The University of Minnesota Kautz Family YMCA Archives holds 'YMCA in Canada records, 1851-1989' which includes records from the Montreal YMCA era when Canadian national administrative headquarters were located in Montreal (before formation of the National Council of YMCAs of Canada in 1912).

Peter Gilling Goddard (August 13, 1953 - October 15, 2016) is confirmed as the Peter Goddard who served at Camp Kanawana. A condolence message on his obituary states: 'I knew Peter years ago at Kamp Kanawana. I remember a warm-hearted and very kind man.' The use of insider spelling 'Kamp' strengthens the identification.

Peter Gilling Goddard was born August 13, 1953, the third son of Elizabeth Anne Goddard (nee Macdonald) and Raymond Gilling Goddard of Smiths Falls, Ontario. Siblings: John, Allan, David, Jennifer, Barbara, and Kathy.

Peter Goddard died suddenly on October 15, 2016 (age 63) while walking Shaw Woods trails with the Mississippi Valley Field Naturalists and his brother Allan. Funeral at C.R. Gamble Funeral Home, Almonte, Ontario; memorial November 26, 2016 at First Unitarian Congregation of Ottawa.

Peter Goddard served Boy Scouts of Canada for 40+ years (teaching, instruction, leading, managing). He worked at the Bill Mason Center as instructor and leader of outdoor activities, and at the Rideau Valley Conservation Authority in outdoor field management and instructing, running summer camp programs at Baxter Conservation Area. He recently retired before his death.
Peter Goddard's father Raymond Gilling Goddard (September 2, 1921 - May 13, 2013) was a WWII veteran (First Canadian Infantry) and graduate of McGill and Bishop's Universities.

Philip Mortimer Caddell was born July 7, 1913 in Brantford, Ontario, Canada, and died July 24, 2004 in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada (age 91). His parents were Captain William Persse Caddell and Florence May Ogden. He had an older brother Shirley Lee Forsythe Caddell (born November 1911).

Philip 'Pip' Caddell was born in Canada (Brantford, Ontario) but raised in Scotland; he returned to Canada as a teenager. He married Elga Ramsey in 1945. Elga (born 1917) was a devout Anglican associated with St. Philip's in Montreal West.

Philip 'Pip' Caddell's employer was a local brewer. He attended the 1936 Montreal Maroons vs Detroit Red Wings six-overtime playoff game (settled by Mud Bruneteau) and the 1935 Maroons Stanley Cup win. His spoken story 'The Black Horse' — about helping his employer honour a commitment to reward Maroons captain Hooley Smith with a Percheron horse — was transcribed from memory by his son Andrew and published posthumously in 'The Goal.'

James Lawrence Caddell was born March 16, 1973 in Montreal. His mother was Norma Lewis, a journalist and communications lecturer at Dawson College who covered John Lennon's 'bed-in' for peace for the Montreal Gazette in 1969. Andrew Caddell was one of her former students.

James Caddell graduated from Cortland High School near Syracuse, NY in 1991. He moved to Montreal and attended Dawson College, then enrolled at McGill University in North American studies before switching to political science and history (BA ~1997). In summer 1997 he was a Normandy Foundation Scholar (six-week tour of European battlefields: Waterloo, Somme, D-Day Normandy).

James Caddell earned an MA in War Studies from Royal Military College, Kingston (1998-2000, as a civilian student). At RMC he met Tara Newell (MA in Public Administration at Queen's); they recognized each other from McGill where James had worked part-time for the Student Society and Tara had signed his paycheques as Student Society president.

James Caddell joined the Royal Canadian Hussars reserve while at Dawson/McGill. In 1995 he took a year off, trained at CFB Valcartier, and deployed to Bosnia: Rotation 5 of Operation Cavalier, May-October 1995, serving in CANBAT 2 (Canadian Battle Group 2), part of UNPROFOR, as a Cougar driver in 42 Troop of 'D' Squadron of the 12e Régiment blindé du Canada. He was awarded the Peacekeeping Service Medal and UNPROFOR Medal.

James Caddell died October 16, 2005 in Tupiza, Bolivia (age 32) of pulmonary edema caused by altitude sickness. He had suffered altitude sickness on Mount Everest 9 months earlier above 5,000m. Tupiza is below 3,000m; no one in the hotel or local hospital recognized the symptoms or had oxygen. His wife Tara Newell was beside him.

James and Tara Caddell's world trip started June 2004. Itinerary: crossed Australia, toured Hanoi and Angkor Wat, humanitarian work in East Timor and Indonesia, 2 months as CMAT volunteer at orphanage in Kannyakumari district (Tamil Nadu, India) working with children orphaned by the 2004 tsunami, trekked in Nepal, toured Gallipoli and Jerusalem, dined in Provence, learned Spanish in Buenos Aires and Santiago, arrived by bus in Bolivia.

Tara Newell (wife of James Caddell) founded the James Caddell Memorial Foundation providing educational opportunities for marginalized girls in India. She spent 16 years with MSF (Médecins Sans Frontières), including Emergency Coordinator deployed to Syria, culminating as MSF's Representative to the United Nations. As of August 2025, she is Chief Programs Officer (VP) at CARE Canada.

Andrew Caddell married Elaine Feldman; children: James (1973-2005), Emily, and Jack. He is a double graduate of Carleton University, Ottawa, with an MA in Journalism (2002, thesis: 'Like Moths to a Flame: the news media's influence on the United Nations and the specialized agencies').

Andrew Caddell's career: broadcast journalist (Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec City, Calgary, St. John's, 1975-1981), political advisor (1980-1986), Director of Communications to Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, Town Councillor Montreal West (1989-1993, Public Security), served with WHO Geneva and UNICEF in Macedonia and Bangladesh, foreign service officer at Global Affairs Canada for 15 years (last role: Senior Policy Advisor, North America Policy and Relations — Mexico), retired GAC July 2017.

Andrew Caddell's current roles include: weekly columnist for The Hill Times (Ottawa), frequent guest on CJAD Radio (Montreal), Town Councillor of Kamouraska Quebec, President of the Task Force on Linguistic Policy, Fellow of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute and Environics Institute, Principal of QIT Canada Inc. (Emergency Management software), and Advisor to the Montreal Irish Monument Foundation.

'The Goal: Stories about Our National Passion' by Andrew Caddell and Dave Stubbs (Deux Voiliers Publishing, 2015; revised/expanded edition 2017) contains Philip 'Pip' Caddell's posthumous spoken story 'The Black Horse' — a secondary source for Pip's biography and Montreal hockey culture of the 1930s.

Nelson McEwen, born c.1897 in Charlottetown, PEI, was hired in 1919 (age 22) as Assistant Boys Work Secretary at Winnipeg YMCA. He personally directed Camp Stephens in Winnipeg from 1924-1927, then was recruited to Montreal YMCA as Boys Work Secretary, where he directed Camp Kanawana c.1927-1947. This extends his documented Kanawana tenure from the previously known 1930-1931 to a ~20-year period.

Nelson McEwen co-founded the Canadian Camping Association with Taylor Statten, serving as Secretary while Statten was President. Note: CCA was formally founded in 1936 at Central YMCA Toronto; McEwen may have been involved in the 1946 reorganization/national assemblies rather than the 1936 founding.
Nelson McEwen developed the Hi-Y program to 'massive size' in Montreal and conducted two National Assemblies of Hi-Y at Geneva Park in 1940 and 1946.

In 1947, Nelson McEwen left Montreal to accept the position of General Secretary of the Saint John YMCA (New Brunswick). At Saint John he recruited Ross Bannerman, Lloyd and Niles Ring, and Doug Allen to YMCA careers.

Camp Becsies was located on Lac des Becs-scie, a lake in Saint-Sauveur (83%) and Mille-Isles (17%), in the same municipality as Camp Kanawana. The lake has a total area of 0.5 km², approximately 2.2 km long, 155-340m wide. It is likely one of the 'three private lakes' on or adjacent to Kanawana property.

Camp Becsies served campers from the Montreal Protestant Orphans' Home in 1934 and 1936. In the 1960-1971 period, Camp Becsies was repurposed for family camping (family camping brochure c.1962, administrative records 1960-1971). Photographs of Camp Becsies exist in the Concordia archives.

Camp Dorval (P0145/12E, 1926-1928, 0.5cm records) was a short-lived YMCA day camp in Dorval, Quebec (West Island of Montreal). Only 0.5cm of archival records survive for its three years of operation, suggesting a small operation.

Camp Thunderbird (P0145/12I) and the Wilderness Survival Camp (P0145/12J) are YMCA Montreal camps listed in the Concordia Archives. CORRECTED 2026-07-09: a direct fetch of the Concordia finding aid found a specific dated item, "Camp Thunderbird - brochure, correspondence, reports, publicity. -- 1942-1943" (Box HA2316) -- dating Camp Thunderbird to the early 1940s, not "the mid-1970s" as this fact previously speculated. The Wilderness Survival Camp's dating is confirmed and sharpened by finding-aid items: "Wilderness camp director's report" (1973), "Wilderness camping programs-brochures" (1973-1974), "Program planning 1974-75 -- Survival camp" (1974), and "Wilderness survival camp" (1975) -- a precise 1973-1975 operating window. The 1974 'Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA' and 1975 'Proposed Hike and Trip Camp' remain plausible context for the Wilderness Survival Camp's origin specifically, not Thunderbird's. No gender assignment is stated in either finding aid.
Camp Perrot (P0145/12G) was a boys' camp operated by Montreal YMCA. A document 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' compares Camp Perrot and Kamp Kanawana from c.1945-1946.

Gabor Ivan Zinner wrote an MA thesis at McGill University (Political Science, 1973) titled 'Noosphere - an experiment in simulation.' This almost certainly documents the Noosphere international development simulation held at Camp Kanawana in summer 1971. Available at https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/concern/theses/6w924d11w

The Noosphere simulation (1971) was modeled on a 'Third World Village' organized in Winnipeg the previous year (1970). It was the first time such an experience was attempted in Quebec. An 'education committee in Montreal with members from various development organizations' established the project.
A second newspaper article about the Noosphere simulation appeared in Montreal-matin on August 24, 1971 (BAnQ: https://numerique.banq.qc.ca/patrimoine/details/52327/4512657).
Gabor Ivan Zinner, author of the 1973 McGill thesis on Noosphere, is now a lawyer in Calgary, Alberta (Zinner Law Office, 100-1100 8 Ave SW). He practices civil litigation and commercial law.

Camp Kanawana held an 'Opening Campfire 2020' as a Facebook Live video, confirming the campfire/council ring tradition was active as recently as 2020 during COVID restrictions. URL: https://www.facebook.com/YKanawana/videos/opening-campfire-2020/1432885173577431/
Camp Kanawana has 4,416 photos on Flickr (flickr.com/photos/kanawana/) and an active Instagram account (@ymcakanawana, 1,835 followers, 573 posts as of June 2026).

The 1974-1975 Camp Kanawana director (who worked alongside Stuart McLean as assistant director) is confirmed NOT to be A. Ross Seaman (left for Dawson College 1974), NOT Dave Twynam (does not appear until at least 1976), and NOT Ross Bannerman (his 1969 report suggests an earlier role). The anonymous commenter who identified himself as this director on Westmount Magazine in 2017 was young enough to sublet McLean's Dorchester flat.

James Caddell was Senior Program Manager at Human Resources Development Canada before his world trip. After moving to Ottawa (~2000), he switched to the 2nd Intelligence Platoon of the Royal Canadian Hussars and received the Queen's Jubilee Medal from his new regiment.

James Caddell's memorial service was held in Ottawa on November 5, 2005. Obituaries were published in the Globe and Mail and Ottawa Citizen. A BillionGraves entry exists under the name 'Lawrence James Caddell.' A Wikipedia article on James Caddell exists.
Andrew Caddell's siblings/half-siblings of James include Emily Caddell and Jack Caddell (from Andrew's marriage to Elaine Feldman). Andrew's Twitter/X handle is @pipson52.
Ross Bannerman established the St. James YMCA branch in Winnipeg (date unspecified, between 1951 and 1956).

Derek Walsh search (32+ queries, 5 surfaces) returned zero new biographical information. He remains biographically opaque. The CCA fonds at Trent University and Concordia YMCA fonds are the only remaining leads requiring physical archive access.

The Pip Award recipients for 2019-2023 cannot be identified through publicly accessible web sources. 42+ queries across 8+ surfaces yielded zero results. The 2019 recipient's title begins with 'Dr.' per Andrew Caddell's LinkedIn. No YMCA Quebec press releases were published for any award 2019-2023.

Nelson McEwen died in 1956 while still in active YMCA service. He was serving as the first Metropolitan General Secretary of the Winnipeg YMCA at the time of his death, a position he accepted in 1951 after serving as General Secretary of the Saint John YMCA (1947-1951).

Nelson McEwen's full career timeline: born c.1897 Charlottetown, PEI; hired 1919 (age 22) as Assistant Boys Work Secretary, Winnipeg YMCA; directed Camp Stephens 1924-1927; recruited to Montreal YMCA as Boys Work Secretary c.1927; directed Camp Kanawana c.1927-1947; General Secretary, Saint John YMCA 1947-1951; first Metropolitan General Secretary, Winnipeg YMCA 1951-1956; died 1956 in active service.

Nelson McEwen founded the 'Order of the Triangle' at Camp Stephens, Winnipeg, during his tenure there (c.1919-1927). Through this program he recruited young men including Mitchel Sharp and Bill Master to YMCA service.

At the Saint John YMCA (1947-1951), Nelson McEwen recruited Ross Bannerman, Lloyd and Niles Ring, and Doug Allen to YMCA careers. This confirms the connection chain: McEwen recruited Bannerman at Saint John, Bannerman later directed Camp Pascobac (1951) and Camp Stephens (1956), then authored the 1969 Report on Kamp Kanawana.

The Camp Stephens Alumni blog states McEwen 'founded the Canadian Camping Association in 1946 with his good friend Taylor Statten.' The official CCA records show the CCA was founded on May 20, 1936, with Statten as president and Dr. George S. Patterson as secretary. McEwen's role may relate to a 1946 reorganization or national assembly rather than the original 1936 founding. The discrepancy between 1936 (CCA official) and 1946 (Camp Stephens blog) is unresolved.

Doug McEwen served as director of Camp Stephens from 1966-1970 and as President of the Canadian Camping Association from 1967-1969. He is listed in the CCA fonds at Trent University Archives as associated with 'YMCA Camp Wa-Sa-Ah-Dun, St. Catharines, Ontario.' His relationship to Nelson McEwen (possible son) is suggested by context but not confirmed.

The McMorris thesis documents Nelson McEwen as camp director in 1930-1931 only. The Camp Stephens Alumni blog documents him as Boys Work Secretary of the Montreal YMCA from c.1927 to 1947, directing Camp Kanawana throughout. The discrepancy is likely explained by McEwen holding an administrative title (Boys Work Secretary) while operational camp directors (Camp Chief / Director) such as Greig Macdiarmid (1935-1938) reported to him. McMorris may document only the years McEwen personally served as on-site camp director.

Concordia Archives sub-series 14D10 contains 'National Council Boys' Work Secretary, Nelson McEwen — E. M. Nelson Correspondence, 1941-1945.' This confirms McEwen's National Council role and his concurrent connection to the Montreal YMCA during wartime.

Nelson McEwen's deep biographical research (20+ web searches across 8+ surfaces) yielded no obituary text, no photograph, no birth/death exact dates, and no family details beyond what the Camp Stephens Alumni blog provides. Find A Grave has no matching record. Winnipeg Free Press historical archives not accessible online. Further research requires: (1) Winnipeg Free Press microfiche for 1956 obituary, (2) PEI vital statistics for birth record, (3) Concordia Archives 14D10 correspondence for biographical details.
Kate Taylor's camp alias/nickname at Kanawana is 'Wawa'.
Kate Taylor holds an Honours BA in Psychology from Trent University (Peterborough, Ontario).
Kate Taylor was previously Camp Director at Camp Ta-Wa-Si Inc. (Johnston's Point, Northumberland Strait, New Brunswick), a camp founded in 1940.

Kate Taylor led the introduction of a gender-expansive tent option at Camp Kanawana — a co-ed sleeping arrangement open to transgender, non-binary, and gender-questioning campers, or anyone who prefers it.

Kate Taylor appeared on three camping industry podcasts: Go Camp Pro 'Beyond Camp' #18 (Social Media Advocacy), CampHacker #147 (Summer Self-Care for Camp Directors), and Camp Code #95 (How to Combat Learning Loss in Your Staff Team).
Kate Taylor also served as Consultant & Graphic Designer at Stephane Richard Development Consulting (concurrent or sequential with Kanawana directorship).
Marie-Pierre Lacasse holds a BA in Leisure Sciences from Concordia University (2004-2006) and also studied at Universite Laval.
Marie-Pierre Lacasse is certified as a Leave No Trace Master Educator, Wilderness First Responder (WFR), and Red Cross First Aid Monitor.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse's career before Kanawana included: Wilderness Safety Systems (Asst Director, 2007-2012), Camp Boisjoly (DG, 2011-2014), Camp Odyssee/Minogami (Director, 2014-2015), Camp Portneuf (DG, 2015-2018), and roles at Loisirs Saint-Sacrement, Domaine du Lac bleu, and Unite de loisir et de sport de la Capitale-Nationale.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse launched the first ADHD-adapted summer camp in the greater Quebec City region at Camp Portneuf in 2018, collaborating with Lyne Guillemette of the Panda Association. The ADHD groups had 1 monitor per 3 youth (vs. 1:5 regular) and included psychoeducators.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse launched 'Aventure a Kanawana' (Kanawana Adventure) day camp in summer 2024 — an English-immersion day camp for ages 5-12, maximum capacity 48 children, with shuttle service from Saint-Sauveur. It is the first day camp program in Kanawana's 130-year history.

Lac Kanawana has RSVL monitoring station number 573, with monitoring data since at least 2013. Precise physical data: surface area 0.2388 km2, maximum depth 12.4 m, volume 1,273,000 m3, altitude 318.4 m, watershed area 5.17 km2, drainage ratio 22.00.
The camp beach is listed on Swim Guide (ID 5490) and Great Lakes Guide as 'Plage du camp Kanawana YMCA camp Beach', indicating formal water quality monitoring for swimming safety.
Lac Kanawana is in the Riviere du Nord watershed; the associated watershed organization is ABRINORD (Organisme de bassin versant de la riviere du Nord).

Philip D. Fagans (spelled 'Fas-ana' in 1918 Gazette, likely OCR error) was Seton's Executive Secretary of the Woodcraft League of America, headquartered at 13 West 29th St, New York City. Before that, he was a YMCA camp director at Trenton NJ and West Side YMCA Camp NYC, and later founded Greenkill Camp in Kingston NY.

A Woodcraft League charter cost $3.00 annually, obtained by application to the Council of Guidance at National Headquarters, 13 West 29th Street, New York City. The charter entitled the tribe to be registered, recognize achievements per the Birch Bark Roll of Woodcraft, and wear League badges.
'Almost all [Woodcraft] tribes operated within the YMCA' — the YMCA was the primary institutional host for Woodcraft Indian tribes before the BSA was formed.

The 1923 Kanawana brochure mentions 'a large Council Ring where woodcraft meetings are held' but does not explicitly reference the Woodcraft League charter, possibly indicating the formal affiliation was being de-emphasized or had lapsed by 1923 even as the physical infrastructure and programming continued.
The Woodcraft League of America grew to approximately 5,000 members at its peak in the 1920s-1930s, with groups in ~20 countries. It went out of existence after Seton's death in 1946.

Harold Herbert Potter (1914-2004) attended Sir George Williams College (B.A. 1935-1939) and worked summers as camp counsellor at YMCA Kamp Kanawana. In 1947, he became the first Canadian-born Black sociologist hired by a Canadian post-secondary institution (lecturer at SGW College). He set up the Department of Sociology and Anthropology at SGW in 1960 and maintained YMCA ties throughout his career.

In 1963, both Hedley G. Dimock and A. Ross Seaman moved simultaneously from YMCA/camp roles into Sir George Williams University — Dimock as first Chairman of Applied Social Science and Director of the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies, Seaman as part-time faculty. This nexus institutionalized the camp-to-university knowledge transfer.

The YMCA-Concordia Fine Arts camp partnership began in 2019 when the Faculty of Fine Arts signed a partnership agreement with the YMCA. By 2024, it expanded to include Science & Engineering Camp and STEAMpunks (ages 13-15). Camp counsellors are primarily Concordia students and Stingers athletes.

Raye Kass presented on 'Leadership on a hot tin roof: Applications for Camp Professionals' at the International Camping Congress, and served as Program Director of the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies (CHRCS) at Concordia.

The QCA/CCA organized a formal Camping School at McGill University from 1937 to 1940 — one of the earliest camp leader training programs in Canada. A related 'camping evening course' at McGill was held in 1952. Records are in Concordia Archives P0145/12N03.

McGill PE students attended a 'Camp School' at Camp Nominingue (founded 1925, north of Mont-Tremblant) as part of their curriculum, learning camping, paddling, portaging, and axe use. This curricular component was recalled by alumni from the 1940s-1950s.

Arthur S. Lamb (1886-1958), 'father of modern physical education in Canada', was a former Vancouver YMCA PE director and Springfield College graduate (BA 1912). He directed physical education at McGill for 37 years (1919-1956), establishing the first university department of physical education in Canada.

Sam Lazarus (1978-2004), a Kanawana camper and staff member, died of cerebral malaria in Ghana while working at an orphanage. His family (Janet Torge, mother; Riel Lazarus, brother) established the Sam Lazarus Fund for camperships at Kanawana. SAM JAM is an annual fundraiser held at Kanawana, running for 17+ years. [CORRECTED 2026-08-14: birth year was recorded as 1979; the obituary and the stated age of 25 at death establish 1978.]
Chris Adam was the 10th recipient of the Pip Alumni Award; the award was established in 2007.
Kevin Slezak held the role of Assistant Director, Camp YMCA Kanawana, and later became Special Projects Consultant at YMCA Quebec.
Audrey Dowse was nominated for the Camp Administrator Hall of Fame in 2022 for her work with Camp YMCA Kanawana and YMCA Day Camps.

Kanawana's early English motto 'Each for all and all for each' was a shared YMCA camp tradition, not unique to Kanawana. At least two other YMCA camps used the same motto: Camp Becket (Becket-Chimney Corners YMCA, MA, est. 1903, one of 8 mottos linked to director Henry Gibson 1904-1927) and Camp Hayo-Went-Ha (Central Lake, MI, est. 1904, primary rallying cry still in use).

Camp Kanawana is the only YMCA camp or YMCA-affiliated organization in the world using the motto 'Non Nobis Solum'. The motto is also used by Lower Canada College (Montreal, adopted 1909), Washburn University, Willamette University, Swarthmore College (Class of 1918), Massanutten Academy, Walnut Hill School, Pennthorpe School (UK), University College Durham (UK), U. of Victoria St. Joseph School of Nursing, and the US Army 1st Maintenance Company.

The LCC school song 'Non Nobis Solum' was first sung at the 1936 return-to-school assembly at Lower Canada College. Lyrics by early alumni, melody from a Brahms symphony. The song made the Latin motto phrase highly recognizable among anglophone Montreal school communities.

Charles Sanderson Fosbery, LCC founder (headmaster 1909-1935), held a BA in classics from Trinity College Dublin and arrived in Montreal in 1900 as choirmaster at St. John's School. He adopted his family crest and motto 'Non Nobis Solum' for the school. Lt.-Col. George Vincent Fosbery VC (1832-1907) bore the same crest with two lions' gambs erased — likely the same Fosbery family heraldic lineage.

The CCA Centenary Journey (1967) was a relay-structure cross-Canada canoe trip organized by the Canadian Camping Association. Each camp/province paddled an assigned section. Key organizers: Bruce Hodgins (Trent/Camp Wanapitei), John Latimer (Camp Kilcoo, OCA President 1967-68, overall coordinator), Kirk Wipper (Camp Kandalore, arranged Lake Superior section using Nor'wester alumni staff in 25-foot Chestnut wood-canvas canoes).

Known CCA Centenary Journey (1967) section assignments: BC/Fraser River — Camp Deka (YMCA, Kamloops); Prairies/Manitoba — Regina YMCA Camp and Camp Stephens (Winnipeg YMCA, Winnipeg River to Lake Winnipeg); Fort Francis to Camp Stephens — Camp Kandalore senior boys; Lake Superior — Camp Kandalore Nor'wester alumni; Quebec/Ottawa River — Camp Kanawana (Deep River to Britannia Beach, Aug 2-9). John Latimer published 'Maker of Men: The Kilcoo Story.'

'A Log of Canada's Centenary Journey' was published in 1971, likely containing the complete route, sections, and participant roster for the CCA Centenary Journey canoe trip. The book appears out of print and not digitized.

Lac des Becs-scie ('bec-scie' = Quebec French for merganser/sawbill duck, from 17th-century New France usage) is approximately 1.5 km west of Lac Kanawana at essentially the same altitude (320.5m vs 318.4m). Physical data: 0.5 km², ~2.2 km long, 155-340m wide, max depth 16.6m, mean depth 5.8m. Coordinates: ~45°51'12"N, 74°12'53"W.

Lac des Becs-scie is definitively NOT one of Kanawana's 'three private lakes.' It is a separate lake with ~240 homes on its shores (mix of primary and vacation residences), governed by the Association du Lac des Becs-scie (formed January 2003). At 0.5 km² it is larger than Lac Kanawana (0.235 km²). Kanawana's three private lakes are Lake Kanawana, Lake Wilson, and Round Lake.

A limerick in the Green Triangle (July 29, 1938) mentions a staff member Wallace who 'found at Leke Becsies his solace,' confirming Camp Becsies was a known location to Kanawana staff in the 1930s, consistent with its ~1.5 km distance.

Chapelle de Sainte-Thérèse-du-Lac-des-Becs-Scies was built 1950-1951 on Chemin du Lac-des-Becs-Scie Ouest in Saint-Sauveur. Listed in Quebec cultural heritage registry and included in Saint-Sauveur heritage circuit.

The Kanawana dam between Lake Kanawana and Lake Wilson does NOT appear in the CEHQ (Centre d'expertise hydrique du Québec) répertoire des barrages. This may mean it is below the 1-metre threshold, registered under an unrecognized name, or predates modern registration requirements. No online source provides a construction date.

Joanna Hode/Houde (director 1995-2000 per oral history) has zero web presence connecting her to Camp Kanawana, YMCA, or any camp director role. 25+ distinct queries across Google, LinkedIn, Facebook, Find A Grave, FamilySearch, and obituary databases all returned null. The only person matching 'Joanna Houde' is in Exeter, NH (b.1977), too young for a 1995 directorship. Spelling variants (Hode/Houde/Johanne/Johanna) and variant roles all returned null.

The 120th anniversary of Camp Kanawana was held September 5, 2014 at Victoria Hall, Westmount (off-site urban venue). The 125th anniversary was a 'Family, Alumni, and Friends Weekend' at camp in summer 2019 (on-site).

Mabel C. Jamieson was NOT a founding member of the Ontario Camping Association (1933). OCA founding members included Ferna Halliday, A.L. Cochrane, H.E. Chapman, Mary Edgar, Mary Hamilton, Taylor Statten, and Ethel Statten — but not Jamieson.

The 'Pupils College in Richmond' where Mabel C. Jamieson reportedly studied (completing 1918) is unidentifiable. St. Francis College in Richmond, Quebec, closed in 1898 — 20 years before Jamieson's alleged attendance. No other 'Pupils College' in Richmond, Quebec has been identified.

The Comité des seize (Committee of Sixteen) in Montreal, of which Mabel C. Jamieson was a member, was founded in 1917 (not 1919 as sometimes reported). It was a moral reform committee concerned with vice and prostitution in the Montreal red-light district.

Rev. John Tudor Harries (B.A., M.Div.) listed Camp Kanawana as an early career formative experience, alongside Manor Road United Church, Central Neighborhood House (Toronto), and Regent Park United Church. He later became Program Director of the United Church of Canada's Cedar Glen Conference and Education Centre near Bolton, Ontario (1976). Died in Aurora, Ontario, following kidney cancer.

George Clouston (d. 2011) was described in his obituary as having been 'an enthusiastic volunteer and member' of the YMCA and its Kamp Kanawana 'as a young man while attending West Hill High School' in Montreal.
Douglas Warren Marston (c.1918-2011) attended Kamp Kanawana as a 'junior summer camp' participant. He died November 14, 2011 in his 94th year.
Harold H. Potter was born March 27, 1914 and died May 8, 2004 in Montreal at age 90.

Harold Potter's father Alfred Moore Westerby Potter (1885-1947) emigrated from British Guiana in 1907 and worked as a redcap porter at Windsor Station, Montreal. He and other CNR porters received official union recognition in 1943. His mother Gertrude Miller Potter (1890-1979) emigrated in 1910 and volunteered for the Negro Community Centre from 1927.

Potter earned his MA at McGill University (1947-1949) supervised by Oswald Hall, with thesis 'The Occupational Adjustments of Montreal Negroes, 1941-48.' The thesis found that nearly 50% of Black male wage earners were sleeping car porters and 80% of Black women were in domestic service. It became a standard citation for decades.
Potter started PhD at University of Chicago in 1950 but returned to SGW without completing the degree because he had a teaching position waiting.
Carl Dawson (founder of McGill's Department of Sociology) recommended Potter to Dean Henry F. Hall for the 1947 appointment at SGW College.

Potter was founding organizer of the SGWAUT (Sir George Williams Association of University Teachers) in 1951 and its president in 1956. He was promoted to Assistant Professor (1949), Associate Professor (1954), Full Professor (1963).
Potter hired Kurt Jonassohn in 1961 (whom he 'knew from the Y') and Hubert Guindon in 1962 to build the SGW Department of Sociology and Anthropology. He served as Chair 1963-64 and 1966-67.

Potter co-authored 'Camp Laquemac: A Bilingual Adult Education Training Centre' with Renee Morin (Toronto: Canadian Association for Adult Education, 1953), demonstrating continued camp/adult education involvement beyond his Kanawana years.
Potter was on sabbatical at Southeastern Massachusetts University during the February 1969 SGW Computer Centre Affair. He maintained he had never experienced discrimination at SGW.

The Harold Potter fonds at Concordia University Archives was donated in 2005 by Jean-Philippe Warren, who obtained the papers from Potter's son Evan. It contains term papers, course outlines, examinations, minutes, and drafts of articles.
Potter married Theresia (Theresa) Hebein, an Austrian emigre, in 1970. Their son Evan Harold Potter was born in 1964. Potter retired from Concordia University in 1977.

Peter Darwin Goddard (July 13, 1943 -- March 23, 2022) was a Canadian music and culture journalist (Globe and Mail, Toronto Telegram, Toronto Star) who won the 1972 Juno Award as Journalist of the Year. An obituary commenter stated they 'knew Peter years ago at Kamp Kanawana' and described him as 'a warm-hearted and very kind man.'
Pascale Audette was named President and CEO of the YMCAs of Québec effective January 6, 2025 — the first woman to hold this position in the organization's 170-year history.
Karen Louise Deterding (d. August 22, 2014, age 57, of pancreatic cancer) was described in her obituary as being deeply missed by 'friends from Kamp Kanawana.'
facts.placement_reason: KB-ONLY BY DECISION (2026-08-25). Karen Deterding was a private individual; the whole of the record is one line in her obituary noting friends from Kamp Kanawana. Placing that in an article would be publishing a private person's death notice for no historical purpose, which the CLAUDE.md Phase 2 privacy rule forbids. Retained in the KB as evidence of the camp's alumni reach, not promoted to the wiki.

facts.claim: Mike Cohen, Montreal media personality, Côte Saint-Luc city councillor, and columnist for The Suburban newspaper, attended Camp Kanawana as a child and described it as his 'favourite' among the camps his parents sent him to.
Hedley S. Dimock created and directed Summer Camp Institutes from 1930 to 1948 at the George Williams College Lake Geneva campus, examining the role of camps in 'character education' of children.

The McMorris MA thesis (2023) full PDF is publicly available on Concordia Spectrum at https://spectrum.library.concordia.ca/id/eprint/992763/1/McMorris_MA_F2023.pdf. The thesis is also indexed on CORE.ac.uk.
Raye Kass presented 'Leadership on a hot tin roof: Applications for Camp Professionals' at the 8th International Camping Congress, October 4-7, 2008, in Quebec City, QC.

Andrew Caddell on his father Pip: 'Like many of the greatest generation, my father did not seek the limelight for the things he did. His grandson, James was very much that sort of person, and he wanted to have an award at camp that recognized those attributes of his grandfather.'

The Pip Award was not given in 2010. Numbering confirms: Mosher (2015) was the 8th recipient, meaning 7 recipients preceded him in 8 years (2007-2014), confirming one skip year. Skinner (2016) was 9th, Adam (2017) 10th, Sharpe (2018) 11th.

Carol Sharman Skinner (full middle name Sharman) served as counsellor and section director at Kanawana from 1990 to 1995. She later became Director of YMCA Camp Hayward in Cape Cod, Massachusetts. Diagnosed with ALS in 2013.

Charles Smillie Buckland (born March 3, 1934), Canadian can company executive from Mississauga, Ontario, attended Camp Kanawana from 1944 to 1951 (ages 10-17). He traveled by train from Montreal Central Station to Saint-Sauveur. A counsellor gave him the nickname 'Smillie' on arrival. His published memoir in Reader's Digest ('How Summer Camp Shapes Lives') credits Kanawana with shaping his life and career.

Leigh Evans attended Camp Kanawana for 6 summers: 1 as camper, 1 as Leader-in-Training (LIT), and 4 as staff member. Camp inspired her to become a teacher. She maintains a WordPress blog with camp memories at leighcevans.wordpress.com.
Peter Gossage, Professor of History at Concordia University, supervised the Grace McMorris MA thesis 'An Experience That Lasts a Lifetime' (2023) on Kamp Kanawana.

YMCA Montreal Annual Reports from 1856, 1876, 1889-1890, and 1891-1892 are digitized on Internet Archive. The 1891-92 report (archive.org/details/sgw-ymca-annual-report-1991-1992, note URL typo) predates Camp Jubilee founding by 2 years and may document the Cushing 1892 camping trip or early outdoor activity discussions.

YMCA Annual Report 1993 is digitized on Internet Archive (archive.org/details/sgw-ymca-annual-report-1993). As the centennial year report, this would likely contain details about the 1993-1994 centennial celebrations and the Cathy Reeves documentary.
The Montreal Gazette published an article about YMCA Summer Camp Kanawana on July 7, 1897, just three years after the camp's founding.
In July 1913, detachments of Montreal YMCA boys left the city for Kamp Kanawana, with a programme for boys aged 3 to 17 that included instruction in athletics, educational subjects, and Bible study.

In July 1918, Camp Kanawana had the largest attendance in its history with 110 members in camp, and instruction included first aid work, basket-making, camp sanitation, wrestling, tumbling, and nature study.
In August 1942, YMCA boys staged a parade and circus at Kanawana, with 'Games of Luck and Skill' entertaining campers at a week-end festival.
In November 1962, citizenship training and educational programs for youth and young adults were planned at Kamp Kanawana.
Sean Day was the regional director of camps for YMCA Québec (as of 2021).

Camp YMCA Kanawana was closed for a second consecutive year in 2021 due to COVID-19. Sean Day said offering overnight services to more than 250 campers at once didn't seem possible with the facilities. YMCA Québec instead offered 10 day camps.
Camp YMCA Kanawana held a 120th anniversary reunion on September 5, 2014, at Victoria Hall, where alumni (former campers and staff) assembled to celebrate.
Camp YMCA Kanawana held a 125th anniversary Family, Alumni, and Friends Weekend in 2019.
YMCA Camp Kanawana maintains a Flickr photostream with 4,416 photos documenting camp activities and history.
A recording of the YMCA Kamp Kanawana radio broadcast on Station CFCF, dated June 26, 1941, is preserved on Internet Archive (added April 29, 2024).
As of fall 2025, YMCA Québec will no longer offer day camps (including holiday and spring break camps), but Camp YMCA Kanawana summer camp continues to operate.

David Leduc managed Camp Kanawana's summer and winter programs, including recruitment, training, and supervision of 75 employees, management of all programs and operational budgets, and overall safety and security of 800 camp participants. His LinkedIn profile title is 'Organisational Executive — Business Strategy and Development for impact driven organizations.'
David Leduc also held a role as Director of Philanthropy (Quebec) at Pathways to Education Canada / Passeport pour ma réussite Canada, per RocketReach.
David Leduc's education includes an undergraduate degree in International Development from Dalhousie University (Halifax) and an MBA in Management from McGill University (2006-2011).

After Kanawana, David Leduc served as Oxfam-Quebec's Lebanon Coordinator for the 'Across Borders Project' (March 2000 – June 2002), managing programs in Palestinian refugee camps and securing $340,000 from international donors.

David Leduc was Director of Operations at McGill University's International Community Action Network (ICAN) for approximately 11 years, strengthening civil society in marginalized communities in the Middle East.

David Leduc was appointed Executive Director of Development and Peace (Canadian Catholic Organization for Development and Peace) on July 28, 2015, replacing Michael Casey. He headed a team of 80 employees across Canada implementing programs in 30+ countries, and served until circa 2020.

R. H. Hanagan's archival title was 'Montreal YMCA camp director' (not specifically 'Kanawana director' — his portfolio covered multiple YMCA camps). His full first name is not confirmed; 'Robert' is unverified.

R. H. Hanagan authored a report to the Camp Board of Management on the American Camping Association Conference (1946) and a Boys' Camping Committee — Survey Committee report (1950), both held in Concordia's YMCA fonds (P0145/12A).
R. H. Hanagan authored a 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (comparing Kanawana and Camp Perrot), c.1945-46, held in Concordia's YMCA fonds.
A Kamp Kanawana reunion took place on April 7, 1989, contemporaneous with Ben T. Hannah's 'Kanawana Reminiscence (of 1948)' document dated 1989.
A Globe and Mail arts piece ('Stuart McLean's bent vision,' c.2003) described McLean's time as a counsellor at Camp Kanawana in his 20s as 'at once magical and developmentally critical.'
Kate Taylor became Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana after Sean Day's departure in 2023. Her social media handle is @thiskatetaylor.

Under Kate Taylor's directorship, Kanawana introduced a gender-expansive sleeping option (tent) for campers who are transgender, non-binary, or who do not wish to be sorted by gender. Any camper can choose it; mainly teens have requested it. Taylor stated Kanawana was not the first camp in Quebec to add such an option.

At Camp Kanawana, dividing by gender is becoming increasingly irrelevant: male counsellors may work with girls (and vice versa), and both boys and girls participate in all camp activities. The sleeping arrangement is the only remaining gender-divided element.

Kevin Slezak served as Assistant Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana, then as Sleep-Away Camp Director and Summer Camp Director at YMCA Quebec. As of 2025, he holds the title Special Projects Consultant at YMCA Quebec.
Kate Taylor appeared on the Go Camp Pro podcast (Beyond Camp #18) discussing social media advocacy for camp programs.

EMSB (English Montreal School Board) schools including Vincent Massey Collegiate (Rosemount), John F. Kennedy High School (St. Michel), and École Secondaire Louis Joseph Papineau's classe d'accueil have sent students to Camp Kanawana for overnight camping experiences focused on canoeing, hiking, conservation, nature, and team-building.
The 'Spirit of Kanawana' blog (kanawana.blogspot.com) is an alumni-run blog dedicated to sharing Kanawana history and traditions, inviting contributions from fellow Kanawanians.

The Spirit of Kanawana blog reports that lost verses of a camp song were rediscovered in the Kanawana Archives at Concordia University in 2006, and that the refrain 'Hail, hail, the gang's all here' derives from the 1915 American song 'Alabama Jubilee.'
Camp Kanawana is available for rental year-round (6-250 persons), with limited capacity during summer and winter (6-26 persons).

The Trailblazers CIT (Counsellor-in-Training) program at Camp Kanawana is a 48-day program (4 sessions of 12 days) for ages 16-17. Participants complete over 200 hours of workshops, training sessions, and activities covering creative programming, risk management, team building, and effective communication. The program includes a 5-day canoe trip. Certifications earned: Standard First Aid and CPR (16-hour course) and a CIT certificate from the Association des camps certifiés du Québec (ACC).
entities: Association des camps certifiés du Québec

facts.claim: "Creatives" at Camp Kanawana are counsellor-designed activities where staff create activities from scratch rather than reserving a regular program area. Examples include puddle jumping/mud fights, makeover the counsellors, pirate-themed overnights with a search for buried treasure, surprise birthday parties/beach parties, paint twister, and water balloon fights. Alumna Leigh Evans described Creatives as consistently campers'  favourite memories each session.

Camp YMCA Kanawana maintains a Facebook photo album titled "1987-1994" on its official Facebook page (facebook.com/YKanawana), documenting the period that includes the Bruce Netherwood directorship and the camp's centennial year.
A Leaders in Training Information Guide for Summer 2026 is published as a PDF on the YMCA Quebec website (ymcaquebec.org), documenting the current LIT program structure.

BaladoDiscovery states 'In 1897, the YMCA acquired two islands of Lake Saint-Joseph' for Camp Jubilee/Otoreke. This conflicts with the QAHN source which says 'three islands.' The 1897 date is not mentioned in other sources — existing sources place the founding at 1894 (Ball) with the first organized use in 1892 (Cushing). The 1897 date may represent a formal property purchase rather than the founding.

BaladoDiscovery states Camp Otoreke 'received 80 campers during seven weeks in its early years.' This contrasts with 20 campers at the 1894 founding (f_0017). The 80-camper figure likely represents a subsequent early year, not the inaugural season.
William Fong's biography describes the YMCA as 'perhaps his [McConnell's] favourite organization since his youth in Toronto,' indicating the depth of his attachment predated his Montreal years.

Concordia University Archives sub-series P0145/5E07 contains a 'Proposal to McConnell Foundation re Organizational Renewal' from May 1971, documenting a formal YMCA-to-McConnell Foundation funding relationship extending after J.W. McConnell's death (1963).
J.W. McConnell came to Montreal to establish the Standard Chemical Company's office. He roomed at the YMCA upon arrival. Within a year, he was selling the company's shares in Europe.

An Yves St-Pierre from Montreal died January 31, 2020, age 76, at CHSLD Argyle. Survived by wife Lucette Gregoire, children Nathalie and Benoit. Born c.1943-1944, he would have been ~23 in 1967 — consistent with a counsellor role on the CCA Centenary Journey. The obituary (cfgrandmontreal.com) does not mention YMCA or Kanawana; confirmation of identity as the trip report author remains unestablished.

In 2010, TELUS donated $50,000 to Camp Y Kanawana for construction of a three-season educational pavilion on the camp site. The pavilion includes a classroom for 50 young people and two accommodations for adults. It was built according to sustainable development principles.
The Lumbermen team in the L&V Games is also called 'Bucherons' in the French context.
The virage vert (green shift) and three-season programming capacity allowed Kanawana to welcome 'four times more young people than before.'

Harold Beveridge Cushing was appointed to the McGill University faculty in 1902. Pediatrics first appeared in his academic title in 1920. He founded McGill's Department of Pediatrics in 1937, the same year the Canadian specialty board was created.

Harold Beveridge Cushing greatly assisted in founding the Montreal Children's Hospital (later Children's Memorial Hospital), alongside A.D. Blackader, with encouragement from Sir William Osler. The hospital opened January 30, 1904 at 500 Guy Street. The Cushing Memorial Prize ($300, highest standing in Pediatrics) at the hospital is almost certainly named for him.

Thomas Hubert Cushing (b. December 10, 1877), son of Thomas Cushing (Montreal Brewing Company), was a Montreal Brewing Company executive who became a minority owner of the Montreal Royals baseball team in January 1908. The deal was brokered with majority owner Sam Lichtenhein and fellow minority owner E.R. Carrington.

A third edition of the Cushing genealogy (1905-1969 supplement) was compiled by Allston T. Cushing and is available on FamilySearch (item 235744). It may contain death dates for Walter Edgar, Harold Beveridge, and Thomas Cushing.

A different Walter Edgar Cushing (b. August 2, 1885, Ashburnham, Massachusetts; Dartmouth Class of 1909) spent his career in New England YMCA work (NY, Newark NJ, Boston). This is NOT the Montreal Walter Edgar Cushing (b. 1870) who wrote the 1943 Lake Saint-Joseph sketches.

The first settlers of cote Saint-Elmire (Saint-Sauveur) included Jean-Baptiste Desjardins alongside Magloire Pagé (père), Augustin Goyer dit Bélisle, Louis Alary, and Pierre Filiatrault. They arrived circa 1837, 'at the time of the troubles of Saint-Eustache' (Lower Canada Rebellion), 'fleeing the rebellion to seek calm and security in the mountains.'

Marvin 'Mickey' Stein married Sheila Joan Vineberg on June 28, 1955. They moved into the old Pagé farmhouse in Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts. With Sheila's father Stanley Vineberg and son Stephen Vineberg, they surveyed the site and hired ski designer Sel Hannah. Mont-Habitant Development Ltd. was incorporated July 27, 1959. Stein innovated night skiing (1961) and artificial snowmaking (1964). He died May 16, 1985.

A second Télesphore Pagé (b. April 1908) existed in the Saint-Sauveur Pagé family. He attended école du Grand-Ruisseau, worked in logging camps, then was hired by Auguste Dionne for his Montreal business. He married Marguerite Amyot in 1935 and returned to Saint-Sauveur to open a grocery store on rue de la Gare. This may be a son or nephew of the Télesphore who married Clarilda Dagenais in 1925. CORRECTED 2026-07-09: this appears to be a mistaken duplication -- see f_1942, which identifies this same biography as belonging to Télesphore Léonard (1908-1997), a Pagé descendant through the female line (son of Léonie Pagé), not a second Télesphore Pagé. Preserved here per the no-silent-overwrite rule; treat as superseded.

Harold C. Cross was based at the Victoria, British Columbia YMCA from 1919 to 1925 before coming to Montreal. A document titled 'Personal Reminiscences-Victoria, B.C. 1919-25, by Harold C. Cross' (written 1967) is held in Concordia University Archives, YMCA of Montreal fonds P0145, sub-series 14H ('Local YMCA Histories Collected by J.M. Duckworth').

The Concordia Archives finding aid for the YMCA of Montreal fonds (P0145) lists Kamp Kanawana records (sub-series 12B) totalling 7.72 metres, spanning [190-]-2003, in 7 sub-sub-series: 12B01 General administration, 12B02 Financial administration, 12B03 Land/facilities/equipment, 12B04 Communications (1913-2003), 12B05 Staff/counsellors, 12B06 Campers, 12B07 Program (1913-1994).

The full Camping series at Concordia (P0145) totals 11.63 metres, 1893-2004. Camp sub-series include: Otoreke (12C, 1921-1983), Becsies (12D, 1929-1936 & 1960-1971), Dorval (12E, 1926-1928), Weredale (12F, 1977-1983), Perrot (12G), Thunderbird (12I), Wilderness Survival (12J), Lake St-Joseph/Jubilee (12L), Day camp (12M).

The name 'Dawson' does not appear anywhere in the retrieved text of the Concordia YMCA of Montreal fonds finding aid, despite Ralph Dawson's authorship of the 1933 'History of Kamp Kanawana' (negative result).
The Westmount Branch and North Branch of the Montreal YMCA both opened in 1912.

The 1971 'Noosphere' event at Kanawana was a 'Perspective-Jeunesse' international development education simulation for about 100 Canadian youth aged 16-19, held in summer 1971. Coverage: Le Soleil (July 7, 1971) and Montreal-matin (August 24, 1971).
The 1976 Lovell's Directory lists the Kamp Kanawana office at 1441 Drummond, Montreal (H3G 1WS, tel. 849-5331), with a second location in Chateauguay (tel. 692-2801).
The Sherbrooke Record (July 21, 1972) reported a three-day counsellor leader training program at Camp Kanawana.
The earliest located newspaper reference to 'Kanawana' is in L'aurore des Canadas, January 17, 1843 — predating the camp and likely a geographic reference.
Le Droit (Ottawa), June 25, 1937, reported a first aid instructor going to Camp Kanawana on July 1.
The Westmount Examiner (November 16, 1962) reported citizenship training planned at Kamp Kanawana.

Ross & Macdonald designed three projects for the YMCA at Kanawana, not one: (1) YMCA Boy's Camp buildings, 1913-1914 (CCA AP013.S1.D37, #48095, 5 working drawings); (2) Dining and Kitchen Pavilion, 1919 (AP013.S1.D46, #48710, 6 drawings); (3) Doctor's Cottage, 1921 (AP013.S1.D67, #50576, 3 drawings ARCH25242-25244). Fourteen drawings total, all for Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts.

As of spring 1892, the 41st Annual Report of the YMCA of Montreal (published May 19, 1892) shows the Association had no outdoor camp or athletic grounds, stating: 'The Out-door Work suffers from the disadvantage of not owning suitable grounds.' This predates the 1894 camp founding.

The Cushing family were active in Montreal YMCA governance in 1891-92: Charles Cushing (Board of Directors, Building Committee), Walter Cushing (Young Men's Meeting committee), and P.H. Cushing (Junior Department committee).
The new Montreal YMCA building at Dominion Square opened in January 1892.

The 1993 Montreal YMCA annual report (Board Chairman Marcel Coté; President/CEO Michael Goldbloom) noted Kamp Kanawana celebrating its 100th anniversary and 'enjoys a special stature within the activities of the YMCA.'
The 1993 Kamp Kanawana Committee comprised: Andrew Caddell (Chairperson), Tim Clark, Barbara Drury, Sue Khan, Bob Lewandowski, Bruce Netherwood (YMCA staff), and Tom Snabl.
The Bill Lewis Spring Race (April 25, 1993) was the first time $5,000 in receipts was used to subsidize disadvantaged children attending camp.

The 1901 'Historical Sketch of the YMCA of the City of Montreal, 1851-1901' (Jubilee Celebration, June 8-10, 1901) contains no references to summer camping; all 'camp' references concern militia/military camps (negative result).
D.A. Budge served as General Secretary of the Montreal YMCA from 1874 to at least 1901 (27+ years continuous), per the 1901 historical sketch.
The 1901 historical sketch lists Lemuel Cushing Jr. as YMCA Montreal President 1867-68 (conflicts with other sources giving 1869-70).
The 1901 historical sketch lists Charles Cushing as a Board Director with term expiring May 1, 1902.

Lac Kanawana RSVL monitoring is Station 0573A, coordinates 45°51'07"N 74°11'37"W, in the Rivière du Nord watershed. Average depth 5.2 m, drainage ratio 21.95; 42% of the lake bottom is colonizable by macrophytes (max growth depth 4.3 m).

Lac Kanawana water quality, 2010 summer means: total phosphorus 8.4 µg/L, chlorophyll a 7.2 µg/L, Secchi 2.5 m, DOC 6.2 mg/L (trophic status: mesotrophe). 2011 summer means: phosphorus 7.5 µg/L, chlorophyll a 3.4 µg/L, Secchi 3.9 m, DOC 3.4 mg/L (oligo-mesotrophe).

Per RSVL/MELCCFP records, Lac Kanawana's volume is 1,239,000 m³ and water renewal time 0.36 years (conflicts with other figures of 1,273,000 m³ and 0.43 years); no RSVL monitoring is recorded after 2011 (conflicts with claims of data since 2013).

Ross Seaman is documented as overall camp director 1959-1967, McCallum was most likely the CIT/leadership-program director that year rather than overall camp director (conflict c_013). The official 'Kanawana' Flickr account holds 4,416 photos in 33 albums (joined 2010). A 'University Concordia Archives' album contains 34 digitized archival images spanning 1900-1960s, with titles including 'Towards St. Sauveur des Monts,' 'To Lake Wilson,' and a 1915 staff photo.

The Concordia Records Management/Archives Flickr holds two ca.1910 Kanawana photos: a flag-raising ceremony captioned 'FLAG RAISING KAMP KANAWANA / MONTREAL Y.M.C.A. BOYS CAMP' (Ref P145) and a camp truck (Ref P145).

FamilySearch record for Mabel Grace Jamieson (b. 8 Nov 1893, Canada; d. 9 Mar 1966, Osoyoos BC; married name Mooney; resided Megantic QC per 1911 census; father William Alfred Jamieson, mother Mary McBride Kean) shows no camp connection — likely NOT Camp Ouareau founder Mabel C. Jamieson.

Hedley Seldon Dimock was born 11 February 1891 in South Rawdon, Nova Scotia, and died 4 October 1958 in Burlingame, California. He immigrated to Vermont in 1895; parents Charles Turner Torry Dimock and Catherine Elizabeth Chase. He married Elizabeth Marguerite Gardiner on 17 August 1922 in Regina, SK, and had three children: Dorothy (1925-2005), Hedley Jr. (b. 1928), and Elizabeth (1934-1988). The son 'Hedley Jr.' born 1928 matches Hedley Gardner Dimock (b. c.1928), strongly supporting the father-son hypothesis.

Cathy Reeves' 1993 VHS film 'YMCA Kamp Kanawana: The Experience that Lasts a Lifetime' is on YouTube (uploaded June 16, 2022 from Concordia Archives); it describes Kanawana as 'the oldest camp in Quebec and second oldest in Canada.'

Silent 1960s archival footage of Kamp Kanawana is on YouTube (uploaded June 21, 2022). A 1941 CFCF radio broadcast about YMCA Kamp Kanawana is on the Internet Archive (item 1941-06-26-ymca-kamp-kanawana-broadcast-station-cfcf).
Tamaracouta Scout Reserve (founded 1912) claims to be the oldest continuously running Scout camp in the world — regional camping context for the Laurentians.

The Stuart McLean fonds at McMaster University (1960s-2016, ~16 metres, 87+ boxes, no access restrictions) contains three camp-related files: F.13 [Summer Camp] (typescript drafts 'Camp' and 'Letter Home,' with an editor's note from Meg Masters dated 8 May 1998), F.16 'Kamp Kanawana,' and F.25 'Vinyl Cafe Show 2.10 Camp — Not Published.'

Stuart McLean (b. Montreal 1948, raised Montreal West) began as a counsellor in the Senior Boys Section at Kanawana in summer 1969, worked 5+ summers, and rose to assistant camp director under director Derek Walsh (summers 1974-75); he returned in 2005 to host a Vinyl Cafe show at camp. McLean later sublet his Westmount apartment to Derek Walsh when McLean moved to Toronto.
Camp Kanawana's address is 673 montée Sainte-Elmire, Saint-Sauveur, QC; phone (833) 505-9622.
The Voyageur program consists of 8+ day canoe camping trips; trip staff are called 'Trippers' (e.g., Justin Caldwell, 2018).

The 'Non Nobis Solum' motto shared by Lower Canada College and Camp Kanawana is coincidental: both derive independently from Cicero. LCC adopted it from founder Charles Fosbery's family crest (1909). LCC's current outdoor programs use Camp Minogami (near Shawinigan), not Kanawana.

The Weskarini Algonquin were dispersed by Iroquois warfare in the 1650s; a major massacre occurred in 1653 near Petit Lac Nominingue, northwest of Arundel — roughly 70-80 km north of the Camp Kanawana site but within the same territorial zone.

Archaeological fieldwork in the Laurentians since 2015 (researchers Francis Lamothe, Karine Taché, and Roland Tremblay) demonstrates the integration of the Laurentian landscape within Indigenous interaction networks spanning several regions of the greater Northeast.

The Rivière du Nord — the watershed in which Lac Kanawana sits — flows approximately 125-137 km, running from Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts through Val-David, Sainte-Adèle, Saint-Sauveur, Prévost, and Saint-Jérôme before reaching the Rivière des Outaouais (Ottawa River) at the Lake of Two Mountains.

The Township of Howard (later Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, site of Camp Jubilee/Otoreke) was created in 1873 and named after Frederick Howard, 5th Earl of Carlisle, a Commissioner of the Colonies during the American Revolution.

Kanawana's Adventurer program (introduced 1998) runs canoe trips in Papineau-Labelle wildlife reserve: a documented route covers ~22 km over 4 days with portages of 100-690 m between Lac Saint-Denis, Lac du Crochet, and Lac Montjoie.
James Orbinski (Pip Award 2024) authored 'An Imperfect Offering: Humanitarian Action for the 21st Century' (2008), winner of the Shaughnessy Cohen Award for Political Writing.

The council-ring concept used at North American summer camps is traced to landscape architect Jens Jensen and to Ernest Thompson Seton's Woodcraft Indians (Silver Bay camp, 1910) — context for Kanawana's own Council Ring.

A handwritten sheet titled 'Medley '81' records camp cheers/chants including a call-and-response opener ('Kamp Kanawana are you ready? We are!! Then let's go!'), 'Hail, Hail the gang's all here / What the heck do we care... We are the guys from Kanawana', a Voyageurs sound-off chant ('Said 1-2-3-4-5 / Said Junior Girls don't take no jive / Ya-Ya'), a nonsense chant ('Alabibo-Alabybo, Alabibo-bybo-boom' and 'Alaman Alaman, Alamandiego sandiego, Hocus Pocus dominocus, Whoa men'), and a girls'-section cheer ('Sr. girls are red hot, let's show them what we've got').
entities: Camp Songs, Cheers, and Musical Traditions

facts.claim: The 1981 'Knights of Kanawana' induction document (artwork and lettering by Greg Shevchenko, May 1981) gives the full oath text: 'I solemnly swear to wear this symbol of the Knights of Kanawana with honour and loyalty. I promise to be a true Kanawanian, and to offer my humble support in all that the Council may decide. I swear, also, to keep secret the proceedings of this ceremony, the persons present, as well as the location thereof. I do solemnly accept the honour bestowed upon me this day, and agree to forfeit my Knighthood or Ladyship if at any time my deeds and thoughts prove contrary to those of the Council.' The crest bears the motto 'Non Nobis Solum' and shows a maple leaf and canoe.

A pre-WWI Concordia Archives photo-album page from the Kanawana collection carries handwritten captions 'Tent C', 'Towards St. Sauveur des Monts', and 'To Lake Wilson' beneath three mounted photographs (a group of boys/staff posed by a tent, a hillside/valley landscape, and a wooded riverbank view).

A photograph of a Kamp Kanawana swim team (seven young men in swim trunks on a shoreline, holding a life ring) shows the life ring lettered 'CAMP KANAWANA'; a separate Concordia Archives photo captioned 'KAMP KANAWANA SR. WATERFRONT' and a 1960s-70s staff-photo t-shirt reading 'KAMP KANAWANA / YMCA / STAFF' corroborate 'Kamp' as the dominant camp-era spelling, distinct from the modern 'Camp Kanawana'.

A Concordia Archives photograph (captioned 'Pop Cameron and the Canoe Trippers') shows a group of boys and men with canoes and packs posed around a car bearing a 1941 Quebec license plate ('54-868 QUEBEC 41'), naming a previously undocumented staff member, 'Pop Cameron', associated with the camp's canoe-trip program circa 1941.

The 1941 hand-drawn Kanawana camp map (three near-identical copies in the archive) carries printed travel directions: 'Kanawana is situated about five miles from the village of St. Sauveur des Monts. Take C.N.R. train from the Tunnel Station. The camp truck meets all week-end trains. By road the camp is reached by highway No. 11 to Piedmont. Turn left up the hill, through St. Sauveur village and follow the Kamp Kanawana road signs.' The map itself labels Lake Kanawana, Lake Wilson, and (tentatively) 'Lac des Beories', with an inset map captioned 'Map showing Camp Property [with] Morgan's to Lock' and small hand-lettered activity labels including 'Junior Camp', 'Camp Cliff', 'Indian Grave', and 'Ski Course'.

A Kamp Kanawana site map (dated by the archive to 1980-2001) labels facilities around Lac Kanawana including a Fitness Course, Ball Field, Hospital, Lookout, Archery Field, Fire House, Rock Climbing Wall, Craft Shop, 'Chez Claude', Barn, Indian Council Ring, Chapel, Boating Waterfront, Sauna, and a Tee Pee site, alongside Senior and Junior parking lots and a Post Office.

A 1982 print advertisement for Kamp Kanawana states: 'In 1894 the Y.M.C.A. pioneered camping in the Laurentians by opening the first boys camp in Canada. Today, 88 years later, Kamp Kanawana continues to lead the way,' and advertises coed enrollment ages 8-15, activities (canoeing, hiking, sailing, campcraft, arts & crafts, orienteering, nature lore), '1200 acres & 3 lakes', a 3:1 camper/staff ratio, membership in the QCA and CCA, and contact details 'Kamp Kanawana, 1441 Drummond St., Montreal, Canada H3G 1W5, (514) 849-5331'.

A 1981 advertisement for 'Les Voyageurs de la Vérendrye' — described as 'excursions en canoë pour les jeunes de 13 à 17 ans' / 'extended wilderness canoe trips for youths 13-17' — run through Kamp Kanawana, carries the YMCA de Montréal's founding date ('fondé en 1851') and the contact address 'Kamp Kanawana, 1441 rue Drummond Street, Montréal (Québec) H3G 1W5, (514) 849-5331'; the program name references explorer Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye.

A handwritten 1970s ad-planning sheet for Kamp Kanawana reads: 'YMCA summer camp. Kamp kanawana for boys + girls age 7-15. Some places still available in 1st 3rd + 4th session. For more info call: 849-5331 ext 749,' with five rough pencil sketches iterating on a YMCA-triangle logo layout for a classified-style newspaper ad.

A 1913 Kamp Kanawana reunion banquet menu card, dated 'Wednesday, Nov. 26th, 1913' and printed on autumn-leaf themed paper, is headed 'Kamp Kanawana Kampers' Kluster to kandidly re-konsider their kapricious kapers and knavery under kanvas' and lists a joking mock-formal menu: 'Cold Meats (Purloined from Harry)', 'Lamb (not Hal of tent 1) à la Filion', 'Pork à la Prevost, très tough', 'Rolls... no Tumbling award allowed', '"Inexpensive, but highly nutritious" Doc. H. Griffiths, M a D', 'Cake (the kind our Bird-ette)', and 'Fruit Salad "General mix up, see tent B"' — the earliest dated primary-source document yet found naming individual campers/staff (Harry, Hal, Filion, Prevost, H. Griffiths) by their in-joke camp roles.

A silkscreen printing film for a 'Kamp Kanawana Reunion, April 7th, 1989' marks the camp's founding-to-reunion span as '1894-1989' (i.e. a 95th-anniversary event), depicted with a stylized torch/plant graphic.

A cyanotype architectural blueprint titled 'Proposed Service Wing to Dining Hall, KAMP KANAWANA Y.M.C.A.' is signed 'J.M. Venters, Architect, 1503 Mackay Street, Montreal' and itemizes a construction cost estimate (store room, tool cupboard, new building, misc.) totalling $5,000, for a workshop, office, staff room, laundry, and truck-packing addition to the dining hall.

Camp staff produced hand-drawn t-shirt and silkscreen art across the 1980s-1990s with recurring motifs of Pacific Northwest Coast-style masks/totems (e.g. 'Staff '91 Kanawana', a design with printer's color-separation notes — 4 PMS colors — addressed to a contact named 'Harriet' at the print shop), parody humour (a Star Wars-logo parody reading 'Kana Wana... A long time ago in a Kamp far, far away' / bilingual French caption), and nature imagery ('Kanawana' silhouetted against a treeline; a beaver-in-a-canoe-hat silkscreen design); dated examples include Staff '86, Staff '88, Staff '91 (two versions), and t-shirt mockups from 1987.

A set of cloth 'KAMP KANAWANA HONOUR AWARD' ribbons, most explicitly dated 1920, covers four departments: Educational (Knot Tying, Signalling, Advanced Basketry, Bible Study, Bandaging, Basketry, Nature Study/Trees), Aquatic (Rowing, Canoeing, Length of Lake Swim, Life-Saving), Athletic (Hike, Wrestling, Boxing), and Social Service (Camp Improvement, Public Health); most ribbons carry a circular YMCA 'Spirit/Mind/Body' triangle emblem. Nearly all use the spelling 'KAMP KANAWANA'; one Camp Improvement ribbon uniquely reads 'CAMP KANAWANA'.

A scrapbook page captioned 'Awards, Circa 1940' documents the camp's felt-badge award hierarchy in period handwriting: a maroon triangle with an embroidered maple leaf is captioned 'This was the leadership crest - Westmount "Y"'; a plain green felt 'K' letter is captioned 'The small "K". The second highest award'; an outlined (unfilled) triangle badge is captioned '▽ - awarded after getting a certain # of badges'; and an orange-and-black circular felt patch bears the YMCA 'Spirit/Mind/Body' triangle motif with the biblical citation 'John 17:21' at its center. Three felt pennants (blue, gold, brown) each carry only a stitched letter 'K'.
A felt badge reads 'KANAWANA OUTING CLUB' around a central YMCA triangle logo, evidencing a camp 'Outing Club' distinct from the main honour-award system.

A felt YMCA pennant reads 'Y.M.C.A.' in large vertical lettering with a shield crest bearing the banner text 'KAMPKANAWANA' (run together, no space) and a partially legible Latin-style motto banner, alongside a small YMCA triangle logo and a torch/flame mark — consistent with, though not fully confirming, the camp's later 'Non Nobis Solum' motto.

When Bruce Netherwood left the Camp Director role at the end of 1994, the YMCA restructured Kanawana's administration into two positions: a year-round Executive Director, headquartered in Montreal and responsible for the organization overall, and a three-season on-site Camp Director. The on-site role was colloquially called 'Chief' -- a title dating to the camp's 'playing Indian' era -- until it was retired in the early 2020s as part of Kanawana's reconciliation efforts, after which the role was referred to as the 'on-site Director'.

Arleen Boyer (previously misrecorded as 'Arlene Boyle') served as Executive Director of Camp Kanawana from 1995 to 2000. Operator corrected both the first name ('Arlene' -> 'Arleen') and surname ('Boyle' -> 'Boyer') on 2026-07-07, confirming that the 'Arleen Boyer' name independently found on Kamp Kanawana's FY2003-2004 local volunteer advisory committee in the Montreal YMCA's own annual report (f_1751) was the correct spelling all along, not a near-miss.

Joanna A.A. Hoad served as the on-site Camp Director of Kanawana from 1995 to 2000, under Executive Director Arleen Boyer. (Previously recorded in the KB as 'Joanna Hode', then miscorrected to 'Johanna A.A. Hoade' -- operator confirms the correct spelling is 'Joanna A.A. Hoad'.)
Gary White succeeded Arleen Boyer as Executive Director of Camp Kanawana in 2001 and served until 2005, when he was succeeded by Sean Day.

Morgan Carter was the on-site Camp Director of Kanawana for the summers of 2001, 2002, and 2003, under Executive Director Gary White. (Corrects/extends the previous KB record of Morgan M. Carter's tenure as 2001-2002 only -- 2003 should be included.)

Dave Leduc was the on-site Camp Director of Kanawana for the single summer of 2004 (succeeding Morgan Carter), under Executive Director Gary White. (Corrects the previous KB record, f_1215, which dated Leduc's directorship to 2003; this superseded that fact and resolves conflict c_014.)

Nicolas Garcia (recorded from oral history as "Nicholas Garcia" -- corrected to the documented spelling, see f_1752) served as the on-site Director of Kanawana under Executive Director Sean Day. Oral history recalled a 2005-2012 tenure; per the standing policy that documented sources take precedence over oral history in direct conflicts (operator directive, 2026-07-07, resolving conflict c_016), the 2012 end date is superseded by documented evidence (f_1753) that he served continuously through March 2014. The 2005-2008 start is not directly contradicted by any document and remains oral-history-only, unconfirmed.
Sean Day served as Executive Director of Camp Kanawana from 2005 (succeeding Gary White) until the spring of 2023, when he was succeeded by Marie-Pierre Lacasse.

Kate 'Wawa' Taylor served as the on-site Director of Kanawana from 2013 through the third session of the summer of 2023, when she left partway through the season without completing it. (Refines the previous KB record, which dated her tenure only approximately to 'the 2020s'.)

Kevin Slezak, previously Assistant Director under Kate Taylor, was promoted to on-site Camp Director for the fourth session of the summer of 2023 after Taylor's early departure, and served in that role for the full summer of 2024.
Marie-Pierre Lacasse became Executive Director of Camp Kanawana in the spring of 2023, succeeding Sean Day. (Refines the previous KB record, which dated her tenure to '2024-'.)
Justin Caldwell has been the on-site Camp Director of Kanawana for the summers of 2025 and 2026, succeeding Kevin Slezak.

The article does not use the specific title 'Executive Director'.
