OPEN QUESTION FOR ORAL HISTORY: the Haunted House is documented at Kanawana 1928-1940 (mapped building, annual cookout pilgrimage, a ghost legend with its own rule that the spirits appear only when the wind is from the east and the moon and stars invisible). Chopsy appears in no document, and its oral telling dates its origin to 1945 -- just after the Haunted House references stop. Whether Chopsy is a successor tradition, a renaming, or unrelated is undetermined and cannot be settled from documents.

A CAMPER DROWNED at Kamp Kanawana in the summer of 1969. The Annual Report 1969 states under Health and Safety: "The tragic drowing of one of our campers this Summer has forced us to look at our standards in the whole area of camping. We are convinced that, especially in terms of aquatics, hiking and tripping, both our training and standards are of the highest possible quality." The camper is not named anywhere in the digitized record; no date, location, or circumstance is given. This is the only known camper fatality in the camp's documented history and appeared nowhere in this wiki before 2026-08-14.

A viral meningitis outbreak at Kanawana in summer 1976 affected at least 19 people including the camp director; three (two of them staff) were hospitalised for a minimum of six days. The 1976 infirmary statistics for the season: 115 sprains, 255 sore throats and colds, 45 earaches, 281 cuts and scrapes, 26 X-ray trips, 48 snake bites, 72 cases of gastritis, 7 fractures.

CORRECTED: Kanawana admitted female campers for the first time in 1968, not 1969. The 1988 report states "1968 Kamp Kanawana admits female campers for the first time. 66 girls registered"; the annual reports' camper-weeks tables first show bracketed girl figures in the 1968 column; and the 1970 season report calls that summer the camp's "third year as a coeducational camp", counting back to 1968. The undated YMCA Kamp Kanawana Facts sheet's "1969" is an error, not a second milestone. The first female waterfront staff were hired in 1969.

Coeducation at Kanawana was RECOMMENDED IN 1965 AND DECLINED, three years before it was implemented. The 1965 director's report argues for it and proposes a costed pilot in the Woodsmen section (ages 10-11, four boys and four girls), noting the only extra expense would be "an adequate wash house with showers for the girls and this would not be an expense of more than $300." It records an earlier constituency survey under Keith Farquharson that found "a very large and positive response", and that the Metropolitan Board declined to act.

The 1969 and 1970 Kanawana season reports record sharply different registers on coeducation one year apart. 1969 anticipates trouble: it "creates some problems for a camp that has dealt with boys only for 3/4 of a century... establishing an identity, showing off, sex experimentation, loss of focus on the tent group". 1970, after two seasons, reverses it: "There were no 'mother or father' roles played (ie boys gathering wood while the girls cooked). Each person shared the responsibility and the dialogue around the fire at night took on extra significance. School, sex, the world, war, ecology, sing songs, etc., were all part of the campfires" -- and frames the whole thing as "not 'coed' camping but a 'coeducational' experience".

Kanawana section extinction dates from the camper-weeks tables: RANGERS last carry campers in 1967; COUREURS DE BOIS and PIONEERS both last in 1972. From 1973 the tables run only Woodsmen (Junior) and Pathfinders (Senior). Since Pioneers and Coureurs de Bois are in use at the camp today, those names were REVIVED after a gap rather than carried continuously.

Kanawana section names were reassigned along gender lines IMMEDIATELY after coeducation, not in the 1970s. The 1969 organisation chart shows PIONEER (M), WOODSMEN (M), CdeB (M) and PATHFINDER (M) under the Camp Director, with WOODSMEN (G) and CdeB (G) under a separate "Camp Director of Girls". By 1970 the chart lists Pathfinder Boys, Woodsman Boys, Pathfinder Girls, Woodsmen Girls and Pioneer; by 1971 Coureur de Bois has gone.

NO document in the digitized corpus states that a 1959 Kanawana section renaming occurred, dates it, or credits A. Ross Seaman with it. The corpus gives only a bracket: 1958 is the last year "Bantam" is used, 1959 the first year "Pathfinders" appears. CAUTION: the ten-year camper-weeks tables in the 1964-66 reports apply the NEW five-section names retroactively to data back to 1955 -- a reporting convention, not evidence the names existed then, and easy to misread as pushing the renaming earlier.
"Rover" at Kanawana in the 1970s denotes a RELIEF-COUNSELLOR post, not a section: "Senior Girls Rover-Counsellor" (1977), "Junior Boys Rover" (1979). It should not be read as a Kanawana section name.

THE ORDER OF THE RED FEATHER was a Kanawana honour, previously unrecorded in this wiki, running from at least 1940 to at least 1965 and tied to the Council Ring ceremonies. It worked by degrees: the Green Triangle of 29 July 1940 reports "Alec Cherney has finally succeeded in passing his third degree, thus entitling him to become a full member of the Order of the Red Feather. This coveted honour is very rare indeed, and to attain it requires a good deal of hard industrious work." It outlasted the "Indian lore" programming -- a 1965 camp publication still refers to "the man in the Red Feather" and "A RED FEATHER REVUE". What the three degrees tested, and when the order lapsed, are undocumented.

THE GOLDEN ARROW was instituted at Kanawana in 1965, previously unrecorded in this wiki. The 1965 report: "At the closing camp fire he was presented with a 'Golden Arrow' which is an award that has been instituted at camp this summer and presented at the discretion of the staff to any boy in camp who shows extraordinary personal achievment during his stay. This is not a 'popularity poll' but an award that is given on recommendation only." The first recipient described is a boy named Gordon, a foster child, almost totally blind, who "learned to go off the high dive at camp".

The Knights of Kanawana was INSTITUTED IN 1979, not 1980. The camp's 1988 report dates it under Programme Highlights: "1979 Knights of Kanawana is instituted. This is a recognition of campers who have acquired an advanced level of various outdoor skills." The charter's "Year of Our Lord Nineteen Hundred and Eighty" dates the charter document, one season after the order began. The same list dates the Order of Owens to 1976 and the WALDEN SOLOS to 1982 ("a programme that enables CITs to participate in a 48 hour controlled solo experience"), and states that as of 1988 all listed programmes were still in effect.

Richard "Itche" Kerr's own first-person account dates the camp song precisely. Writing in the alumni newsletter The Lookout in autumn 1993: "My invitation to this year's closing banquet was written at summer's end 1977. I wrote it myself late one night with some help from three friends... Somehow, the next summer it was remembered and it has been sung every summer since." So: written in one night at the end of summer 1977 with three unnamed collaborators, revived 1978, annual thereafter. CAUTION: no contemporaneous 1977 or 1978 document naming Kerr as composer has been found; this 1993 memoir, sixteen years after the fact, is the sole source. Kerr was on staff in 1975, 1976 (took over the CIT program mid-summer) and 1977 (CIT Director), and ran a song workshop at pre-camp in 1992.

The CBM radio broadcast "The Voice of Youth" of 10 November 1938, performed by the boys of Kanawana, gives a set list: 1. "Kanawana Marching Song" (a distinct title, not otherwise attested); 2. "Hi-Ho, Hi-Ho"; 3. "My Old Kentucky Home" (solo by 12-year-old Sandy Spence); 4. "The World is Waiting for the Sunrise" (chorus only); 5. "Johnny Verbec", introduced as Dick Abraham's "Kanawana song specialty" with guitar and called "the sausage song"; 6. "Taps". "Johnny Verbec" is the folk song usually spelled Johnny Verbeck / Dunderbeck's Machine -- a second borrowed-song lead of the "Alabama Jubilee" type. The script names John Pearson as song leader and lists the singing venues: the dining hall, Farewell Rock, around the fire-rafts on the lake, and the Saturday Night Shows.

Four Kanawana song titles from 1933, from the Green Triangle of 29 July: "Marois", "The Nonsense Song", "Sea-Side" and "Yo Triumphy", plus an unnamed "the camp song" distinct from all four. "Yo Triumphy" is the 1922 brochure cheer, still in the repertoire eleven years later. NO LYRICS survive for any Kanawana song anywhere in the digitized corpus -- only titles, plus one complete yell text (the 1965 Pathfinder yell).

The 1965 Pathfinder yell is the only complete Kanawana cheer text recovered from the season-report corpus besides the 1922 brochure cheer. Reconstructed from damaged uppercase OCR: "Tents, trails, trees and tracks / Paths, paddles, pets and packs / We're the boys with the strongest backs / We're the boys who swing the axe / Here we are, there we are / Tripping men from near and far / Swish, swash, splish, splash / We're at Kamp to have a bash / YEA, PATHFINDERS!" The article printing it says the yell "was original to the Pathfinders in 1965, required maximum participation and group effort in order for it to sound really good in the dining hall", gives the section motto "one for all and all for one", and a call-and-response closing. An all-camp "Kanawana Yell" existed by 1932.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-14: canoe-trips.md carried numeric citation markers ^3 through ^7 in its body while its Sources section was an UNNUMBERED bullet list, so none of those five citations resolved to anything. Only ^7 had a label, attached to the eighth bullet. Pre-existing, not introduced by any recent pass, and invisible to the draft-only mechanical harness because the article is E1-reviewed. Found by extending the marker-resolution check to all 91 articles rather than the 28 drafts. The list is now numbered.

THE LONG HOUSE was built and dedicated in mid-July 1952 and demolished in 1978. The 1952 Annual Report: "Campers and staff will look back on 1952 as the year of the 'Long House'. Officially opened and dedicated in mid-July, this spacious waterfront recreation hall was a great asset, especially for rainy weather program, with its large stone fireplace and stage. It also provides winter storage space for the entire camp fleet of 50 boats and canoes, and quarters for the waterfront directors." The 1978 director's report records "demolition of the old 'Longhouse' (32' x 70')", giving both the year and the dimensions. SUPERSEDES the wiki's "demolished c.1979 by controlled fire" as to date.

Kanawana Council Ring construction chronology: first erected c.1917-1920 per the Green Triangle of 13 August 1932 ("first erected some twelfe or 15 years ago"), which conflicts with the wiki's 1922; enlarged and rebuilt to seat 325 in 1928 under KAROL PERRY (the 1929 Annual Report describes the 1928 season -- the wiki dated this 1929, a one-year offset from misreading the report year as the season year); COMPLETELY REBUILT with stronger foundations in 1932 under JIM CARNEGIE; razed and rebuilt in 1987 by a senior boys' tent under TOBY DESJARDINS. The 1988 facilities survey specifies a large fire bowl and seating for 300, in a wooded area removed from the camp core.

UNRESOLVED: the 1954 Annual Report states "The Y's Men's Club of Westmount provided Kanawana with an Indian Council Ring, which greatly enhanced the Indian Lore Program." Read literally this implies a NEW council ring in 1954, which is impossible -- a council ring is continuously documented from c.1918. Most likely a donated rebuild or a second ring for the junior sections. 1954 must NOT be presented as a founding date.

The time-capsule tradition at Kanawana -- burying a record of the summer at the closing council ring and unearthing it at the next season's opening fire -- is DOCUMENTED FROM 1923, twelve years earlier than the wiki's "believed to date to the 1920s or 1930s". The Gas Bag camp diary of 1923 records at the closing council ring: "Record of Camp's activities buried with avpropriate ceremony." The 1935 season chronicle closes with the other half: "we are about to bury this short History, in order that it may be unearthed at the first all-camp fire next Season."

Kanawana building chronology from the 1951 camp history: the lower pavilion on the lake front built early; the present dining hall and kitchen unit completed 1920; the lodge and museum built 1927; Bantam cabins 1936; water system and latrines 1938; showers 1939; Junior cabins and fourteen new tent platforms 1942, with seven open-sided Junior cabins that fall under Ross Wiggs, contracted to E. C. Page; and under Roy Locke from 1947 a new main wharf, a new Senior Section Director cabin, electrification, an automatic chlorinated water system and electric refrigeration. A new boat house to replace the lower pavilion was planned for September 1951.

CONTRADICTION between two camp documents on two building dates. The 1988 facilities table gives dining hall [1919] and lodge [1880's]; the 1951 camp history gives dining hall 1920 and "In 1927 the lodge and museum was built". The dining-hall difference may be construction-start versus completion. The LODGE difference is harder: the Saint-Sauveur site was not purchased until 1910, so an 1880s lodge would have to be a pre-existing farm structure later converted. Both readings are defensible; neither is adopted.

CATALOGUING DEFECT: the Kanawana orienteering map in the digitized fonds is catalogued as 1974 and cannot be. It shows KATIMAVIK (the 1978 director's report calls it "the new recreation hall"), the SAUNA (built summer 1974) and the GRAND PORTAGE (first named 1976). The map is c.1978-1982 at the earliest. Its 32-structure legend is the fullest building list the project has, and it reveals a compass-and-light naming scheme (North Wind, South Wind, Northern Light, Midi du Soleil, Lighthouse, Compass) confirmed live in the 1979 report.

"The Ritz" was a Kanawana BUILDING, not a hill, and is the likely origin of the toponym "Mount Ritz" (which returns zero hits corpus-wide). The Gas Bag Extra reports "GREAT ENGINEERING FEAT / Removing the 'Ritz'. This building in its time has served as hospital, library, barber shop and directors' office. It will be moved to the brow of the hill between Tent A and Chute." A new Ritz opened in July 1933 as the Junior Director's cabin, "situated just back of the monument", the old one having "outlived its usefulness". INFERENCE, labelled: a building moved to the brow of a hill is a plausible source for a hill name.

"The Suez" is a Kanawana channel or narrows, bridged and re-bridged across 64 years: the 1923 Gas Bag records "bridge over the Suez completed after much hard work"; a 1937 Green Triangle recalls "Paddling through the Suez at sunset"; and the 1987 director's report records that "The entire senior boys section spent the second and third session rotating their time in razing and re-building the bridge across the Suez canal. Thousands of man hours were used."

The 1970 Kanawana annual report records severe erosion in the camp's own words: "Since we use only a small area of our 1,000 acres we have finally worn all the earth away. One section (Pioneers) is eroded so badly that there is no green area over most of the section... The main areas we use 90% of the time (camp proper) do not look like a camp but a section of St. Catherine Street." Thirty-six years before the camp's "green camp" branding.

The 1987 director's report documents four camper-led restoration projects in one season -- a Junior Boys forest project with 100 seedlings, a CIT reforestation project, a CIT stair-and-retaining-wall project for erosion control, and path closures directed by camp naturalist Chris Adam -- and records acid-rain damage: "Many of our large maples are dead or dying and the Tasses must cut more down each year. At this rate, in 5-7 years there will be no large trees left."

Kanawana's stated land area varies by nearly a factor of seven across the record: 150 acres (1936 CFCF broadcast); 600 acres (1949-1959 annual reports); "a sixty acre site" (1957, almost certainly an error for 600); "approximately 1,000 acres" (1964, 1969, 1970) after a 1964 purchase of ~120 acres at the south end of Lake Wilson; and 455 acres land / 537 total (1989 Royal LePage figure). The 1988 report supplies the explanation: "There was no record found that showed the Kanawana site has ever been surveyed."

The 1964 Kanawana land purchase was partly defensive: lot 215 was bought JOINTLY WITH THE BOY SCOUTS' CAMP TAMARACOUTA and lots 216-217 outright, expressly to block "a proposed summer colony of some 200 lots" at the south end of Lake Wilson.

In his 1971 parting report, Camp Director James H. Turner recommended effectively abolishing Kanawana as it then existed: "Kanawana program should focus specifically on hikes and canoe trips... this would reduce budget expenses by cutting back on all other program staff and equipment... all meals would be cooked out - just as when they are on their trip. Kanawana should move this aspect of its operation 50-100 miles further north to a smaller base camp site... buildings and program areas are no longer needed... Kanawana's present property to be used for experimental programs or rentals." He also recommended selling the Lac Becsie property, which WAS sold in 1986.

Kanawana hosted campers with cystic fibrosis from 1970 -- seven in the first year (3 girls, 4 boys), one of whom "swam two miles for his double black cord" at age 10. The 1970 report is candid about the partnership: "Our relationship with the C.F. Association seemed shaky all through the pre-arrangements and during camp. There seemed to be no clearing house for them and everyone did pretty well what they wanted when they wanted." From 1986 the camp partnered with the West Island Association for the Handicapped, Giant Steps, and the Montreal Oral School for the Deaf.

The 1978 Kanawana director's report is unusually candid about internal difficulty: "In my six years at Kanawana, I don't think that I have ever written a report that talked about problems as much as this", and "Some staff have intimated that they feel the strictness of the Director inhibits the kamp spirit." Seven campers were sent home that summer -- four for drugs, two for cigarettes, one for an injury. The following year the returnee staff rate was 10%.

PRIVACY NOTE, deliberately recorded without names: Kanawana directors named individual staff under a "Do not re-hire" heading in season reports that are now publicly digitized -- the 1973 report lists three people by name and gives two further paragraph-length negative character assessments naming individuals. The 1975 report records a Senior Waterfront Director "asked to leave during the fourth session". The EXISTENCE of the practice is recorded here as a fact about how the camp documented itself; the names are NOT extracted, per CLAUDE.md's Phase 2 rule against extracting personal information about living private individuals.

EXHAUSTIVE SEARCH, NULL BEYOND FOUR YEARS: the complete digitized YMCA of Montreal fonds contains L&V Games RESULTS for exactly four seasons -- 1966 (Voyageurs), 1977 (Lumbermen), 1978 (Lumbermen, 'again', which also corroborates 1977) and 1993 (Voyageurs, narrowly). All four are already extracted. Every surviving Kanawana season report (1964, 1965, 1966, 1969, 1970, 1971, 1973, 1974, 1975, 1976, 1977, 1978, 1979, 1987), the Green Triangle run, the Ka-News run, the Gas Bag, the 1988 'A Place to Grow' report and the SGW annual reports 1856-2009 were searched for both 'lumber*' and 'voyageur' with and without a win verb. The Games are mentioned in 1949/50, 1960, 1969, 1975, 1976, 1982, 1987 and 1988 WITHOUT naming a winner -- the reports record that the event happened, not who won it. CONSEQUENCE: p_244's premise, that up to a dozen further seasons were available to corroborate the trophy roll, is WRONG; four is the ceiling from this corpus. Conflict c_025 (the 1966 discrepancy) and the missing 1961 shield CANNOT be resolved from these documents and need the physical trophy or a source outside this collection.

Camp YMCA Kanawana's modern residential attendance, from the YMCAs of Quebec impact reports: 655 kids and teens in 2022 (the reopening season) and 780 in 2023, a 19% increase. These are the first hard residential-attendance figures this wiki holds for any year after the 1980s.

The YMCAs of Quebec 2022 impact report records that the association 'reopened Camp YMCA Kanawana after two years of closures' -- corroborating the two lost summers of 2020 and 2021 from the association's own reporting.

CAUTION ON A NUMBER: the 2022 impact report states 'Close to 300 campers, including Ukrainian refugees, had a memorable summer in our day camps and at Camp YMCA Kanawana.' This is the FINANCIALLY-ASSISTED subset across day camps AND Kanawana combined -- the preceding sentence is about financial assistance -- and is NOT a Kanawana attendance figure. It must not be added to or netted against the 655. The substantive fact is that the camp took in children displaced by the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

The YMCAs of Quebec 2024 impact report marks the 130th anniversary of Camp Kanawana and the launch of 'Adventure at Kanawana', a DAY-CAMP format run on the Saint-Sauveur site -- distinct from the residential camp and from the YMCA Concordia science, engineering and fine-arts camps.

During the 2020 closed summer the YMCA ran a virtual campfire singalong with the Camp YMCA Kanawana team as part of a fundraiser that raised $81,520, with donations doubled by the Trottier Family Foundation. The same report lists Sean Day as Regional Camp Director.

THE 1894 FOUNDING IS DOCUMENTED CONTEMPORANEOUSLY. The YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1894-95 states in its Junior Department section: "We are able to report the holding of our first Summer Camp, which was in every way a decided success, and will become an established item in our prospectus. This Camp was composed of 23 workers and boys." The statistical summary confirms "Attendance at Summer Camp ... 23". The preceding 1893-94 report contains NO mention of a lake, lease, fishing rights or Ste-Agathe -- a null result confirming 1894 as the first year.

CRITICAL NULL: the YMCA of Montreal annual reports NEVER call any camp "Camp Jubilee." Every pre-1921 report was searched. "Jubilee" appears only in the YMCA-worldwide sense -- the 1893-94 report's "This is the Jubilee Year in the history of the Young Men's Christian Association" (the 1844-1894 golden jubilee) and the 1894-95 report's "The World's Jubilee Convention, London, Eng., June 6-10, 1894." That the association's first boys' camp began in the YMCA's Jubilee Year is a real coincidence, but the association's own records do not make the connection or use the name. This wiki uses "Camp Jubilee" throughout and should attribute it to whichever source actually supplies it.

The 1894 camp ran as TWO PARALLEL STREAMS on one leased lake. The 1894-95 report's Junior Department section reports the first boys' camp (23 workers and boys); its Physical Department section separately records "The Association has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe... Last year 53 members took advantage of this privilege" -- adult/senior members. From 1896 the reports state the split explicitly (28 junior, 40 senior). INFERENCE, labelled: only the Junior line becomes Kanawana; the Senior line stays on Lac St. Joseph and becomes Camp Otoreke.

The first Summer Camp committee, named in the 1894-95 annual report's officers list: "Summer Camp. John W. Ross, Chairman. E. J. Coyle. R. L. Charlton." John W. Ross recurs as camp chairman for roughly thirty years and later becomes Association President and Honorary President. By 1896 a "PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE" exists: John W. Ross (chairman), Jas. Wilson, W. E. Cushing, R. B. Ross Jr. -- putting W. E. Cushing on the camp committee from 1896.

KANAWANA'S FIRST SEASON IS SUMMER 1910, announced in the forward tense in the 1910 annual report: "A new site has been secured for the Boys' Camp on Lake Kanawana, near Shawbridge, in the Laurentian Mountains... a summer vacation camp for boys, from July 1st to August 15th. They will have accommodation for 70 boys. This camp will be under the charge of Mr. W. J. Holliday, of the Central Branch. The Summer Camp at Lac St. Joseph will have renewed equipment, and will be given over entirely to the senior members." Two internal confirmations: the 1931 report says the camp "HAS BEEN IN OPERATION FOR TWENTY-ONE YEARS IN ITS PRESENT LOCATION" (of the 1930 season) and the 1939 report calls 1938 "The twenty-ninth season at Camp Kanawana" -- both giving 1910.

NAMES FILLING THE 1902-1920 DIRECTORIAL GAP, from the annual reports (season years): 1908 Junior Camp under W. J. Holliday; 1910 Kanawana opens under W. J. HOLLIDAY of Central Branch; 1913 "in charge of Messrs. D. J. EVANS, HAROLD CROSS, and H. A. LORDLY for successive portions of the season"; 1915 T. HICKS MILLER (Physical Director, Westmount) in July and JOHN McKINNON (Boys' Work Secretary, Central) in August; 1916 "Mr. MacKinnon acted as Leader throughout"; 1917 supervised by J. G. MacKINNON with Jos. DALLEY and John BRADFORD; 1918 John MacKinnon to 3 August, G. D. BRANDON relieving to 17 August; 1919 "Mr. MacKinnon has been appointed Director for this season". NOTE the 1913 entry: Harold Cross running part of the 1913 season predates by a decade the c.1925-1928 directorship the wiki records for him.

THE ASSOCIATION RAN TWO COMPETING ANNIVERSARY CLOCKS, which explains two long-standing confusions in this wiki. A "camping since 1894" clock is used in the reports of 1946 ("the 52nd for boys arranged by the Montreal Association"), 1948 (54th), 1949 (55th), 1966-67 (73rd year), 1967 (74th), 1968 (75th anniversary), 1977-78 and 2005-06. A "Kanawana site since 1910" clock is used in 1931 ("TWENTY-ONE YEARS IN ITS PRESENT LOCATION"), 1939 (29th season), 1984 ("its 75th year of service") and 1985 ("for the past 75 years"). CONSEQUENCES: the 75th anniversary was celebrated TWICE, in 1968 and again in 1984; and the 1993 report announces the camp "celebrating its 100th anniversary this year" while the 1994 report says "This was Kanawana's 100th year of operation" -- two centennials, one from each clock.

The earliest founding-date claims in the annual reports are UNRELIABLE and conflict with the contemporaneous record: the 1931 report says "IN 1898, OR FORTY YEARS AGO, THE FIRST BOYS CAMP OF THE ASSOCIATION WAS OPENED AT LAC ST. JOSEPH"; the 1932 and 1933 reports date Lac St. Joseph activity to 1891/92; the 1954 and 1955 reports say "the site of the first Y.M.C.A. camp established in 1892"; the 1953 and 1965 reports say 1893. All postdate the events by three to four decades and conflict with the 1894-95 report's own first-person "our first Summer Camp". The corpus also holds a document titled "1900-12-10 seventh annual report of the current camp committee" -- 7th annual in 1900 gives 1894.

The scarlet fever outbreak that quarantined Kamp Kanawana for about four weeks is recorded in the YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1941: "a mild case of scarlet fever developed, followed by two others, so that the camp had to be quarantined for about four weeks." DATE UNRESOLVED BY ONE YEAR: the wiki dated it 1941 from McMorris, but the association's fiscal year then ended 31 March, so the 1941 REPORT describes the summer of 1940. Three cases and four weeks match McMorris's "full month" closely enough to be the same event, but a different source-dating on her side, or two outbreaks in consecutive years, cannot be excluded without reading her citation. Same one-year offset class as the Council Ring rebuild (recorded 1929, actually 1928).

CORRECTION TO THE POLIO RECORD: the 1947 annual report (1946 season) does NOT state that polio cases occurred at camp. It says "The polio epidemic affected attendance for the last half of the season, although most doctors advised parents that conditions at camp were more favorable for children than were those in the city" -- i.e. the city-wide Montreal epidemic as an attendance depressant. The six-case figure this project holds comes from the McMorris thesis, which remains its sole source. The annual report corroborates the YEAR and the ATTENDANCE EFFECT, not the case count.

The camp's water supply failed in 1932: "PROBABLY THE MOST SERIOUS PROBLEM THE CAMP IS FACING AT THE PRESENT TIME IS THAT OF AN ADEQUATE WATER SUPPLY. THE FACT THAT BOTH WELLS PRESENTLY BEING USED WERE DRY DURING THE PAST SEASON LEADS ONE TO BELIEVE THAT IT IS SURFACE WATER WHICH IS BEING USED." Resolved the following year -- the 1934 report records "two new wells were sunk."

NULL RESULTS ACROSS ALL 114 ANNUAL REPORTS MENTIONING KANAWANA: no fire, no storm destruction, and no death at camp is reported in any of them. The 1969 camper drowning appears ONLY in the Kanawana season report, not the annual report (whose sole 1969 Kanawana passage is an attendance line, and which returns zero hits for regret/sorrow/died/death/accident/tragic/drown). The 1976 viral meningitis outbreak likewise appears only in the camp's own director's report. Two apparent hits are false positives: a 1938 "two or three drownings" line concerns a city branch waterfront, and a 1962 "water pollution cancelled swimming" line concerns the Ile Perrot day camp.
NULL: Camp Weredale and Camp Ouareau appear NOWHERE in any of the 114 YMCA of Montreal annual reports that mention Kanawana.

THE FISCAL CONVENTION OF THE YMCA OF MONTREAL ANNUAL REPORTS, needed to date anything drawn from them. Reports up to and including 1925 cover a year ending 30 APRIL. Reports from 1926 through 1950 cover a year ending 31 MARCH. From 1951 the fiscal period is the CALENDAR YEAR, decided explicitly: 'It was decided ... that effective January 1st, 1951, the fiscal period should accord with the calendar year.' CONSEQUENCE: for every report up to 1950, report YYYY describes the summer of YYYY-1, and any month named in it falls in the twelve months BEFORE the March/April year end. THE KANAWANA FEE WAS $8.50 PER WEEK IN 1923, extending the documented fee series back four years from the 1927-1929 figures. The 1923 Gas Bag Extra: "The cost is $8.50 per week. This includes one return trip from Montreal to Camp." So the fee was UNCHANGED across at least 1923-1929, through a period when the annual reports repeatedly note it was deliberately below every other permanent camp "to keep the cost within reach of the average home."

Visitor charges at Kanawana in 1923, from the Gas Bag Extra: 50 cents per night, 50 cents per meal, and $1.50 each way for the rig to Piedmont. The Camp Management "prefers to know in advance if visitors are expected."

R. L. CHARLTON WAS ACTIVE AT KANAWANA IN 1923, not only in the founding era and the 1943 manuscript: the 1923 Gas Bag Extra reports "Mr. R. L. Charlton reports that he hopes to complete arrangements for a Senior Log Cabin. On rainy nights the Cabin, with a roaring fire throwing out its warmth and comfort, will be more than welcome." Charlton sat on the first Summer Camp committee in 1894 and wrote the "Notes re Early Days" manuscript in 1943 -- this places him still working on camp buildings nearly thirty years after the founding.

RESOLUTION (c_024, operator, 2026-08-14): the 1919 memoir's Lac la Croix passage records a SITE-SELECTION SEQUENCE, not a rival account of where the 1894 season was held. The syndicate decided to locate the first camp at Lac la Croix; the first group went out in 1894; a better location was found 'just a little further on'; property with fishing privileges was secured at Lac St. Joseph. Lake Saint-Joseph stands as the 1894 camp site; Lac la Croix is recorded as the site originally selected and abandoned.

CORROBORATION of the 1919 memoir's reliability: the memoir says property 'with fishing privileges' was secured at Lac St. Joseph, and the YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1894-95 -- written within a year of the events -- says the Association 'has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe'. Two independent documents twenty-five years apart describe the same transaction in the same terms.

ATTRIBUTION CAUTION: the August 1919 'Brief Autobiographical Sketch of Association Career' is NOT by W. H. (Billy) Ball. Ball appears in it in the third person as a fellow member of the founding syndicate ('a small group composed of W. H. Ball, John W. Ross, Will Wilson, myself and others'). The author is the man who became the third General Secretary of the Winnipeg YMCA in June 1894.

NULL/SCOPE RESULT (p_255): the phrase 'Camp Jubilee' appears in exactly ONE of the 634 digitized text items in the YMCA of Montreal fonds -- the 1988 retrospective report 'Kanawana... A Place to Grow'. Every other corpus use of 'Jubilee' is the YMCA movement's own jubilee sense (the 1844-1894 World's Jubilee Convention; Montreal's own 1851-1901 jubilee celebrated June 1901). No contemporaneous 1894-1910 document in the corpus calls the camp 'Camp Jubilee'.

The 1988 report 'Kanawana... A Place to Grow' is the source of the 'Camp Jubilee' name in this wiki's chain, and its 1894 entry is demonstrably unreliable in detail: it states 'Three islands were purchased on Lake St. Joseph' in 1894 with '20 participants'. The contemporaneous 1894-95 report says the land and fishing rights were LEASED from the Government, and gives 23 workers and boys; the 1902 report records that three islands in Lac St. Joseph were sold by public auction on 26 November 1901, the Committee purchasing one small island adjoining 'our present island' for $50.

The 1988 report also states that in 1910 'Camp Jubilee was renamed Camp Otoreke' -- making Otoreke, not Jubilee, the name with contemporaneous documentary support for the original site. The earliest Otoreke attestation in the corpus is the 1921-22 Annual Report: 'CAMP OTOREKE -- The Camp for men was again conducted during the months of July and August', carried as a budget line separate from Kamp Kanawana.

What the YMCA of Montreal actually called the original camp, contemporaneously and consistently, was descriptive rather than a proper name: a standing committee simply titled 'Summer Camp' (chaired by John W. Ross, in the Committees for 1895-96 list); 'the summer camp at Ste. Agathe' (1895-96); 'the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph' (1897-98); 'THE ASSOCIATION SUMMER CAMP, LAKE ST. JOSEPH' (1899); 'SUMMER CAMP, ST. AGATHE' (1902); 'The Camp at Lac St. Joseph, Ste. Agathe' (1903).

EARLIEST RECORDED REFERENCE to the original camp location: the YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1894-95, Physical Department section -- 'The Association has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe, and purpose using it as a summer camp for our members.' The LAKE IS NOT NAMED. The earliest naming of the lake in the corpus is the following year's 1895-96 report: 'In July and August the Association carries on a camp at Lac St. Joseph, near St. Agathe, for the use of the members on their vacation.'

MATERIAL QUALIFICATION to the p_255 'Camp Jubilee' null: while the name appears in only one of the 634 digitized corpus items, it IS the name used by CONCORDIA'S OWN ARCHIVAL DESCRIPTION of the YMCA of Montreal fonds -- sub-series 'P0145/12L - Lac St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee', and a series description reading 'Season reports of the Junior Camp (Camp Jubilee/Otoreke)'. QAHN uses it too: 'That camp, called Camp Jubilee after the fiftieth anniversary of the YMCA'. So the name is the received archival and heritage-sector name for the site, not a wiki invention -- it simply has no attestation in the association's own 1894-1909 records.

The camp's two in-house histories do NOT use the name 'Camp Jubilee' either. The 1935 'A History of Kamp Kanawana' does not contain the word; the 1951 'Kamp Kanawana History' says only that 'After much searching a site was chosen on Lac St. Joseph at Ste Adolphe de Howard' -- wording which is itself consistent with the Lac la Croix site-selection sequence recorded in the 1919 memoir. || CORRECTION 2026-09-02: this fact previously rendered the 1951 quotation as 'at Ste [Agathe]', with Agathe supplied in brackets. The document does not say Agathe. It says 'Ste Adolphe de Howard' -- Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard -- and mentions Sainte-Agathe separately and earlier, as the REGION toured in spring 1893 before a site was picked. The bracket inverted the document's own distinction between where they looked and where they landed, and it pointed away from Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, which is exactly where QAHN places Camp Jubilee. Found on the first end-to-end read of the full cached text.

QAHN dates the renaming of Camp Jubilee to Camp Otoreke to 1909; the camp's own 1988 retrospective dates it to 1910. Both postdate the events by decades and neither is corroborated by a contemporaneous document; the earliest corpus attestation of 'Otoreke' is the 1921-22 Annual Report.

The QAHN photograph 'Camp Otoreke (YMCA Camp), Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, 1944' is an old photographic postcard whose verso, transcribed by QAHN, reads: 'Camp Otoreke. 3 August 44. So by August 1944 Otoreke had a NEW LODGE with an upstairs dining and function room and downstairs showers and changing rooms, and its campers took fifteen-mile paddles.

QAHN's historical note on the Otoreke photograph, credited to the Concordia University Archives, records the site's post-1910 career: after the YMCA's main camping program moved to Kanawana in 1910, Otoreke 'operated variously as a camp for men over 18, for women and men over 18, for married couples, and for low-income families. It was sold in 1987.' It also describes the site as 'several islands plus a landing area on the mainland'.

CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW CONFLICT (p_263): QAHN, citing the Concordia University Archives, says the original Montreal YMCA camp 'began operation in 1893'. This does NOT contradict the 1894 founding; it matches material this wiki already records -- Concordia fonds P145 sub-series 12L holds camper lists, financial records and fishing-rights documentation dated 1893, and sub-series 12A holds an 1893 report of a trip to St. Agathe to scout a lake. The wiki's own framing already treats 1893 as documented precursor activity and 1894 as the first camp proper, on the strength of the contemporaneous 1894-95 report's 'our first Summer Camp'. THE 1918 SEASON IN DETAIL, from the Gazette of 27 July 1918 (recovered via Google Books after newspapers.com blocked access): 'At the Y.M.C.A. boys' camp at Kanawana there are now about 90 boys whose ages range from 12 to 17 years.' The boys 'sleep under canvas' and are 'wakened at [6].30 a.m. by a bugle', a welcome summons because it means 'the morning dip, which is preceded by physical exercises'. 'Nearly all the boys can swim, and many become expert oarsmen -- twelve rowboats and six canoes are at their disposal.' Meals were 'served in the dining pavilion'.

TWO NEW 1918 STAFF NAMES from the same Gazette report: 'the camp cook is Mr. Harry Smith, from the Montreal High School, and being well acquainted with boys' appetites, the campers never have to go short'; and 'Lessons in basketry and woodwork are given by Mr. Robert Spinney'. Woodcraft was 'one of the special features of this year's camp', with 'long rambles... giving the boys a chance to study nature'. Neither man is otherwise known to this project.

THE 1974 SEASON, from the Gazette summer-camp feature of 18 April 1974 (recovered via Google Books): Kanawana is listed under 'RESIDENTIAL CAMPS - CO-ED' and 'was billed as Quebec's oldest boys' camp until sister campers invaded four years ago'. That summer '90 boys and 90 girls' were expected. Facilities: 'canoes, sailboats, handicraft shop'. Location 'just outside St. Sauveur'. The stated rationale for coeducation, quoted from a YMCA public relations manager: 'We went co-ed in response to requests from parents who wanted their daughters to have the same opportunities as their sons.' And a striking demographic figure: 'French campers constitute 30 per cent of the Kanawana population.'

DOES NOT REOPEN THE COEDUCATION DATE. The 1974 Gazette's 'sister campers invaded four years ago' would put coeducation at about 1970, but the date is settled at 1968 on three independent traces: the camp's own 1988 report ('1968 Kamp Kanawana admits female campers for the first time. 66 girls registered'), the annual-report camper-weeks tables where bracketed girl-camper figures first appear in the 1968 column, and the 1970 season report calling that summer the camp's 'third year as a coeducational camp'. A newspaper feature's round 'four years ago' is loose journalism against a hard enrolment figure. Recorded so the settled question is not reopened by a later pass.

The 1988 Kanawana Camping Task Force chronology records, for 1964: "The Y purchases 120 acres of land south of Lac Wilson which connects Kamp Kanawana to Camp Tamaracouta. A portion of this is sold to the Boy Scouts of Canada." The same chronology records a second 1964 purchase: "The Y purchases the Page's property. This land is the entrance to Kanawana and contains the Farm house and the Block house." This is the first documented statement that Kanawana's property was made physically contiguous with Camp Tamaracouta, and that part of the acquired land passed to the Boy Scouts rather than remaining with the Y.

The 1988 Task Force report gives the only itemised property breakdown in the record, attributed to "a report submitted to the Y from Royal/Lepage in 1989": Land 455 acres; Lac Kanawana 60 acres; Lac Wilson 17 acres; Lac Rond 5 acres; TOTAL 537 acres. The report states in the same paragraph: "There was no record found that showed the Kanawana site has ever been surveyed." The report adds that the property "completely encompasses three lakes: Kanawana, Wilson, and Rond, and touches the tip of Lac Spring," and that the 455 acres are "mostly hilly, rolling terrain" with facilities on "a thin strip of land north of Lac Kanawana."

The figure "Between 1,000-1,500 acres" in the 1988 Task Force report is NOT a statement of Kanawana's size. It appears under a "SITE / Size:" heading in a specification for a hypothetical REPLACEMENT property, written in support of the Task Force's recommendations that the Board consider "A) The sale of the Kanawana site; B) The purchase of a new site." The adjacent criteria are prospective, not descriptive -- "Undeveloped, wooded area that contains 2-3 lakes"; "Adjacent to a national or provincial park"; "Preferably near downhill ski area"; "Facilities be developed on northern shore" -- and the report's costing section budgets "Land Cost 1,000 acres @ $1,000" for the purchase. Neither the sale nor the new site took place. This passage is a documented trap: read out of context it would appear to corroborate the 1974 Gazette's 1,200-acre figure, and it does not.

Six independently cached documents spanning 1964-1970 state Kanawana's size as roughly 1,000 acres, establishing that the large figure was the camp's own settled self-description for at least that period rather than a one-off error: the 1964 Kamp Kanawana annual report ("over approximately 1,000 acres"); the SGW YMCA annual report 1964 ("1,000 acres"); a YMCA news release of 13 May 1969 ("it covers more than 1,000 acres"); the 1969 Kamp Kanawana annual report ("We occupy 1000 acres of valuable land"); and the 1970 Kamp Kanawana annual report ("a small area of our 1,000 acres"). The series begins in the same year as the 120-acre purchase that connected the property to Camp Tamaracouta.

Camp Kanawana cancelled its residential season for a second consecutive summer in 2021, and the decision reached camp families in the last week of April 2021: 'This week, the family learned Kanawana is pulling the plug on camp for a second consecutive summer due to COVID-19.' The article is by Jessica Wong, CBC News, posted 29 April 2021 -- a month before the 28 May 2021 CBC report that Quebec sleepaway camps had been given a greenlight 'too late'.

IDENTIFICATION NOT ESTABLISHED (2026-08-25 RALPH loop, p_272): whether the Gaetane Verna named as a former Kanawana counsellor and section leader is the internationally known curator of the same name is SUPPORTED BY FOUR CONVERGING ATTRIBUTES but confirmed by no source. FOR: (1) the name is rare and matches exactly; (2) CBC says she grew up in Quebec, and the curator was raised in Montreal after her family moved to Canada from Kinshasa when she was two; (3) CBC says she was 'now based in Toronto' in April 2021, and the curator directed The Power Plant in Toronto from 2012 until her 2022 move to the Wexner Center; (4) the curator holds a bachelor's degree in management and international business from Concordia University, Montreal -- the institution descended from the Sir George Williams YMCA, the same institutional lineage that supplied Kanawana staff. UNRESOLVED AND UNREADABLE: a Toronto Life feature is reported by search engines to give her daughters' ages as six and ten, which if paired with the reported October 2015 publication date would NOT match CBC's April 2021 description (elder daughter plus a 15-year-old), but WOULD match it if the piece dates from her 2012 appointment.
