Campers built the rockets, a wooden bunker, a flag pole and a cleared recovery area; launch teams were drawn from those who helped. Cost: under $100 for four camp periods. His rationale is the one that recurs through this decade: "rocketry... is a program which cannot easily be duplicated in the city."

Ann Prewitt's first-hand account of Greek children's camping in 1969, guided by George Stathos, Head of the Foreign Press Division of the Prime Minister's Office: out of 8 million people, about 400,000 children go to camp each summer for three weeks or longer -- "probably the highest percentage of any country." Employers run camps for employees' children (the National Bank runs a free mountain camp funded by an automatic payroll deduction), as do lawyers, accountants and Athens shop owners; plus private, Scout and YM/YWCA camps; the Municipality of Athens; and, largest of all, camps run by the Departments of Education and Social Welfare, to which classroom teachers select campers, "favoring those who particularly need camp from the health point of view." St. Andrew's Camp on the plain of Marathon takes 3,000 children at a time, in sections of forty, each with one professional teacher and four high-school assistants, all unpaid volunteers. The detail that stops the reader, recorded exactly as written and dated to the Greek military dictatorship: "Like most Greek camps, Kinderland is completely fenced with high cyclone wire fencing, topped with barbed wire. There are guards all night and all day. On the drive down to Sounion with Mr. Stathos we looked into camp after camp, all securely fenced." Prewitt reports it without comment; the government press officer was her host.

Laurence J. Taylor's "17 Ways To Block Communication," reprinted in December 1969 from the Hillsdale College Leadership Letter of December 1964, is the management theory the camping movement was importing. Among the seventeen: misreading one's own authority ("His people will give him what he seems to want by screening their words and actions to match his expectations. Good news and happy thoughts will be given to him at once. Bad news and conflicts will be withheld"); failing to keep people informed ("strip a man of information that he needs for successful operation and you have robbed him of his dignity"); suppressing feeling ("a person has not communicated unless he has stirred the emotions"); disciplining in front of others ("Cause a man to lose face before others and you may lose him... A man is much more concerned for the opinions and feelings of his peers than he is of his superiors"); reacting badly to mistakes ("The leader who concentrates on 'Who did this?' as against 'What caused this and how do we avoid it?' will find a blank wall against him"); and tone of voice ("Your tone of voice gives you away, no matter what you say"). It belongs with the Moon interview methodology and the CIT evaluation practice as the professional framework under which camp staff were being observed and assessed.

Carolyn Ann Bennett's "C.I.T. Speaking," an essay written in November 1967 after leadership training at the Ontario Camp Leadership Centre at Bark Lake and printed two years later, is rare in this run for being a trainee's own voice. She quotes the Camp Counsellor's Manual foreword -- that the cabin counsellor is "the focal point of success or failure in morale, camp spirit, harmony, co-operation, true education, and character growth" -- and calls it "frightening to the first-year counsellor." Her observations: that "often the skill experts are not the best teachers," since "an instructor who herself has had difficulty mastering a skill will be more alert to the problems experienced by the learners" ("Some of the best diving coaches in the world cannot themselves perform the dives they teach"); that counselling is "a twenty-four hour a day job" including being "prepared to awaken at three or four in the morning to talk intelligently to a homesick or frightened camper"; the working rule "If in doubt -- don't"; and that the quality campers actually remember is "emotional maturity" -- "As a camper one could never find a name for it, but it was just that she knew how to handle every situation; make the fairest decision; was patient and always had a sense of humor." Note the term: "emotional maturity" is the first heading on Peter Moon's interview-assessment checklist, here reported from the other side of the desk by someone being assessed by it.

A roll of provincial presidents from the CCA annual dinner of February 1970, from the cover montage: CCA David Hartry, with secretary Barry Bryant and treasurer Robert Gregory; Manitoba Arnie Cohen and president David Loewen; Nova Scotia Mrs. Campbell and Tom Creighton; Saskatchewan president Eileen Mayotte -- the QCA secretary of the 1940s, her prairie presidency now dated; Newfoundland president Eric Russell; Ontario president Ivan Robinson with Ron Johnstone; British Columbia president Grant McKeen; and "LA BELLE PROVINCE'S PRES. L. PERRAS with BOB LAZANIK and CY BEKOFF." So Quebec is represented at the 1970 national dinner by Father Lionel Perras as president, with Lazanik and Cy Bekoff, the merged association's public face one year after affiliation. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the next issue prints "Sorry the names were mixed on the cover of the last issue!" and reprints three captions, so the names and offices are the magazine's own and are real, but which name went with which face -- and so some of the name-to-province pairings -- cannot be confirmed from this reading. Mary Edgar "delights with her poetry" at the same dinner.

Charles F. Plewman's tribute to Ethel Statten, March 1970, on her death: "the surviving partner of one of the most remarkable teams in Canadian Camping." Its substance: "it was Taylor who decided to launch a camp for girls, a girls' camp that would be different in that it would mesh activities with the boys at Ahmek, but it was left to Tonakela to make a dream come true"; "If Taylor Statten by nature and temperament was destined to work in the limelight, Tonakela, by the same token, was ordained to labour behind the scenes"; and "Certainly no married couple throughout the first fifty-five years of organized camping in Canada contributed as much" -- which incidentally dates organized camping in Canada from about 1915 by Plewman's reckoning, a later start than Ebbs's "more than 70 years" and than Kanawana's own 1894. Both are estimates by different men, not conflicting evidence. The tribute also confirms from a third source that Ethel Statten's camp name was Tonakela, used throughout as her name.

An inference recorded as inference, not asserted anywhere in the sources: Wallace Forgie's Camp Tonakela near Madras, opened officially by Mr. and Mrs. Taylor Statten, may have been named after Ethel Statten's camp name Tonakela, with the reported Ojibway and South Indian double meaning "you first" as the justification. Forgie was Adele Statten Ebbs's uncle and so connected to the Statten family. No source makes the connection, and it does not affect the open Tonakela founding-date question of 1935, 1937 or January 1938, which stands with none of the three superseded.

Three medical notes by Dr. J. H. Ebbs, March 1970. On lightning and electrocution: an average of 11 deaths a year from lightning and 82 from electrocution in recent years, with the operational advice that during severe electrical storms individuals should not be "on open bodies of water in metal canoes, on heights of land, or in open spaces" -- a dated safety standard for canoe tripping. On campers' injuries, from a children's camp health department: July has more injuries than August in some summers -- fewer abrasions, blisters, sunburn, concussions, cuts, foreign bodies, insect bites, sprains and stubbed toes as the season goes on, suggesting campers become "more seasoned"; and the younger age group suffers three times as many minor injuries as older campers and staff, and nearly twice as many infections. And on teaching nonswimmers, reporting Cressy A. McCatty of the School of Physical and Health Education, University of Toronto, in Research Quarterly: no evidence that a flotation device accelerates learning, but "a statistically significant difference between the scores of pupils taught by two different instructors" -- "it did not matter if a flotation was used or not, the significant thing was the quality of the instruction."

David Loewen, Director of Camp Arnes, Manitoba, gives the practical manual for year-round conversion in March 1970, in the camp's third year of winter operation: "The demand for rental facilities is so great... we have opened a second site for winter use." Who rents: "predominately high school and university students, church youth groups, clubs of various natures, private and public schools, and adult conference groups," but "the initial selling job must be done by you." The camp also runs its own winter retreats, because "our summer campers... like nothing better than to see and enjoy 'their camp' in its winter splendor," and staff "look forward to a week-end back at their camp in winter." Programme: toboggan, tube and ski slopes, but ski tows are not worth the cost -- bus to an existing tow; invest in snowshoes, "quickly learned and opens up otherwise impassable hiking areas"; ice fishing, skating, broom ball ("Visit the curling rinks for their discarded brooms -- they're ideal for broomball, and free"), snow sculpturing, survival stalking, and cooking over an open fire in the snow. And a firm rule: groups that expect no planned programme "we do not permit to rent our camp," because "where there is no program there usually is a high degree of misuse of camp facilities as well as more opportunity for accidents."

Loewen's winterization detail, March 1970 -- the answer to what winterizing a camp actually involved: "Any well-built cabin is probably worth winterizing." Propane heat over electric because it gives instant warmth, or cheap oil space heaters "very quickly installed into a building." Cabins work as well as dorms. And the water decision, which is the crux: Camp Arnes runs no running water in winter -- "the campers like it that way" -- because "if you have running water, you will have to heat your building all winter, or drain the pipes each week-end. One is costly, the other time consuming." They have a year-round artesian well but "campers are quite ready to melt snow." One large building with a good fireplace, washrooms and food service is essential; the walk-in cooler is run in reverse in winter with a small thermostatically controlled electric heater inside, "and that solves all our food storage problems"; summer washrooms are used with stalls blocked off in BP board, small electric space heaters, and flushing by dipper of water from a bucket. On charging: renting groups carry all the water, sweep and tidy, wash dishes, set tables, serve at meals and provide their own nurse, so the camp employs only a custodian and a cook and passes the saving on; a minimum fee to open camp covers fixed costs, and food costs are then divided per head, "the larger the group, the lower the rate per person." A complete off-season rental business model, from 1970.

The keynote address at the Camp Counsellors' Conference, York University, 10 May 1969, was given by two twelve-year-old campers, Ian Fleming and Neil MacLean -- the rarest voice in this run. Neil on what he likes: a counsellor who participates ("in this way the cabin will always do things together and become a good group"); one with humour -- "That doesn't mean that he should be as funny as Bill Cosby, but he should be able to appreciate the humour of the campers"; "A really serious counsellor TAKES THE FUN OUT OF CAMPING"; one "strict but manages to control the cabin, without us knowing it"; the one who appointed a "DIRECTOR OF FLOORS" and "A SUPERINTENDENT" so that "cleaning the cabin was always fun and we didn't mind doing a rotten job... besides we usually won the 'CLEANEST CABIN' award"; and one active beyond his own cabin -- "HE makes the cabin proud that HE is THEIR leader." Ian on what he dislikes: the counsellor who doesn't associate with the cabin; the one who "used to sit down every time we had a race, and watch us run all over the place... and NEVER help us at all"; the too-strict one, because "everything has to be done HIS WAY and sometimes the campers, who have some pretty good ideas, can't say anything"; and the lazy one -- "If he sleeps in, so will his campers." His closing: "This has been pretty hard to talk about because MOST of my counsellors have been good, and, if you have a good counsellor you will do anything for him."

A dated, named camp hoax with its mechanics, described by a twelve-year-old camper to a counsellors' conference in May 1969: the PACKASORUS, "a mysterious [creature] wandering around... identified by the pack on his back and by the fact that he ate paper," tracked by paper trails all over camp until "we finally caught him. It was our Director sitting in a tree with a pack on his back... It was a great program, and besides... we got all the papers picked up around camp." The same speaker describes free-choice interest groups in the morning at three levels with crest work as the incentive ("The crest work was up to us... Most campers do it because it is a good challenge. It also made us better trippers because we learned axemanship and how to pitch camp really well"), all-camp cook-outs every two weeks, and campfires "always better if you can participate" rather than "just sit around and sing songs."

Two counsellors on homesickness, printed together in March 1970, one of them writing from experience of it. Donna Richardson, at Camp Ouareau in Quebec: homesickness peaks at mealtimes, "the gnawing realization that she is alone in the midst of a great many strangers"; stay with the child as long as needed "even if we are missing lunch"; stay cheerful, "not wishing to increase her unhappiness by looking depressed myself"; and touch -- "I am not afraid to put my arm around those quivering shoulders... It is comforting to a child to have the hair which may be clinging to her flushed face brushed away." Lela Shepley, seventeen, a first-year counsellor at Camp Northway, writes as a former sufferer: "I spent the first two and a half weeks of summer camp wishing to Heaven that I wasn't there... I'm thankful that I had the experience of being homesick. It gave me an insight to all of the frightened and miserable campers I have encountered." Her list of what not to say: not "You're too old to be homesick" -- "A person is never too old to be homesick. Whether you're five or fifty"; not "Give this place a chance," because "that automatically makes the camper hate it even more. No one likes to admit it's her own fault"; not "EVERYONE loves it here, why don't you?" because "that only makes the camper feel even more out of place and that she must be 'weird'"; and never "I'm too busy, I'll talk to you later" -- "What a confidence destroyer!"

Doreen Kronick, Director of the Integra Foundation in Toronto and sponsor of Camp Towhee, gives the earliest full statement in this run of integrating disabled children into a mainstream camp, reprinted March 1970 from the Journal of Health, Physical Education, Recreation of May 1969. Her argument: many such children "have spent their lives being sheltered and overprotected at home, attend 'special' classes and therapy groups with other 'special' children. They experience their first real opportunity to learn to live with their normal peers at camp"; and for the other campers, "just as sleeping beside a youngster of different race or nationality can help a child appreciate his sameness and humanity, so can a special child teach an invaluable lesson." Her procedure: request a detailed report from the sending agency; furnish a report back at the close of summer "so that they can maintain a twelve-month picture of the child's progress"; an extended family interview covering medical services, physical facilities, meals, demands made of campers, staff qualifications and programme, plus "a detailed description of the trip to camp, from the time he leaves home until he is settled into his cabin"; and an eight-point intake list including how the child feels about the handicap. The period's vocabulary is recorded as written and read as of 1969-70.

Kronick's operational findings on integrating disabled campers, March 1970: facilities meeting ACA standards for non-disabled children are sufficient "provided leniency and extra time to move from place to place are allowed"; suitability depends "not... upon program orientation as upon maturity of staff and flexibility of programing"; a group-centred camp suits integration because of close supervision and minimised competition; always provide an alternative activity when the disabled child cannot join in, so cabinmates are not held back and do not resent it; and give the counsellor only "the specifics wherein his handling of the camper will differ," not "technical terminology or extensive material on the etiology." Her warning is the structural one: because so few directors will take such campers, the willing ones "become overwhelmed with applications... Their camps threaten to adopt the characteristics of a 'special' setting which negates the original purposes."

Joyce Bertram's "Now at My Camp," March 1970, records an experiment that failed. Camp Ouareau spent years letting campers choose every period of every day, and abandoned it -- "when a different child showed up for the activity each day of the week the staff had no feeling of accomplishment, no feeling of continuity and no reason to make out a lesson plan," and the campers "often went home with a lopsided basket and a half-ass copper bracelet when what they really wanted was their Senior Red Cross and their Skipper." Her conclusion: "THEY LIKE RULES AND REGULATIONS AND LIMITS. Partly because they like to be able to fight against them: there is no fun in fighting a cream puff. But partly it is because they want to feel that someone is interested enough in them to INSIST that they make the most of their God-given talents... We offer a lot of choice but that choice is between a number of things. It is never between something and nothing. Give a kid a chance and he'll choose nothing every time!" Her fear at the outset: a child saying "'Oh nah, it's just like school'... some camp programs made up ALREADY, and some Program Directors know NOW just what Bunks 4, 5 and 6 will be doing on Wednesday, July 15th."

Camp Ouareau's structure as Joyce Bertram describes it in March 1970: two chosen concentration activities plus an instruction swim in the mornings, changed weekly; free-choice afternoons adding diving, synchronized swimming, dramatics, photography, modern dance, music, poetry and nature lore; section programmes two or three evenings; two all-camp nights; Monday Cabin Nite, Saturday dramatics, and Sunday "a special quiet time with music and poetry and story telling around the fire in the Lodge." On self-reliance her arrangement is distinctive: campers live four to a tent or cabin, with their counsellor living nearby among her own contemporaries -- "close enough for supervision and safety but not close enough to mediate every quarrel or referee every fight." And her Sunday chapel story, which became a camp saying in a single season: her father's rabbit that climbed a tree to escape the dogs -- "But Daddy, rabbits don't climb trees." "THIS rabbit had to!" -- adopted at Ouareau "for every youngster faced with something difficult -- whether it was a Red Cross test, a first night on the stage or sitting at a new table in the dining room."

Colin Hatcher, Director of Camp Keewaydhin for the YMCA of Edmonton, describes a YMCA camp's scheduling mechanism in March 1970. Four "givens": scheduled meals unless a group eats out or is on an out-trip; a morning camp and cabin clean-up; an afternoon rest hour; and sleep quotas of 9 to 10 hours for juniors and at least 8 hours for seniors aged 11 to 13. The mechanism is the "sloosh" board: after supper a section director clears the chips, and each counsellor bids for his group's time by placing chips on the board against activity and period. The activities listed on the reproduced board are archery, axemanship, boating, canoeing, crafts, nature lore, orienteering, riflery and swim instruction, over two one-hour periods each morning, three each afternoon and one early evening; counsellors accompany their campers and act as resource person, and groups collect and return their own equipment. "Bidding... is tight when all groups are in camp. However, as groups leave for out-trips, it is not unusual to have one of the remaining groups take two consecutive periods." The closest thing in this run to a YMCA camp's own scheduling system set out in full.

Jaye Hickey's riding safety standard, March 1970: "It is unrealistic to hope that two weeks, even a month, can produce polished equestrians. Therefore, camp riding should aim for the more functional and desirable end -- that of basic safety." Teach the horse's psychology, not just rules. On fear: "a frightened child is instantly relieved, forgives, and at times feels a great sympathy for a horse who has just tossed him when he is told that the animal shied because he was frightened." Practice: schooling helmets with chin straps worn at all times, even unmounted, against bumped heads in the stall; quick-release knots; cross-tie in aisle or box stall for grooming; inspect all tack before horses leave the barn if campers tacked up; check every saddle before the season for pinched withers, overdue restuffing and decayed stitching; a restricted, well-stocked medicine cabinet, since "a carelessly applied bandage can cause permanent damage to a tendon"; a NO SMOKING sign in the stable area; and a red ribbon braided into a kicker's tail as a visual warning. In the ring: one horse length between riders at a walk, and never "Everyone canter" -- riders go one at a time from the back of the ride, which "negates the possibility of 'races', fighting, bucking."

Canadian Camping went bilingual in April 1970. The cover reads "APRIL 1970 AVRIL," the masthead is set in both languages throughout, Pierre Trudeau's editorial runs in both, Elsie Palter's article is printed twice in English and in a French translation by Janina Klee, and Lionel Perras contributes a full-length article in French only. This is the visible consequence of the 1969 merger, thirteen months later, and it is a fact about the source itself: from April 1970 this run carries French-language content that an English-only search would never surface. The provincial offices now list both bodies separately: Quebec Camping Association at 2233 Belgrave Ave., Montreal 261, and L'Association des camps de Quebec at 952 Cherrier Ave., Montreal.

Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau wrote the editorial for Canadian Camping in April 1970, in both languages and from Ottawa. English: "Canoeing down a fast moving stream, the smell of a smoking campfire, the fresh air of early morning in the woods. These are some of the happy and nourishing experiences that many of us have shared. Nature provides us with an opportunity for enjoyment, solitude and self-renewal. How fortunate we are to live in a country so abundantly blessed with unspoiled streams, forests and mountains!" The French is not a translation but a separate composition: "Un canot qui bondit au milieu des rapides, l'odeur inoubliable d'un feu de bois et la griserie d'un reveil matinal au creux d'une clairiere: ce sont la des moments privilegies que plusieurs d'entre nous ont vecus."

Lionel Perras's "L'Accreditation Des Camps, Tremplin Vers l'Excellence," April 1970, is the fullest statement anywhere in this run of what camp accreditation in Quebec required, written by the president of the ACQ -- the apparatus Kanawana was inspected under, set out by the man who ran it. His definition: "LA RECONNAISSANCE OFFICIELLE, par un organisme competent et reconnu, du serieux des objectifs que s'est fixes une institution et de la valeur des moyens qu'elle utilise pour atteindre ces objectifs." On chronology and provenance: accreditation "fut l'une des premieres preoccupations des fondateurs de l'ACQ en 1958... il suffit de relire les proces-verbaux des assemblees" -- a direct pointer to surviving ACQ minutes. And the key sentence: "L'Association fournit aux camps avec le texte des normes actuelles dernierement traduites de la QCA" -- the ACQ's current standards are a recent translation of the Quebec Camping Association's. If the English QCA standards Kanawana was measured against are lost, the French ACQ text is a translation of them and recovers their content. He also refers to "des camps visites au cours de l'ete 1966" -- a 1966 visiting round, one year after the McFarlane round of 1965.

Perras's eleven characteristics assessed in Quebec camp accreditation, April 1970 -- effectively the inspection checklist: staff whose training meets qualification and age norms and who are numerous enough to form a stable team; an efficient and creative administration where the director holds full responsibility for the camp's general running; a programme with long-term forecasting aimed at the camp's maturity; premises whose plans and equipment serve the education being given; a sense of the camp's own identity and prestige, hard to achieve "si on n'oeuvre pas dans des locaux fonctionnels, appropries et convenables"; a programme respecting physiological and psychological norms in theory and practice; conditions of employment ensuring recruitment and staff stability, which "supposent des salaires et retributions conformes aux usages des camps"; statutes approved by the camp's board defining the organigramme and each person's functions and responsibilities, codifying terms and conditions of employment; an admissions policy and a policy of relations with parents; financial administration norms letting other administrators stay informed and exercise control; and administrators who understand and accept their responsibilities and are "les interpretes les plus enthousiastes et les mieux informes" to the public. Once accredited, the ACQ Standards Committee follows the camp closely and "tous les 2 ou 3 ans environ, un controle des resultats et une reevaluation de ses progres sera reprise."

Perras's two stages of accreditation, both self-directed: defining the camp's objectives, and a self-critique. On the first his advice is a research method in itself: study the camp's charte civile if incorporated -- "c'est le document qui renseigne le mieux sur les buts que se proposaient les fondateurs du camp" -- and if not incorporated, find the documents or the people who know why the camp was founded; the inventory "racontera qu'il y a eu des amendements qui ont oriente le camp et l'ont fait evoluer autrement." The self-critique has six headings, each a template for what a camp's own accreditation file would contain: administration (is the structure fit to make the camp progress? is it outdated? is the line of authority respected in the organigramme? "Y a-t-il un Coutumier du camp?" -- a book of the camp's own customs, a striking thing to find as an accreditation requirement); programme; resources; la vie des campeurs (do the young accept the activities willingly? what climate reigns among the campers? are counsellors involved in campers' lives? "La vie spirituelle du camp est-elle integree dans l'oeuvre ou fait-elle partie d'activites qui s'ajoutent sans lien avec le reste?"); finances; and hygiene, health and safety. His refrain, repeated three times: "Ce sont les camps qui feront leur propre accreditation, le visiteur va seulement la constater officiellement." He closes by noting the standards are wanted by all "depuis que les camps de langue francaise sur le modele de ceux de langue anglaise ont decide de se grouper en association."

Kirk Wipper's "Spacemen Are We!", from a paper to the Society of Camp Directors dated by its opening to just after the Apollo XIII splashdown of April 1970, sets outer space against "middle space" (the natural environment) and "inner space" ("that which lies within each of us"), arguing that outer space gets the attention because "this planet's wilderness has been explored and charted... even the undersea regions have been investigated," while "the middle and inner spaces are the immediate and real concerns." He reports that the Conservation Council of Ontario, "in which our O.C.A. participates," counted 500 to 600 chemical poisons in use in the United States, with "roughly 70 million pounds of those poisons used each year" in Canada, against "so little experience or information regarding the long-range effects" -- "The recent recall of D.D.T. is an example of a major admitted error." He names contemporary controversies: "We blunder along over Spadina Expressway issues, waste disposal, highways, mines and quarries, energy plants, subdivisions, huge public campsites in parks and industrial developments."

Kirk Wipper's passage on Indigenous land relations, April 1970, recorded as written and as a non-Indigenous camping leader's framing of its date: "The Indian for centuries tended to approach his natural surroundings as a friend... never really depleting his living environment... Maka-ina, mother earth, and the four winds received his salutes around the council campfires." Against this he sets "the white man [who] looked upon the wilderness as an enemy to be subdued... Hacking, gouging, blasting, burning, scraping, digging, burying, flooding, cutting, draining, stripping, hunting and trapping." The same council-ring vocabulary this project has traced through camp ceremonial, here doing argumentative work in an environmental essay. It should be recorded and dated, not adopted.

A named research citation for camping's effects, from Kirk Wipper in April 1970: Jerome Beker of Teachers' College, Columbia University, "The Influence of School Camping on the Self-Concepts and Social Relationships of Sixth Grade School Children," finding that five days of camping "can have a marked positive impact on children's self-concepts and to a slightly lesser degree on their social relationships," though "the precise nature and depth of this influence and its specific determinants... remain obscure." A findable study, and the kind of evidence Ebbs's new Society of Professional Camp Directors was calling for.

William J. Babcock of Camp Richildaca gives a camp's complete twelve-year record of school use in April 1970 -- the best single answer in this run to what "year-round use" meant in practice. The programmes run at one camp: canoe trips; canoe-skills training; water safety; a resident art camp; biology and natural science; work-study with four-year technical students; a geography regional study; leadership training with vocational students; "La Maison Francaise," a resident French language camp; junior high camping and geography; senior elementary interdisciplinary days; grades 2 to 5 day experiences; and preschool half-days. Two schools trained students in swimming, canoeing, campcraft and water safety at the camp and used the test results as a selection criterion for who went on canoe trips; Richmond Hill High School has an "Outfitters Club" providing information, maps and routes, and has sent out trips since 1958. In the work-study programme, technical students from Cedarbrae Collegiate and Thornlea Secondary built eight tent floors, a bridge, a sauna bath, forestry work and fence building -- school labour as camp capital works. La Maison Francaise took forty students for a week, all agreeing to speak only French.

Babcock's full winter outdoor-education day programme, April 1970 -- twelve activities of which eight must be completed: melting snow to find the snow-to-water ratio; measuring snow depth to compute precipitation; temperature readings at different depths of the pond; bud formations; impressions of bark taken in cobbler's wax for later identification; winter damage to trees including rodent damage; animal tracks; construction of a shelter for two; winter first-aid problem solving; language arts descriptions in French and English plus lab reports; orienteering on snowshoes or skis; and cooking their own lunch over an outdoor fire. Snowshoes provided. Woodland Senior Elementary ran eight such days in January and February. His advice to camps wanting the business: contact local teachers of science, physical education, geography, art and languages, invite them to the camp, and write to the Director of Education; and note that the Ontario Teachers' Federation "will soon publish a Handbook on Outdoor Education in which will be listed camps which have shown an interest."

Elsie Palter's "When Stealing Occurs at Camp," printed in both languages in April 1970, gives a taxonomy of causes: lack of a sense of property rights (uncommon); the desire to please rather than to possess -- "very often the child steals things he does not need and gives them away to ingratiate himself with his fellow campers... When money is stolen, this, too, is often used to 'buy' acceptance"; vengeful feelings against authority, "in order to annoy the parent or counselor"; and, commonest in the school-age child, "a need to overcome a sense of inferiority or a feeling of being different from the group due to perhaps a physical handicap, shabby clothes, overweight, and even being too well dressed," expressed as bribery or "splurge stealing." Her observation about camp as an environment: "At camp, there is very little privacy and all behaviour is exposed, so that stealing is quickly detected and usually the culprit is readily identified." Her recommended procedure is a documented 1970 camp disciplinary method and an uncomfortable one: call a meeting of the small group; have the children say in turn what they expect of each other regarding personal property, with no accusations, reaching a consensus; then "Each child could be asked to write the name of the person whom they believe has been guilty of stealing and this information must be treated confidentially," after which the child is helped privately. Her aside on class is of its time and should be dated, not repeated: "in slum areas of large cities, stealing by children is quite acceptable and condoned, but getting caught is the offence."

Mary Leggatt's "Laurence Taylor in Practice," April 1970, is the Hillsdale small-group method actually implemented at a camp, and the most concrete pre-camp training record in this run: an eight-day pre-camp for counsellors plus two extra days for department and section heads. Her preparation as leader: find the warmest spot with a suitable table and chairs, paper and pencils for everybody, an ash tray, brown paper pinned to the wall for writing major decisions "since we have no easel or chalk board," arrive early to greet each person, coffee available -- "The right atmosphere is so important." Ground rules: introduce yourself by name "and our camp names if we had them" plus what you did during the year, one minute each with an appointed timekeeper; then three minutes' thinking on the question; a volunteer speaks first and the group follows clockwise; one minute each; and you may speak to the question, comment on a previous answer, pass and take your time later, or "ask for silence for her time so that everyone could do some more thinking." Her honest finding: "Actually the program was not very different from what we might have planned... The big difference compared to former was the much greater participation, and enthusiasm." Also: "We used a tape recorder which I felt inhibited some of the staff," and the warning, "Like all techniques it must not be over-worked."

Mandatory national camp standards arrive in 1970. The April 1970 provincial column reports Ron Johnstone, National Chairman of Standards, with co-chairman Al Goodman, implementing "a new set of Mandatory Standards -- Over 20 items are mandatory for a Camp to be an accredited member." The same column records the Ontario Counsellors' Conference at York University on 9 May drawing 1,200 delegates; Stanley Burke, "the ex-voice of the National News," and Pollution Probe at the OCA annual meeting of 29 April, introducing "an exciting programme which will bring Ontario Camps into the fight against pollution"; and the Society of Camp Directors meeting in April with papers by Don Groff on Intercultural Camping and Bruno Morawetz on Drugs.
The June 1970 issue of Canadian Camping carries the association's French name, "L'Association des camps du Canada," beside the English name on the cover masthead.

The provincial officers list in Canadian Camping, June 1970, names the Quebec Camping Association's president as Cy Bekoff (2233 Belgrave Avenue) and L'Association des camps de Quebec's president as Lionel Perras (952 Cherrier Avenue) — two separate presidents at two separate addresses as of June 1970.

The provincial presidents listed in Canadian Camping, June 1970, are: British Columbia Grant McKeen; Alberta Colin Hatcher, with J. E. Hanlin for the Northern Alberta Branch; Saskatchewan Eileen Mayotte; Manitoba David Loewen; Ontario Ivan Robinson; Nova Scotia Tom Creighton; Newfoundland and Labrador Elizabeth Mouland.
Bob Lazanik is listed as 3rd Vice-President of the Canadian Camping Association in June 1970, c/o 2233 Belgrave Avenue, Montreal — the Quebec Camping Association English section's address.

An editorial note in Canadian Camping, June 1970, describes Charles Plewman as "former Owner and Director of Kilcoo Camp, and former President of O.C.A.," appointed an Honorary Member at the Society of Camp Directors' Founders' Meeting.

Charles Plewman, addressing the Society of Camp Directors' Fall Dinner Meeting at Hart House, University of Toronto, on 26 November 1969, dated his own start in camping: "I think it was in 1909 I took my first group camping."

In his 26 November 1969 address to the Society of Camp Directors, Charles Plewman warned the new profession against credentialism: "What we do not need is a lot of efficient technocrats... no amount of knowledge and no amount of skill is going to suffice if a man lacks a sympathetic understanding of youth on one hand, or hasn't got his heart in the right place on the other."

Charles Plewman, in his November 1969 address, recounted his fifteen-year-old granddaughter telling him "Grandad, 50% of the kids in Grades 9 and 10 in our school use drugs," and added his own qualification: "Now let's say that's an exaggeration, but it's significant that the kids think that."

Jack Pearse, Director of Camp Tawingo, published "Song Leading" in Canadian Camping, June 1970, setting out a five-category taxonomy of camp songs: novelty numbers, action songs, rounds, spirituals and folk songs, and quiet songs.

Jack Pearse's June 1970 "Song Leading" article lists the novelty numbers of the period repertoire as: One Flea Fly; Hole in the Bottom of the Sea; Tipperary; Pack up Your Troubles; Long, Long Trail; She'll Be Coming Round the Mountain; Bingo; My Bonnie; Beans in my Ears; Old MacDonald.

Jack Pearse's June 1970 "Song Leading" article lists the action songs of the period repertoire as: My Hat it Has Three Corners; The Old Mill Stream; Deep and Wide; Under the Spreading Chestnut Tree; Heads and Shoulders, Knees and Toes; This Old Man; Little Cabin in the Wood; One Finger, One Thumb, Keep Moving; Grand Old Duke of York.

Jack Pearse's June 1970 "Song Leading" article classifies camp rounds as rousers (Little Tommy Tinker, Row Row Row Your Boat), fun (Kookaburra, Three Blind Mice), and quiet (Fire's Burning, Oh How Lovely is the Evening, Rosen Fra Fjun, Hey Ho).

Jack Pearse's June 1970 "Song Leading" article names Alouette among the folk songs in the standard Canadian camp repertoire, alongside Blue Tail Fly, Green Grow the Rushes Ho, Matilda, If I Had a Hammer, Workin' On the Railroad, Loch Lomond, On Top of Old Smokey, Home on the Range and When I'm on My Journey.

Jack Pearse credits the camp folk-song revival of the period to "the Weavers, Pete Seeger, Woody Guthrie, Harry Belafonte, Bob Dylan, Joan Baez... as well as Canada's Oscar Brand, the Journeymen, Ottawa's Couriers," and names We Shall Overcome, This Land is Your Land, Where Have All the Flowers Gone and Deep Blue Sea as songs that entered camp singing through it.

Jack Pearse's June 1970 rule for the shape of a camp sing-song is stated in capitals: "ALL SING SONGS SHOULD END WITH QUIET SINGING," and he notes the change from an earlier era "when the louder and more boisterous was the singing, the more successful was the sing song."

Jack Pearse advises camp song leaders to "be original" — "It's fun, too, to make up songs, particularly for the group you are leading" — establishing that composing songs for one's own camp group was standard advised practice in Canadian camping in 1970.

Kirk A. W. Wipper wrote in Canadian Camping, June 1970, that the search for historic original watercraft had been under way "for more than twenty years" — dating the origin of the collection that became the Canadian Canoe Museum to about 1950.

Kirk Wipper reported in June 1970 that "a building of pine logs two storeys high and sixty-six feet square is being constructed to house the collection" at Camp Kandalore, twenty-two miles north of Minden, Ontario, with visitors welcome.

Kirk Wipper's June 1970 account of his watercraft collection includes "the canoe of a chief from near Ft. Coulonge, Quebec" (photograph caption), a Labrador freighter canoe built from one immense piece of birch bark, a butternut kayak by the Lakefield Canoe Company predating 1900, and a racing shell over 100 years old and still usable.

Kirk Wipper's June 1970 article states that "In 1844, four grey nuns undertook to travel in canoes from Montreal to the Red River Settlement," and names Simon Fraser's descent of 28 May to 1 July 1808 among the canoe journeys of Canadian history.

Jocelyn Palm, Executive Secretary of the Royal Life Saving Society Ontario, published "Waterfront Activities — What Can Be Accomplished At Camps With 8-12 Day Periods" in Canadian Camping, June 1970, holding that one organised swimming lesson a day is sufficient and that camps should teach to national standards even where the award cannot be completed within the period.

Jocelyn Palm's June 1970 waterfront article states that non-swimmers should not be permitted in canoes at all, and in rowboats only while wearing lifejackets, and names the awards achievable in an 8-12 day camp period as the Beginner Red Cross and the Elementary and Junior Resuscitation Awards of the Royal Life Saving Society.

Jocelyn Palm's June 1970 canoeing teaching progression runs: introduction, bow strokes, launching/docking/beaching, capsize procedure, stern strokes, landing, a specified course, solo, jump out and in, canoe-over-canoe rescue, portaging, artificial respiration by the Direct Method using the canoe as a buoyant aid, and gunwale bobbing and other stunts.

John Latimer of Camp Kilcoo published "Cabin Counselling: How to Stay on Your Toes From 'Wake-up' to 'Flake-out'" in Canadian Camping, June 1970, printed also in a French translation by Anne Thompson of Camp Ouareau under the title "Grand Frere? Grande Soeur? Maman? Moniteur!!"

John Latimer wrote in June 1970 that "Bed time, in my view, is just about the most important time of day in working with children," naming the topics campers raise then as "religion, space, history, drugs, sex," and directing counsellors to add "information and accurate knowledge... not necessarily his own prejudices and biases."

John Latimer's June 1970 counsellor guidance holds that "the punishment should fit the crime" — misbehave at table, leave the table; push someone off the dock, leave the swimming area — and that "a good Counsellor will not hesitate to consult with his unit head or Director... Asking for advice is not a sign of weakness."

John Latimer's June 1970 article names the experiences he believed campers remember for life: "Wake the group up at night to see the Northern Lights; if the Camp rules permit it take the group out in the lake on a starry night, lash the canoes together and drift; dress them properly to watch a good storm coming across the lake... or if it's warm enough and not dangerous let them get soaked in a good storm."

Joyce Bertram of Camp Ouareau described a bilingual experiment at a Quebec camp in "L'Amie de ma Tente," first published in Canadian Camping in December 1964 and reprinted in June 1970: a compiled camp vocabulary list of words absent from school grammars (ant, snake, spider, thunderstorm, sailboat, "summer complaint"), about thirty idiomatic expressions, French on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday and English on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and a rule of "pas de mains pour parler" — no hands while speaking.

Joyce Bertram's account of bilingual practice at Camp Ouareau notes campers "huddled in corners with English-French dictionaries, au contraire French-English ditto depending on whether elles demeurent a Outremont ou Westmount" — a Montreal class-and-language marker recorded as written in 1964.

Eanswythe Flynn's June 1970 account of the Duke of Edinburgh's Award Scheme states it was introduced to Canada in 1963, with two separate schemes for girls and boys, each of four sections at three levels (Bronze, Silver, Gold), non-competitive, all four sections required; the Canadian office was Commander George Manson, Suite 810, 135 James Street South, Hamilton.

The Duke of Edinburgh's Award girls' scheme as described in June 1970 included a "Design for Living" section with topics such as "Art of Make-up and Hairstyles," "Entertaining," "Food and Your Health" and "What to Wear and When To Wear It," while the boys' equivalent sections were The Expedition and Physical Fitness — the girls' scheme domestic where the boys' was physical. Recorded as the period's own design, not endorsed.

W. Bertram Danson wrote "Do's and Don'ts for Counsellors" in Canadian Camping, June 1970, from Camp Winnebagoe — identifying the Danson whom J. Harry Ebbs named among the founders of Canadian boys' camping as Camp Winnebagoe's director.

W. Bertram Danson's June 1970 "Do's and Don'ts for Counsellors" instructs: "Don't resort to physical punishment, or other off-beat methods that might have been used on you when you were a camper" — a prohibition of corporal punishment framed as breaking a generational chain.

W. Bertram Danson's June 1970 counsellor list also forbids profanity and slang ("never tell your campers to 'shut-up'!"), embarrassing a child in front of others, "docking" as a punishment, brow-beating, threatening, nagging, sarcasm and belittling, allowing campers to use a counsellor's last name only ("It is a mark of disrespect"), and taking food from the cabin tuck larder other than when shared by everyone.

The Newfoundland and Labrador Camping Association held its annual meeting and conference on 17-18 April 1970 with a keynote by CCA president David Hartry and Dr. Richard Warner, Director of the Centre for Environmental Biology at Memorial University, speaking on the theme Pollution; Elizabeth Mouland was elected president.

Canadian Camping, June 1970, carried an advertisement from the Rural Toilet Specialty Co. under the slogan "Well Equipped Camps Have Inside Toilets," offering septic tanks serving six or more toilets and gasoline pumps and pressurised tanks "for camps with no hydro facilities" — dating the point at which indoor plumbing was being sold to Canadian camps as a competitive feature.

Huguette Dagenais reported in Canadian Camping, November 1970: "Le programme d'accreditation de l'A.C.Q.C.A. s'est poursuivi durant tout l'ete '70. ENVIRON 75 CAMPS DANS LA SECTION ANGLAISE ET LA SECTION FRANCAISE ONT ETE VISITES PAR TROIS EQUIPES D'INSPECTEURS" — about 75 Quebec camps in both sections visited by three inspection teams in the summer of 1970.

Three documented Quebec camp inspection rounds are now on record from Canadian Camping: Murray McFarlane's visits to twenty-seven camps in summer 1965, Lionel Perras's account of a 1966 round, and about seventy-five camps visited by three teams in summer 1970 — each round producing a written report on each camp. Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp throughout this period, so a written accreditation report on it is likely to exist, though none has yet been located.

L'Association des camps du Quebec received a letter of intent for renewal of a $30,000 grant for its provincial secretariat in 1970, after representations to the Hon. Jean-Paul L'Allier, minister responsible for the Haut-Commissariat a la Jeunesse, aux Loisirs et aux Sports.

A commission d'etudes sur les vacances familiales a prix modique was formed in late August 1970 by the ACQ, the Confederation des Loisirs du Quebec, the Touring Club du Quebec, the Cooperative de vacances familiales, the Conseil des Oeuvres de Bienetre de Quebec and the Unions de familles, reporting on 6 November 1970.

The Quebec Camping Association (English Section) executive elected at the annual meeting of 2 June 1970 for 1970-72 was: Past President Cy Bekoff; President Peter Van Wagner; Vice-Presidents Mrs. Nicholas D. Demetelin and Zave Ettinger; Secretary Mrs. Kenneth R. Willis; Treasurer Mrs. D. Jacques Reeves.

Ron Johnstone, Director of Camp White Bear and Chairman of Standards for the Canadian Camping Association, introduced the Ontario Camping Association's Mandatory Standards, approved at the OCA's November 1969 board meeting after a standards programme "going on for over twenty-five years" — dating the OCA's standards work to about 1945.

Ron Johnstone framed the 1969 OCA Mandatory Standards as "MINIMUM standards for safe camping... no more than a minimum guarantee, to the camping public of our Province, that their children will be safe both physically and mentally," with "Desirable Camping Practices" remaining the basis of accreditation alongside them, and a third purpose in liability protection: "The liability we face is equated on what is the 'accepted common practice' within our profession."

The Ontario Camping Association's Mandatory Standards for resident camps, printed in full in Canadian Camping, November 1970, comprise 23 items including: a current Ontario Department of Health licence under Public Health Act O. Reg. 518-1960; a signed medical history form for every camper and staff person; toilets at one seat per 8-10 people; water supply tested before camp and re-tested weekly; a camp director aged 25 or older with at least two years' staff leadership experience; a minimum of one third of counsellor staff being new; facilities enabling staff privacy from campers off duty; emergency numbers posted by the telephone; safety inspections carried out personally by the director and re-checked within 24 hours; and a minimum of one staff member per five campers on trips away from camp, never fewer than two.

The OCA's 1969 Mandatory Standards require that the person in charge of an out-of-camp trip be at least 18, familiar with the territory and aware where help can be obtained, with an assistant at least 17; the day-camp equivalents are a trip leader of 18 and assistant of 16, one trained person per ten campers, and a director aged 21 or older with two seasons' experience.
The OCA's 1969 Mandatory Standards include a consumer-protection clause: "Does the Camp adequately provide all facilities and activities listed in its brochure and advertising material?"

David Palter, B.Sc., P.Eng., Camp Consultant, told the Society of Camp Directors on 26 November 1969 that "As early as 1952, the Board of O.C.A. adopted accreditation of children's camps in principle," that the first attempt at "Minimum Standards" failed because "there is no minimum when it comes to the physical property," and that a 1954 self-evaluation questionnaire brought only 44 responses.

David Palter quoted the Ontario Camping Association's own archives: a minuted meeting of the Legislative Committee at the Park Plaza Hotel, noon, Thursday 7 March 1957, present Lloyd Perry, Dr. J. Harry Ebbs, Irwin Haladner, W. E. Yard, Mrs. Ralph Raymer, W. B. Danson and Mrs. G. W. Flynn, recommending "that the Ontario Camping Association endorse and encourage the formation of an association of professional camp directors... to provide a government-recognized organization through which the public will be protected against the operation of children's camps by undesirable and untrained directors." It was approved in principle in 1957.

David Palter was appointed chairman of the Ontario Camping Association's Standards Committee on 29 April 1957 and charged with initiating accreditation; camp visiting began on a friendly, voluntary basis, with visitors chosen from directors having at least five years' administrative experience.

David Palter warned in November 1970, with camp visiting now mandatory in the OCA, other provincial associations and the American Camping Association: "there is a great danger that the visit could become an inspection. If it becomes a mechanical routine chore that a camp must submit to, in order to receive the blessing of the Association and in order to show the emblem to the public, all value of the program is lost." He recalled the practice it replaced: "I am sure you can recall the day when it was unheard of to go to see your competitor... Directors met at arms length — fully extended — at association meetings."

David Palter, camp consultant and OCA standards chairman, and David Paltiel, a Kanawana name appearing on the Knights of Kanawana roll, the 1975 board and the 1976 staff list, are different names appearing in different records. No evidence links them and they must not be merged.

The Ontario Camping Association's archives were presented to Trent University, Peterborough, on 22 October 1970, past president John Latimer handing them to Dr. T. H. B. Symons, president of the University, with about thirty OCA members attending.

Mary L. Northway records that the Ontario Camping Association archives deposited at Trent in October 1970 were assembled over six years by an archives committee under three successive chairs — Mrs. Adele Ebbs, Miss Margaret Govan and Dr. Mary Northway — with records collected, stored and catalogued at the OCA office by Mrs. Shirley Hall; the holdings comprise "early brochures, photographs, programmes and schedules, films, financial accounts, diaries, and taped interviews of prominent camp personalities," with a duplicate file kept at the camping office and the originals at Trent.

Mary Northway states the collecting policy behind the OCA archive: asked what to collect, the answer was "everything. Let the archivist decide what is not important," and material "should not be sorted by amateurs, but stored in its original packages and catalogued from these."
The authors of The Camp Counsellor's Book turned over the book's royalties to the Ontario Camping Association to fund its archive, and the manuscript of the book is itself part of the Trent archives.

Mary S. Edgar's "A Page of Poems" in Canadian Camping, November 1970, prints four texts: "A Director's Meditation," "Hymn for the Space-Age" (Tune: Forest Green), "Postpone the Verdict" and "Outdoor Beauty Clinic."

Mary S. Edgar's "Hymn for the Space-Age," printed in Canadian Camping in November 1970 to the tune Forest Green, is explicitly a conservation hymn: "Keeping our skies and waters clean / Our forests freshly green / Thus through the ever-circling years / True gratitude is seen," with the verse "Inheritors, our debt is paid / By passing beauty on." It is the third Edgar hymn found in this read, after "Canada's Our Country" (June 1967) and "This Fair Land, Our Canada" (1969).

Once There Was a Camper — Rhymes and Drawings by Mary S. Edgar, "a little book of 23 delightful rhymes on kids at camp" with line drawings by the author, was published by G. R. Welch, Toronto, and announced in Canadian Camping in November 1970.

Bruno Morawetz delivered "Youth and Drugs" to the Society of Camp Directors on 9 April 1970; the paper was copyrighted by the Society and Morawetz, with reproduction permission from Box 173, Station S, Toronto. It is a named, dated, formally copyrighted position paper of the professional body of Canadian camp directors on drug use.

In "Youth and Drugs" (9 April 1970) Bruno Morawetz argued his fellow camp directors out of panic about drug use, admitting "the spectre of a drug using youth haunted me terribly a few years ago. I remember the panic which came over me when I imagined my counsellors or campers stealthily smoking pot behind the craft area," reading the counterculture as "a spiritual revolution" happening "in every industrialized society," and predicting that "when this Society meets again in 1990 the smells of marijuana cigarettes may well waft through this room." Recorded as evidence of what Canadian camp leadership said in 1970, not endorsed.

Canadian Camping, November 1970, printed the badges-and-awards question as two facing essays: Jocelyn Palm of the Royal Life Saving Society for, and John H. Walker of Springfield College and Kilcoo Camp against.

Jocelyn Palm's November 1970 argument for camp badges rests partly on staffing: "A prospective staff member may claim to have all the required safety skills in riflery and aquatics, but without credentials to prove his capabilities the camp director should be reluctant to hire such an individual. The legal implications in hiring staff without current qualifications are of the utmost significance. Most camps obtain their senior personnel through the ranks of their own organization. Then, is it not fair to provide the opportunity for campers to achieve recognized awards while they are campers?"

John H. Walker's November 1970 argument against camp badges holds that "Camp should be a place where there is no system of badges and awards... The achievement of a badge or award overshadows the amount of learning which takes place," and that "It is often the weak instructor who relies on tests to accomplish what he himself can not do."

Pierre Cote, S.J., delivered "Besoins spirituels dans les camps" to the ACQ congress on 21 February 1970, defining the spiritual dimension without requiring religious practice or Catholic faith — "Par dimension spirituelle faut-il entendre une pratique religieuse intense? Non. Faut-il entendre une foi en l'Eglise Catholique? Non" — and holding that a director must not impose "un horaire et une facon de vivre contraire a l'option du milieu dont ils sont issus."

Pierre Cote, S.J., graduated the demand on camp staff by their own belief: a staff member who believes nothing must still "respecter une option differente de la votre, sans la mepriser... sans en rire et sans la ridiculiser"; one who believes a little should help the camper discover the dimension; one who believes much may share it.

Eanswythe Flynn's obituary of Gertrude Evelyn "Dinty" Moore records that she was born and educated in Toronto, graduated from the Margaret Eaton School of Physical Education, was waterfront director at Glen Bernard Camp, Director of Physical Education at the Vancouver YWCA and Director of Women's Physical Education at UBC, and opened her own girls' camp near Nanoose Bay in 1934, "the first private camp for girls in the West," selling the seventy-five-acre site on retirement to the United Church, which runs it as Moorecroft.

Gertrude "Dinty" Moore founded the British Columbia Camping Association in 1939 and was its first president, and was its honorary president at her death; during her ten years in executive office the association drew up standards for camping in the province in co-operation with the provincial government, and "Later this research and study was used as a basis for Government licensing of summer camps in B.C."

CCA president David Hartry's November 1970 letter names as "prominent Camp Directors in Canada" John Latimer, Robert Lazanik, Sophia Demetelin, Zave Ettinger, Tony Fry, Ivan Robinson, Tom Creighton and Peter Harris — three of the eight from Quebec.

David Hartry's November 1970 president's letter records visits to B'nai Brith Camp in Ste. Agathe du Mont, "with over 800 people in camp at one time," directed by Zave Ettinger; Bob Lazanik at Pine Valley, with "hundreds of people in Pine Valley's week-long grey cup games"; John Latimer's Kilcoo; and Tony Fry at Pine Crest YMCA Camp, Toronto.

Joint Canadian Camping Association / American Camping Association standards visits began in the summer of 1970 at two Ontario camps, saving those camps two visits in one year, under a new ACA rule that a camp outside the USA must first be a member of its own national camping association before the ACA will accredit it; all accredited camps must now sign an undertaking to abide by the mandatory standards before membership renewal and directory listing are approved.
The Ontario Camping Association moved on 1 November 1970 to 102 Eglinton Avenue East, Suite 203, Toronto, and Stan Wild was promoted to Executive Director.

Jack MacKenzie, Supervisor of Physical Education for the Regina Board of Education for thirteen years, became president of the Saskatchewan Camping Association in 1970; profiled by Eileen Mayotte, his camping work included "canoe trips on the Churchill River for boys, including inter-cultural trips (Indian boys and white boys)," and he chaired the Saskatchewan section of the CCA Centenary Cross Canada Canoe Journey of 1967. Terminology recorded as written in 1970.

The Canadian Camping Association scheduled a National Conference on Camping Standards and Research at Halifax on 22-23 February 1971, one delegate per member camp, with the board meeting 20-21 February and the annual meeting on the evening of the 21st; delegates were asked to propose topics under standards and accreditation, health and safety, leadership development, and pollution and conservation.

Harry Brown of Camp Tawingo argued in "Everybody Talks About It" (November 1970) that "Nature is the prime reason for having or going to camp... when the site is destroyed so too, is any camp," proposing that camps measure the pollution around them and identify its sources, run a camper-oriented Nature Centre with live animals, build their own weather station, and have campers plant trees.
A photograph in Canadian Camping, November 1970, is captioned "Camp Northway Lodge; Circa 1910" — an image caption independently placing Northway Lodge in existence by about 1910.

The provincial offices entry in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971, reads: "L'association des camps du Quebec, and Quebec Camping Association — 952 Cherrier Ave., Montreal, P.Q. (Lionel Perras, pres.) English Section: 2233 Belgrave Ave., Montreal 261 (Peter Van Wagner, Pres.) Section francaise: 952 Cherrier Ave., Montreal. (Rosaire Corbin, pres.)" — one president over the merged body with a separate president and address for each section.

A New Brunswick Camping Association appears in Canadian Camping in Winter 1971, based at the Moncton YMCA with Robert Cameron as president — the ninth provincial body and the last Atlantic province to organise.

The Canadian Camping Association's address in Winter 1971 is Suite 203, 102 Eglinton Avenue East, Toronto — the Ontario Camping Association's new office — so the national office left Ottawa less than two years after moving there.

Robert Lazanik's Canadian Camping Association address changes in Winter 1971 from 2233 Belgrave Avenue to 5465 Queen Mary Road, Suite 460, Montreal 29 — his own office rather than the Quebec Camping Association's.

David Hartry, president of the Canadian Camping Association, wrote in Winter 1971 that "the first official snark hunt was held in the year 1968... on the shores of Mason's Point" at the Anglican Youth Camp twenty miles outside Halifax — a dated, first-hand account of the invention of a camp legend by the staff who invented it.

David Hartry's Winter 1971 account describes the snark as "a cross between a fish, an animal and a human being. It goes on land; it goes on water, but it cannot go too far on land or too far in the water... sometimes eighty feet long, sometimes only ten. Many bumps protrude from his back. He has antennae and his eyes usually shine in the dark," catchable only "at 3 in the morning on a foggy night on the Atlantic coast" and only with a WHOMPHUM STICK, "a very large stick with a huge bump on the end."

David Hartry describes the staging of the snark hunt without concealment: staff set the campers' watches ahead and woke them soon after they fell asleep; the snark was built by campers who knew the secret from the previous year, from green garbage bags stuffed with styrofoam and tied in a row, with bicycle reflectors for eyes and coat-hanger antennae, floated off the wharf; the waterfront director lay hidden on the wharf blowing through a long cylinder to make gurgling sounds and once used a hand-pressure fire extinguisher for the spout; the director waded in to the knees and struck three times shouting "WHOMPHUM! WHOMPHUM! WHOMPHUM!" after which "everyone gives the camp yell or sings the camp song."

David Hartry records that the snark hunt acquired a spurious documentary pedigree: "much to our surprise at one time, we found, in the library a book actually called 'Snark Hunting'... we showed this to the children and this made our fictitious story even more convincing!"

David Hartry records that within three years of its invention the snark hunt was expected annually ("it is quite amusing each year as we are asked, 'When will the snark hunt be?'") and that campers were already elaborating its vocabulary, one writing: "The bump on the snark stick is called sarcophagus and the part you hold onto is called the handle. The part above the bump is called the framis."

David Hartry's snark-hunt account carries his own caution: "One has to be careful that the children don't become frightened by the darkness and the whomphum stick and the enthusiasm of the staff. I found that I got so excited one time that it was almost dangerous in the sense that some child might panic and get really scared."

Hartry's 1968 snark hunt is a documented instance of how a Canadian camp legend was made, staged, elaborated by campers, given spurious corroboration and then expected annually, all recorded by its inventor within three years. It says nothing about Kanawana's Chopsy legend directly, but it indicates what evidence of such a legend would and would not survive: the staging is remembered, the invention is not, and the corroborating "old book" was part of the hoax. Any oral history instrument on Chopsy should ask about staging and about who knew the secret, not only about the story.

Adele Ebbs of Camp Wapomeo wrote "The Campers — They Are Yours to Motivate" in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971, drawing a distinction she states plainly: "Award and reward are not synonymous." She quotes "A. J. Neil of Summerhill school in England" (A. S. Neill): "To offer a prize for doing a deed is tantamount to declaring that the deed is not worth doing for its own sake."

Adele Ebbs reports in Winter 1971 that one camp surveyed its campers and 97% favoured the competitive programme; the following year the camp eliminated competition and "the final consensus of opinion was that the summer had been more fun." Her four motivating techniques are positive suggestion rather than negative command, co-operation rather than bossing, faith, and commendation.

In the Winter 1971 letters column the editor of Canadian Camping conceded, replying to Mrs. Gail Brown, that the two badges-and-awards essays were "incorrectly titled" as positive and negative viewpoints and stated: "There is no official Association viewpoint" — establishing that the Canadian Camping Association had no policy on badges and awards in 1971, so a camp's badge scheme in this period was its own choice rather than a national requirement.

John R. Latimer, president-elect of the Ontario Camping Association, told its conference on 7 March 1970 in "The Youth 'Revolution' — How It Can Save Our Camps" that camp staffing depended on taking the young seriously, quoting Barry Lowes: "this is the first generation in history in which our young people have not been needed. There's no depression — There is not a world war — They aren't needed."

John Latimer described an experiment in camper self-government: the six oldest campers, the "Super Senior Cabin," were given no counsellor, with safety rules and camp relations set but programme, bedtimes and discipline their own. "For two weeks they operated on their own. However, near the middle of the third week, they came and asked me if they could please have a Counsellor."

Bruno Morawetz's "Bermudians Camping in Canada" and Richard Kinch's "Camping in Bermuda" in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971, record the first Bermuda-Canada camper exchange, of twelve campers each way, arranged with Mr. Reginald Ming, Director of Youth, for August 1970 "with very little red tape."

Bruno Morawetz recorded of the twelve Bermudian campers who visited Ontario in August 1970: "The revelation that white people are not ogres came as quite a surprise to some of them. One boy said that he had never shaken hands with a white person and most of them had had no previous contact with white people." Morawetz, a white Canadian camp director writing about Black children in 1970, also described them as "polite, clean, well-spoken, well-mannered and well-dressed." Recorded exactly as written and dated, not endorsed.

Bruno Morawetz reported that the visiting Bermudian campers found it hard to split into different tent groups "because as members of the Pembroke Youth Club, they had been accustomed always to do things together," that Ontario lakes were much colder than they expected, and that "several of them could not swim at all and most of the others had never developed a clearly definable stroke. The waves around Bermuda do encourage bathing, but not swimming."

Richard Kinch of Camp Ponacka recorded that the Canadian campers visiting Bermuda in 1970 were met at the airport by television cameras and newsmen and made a presentation to the Hon. Lancelot Swan, Member of Parliament for Youth, with Lloyd James as their government guide; housed at the former British officers' headquarters at Somerset after plans to stay at Camp Wahoo fell through.

Richard Kinch described Camp Wahoo, the government-owned Bermuda camp on Port's Island, as taking close to 100 boys, offering leather crafts, nature, sports fundamentals and swimming, booked about a week at a time by church clubs and scout troops, and providing "only the physical layout. The campers themselves do most of their own work, housekeeping, assisting in main meal preparation" — concluding "We couldn't help wondering if this camp with its limited facilities didn't offer a great deal more than our modern multi-programmed set-ups in Ontario. It really helped point out the importance of the human side of camping."

M. C. MacCulloch, Director of the Bolton Summer Camp (Rotary Unit), wrote in "The Camper in the Dining Room" (Winter 1971): "eating is a right, not a privilege. For that reason, meals, nor any part of them should ever be denied the camper. Coaxing, rewarding, punishments or ridicule at the dining room table are wasted. Desserts are never denied the camper. It is an unfair and unnecessary punishment."

M. C. MacCulloch listed poverty at home twice among the causes of poor appetite at camp in 1971: "at some homes, the family diet which the child is accustomed to is inadequate from a dietetic point of view and the foods provided at camp will appear unnecessary and too much... Some children from the metropolitan areas make their own meals due to family circumstances and three courses at a meal is out of proportion to a jam and peanut butter sandwich for lunch... Limited budgets at home which provide spaghetti and bread as fillers will cause the child's perspectives re his own needs to be shaded."

M. C. MacCulloch's 1971 dining-room guidance directs camps to "hold off section cheers, and camp songs, until after the meal is completed, or at least towards the end of dessert," to schedule open periods for free time before meals, to allow no seconds on dessert until every camper has had a first, to ration sugar and jam as the most expensive items on a tight budget, and not to pour milk until dessert is served.

J. D. Walker, Provincial Supervisor of Camping and Recreation for the Alberta Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled, published "Handicapped Camping in Alberta: A Five-Year Projection 1970-1975" in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971, recording that five years earlier an observer had objected that for the money proposed "two hundred youngsters could be flown to Hawaii every summer for five years"; Alberta built two camps instead. Terminology of 1971 recorded as written.
entities: Alberta Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled

facts.claim: J. D. Walker's 1971 Alberta projection admits that "maximum occupancy has been the goal, and very, very few applications have been refused," with the result that "some children with multiple handicaps and behaviour problems, which are beyond the competence of the staff to deal with, have been accepted," and proposes structuring camp periods "on the basis of level of activity, area of interest or intellectual capacity rather than an arbitrary age or disability structure."

J. D. Walker's 1971 Alberta staffing figures give a maximum twelve-week season, staff drawn from university and senior high school students available for about four summers, at least 25% turnover a year, an age range of 17 to 21 with a median of 19, senior staff encouraged to commit to three consecutive seasons with stipends set accordingly, and training comprising a three-day May seminar plus an on-site orientation weekend immediately before opening.

Charles A. Ceglar, sdb, of Camp Savio published "Quelques notions generales sur le repos et le sommeil" in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971, a physiological essay on sleep for camp staff citing Dr. L. Boisvert, the Encyclopedie Larousse pour la jeunesse, Paul Chauchard, C. T. Morgan, Brown-Sequard and Kleitman (1949).

Charles Ceglar's 1971 essay on sleep notes that during sleep "la calorification est moins energique, aussi l'homme a-t-il besoin d'etre plus chaudement couvert durant le sommeil" — a physiological reason for extra blankets at camp — that "on ne dort jamais 'comme une pierre'" with a small movement about every quarter hour, that "le sommeil est plus long et plus necessaire dans la jeunesse," and that "il n'y a pas de lien direct entre l'intensite du sommeil et sa valeur recuperatrice; les dernieres heures sont aussi importantes" — an argument against cutting the morning end of a camper's night.

Tremblay Canoes of St-Felicien, Quebec, advertised a full page in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971: "60 years experience," cedar canoes with "Verolite," a plastic-coated canvas in use six years by "more than 60 Boys' and Girls' camps and by various police units and several governmental departments in Ontario and Quebec," in 38 sizes and models, of No. 1 Eastern Canada cedar with solid brass nails and screws and white birch decks and thwarts.

Continental Casualty's Camp-Guard advertisement in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971, had changed its pitch to cover "the extra medical expenses not covered by Government Health Insurance Plans" — the arrival of public health insurance visible in camp insurance advertising.
Camp Nagiwa advertised its complete camping equipment and supplies for sale through the Guelph YM-YWCA in Canadian Camping, Winter 1971 — a camp closing.

Canadian Camping, Spring 1971, announces that the Centenary Journey Committee's "Journal" is published: "the 'Journal' which tells the story of the project is now available. It includes 'their story' which relates the historical significance of each segment of the journey and 'our story' of the experiences of Young Canadians in 1967. Maps are provided to show the route taken," at $1.50 plus 25c from the Canadian Camping Association, 102 Eglinton Street East, Suite 203, Toronto.

The Centenary Journey Journal is the national volume at the top of the record chain in which each camp's log fed a provincial log which fed a national book. If Kanawana's 1967 crew, which reached Britannia Beach on 9 August 1967, contributed a log, its account would be in this volume.

June Labbett's memorial for Ferna Graham Halliday in Canadian Camping, Spring 1971, states: "Upon graduation in 1917 Miss Halliday went on to New York to study social work and from there to Montreal and a job with the Y.W.C.A. It was here that she received her first real camping experience at 'Oolawhan,' the 'Y' Camp north of Montreal. This whetted her appetite for camping and in 1922 she and Miss Mabel Jamieson started Camp Ouareau in the Laurentians."

Ferna Graham Halliday was born in Chesley, Ontario, studied at Queen's, and kept lifelong ties with the Queen's alumnae including Charlotte Whitton of Ottawa; she chose the Eagle Lake property north of Kingston deliberately, wanting a site "approximately half-way between Toronto and Montreal" so as to draw campers from both cities.

June Labbett's 1971 memorial states that "in 1925 Oconto opened for its first summer" and calls Ferna Graham Halliday "its Director from 1925 to 1949." This is a one-year discrepancy against camp-oolahwan.md, which gives Camp Oconto in Tichborne, Ontario, as 1924. Both dates are recorded; neither is resolved.

Camp Oconto "virtually doubled its size in a few years" during the Second World War, when "many young British war guests were amongst the campers"; Ferna Graham Halliday retired in 1949 to a cottage at Kincardine, sat on the board of the Julia Greenshields Home in Toronto, raised her niece and nephew Barbara and Jack Halliday after their father's early death, and died in October 1970 after a severe heart attack earlier that year.

June Labbett records that the Ontario Camping Association archives refer to Ferna Graham Halliday as "Halliday the colourful," and tells the story of Camp Ouareau's first day, when the beds ordered weeks ahead had not arrived: "Undaunted, Miss Halliday announced she had a wonderful surprise for them — they were all going to sleep on the floor! The children loved this."

Charles Plewman wrote in "Our First Seventy-Five Years of Camping" (Canadian Camping, Spring 1971): "That was my experience as a boy of thirteen when I went to camp in 1903," and "All of the boys that I took camping from 1910 to 1920 had also taken the initiative themselves." Set beside his June 1970 statement that he first took a group camping in 1909, both can stand — 1903 as a camper, 1909-10 as a leader — and together they place his birth at about 1890.

Charles Plewman wrote in 1971 that "Older boys had been going to camp for twenty-five years before it had become the accepted thing for girls," attributing the lag to "a carry over from the Victorian era when it was considered a greater asset for a fragile girl to be able to swoon at the right moment than to stand on her own two feet," and adding: "As a teen-age boy I would never have dreamed of my sisters going to camp."
