Charles Plewman wrote in 1971 that during the first twenty-five years of organized camping in Canada camping was limited to teenage boys: "'Cradle snatching!' is the exclamation that would have been made if you had taken a ten year old boy to an organized camp in the year 1910," and that early camps were "very much a rough and ready he-man affair with nary a skirt in sight... minus buildings, doctors, or women in any capacity."

Charles Plewman wrote in 1971: "Today in most instances it is the parents who persuade the boy to go to camp; not so in 1915. Then, in nine out of ten cases, it was the boy who persuaded his parents to let him go camping."

Charles Plewman recorded a named, dated objection to the founding of Camp Wapomeo: "I can still remember Holt Guerney telling Taylor Statten back in 1923 that it would be a big mistake to start a girl's camp on the same lake as Camp Ahmek for boys, particularly because he contemplated having some joint activities."

Charles Plewman wrote in 1971 that early Canadian camps had "a star system, in which the camp director was the dominant figure in all activities... many early camps actually were built around the personality of the director! He was not adverse to playing to the gallery and in some extreme cases he became a stunt artist with a bag full of tricks."

Charles Plewman wrote in 1971 that "Even as late as 1923 you could count the number of Travel Camps in Ontario on the fingers of one hand," and that "it took over twenty-five years of organized camping to convince the general public of its value."

Charles Plewman's 1971 article title, "Our First Seventy-Five Years of Camping," dates organized Canadian camping from about 1896 in his reckoning — a third round-number estimate beside J. Harry Ebbs's "more than 70 years" (1969) and Plewman's own "first fifty-five years" (1970). None is evidence against Kanawana's 1894 founding; all three are recollections stated in round numbers.

Huguette Dagenais reported in Canadian Camping, Spring 1971: "Felicitations au Camp Ecole Trois Saumons qui fete cette annee son 25e anniversaire. Bravo a M. l'abbe Raoul Cloutier son fondateur et a Mlle Lucie Samson et l'abbe Patrice Turcotte les deux co-directeurs actuels" — a 25th anniversary in 1971 dating the camp's founding to 1946, against Cousineau's "some 21 years ago" in 1969, which points to about 1948. Both dates are recorded; neither is resolved.

The merged Quebec association had a paid executive director, Yves Beauregard, who left on 1 February 1971: "M. Yves Beauregard, le directeur-executif de l'A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. a quitte le 1er fevrier dernier." Dagenais also records the provincial grant arriving in late instalments: "La deuxieme tranche de l'octroi du Haut-Commissariat nous est enfin parvenu fin fevrier. Et la troisieme?"

Lionel Perras, in "Variations sur le camp de jour" (Spring 1971), dates day camping to 1922 and to the United States — "Elle est nee aux Etats-Unis en 1922" — and defines it against the resident camp as an "externat de Plein Air pour une duree de 7 a 10 heures par jour," noting that early day camps used parks on the outskirts of cities before the trend moved toward camp sites.

Lionel Perras's 1971 account of day camping lists its disadvantages honestly: transport costs more when the camp bears it; the child's return home each evening "diminue l'influence du camp et contribue a replonger les enfants dans les problemes familiaux"; attendance is less regular; and "les enfants manquent des avantages des soirees." He names its constituency as families "de milieux economiquement faibles."

Kirk Wipper argued in "The Quest for Zest" (Spring 1971) that the quest for vertigo is universal and cannot be suppressed, plotting a continuum from skiing, shooting rapids and mountain climbing through snowmobiling and auto racing and carnivals to drugs, alcohol and glue, and concluding that "a significant rise in zestful experience of the positive form, could very well waylay, arrest, replace or impede the less desirable patterns" — with the by-product that positive forms involve the natural environment: "When people care there is hope for the survival of both man and the planet."

David Hartry's "C.C.A. — New National Office," dated 14 December 1970, explains why the Canadian Camping Association's Ottawa office lasted less than two years: after meetings with Fitness and Amateur Sport consultant Cor Westland, the OCA executive and the head of the Ottawa Administrative Centre, "it was felt strongly that the establishment of a National Office in Ottawa would be of no benefit to C.C.A." The financial reason is stated plainly: "Project Grants are still available to C.C.A. but little is available for administrative Grant to operate office anywhere... With the offer of O.C.A., C.C.A. will be able to operate from its own income."

The Ontario Camping Association's terms for housing the Canadian Camping Association from 1971 were desk and filing space at $45.00 per month, use of typewriter, duplicating machine, collator, folding and addressing equipment, use of the board room for executive, committee or editorial meetings, and office supplies at cost; the Ottawa Administrative Centre was retained only for translation services and consultation on legislation.

Paul Chamberlain, Chairman of the Watercraft Committee, described in Spring 1971 a costed model for an OCA canoeing clinic funded for three years from Ontario Department of Education annual physical fitness grants: minimum enrolment fifty, sixty-four counsellors at each of the last two clinics, $17 per person Friday afternoon to Sunday afternoon plus a $6 return bus fee, covering two dinners, two breakfasts and two lunches for seventy-two including staff and housing thirty-three men and thirty-one women, requiring at least forty canoes.

Paul Chamberlain distinguishes the Ottawa Canoeing Instructors' Course — national, a full week, conferring Instructor and Assistant Instructor standing — from the provincial canoeing clinic, which runs two or three days and confers no award. He also warns that "in planning transportation it is important that one checks what modes of travel the Association's insurance policies cover."

Carolyn Jack reported in Spring 1971 that the Amherst Rotary Club had sponsored camps at Camp Tidnish, Nova Scotia, for thirty-three summers, since 1937, an operation "considered to be a $100,000 investment," with 178 campers in 1970 in two-week sessions. Her statement of the difference from an ordinary camp: "The normal child can adjust to a camp schedule easily. At Tidnish, the schedule must be adjusted to the campers." Among Tidnish's five stated purposes is "to support family relationships by providing a program outside the home which will permit the parent some freedom from the daily care of the child." Terminology of 1971 recorded as written.

Allison Hagen reported on Camp Atlantic, the Nova Scotia Diabetic Camp in Pictou County, in Spring 1971: its purpose was "to help teach the kids to become independent," and "by the end of camp all the campers could inject their own insulin and knew how to care for the equipment"; the programme had to be planned around snack times and meals. Named staff: Dr. Phil Bagnell, nurse Ann Johnson, dietician Valerie Aylward. A "Women's Liberation Day" is recorded among the camp's 1970 events.

Ginny Baker reported that the Westmount Day Camp of the Halifax Recreation and Playground Commission ran its twelfth season in 1970, with two camps of about 45 and 30 children, staff including three junior leaders who attended Ardmore School, two high school volunteers and six paid staff "one of whom was handicapped"; because of its playground siting, "we were integrated with non-handicapped children on the playground... It was a new experience for both." Camper criticism from the previous year that the programme "did not meet the needs and interests of the older children" changed the following year's programme.

Charles Cook of Camp Sharbot argued against specialised camps in Spring 1971: "We have music camps, riding camps, French camps, drama camps, hockey camps... I think we have gone too far already. As the concrete spreads across southern Ontario, the need for summer camps to offer an all-round outdoor experience increases, not decreases," adding "Let them flit from flower to flower and, when they eventually settle, they will at least know what the whole garden looks like," and, on measurement, "You can't measure them, but they are real."

Rob McKinnon, aged 22, of Camp Kilcoo, published his chapel talk to his own eight campers in Spring 1971, including a plain statement of the period's gender policing recorded as written: "This Society has taught me... don't be warm and feeling (That's not masculine)... don't cry (That's feminine)."

A review of Mary Edgar's Once There Was a Camper in Canadian Camping, Spring 1971, prices it at $1.75 and records that "she has donated all royalties from the sale of the book to the Canadian Camping Association."

Canadian Camping, Spring 1971, reports that "For the first time in the history of camping, a Canadian mountain peak has been named in honour of a camp director" — Mount Peskett, Alberta, for the Reverend Louis "Lou" Peskett, founder of Frontier Lodge off the David Thompson Highway midway between Banff and Red Deer, who was struck by a falling rock on a mountain climbing expedition near the camp and died a few days later. The camp was "an outgrowth of Rev. Peskett's parish work with troubled youths."

Helen Stewart's "Outdoor Cookery" in Canadian Camping, Spring 1971, supplies eight recipes from Cookery for Kids, Kamp 'n' Kicks: Frank Canoes, Bar-B-Q Beans and Franks, Spoon Cakes in Chocolate Sauce, California Settler's Stew, "Squaw Corn," Beach Boy Bread, hot gingerbread with apple sauce, and Toasted Jamwiches. The third-listed name is recorded exactly as printed in 1971 and is not used in this project's own voice.

Ron Johnstone became president of the Ontario Camping Association and John Latimer president of the Canadian Camping Association, with David Hartry past president, as recorded in the officers list of Canadian Camping, Spring 1971; Arnold Cohen is Manitoba president.

Huguette Dagenais reported in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971: "Au nouveau president; M. Robert Lazanik, meilleurs voeux de succes. A M. Lionel Perras, President sortant et recipiendaire de l'insigne A.C.Q.-Q.C.A." — so the presidency of the merged Quebec association passed from Lionel Perras to Robert Lazanik in 1971, and Perras received the association's insignia on leaving. Lazanik was simultaneously CCA Vice-President for the Quebec Region.

The merged Quebec association held a seminar for camp directors and their principal colleagues attended by 115 people, on "politiques de personnel et des questions de financement dans les camps" — staff policy and camp financing — conducted bilingually without simultaneous translation, "anglais et francais ont echange en s'exprimant dans leur propre langue; des animateurs bilingues faisaient le lien." Huguette Dagenais argued the province should issue a certificate accrediting those who completed it. Thirteen people represented Quebec at the CCA congress in Halifax.

C. B. Powter signed a visiting policy statement for "Powter's Camp for Boys, St. Donat de Montcalm, Quebec" in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971 — so the Powter family camp, whose founding near Lac St. Joseph, Ste-Agathe-des-Monts, in 1893 is described in N. B. Powter's "Sixty Years Ago" (Canadian Camping, February 1962), was still being run by the family in 1971 at St-Donat-de-Montcalm. The run therefore documents the Powter camp across at least 1893 to 1971.

Powter's Camp for Boys' 1971 visiting policy allowed parents every Sunday except the first Sunday of each month, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., permitted to take boys out for lunch or picnic on camp property; staff might have Sunday visitors only in non-scheduled time, with no meals or accommodation provided at counsellor level, "although permission is sometimes granted to members of the Senior Staff."

John Latimer's first president's letter (Summer 1971) records the Canadian Camping Association's restructuring into regions: "since the Association was founded, the Executive moved from province to province every two years. Now there are five Vice-Presidents on the Executive of C.C.A. who represent various regions in Canada" — Tom Creighton (Atlantic), Bob Lazanik (Quebec), Jack Pearse (Ontario), Eileen Mayotte (Prairie), Tanya Krisman (British Columbia) — with Brian Graham treasurer and Rick Bendera secretary, both of Toronto. "The Board of C.C.A. is now made up of the Executive, the Provincial Association Presidents and the Committee Chairmen."

The rotating provincial executive of the Canadian Camping Association, which moved the national office from province to province every two years — Winnipeg, then Halifax, then Toronto across the period this read tracks — ended in 1971 with the adoption of five regional vice-presidencies.

John Latimer's Summer 1971 letter records a CCA resolution "that all provinces have minimum standards prepared so that they can be used in the study of provincial standards development and the development of national standards," a CCA workshop to be held no later than 31 January 1972 with funds requested from Cor Westland at Fitness and Amateur Sport, and National Camping Day on Wednesday 21 July 1971 under chairman Doug Dent of Victoria.

Don Groff's foreword to "The Youth Culture and Camping" (Summer 1971) records that the Canadian Camping Association's Publications Committee could not agree to print the articles it had solicited: "Concerns about language forms and philosophies expressed or implied in some of the articles caused sufficient apprehension for some committee members (camp operators and directors) that we could not reach a consensus as we usually do for our editorial decisions. As a result, these articles appear by a majority but not unanimous decision." One of the three is marked "(This article is unedited.)"

Doug Caldwell wrote in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971, that "Our Canadian camps are involved with over four-hundred thousand campers every summer" — a national camper count for 1971, twice John Latimer's Ontario figure of 200,000 given in 1969.

Doug Caldwell set out in Summer 1971 the three staff-hiring questions Canadian camps were facing, leaving the answer to each camp: "Is there any moral significance in a male staff member with long hair? Should we be discriminatory towards staff members who have used drugs? How far should we go towards hiring staff members who do not have ideas in keeping with the philosophies of the established order?" His own position was that terminating staff who had used drugs would be "inconsistent with our goals," coupled with the principle that "it should never be necessary to impose on campers the personal life-styles (political, social, or religious) of individual staff members."

Doug Caldwell warned in Summer 1971 against the phrase "youth culture" itself: "The very phrase 'youth culture' all too often conjures up visions of a long-haired, drug-oriented, morally deficient, radical counter-culture... we must recognize a set of people as diversified in their beliefs as any other given age group."

Bob Osborne of Trent University argued in Summer 1971 that camp was the natural home of the new naturalism, noting that "the youth of today however are aware of the pressing urgency of their task while ecologists predict the complete breakdown of life by the year 2000," and proposing crafts on creative design in natural materials and music "expanded from note singing of old camp songs to include chanting, hand clapping, screaming and free-form dancing." His sentence "A lesson can be learned from the satisfaction that the so called 'primitive' savages obtain from their frenzied dancing around a flickering fire" is recorded exactly as written in 1971 and is not adopted in this project's voice.

ed la Pierre of Dalhousie, formerly CIT Director at YMCA Big Cove Camp, Nova Scotia, wrote the article Canadian Camping printed unedited in Summer 1971: "Most Canadian camps are unisexual. Most camp administrators and supervisors look upon their authority as replacing that of the parent. Sex is worried about and it is hoped that no accident happens which would put Camp Director Short Pants in the embarrassing situation of relaying the news to dear mother. Control is assured by authority rather than individual responsibility. Most camp directors and senior staff are flagrantly ignorant about drugs."

ed la Pierre proposed in Summer 1971 that "Resident camps should be controlled by the campers themselves. They should become a commune"; that university students with specialised skills be hired and "paid adequate salaries"; that directors be appointed for two-year terms with an M.A. and "varied experiences on the road," evaluated by the campers, staff and supervisors; and that camps near towns become year-round hostels supported by fees and provincial or federal subsidies.

M. C. MacCulloch's "Homesickness: Diagnosis and Preventive Measures" (Summer 1971) lists fourteen causes, among them "Inadequate spending money, or personal effects in comparison with more fortunate campers," physical differences such as stammering, limping or cross-eyes, "lack of privacy in the camp cabins," bed-wetting and constipation, being sent to camp against his will, and "No one on staff has shown any real concern for him; due to numbers and opening day programming."

M. C. MacCulloch's twelve preventive measures against homesickness (1971) include decorating the cabin with camper names on bunks and lockers before arrival, a personal letter from the counsellor in small camps, camper lists drawn up in advance so the counsellor knows the names — "Nothing makes you feel more insignificant than to watch your leader grope for your name on a list" — a welcoming committee for cars and buses, cabin name cards above the dining room tables, and respect for nicknames: "If the camper prefers 'Skip' there is no reason to call him 'Wardell' just because your list says so." His conclusion: "To send the camper home the first day is to cheat him."

Huguette Dagenais's "Le camp de jour et son transport" (Summer 1971), printed in French with an English translation by the Administration Centre for Sports and Recreation, Ottawa, sets out a complete tender procedure for camp bus transport: go by tender but "ne pas necessairement arreter son choix sur le cout le plus bas"; specify numbers, exact dates and hours and a preliminary route; require commercial permits and a copy of the insurance policy for each bus; and verify personally that policy, permit and serial number match the same vehicle, because "il arrive que les compagnies peu consciencieuses transportent les licences et les assurances d'un autobus a l'autre."

Huguette Dagenais's 1971 day-camp transport procedure requires a monitor on every bus so the driver is not responsible for the children, a named person holding the director's delegated authority for transport, camp rules for drivers supplied in writing, a first aid kit and plastic bags in every bus, one driver a mechanic if there are several buses, and that the whole arrangement be completed at least four months before opening. Her closing: "Le succes d'un camp de jour repose en grande partie sur son transport."

Canadian Camping, Summer 1971, printed four camps' visiting policies together at the editor's invitation. Bruno Morawetz of Camp Ponacka: "If it were possible, every day should be visitors' day... In this way the camp would run normally and this is what parents should witness," with three weekends in practice, a changing hut and picnic tables at the beach so families are independent of the camp during meals and swims, and the programme not changed on visiting days. Eanswythe Flynn of Camp Brigadoon, with thirty campers and twelve staff, allowed every day after a two-week breaking-in period, noting that "a camp of two hundred or more could not possibly cope with daily hordes of parents, friends, relatives, dogs, Siamese cats, budgies and white mice."

Sphairee, a cheap camp racquet game specified in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971, was invented about 1961 by Frederick Beck of Sydney University and brought to Peterborough by John Lucas of Canadian General Electric: a court 20 feet by 9 on concrete or asphalt, net 18 inches high, five-ply wooden bats faced with cork or pimple rubber, and a perforated heavy-gauge plastic ball 2.5 inches across sold in Canada as a "Fun ball." "To equip one court with four bats, three balls and a net, will probably cost less than $15.00."

The organizational meeting for a cross-Canada foot trail, originated by L. Doug Campbell of the Chinook Trail Association, Calgary, was held at the Toronto YMCA on 29 April 1971, with Ann Prewitt attending as the Canadian Camping Association's official representative appointed by the Board at Halifax. Organisations present included the Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, YM-YWCAs, National and Provincial Parks Associations, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Waskahegan Trail Association, the Bruce Trail Association, the Canadian Audubon Society and the Federation of Ontario Naturalists; the first of six stated objectives was "to preserve places of natural and historical value."
Copies of the Centenary Journey Journal were sent to the organizational leaders of the cross-Canada foot trail project in 1971 — so the 1971 volume circulated beyond the camping movement.

Deputy Chief Bryan N. Mitchell of the Etobicoke Fire Department set out camp fire safety in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971: camp on the north or west side of a clearing so prevailing westerlies carry smoke and sparks away from tents; use a large flat rock settled flush to the ground for a fire site, or a scraped circle four feet minimum and ten preferred, with tree roots under the topsoil chopped off "to prevent your campfire from tunnelling underground and starting another fire"; obtain a fire permit from a ranger or the Department of Lands and Forests; never use gasoline, kerosene, alcohol or barbecue lighter to start a fire; and on leaving soak the fire until "cool enough to stir with your hands."

Bryan Mitchell's 1971 fire-safety article directs camps to store flammable liquids in metal containers with a safety vent or spring-loaded lid, painted red and labelled, never in glass bottles or plastic water jugs; warns that L.P. gas is heavier than air so leaks travel along the ground, with an odourant "similar to that of a skunk or rotten cabbage"; states that "a gallon of gasoline, when completely vapourized, has the explosive power of eighty sticks of dynamite"; and forbids using a stove as a tent heater, which "in an air-tight tent will soon devour the oxygen from the air and cause the sleeping occupants to suffocate."

Margaret Govan's report on the CCA conference at Halifax (Summer 1971) records seventy-five people from across Canada, every province represented except Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick present for the first time; delegates were made members of "L'Ordre de Bon-Temps," founded 1606, "the oldest social club in Canada," by the deputy minister of education. Western delegates travelled on "the 'milk plane', an all-night journey with a stop-over at almost all the capital cities."

Canadian Camping offered a special subscription to camp staff at $2.00 a year, "below cost," enrolled through camp directors — the magazine deliberately broadening its readership from directors to staff and campers in 1971.

Charles F. Plewman's "The Canadian Camping Magazine and How We Came By It" (Canadian Camping, Fall 1971) is the magazine's own founding history, written by the man who founded it. He was drafted into the presidency of the Ontario Camping Association in the autumn of 1944, the OCA having been formed "eleven years before" — that is, 1933.

Charles Plewman's diagnosis of the Ontario Camping Association in 1944: "Ninety percent of all the camps in Ontario emanated from Toronto and all of the O.C.A. officers came from the same place. We were an Ontario Camping Association but in name only." With war having reduced camp conferences to sporadic events, "the answer was clear, we needed a magazine or bulletin of some kind to draw us closer together."

Charles Plewman records that the T. Eaton Company financed the first edition of the Ontario camping bulletin — "As an association we were poor and just didn't have the money" — and that "Next I asked the one and only Mary Edgar to act as Editor and she agreed."

Charles Plewman wrote in 1971: "Before very long, I think it was in 1946, the Canadian Camping Association was formed at a meeting held in the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa," adding that "while it was called the Canadian Camping Association, in reality, nearly all of its members were representatives from the Ontario and Quebec Associations. To the best of my knowledge no other Province had a camping association," and that "for the moment it had no corporate existence."

Charles Plewman is a second, independent, first-hand source for a Canadian Camping Association founding event in 1946, and supplies a venue the project did not have: the Chateau Laurier, Ottawa. He hedges the year ("I think it was in 1946") but not the event. This does not overturn the documented 1936 founding at the Central YMCA, Toronto, but it makes the 1946-reorganisation reading of the Camp Stephens claim about Nelson McEwen substantially more likely than an error, and turns it into a checkable question: what happened at the Chateau Laurier in 1946. The CCA's own minutes should be in the OCA archives deposited at Trent in 1970.

Charles Plewman records that "To the credit of the Ontario Camping Association, and its vision of the Canada of to-morrow, it closed out the Ontario Bulletin in 1947 and threw its entire resources behind 'Canadian Camping', a mimeographed bulletin published quarterly and edited as before by Mary Edgar... It was not by accident that we called it the Canadian Camping 'bulletin'. One could not call a mimeographed affair a magazine."

Charles Plewman states that "The first real Canadian Camping 'magazine' was published in February of 1949 when for the first time it appeared in print" — which is exactly where this project's 164-issue cached run begins. The run is therefore complete from the magazine's first printed issue, and the mimeographed 1947-48 quarterly bulletin that preceded it is a separate, earlier body of material that this project does not hold.

Charles Plewman records that the move from mimeograph to print in 1949 "would not have been possible had not Mr. Fred Haiblen of Toronto stepped in and assumed the financial responsibility," and that Mary Edgar "gave continuity to the magazine by acting as its editor for five more years and was succeeded by Mrs. G. W. Flynn."

Charles Plewman identifies the author of Canadian Camping's first editorial as "Miss Dais L. Gass, president of the C.C.A. in 1946," quoting it: "Now it starts in its humble way — may it grow like the acorn and the oak, but most of all may it prove a tie between all of us in Canada. We can learn much from each other. May Canadian Camping weave a bond of understanding, of mutual helpfulness and good will from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the end of the earth."

Clifford Labbett, Director of Camp Oconto and President of the Society of Camp Directors, gives the Society's inaugural dinner as "held at the Rosedale Golf & Country Club, Toronto, on May 12, 1969," with fifty-seven members attending. J. Harry Ebbs's founding address as printed in Canadian Camping in 1969 was delivered at "the Founding Banquet held at the Rosedale Golf Club, Toronto on May 21st, 1969." Same venue, same event, nine days apart in the magazine's own two accounts. Both are recorded; neither is resolved.

Clifford Labbett records that "The Society is the brain child of Dr. Harry Ebbs of Taylor Statten Camps," the first seeds being a questionnaire sent to Ontario Camping Association members in 1968 and reported back at the OCA spring conference that year; its purpose is "to establish and maintain professional practices in the directing of childrens' camps and to ensure qualified directorship in such camps."

The Society of Camp Directors has a board of five serving three-year terms and three membership classes — Fellows, Honorary Fellows and Emeritus Fellows. The Honorary Fellows elected at the inaugural dinner in May 1969 were Mary Edgar, Ferna Halliday, Mary Hamilton, Charles Plewman and Mrs. Taylor Statten; the first board was Ebbs, Ron Johnstone, Clifford Labbett, Bruno Morawetz and Dr. Elsie Palter, with Ebbs elected first president.

Four of the five Honorary Fellows elected by the Society of Camp Directors in May 1969 had died or would die within four years — Ferna Halliday in 1970, Ethel Statten in 1970, Mary Edgar in 1973. The roll is effectively the movement's surviving founders honoured at the last moment.

The Society of Camp Directors met twice a year, on the second Thursday of November and April, at a fee of $25 a year covering two dinner meetings and copies of the papers; its secretary in 1971 was David Palter, 80 Old Colony Road, Willowdale. Papers delivered to it by 1971 were by Donald Groff, Joseph Kronick, Bruno Morawetz, Mary Northway, David Palter, Jack Pearse, Elizabeth Raymer, Stanley Wild and Kirk Wipper, "many of these papers have been reproduced in Canadian Camping and American publications."

The Society of Camp Directors had two projects under way in 1971: a $500 Research Fund for any undergraduate wishing to research some aspect of children's camping, and, with the Ontario Camping Association, "a joint proposal to have stricter licensing of childrens' camps in Ontario and to have the O.C.A. made the governing body in Ontario."

Charles Plewman replied in print to ed la Pierre's unedited article of the previous issue, defending directors' parental authority: la Pierre had written that "most camp administrators and supervisors look upon their authority as replacing that of the parent"; Plewman answered, "What is wrong with that? I would say that it is to the credit of Camp Directors that they have personally felt a real responsibility for everything that had to do with the welfare and happiness of those entrusted to their care. Organized camping has flourished in Canada because of the confidence that parents have come to feel about those who operate them."

Charles Plewman conceded to ed la Pierre in Fall 1971 that "adults should have done a better job in sharing with the campers on the decision making level, but to say that we should abdicate and turn everything over to inexperienced youngsters to run is sheer unadulterated nonsense... The program and the ongoing life of camp should be the results of two age groups sharing and not of any one age group dominating," and objected that la Pierre's argument applied to those aged 17 and over but not to campers of 7 to 16.

Charles Plewman, aged about 81, offered a corrective to the period's own crisis talk about camps losing children: "I have just passed through a camp of 200 boys. I don't know where you could find a happier gang of kids... camps are just as popular as ever with the 8 to 14 year olds and as for those older, it never has had too great an appeal." He closed his reply by turning on his own generation: "a good group of 35-year-olds, if sitting in the seats of the mighty, would do a better job of solving the world's problems than the present tired outfit schooled in the out moded practices of the past."

Andrea Dillon records that "The Canoeing Instructor's School was first started in 1967 with a small group of enthusiastic canoeists under the direction and guidance of Claude Cousineau and Professor Kirk Wipper. The canoe school has just finished its fifth year." After four years the single course split into two eight-day sessions, one French and one English, because "much of the course's time was taken up in translating material due to the two languages."

The 1971 Canoeing Instructors School was held at the University of Ottawa Camp near Gracefield, Quebec, with the French session 8-15 June and the English 16-24 June, administered by the Department of Recreology, University of Ottawa, with a second-year grant from the Fitness and Amateur Sport Division covering travel for candidates from outside Quebec and Ontario and reducing the fee to $30.00 for eight days; about seventy candidates attended from almost every province and 34 received the "Instructor" mention. Staff included Claude Cousineau as director and Kirk Wipper as guest professor.

The 1971 Canoeing Instructors School introduced a canoe trip within the session and the use of a video-tape machine ("L'introduction du ruban magnetoscopique facilita l'apprentissage de certaines manoeuvres en canot"), and shifted its emphasis from stroke and dock teaching toward tripping programme organisation — budgeting, equipment, food and pre-trip training — because "many canoe programs are now increasing the performance of tripping."

Bruno Roy of Camp St-Arsene published "Relations moniteurs-campeurs" in both languages in Fall 1971, working through three leadership types — autocracy, anarchy and democracy — and stating on discipline: "la discipline est avant tout une attitude de cooperation. Cette attitude elimine le pesant probleme de l'autorite," and "moins on a d'autorite reelle plus les marques exterieures se font importantes et repetees."

Bruno Roy wrote in Fall 1971 that where a sanction must be imposed "elle ne sera ni collective ni corporelle" — neither collective nor corporal — adding "Il doit eviter egalement d'humilier un campeur en public." This is the fourth explicit prohibition of physical punishment recorded in this run of Canadian Camping, after MacCulloch (1969), Danson (June 1970) and MacCulloch again.

Bruno Roy wrote on fairness in 1971 that "La segregation reside souvent dans la tete du moniteur" and that "justice ne veut pas dire 'rasage' (tout le monde au meme niveau)... Chaque campeur a un droit strict d'etre eduque pour lui-meme"; and on affection, warning that young counsellors must not seek gratitude, quoted a teacher friend: "Il n'y a pas de plus riche amour que la depossession... Ce sont mes eleves et non pas 'mes' eleves 'a moi'. Ils s'appartiennent."

Hendrick "Hank" Roessingh of Silvercreek Ranch, Calgary, National Standards Chairman of the CCA, wrote in Fall 1971: "After twelve years of operating a camp with a horseback riding program as one of the main features, my wife and I have come to the firm conclusion that it isn't worth it... We are going to trade in our horses for canoes, flood part of our campsite, and have a waterfront program," citing staffing, the year-round cost of horses against canoes, and dishonesty in the horse trade — "No seller will ever admit to selling a horse more than eight years old."

M. C. MacCulloch's "As Camp Closes" (Fall 1971) prints four letters between a director and a departing counsellor. The counsellor's case for not returning: "There is a magic about camp — but prolonged magic is unreal... Camp is for the kids — and if I went back for the purpose of having a good time or recapturing memories rather than for the kids, I would be a hypocrite." The director's reply: "Camp doesn't drain into your system any 'X' amount of happiness, fulfilment, reward or experience and then stop, measuring your portion as complete... the magic is not childlike. It is not prolonged for adults. Every new camper, every new counsellor, every new day starts it all over again."

Tom Creighton, Director of YMCA Big Cove Camp and former president of the Nova Scotia Camping Association, wrote the only saltwater-camp article in this run, "Unique Aspects of Waterfronts in Ocean Environments" (Fall 1971), stating that camps in the Bay of Fundy "must realistically develop swimming pools rather than utilize the ocean as the costs and difficulties of dealing with 24-foot tidal variations are staggering," that a tidal waterfront "may only be one third usable at low tide," and that "A piece of wood left in warm salt water will be reduced to a sponge-like consistency within a summer," with "aluminum construction impossible as electrolysis develops."

Tom Creighton recorded in Fall 1971 that his own camp's cove had been polluted out of use: "Our beautiful cove now has phosphate enriched eel grass growing abundantly, its shell fish are now condemned because of the effluent from nearby communities." He also noted a season when jellyfish "were particularly virulent" and "we had an alarming drop in swimming participation."

Canadian Camping advertised a "FRENCH-ENGLISH CAMPER EXCHANGE" for summer 1972, camps to send brochures to the editor: "CANADIAN CAMPING is interested in promoting bi-lingualism and friendship among our Canadian Campers."

John Latimer's Fall 1971 letter announces a National Standards Workshop at Banff, 20-23 January 1972, tied to the Alberta association's annual meeting, with two representatives per provincial association "perhaps your President and Standards Chairman"; Claude Cousineau to chair a National Canoe School committee; and a Constitutional Task Force meeting in Vancouver 11-13 November because "the constitution of C.C.A. has many inadequacies."

A full-page thank-you in Canadian Camping, Fall 1971, lists forty-six advertisers and states: "CANADIAN CAMPING is a 100% Canadian magazine and is not subsidized in any way. It is supported solely by advertisements."
Eric Russell of St. John's, who founded the Newfoundland and Labrador Camping Association and was its president when the association became a member of the Canadian Camping Association, died in 1971.

Charles F. Plewman's biographical note in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972, is the fullest account of him the run carries: eight years Boys' Work Secretary for the YMCA in Ottawa and Winnipeg; eleven years Secretary for the Ontario Boys' Work Board; founded Kilcoo Camp for boys in Haliburton in 1932; later assisted in the formation of the Ontario Camping Association, of which he is past president and Honorary member; Honorary member of the Society of Camp Directors; during the Second World War Secretary for the Toronto Branch of the Canadian Red Cross with a staff of 65 and 40,000 volunteers, where he instituted the Toronto Mobile Blood Donor Service; and "although in his 83rd year... still active in Rotary and Camp circles."

Charles Plewman held the YMCA Boys' Work Secretaryship at Ottawa and Winnipeg before founding Kilcoo Camp — the same office Roy Locke and Nelson McEwen held at Montreal, and the standard route into camp directing that this project has repeatedly traced.

Charles Plewman published an eyewitness account of Tom Thomson's burial in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972, fifty-five years after the event: he arrived at Mowat Lodge, Algonquin Park, in July 1917 for a two-month stay after his health broke down — "Taylor Statten, who was interested in my welfare, arranged for me to go to Mowat Lodge" — and acted as a pallbearer, one of a group of "something like 12 or 13" at the graveside, in rain, with no minister, no family member and none of the painters present. "The Stattens, whose cabin was nearby were absent." Park Ranger Mark Robinson "appeared to be in charge." Marked "Copyright, Canadian Camping."

Charles Plewman's 1972 account records Winnie Trainor demanding to see Tom Thomson's remains and insisting on foul play, and Shannon Fraser of Mowat Lodge confiding afterwards that Thomson was engaged to Trainor, that she was coming for a showdown, and that "Tom was a shy and sensitive person and... he just could not face the music." Plewman sets out all three theories with the evidence for each and declines to choose: "Actually the truth regarding what happened to Tom may never be known with certainty." His reason for speaking: "At 82 I now feel that I should say what I know. It is quite possible that I am the only person living who participated in Tom Thomson's burial in Algonquin Park."

Charles Plewman recorded how little Tom Thomson's death meant at the time: "When I arrived back at the Lodge I was still quite oblivious to the fact that we had just buried a man who is now recognized as one of Canada's foremost artists... he might as well have been Algonquin Park's 'Unknown Man'... I was back at Canoe Lake in 1921, four years later, but no one up there was talking about Tom Thomson. He seemed 'forgotten'." And: "Mowat Lodge was full of 8.5 by 10.5 inch sketches that Tom had painted. I could have had them for about a dime a dozen."

Dr. Elsie Palter's "Exceptional Children" / "Enfants inadaptes" (Canadian Camping, Winter 1972), printed in both languages, is the most complete statement in this run of who was actually attending Canadian camps. Her test for admitting a child with a physical disability is the camp's programme, not the child's condition: "If a camp is geared to an athletic type programme... then a child with a physical handicap does not belong there. However, in camps where the programme offers a choice of activities... then a camp experience with normal children should be planned for him." She states that "The deaf can fit into a regular camp with very little trouble, and should not be excluded for this reason." Terminology of 1972 recorded as written.

Elsie Palter wrote in 1972 that perceptual handicap was a category "fifteen years ago... a term seldom heard," and gave a figure: "Many of our campers have some perceptual deficiency, statistically 10-15%... They need extra help, in order to keep up with their fellow campers, but they do belong with other 'normal children'." She notes that "the simple act of walking up an inclined plank comes easily to most children, but to the perceptually handicapped it is an insurmountable task."

Elsie Palter distinguished slow learners from children described as retarded in 1972: "Sickness, emotional disturbance, poverty, may have held a child below his age level... These children are often sensitive, the butt of jokes... wander by themselves at camp, unless someone is aware of their deficiency and has helped that child to find some area in which he can be made to feel competent." On aggression: "A child who has suffered physical abuse in his home often resorts to aggressive behaviour." On withdrawal: "A child who is excessively timid... who internalizes all his feelings, is just as ill mentally as the overly aggressive youngster."

Elsie Palter's section "Culturally Enriched or Culturally Deprived" (1972) describes agency camp children in the period's own terms: their "communication is often physical, and their language, limited as it is, coloured with obscenity. Social behaviour and personal hygiene do not fit middle class standards. Agency camp staff are more familiar with these children" — and itemises what camp offered them: "He is assured three good meals, seated in a dining room, a clean bed of his own, facilities for washing and bathing... away from the city slums... and is exposed to adults who care about him." Recorded exactly as written and dated, not adopted in this project's voice.

Elsie Palter names foster children as a distinct part of the agency camp population in 1972: "They often come from culturally deprived settings, have been rejected by their parents, and are as they call themselves the 'Aid' or 'Children's Aid'... they may have been in several different foster homes, sometimes returned to their natural parents and then placed again... They have witnessed desertion, alcoholism, promiscuity and neglect in their homes... Camp is often the most meaningful experience in their lives." Children placed by Children's Aid Societies were therefore part of the agency camp population, and some arrived with case histories attached.

John Latimer's Winter 1972 newsletter dates and locates the CCA's Montreal meetings: the Board meeting at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel, Montreal, 19-20 April 1972, the Annual Meeting the night of 20 April, and the QCA-ACQ Conference 20-22 April at the same hotel, with a separate Quebec Camping Association annual meeting on 24 May.

The Girl Guides Association of Canada was welcomed as the Canadian Camping Association's first Affiliate in 1972; the Constitution Task Force met in Vancouver under Stan Wild; membership certificates in French and annual seals for member camps were to be issued; and National Camping Day was set for Wednesday 19 July 1972 under Doug Dent.

Bob Lazanik and David Hartry were working in 1972 on a committee to establish a Canadian Camping Association Award for significant contribution to camping in Canada — the origin of the CCA award scheme under which Derek Walsh received an Award of Excellence in 1983.

A new Canadian Camping Association Committee on Outdoor Education first met on 1 January 1972 with Brian Blackstock, David Brown, Margaret Govan, Sam Hambly, Marjorie Howard of the Girl Guides and Flo Woods of the National Council of the YWCA; a separate committee was formed to counteract press coverage "which give a completely misleading picture of camping in Canada."

John Latimer reported in Winter 1972 that "Camping Sunday" had been introduced into the Anglican churches of Newfoundland in spring 1971 and would be extended in April 1972 to the United Church and the Salvation Army — special services across the province conducted largely by campers and young staff, "highlighting the importance and value of camping."

Max Campbell, Director of Arrowhead Ranch, objected in print to Hank Roessingh's "Horses for Sale," making a structural criticism of the movement: "Both the Ontario Camping Association and the Canadian Camping Association have on occasion conveyed the impression of being unquestionably waterfront camp-oriented with an inherent lack of interest in the merits of any other type of Camp Program. Question — would the Executive of the Canadian Camping Association have permitted the publication of a similar article on canoeing — even if it had been written in jest? I doubt it." Roessingh replied that "for too many of us being dedicated to camping is synonymous with being deadly serious about it at all times," made the case for riding as work with a living creature, and withdrew his offer to sell his horses.

Sam G. Hambly, Director of Camp Allsaw, published a complete buildable camp composting system in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972: a 12-foot circle of snow fence, an 18-inch layer of dry organic material inside it, a 45-gallon steel drum with top and bottom removed set in the centre as a funnel for kitchen waste with a tight fly screen on top, dry material packed between drum and fence, and the drum rocked and raised as the pile fills. Re-piling to admit air "will produce offensive odours and for this reason should be avoided during the camp period."

Sam Hambly connected camp composting to the waterfront in 1972: garden soil made "open and porous... absorbs the rain and melting snow water. Underground reservoirs are filled up. Hence, the water emerges to provide crystal clear water for swimming and canoeing... campers who like to have quality conditions on the waterfront have a responsibility for the conservation practices of the watershed."

David Hodgetts, Director of Hurontario Wilderness Camp, set out a whitewater teaching document in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972, with a threshold: "I think not for campers under twelve... I think not if the staff members are inexperienced or if your equipment is not suited to running rapids," and three hard rules — wear lifejackets, always carry a spare paddle in each canoe, never underestimate the power of running water, especially if it is cold. He teaches the terminology of the "V," standing waves (runnable if not over 2.5 feet), rock, boil and back eddies, and the two-man division of labour between the critical man and the power man.

David Hodgetts's 1972 whitewater article states the key safety point twice — "always have the canoe tilted downstream on a turn" — because eddy turns "cause about 80% of all turn-overs in rapids," and advises on standing waves: "If they are huge — portage. If between 2 and 3 feet hit them right dead centre... If you hit them sideways you'll probably have to build a drying fire that evening."

Margaret Govan, the former Camp Onawa director, in her seventies, made a 200-mile inflatable-raft float down the Teslin and Yukon rivers with Wilderness Unlimited (John and Mickey Lammers), sponsored by the Federation of Ontario Naturalists — six adventurers from Ontario, four days on each river with two lay-off days, eight campsites, ending at Carmacks. Her account was reprinted in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972, from The Liberal, Richmond Hill, 7 October 1971.

Helen Stewart, Director of Camp Wahcahmie, described a Mother and Daughter Weekend in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972, held the second weekend in June "so that Camp will be ready for parental inspection and we have a 'breather' of a few weeks before Pre-camp begins," and offered explicitly as a homesickness preventive. Terms: expenses divided equally, dish-washing shared by the group, staff present with their own mothers NOT on duty, and all participants required to abide by the camp's waterfront and safety rules.

Joyce Bertram of Camp Ouareau published "Camping on the Avon" in Winter 1972, a comic essay arguing from quotation that Shakespeare was a camp director — a period inventory of a director's grievances hung on quotations: the bank, the health inspector, staff, senior staff, Parents' Day and the queue of cars, duty counsellors, the weather, the night rounds, and the maintenance man at dawn.

Officer changes recorded in Canadian Camping, Winter 1972: Levi Mehaney succeeds Elizabeth Mouland as Newfoundland president, Mouland having gone to head a national Girl Guide Ranger training programme; Marion Rosborough is Nova Scotia president; Robert Lazanik is listed as president of the merged Quebec association in the provincial offices block; and Huguette Dagenais joins the Publications Committee.
Canadian Camping sold at $1.00 a single copy from Winter 1972 and printed its subscription rates on the masthead for the first time.

Bob Attfield's article in Canadian Camping, Spring 1972, is headed "Camp Hoax Costs Director $25,000 In Legal Damages," but the headline is itself the hoax: "Did you believe the headline of this article? If you did, you have just been successfully hoaxed into reading about the value and fun of the camp hoax." There was no lawsuit, no director and no damages award. The article is a practitioner's how-to, printed in the national magazine, arguing that the camp hoax is something a camp should deliberately do.

Bob Attfield defines the camp hoax in Spring 1972 as "a dirty, underhanded, ingenious, demonic and dastardly plot that will have your entire camp believing that Mrs. Trudeau has just arrived, or that last night's explosion was a crashed space-ship, or that the scrap of curved white plaster unearthed by the campcraft people is a section of prehistoric GLABERGOOF egg," and describes two worked examples: a staged spaceship crash on a balmy night in late July 1968, after which "two R.C.M.P. in plain clothes arrive to investigate the explosion," and a fake newspaper flash announcing a visit from Mrs. Trudeau, who arrived in a cottager's Cadillac with a uniformed chauffeur and stayed for dinner.

Bob Attfield names Camp Ponacka's "George the Leprechaun" as a camp hoax that grew into a programme — green footprints on clothing, walls and foreheads at night, paddles gift-wrapped in toilet tissue in the dining hall — and because it was non-frightening it produced "an Irish Day, an Irish Pub evening, shamrock cookies, and even a race to the end of the rainbow."

Bob Attfield's 1972 craft notes on starting a camp hoax: "a whispering campaign may provide the answer," seeded through a talkative camper; and on senior campers, "If your plan is especially sophisticated, you can baffle the sharpest of your seniors. If not, for goodness sake let them in on the action, or they will destroy the whole show" — the mechanism by which a camp's older campers become co-custodians of a legend rather than its debunkers. His stated limit: "The best camp hoaxes always seem to combine the greatest amount of imagination with the least amount of scare... It's great for kids who can take it, but a pretty poor idea if the goal is to scare the life out of them."

Walter Greenway of Camp Ponacka lists as the third objective of pre-camp staff training, in Canadian Camping, Spring 1972, "To pass on traditions and established practices": "one of the camp's most precious possessions, its traditions, should be explained and discussed with the staff. Whether it is celebrating birthdays with the Saturday morning throw-in, a hoax, or an Indian Programme, the staff must be ready to participate actively to make them a success." A camp hoax was therefore not an outbreak but curriculum, handed over deliberately at pre-camp to each year's new staff so that it survived them.

Three items across two issues of Canadian Camping describe the same practice from three sides: David Hartry's "Snark Hunting" (Winter 1971) on how a camp legend is built, Walter Greenway's pre-camp objectives (Spring 1972) on how one is taught to staff, and Bob Attfield's hoax article (Spring 1972) on how one is seeded and sustained. Together they set out what evidence a legend like Kanawana's Chopsy would leave: the transmission is through pre-camp staff training, not through campers, and the older campers are let in on it deliberately.

Walter Greenway's week-long pre-camp timetable (Spring 1972) runs Friday staff arrival to Friday campers arrive at 5:00 p.m., with work gangs deliberately mixing old and new staff ("they should not be regarded simply as a source of cheap labour"), an ice-breaker session at which every staff member brings a cabin game, a heading "Beware of Fatigue" prescribing a night off and transport to town before campers arrive followed by a late breakfast, and all staff including kitchen and maintenance attending sessions.

Kirk Wipper's "Haida Voyage" (Spring 1972) records the commissioning, carving and launching of a Haida dugout in 1971, marking both British Columbia's centenary and Camp Kandalore's twenty-fifth anniversary — which dates Kandalore's founding to 1946. The carvers were Victor Adams and Adam Bell, of whom Wipper writes that "out of the 1800 surviving Haidas only [they] had any idea of how to build this ancient craft."

Kirk Wipper recorded two passages in 1972 to be read as period voice with its frame stated. At the launching of the Haida dugout: "the children became passengers in their native craft, but the art of paddling is lost for them. This fact is regrettable." And at Skidegate the party found an old unfinished Haida canoe abandoned in the forest, its builders "silenced by the smallpox epidemic" — "mute evidence of an occurrence that had nearly destroyed the Haidas and their culture forever."

The Canadian Camping Association's 1972 constitution revision, presented by Stan Wild in John Latimer's president's column, proposed: the name "THE CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION — L'ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU CANADA"; publication of documents and training courses in both official languages; a board member representing "les colonies de vacances d'expression francaises du Canada"; the five regional vice-presidents replaced by one board member per provincial or territorial association plus a single vice-president; two voting systems, one vote per board member for administrative decisions and postal voting weighted by membership for national ones; the CCA redefined as "une federation nationale, refletant les deux langues officielles, composee des associations provinciales et territoriales des camps au Canada"; seven membership categories; and affiliation invited from the Guides, Scouts and YM-YWCAs, to be in force by the end of 1972.

The Canadian Camping Association's past-presidents list in Spring 1972 marks with asterisks, as deceased, Taylor Statten of Toronto and Dais L. Gass of Montreal — the first bound this read has produced on the date of Gass's death, which was therefore before Spring 1972. The Montreal past presidents listed without asterisks, and so living in 1972, are Anne I. Vail, F. M. Van Wagner and Kenneth H. Murray.

Walter Mingie, Director of Camp Carowanis, wrote in Spring 1972 that Georges Hebert "was charged with the responsibility of training or conditioning the men of France's navy during World War I... giving the men three week's training on an obstacle course in the forests of France." This conflicts with Claude Cousineau's account in Canadian Camping in 1969, of a pre-war methode naturelle demonstrated in 1913 and carried to Quebec after the Second World War. Both are recorded; neither is resolved.

Walter Mingie reported in Spring 1972 that "The Quebec Department of Education has recently recommended in their norms that provision be made for a hebertisme area when land for a school is obtained."

Walter Mingie's 1972 hebertisme course description gives a course of about three acres ("nearby camps have courses covering up to five acres"), all apparatus built from trees, logs and branches with only rope, wire and nails supplied, one senior staff member in charge who must approve every apparatus, the course rebuilt each season as campcraft projects for tent groups in the first week, and a flagpole and flag at the course entrance "similar to the waterfront, in order to indicate when the course is open." Nineteen apparatus are specified, including Tarzan, spider web, log wall, stump walk, monkey bridge, teleferique and elevator. On racing: "the fun derived from becoming good on a particular apparatus is motivation in itself, races are not really necessary."

National Camping Day 1972 was set for Wednesday 19 July, with all Canadian camps celebrating simultaneously at 9 p.m. Pacific — midnight Eastern, 1:30 a.m. Newfoundland — climaxing at a special campfire by shooting a flaming arrow toward the north, then "Taps," then the flag lowered to "My Country is my Cathedral."

Michel Corbeil's "Education de la conscience sociale — l'experience du camp familial Bleu et Blanc," reprinted from RELATIONS (October 1971), records that four Montreal family agencies began work in September 1970 to build a family camp conceived as social-conscience animation, drawing families from Saint-Henri, Pointe-Saint-Charles, Lafontaine and Verdun; from 25 June to 21 August 1971 the camp at La Conception north of Saint-Jovite received 64 families, sixteen at a time for fifteen days, grouped by home district, prepared by an executive of twelve couples and supported by the Haut Commissariat aux loisirs et aux sports, the ministere des Affaires sociales and Perspectives-Jeunesse.

Michel Corbeil's argument for the Bleu et Blanc family camp was that "il faut liberer la personne exploitante aussi bien que l'exploite," and his concession was equally plain: "Certaines familles plus alienees, plus ecrasees, prennent du temps a passer de la consommation passive a une certaine forme de participation. D'autres demeureront dependantes malgre les efforts de leur entourage."

John Latimer's "Unemployment Insurance Changes" (Spring 1972) records that from 1972 counsellors and instructors in summer camps are in insurable employment with premiums payable by employee and camp; citizens of other countries working in summer camps are not exempt; there is no minimum age exemption; camps operated by a charitable institution get a reduced rate for 1972, 1973 and 1974; and camp personnel otherwise employed as teachers and nurses are no longer exempt.

1972 is the year Canadian summer camp staff began generating federal employment records: after the unemployment insurance change there is a payroll paper trail on summer camp staff that does not exist before it. For a YMCA camp this is a real archival lead into staff records from 1972 onward.

Allan A. Webber's poem to his granddaughters at camp, printed by Al Goodman of Camp New Moon in Spring 1972, is an undated first-person recollection of a charity fresh-air camp near Orillia on Lake Couchiching where Webber was a counsellor and swimming instructor: the camp "didn't cost a penny / For it was just for boys / Whose parents had no money," with the scrubbing-down of arriving campers and deliberate feeding to "fatten them a bit," and the closing couplet "And now and then I chance upon / Some man at an affair / Who came to camp a poor boy / And is now a millionaire."

Mary S. Edgar's "Our Indebtedness to Our Indian Friends," a talk given in the Glen Bernard Camp chapel on Sunday 15 August 1971 as part of the camp's fiftieth-anniversary ceremonies and reprinted in Canadian Camping, Summer 1972, is a first-person account by the founding generation of Canadian camping of how "Indian programming" reached a Canadian camp.

Mary S. Edgar states in her 1971 talk: "When I was director of Camp Oolahwan in the Laurentians, (the Montreal Y.W.C.A. camp), it was difficult to have a council ring ceremony, for our campers changed practically every week." This confirms in her own words that she directed Oolahwan, uses the spelling "Oolahwan" that this wiki uses (against the "Oolawhan" of the Halliday tribute of Spring 1971), and records that the camp's intake turned over roughly weekly — the reason the council-ring form could not take root there, and her stated reason for wanting a camp of her own.

Mary S. Edgar's 1971 account of how the "Indian theme" reached her camp names three sources: Pauline Johnson, "the Mohawk Princess," who performed in Sundridge about 1899 when Edgar was ten and stayed as a guest in the Edgar family home; a rescue in the summer of 1900 on Lake Nipissing, when her father's launch failed in a storm and two friends of his from the Dokis Reserve brought the party safely to Sturgeon Falls — "We felt that we owed our lives to them. We had a debt to pay"; and her YWCA training course in New York in 1914-15, where she met Miss Ruby M. Jolliffe, Superintendent of State Camps for New York and New Jersey, and at Jolliffe's Bear Mountain cabin met "Princess Ti-ata" from a southern tribe, a storyteller Jolliffe "often engaged... for Council Ring programs."

Mary Edgar's 1971 talk states the transmission route for camp "Indian programming" outright: American state-camp practice, via the YWCA national training school in New York, into a Canadian camp director's programme — arriving in Montreal at the YWCA's own Laurentian camp before going on to Glen Bernard. Kanawana's totem pole (1927), Council Ring and "Council of Tribes" belong to the same period and the same movement, and this is the clearest contemporaneous statement of that pipeline the project holds.

Mary Edgar's own account of founding Glen Bernard: "In July 1921 when I returned with my parents from a trip around the world, I was eager to get to work on my dream — 'a camp of my own'. On the first trip to my new property on Lake Bernard I discovered the Glen, a perfect amphitheatre for a Council ring. It seemed quite natural then to name the new camp Glen Bernard." This is compatible with the property being purchased in 1920 and the camp opening in 1922, and it makes the Council Ring the reason for the site and the name rather than a later addition.

Mary Edgar records that the old totem pole at the entrance to the Glen at Glen Bernard Camp was carved by campers, that by 1971 "Time and the woodpeckers" had damaged it "probably beyond Repair," and that a taller replacement was being carved for the fiftieth anniversary by Mr. Tom Bowie of the Ontario College of Art. Every camper was made a member of a tribe, with a council ring "practically every Saturday evening for fifty summers."

Mary Edgar names three Indigenous guests to Glen Bernard Camp across fifty years, with dates: Dawendine, daughter of a Mohawk chief from the Six Nations Reserve, first invited in 1934 and returning in 1969, who gave Edgar a paddle her father had cut and shaped, decorated with the totems of the six tribes, which Edgar used on every canoe trip and gave back to her in 1969; Chief Mudjeekwis of the Ojibways from the Rice Lake reservation, who named Edgar "Ogimagua, Children's friend" — which is how she acquired her camp name; and "Nanaki" of the Blackfeet, whose English name Edgar gives as Norah Gladstone, daughter of Senator Gladstone, met by Helen Stewart on the ship home from the coronation of Queen Elizabeth, which Nanaki attended representing Canada, and who came to the Council Ring in the beaded white doeskin costume made for the coronation.

Mary Edgar's 1971 talk holds statements of debt, sympathy and appropriation together in one text and does not resolve them: "We need often to remind ourselves that this country which we proudly call 'This land of Ours', once belonged to the Indians"; on the July 1971 Life magazine special edition on the Indian in North America, "It is a sad story. It is a story to make one blush with shame. They have not had a fair deal"; and "we hope the Indians will treasure their old legends, customs and traditions and that the white race will learn to appreciate those things that are unique and precious in their culture." The fiftieth-year project of the old campers was a fund to bring Indigenous girls to camp, which had not yet happened — "we found it takes time to work out worth-while arrangements." Recorded exactly as written and dated, not adopted in this project's voice.

Tanya Krisman, British Columbia vice-president of the Canadian Camping Association, was killed in a motor accident on 28 April 1972. An active YWCA Vancouver worker, she had envisioned a year-round outdoor centre on Salt Spring Island and would have been director of the new Camp YaWaCa that summer.

James C. Moore ("J.C.") of the Boy Scouts of Canada died on Saturday 10 July 1971; he was involved with the Haliburton Scout Reserve from its founding in 1947 ("a few experimental Camps") to 1970, when it was running about 350 campers per week, and sat on the OCA board representing the Boy Scouts, Greater Toronto Region.

Doug Dent gives the prior history of National Camping Day in Summer 1972: Canadian Camp Week in 1957 and 1958 (he believes), dropped on that committee's own recommendation; the biggest attempt in 1967 for Centennial; 1968 curtailed by the postal strike; nothing in 1969; and the committee re-created in 1971. The 1972 observance is therefore a revival of a revival, not a new thing.

Doug Dent's 1972 National Camping Day instructions include half a column of safety directions for the flaming arrow: bind a 3-inch by 10-inch burlap swath to a good arrow with fine wire, soak the binding in coal oil or kerosene "for a few hours before use (not 60 seconds ahead of time in gasoline!)," fire toward water if possible, and "pick an archer who will fulfill that responsibility as is required — possibly an award to a senior camper."

Canadian Camping, Summer 1972, printed two camp song texts in full for National Camping Day: "Taps" ("Day is done / Gone the Sun / From the lakes, from the hills, from the sky / All is well safely rest / God is nigh") and all four stanzas of "My Country is My Cathedral" ("My country is my Cathedral. / The northern sky its dome. / They all call it Canada / But I call it home"). The music was held by provincial co-ordinators rather than printed.

A national camp song circulated top-down through the Canadian Camping Association in 1972 for simultaneous singing on National Camping Day — a different transmission path from the ones this project has traced, and one that would explain a song appearing at Kanawana without any local origin.

Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau's message for National Camping Day 1972, printed in facsimile in both languages, gives the Canadian Camping Association's participation figure as "almost half a million young Canadians who participate in organized camping activities each year," and quotes himself on wilderness: "Denied an opportunity to breathe the brisk freshness of an Atlantic gale, to view the unbelievable glory of a prairie sunset, to feel the overwhelming silence of a northern lake, we would no longer be Canadians."

Jocelyn Palm's "Aquatic Danger: Spinal Injuries" (Summer 1972), written as Executive Secretary of the Ontario Branch of the Royal Life Saving Society Canada, cites Megan Wynne-Jones, M.D., of Lyndhurst Lodge Hospital: "In one hospital in Toronto 523 cases of paralysis from the neck down have been treated prior to 1972; 109 of these cases were a result of diving accidents." Her prevention standards give minimum depths of 9 feet for a one-metre board, 12 feet for five metres and 15 feet for ten, plus marking of underwater hazards and the diver's flag at 100 feet.

Brian Blackstock, Director of Camp Mazinaw, published "Age Group Characteristics in Camp" in Summer 1972, from a study made at the camp financed by The Neathern Trust and presented earlier to the Society of Camp Directors, written expressly "to assist Camp Leaders in their staff training programs." It gives six age bands — 8-9, 9-11, 11-12, 12-13, 13-14, 15-16 — each with characteristics and the counsellor's changing role, from "very dependent on counsellor for direction and support" at 8-9 to "counsellors should be very observant but in the background" and "'silent lessons' — by example are most effective" at 15-16.

Eanswythe Flynn's "What's With Your Storage" (Summer 1972) is a four-page winterising checklist that doubles as an inventory of what a Canadian summer camp of 1972 physically contained: a piano left in place uncovered with the keyboard exposed and a cup of powdered camphor inside against mice; mattresses left on the beds with naphtha flakes and cedar fronds and never stacked, on Fire Department advice; oily rags to the dump and never the camp incinerator; temporary log studs between floor and beams under long spans against snow load; windows covered because grouse and partridge fly through clear glass; and canoes stored keel up, supported at bow and stern thwarts.

"Enjoyment of Mutual Aid Holidays" / "Plaisirs de l'entraide et des vacances," reprinted from RELATIONS (November 1971), records twelve families of the Saint-Jean-Baptiste quarter of Montreal at Lac-des-Plages from 26 June to 10 July 1971 — the second Montreal working-class family camp in two issues of Canadian Camping. It was financed by the ministere des Affaires sociales and the Club Richelieu, its leaders trained under Perspectives-Jeunesse; the families met from April to June to plan it themselves and paid their own food bills, each family having a cabin and cooking for itself. Its argument: two weeks "ou chacun est accepte comme il est... ou il ne se sent pas a part parce qu'il a moins d'argent, parce qu'il est handicape, parce qu'il est separe, parce que ses enfants sont turbulents."

A follow-up notice in Canadian Camping, Summer 1972, states the unemployment insurance threshold for camp staff: anyone receiving a minimum salary including room and board of $30.00 a week or more must pay, "no matter what age — no matter what nationality"; a counsellor whose services consist mainly of teaching or instructing is in a "teaching class" and gets the reduced premium rate for 1972, 1973 and 1974.

Helen E. Stewart became editor of Canadian Camping with the Fall 1972 issue, with Bill Henderson as Publications Committee chairman, replacing Ann Prewitt and Don Groff. Her first editorial says she "inherited no statement of editorial policy," asks for one to be formulated, and states the intended readership as "not only... camp directors old and new, but... counsellors, senior staff and anyone involved in camping," adding that it does not matter "whether the article is written by a camp director, a counsellor or a maintenance man."

Canadian Camping, Fall 1972, printed a national call for camp songs: "We need your assistance — We want to compile a songbook and make it available to all camps in Canada. You must have a popular camp song. Would you please send in to the magazine the words and list the tune of your camp song so that it can be shared across Canada." If Kanawana answered it, the words and tune of a Kanawana camp song exist in the CCA's papers or in a published CCA songbook.

Canadian Camping, Fall 1972, asked all camp directors to send the CCA office "Two copies of your camp brochure — they are needed for the C.C.A. Archives and for display at the February Conference at Geneva Park." There was therefore a C.C.A. Archives actively collecting camp brochures in 1972, separate from the Ontario Camping Association archives deposited at Trent in October 1970.

Canadian Camping reported in Fall 1972 that "Jack Pearse is working on the establishment of a committee to investigate ways and means of gathering together material which can be compiled into a master document on the history of the camping movement in Canada." Pearse was the CCA's Ontario vice-president.

Helen Stewart announced in Fall 1972 that the Canadian Camping Association had asked the president for a list of the types of camps in every province and the number in each category — a national camp census that would name Kanawana if it survives.

Claude Cousineau's "Have a 'Wigwas Teiman' in Your Camp," printed in English and French in Fall 1972, records that William Commanda, Traditional Chief of the Algonkin Nation of North America, was building birch bark canoes on the Maniwaki Reserve about 90 miles north of Ottawa, and that "This past summer, a few camps had the opportunity to acquire a Commanda birch bark canoe." Materials given: white cedar frame, birch bark covering, ash thwarts, black spruce roots for lashing, spruce gum mixed with animal fat for pitch. Photographs show Commanda teaching Gaston Lemire, instructor at the CCA Canoeing School, and an Algonquin model built in July 1972 at the University of Ottawa camp.

Canadian Camping, Fall 1972, printed within two pages both a genuine transmission of Algonquin craft knowledge from a named living chief (Cousineau on William Commanda's birch bark canoes) and "An Indian Version of the Twenty-Third Psalm," a missionary composition presented as an Indigenous one, with an editor's note that it "originated many years ago with Arizona Indians... A white missionary then retranslated it into literal English — Indian style." The magazine does not appear to notice any difference between them. That juxtaposition is the most economical illustration this read has found of what "Indian programming" meant in Canadian camps in the 1970s.

Miss Mary G. Hamilton died in July 1972; Elizabeth Raymer's tribute calls her "a pioneer in two fields: physical education and camping," Principal of The Margaret Eaton School from 1926 through 1934 and founder and director of Camp Tanamakoon from 1925 until 1953, known as "Hammy," "Mary G" or "Merrigee," and author of The Call of Algonquin (Ryerson Press, 1958).

Elizabeth Raymer's 1972 tribute to Mary G. Hamilton records that Margaret Eaton School graduates "taught in every YWCA and in almost every private school for girls in Canada... Many of them eventually became camp directors" — a second named training pipeline into Canadian camp directorships, parallel to the YWCA National Training School route Mary Edgar describes, and a place to look for the women who ran girls' camps in Quebec.

C. Labbett of Camp Oconto set out a full budget template for a Canadian camp in "Money in the Bank — Budget, or else..." (Fall 1972), with expenditure headings including food, salaries and wages (counsellors, kitchen, maintenance), supplies, insurance (fire, auto, burglary, business interruption), repairs and maintenance, Red Cross and Royal Life Saving Society examination fees, publicity and advertising, tuck purchases, vehicle, boat, taxes and mortgage or loan interest, and unemployment insurance, Canada Pension Plan and Workmen's Compensation.

Clifford Labbett's 1972 budget article gives hard figures for Canadian camp operation: raw food cost "anywhere from $1.00 to $1.75 per day" per camper; the employer's unemployment insurance contribution "is now 1.4 times that of the employee — not equal to his" since the rules changed on 1 January 1972; the Canada Pension Plan matched by the employer; and, in Ontario, sales tax applying where the fee exceeds $66.50 per week and the camper stays less than 30 days. He also notes that the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Ontario Workmen's Compensation Board "maintain auditors who may examine your salary and wage records at any time."

Bruno Morawetz's "The Counsellor in the Public Eye" (Fall 1972) frames the camp counsellor as a member of "the teaching fraternity, with the obligation of observing their code of professional ethics," who "probably spends almost as much time with them in one month as their classroom teacher does in one year" and "is more of an idol than the teacher." Its prohibitions concern conduct off the camp site: the "swelled head" syndrome and the night-off invasion of the nearest town, trespass including on abandoned buildings, the collecting of "trophies" such as highway and cottagers' signs, nuisance-making at country stores, and, within camp, avoiding "gossip, 'borrowing' or running people down."

The Ontario Camping Association's "Guidelines for Job Negotiation," reprinted in Canadian Camping, Fall 1972, state that an oral offer and oral acceptance bind both parties, that once agreed "it is unethical for you to apply or continue negotiations elsewhere," and list the grounds on which an application may be rejected: "age, school grade, lack of experience, previous performance at another job, references, your personal interview, no suitable openings available, or your unreasonable salary requirement in view of age and/or experience." Applicants are told to establish at interview "all Camp policies e.g. bed hours, days off, camp dress, smoking" and which benefits are taxable.

Canadian Camping's personnel news column of Fall 1972 records that Don Beauregard was appointed Executive Director of the Quebec Camping Association and Zave Ettinger elected President of its English Section, replacing Peter Van Wagner between the Summer and Fall issues; the section francaise was headed by Rev. Pere Rosaire Corbin.

Canadian Camping reported in Fall 1972 that Don Pringle "recently retired from the Y.M.C.A. in Regina and has been appointed Director of Camp Pine Crest, Toronto Y.M.C.A.", with the bracketed joke that "Saskatchewan people are now complaining that they train all the good people and then Ontario grabs them off" — a statement about how YMCA camp directorships were filled nationally.

Saskatchewan was described in Canadian Camping, Fall 1972, as the only provincial camping association to have dealt with environmental protection in its standards programme, and the only one to have presented briefs — five of them, on the Qu'Appelle Basin, Churchill River and Peitahigan — to its provincial government.

The Canadian Camping Association's meeting calendar for 1972-73, printed in Fall 1972, includes a National Camp Directors Workshop at Geneva Park, Ontario, 1-4 February 1973, titled "The Threat to Camping — What does Camping have to do to survive?", alongside the CCA Executive and National Standards Committee Workshop; the Ontario Camping Conference in Toronto 8-10 March 1973; and the CCA Canoe Instructors School, French section 1-10 June and English section 14-23 June, both in Ottawa.
