John Latimer's president's letter in Fall 1972 states the movement's own sense of crisis: "Camping is having difficulties... Government legislation and 'red tape'; increased operational and land costs; more competition; more alternatives for parents and children; less public awareness; higher standards... We are being threatened and we must do something about it!" The sense of crisis in Canadian camping is therefore firmly dated to the 1972-73 season, which is the frame in which any account of Kanawana's own difficulties in the 1970s should be written.

John Latimer reported in Fall 1972 that the Canadian Camping Association was lobbying Ottawa over the Opportunities for Youth / Perspectives-Jeunesse programme, expressing "deep concern over some of the projects relating to children and camping which were submitted to the Government" and wanting a closer liaison so the CCA could help select "only those leaders who are qualified and experienced," plus a complaint that national organisations were not permitted to submit project proposals to the Secretary of State. The two Montreal family camps recorded in the Spring and Summer 1972 issues were both Perspectives-Jeunesse-staffed.

Eanswythe Flynn's "Do It Now! A Camp Director's Check List" (Fall 1972) gives month-by-month duties for November to February, implying the shape of the camp year: staff engaged and "contracts signed and sealed" in January, out-of-town interviews arranged then, counsellor rules on "duties, responsibilities, time off, behaviour in camp and out of camp, supervision of campers and cabins" reviewed and discussed at February interviews, and agency camps advised in December to ask for surplus commodities, including "clearance of fire-damaged goods which can be used in arts and crafts."

David Keast of Camp Ponacka set out a camp naturalist's working method in Fall 1972: scout the site first, read everything, teach by question rather than statement, and "never be afraid to say 'I don't know', but be sure to add 'Let's look it up and find out'." He argues for stocking the nature hut mainly with domesticated animals — ducks, turkeys, chickens, pheasants, mice, white rats, gerbils, guinea pigs, rabbits, a goat — because campers want to handle animals and wild ones sicken in cages and carry rabies risk, with wild animals kept only a few days and released; the ratio given is ideally 6-8 campers per instructor.

Theron Kramer of Camp Edgewood argued in Fall 1972 that non-profit camps turning to off-season rentals to cover fixed costs "incurred both before and after the fee-paying campers are there to cover them" had an obligation to know what programmes the renting groups ran and to offer "professional consultation" over and above food and accommodation. His examples of who rented a camp in 1972: drum and bugle corps, a police detachment training school patrols, youth groups, senior citizens, boy scouts and church councils.

Brian Blackstock, Director of Camp Mazinaw, printed a model camp staff contract in Canadian Camping, Winter 1973, described as "a compilation of forms from a number of Camps," thanking the directors of Camps Oconto, Pinecrest, Ponacka, Timberlane, Wahcahmie and Wapomeo. Pinecrest is a Toronto YMCA camp, so at least one YMCA camp's contract is in the composite.

The 1973 model camp staff contract's conduct clause reads: staff must be "aware of the role you must play in maintaining good Public Relations in Camp and wherever you come in contact with the public. Conduct on your part which would reflect unfavourably on the Camp's reputation could be considered a breach of this contract." Its termination clause: "The Camp retains the right to terminate this agreement at any time without notice if, in our opinion, there is sufficient cause," with pro rata pay; resignation requires two weeks' notice.

The 1973 model camp staff contract makes optional, bracketed clauses of the following: that "'Drugs' have no place in Children's Camps and are not permitted"; that smoking is permitted only in specified areas and only when campers are not present; and that alcohol is not permitted in camp. It also brackets as optional that a staff member may be charged for damage due to their negligence and for loss or theft of their belongings, and that "Should you be unable to satisfactorily handle all of your responsibilities and, as a result, have some of them handled by another party, your salary may be adjusted accordingly."

"Two Approaches to Camp Staff Manuals" by Bruno Morawetz, Fred Dier and Don Groff, ex-Director of Camping for the Kitchener-Waterloo YMCA, printed an eight-part outline of what a camp staff manual contained in 1973. Under "Sample forms used at camp," alongside test sheets, tripping reports and parent reports, is "counsellor evaluation" — so a written counsellor evaluation was a standard, expected, template-driven part of camp administration in 1973, not an exceptional act.

The 1973 staff manual outline directs that the Discipline section state "meaning of discipline — what kinds of punishment, if any — factors in group discipline — building of esprit de corps — do's and don'ts of discipline." The phrase "what kinds of punishment, if any" is the period's own formulation, and stands beside the explicit prohibitions of physical punishment by MacCulloch (1969), Danson (1970) and Bruno Roy (1971) recorded elsewhere in this run.

The 1973 staff manual outline names what a camp was expected to write down about itself: "a brief historical sketch of the camp," statements of "traditions, philosophy," and "explanation of role that camping plays in the total program of the sponsoring organization, where such exists" — which is precisely the YMCA-of-Montreal section a Kanawana staff manual would have carried. Personnel policies were to cover "sickness allowance — employment and dismissal procedures — salary scales and payment procedure."

The bibliography of the 1973 camp staff manual outline is the profession's reading list: "Talks to Counsellors" by Dimock and Statten (Association Press); "The Camp Program Book" by Catherine Hammet; "The Call of Algonquin" by Mary G. Hamilton; "The Camp Counsellor's Book" by Northway and Lowes; "Summer Magic" and "Lights from a Thousand Campfires" by Kenneth Webb; "Camp Waterfront Programs and Management" by Pohndorf; plus OCA Conference Digests for 1966, 1967 and 1968 and Reports for 1971 and 1972. Its closing hint: "the tone of the Manual sets the tone of the future counsellor."

Ed. H. Devitt, former Director of Camp Comak, argued in Winter 1973 that a camp counsellor's manual should be mimeographed and loose-leaf rather than printed, because "a printed page is too final and discourages revision," and should never be finished but always evolving, compiled with contributions from campers, counsellors, senior staff and the director alike — "there is no reason to bring it down from on high, engraved on stone tablets." A working reason why few camp staff manuals survive in fixed, datable form.

Judy Richards of Camp Wahcahmie described a girls' camp Saturday council ring from inside in 1973: "Every Saturday night is Indian council ring which means a tribal gathering on council rock. We parade single file dressed in colourful blankets and Indian headdress to greet the Big Chief who then lights the council fire. We have three tribes. Each challenges the other to a feat of physical or mental skill." Sunday brought white shorts and shirts, outdoor chapel "under the arch of birch," and the camp leaving chapel singing the camp hymn, "God who touchest earth with beauty" — Mary S. Edgar's 1925 prize hymn.

Judy Richards's 1973 account of Camp Wahcahmie records cabin groups of six, a "Blue Moon Night" on which campers are woken at full moon with "Arise and come away with me" and paddle across the lake for a fire and marshmallows, a breakfast hunt with oranges hung in the pines and cereal boxes under the boughs, a Sunday regatta, cabin picnics and a sauna, and a canoe-trip send-off sung to "So Long We'll See You Again."

Canadian Camping, Winter 1973, printed "A Singing Grace" courtesy of Jack Pearse of Camp Tawingo, set to the tune Edelweiss: "Thank you, Lord, on this day, / For Your many great blessings... Glory to God. / May You hear our prayer." The mechanism — a devotional text fitted to a familiar popular tune — is identical to Kanawana's grace rotation set to Johnny Appleseed and to "Jeremiah was a Bullfrog," and a national magazine circulating one in 1973 is a plausible route by which such graces travelled between camps.

Taken together, the 1972 songbook appeal, Blackstock's composite staff contract, the staff manual outline, the OCA job-negotiation guidelines and the printed standards documents show a Canadian camp of the early 1970s running on shared, published forms rather than purely local practice. Where Kanawana's own paperwork is missing, the template it would have been built from is not.

Patricia M. Russell's "YaWaCa Comes Home" (Winter 1973) gives a dated institutional history of a YWCA camp: in 1962 the Vancouver YWCA studied the need and found a shortage of resident camping for girls in British Columbia; Camp YaWaCa began the following summer on rented premises at a seaside site on Howe Sound, moved repeatedly, and by its ninth year was two hundred miles inland on Okanagan Lake. In 1969 a task force began scouting for a permanent property; the old Bulman Farm on Salt Spring Island was leased from McMillan Bloedel Ltd., the farm surrounded by some twelve hundred acres of forest reserve, with capacity for forty-eight campers plus staff and all buildings winterised for year-round use.

Tanya Krisman was director of Camp YaWaCa from 1967 to 1972, succeeded by Mrs. Sally Schwetz in June 1972; on National Camping Day the camp's farmhouse was named "Skipper's Shack" in her memory, chosen by her daughter Pat, and the British Columbia Camping Association dedicated a memorial fund for the $5,000 renovation.

Camp YaWaCa's 1972 activity list includes "Hebertisme" — on Salt Spring Island, British Columbia. Claude Cousineau's 1969 account had over fifty pistes d'hebertisme in Quebec and none elsewhere in Canada. By the summer of 1972 a British Columbia YWCA camp was running one, so the practice crossed the country within three years.

Mrs. Sandy Hyman, M.S.W., Camp Co-ordinator of the Children's Aid Society of Winnipeg, reported in Winter 1973 that during 1971 the Society helped 862 unmarried mothers, of whom 54% kept their babies, and described two camp programmes: one for mothers who kept their children, begun in July 1970 with eight girls and their children placed into an existing session of Mothers' Camp at the United Church Fresh Air Camp at Gimli, 60 miles from Winnipeg, growing to twenty-eight girls and thirty-three children in 1971 and twenty-two and twenty-six in 1972; and Lifeline Camp for pregnant girls, sponsored by Greater Winnipeg Youth for Christ on an island in the Lake of the Woods, with ten girls in 1971 and eleven in 1972, none beyond the end of the seventh month.

Mrs. Teddy Hoyle died in the autumn of 1972; Peggy Latimer's tribute records that she was born on a riverboat in Kashmir, came to Canada in 1929, and about thirteen years after marrying John Hoyle — "The Major" — the couple founded Camp Gay Venture, Haliburton, Ontario, in 1946. After his death she continued at the camp, then at 60 bought a farm north of Toronto and began boarding and raising horses.

Claude Cousineau's "A Case for the 'Canadian Stroke'," printed in English and French in Winter 1973 from the CCA Canoeing School at Ottawa, compares five stern strokes — the "goon" (French: le coup du "touriste"), the "J," the "Indian," the "pitch" and the "Canadian" — with a four-phase diagram, citing Rutstrum (1958, 1964), Handle's Canoe Camping (1953), Riviere's Pole, Paddle and Portage (1969) and Malo (1969).

Claude Cousineau examined the term "Indian stroke" sceptically in 1973: "The origin of the term 'Indian' stroke is not clear. Some writers describe the Indians using this stroke to sneak up behind their enemies or to stalk prey. It is very doubtful that the Indians used it for long distances as it requires more energy to use the shoulder muscles as a fulcrum rather than the gunwale of the canoe." He kept the term "for a lack of a better term." He also recorded a camp custom: "In some camps the contact of the paddle with the gunwale is considered a very bad practice. The object is not a quiet and efficient stroke but rather to protect the canoe from wear and tear."

The Canadian Camping Association's executive meeting at Regina in November 1972 established an Awards Committee under the chairmanship of Bob Lazanik "for the purpose of recognizing those individuals who have strongly contributed to camping in Canada" — the Quebec vice-president chairing the national awards body. It also set National Camping Day for 18 July 1973, added a Maritimes canoe instructors' school organised by Bill Palmer to the existing Ottawa and Lake of the Woods schools, re-elected John Latimer for a second term, and approved in principle an investigation of an International Camping Workshop in Ottawa in 1975.

"Additional copies of the Centenary Journey Log are now available through the Canadian Camping Association Office," reported in Winter 1973 — the 1967 centenary publication was still in print and orderable six years later.

John Latimer ended his Winter 1973 president's message "The Camping movement is NOT 'in trouble'" — in the issue after the one that booked a national workshop titled "The Threat to Camping — What does Camping have to do to survive?" Both are the same man in successive issues.

John Walker of Cornwall, studying for a master's at York, was the recipient of the first Research Award of the Society of Camp Directors, reporting to its fall gathering on "professionalism and the training of Camp Directors."

The editor of Canadian Camping complained in Winter 1973: "for this Winter Edition, we have one article from B.C., one from Manitoba and the rest are from Ontario. Isn't it time to make this magazine a true Canadian one?" Ontario is therefore over-represented in the run by the editors' own admission, and the near-absence of Quebec English-camp material is partly an artefact of submission patterns rather than evidence about Quebec.

Eanswythe Flynn's "Do It Now!" checklist for May directs camp directors to "Find out from your provincial camping association whether or not this is your year for a Standards Visitation," confirming the two-to-three-year inspection cycle Lionel Perras described, and to "Send water samples (both drinking and swimming) regularly to Provincial Health Department" — a routine that would have generated a dated provincial paper trail for Lake Wilson.

Jack Eastaugh, Assistant to the Director of the Taylor Statten Camps, wrote in Canadian Camping, Spring 1973: "The Indian Council Ring Ceremony, devised by Ernest Thompson Seton in the years following the first great war and refined by Taylor Statten who taught the ceremonies to camp leaders in the 20's, needs no apology and is still viable today."

Kanawana's "Tribes of Kanawana in Council" script is dated c. 1925-1927 and its totem pole went up in 1927 — precisely the years in which, by Jack Eastaugh's 1973 account, Taylor Statten was teaching Ernest Thompson Seton's Council Ring ceremony to camp leaders. Eastaugh's list of the ceremony's standard parts — "the Fire Lighting, Peace Pipe Ceremony, Indian Games, Dances or Departure of Hiawatha" — is item for item what Kanawana's own scripts and The Green Triangle describe.

Jack Eastaugh records that campers remembered "a spine-tingling sensation at the close of the council ring when the entire group rose to sing 'Wakonda dhe dhu' — 'Father a needy one stands before thee; I who sing am he.'" Kanawana's c. 1925-27 script closes with "Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe," and the same deity name recurs in the staged chemical-flash firelighting of 21 July 1940. The words Kanawana campers chanted for at least fifteen years are therefore part of the same Seton-Statten text, and are a prayer of supplication. Recorded as Eastaugh's 1973 rendering, not as an independent translation.

Jack Eastaugh's 1973 defence of camp Indian Lore contains its own concession: "Candor is also required in levelling with the purist who can quite legitimately claim that Indian Lore in the summer camp is guilty of ignoring cultural facts. We have not limited ourselves to archaeological truths. We have stolen the tepee from the people of the plains, the grotesque and marvellously hideous masks of the Iroquois, the birch bark crafts of the Hurons and the rich and colourful designs of the West Coast Indians." His remedy is disclosure, not discontinuation: "there is nothing wrong with this practice as long as we recognize the source of our material and make the facts known to our campers." Recorded exactly as written and dated, not adopted in this project's voice.

Jack Eastaugh wrote in 1973 that "the Y.M.C.A. camps in Eastern and Western Canada for years have welcomed the participation of, and appreciated the contribution of local Indians in their programs," naming people from the Golden Lake, Couchiching, Georgian Bay, Brantford and Moosonee reserves working in Ontario camps. No Kanawana source has yet confirmed or denied a comparable practice at Kanawana.

Jack Eastaugh is frank in 1973 that the Council Ring ceremony works as religion: "why not admit that much of the appeal of the Indian Council Ring Ceremony is dependent upon the observance of primitive ceremonies and a reliance upon the mystery of the wild?" He notes that "the lighting of the fire and the Peace Pipe Ceremony are certainly prayers" and that reliance on Wakonda, "the one great knowing spirit of the universe," "has its counterpart in white society religion."

Jack Eastaugh states an operational requirement for the council ring: it "must be a total, all-camp program," because "distractions of any kind are 'killers'" and a few scoffers can conspire to interrupt the make-believe atmosphere. At Camp Ahmek the camp was split — eleven-and-under at one sitting, twelve-and-up at another — after early years of interference, and attendance was compulsory where theatre, chapel, musicales and movies were voluntary.

The Canadian Camping Association's Publications Service catalogue, printed over two pages in Spring 1973, lists "CANADA'S CENTENARY JOURNEY — the Centennial project of C.C.A. — a collectors' item — cross-Canada by canoe. 145 p. $2.00" — the first sighting with a page count, and enough to search a library catalogue with. Also listed: "ONCE THERE WAS A CAMPER — Mary Edgar's popular book of poems... 48 p. $1.75"; the 1972 Ontario Conference Digest "CAMP IS GROWING UP," 104 p. $4.50; and "COOKERY FOR KIDS, KAMP 'N KICKS" by Stewart, 81 p. $3.50. CCA members received a 10% discount.

J. Harry Ebbs, M.D., F.R.C.P., published an itemised list of medical supplies "suggested for a residential summer camp for children with an enrolment of about fifty to one hundred campers" in Spring 1973, including 500 ASA tablets, 100 ASA-and-codeine, 100 Phenobarbital (half grain), 100 Pyribenzamine, 100 Penicillin 250,000 units, 100 Triple Sulpha, 100 Achromycin capsules, 25 disposable hypodermic syringes and 25 needles, a folding stretcher, an electric steriliser, crutches, two bed pans, a locked metal cabinet and a small refrigerator; the attending doctor would additionally provide scalpel, suturing material, rubber gloves, local anaesthetic and narcotic drugs.

J. Harry Ebbs closed his 1973 camp infirmary list with an administrative expectation: "The director in consultation with the doctor should have suitable and adequate illness and accident record forms." Dated illness-and-accident records were therefore a professional expectation at camps of Kanawana's size in 1973 — another record class to ask Concordia about.

W. Bertram Danson, Director Emeritus of Camp Winnebagoe, described the camp tuck shop in Spring 1973 as "The only activity that was NOT included in our fee! Always an 'extra'." His policy: as many non-candy treats as possible because "anything containing sugar is not good for the teeth of a growing child"; never sell gum, because "gum always ends up on the underside of the tables, benches, bed rails or on the floors"; and camp T-shirts placed with a town outfitter rather than stocked, because "It has been our experience that it NEVER pays."

W. Bertram Danson describes the camp tuck card system exactly in 1973: a serial-numbered card about 3 by 5.75 inches, worth $5, with the camper's name and cabin number and boxes around the edge in 5-cent, 10-cent and 25-cent denominations punched out with a ticket punch as purchases are made; a $5, $10 or $15 tuck deposit billed with the spring camp fees; unspent money returned in an envelope as the camper boards the bus home. He also records paddles sold through the tuck shop "on which he can paint the OCA canoeing awards he has secured" — a documented practice of recording awards on a camper's own paddle.

Ron Johnstone, President of the Ontario Camping Association and Director of Camp White Bear, wrote in Spring 1973: "I have on my Camp Staff today the man who was my Camp Director when I was an eight year old... He is 76 years old" — named as C.T. Sharpe. Johnstone argued against the "ideal counsellor" model and denied there was a new morality: "today's youth can no longer stomach the double standard that society seems bent on expressing."

Ron Johnstone reported in Spring 1973 that 600 leaders in outdoor education had gathered at Dorset in October 1972, whose finding was that the experience should be "in small groups, in depth with trained leadership" — on which he remarked, "Camp directors of fifty years ago could have told us this!" He also cites Dr. John Rich at an OCA conference: "you can teach a camper how to paddle a canoe, but you cannot teach him how to spend time in a canoe — only the calm, peace, beauty and serenity of the country can do that."

Three consecutive presidential messages in Canadian Camping contradict one another on whether Canadian camping was in crisis: Fall 1972 books a workshop called "The Threat to Camping"; Winter 1973 says the movement is "NOT in trouble"; Spring 1973, after Geneva Park, is optimistic — "While it is true that some camps are closing and many are facing registration difficulties, we see in Canada that many new camps are opening... and that more children are going to camp." The swing is the record of the sector's mood in 1972-73 and should be recorded rather than resolved.

The Quebec Camping Association's delegation to the Canadian Camping Association's National Workshop at Geneva Park, 1-4 February 1973, promoted the Carnaval de Quebec with posters, its president Bob Lazanik presenting the editor with a replica Bonhomme, and the workshop's "warmest experience was the rousing singsong with Bob at the piano on the last evening."

The YWCA and YMCA held separate national meetings in Toronto on 4 February 1973 in conjunction with the Canadian Camping Association's National Workshop — so there was a national YMCA camping meeting that week, whose minutes, if they survive, are a place Kanawana could appear.

Paul Rushton's "Watch Those Pocket Rockets!" (Spring 1973) records that some Canadian camps ran model rocketry programmes, now governed by Amendment No. 13 of the Air Regulations and Aeronautics Act of Canada: no model rocket launch within 10 miles of any airport, control zone or aerodrome traffic zone, none into cloud, and none "unless a firing supervisor approved by the Royal Canadian Flying Clubs Association is present."

Eanswythe Flynn's "Do It Now!" for June (Spring 1973) directs that "Your Staff Manual should be distributed to all your staff members by the first week of June at the latest," and asks "Are campers' Health Forms and their Doctors' Certificates coming in? Have you enough file cards for your records?" — camper health records as a routine annual paper class at Canadian camps.

The Canadian Camping Association's board meeting at Vancouver in April 1973 resolved that "A new Committee, ARCHIVES, is to be established to gather material and documents to be housed at the University of Waterloo and made available to anyone in Canada and the world." This was the 1973 plan; by October 1976 Adele Ebbs, as chairman of the CCA Archives Committee, reported that a home had been found for the Canadian Camping Archives at Trent University in Peterborough, with F. M. Van Wagner's papers as the founding deposit. The destination changed in between.

Mary L. Northway, co-author of The Camp Counsellor's Book, wrote in Canadian Camping, Summer 1973: "One of the strange beliefs of our society is that it is wrong to be afraid. A counsellor who ridicules or condemns a child's fears may succeed only in having the child repress, rather than express them... Supernatural fears from spooky stories and myths about malicious ghosts have no place in the young camper's life, nor have unnecessary fears of night raids or hazing. There are enough things to be afraid of in the civilized, atomic world, that there is no need to produce artificial terrors."

Within eighteen months the same magazine printed a how-to for the camp hoax (Attfield, Spring 1972), a director naming "a hoax" among the traditions taught at pre-camp (Greenway, Spring 1972), and the country's leading authority on camp counselling stating that ghost stories have no place in a young camper's life (Northway, Summer 1973). A camp running a Chopsy in the 1970s was therefore doing something the profession was actively arguing about — a better documented fact than either approval or disapproval alone.

Mary Northway reduced the camp counsellor's requirements to two in Summer 1973 — the ability to camp and the ability to counsel — against a job description in which "The modern camp counsellor apparently should be a mixture of Superman and an archangel... trained, presumably at the graduate level in sociology, psychotherapy, group dynamics and perhaps even nuclear physics." On camping: "One has to be clever to live simply," skills being "important, not as ends, but means," and the counsellor "should know the value of time spent in doing nothing but watching... 'Program' is often so full there is no time left for living." On counselling: being "more interested in children than in himself."

The Canadian Camping Association reported at its April 1973 Vancouver board meeting that "The C.C.A. is having financial difficulties... Fees to C.C.A. have not increased for over 15 years," with the provincial associations asked to help cover "a deficit budget of over $2500 for the coming year." Each provincial president undertook to find an advertising agent to produce one page of advertising per issue of the magazine, "since the advertisements must pay for the printing of the magazine," and "all the advertisements appearing in the last three issues have been tracked down by Paul Rushton" alone.

The Canadian Camping Association reported in 1973 that it had "about 600 Member Camps serving some 400,000 campers" — a national scale figure, against Prime Minister Trudeau's "almost half a million" of the previous summer.

Claude Cousineau was appointed the Canadian Camping Association's liaison with the Ministry of Transport on the policy-forming committee regarding life jackets in April 1973, with every province asked to send him its views — a datable moment in how Canadian camp waterfront regulation was made. At the same meeting Val Willis accepted responsibility for putting together a National Code of Ethics, and Stan Wild reported the revised constitution circulating in both official languages with the final vote due no later than 30 October 1973.

Officer changes reported in Summer 1973: Ron Johnstone becomes regional vice-president as Jack Pearse moves to the board as the new president of the Ontario Camping Association; Gordon Stewart (Manitoba), Michael Pezderic (Saskatchewan) and Rev. Pere Rosaire Corbin (l'Association des camps du Quebec and QCA) join as new provincial presidents. John Latimer read telegrams of good wishes at the annual meeting from Mary S. Edgar and Pierre Trudeau.

Canadian Camping, Summer 1973, records: "A belated but gentle tip of our hat to another gracious lady who has, for many years, been a firm supporter of the Q.C.A. — Mrs. Alta Kahn. A richly deserved honour will be bestowed on her by Q.C.A. in May and our fall edition will feature an article about her."

Six letters on the Geneva Park National Workshop of February 1973, one per province, record its structure: camp directors chose three from eight workshops, among them "Recruiting Campers" led by Bruno Morawetz and "Funding" led by Ross Seaman, plus sessions on recruiting and training camp staff, on meeting the changes of society, and a Standards Workshop. Opening and closing were an audio-visual presentation by John Latimer and Jay Haddad and a final session featuring Mary Edgar and Ron Johnstone. Joy Rennick of New Brunswick records the formulation that came out of it: "Camping today is not one of physical survival but of psychological survival."

Doug Dent notes that "all sessions were recorded to allow for a written resume for all who attended" at the Geneva Park National Workshop of February 1973 — so a written record of that workshop, including A. Ross Seaman's session on funding, was produced and circulated, and is a findable document.
Yves Beauregard wrote the only French letter on the Geneva Park workshop, calling it "un pole important des professionnels que nous sommes... Apres tout, les camps... c'est nous!"

Jack Pearse's "Camp — An Oasis" (Summer 1973) records his return in spring 1973 to the camp where he first swam, tripped, held staff position and led a singsong, unvisited since 1953: the boathouse burned down and replaced by an outdoor theatre; the Tent Alley gone, with its "roughly-hewn archway" bearing the camp motto in logs, "I'm third" — God first, the other fellow second — replaced by cabins; and "a post that was once a corner of the stage was all that remained of the Council Ring." "I didn't know a single person I met in my stroll around my camp." But he found a rock painted "J.P. 1946" and heard a noon-hour singsong from song sheets he had compiled in 1941, including a song composed by his father in 1934 — "And I knew those songs as well as anyone in the dining hall."

Jack Pearse's conclusion in Summer 1973, quoted by John Latimer as the issue's keynote: "it is not a generation gap but a lack of common experience that creates a gap between people." He also cites Fiddler on the Roof for the defence of tradition — "Without our tradition, we are as shaky as a fiddler on the roof" — qualified: "If it is a good tradition, then it is worth keeping," set directly against Latimer's "certain traditions must be maintained — but they must make sense."

The Ontario Camping Association published "It's Wise to Supervise," advertised at $1.25 in Summer 1973 as "An authoritative discussion on Staff Supervision in Summer Camps" — a purchasable statement of what camp staff supervision was supposed to be in 1973, and the fifth period document on camp staff practice this read has found.

Mary S. Edgar composed three poems for the Geneva Park conference of February 1973, printed in Canadian Camping that summer — "An Everyday 'Thank-You'," "A Camp Vesper Prayer" and "The Bumble Bee" — with an editor's note that she "has provided extra copies of these poems for distribution" on request; Doug Dent's National Camping Day programme then recommended "A Camp Vesper Prayer" as "a fitting part of the evening." Edgar was eighty-four.

National Camping Day 1973 was set for Wednesday 18 July, culminating at 9:30 p.m. Daylight Saving in each time zone — a change from 1972's single simultaneous instant, because "some camps prefer not to be restricted and some may not be so physically located." A song list was printed and circulated from the CCA office to every member camp: "This Land is Your Land," "It's a Long Road to Freedom," "Get Together," "My Country is My Cathedral," "Four Strong Winds," "Sounds of Silence," "As I Open the Door," "Happy Wanderer," "Jacob's Ladder" and "Something to Sing About, This Land of Ours."

The editor's note on National Camping Day 1972 is blunt: "the response last summer was rather disheartening... the bulk of the response coming from the Girl Guides and Ontario." National Camping Day was therefore largely ignored outside Ontario, and the absence of any recorded Kanawana observance is unsurprising rather than significant.

Jack Pearse ran the whole pre-camp week at Camp Tawingo under one theme, "A happy Camper is...", each session leader prefacing his presentation with it — "A happy camper is a healthy camper" from the health director, "a singing camper" from the music director — with staff given a "MATCHED" button, the letters standing for Make A Tawingo Camper Happy Every Day.

Bruno Morawetz's "Make Your Own Paddles" (Summer 1973), demonstrated at the OCA conference by one of his campers, specifies clear basswood free from knots, a rough 1 by 6 inch board six feet long, and a method of tracing an existing paddle, sawing relief cuts about 6 inches apart, roughing out with drawknife or chisel, shaping blade and grip first and leaving the shaft square until they are finished, and finishing with several coats of linseed oil — "stay away from varnish altogether." Paddles were also made at Camp Ponacka from maple and black cherry.

Dr. Bruce Bocking of Camp Ponacka opened "Campcraft Can Be Fun" (Summer 1973) with an accusation directors would recognise: they "search diligently for months looking for a super qualified instructor to head their swimming programme... but then turn around and, at the last minute, quickly hire one or two counsellors who are relatively inexperienced to instruct in campcraft." He describes a survival hike in which the most experienced campers were dropped in pairs at isolated sites for 48 to 72 hours with "only the clothes on their back, a survival kit and an axe," campers "unable to cope in foreign situations" screened out.

Camp Ponacka's "Diplomacy Day," printed in Summer 1973 as a replacement for "traditional Sunday afternoon programs such as Gold rush Day and Olympic Day," divided the camp into countries of about fifteen campers and two counsellors, each given a disproportionate share of raw materials and 100 "Ponax," with a Central Trade Board manned by counsellors and counsellors as ship captains and truck drivers to prevent border-hopping. Each country was given five bombs (painted sticks), each dropped costing the victim 5 Ponax, with losing nations forming alliances to pool bombs against the leader.

R. M. Semple, Director of Dietetics at Humber Memorial Hospital, wrote in Summer 1973: "if I were to ask you the actual food cost per camper per day, doubtless no one would know," recommended standardised recipes and making the camp nurse responsible for daily kitchen sanitation inspection, and added two harder passages — "Most camps are over-staffed and over-paid. If you hire students on an ego trip, that's all you will get," and "Look at the possibility of hiring some of your campers to do some of the kitchen duties, e.g., floors and dishes. You could pay them at student rates or make allowances on the price of the vacation."
The Saskatchewan Camping Association was six years old in the spring of 1973, so founded in 1967.

W. Bertram Danson advertised himself as a camping consultant in the classified pages of Canadian Camping, Summer 1973: "Director with over 25 years experience in all phases of camping, able to come to your assistance!"

On 23 May 1973 the Quebec Camping Association's English Section made Mrs. Alta R. Kahn the first Honorary President in the Association's history; the tribute read on that occasion, printed in Canadian Camping, Fall 1973, is the fullest internal history of the Quebec association in this run.

Alta R. Kahn began with the Quebec Camping Association in 1946; in 1958 she chaired the joint QCA/CCA conference and "courageously suggested that the Quebec Camping Association celebrate its 'coming-of-age' party by holding, for the first time, its Conference in a hotel." A twenty-first birthday in 1958 puts the Quebec Camping Association's founding at 1937 — independent corroboration of the date this project holds from archival sources.

Alta R. Kahn was Co-Chairman of the Quebec Camping Association's Standards Committee in 1959-60, "when inspection of camps and accreditation were in the pioneer stage." This pushes Quebec camp accreditation back to 1959-60, several years before the 1965 round under Murray McFarlane that this read had as the earliest documented. Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp, and the accreditation machinery existed earlier than the project had assumed.

Alta R. Kahn was President of the Quebec Camping Association's English Section from 1960 to 1962 and simultaneously a CCA executive member; she was "a major contributor to the realization of the founding of the Provincial Board (co-ordinating body of the English and French Sections), and served as the Board's second President from 1963 to 1965."

"It was through Mrs. Kahn's efforts that the Quebec Camping Association finally secured its Provincial Charter in 1961" — a checkable corporate fact, which Quebec's register of enterprises should hold.

In 1973 Alta R. Kahn was still Chairman of the Quebec Camping Association English Section's Standards Committee, Co-Chairman of the joint QCA-ACQ Provincial Board Standards Committee, and a member of the Canadian Camping Association's National Standards Committee, credited with having "assisted greatly in the establishing of Standards in the French-speaking Camps."

Alta R. Kahn's career before camping, as given in the 1973 tribute: in 1908 the first Jewish teacher to graduate from Macdonald College, then five years teaching; 1909 active in Zionist work and the first campaign of the Federation of Jewish Charities; 1918 a founder of Montreal Hadassah; 1920 organiser of the first Junior Hadassah chapter in Canada; 1928-30 vice-president of the Eastern Division of Canadian Hadassah; 1931-33 its Chairman of Education; 1936-45 Executive Director of the Young Women's Hebrew Association; and 1946-49 Executive Secretary of the Jewish Community Camps (B'nai B'rith, Jewish Laurentian Fresh Air, and Wooden Acres), during which she "instituted many new projects, including the first Pre-Camp Training Programs for Staff."
Mary S. Edgar died on 17 September 1973. Mary L. Northway's memorial in Canadian Camping, Fall 1973, is the fullest account of her in the run.

Mary Northway records the moment the Glen Bernard programme was invented. Aged about eleven in April 1922 she was taken to tea to meet the woman starting a girls' camp, having announced "I'll only stay five minutes because I'm not going to her silly camp," and told Edgar about the Knights' club she had founded and her secret love of poetry. Edgar replied: "Well, we won't have Knights at camp but we will have Indians. Perhaps you would help me organize the tribes," and offered her the chance to write poetry "for the Scroll which would be read out in Council Ring."

Mary Northway's 1973 memorial adds biographical facts about Mary S. Edgar: her parents Joseph and Mary Edgar settled Sundridge in 1885, before the railway, running the general store; her father went into lumbering and later became M.P.P. for the District of Parry Sound; her sisters were Margaret (Gilchrist), Anne and Betty (McTavish); her nephew John Gilchrist and his wife Barb took over Glen Bernard in 1955; she was made Honorary Reeve of Strong, Joly Township and Sundridge in 1967; and as a centennial project she bought the "High Rock" property and made it a park for the village "because the cottagers have taken all the lakeshore and the village people have no campsite of their own." She is buried at Sundridge.

Mary Northway records a near-complete unpublished manuscript by Mary S. Edgar on her family's early days, under the working title "Turn of the Century for Suzanne Marie," and calls its publication "a challenge to the Canadian Camping Association" — a findable lost document.

Mary Northway writes that Mary S. Edgar was "the right person to initiate and become first editor of the Canadian Camping Bulletin (February 1949, and remained such until April 1953. The Bulletin has evolved into this Magazine.)" Charles Plewman credits Edgar as first editor of the earlier Ontario bulletin financed by the T. Eaton Company, and dates the first printed national magazine to February 1949. The two accounts are reconcilable but are separate claims from separate witnesses, and neither is being used to settle the other.

Mary Northway states that Mary S. Edgar had recently established a trust fund for publications of the Canadian Camping Association, and was made Honorary President of the CCA in April 1960. The same issue's masthead reads "The Canadian Camping Association is indebted to The NEATHERN Trust for its support of 'Canadian Camping' through a substantial donation to assist in the publication of this issue," and Brian Blackstock's 1972 age-group study was financed by the same Neathern Trust. Whether the Neathern Trust is Edgar's publications fund is not stated anywhere and is not assumed here.

Mary S. Edgar's last public address was at the National Camp Directors and Camping Standards Workshop at Geneva Park in February 1973: "I don't know whether you realize how fortunate you are in just having the Canadian Camping Association," followed by three of her own poems, her favourite quotation — "To the worker who can dream and the dreamer who can work, life surrenders all things" — and a standing ovation. The Glen Bernard camp hymn she wrote in 1924 was sung at her funeral.

The Canadian Camping Association abandoned National Camping Day in 1973: the president's message states "National Camping Day will not be held again until 1976," and the news column gives the evaluation that killed it — "The Committee mailed out approximately 600 evaluation forms to member camps across Canada and received 48 replies indicating that 24 camps participated, 24 did not." Of roughly 600 member camps, twenty-four are known to have taken part, so the absence of any recorded Kanawana observance is not evidence of anything.

Stan Wild reported in Fall 1973 that "sufficient votes were received by the deadline date, Nov. 20th, to approve the new Constitution" of the Canadian Camping Association, to be instituted by the April 1974 annual meeting, with a National Vice-President to be elected by 31 January 1974. He credited Quebec for the bilingual text: "It is completely bilingual, accomplished by our friends in Quebec, Yves Beauregard in particular."

The Canadian Camping Association's 1973 government relations, as reported by John Latimer: dialogue continuing with the Secretary of State, Hon. Hugh Faulkner, on Opportunities for Youth grants and camping programmes; communication with Hon. Robert Andras, Manpower and Immigration, concerning foreign students, with no indication yet whether "another year's exemption will be granted" — a live employment-law issue for camps hiring foreign staff in 1974; and continuing financial support from Recreation Canada.

A "Central Information Bureau" under Brian Blackstock was announced in Fall 1973, to be built from provincial reports, documents, research papers and books solicited by the president — a second national collecting effort alongside the archive the CCA planned to deposit at the University of Waterloo.

The Quebec Camping Association / Association des camps du Quebec conference for 1974 was set for the Queen Elizabeth Hotel, Montreal, 28-30 March — a joint English-and-French provincial conference in Kanawana's own city. The Canadian Camping Association's own 1974 calendar also included a National Workshop at Camp Richildaca near Toronto, 26-28 February, with emphasis on day camping standards, and its Board and Annual Meeting at St. John's, 25-26 April.

Helen Stewart met Chief Dan George at the Toronto Camping Show in 1973, where his voice over a loon's cry had been used in radio advertising: "To set up camp beside a lake or stream, to know the freedom of the winds, the dancing of the sun on the water, it makes my heart soar like an eagle." She told him "about the many campers across Canada and our keen interest in Indian Lore," and he inscribed his photograph "To all campers of Canada." The note gives him as Honorary Chief of the Squamish and Shuswap, Academy Award nominee for Old Lodge Skins in Little Big Man, twenty-seven years a longshoreman, and recently awarded the Human Relations Award by the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews.

Mors Kochanski's "Winter Wilderness Survival" (Canadian Camping, Fall 1973) is an early published piece by the freelance instructor who later became the standard authority on northern bushcraft. Its governing formulation: "a person of average health can last four days without water and ten times longer with unlimited drinking water. It is the cold that makes the difference because, in general, the cold may allow an hour of survival for each day of survival in the summer." Being prepared means "carrying matches and an axe with a handle at least 28 inches long and a head at least 3 lbs."

Mors Kochanski's 1973 survival article states that "it takes an average of five days for a search to get underway when someone realizes that you are missing"; that three of anything signals distress and one of anything is the answer; that "Their greatest asset at that moment was time and the situation could best be handled by 'hibernating' rather than frenzied activity... Once you lose your will to live, the inevitable will happen"; and that "As the bush is neutral, neither for nor against you, it will be up to you what you get out of it."

Brian Blackstock's "Extend Your Season by Winterizing" (Fall 1973) describes how a Canadian camp converted a summer cabin for off-season school and community use: choose a building close to a water source, preferably with sleeping quarters separate from living and dining; work done by "former staff or friends who would like to 'get away from it all and do something'"; electric heating, "not as expensive as we were warned it would be"; and a wall build-up of stapled insulation, a plastic moisture barrier, tar paper stapled horizontally, then unfinished pine boards nailed a quarter to half an inch apart so the tar paper shows.

Kirk Wipper reviewed "Outdoor Education — 'Without Boundaries', Proceedings of the International Conference in Outdoor Education held at Camp Kandalore and the Forest Technical School, 28 September - 1 October 1972," conducted "for nearly six hundred persons" and available from Wipper at the University of Toronto for $3.00 plus 50 cents postage; its contents include summaries of the Chapel Service and an Indian Council night, and a full list of speakers and delegates. Ron Johnstone placed the same October 1972 gathering of 600 outdoor-education leaders at Dorset; the two locations are both in the Haliburton area and the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved.

Tony Fry of the YMCA of Metropolitan Toronto Camping Service advertised in Fall 1973 for a Director of an Ontario co-ed resident camp of one hundred six-to-ten-year-olds and thirty staff, minimum twenty-five years of age — a YMCA co-ed camp directorship specification from 1973.

Canadian Camping's subscription rose from $3 to $4 a year and single copies from $1 to $1.25 with the Fall 1973 issue; the editor admitted the editorial committee "with the exception of two people... is Ontario-oriented," and reported that the CCA's fee income "has for several years been around the $3000.00 figure, but it is now quite unrealistic."

Al Knox, former Director of Camp Wanakita, wrote in Canadian Camping, Winter/Spring 1974: "If you want to pursue the concept of participative camping further I recommend that you read Hedley G. Dimock's address to the Canadian Camping Association meeting (March 2-4, 1967), 'Canadian Camping — Its Resistance to Change'. Hedley discusses these concepts in depth from the perspectives of 1) camper development and 2) the function and influence of the camp director."

Canadian Camping's own April 1967 conference report records: "the delegates were in a position to hear Dr. Hedley Dimock's keynote address on the Individual. From 'Springboard No. 1' Dr. Dimock lectured to camp directors urging them to change from repressive to participative methods of programming. In the 'Feedback' sessions the directors 'participated' by getting back at him."

A Manitoba camp director wrote in Canadian Camping, Autumn 1967: "Heavily impressed by Hedley Dimock at the Canadian Camping Association Conference we are introducing some measure of participatory camping at the camp this year."

Hedley G. Dimock, who spent 1960-61 studying counsellor effectiveness at Camp Kanawana, gave the March 1967 Canadian Camping Association keynote address "Canadian Camping — Its Resistance to Change," which put "participative camping" into the working vocabulary of Canadian camp directors; camps were still citing it by name seven years later. The address itself has not yet been located; the OCA Conference Digests for 1966-68 and the CCA's own archive are where to look.

Al Knox's 1974 statement of participative camping distinguishes "a more traditional style in which the benefits of good camp program are stressed" from "a more 'participative' style in which program is seen as a tool to help the participant learn more about himself" — the difference being "the extent to which program is seen as a goal or as a tool." His challenge to camps: "How many of our camps or programs are evaluated on the extent (or the effort made) to which such growth has been achieved versus evaluation based on number of participants, degree of fun (alone)? For that matter, do criteria exist in our evaluation processes to measure such personal development?"

Al Knox names three participative mechanisms tried at Camp Wanakita: camper councils open to any interested camper ("Don't sell the junior campers short. You will find that they have the creative ideas — not being hindered by tradition"); a three-phase system in the junior section moving from counsellor-planned programme, to campers and counsellors planning together, to campers planning as a group with the counsellor "assuming a truly advisory role"; and decentralised cabin-centred seniors where "counsellors are challenged to be 'advisors' vs. leaders."

Madelene Allen, Director of Camp Ouareau and a member of the Quebec Camping Association Standards Committee, described the provincial standards from inside an accredited Quebec camp in Winter/Spring 1974: "We, in Quebec, are familiar with our provincial standards. We view this tome in different lights depending on the time of year... Even though we know we have done our best, we view it with slight trepidation as we leaf through its pages the night before the visitor is expected."

Madelene Allen gave the Quebec standards document and its marking scheme to her five CITs at the six-week point of their training, in pairs, a week each on different sections: they interviewed the director with pencil and notebook, shadowed senior staff, were given the records of programmes and staff lists, and "inspected the waterfront, examined the canoes, counted the toilets, and checked the outlets of the septic tanks after a heavy rain." This is what a Quebec standards visitation covered in 1974, and it confirms there was a written marking scheme as well as a standards document.

Rev. Philip A. Giberson of the Saint John Valley Bible Camp, New Brunswick, summed up twenty-five years of watching camping change in Winter/Spring 1974: "I have watched the changes in camping patterns in the past 25 years and see little change in the actual camper. They still want camping and not glorified entertainment."

Neil Graham of Pioneer Ranch Camp defines a wide game in Canadian Camping, Winter/Spring 1974, as "a game involving large teams of people over a large area of land," credits Joe Curry as "the basic 'brain' behind many of these games," and sets out Capture the Flag in full: two teams, territories with a clearly marked boundary, flags placed in a circle of flour or toilet paper and visible from a stated distance, attackers "killed" by having an article seized — "a crepe paper arm band, a piece of adhesive off the forehead, a hat" — and a prisoner's base freed by a comrade touching a prisoner without being caught.

Neil Graham's 1974 wide-game design principles include: make sure everyone can play to the end and that "people are 'recycled'"; "try to design your games so there is a role for the quieter, non-athletic campers"; make the scores high; check the ground beforehand and "get rid of barbed wire, open wells, dangerous holes"; "Night games in the bush are dangerous. Emphasize skulking at night rather than running. You've got to be sneaky, not fast"; and "get the whole camp excited about the game ahead of time, by having some kind of confrontation between the teams before the game — even just a put-on fight or verbal attack between the leaders will help to polarize feeling in the camp." Wide games were "generally given some added meaning by involving a theme taken from past or contemporary history" — the same device as Kanawana's Lumbermen and Voyageurs.

Neil Graham records a co-ed convention and its reception in 1974: "In Co-ed games we sometimes make a rule that only girls can attack other girls, but often the girls want to be 'liberated' from the role!"

Arnold R. Cohen described a 1973 "Earth Day" at the Y.M.H.A.-B'nai B'rith camp on Lake of the Woods — 120 boys and girls aged 9 to 16 in three two-week sessions. Campers were woken at 11 p.m. for a mass assembly and the film The Rise and Fall of the Great Lakes, with an oil drum hung in effigy and a scroll proclaiming Earth Day; at breakfast staff read world news bulletins every two or three minutes; swimming and canoeing instructors then presented what Lake of the Woods would be like in 1980; and the whole camp was taken by canoe and chartered boat to a littered public island and cleaned it. The argument put to the campers: "it really does not matter if we personally litter... The result affects us."

Sam G. Hambly of Camp Allsaw published a buildable year-round camp composting unit in Winter/Spring 1974 — quarter-inch aspenite panels 2 by 4 feet in 2 by 2 frames bolted into a square, two squares making a two-storey unit, a plywood lid and a plastic lid that "conserves moisture and keeps out flies in summer weather. It also enables the facility to be used as a hotbed for growing seedlings in the spring," a 4-to-1 mix of organic waste to farm manure, and a bottomless plastic garbage pail set in the centre to funnel fresh waste to the bottom of the mass. His framing: "If Youth as citizens, electors and legislators are to solve environmental problems on which survival depends, it seems logical that practical experience be provided at an early age... Camp is a good place for this experience."

Viiu Kanep of Camp Wapomeo wrote to contracted counsellors in mid-winter 1974 against amateur psychology: "So often, inexperienced counsellors feel they should carry out psychological experiments with their cabin group, or use each camper as a case study for a sociological report... In my opinion this is not summer camp counselling." Her self-audit runs under six headings including self discipline and discipline: "no matter what your philosophy is, you must have the ability to say 'NO'. Saying 'YES' to everything does not automatically make you a good counsellor."

Viiu Kanep's 1974 list of what a counsellor should prepare before camp includes a stock of bedtime and rainy-day stories from the public library; a long list of songs, because "a singing camp is a happy camp"; group games for every size and energy level; knowledge of the camp's own surroundings, "points of interest and areas of historical importance"; local natural history; the weather; and the night sky.

Paul Belanger began reporting the Quebec scene in French in Canadian Camping in 1974, recording that Yves Beauregard, "directeur executif permanent de l'A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. depuis plusieurs annees," had been appointed Directeur du Camp des Enfants Infirmes (Societe des Enfants Infirmes du Quebec) — so the joint Quebec association had a permanent paid executive director.

From January 1974 the ACQ-QCA ran several training courses for camp monitors, basic and specialist, in both Quebec City and Montreal, "en grande partie subventionnes par le Haut-Commissariat a la Jeunesse, aux Loisirs et aux Sports du Gouvernement du Quebec" — a provincially subsidised camp-staff training system in Kanawana's own province. The theme of the 28-30 March 1974 ACQ-QCA congress at the Reine Elisabeth, Montreal, was "Une Dynamique du Changement."

Kirk Wipper received an Ontario Government plaque in 1973 for his contribution during the Queen's visit: the International Museum of Canoes and Kayaks, "located adjacent to Camp Kandalore in Dorset," provided a Canot du Maitre, "known as the Montreal canoe" — 36 feet long, entirely birch bark and natural material, no nails — with paddles and sail, for the pageant at Old Fort William.

The Canadian Camping Association's canoe schools for 1974: Atlantic at Camp Wapomeo, Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, 10-19 June, Susan Cousineau director; English Eastern at the University of Ottawa camp at Gracefield, Quebec, 30 May-8 June, Doug Wipper; French Eastern at the same site 10-19 June, Gaston Lemire; Mid-West at Camp B'nai B'rith, Kenora, 1-10 June, Jim King; Western at Camp Chief Hector, Banff, 19-28 June, Claude Cousineau and Kirk Wipper.

John Latimer's president's message of Winter/Spring 1974 is a sustained complaint — "I'm frustrated, discouraged and just plain mad!" — against "phony make-work programs of certain Governments — programmes which allow some incompetent teenagers to operate Camps on their own, at salaries which Camps are unable to afford," against the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and, substantively, against the camping movement having let outdoor education be taken from it: "Since the beginning of the Century, Camps have been in the field of Outdoor Education. Now some outsiders have found a label... And that's our fault! We let Camps sit idle, complain about high costs, and watch School Boards build elaborate, beautiful Outdoor Education Centres."

Jocelyn Palm, writing as the new Managing Director in Canadian Camping, November 1974: "In the last three years, the magazine was financially sliding downhill to the extent that an unrealistic portion of the CCA budget was consumed to keep Canadian Camping coming off the press. As a result of this situation, the Board of Directors temporarily suspended publication of future magazines effective in February 1974." A Task Force was appointed at once and reported to the April 1974 board meeting.

The run of Canadian Camping is not continuous across 1974: Vol. 26 No. 2 is a combined "Winter/Spring 1974" issue, then nothing until Vol. 27 No. 1, November 1974. The gap is a real suspension of publication, not a hole in this project's holdings.

The 1974 Task Force on Canadian Camping reported six findings: direct mail to members essential; a newspaper format rejected because it "would not serve as an effective reference tool for schools and camp staffs nor would it be as appealing to advertisers"; the magazine format retained "because of the public relations values"; content to "inform and educate in order to upgrade camp directors and staffs in all provinces"; "the information should be as bilingual as possible"; and the magazine to be self-supporting "and be set up on a more professional basis." The new masthead was Managing Director Jocelyn Palm, Editor Helen Stewart, Circulation Manager Mary Pat Bradbury, Advertising Manager Doug Dent, Directory Issue Peter Gilbert; subscription $5 a year, $1.50 a copy.

Canadian Camping announced in November 1974 that "the January Issue of the magazine should be a 'Directory Issue' and contain a complete listing of all CCA Member Camps in each province along with the full editorial content... The Directory Issue has been accepted by all provinces and over 20,000 copies will be issued as the next magazine."

The January 1975 Directory Issue of Canadian Camping lists Kanawana: the directory line reads "KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)," with St. Sauveur des Monts and a "c/o Kamp Kanawana" address nearby. This is the first direct Kanawana appearance in the 1970s stretch of this read.

Robert P. Attfield's "Things Go Better With... Good Public Relations" (November 1974) lists what a parent should find in a camp brochure: director's qualifications; camp philosophy; camp location and physical structure; number and sex of campers accommodated; religious or other ties; number and qualifications of staff; fee scale; activities offered; length of camping periods; transportation routes and arrangements; information on communications; nearby lodging and visitors' day; description of meals and camp policies; and a guide to clothing and weather conditions. That is a checklist for reading any surviving Kanawana brochure of the period, and for knowing what is missing from one.

Robert Attfield printed a dismissal anecdote as a cautionary example in November 1974: "If it becomes necessary to dismiss a staff member, how is the situation handled? Not too long ago in one camp a counsellor was told over the loudspeaker system to leave the premises within an hour!" It is offered as a public-relations failure rather than an ethical one, and records both that summary dismissal happened and how the profession judged that handling of it.

Robert Attfield's 1974 guidance on counsellor conduct off site: dress the group properly leaving camp because "Campers fitted out like hobos for a canoe excursion won't feel like voyageurs, and may give the impression that they come from a shoddy camp"; the local store owner "acts as a barometer of good or bad will"; ask permission to cross private land; telephone ahead before visiting a neighbouring camp. For directors: invite local residents to camp shows, join the area cottagers' association, buy food and supplies locally "if it is financially feasible," tell neighbours what camp facilities they may use in an emergency, and keep photographs of cabin groups hung "in a suitable area for permanent display" as "a good historical camp record."

Roger Coles, former Director of Camp Belwood, Belwood, Ontario — "the first camp in Ontario operated by the Ontario Association for the Mentally Retarded," founded 1956 — described in November 1974 how for five weeks each summer the camp became "Belwood Lodge" for adults, who "like other adults... get time off from jobs" and come "as full persons — persons with the need of self-worth, the need to feel useful, the need of responsibility," with counsellors becoming "resource staff and friends," choice of activity "paramount," and the operation running under a Lodge Council elected at the start of each session. Terminology recorded as written in 1974.
entities: Ontario Association for the Mentally Retarded

facts.claim: Jocelyn Palm's Alert: Aquatic Supervision in Action, "the textbook of The National Lifeguard Service," was published by the Royal Life Saving Society Canada at $5.95 with a French edition due December 1974; its chapters include "Liability for Swimming Accidents and Drownings" and "Regulations, Legislation and Good Sense." Palm was by then Executive Director of the Canadian National Branch of the RLSS and Managing Director of Canadian Camping.

Rev. Morley G. Clarke's "Church Camping Futuribles" (November 1974) prints sixteen future scenarios written as cards for a learning game played at a Presbyterian camping consultation in February 1974. The pessimistic one: "Legislation may force some camps to close down because of exorbitant costs — e.g., full taxation; minimum wage requirements for all leaders, including Counsellors; unattainable accommodation requirements; unattainable acreage standards; school boards may buy up some of our Church Camps to use for outdoor education programs; Churches may rent them back as needed." Others foresee language immersion camps in Quebec, consolidation of less effective camps into larger operations, year-round sites with a full-time director, and "camping without camps" run out of a church hall.

J. A. Craig's camp astronomy programme in Canadian Camping, November 1974, lists Canadian observatories and planetariums for camp use, giving for Montreal the Royal Astronomical Society centre and the Dow Planetarium at 1000 St. James Street West.

Provincial officer changes recorded in November 1974: Val Willis is President of the Quebec Camping Association English Section, Abbe Rosaire Corbin heads the joint association and Abbe Robert Maisonneuve the section francaise; Rev. Philip Giberson is president in New Brunswick and Barbara Taylor in Newfoundland — the first woman president named in that province in this run.

The Canadian Camping Association's national Directory Issue of January 1975 lists Kanawana as printed: "KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA); Director Derek V. Walsh; Summer: P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts, Que. (514-227-2414); Winter office: 1441 Drummond St., Montreal, H3G 1W5 (514-849-5331); Activities: Tripping, Swimming, Sailing, Arts & Crafts, C.I.T. Program; Accommodation: 90 boys 8-15 / 90 girls 8-15." It is filed in the Quebec grouped index under "Organizational Residential — Co-ed."

The Quebec Camping Association's own accredited-camp listing, printed nationally in 20,000 copies in January 1975, gives Kanawana's founding year as 1894 — the camp's own claim as the provincial association held it.

Kanawana's January 1975 directory entry gives its registered capacity as 90 boys aged 8 to 15 and 90 girls aged 8 to 15 — exactly equal capacity by sex — and the Quebec Camping Association classified it as co-ed. This is the camp's own registered capacity rather than an inference that it had become co-educational by that date.
Kanawana's January 1975 directory entry lists a C.I.T. programme among its five headline activities, alongside tripping, swimming, sailing and arts and crafts.

The January 1975 national directory lists Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye as a separately accredited camp in its own right: "LES VOYAGEURS DE LA VERENDRYE (YMCA); Director Derek V. Walsh; c/o Kamp Kanawana, P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts, Quebec (514-227-2414); Winter: 1441 Drummond St., Montreal H3G 1W5; Activities: Wilderness, Canoe Trips, Fishing, Campcraft; Accommodation: 15 boys 13-17 / 5 girls 13-17." The La Verendrye canoe trip programme was therefore, in the eyes of the Quebec Camping Association, a distinct wilderness camp operating out of the Kanawana site, with fifteen boys' and five girls' places for ages 13 to 17.
Kanawana's winter office in January 1975 was 1441 Drummond Street, Montreal H3G 1W5, telephone 514-849-5331 — the YMCA of Montreal's address.

The January 1975 directory carries a SEASON/FEES column, but in the OCR of the cached scan it appears as a floating block of dates and prices detached from their rows. Kanawana's season and fee are present on the printed page but are not safely attributable from the OCR, and are recoverable only from the scanned images.

The Quebec association's own corporate history, printed in both languages in the January 1975 directory: "The QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION INC. — L'ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC INC. is a bilingual non-profit organization incorporated under Quebec law, January 23rd, 1961. The English Section was started in 1937, and was incorporated by Federal Charter in 1949. It is affiliated with the CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION."

The Quebec Camping Association's English Section was incorporated by Federal Charter in 1949 and the joint bilingual association by Quebec provincial charter on 23 January 1961 — two separate incorporations twelve years apart, federal then provincial. The 1949 federal charter is previously unrecorded in this project, and it explains how a body founded in 1937 could describe itself as newly chartered in 1961 without contradiction.

The joint Quebec association's officer list of January 1975 gives its Past Presidents as M. Lionel Perras, M. Tony Shorgan, Mme N.D. Demetelin, Mme Alta R. Kahn and H. Capt. Abbe Raoul Cloutier, and lists Cloutier separately as an Honorary Member alongside Jules Leavitt, Q.C. The rank "H. Capt." — Honorary Captain, a military chaplaincy title he still carried in 1975 — independently corroborates the wartime service Claude Cousineau described. The founder of hebertisme in Quebec presided over the province's camping association and was still an honorary member of it in the year Kanawana was accredited by it.

John Hasell, Chairman of the Canadian Camping Association's National Standards Committee, wrote in January 1975 that re-accreditation intervals varied "with some provinces requiring a visit every two or three years, but Quebec has developed its programme to the point where every camp is re-accredited annually" — repeated in French as "quelques-uns sont raccredites tous les deux ou tous les trois annees tandis qu'au Quebec chaque camp est raccredite chaque annee."

If Quebec re-accredited every camp annually, then a written visitation report on Kanawana exists for every year of its accreditation rather than one every two or three years — a series, not a document. Combined with Quebec accreditation dating to the pioneer years of 1959-60 and Madelene Allen's account of what a visitation covered, the shape of the missing record is an annual, itemised, externally written assessment of Kanawana's administration, personnel practices, site, programme, health and safety, running from about 1960.

John Hasell specifies what a 1975 accreditation visitation covered: written and implemented objectives; "sound financial control... through the use of budgets, financial statements and properly maintained accounts, records and inventories"; insurance including comprehensive liability, motor vehicle, fire and theft, passenger hazard, health and workmen's compensation; that "the visitation or accreditation team will make certain that the camp publicity is accurate and not misleading"; programme; facilities, site, equipment and transportation; diet and feeding; and staff, with "at least one experienced camp director who will be able to assess the effectiveness and competence of the staff." His framing: visitations are "regarded not so much as an inspection as a consultative service," and "Standards do not mean standardization."

The Quebec Camping Association English Section's officer list of January 1975 names Mr. Derek Walsh as chairman of Publicity and Public Relations and Mr. A. R. Seaman among its Honorary Members — Kanawana's serving director and its director of 1959-67 both on the provincial association's English Section at the same time. Walsh chaired that committee in January 1975 and was President by October 1976, so the presidency followed a committee chairmanship in the same portfolio he would later hold nationally.

The Quebec Camping Association English Section's full 1975 list: Honorary President Mrs. Alta R. Kahn; Honorary Members Mr. and Mrs. Neil B. Powter, Mr. A. R. Seaman, Mr. T. Shorgan, Miss A. I. Vail and Mr. F. M. Van Wagner; President Mrs. Val Willis; Vice-Presidents Mrs. Barbara Patterson and Mr. Wilfred Jackson; Treasurer Mrs. D. Jacques Reeves; Secretary Mr. Joseph A. Friedman; Past President Mr. Zave Ettinger. Anne I. Vail — the Montreal CCA past president unasterisked in the 1972 list — was alive and honoured in 1975.

The Quebec Camping Association English Section's committee chairmen in January 1975 included Mrs. J. Robin Allen and Mr. Doug Anakin on Staff Training, Mrs. Nicholas D. Demetelin on Directory of Membership, Mr. Joseph A. Hood on Archives, Mr. Isaac Katofsky on Senior Citizens, Miss Frances M. Kelly on the Staff Placement Bureau (she was also the Section's Executive Secretary at 2233 Belgrave Avenue), Mr. Walter Mingie on Outdoor Education and Mr. Peter Van Wagner on Standards. An Archives chairman means the Section was actively keeping records in 1975 — where annual Kanawana accreditation reports would most naturally sit — and a Staff Placement Bureau means there was a central Quebec clearing-house for camp staff, generating its own records of who worked where.

An advertisement on the back page of the January 1975 Directory Issue announces a "DIRECTORY OF YMCA/YM-YWCA/YWCA RESIDENCE CAMPS IN CANADA — to be available soon at all Y's," from the National Council, YMCA of Canada, 2160 Yonge Street, Toronto, and the YWCA of Canada, 571 Jarvis Street, Toronto. A national directory of YMCA residence camps published about 1975, in which Kanawana would necessarily appear.

The January 1975 Quebec directory lists "PERROT DAY CAMP (1948) (Y.M.C.A.)", director Mr. Paul Cappelli, 2467 Ile Perrot Blvd., office 170 St. Louis Ave., Pointe Claire; activities swimming, gymnastics, archery, games, arts and crafts; 410 boys and 291 girls, ages 4 to 12 — seven hundred children, by far the largest camp in the Quebec listing.

Camp Oolahwan and Camp Lighthall were both still accredited and operating in January 1975, listed in the Quebec directory under Organizational Residential — Girls, alongside Marian, Quebec Lodge and Wa-Thik-Ane (GGOC).

The January 1975 Quebec directory lists "JEWISH LAURENTIAN FRESH AIR CAMP (1927) (Golden Age Association)," St. Hippolyte, for 35 men and 35 women aged 60 and over — one of the three Jewish Community Camps Alta Kahn ran as Executive Secretary from 1946 to 1949, now a seniors' camp under a different sponsor. Wooden Acres, another of the three, is also still listed.

Val Willis's National Code of Ethics, printed in full in both languages in January 1975 over her name as Chairman of the National Ethics Committee, sets out nine principles including: "We will familiarize ourselves with and comply with all government laws and regulations governing the operation of camps"; "We shall concern ourselves with the welfare of our natural environment and encourage others to do likewise"; "Our advertising and publicity shall avoid misleading statements and superlatives"; and "We shall refer to the Executive Committee any unethical practices which could be detrimental to the integrity and dignity of the Association." Willis was simultaneously President of the QCA English Section that accredited Kanawana.

Jack Pearse's "If I Were to Send My Child to Camp" (January 1975), drawn from the OCA directory's "In Choosing your Child's Camp Be Sure," gives a parent's checklist and a diagnostic reading of a camp's equipment: "if there are a dozen power boats, six dozen pairs of water skis and one leaky canoe, that should tell you something about the waterfront program. If the horseback riding stables are in better shape than the camper cabins, that ought to tell you something." On staffing: "As a good rule of thumb, a camp should have one staff for every three campers." He quotes John Ledlie's Managing the Y.M.C.A. Camp at length, and a director's line, "We don't teach the reef knot, we teach the camper."

Frances M. Kelly's tribute to F. M. Van Wagner (Canadian Camping, April 1975), written on his being made an Honorary Member of the CCA, states: "As early as 1937, as promoter and charter member of the C.C.A., Mr. 'Van' organized the Quebec Camping Association, English Section, to improve the camping methods and to raise the standard of the camps throughout the Province of Quebec. He was also the first President of the Q.C.A."

"In 1955 he formulated and first introduced a Manual of Standards for children's summer camps in the Province of Quebec" — F. M. Van Wagner is the author of the first Quebec camp standards manual, and it has a name and a date. The chain of Quebec standards is therefore: Manual of Standards, Van Wagner, 1955; accreditation practice "in the pioneer stage" under Alta Kahn, 1959-60; the association's provincial incorporation, 23 January 1961; annual re-accreditation of every Quebec camp by 1975. Kanawana was measured against a document written by a named man in a named year.

F. M. Van Wagner "was President of the Canadian Camping Association with Office in Montreal from 1958 to 1961" — the national association's office was in Montreal for three years under a Montreal president, a period in which national camping records were kept in Kanawana's own city.

F. M. Van Wagner was born in Hyde Park, New York, had a farm childhood and a career in physical education, and was aged 80 in 1975, so born about 1894-95. He founded Camp Nominingue in 1925 on Petit Lac Nominingue in the Laurentians, and "In 1974, the camp celebrated its 50th season." He received the Centennial Medal in 1967, an Award of Merit from the Provincial Board of the QCA English and French Sections in 1968, and Honorary Membership of the CCA at the Annual Meeting in October 1974; he had been ski-touring since the mid-1930s and "next to the famous 'Jackrabbit' Johannsen, 'Van' has probably travelled more ski-miles in the Laurentians than anyone."

F. M. Van Wagner's 1975 tribute gives Camp Nominingue's founding as 1925, and the fiftieth-season arithmetic (fiftieth season in 1974) agrees. This project's records carry a 1924/1925 discrepancy for Nominingue; the founder's own tribute is recorded here as evidence for 1925 without unilaterally resolving it.

The Canadian Camping Association's Annual Meeting of October 1974 was held in Montreal, stated twice in the April 1975 issue in the tributes to F. M. Van Wagner and Charles Plewman, both of whom were made Honorary Members there. Its minutes would name the Quebec camps and people present.

Charles Plewman's career as dated in his April 1975 tribute: first attended camp as a camper in 1903; ran his first short-term camp in 1909; Director of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks 1913-1916; then three years directing Camp Stephens; Inter-Church camps thereafter; opened his own boys' camp, Kilcoo, in 1932 and owned it until 1955; helped found the Ontario Camping Association and was its President in 1945. "He and some of his associates began publishing a 'Camp Bulletin'... the forerunner of 'Canadian Camping'."

Three accounts of Canadian Camping's parentage now stand together without needing to be reconciled: Charles Plewman's own (1971), Mary Northway's on Mary Edgar (1973), and Plewman's 1975 tribute — an Ontario "Camp Bulletin" begun by Plewman and associates, with Mary Edgar as its first editor, becoming the national Canadian Camping Bulletin whose first printed issue was February 1949.

Abbe Paul Belanger, Director of Camp Ecole Keno and the magazine's Quebec correspondent, opened his April 1975 Viewpoint with the practice he was arguing against: "due to our selection processes, we have taken the habit of accepting in our camps normal children only, refusing systematically children with behaviour problems or with physical handicaps. These children were grouped in specialized camps, sheltered from the 'dangers of the outdoors', where they could not contaminate 'good children' or run the risk of being ridiculed by them." Recorded exactly as written in 1975.
