Paul Belanger records that Camp Ecole Keno had integrated blind campers since 1971: "with the help of people responsible for the education of blind and half-blind children, we have continued each summer to take as campers 8 to 10 of these children and integrated them in groups of 10 campers, one handicapped child to a group." His four stated conditions: do not water down the programme; aim at true integration and avoid treating the child as "a second-class camper"; keep one or two staff who know the children as resource persons, not necessarily as their counsellors; and never more than one such camper per cabin.

Paul Belanger's 1975 case study is Francois, blind from birth and twelve at his first summer at Camp Ecole Keno, integrated fully into a normal cabin group. Two of his teachers were on staff that year and it was deliberately decided neither would be his counsellor; they "insisted that nothing be changed in the camp program because of Francois." He swam, did hebertisme once he had learned the course, shot archery using a small bell pinned to the centre of the target sounded by a rope he touched with his foot when ready to aim, passed all the canoeing safety tests, and went on canoe trips. Walking the beach he stayed exactly at the water line without getting wet, and when asked how, said "I can smell the water!"

Stan Talesnick of the Camp Tawingo Outdoor Centre described group initiative tasks used in Staff Orientation Week in April 1975: staff split into twelve groups of ten, deliberately mixed for "ages, experiences, camp responsibilities, leadership abilities and personalities," rotating through ten of twelve fifteen-minute tasks over two and a half hours. The sources are named: "Most of the tasks are collected from the Colorado Outward Bound School, via Bob Woodburn of York University, or from the Canadian Outward Bound School."

The twelve group initiative tasks Stan Talesnick printed in 1975 are the recognisable ancestors of the modern team-building course: the Beam (a 6-inch log lashed 8 feet up between two trees, everyone over including the last person, who cannot be helped from below); Pole and Tire; Electric Fence; setting up a tent with no talking and optionally blindfolded; blindfold walks led non-verbally; simulated first aid situations using red dye; measuring tree heights without instruments; Diverging Bridge; Tea in a Tree; getting the whole group onto a rock or stump; loading a canoe anchored five feet out without touching the water; and a rope maze crawled out of blindfolded. The debrief questions are the point: "Did one or two people repeatedly assume leadership, or was the role passed around? Was everyone listened to? Did any group members behave 'out of character'? If so, how?"

Dr. John J. Kirk, Director of the New Jersey School of Conservation, dated organized camping's origin to 1861 at Milford-on-the-Sound, Connecticut, under Fred Gunn, headmaster of the Gunnery School, who moved his whole student body to a camp site for two weeks after students asked "to be given the opportunity to live like soldiers," and gave about ten million children in Canadian and American camps in the summer of 1975.

John J. Kirk's April 1975 critique of camping is the period's own indictment from inside: "Many children attend organized camps today, and in the four-, six-, or eight-week experience may never have the thrill of cooking a meal over an open fire, may never have the challenge of pitching a tent or the enjoyment of sleeping under the stars"; camps use the natural environment "as a theatrical backdrop"; the old nature study required campers to learn "the names of ten trees, fifteen flowers, six birds and three animals; and for this monumental achievement they would receive the 'looney bird award'"; and "Camping people will sit around the campfires, sing their quaint little songs and toast their marshmallows while the world collapses around them. This unrealistic approach, if allowed to continue, may well cause the camping movement to become an endangered species and ultimately to become extinct."

Grant McKeen reported that the British Columbia Camping Association surveyed its camps in 1974 and 43 returned material: "Over 20,000 children were registered in these camps — 2,100 staff were employed — $400,000 was spent on salaries — $275,000 was spent on food." Registration was increasing at 22 camps, constant at 17 and decreasing at only 4. From the start of 1974 only accredited camps could join the BCCA.

J. Harry Ebbs reported in April 1975 that "The camp Health form for both campers and staff should have smallpox deleted from the list of vaccinations" — so camp health forms before about 1975 asked for smallpox vaccination and after it did not, which dates a form. He also noted tetanus toxoid was now known effective for at least ten years.

Catherine Thomas of Camp Northway set out how to organise a camp sailing programme in April 1975: minimum recommended age nine; sessions of at least two weeks and preferably three or four; a waterfront needing "a traffic-free area on the water... It is unnerving for the novice sailor to have to negotiate his way through the canoeing program"; and twelve rules for choosing a boat, of which "be sure the boat you choose is CAMPER PROOF" and don't buy the racing model, "too light and... equipped with too many lines and gadgets." The Canadian Yachting Association administered a loan fund for boats bought for junior training, open to camps holding CYA membership.

Wilfred A. Jackson of Quebec reported in April 1975 that "the Keynote Speaker, Dr. Don Ehat, has been secured for the Q.C.A. Director and Senior Staff Seminar to be held March 14-16 in Montreal" — a Quebec directors' and senior staff seminar in Montreal in March 1975, which Kanawana's director, then on the QCA English Section executive, would have been in a position to attend.

The Canadian Camping Association sold seventeen cassette tapes of its January 1975 Geneva Park national conference at $4.00 each, including seven Don Ehat sessions and ten Canadian ones: "Recruiting, Hiring, Interviewing" (Bruce Harris), "Evaluating Your Camp" (Barry Lowes), "Staff Training" (John Boutin), "Staff Supervision" (Brian Law), "Develop Staff From Within Your Camp" (Al Knox), budget (Ron Johnstone), recruiting and PR (Doug McEwan), camp philosophy (Arnie Cohen) and working with committees (Tony Fry). A recorded 1975 seminar on camp staff supervision and evaluation, sold on tape, which may survive.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1975 publications catalogue announces "CAMP COUNSELLOR'S HANDBOOK. Blackstock & Latimer. — 1975 publication. New, up-to-date! 128 p. $4.95" — the CCA president and the publications chairman co-writing the national counsellor manual — and "Counsellor's Guide to Camp Singing" by Tolbitt, 44 pages, which is the nearest thing yet found to the national camp songbook.

The February 1974 National Standards Workshop at Camp Richildaca, Kettleby, defined day camping: "Day Camping was defined as an experience in group living in a natural environment. It is a sustained experience carried on during the daytime under the supervision of trained leadership." It also recorded that "In response to concern for a low standard of supervision in some government-funded day camps, letters were sent to government project officers requesting them to consult with the Standards Committees of provincial camping associations before approving outdoor recreation projects" — the camping establishment lobbying in writing against government-funded youth camps.

Bruno Morawetz, Director of Camp Ponacka, wrote in Canadian Camping, June 1975: "The one thing which occupies a large part of our time is our annual Hoax (Indian Burial ground, unidentified flying object, glabergoof egg, etc.). With the bombardment from noise and the mass media, the imagination is frequently overlaid and buried. Camp is a good place to re-awaken it." The camp hoax was therefore annual, institutional and directed from the top at that camp, and the glabergoof egg invented in Bob Attfield's 1972 article appears here three years later as a past year's hoax.

A staged "Indian Burial ground" is documented as a recognised camp-hoax type of the period, named by a camp director in the national trade press in June 1975. Kanawana's camp map carried an "Indian Grave" marking for which no documentation has been found explaining whether it referred to an actual burial site, a naturalistic feature or a campfire-story location. A staged hoax is a fourth possibility, not an answer, but it is the first evidence of any kind bearing on that question.

Bruno Morawetz argued in June 1975 that a camper's "fourteen hour day consists of hundreds of minute incidents" which "make or break his camping experience," so the director should delegate the important things — daily routines, maintenance, buying — and keep himself free for the unimportant ones, "being free to talk to a camper on the path or tell a bedtime story to one little group." On staff applications: "I am always suspicious when a staff application is accompanied by a long resume listing dozens of qualifications, courses taken, tests passed... A good counsellor needs ears tuned to the ripples of a child. He needs more the ability to listen than the skill to teach." On facilities: "A highly developed campsite may prove to be a real handicap. When our camp was young, the campers derived great satisfaction from creating a new path or cutting trees for a new tent. Now it's all done."

Don Dickie, a Royal Life Saving Society summer field representative, printed a timed water search procedure in June 1975 in which everything is done correctly and the camper dies: buddy check at 0 seconds, missing camper discovered at 10, emergency signal at 15, waterfront cleared at 20, counsellors report at 40, attendance taken at 1 minute, search groups formed at 1:10, full water search begun at 1:30, one sweep concluded at 3:00, the body found within five feet of where the camper was last seen at 3:05, artificial respiration commenced at 3:30. "The camper has been without oxygen for a minimum of 3 min. & 30 sec.... Brain damage may have set in after 3 min." His conclusion: "It took 1 min. & 15 sec. from the time the camper was discovered missing until the water search was initiated. It was in these wasted seconds that the chance of reviving the subject was lost."

Don Dickie's 1975 article gives the signs of a non-swimmer in difficulty — vertical body position, no supporting kick, eyes wide open, no call for help because "priority is breathing" — notes that a drowning non-swimmer usually stays conscious about forty seconds after his last breath and that a body after unconsciousness is usually within eight feet of the surface, and requires that a camp's search procedure be "written up and posted," taught to each new intake of campers, and tried at least once a season with no advance warning: "Many procedures that look adequate on paper and in controlled trials, may not work in practice."

A boxed note in Canadian Camping, June 1975: "Legislation under Small Vessels Regulations now requires a Ministry of Transport approved lifejacket or Personal Flotation Device for each person in any vessel at all times. Canoes and rowboats were previously exempted but are now included." This is the outcome of the life-jacket policy committee Claude Cousineau was appointed CCA liaison to in 1973, and 1975 is the year canoes came under the requirement.

Bob Attfield's "The Successful Singsong" (June 1975) records that "Some of our best song leaders seldom, if ever, use any song books," because distributing books and flipping pages "detracts from the spontaneity," and "If song words can be taught without the use of books, so much the better" — a direct explanation of why camp song repertoires of the period are so poorly documented: the good practice was deliberately not to use printed books.

Bob Attfield's 1975 singsong method: start the day with a quick singsong right after breakfast; three or four songs is enough, and "it is better to cut a song period short than to let it drag on." His named repertoire: warm-ups "The Grand Old Duke of York," "When the Saints Go Marching In" and "The Junior Birdsmen"; competition song "The Quarter Master's Store," "great for inducing each cabin group to produce an original rhyme"; rounds "Frere Jacques," "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" and "Good News"; and the daily bookends — "How rewarding for a camper to be able to begin the day with 'Alouette' and retire with an appropriately soothing melody like 'Land of the Silverbirch'."

"L'Expedition Bostochouane" (Canadian Camping, June 1975) records a 150-mile canoe expedition by Camp Richelieu Quatre-Saisons, Ste-Therese: eight people, Jean-Pierre as animateur on his fourth such expedition, Denis as co-animateur, and six boys aged 14 to 17. Preparation began in January with fortnightly meetings, each boy taking a portfolio — Alain cartographer, Michel F. treasurer, Andre minutes and correspondence, Pierre canoe repair, Michel B. menu and food, Daniel equipment. It was financed at about $100 a head by member contributions, a sale of kites the team built themselves, circular distribution and grounds-clearing work in May.

The Bostochouane expedition departed on 15 August from Lac Montagnais in the Parc des Laurentides, down the Metascouac to the Metabetchouane, then Grand lac Bostonnais and the Bostonnais river to La Tuque — about 150 miles. The hard section was "les Neuf milles de rapides," which they were advised to run without baggage in open canoes; one canoe was swamped in a class 3 rapid hidden in a sharp bend, the occupants saved by life jackets and companions with only leg grazes, the canoe patched with strong adhesive tape for the rest of the trip.

The Canadian Camping Association's executive from mid-1975 was President Ron Johnstone, Vice-President Jack Pearse, Secretary Jay Haddad, Treasurer Bill Swift; John Latimer left the masthead after four years as president.

Catherine Thomas's second sailing article (June 1975) requires an approved life preserver per person in all sailboats "and they are to be worn," plus two paddles and a bailer secured against a capsize, and notes that the Canadian Yachting Association Standards were new — "Until recently there was no standardized criteria available for the evaluation of sailing ability from one program to another" — recommending that camps add their own swimming requirements at the higher sailing levels since the Standards do not.

Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 1 (November 1975) is a four-page newsletter rather than a magazine. The editor's note: "Without any doubt, the mail strike has brought its hardships and 'Canadian Camping' is no exception. Unfortunately, when the time for typesetting arrived, we were lacking in advertisements and editorial content which included resumes in French... the decision was made to publish a four page Newsletter." The 1975 Canadian postal strike is therefore the reason anything expected in a Fall 1975 issue is not there.

A boxed notice in Canadian Camping, November 1975: "'HEBERTISME' — a new booklet written by Claude Cousineau and published by the Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation. 50 cents each from: Ontario Government Publications Service, 3 B-7 Macdonald Block, Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario." Cousineau is the author of one side of this project's open conflict over hebertisme's origin, and here writes it up at length for a provincial government publisher — a catalogued, findable item rather than a magazine article.
entities: Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation

facts.claim: Gil Cardinal became Executive Director of the ACQ-QCA in 1975, succeeding Yves Beauregard, who had left for the Camp des Enfants Infirmes.

A train-the-trainer pilot ran in Quebec camps in 1975-76: "A pilot project is now in progress with a new slant on the training of counsellors. Selected counsellors from Quebec Camps are given a course at a central location on the understanding that these people will return to their own camps and train their camp staff." Kanawana, as an accredited member camp, would have been eligible.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1976 Annual Meeting was set for Quebec City, 28-30 April, in conjunction with a French Language Conference, "Activite Educative du Camp de Vacances — Educational Activity of Camping" — the second national gathering in Quebec in two years, after Montreal in October 1974.

Rick Ryan, former president of the British Columbia Camping Association, moved to Montreal in 1975 to become Executive Director of Boys' Clubs of Canada. The Alberta Camping Association visited over 60 camps in its 1975 accreditation programme, and 99% of camps in Newfoundland and Labrador were NLCA members. The American Camping Association's January 1976 conference was booked for the Yamnuska Centre, "the new YMCA training camp about 25 miles from Banff."

Ottelyn Addison's "Naturecraft Collectibles" (November 1975) describes camp crafts built entirely from gathered natural material with a conservation ethic stated throughout — "a big 'if': none of them will deplete the environment"; "always remember there is no picking of any sort in Conservation Areas or Provincial Parks"; "only take what you actually can use." Techniques include cones threaded on nylon fishing line, a sack of cones from the Ministry of Natural Resources Seed Extraction Plant at Angus, Ontario, for $2.00, plaster casts of animal tracks, goldenrod-gall figures, cobweb pictures sprayed with paint and lifted onto coloured paper, and plant printing on sensitized paper from a drafting office developed with 24% ammonia.

The January 1976 Directory Issue of Canadian Camping lists Kanawana with its sessions and fees intact: "KANAWANA (1894) — Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye; Director Derek V. Walsh; P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts, Que.; 1441 Drummond St., Montreal H3G 1W5; Activities: Tripping, Canoeing, Orienteering, Arts & Crafts, Sailing; 98 boys 8-15 / 91 girls 8-15; June 28 - July 12; July 12 - July 26; July 29 - Aug. 12; Aug. 12 - Aug. 26; $210.00 / 2 weeks. Add. 2 weeks / $190."

Kanawana's 1976 fee was $210.00 for two weeks with each additional two weeks at $190 — a deliberate marginal discount for longer stays, and the first Kanawana fee figure this project holds for the 1970s.
Kanawana ran four two-week sessions in 1976 — 28 June to 12 July, 12 to 26 July, 29 July to 12 August, and 12 to 26 August — with a three-day break between the second and third.

Comparing Kanawana's 1975 and 1976 directory entries gives a two-year operational series: the two camps listed separately in 1975 (Kanawana and Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye) are combined under one heading in 1976; capacity rises from 90 boys and 90 girls to 98 boys and 91 girls in the same 8-15 age band; and the headline activity list changes, with swimming and the C.I.T. programme dropping out and canoeing and orienteering coming in.

Kanawana's 1976 season ran through the Montreal Olympics of 17 July to 1 August, which fell across the end of its second session and the start of its third. Camps nearer the city were advertising group accommodation to Olympic visitors in the same issue. Whether the Games affected Kanawana is unrecorded.
The Newfoundland and Labrador Camping Association's entry in the January 1976 directory states that the Canadian Camping Association "was incorporated by Letters Patent at Ottawa November 5, 1949."

The Canadian Camping Association's competing founding dates may be three stages of one process rather than a dispute: organising activity from 1936-37 (the Concordia holdings, and F. M. Van Wagner describing himself as "promoter and charter member" in 1937); a founding meeting at the Chateau Laurier in 1946, which Charles Plewman qualified by saying "for the moment it had no corporate existence"; and incorporation by Letters Patent at Ottawa on 5 November 1949. The Quebec Camping Association English Section took its own Federal Charter in 1949 as well, suggesting one round of formalisation.

F. M. Van Wagner's byline in Canadian Camping, January 1976, reads "Director, Camp Nominingue 1925-1967" — a forty-two-year directorship, exactly dated. His article "Lunch on the Ski Trail" describes a technique he says he has used "some hundreds of times, along Laurentian ski trails, during the past forty winters," so from about 1935: lay several layers of two-foot logs on the snow as a base "to keep the snow from melting away quickly, forming a hole under the fire"; standing dead wood is drier in winter than summer; one fire for every four to six skiers; skis running-surface-down make a seat; "stop for lunch as soon as the first member of the party feels hungry."

Bruce W. Hodgins's Trent honorary-degree citation for J. Harry Ebbs, read on 6 June 1975, records: born in England, arrived in Peterborough as a child in 1912; graduated in medicine at the University of Toronto in 1931; joined the Hospital for Sick Children in 1938 and was its Senior Staff Physician from 1946 to 1968; Director of the University of Toronto's School of Physical and Health Education from 1952 to his retirement in 1973; author of more than sixty scientific papers; a Depression-era nutritional study of expectant mothers in Toronto whose recommendations were adopted by Britain's Chief Medical Officer, after which "that country's infant mortality rate was reduced by fifty per cent"; a pre-war study of nutritional needs in the far North whose findings were used in 42 million food packages sent to Allied prisoners of war; and service as a Captain in the 48th Highlanders.

The 1975 Trent citation names J. Harry Ebbs "Founding President of the Society of Professional Camp Directors" and President of the Brora Research Centre for Children — Mary L. Northway's Brora Centre. It also records that over fifty years earlier, "through the efforts of Alex Edmison," he became a counsellor and canoe instructor at the Taylor Statten Camps, "There he fell in love with Adele or 'Couchie', the Director's daughter, whom he married. Since 1938 he has been the Chief Medical Advisor for these camps, while his wife has directed Taylor Statten's Camp Wapomeo."

Doug Dent reported in January 1976: "First of all, the YMCA lifesaving program was revamped, and in its place the RLSS program (Bronze Medallion and upwards) has been adopted." By 1976 the YMCA had dropped its own lifesaving programme in favour of the Royal Life Saving Society's. He printed a three-column equivalence chart between the YMCA, Red Cross and RLSS levels — YMCA Pre-Beginner, Beginner and Star I-VI against Red Cross Pre-Beginner, Beginner, Junior, Intermediate and Senior and RLSS Survival and Life Saving I, II and III. The YMCA "Star" levels are the system a Kanawana swimmer of this era would have been graded on.

Jocelyn Palm's "Adventure versus Risk," her paper to the National Outdoor and Environmental Education Conference of 4 October 1975, defines risk as "the exposure of the participant to injury as a result of the adventure" and notes that "many of the things the pioneers did in order to survive, we are now doing for 'kicks'." She sets nine preparation factors against nine severity segments on a rotating paper wheel so a leader can work each possible accident against each preparation factor, and calls for "more adequate investigation of the accidents which occur (not just the deaths but the total injury picture)."

Jocelyn Palm wrote in 1975 that rescuers "had the skills and the theories but they were not ready for the unpleasantness of pushy uncontrollable crowds, of violent regurgitation of victims while rescuers performed A.R., of sobbing relatives and friends close by"; that leaders must recognise "an individual's desire to do an activity may not be desire at all, but pressure from peers"; and that "Teachers have been embroiled in law suits and have lost their cases in court resulting in a public suspicious rather than enthusiastic for outdoor adventure."

John Pratt's "The Adventure Trail" (January 1976) describes what is elsewhere in this run called a piste d'hebertisme, a Swedish exercise course and group initiative tasks: "Many camps and outdoor centres today have, or are planning to have, an adventure trail... It is an obstacle course or a combination of an obstacle course and nature trail... Adventure trails are very common in some Western European countries," with a full materials list and stencilled plywood signs 12 by 16 inches, black on white, at each apparatus. A camp's rope or obstacle course of this period may therefore appear in its records under any of four names.

Frank Jennings died in September 1975. Commissioned a Salvation Army officer in 1944, Youth Officer at Corner Brook, married Eva Lundrigan in 1954, latterly Salvation Army Sub-Director for Canada, retired through ill health in 1967. As Newfoundland and Labrador Camping Association standards chairman he produced a Camp Standards Book for Newfoundland; as president he started a newsletter, initiated the camp visitation and accreditation programme, published the Newfoundland Camp Directory for the first time, revised the constitution, and brought the CCA annual meeting to Newfoundland in May 1975. He received the CCA's Award of Merit.

Madelene Allen's "Camp Is" collects lines written by campers at Camp Ouareau in the summer of 1975 for a Sunday evening programme, including camp vocabulary the campers plainly understood: "Tent hopping"; "Making 'Heavy Dew Days' into sunshine days"; "Learning to be 'copesetic'"; "Bymph"; "Feeling safe as the fire plane drones overhead."

Ann Prewitt, the magazine's former editor, records in January 1976 that Russ Rutter, naturalist and wolf authority, had come to her camp on Cache Lake, Algonquin Park, and talked to the girls about wolves with tape recordings of their howls, having "impressed us all that there was no reason for humans to fear wolves" — a dated instance of wolf education at a Canadian camp.

The Quebec grouped index in the January 1976 directory carries a new heading, SPECIALIZED CAMPS, listing Carowanis (diabetic children), the Centre de Vacances de l'Association de Paralysie Cerebrale, Centre de Plein Air La Caleche (socially-emotionally disturbed) and Centre Marronniers (mentally retarded adults) among others — a category that did not exist in the 1975 index, and evidence that Quebec was formally accrediting specialised camps by 1976. Terminology recorded as printed.
Canadian Camping carried an ISSN for the first time with the January 1976 issue: 008-3119.

Helen Stewart's editorial in Canadian Camping, June 1976, opens: "This issue of Canadian Camping is its last. The decision was made by the CCA Board at the recent meetings in Quebec City and was one based wholely on financial considerations." She adds that "no decision has been reached if or when anything else will be devised to take the place of Canadian Camping" and closes, "And so we have come to the end of an era."

The magazine was not ended in June 1976 but replaced: the next cached issue is Vol. 28 No. 4, October 1976, and from there the frequency rises to five or six numbers a year through 1977 and 1978 where the magazine had been quarterly. Stewart's own French text says so — "il y aura peut-etre une publication moins couteuse pour remplacer Canadian Camping." Together with the February-November 1974 suspension and the 1975 postal-strike newsletter, that is three structural breaks in the run in three years.

Helen Stewart's farewell names the people behind the run since Fall 1972: Mary Jane Sanderson, responsible for all the unsigned sketches, and Paul Belanger for the translations — so the French half of every bilingual article in the magazine's last four years is one Marist priest's work.

Alex Peepre died in 1976 aged 58. Colin C. Kelly's tribute records him as champion of Estonia and the Baltic countries, whose hope of skiing the combined event at the 1936 Garmisch-Partenkirchen Winter Olympics "was dashed at the last minute"; a second career in Sweden ending as Sports Director for the city of Stockholm; arriving in Canada in 1950, where he began as "probably the most distinguished dishwasher Camp Pinecrest ever had," then ran its waterfront, then spent five years as Director of Camp Nagiwa which he developed for the Guelph YMCA, then Camp Beausoleil and Camp On-Da-Da-Waks, then seven more years at Pinecrest while joining the faculty of what became the University of Guelph. "He fathered [orienteering] in North America and proudly nursed it to its current state of popularity."

Kanawana's 1976 directory entry lists orienteering among its five headline activities where its 1975 entry did not. Alex Peepre, credited in 1976 with fathering orienteering in North America, spent his whole Canadian career in YMCA camps. That is a plausible transmission route and is recorded as context, not causation: no source connects him to Kanawana, and orienteering was spreading through several channels by the mid-1970s.

Lorne Brown died in 1976. A physical educator who taught "in the YMCA and its camps; the elementary schools, the teacher training college and later in the faculty of education — U.B.C., in his own private camp and through being an elected member of the Vancouver Parks and Recreation Board," he was President of the Canadian Association for Health, Physical Education and Recreation from 1955 to 1957, and had been asked in 1973 to investigate a national programme for instructors in Nature Lore, Campcraft and Survival.

Jacques Grenier's "Comment se preparer a une expedition en canot" (June 1976) was written against a rising toll: "more and more people are travelling by canoe in the northern parts of our country and more and more tragedies occur because of a lack of preparation." Its long-term planning horizon runs from as much as eighteen months out and includes obtaining "a written governmental permit to travel north of the 52nd or the 60th parallel"; the short term, two to six months out, requires testing all equipment in a mini-expedition of two to four days, eight to ten weeks before departure; and immediately before departure the party must notify the RCMP, local police and the air and seaplane bases that overfly the region of the route, names and expected timing, arrange for a search to be raised if no word comes by a set date, and report success on arrival.

Jacques Grenier's 1976 pacing rules for a northern canoe expedition: never paddle or portage past 17:00; eat properly at every meal; eight to ten hours' sleep; a full rest day every four or five days; and fifteen-minute breaks at regular intervals. "Une malchance ou un incident dans un environnement urbain peut s'averer fatal dans le grand nord canadien ou les secours sont lents et difficiles a obtenir."

Liz Greenway's "Just What Do You Do All Day?" (June 1976) describes the ordinary machinery of camp staff supervision: "I found it best to make a specific effort to speak to each counsellor alone every week or so, to talk over any problems and to get some feedback. You don't need to tell the counsellor that she's scheduled for an interview since that can sound rather formidable but you should make an interview schedule for yourself." On campers she describes "cruising" — walking the section at the start of each activity period, especially in the first fortnight, and noticing who is alone: "if it's the same girl three periods in a row then perhaps there is some problem. She may need some friendly interest (which is not the same thing as prying)."

Eileen Mayotte's Viewpoint of June 1976, built on Haim G. Ginott's Parent-Child, draws the line on camper participation: "Responsibility is fostered by allowing the campers a voice, a choice in matters that affect them," but "the selecting belongs to the administration — the choosing should be the right of the camper."

Paul Rushton's "The Garden of Eatin'" (June 1976) describes a camp vegetable garden built on an old horse corral, the years of hooves having left "a reasonably flat surface" over enriched soil, and argues for organic gardening over inorganic fertilizer, "brought about not only by skyrocketing cost of inorganic fertilizers but by the startling results that farmers and gardeners alike are deriving," naming milorganite, compost, rock phosphate, bone meal, colloidal phosphate, potash rock, ground limestone and dolomite, and recommending a free soil test from the local government agricultural representative.

Officer changes in June 1976: Kirk Wipper became President of the Ontario Camping Association; Bill McCarthy headed the joint ACQ-QCA with Georges Robitaille for the section francaise; John Hasell led the British Columbia Camping Association.

Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 4 (October 1976) is a typewritten, mimeographed newsletter of eight pages, about a quarter the size of the magazine it replaced, with its own note: "The format might be different... but the intent is still the same... Costs have forced us to look carefully at ourselves (probably a very good thing from time to time)."

Adele Ebbs wrote in Canadian Camping, October 1976: "In 1967 official collecting and sorting of camping records was started by a small group, all of whom are still involved, and now there are concerned people in every provincial association. We have been fortunate in finding a home for our Canadian Camping Archives at Trent University in Peterborough. Their Department of Canadian Studies is very supportive of our efforts... Since the Canadian Camping Archives Committee was established in 1975, made up of representatives from each province, the biggest thrust has come from the first Geneva Park Conference... The Archives at Trent are National... Such national papers belong at Trent." She names the archivist: "Mr Kenneth Johnson, Archivist, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8."

The Canadian Camping Association's archive went to Trent University, not the University of Waterloo. The 1973 board resolution named Waterloo; the 1976 statement by the chairman of the Archives Committee names Trent, its department, its archivist and its postal code, and describes a committee already two years old with material already deposited. The 1976 statement is the later, more specific and more authoritative one.

Adele Ebbs records the founding deposit of the national camping archive: "The first and very valuable contribution of papers came from F.M. Van Wagner who was C.C.A. President 1958-60. From these papers we have many records of the early days of our Association." Van Wagner founded the Quebec Camping Association in 1937 and was its first president, wrote the 1955 Manual of Standards for children's summer camps in Quebec — the document Kanawana was accredited against — and was CCA president with the national office in Montreal. His papers at Trent are therefore the most likely single location for the 1955 Manual and for early QCA records.

Trent University holds three separate camping deposits: the Ontario Camping Association's, given 22 October 1970 with its taped interviews of camp personalities; the Mary S. Edgar fonds; and the national Canadian Camping Archives, whose founding deposit was F. M. Van Wagner's papers.

Adele Ebbs reports a national camp oral history project agreed in spring 1976: "At the Quebec Board meeting last spring a long list of camp pioneers was drawn up and agreement was reached by the Provincial Presidents that their associations would start taping oral biographies of those people. It is an arduous and costly task, but well worth the effort, and it must be done NOW! The Trent Archivist will make a copy and return the original." The Quebec Camping Association was party to that agreement, and Kanawana's own director sat on its English Section executive.

Don Smith died in 1976; he was Canadian Camping Association President from 1963 to 1965. Reg Blackstock's tribute records that "He was one of the first people to establish courses in camping at the university level," that he pressed for resident outdoor education during the school year, and that he helped set up the outdoor education committees in the provincial associations and the CCA. On his philosophy: "he knew that camping provides vivid learning experiences; that the risk-laden adventure is a strong motivator to sharpen skills; and that stressful activities enhance self-knowledge and self confidence."

The Kanawa International Museum of Canoes, Kayaks and Rowing Craft acquired, after negotiation with the Museum of the American Indian-Heye Foundation, ten kayaks, twelve dug-outs, eleven bark canoes and eleven miscellaneous canoes, "on the understanding that special care would be taken to preserve, restore and display the collection. This has expanded the Kanawa collection to three hundred or more," requiring an extension to the log display house built by a Log Construction School under Alan Mackie of Prince George and Paul McNab of Ignace.

The Kanawa Museum's 1976 public events included "a journey to the Olympics in Voyageur costume in the 36 ft. Montreal Canoe," the same canoe sent to the French Festival at Detroit for the U.S. Bicentennial, and a historic canoe and kayak display at the Barrie-Orillia-Kempenfeldt Bay Festival. A voyageur-costumed Montreal canoe went to the Montreal Olympics in the summer Kanawana was running four sessions forty miles north of the city.

The Woodsmanship Instructor School, first run nationally in 1976, grew out of the National Canoe Instructor Schools from the realisation that "it becomes the responsibility of wilderness travellers to be fully aware of the consequences of such encounters for the natural environment," with "a strong 'ethic of the land' theme... so that the principle of 'wise use without abuse' could be honestly respected." Two experimental Ontario schools preceded the first national one, whose purpose was "to inspire a group of leaders who would conduct such programmes in their own areas."

"A Wilderness Dilemma" (October 1976) reports the September OCA board meeting voicing "concern... regarding the number of accidents occurring in adventurous outdoor activities; this, because participants are not properly prepared by those who offer such programmes," and gives a case: "A young man of twenty-five recently perished on a western river when his canoe capsized. The Package Tour in which he invested included a flight to the West and a run down a river to a rendezvous spot. He was given a helmet and a water-ski belt and sent on his way by canoe with a friend, but no second canoe to accompany the pair in strange country." Its conclusion: "mismanagement at this crucial stage of development may lead to unfortunate negative results, if such wilderness treks and trips are not controlled intelligently in the very near future."

Raymond Hade replaced Gil Cardinal as Executive Director of the ACQ-QCA in 1976 — the third executive director in three years, after Beauregard and Cardinal. "The High Commission of Leisure and Sports has provided funds to ACQ-QCA so that a full time person may be hired to set up provincial training programmes in camping" — a provincially funded, full-time camp training post in Quebec from 1976.

Canadian Camping, October 1976, lists Derek Walsh as President, Quebec Camping Association Inc. (English), at 2233 Belgrave Avenue — confirming from the association's own masthead the presidency the derek-walsh stub dates to "by Oct 1976." Robert Maisonneuve headed the ACQ and W. McCarthy the joint Provincial Board.

New Brunswick reported in October 1976 that "Hebertisme continues to grow in many camps... due to the tremendous influence of Claude Cousineau's book on the subject" — so the booklet published by the Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation in 1975 was having measurable effect within a year, two provinces away from where hebertisme started in Canada.

Eanswythe Flynn's camp closing-up list, reprinted in expanded form in October 1976, adds items not in its 1972 version: fill the tiniest crack or hole in woodwork, walls or floors with putty or plaster of paris "mixed with cayenne pepper or mustard (powdered)"; spread fireplace ashes one or two inches thick on the mass in pit toilets to break down odour; and "all drugs should be carefully examined to determine whether or not there is an expiry date... Throw out all drugs whose dates have expired" — a change reflecting new pharmaceutical labelling. The 1972 advice to leave a piano uncovered is now stated as a rule: "the secret is never cover a piano."

Canadian Camping's Quebec column of December 1976 reports: "A somewhat scary proposal is now being made by the Department of Labour...Waterfronts in camps may not be deeper than six feet!!! Another highlight in Quebec is that they have formed a very active Day Camp Standards Committee." The exclamation marks are the association's. A six-foot depth limit is not a rule a camp on a natural lake can comply with by adjusting anything; whether it was ever enacted is not stated.

By 1976 the Quebec government appears on both sides of the ledger at once: the High Commission of Leisure and Sports was funding a full-time provincial camp training post at the ACQ-QCA, while the Department of Labour was drafting a camp waterfront rule of its own. If a ministry was regulating camp waterfronts from 1976-77, a governmental inspection file on Kanawana may exist distinct from the association's annual accreditation reports.

Voluntary camp accreditation had become the gatekeeper for public money across Canada by December 1976: New Brunswick — "The government has been very helpful in giving grants to camps — but such grants are only given if a camp is a member of the N.B.C.A."; Saskatchewan — "Government grants are not given to camps which are not accredited by the S.C.A."; Manitoba — a $46,000 government student-employment grant to MCA camps, the province paying the salary of a standards visitor, and the government having purchased six camps; British Columbia — "The B.C. Association has been asked to operate an in-service training programme for those inspectors hired by the Department of Health who will be visiting camps."

The Taylor Statten Memorial Fellowship as announced in December 1976: annual value $1,000, open to applicants from any Canadian university and tenable at any university considered appropriate, "to assist post-baccalaureate study in any professional field or career related to youth services, such as, but not restricted to, physical and health education, psychology, teaching, the ministry, and social work." Applications by 1 March with a transcript and three letters of recommendation, at least two from university teachers; "Only candidates under the age of 25 will be considered"; forms from the Office of Student Awards, Room 107, Simcoe Hall, University of Toronto.

The memorial to Taylor Statten, the central figure of Canadian camping, took the form of a graduate award in youth services generally, held at a university rather than by the camping association: the Taylor Statten Memorial Fund launched at the University of Toronto in 1962 with over $20,000 from 400 contributors, the first Taylor Statten Memorial Lecture given by Charles Hendry at Hart House on 24 March 1962, and the Fellowship in its mature form by 1976.

Cliff Labbett wrote in December 1976: "In 1976, the Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association took over the operation of the Canoe Instructors Schools which were founded in 1967 by Professors Kirk Wipper of the University of Toronto, and Claude Cousineau of the University of Ottawa. This modest beginning at the University of Ottawa's camp site near Gracefield, Quebec has now blossomed into six schools across Canada." The 1967 founding and the two founders match Andrea Dillon's 1972 account exactly — two independent attestations of the same origin.

The 1976 canoe instructor schools produced 189 candidates in one summer, 84 of them certified as instructors: Atlantic at Camp Kadimah near Bridgewater, N.S., 11-20 June, 25 students; French-language Gracefield, 41 students; English Gracefield in early August, 30 students; Ontario at Camp Kandalore, "overwhelmed with applications," 44 students; Mid-West near Kenora, 24 students; Western near Calgary, 25 students. Two of the six schools were held in Quebec.

Alberta's Department of Recreation and Parks gave funds to three camps in 1976 to set up hebertisme courses, from whose experience a "Practical Guide to Hebertism" was to be produced. With New Brunswick's report that hebertisme was spreading "due to the tremendous influence of Claude Cousineau's book on the subject," this is the method reaching Alberta with provincial funding within a year of the booklet.

The December 1976 masthead states: "Canadian Camping is published 6 times a year. Subscription Rates: $5.00 — 1 year; $12.00 — 3 years. C.C.A. membership includes subscription." That confirms the newsletter-era cadence of five or six issues a year against four in the magazine era, and gives the subscription price at the changeover.

The Canadian Camping Association's water-safety concern of December 1976 locates the problem in retail equipment rather than training: drownings in canoe accidents due "not only to inexperienced people; cold weather and water; but above all, to the poor quality of canoes sold extensively in super markets," together with "a great concern about the quality of some of the approved P.F.Ds. as well as the fact that there is not a wide variety of such approved P.F.Ds."

W. Grant Kerr's camp insurance article, reprinted from the United Church publication Church Camping (Spring 1976), gives recommended minimum liability cover in 1976 as "not less than $200,000 for bodily injury and $20,000 for property damage," better $500,000 with some camps carrying a million, and automobile liability from $100,000 up to $5,000,000. Liability is scheduled "in the per-camper per day charges," with rowboats, canoes, power-driven boats, motors, sailboats, malpractice, products coverage and horses scheduled separately. Fire rates were reduced by a full-time caretaker on the property, fire-resistant roofing, distance between structures and extinguishers in all buildings, with 90% co-insurance typical.

John Beedell of the Bark Lake Camp Leadership Centre set out winter camping requirements in December 1976: sleeping bags at $100-$150, or a summer down bag inside a Black Icelandic Special or Woods Mount Whitney, with closed-cell foam beneath; layered clothing; moccasins with rubber bottoms or oversized boots with snowmobile liners; chopping a three-foot ice hole for water; snow shelters entered below floor level so cold air cannot pour in; toboggans fitted with a wooden box; and the governing rule that "the biggest fear is sweating."

Canadian Camping's Quebec column of February 1977: "Support from the Provincial Government is still very evident in this Province, and a close liaison exists when it comes to new legislation. $300,000 is being given to the Association for their spring Training Programme." Set beside Nova Scotia's $3,600 provincial recreation grant reported two months earlier, this is the scale of Quebec's investment, and it was for staff training — the function the association had performed on its own since 1937.

Quebec ran a provincial "Camp Week" from 5 to 11 March 1977, with "promotional spots on radio and television; advertisements and public service announcements in every newspaper; buttons, posters, badges etc." — a government-funded advertising campaign on behalf of every accredited camp in Quebec, inside which Kanawana's 1977 recruitment took place.

The Quebec Camping Association English Section held its 40th Anniversary Banquet on 26 March 1977, dating its founding to 1937 for the fourth independent time — after the Concordia holdings, Alta Kahn's 1958 "coming-of-age" conference, and F. M. Van Wagner's 1975 tribute. Rosaire Corbin had returned to the ACQ-QCA staff and was responsible for all its training programmes.

Canadian Camping, February 1977: "The Employment Visa Certification Waiver has been amended to permit non-immigrants to work as camp counsellors, or in similar leadership roles, (not as kitchen staff or maintenance workers) in camps operated by the Canadian Camping Association. They do not need Canada Manpower certification that residents of Canada are unavailable for such employment." The mechanism required a letter from the camp director naming the occupation, location and duration "and particularly, that the employer is a member of the Canadian Camping Association," presented with a passport or birth certificate at the point of entry; provincial associations were told to send their member-camp directories to every port of entry.

Camp accreditation in 1977 was a standards regime, a condition of government grants and a hiring instrument at once: any foreign staff member at an accredited Canadian camp from 1977 onward entered the country on the Employment Visa Certification Waiver, which applied only to member camps of the Canadian Camping Association.

Charles Plewman, on being made an Honorary Member of the Canadian Camping Association, said: "When the Canadian Camping Association was formed back in 1936, it was an act of faith, pure and simple. It was only a dream... because after all there were only two provinces in the whole of Canada that even had Camp Associations. In the thirty-eight years that have elapsed since that time, we have made that dream come true." The internal arithmetic — 1936 plus 38 — places the address at the October 1974 annual meeting in Montreal; the February 1977 newsletter is reprinting it.

Charles Plewman was 87 in February 1977, which places his birth at about 1889-90 — the first birth estimate this project has for him. In the same address he gave organized camping as reaching "some 500,000 of our Canadian youth," complained that "the Federal Government had not begun to appreciate" it, named "Taylor Statten and Mary Edgar, just to mention two" among the founders, and held that "the Golden Age of Camping still lies ahead."

John Latimer, Director of Kilcoo Camp, set out the Canadian Camping Association's promotion doctrine in February 1977: the primary source of campers is old campers, so leave room on the application for names of friends and relatives; "be wary about advertising in large urban newspapers" — suburban weeklies, school yearbooks and home-and-school publications reach the right homes more cheaply; brochures should last three or four years with only the application reprinted annually; then a home visit at which "the first item to be 'sold' is of course — the Director"; then birthday cards, Christmas cards, calendars, two or three newsletters a year, and separate reunions for new campers. Chase every unreturned application, "because those with the criticisms... are those who are the most reluctant to let you know what went wrong the previous year." The summary word is "PERSONAL."

John Latimer told directors in February 1977 that "at the end of the summer, a letter of assessment from the Director" should go to each camper's parents, and that this "will mean that there must be a very accurate method of receiving a full report from each counsellor." This is assessment of campers, not of staff, so it is a different document type from a staff evaluation; but it establishes that a director writing down judgements of the children who passed through his camp in August was following national practice.

The Canadian Camping Association's five best-selling books of 1976: Camp Counsellor's Handbook by Blackstock and Latimer ($4.95); Acclimatization ($5.25) and Acclimatizing ($5.95) by Steve Van Matre; The Camp Counsellor's Book edited by Northway and Lowes ($1.95); and Nessmuk's Woodcraft and Camping ($1.75). Punch Jackson of Winnipeg was building a book service for directors through the CCA, and Sharon Brown "a complete bibliography of all books, catalogues, papers, magazines etc. which would be of any interest to anyone in the camping and related fields," due mid-April 1977.

The six Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association instructor schools for 1977 included only one in Quebec — the French-language school at the University of Ottawa Camp near Gracefield, 20-30 June, under Jacques Grenier. The English-language Gracefield session of 1976 is gone, so English-speaking Quebec candidates would have had to travel to Ontario. Three Woodsmanship Instructors Schools were promised conditionally: "If Government funds are available to be used by the C.C.A. for certain projects in 1977."

Hart M. Devenney's obituary by Kirk Wipper (February 1977) records a Springfield College B.Sc. and a McGill M.A., a year at Yale Divinity, marriage to Rena Bickerton in 1929, Director of Urban Youth Centres in Manitoba in 1939, RCAF auxiliary services in England, the Middle East, North Africa and Italy, Director of Physical Education and Recreation for Manitoba for a decade from 1945, inspector then consultant in Physical Education and Camping for Ontario from 1955, managing editor and assistant director of CAHPER for thirteen years, President of CAHPER 1952-54, and from 1957 Director of the Ontario Camp Leadership Centre at Bark Lake.

May Brown closed Camp Deka in British Columbia in 1977 — "truly one of the finest independent camps in this country... An era has come to an end!!!" — her husband Lorne Brown having predeceased her; she moved on to Vancouver municipal politics.

Canadian Camping, March 1977, reports the Quebec Camping Association English Section's 40th anniversary conference: "The 40th Anniversary of the English section of the Q.C.A. was indeed a great celebration. Telegrams from several spots around the world were received by President Derek Walsh and the weekend Conference (March 25 - 27) was a tremendous success due to the efforts of so many people including Chairman Wilf Jackson. There was an impressive list of past presidents of Q.C.A. in attendance, namely; Norrey Owens, Zave Ettinger, Ross Seaman, Bob Lazanick, Peter van Wagner, Bill McCarthy and Val Willis. Special recognition was given to Miss Frances Kelly who for many years has been the backbone of the English section of Q.C.A."

Three Kanawana-connected people were at the Quebec Camping Association English Section's fortieth anniversary conference of 25-27 March 1977: Derek Walsh, then Kanawana's director, presiding as Section president; A. Ross Seaman, Kanawana's director of 1959-67, among the past presidents; and Norrey Owens, eight months after he endowed the Order of Owens at Kanawana. Seaman and Owens had sat on the same QCA executive in 1954, Owens as president and Seaman as conference chairman.

Frances Kelly is described in March 1977 as "the backbone of the English section of Q.C.A." She appears in this run as the office secretary of the early 1950s, the executive secretary of the 1960s and 1970s, and the author of the F. M. Van Wagner tribute in 1975 — twenty-five years in the same office.

Robert Lazanik's surname is spelled "Lazanick" in the March 1977 newsletter against "Lazanik" elsewhere in the run. The same man; the spelling is unstable in the source and should be flagged before any name-matching pass.

The Canadian Camping Association published the results of its first annual statistical questionnaire in March 1977: "68,000 Camper Spaces Available in 1976. 260,000 Campers attended Member Camps. Of the 32,000 staff members in 1976, 22,000 were paid and 10,000 were volunteers, while 1,600 came from outside Canada. Food Costs equalled $8,000,000 (not including Salaries, fuel and kitchen supplies); Other costs (excluding food and salaries) totalled $14,000,000." Quebec was among four associations — with New Brunswick, Alberta and British Columbia — whose members responded at over 50%.

The Canadian Camping Association wanted 1976 statistics "in order to appear to be an organization with a strong foundation, and a knowledgeable spokesman for camping" when facing "members of the media, as well as Government officials," and reported that "some Camp Directors refused to co-operate... feeling that we were invading their privacy, or that the figures would be used to embarrass them," to which the editor replied: "if we are unable to provide reasonable figures for the Government, we will then be legislated into answering certain questions... with no option to be coy or evasive!"

Madeleine Allen's "Parental Motivation Affecting the Attendance of Children at Summer Camp" (March 1977) surveyed parents at Camp Ouareau: 150 questionnaires sent with the May camp mailing against a registration of 195 campers over the two-month season, unsigned and uncoded "to encourage frankness," 100 returned — 66%. Of seven ranked reasons, living with others was the first choice of 40%, fun in the out-of-doors of 28%, and skills last, the last explained by her clientele since "eighty-two per cent of the families have summer cottages available." Fun was first for 45% of parents of 13-15s against 15% for 6-9s.

Madeleine Allen drew a conclusion from her 1977 parent survey that questions her own profession's senior programming: "This leads me to question camps' emphasis on skills and of giving this older age group any automatic, built-in over emphasis of responsibility. Should we not continue, or go back to, letting them just be themselves, to relax and have fun without the stresses and challenges of responsibility... be it tribal chiefs, test passing, 'super senior' programs, team leadership, or what have we, unless they themselves, the individual camper, really wants it?"

Madeleine Allen describes Camp Ouareau in March 1977 as "the only English speaking, private, girls' camp in the province of Quebec," with francophone registration capped at 10% per section so those who came would get "almost total immersion in the English language." Her survey also records that 44 mothers and 47 fathers had been campers (14 and 15 of them staff), 35 families had neither parent at camp and 26 had both, and only a third of campers had been to any other camp.

Jack Pearse was elected incoming President of the Canadian Camping Association in 1977, with Paul Belanger acclaimed Vice-President. The Ontario Camping Association elected Jocelyn Palm incoming President, Mrs. Barbara Gilchrist President Elect and Mrs. Phil Lowes Vice-President; its annual conference of 3-6 March at the Royal York drew "a record number of 552 Directors and Senior Staff," and a lucky draw raised "a little more than $3000.00, thereby putting the O.C.A. out of the red for the first time in a couple of years."

The newsletter that replaced Canadian Camping magazine in October 1976 was "Design and/Dessin et Printed by/Imprime par National Sport and Recreation Centre Inc. / Centre National du Sport et de la Recreation Inc." — the federal sport body, which is part of how the association cut the cost that had killed the magazine.

Jocelyn Palm's survey of camps on the Small Vessels Regulations, reported in May 1977, records the reception of the November 1975 federal rule requiring an approved lifejacket or Personal Flotation Device for every person in every craft: "Almost 50% of the camps responding required the presence of the lifejacket or P.F.D. prior to the regulation... 18% of the camps were unaware of the regulation until they read about it in the June 'Canadian Camping' magazine, and another 10% of camps were unaware of the regulation prior to receiving the questionnaire." More than a quarter of accredited Canadian camps were operating boats in breach of a federal regulation they had not heard of, and this magazine was the instrument that told 18% of them.

Jocelyn Palm's May 1977 waterfront syllabus distinguishes a lifejacket — 29 lb buoyancy, with a righting movement — from a PFD, 15 lb and less bulky, "designed to encourage Canadians to wear the devices"; notes that the regulation requires the device to be carried, not worn; and teaches donning on land, in the craft and while immersed, entering the water from a low dock to see what position the body takes, HELP (heat escape lessening posture) for water below 60 degrees Fahrenheit, and helping an injured partner into a device in the water.

Every La Verendrye trip from the summer of 1976 carried approved flotation for every paddler because federal law required it from November 1975, so any 1975-76 bulk purchase of flotation devices in Kanawana's records is explained by the regulation rather than by a change of camp policy.

Charles W. Tisdall, managing partner of Tisdall Clark Lesly & Partners, reviewed some 50 Ontario camp brochures with his graphics staff for the 1977 OCA annual meeting and reported what he found: staff group photographs "sitting and standing row after row, clean and neat in their Sunday best," never with names; collages; under- and over-exposed pictures; inconsistent writing, "good basic English on one page, and then, an informal and 'slang' English on the next"; trite phrases — "our camp is a melting pot," "we are one big happy family"; logos "tucked away in corners... as if camps were ashamed of them"; loose inserted fee schedules; and "the fifty brochures reviewed, submitted from Ontario camps, all said pretty much the same thing."

Charles Tisdall's 1977 prescribed contents list for a camp brochure is a checklist against which any surviving camp brochure of the period can be read: management qualifications, activities, senior staff backgrounds, safety precautions including water safety, supervision, doctors and nurses, first aid and emergency measures, fee schedule, contact telephone and address, a short history of the camp, directions, arrangements for eating, sleeping, clothing and washing, a statement of what kind of camp it is, a return envelope, and "Display your accreditation logo clearly, and large enough to be seen — the Canadian Camping Association — your Provincial Association. Be proud of it."

The Canadian Camping Association held its annual meeting in late April 1977 at the Easter Seal Camp in Squamish, British Columbia, concurrently with the Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association's: "Musical Chairs was played by Ron Johnstone, who became Past-President of the C.C.A., and the new President of C.R.C.A. John Latimer became Past-President of the C.R.C.A." Awards of Honour went to May Brown, Adele Ebbs, Bryan Graham, Ron Johnstone, Cliff Labbett, Barry Lowes, Grant McKeen, Bill Swift and Barbara Taylor; Certificates of Thanks went to Recreation Canada, Fitness and Amateur Sport Branch, "in appreciation for their tremendous financial support." The 1978 annual meeting was set for Winnipeg.

The Canadian Camping Association's Task Force, created "with the support of Recreation Canada" and reporting in 1977 after "several meetings with hundreds of Canadian Camping leaders," recommended that camps continue to join the CCA only through their provincial associations; that many committee tasks be devolved to provincial associations; that the CCA keep organising national conferences of the Geneva Park type; that the national board keep meeting in conjunction with provincial workshops; and that "A National Publications Service should be a strong priority," covering new books, reports, theses and speeches. Its committee was John Latimer (Chairman), Paul Belanger, Barry Lowes, Jack Pearse, Jay Haddad and George Robitaille, with Ron Johnstone as consultant. The full report "along with all of the background material is available in every Provincial Association office," so a copy was deposited in the Quebec office.

The Employment Visa Certification Waiver for foreign camp staff was narrowed and confirmed in May 1977: "The ruling about foreign staff applies only to those young men and women who will be instructing and counselling... and only in Accredited Camps." Directors were urged to notify the point of entry of names and addresses in advance.

The Canadian Camping Association adopted a new logo in 1977, chosen from a competition and designed by Mrs. Daphne Kaye of Camp Voyageur, Ontario, with "a cut of the Logo... made available to Camp Directors so that our National symbol can be part of all publicity and correspondence sent out from every accredited Camp in Canada." Any Kanawana letterhead or brochure of 1977 or later may carry it, which is a dating aid for undated printed material.

The provincial association addresses printed in May 1977 give the Quebec Camping Association, Inc. (English) at 2233 Belgrave Avenue, Montreal H4A 2L9, and the Association des Camps du Quebec, Inc. (French) at 1415 est, rue Jarry, Montreal H2E 2L9.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1977 publications catalogue lists among its Canadian titles the Log of Canada's Centenary Journey, published by the CCA at $3.00 — the Centennial canoe-journey record, still purchasable ten years after the event.

Brian Blackstock is named as Editor of Canadian Camping for the first time in the newsletter era, in the May 1977 masthead — the same Blackstock who co-authored the Camp Counsellor's Handbook the association was selling. The masthead's French line in that issue reads "Publication Officielle L'Association des Camps du Quebec" where every other issue reads du Canada — a printing error, not a fact.

Song-leading advice from the Boy Scouts of Canada, Greater Toronto Region Training Resource Library, printed in May 1977, includes "Consider the songbook as a teaching aid. Use the books when you need them; put them aside when you don't" and "Keep a File or List — Start now to accumulate songs that your group likes to sing" — the practice that would have produced a camp songbook had anyone at a given camp followed it.

The 1978 Geneva Park national conference was set for 19-22 January 1978, with a charter committee including Rosaire Corbin of the Association des Camps du Quebec, Virginia Fraser of Etobicoke Parks and Recreation for day camping, Bruce Harris of Camp Kawabi for independent camps, Wayne Perkins of Camp Wanakita for the YMCA, Mardi Tindal for United Church camping, Barry Lowes of Camp Timberlane, and Dorothy Walters on Government Liaison — a standing government-liaison post on a conference committee.

Canadian Camping's Quebec paragraph of June 1977: "Abbe Robert Maisonneuve is the new President of the A.C.Q. - Q.C.A. Provincial Board. The Vice-Presidents are the Presidents of the English and French Sections, respectively. Mr. Derek Walsh begins the second year of a two year term, while Abbe Paul Belanger will combine the Presidency of the French Section with his position as Vice-President of the C.C.A. M. Rosaire Corbin is the Chairman of the French language Camping Committee."

Derek Walsh's presidency of the Quebec Camping Association English Section was a two-year term whose second year began in June 1977 — so roughly spring 1976 to spring 1978, overlapping his Kanawana directorship of 1974 to February 1979 entirely. Because the joint Provincial Board's vice-presidents were the two section presidents, he held provincial office in the bilingual body at the same time, under Abbe Robert Maisonneuve, while also being a Vice-President of the Canadian Camping Association nationally.

The Canadian Camping Association's executive from mid-1977: President Jack Pearse; Past-President Ron Johnstone; Vice-President Paul Belanger; Secretary Eileen Mayotte; Treasurer George Simonett. Two of the five were Quebec men, with Derek Walsh also a vice-president — the strongest Quebec presence in the national body this run has shown.

Bruno Morawetz's essay "The Importance of the Unimportant" appears twice in this run — in Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 4 (June 1975) and again in Vol. 29 No. 4 (June 1977) — and the two printings differ. The sentence "Woe to the camp which yearly changes its directors!" appears only in the 1977 reprint; the 1975 original ends that passage at "a camp is the expression of the individual who runs it." The 1975 text also reads that camps "should" be made into little Switzerlands where 1977 reads "could." A third printing, in Winter 1983, carries the attribution "Reprinted with permission from the CCA Conference Digest, 19[??]" — the year is not legible in that scan, and is consistent with 1961 or 1971.

D. R. Offord, M.D., writing for counsellors in June 1977, holds that there are two groups of campers, those "who feel 'good in their own skins'" and a smaller group arriving "with some needs that really should have been looked after long before they got to camp"; that from a camper's point of view "the more I like him, the worse I'll behave, maybe"; that "some cabins where the kids are the best behaved are the cabins where very little of any lasting learning has gone on"; that it is worth telling campers "when you feel you've been a poor counsellor"; and on discipline, "Anyone of your campers has a right to be angry but he doesn't have the right to hit someone every time he feels that way."

The Special Report on John Bosco Camp (June 1977) gives an unusually complete financial picture of a small Canadian camp: eighteen years on ZN Lake in Nipawin Provincial Park; 5,176 campers served in the ten years since 1967; 820 campers and 81 staff in 1976; the camping budget "trippled in the last five years"; camper fees of $7.50 per day in 1977 covering only the cost of feeding them; and a spring forest-fire loss of $62,177.48 of which $32,210.00 was insured, leaving $29,967.48 uncovered. 256 man-hours, 48 of them by air, were spent searching 1,000 square miles for a relocation site without success.

The Canadian Camping Association renamed its Standards committee the Professional Development Committee in 1977, under Lorne Bowering — worth noting for anyone searching CCA records by committee name.

Barry Lowes, Director of Camp Timberlane and a member of the CCA Task Force, set out the association's recommended staff evaluation sequence in October 1977: "The Unit or Section Heads — They do evaluations on all staff. We do formal brief, sit-down evaluations of staff at the end of the first few days... We have each counsellor do a self-evaluation at the mid-point in the summer. They fill out the same form that the unit head will use at the end of the summer... At the end of the summer each counsellor has a final evaluation to learn how others have viewed his summer." And: "The Directors — Collate all of these reports. From them develop lists of repairs, items to be purchased, staff to be rehired, programs to change, etc."

Leo Robitaille's Kanawana line "All '73 staff could be re-hired unconditionally with the following exceptions" is the last step of a nationally recommended procedure, written four years before Barry Lowes set that procedure out in print but describing the same practice.

Barry Lowes states the safeguards that were supposed to accompany camp staff evaluation in 1977: counsellors' reports on campers are "brief, confidential and must be written candidly to be of value"; "You must be sure to let staff know who will have access to the evaluations. Confidentiality is vital!"; and, of counsellors-in-training but stated as a general principle, "they have, like all staff, a right to know how they are doing during the season and a final evaluation of how they did overall at the end of the summer... The C.I.T. has a right to discuss the report with the person doing them. It is a basic human right and also a sound evaluation technique."

Barry Lowes's 1977 account of how a Canadian camp was supposed to examine itself: campers evaluate anonymously ("Handwriting will enable you to determine roughly the age group"); counsellors evaluate the camp anonymously and are asked specifically whether supervision was "Too little, too heavy, helpful, hindrance?"; specialists inventory their equipment under "Item, Quantity, Good Condition, Need Repairs, Discard, Quantity to Purchase Next Year, Where is it Stored?"; kitchen staff are consulted; and parents who simply stop sending their child get an anonymous questionnaire asking why. He kept it all in a large loose-leaf notebook divided by department, so that "year by year you will build up a valuable historical pattern of evaluations, recommendations and results."

Barry Lowes's test of a camp's success: "How many of your campers and staff want to return to camp this summer? Turnover is your barometer of success." And against the objection that a change must wait for next year: "It angers me to hear someone say 'it's too late to change this year'. The devil it is! We have made major changes on the second last day of camp in order to see some idea in action."

Eanswythe Flynn's off-season checklist for November and December, reprinted in October 1977, includes reprinting the camp folder "using new photographs and copy if necessary" with an explicit cross-reference to Charles Tisdall's brochure article of May 1977; checking letterhead, statement forms, staff contract forms and invoices; planning a Christmas-holiday camp reunion including parents; and, for agency camps, "Agency camps should investigate the availability of surplus commodities and supplies. These can be available for the asking, but requests should be in early," including arts-and-crafts scraps, linoleum and carpet ends and "clearance of fire-damaged goods."

Canadian Camping reprinted American food-cost advice in October 1977 giving the scale of the inflation camps were absorbing: "sugar, for example, increased over 400% in a two year period." The recommendations were to buy Standard rather than Fancy grade, "costs less and has just the same nutritive value"; judge a case of canned goods by usable yield rather than can count; eliminate menu items "that historically end up in the garbage can"; and increase initial orders and storage capacity to buy pre-season.

Rona Wasserman's month-by-month camp public-relations programme, reprinted in October 1977, centres on a November Yearbook mailed to campers, counsellors and prospects and deliberately amateur — "It is imperfect, photo-offset, obviously written by children. The pictures are not professional. But the Yearbook gives the feeling of the camp much better than the slick brochure we used 18 years ago" — which sold about half their prospects; with December enrolment carrying an "early sign-up appreciation souvenir" and different souvenirs by year of return, "pennants, banners, camp nightshirts."

The Canadian Camping Association's third National Conference at Geneva Park, 19-22 January 1978, ran "through the co-operation of Recreation Canada and the Canadian Camping Association" on the theme "Keys to Success," at $75.00 per delegate with economy return air fare to Toronto covered for delegates from outside Ontario — federal money paying for a national camp conference. Delegates were selected by each provincial association rather than by application, so the Quebec association chose who went.

The newsletter's front page from late 1976 reused the dead magazine's cover design: "We have incorporated the cover of the 'Canadian Camping' Magazine, Vol. 27 No. 1 to Vol. 28 No. 3, designed by Violet Catlin, Graphics, 4 Canzone Dr., Toronto, into the front page of this and the previous six newsletters."

The Canadian Camping Association's committees and projects for 1977-78 were: Archives, Adele Ebbs (Ontario); French Language, Rosaire Corbin (Quebec); Leadership Training, Jean Funk (Alberta); Liaison with National Agencies, Clare Magee (Ontario); Outdoor Education, Bob Cameron (New Brunswick); Professional Development, Lorne Bowering (BC); Publications, Punch Jackson (Manitoba); Public Relations, DEREK WALSH (Quebec). Projects: National and International Conferences, John Latimer; Newsletter, Brian Blackstock; Oral History, Jay Haddad; Skill Schools, Jim Winter; Woodsmanship, Kirk Wipper.

Derek Walsh chaired the Canadian Camping Association's Public Relations Committee from 1977-78 — three years earlier than this project had it from the 1980 committee list — while still Kanawana's director, while holding the Quebec English-section presidency, and while a national vice-president. He was the only Quebec name among the eight committee chairmen, and the line from here to his 1981 pamphlet How to Promote Your Camp is four years long and continuous.

The Canadian Camping Association's oral history work was a standing national project by winter 1977-78 with a named chairman, Jay Haddad of Ontario, who also sat on the Task Force that reported in April 1977. The taping of camp pioneers agreed at the Quebec board meeting in spring 1976 was therefore institutionalised.

The Canadian Camping Association became formally bilingual at one meeting, dated in the December 1977 tribute to Paul Belanger: "When the C.C.A. Board was struggling with the revision of our constitution at a meeting in Regina in 1971, it was Paul Belanger who convinced us in his delicately kind and inimitable way that we ought to give warm recognition to our two languages in the C.C.A. We became convinced, committed and constituted and, out of the Regina meeting, emerged Le Comite des Camps Francais and a new constitution with this stated purpose — 'To promote the development of Camping in Canada with the highest ideals and traditions of both language groups consistent with the national heritage of Canada.'"

Abbe Paul Belanger founded Camp-Ecole Keno in 1964, sixty miles northwest of Quebec City; sat on the Quebec Provincial Board; was President of the Association des Camps du Quebec; was first President of the CCA's French Language Camping Committee; was ACQ delegate to the Federation de canot-camping; chaired the first Canadian Conference on French Language Camping at the Montmorency Forest in April 1976; was CCA Vice-President; and was called to Rome as Assistant General of the Marists with responsibility for Quebec, New England and France, honoured at an ACQ-QCA dinner in Quebec City on 24 November 1977.

Canadian Camping printed a STAFF INTERVIEW EVALUATION chart in December 1977 with seven headings to be rated one to ten — Appearance, Composure, Maturity, Self-Confidence, Frankness, Leadership Potential, Experience with Children — with a note to add "patience, fairness, sense of humour, honesty, imagination, reliability, enthusiasm and a high set of personal standards." Directors were told to keep the ratings and "look at the ratings during the summer and compare your rating then to the initial interview," and to "be sure to keep the autobiographies of those you hire as they are often useful for reference during the summer."

The full documentary cycle of a 1970s Canadian camp staff record is now described in the association's own pages: interview rating sheet, autobiography on file, first-week sit-down, mid-summer self-evaluation, end-of-summer written evaluation, and the director's collated rehire list. Kanawana's embargoed 1973 staff assessment sits at the end of that cycle.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1977 hiring advice gives a memorable test — "How would I feel about letting this person take a group of my campers on a trip?" — with suggested interview questions "What would you do if one of your campers was missing when you woke up in the morning?" and "Suppose you broke your leg on a trip fifty miles from camp." On personality: "a Camp can handle a limited number of 'characters'... they are like the paint on the paddle. The blade, however, is what does the work." On references: "Some of those 'saints in script' you may read of in letters of reference don't turn out that way on the job. PHONE one of the referees if you want more information in confidence."
