A joke column in Canadian Camping, December 1977, pairs polite formulas with what a director actually means, ending: "You have learned a great deal from your summer with us, I am sure. Perhaps another year you might find it challenging to try a (a) larger, (b) smaller, (c) different, (d) American camp." = "Thank heavens you won't be back!" Published as humour in the association's own newsletter, it is evidence that the not-rehire decision was an ordinary and even jokable part of camp directing culture in the period.

The Quebec camping calendar for 1978 shows an annual provincial campaign: "2-9 March 1978, ACQ-QCA semaine de Camps" — so Camp Week was a yearly March fixture and not the one-off of March 1977. The Montreal souper-causerie series had published themes: "Plein air — publicite, depliants" on 30 January, "Recrutement — mode de selection" on 22-23 February, and "formulaires — Mecanismes de controle" on 15-16 March, with a seminaire des directeurs de camps 7-9 April.

On Paul Belanger's departure for Rome, Eileen Mayotte of Saskatchewan became CCA Vice-President and Jane McCutcheon of Ontario replaced her as Secretary; M. Rene Rousseau, Director of Camp Edphy at Val-Morin, Quebec, became the new President of the Association des Camps du Quebec; and Jocelyn Palm, President of the OCA, became the new owner and director of Camp Glen Bernard.

Jack Pearse's presidential travelogue of December 1977 records that he directed Holland Cove Camp on the south shore of Prince Edward Island in the summer of 1949; was at Burry Heights Camp, Newfoundland, in 1969, the year the Newfoundland and Labrador Camping Association "had just been born"; that the CCA Annual Meeting of late winter 1976 was at the Montmorency Forest outside Quebec City, joined to Canada's first French Language Camping Conference; and that in June 1967 he opened Bird's Hill Park north of Winnipeg and sang camp songs with twenty-four thousand Guides, Brownies, Scouts and Cubs.

Eanswythe Flynn's January checklist directs directors to order crests, pennants, camp T-shirts and postcards; to "Engage staff, nurse and doctor for the summer as soon as possible. Have contracts signed and sealed"; and to "get last year's staff together for suggestions — new canoe routes or out-trip hikes to new sites." Her February checklist directs them to consult the Counsellor Placement Service and to "Review and prepare rules for counsellors, regarding duties, responsibilities, time off, behavior in camp and out of camp, supervision of campers and cabins, and discuss them with staff during interviews."
The Royal Life Saving Society Canada convened a national symposium, "Alcohol & Aquatics," and published the proceedings at $3.50 in 1977 — a findable Canadian document on drinking and drowning.

Winter maintenance advice in Canadian Camping, December 1977: mothballs on mattresses; screens taken off, "they will last about three times longer"; wax paper over stove grills; the walk-in refrigerator left open because it is "a great place to grow MOLD"; canoes stored on benches or rafters so both gunwales carry the weight rather than flat on the floor; and mattresses left in their own cabins rather than piled, "also combustion hazard."

Canadian Camping printed Ernest Thompson Seton's "The Indian's Creed" in full in February 1978 — all fourteen articles verbatim over Seton's name, cited to The Book of Woodcraft and Indian Lore, without comment, introduction or context. It is a white naturalist's idealised composite in the past tense and the singular: "he believed in the sacredness of property. Theft among Indians was unknown"; "he believed that the noblest of virtues was courage... the most shameful of crimes was being afraid." Recorded exactly as printed and dated, not adopted in this project's voice.

The Seton framework this project traces from Seton through Taylor Statten into Kanawana's council ring had not been retired by the Canadian camping establishment by February 1978: it was reprinted verbatim and without comment eight years after the Red Power movement and five after Wounded Knee, in the same run that had already carried Mary S. Edgar's and Jack Eastaugh's more self-conscious pieces on the same subject. That is a datable fact about the institutional context of Kanawana's own ceremonies in the late 1970s.

J. Harry Ebbs's camp infirmary inventory was reprinted in Canadian Camping in February 1978, five years after its first appearance in Spring 1973. The drug list is the striking part: beyond ASA, milk of magnesia, calamine, kaopectate and ear and toothache drops, a camp was expected to stock ASA with codeine, 100 tablets of phenobarbital, 100 tablets of penicillin at 250,000 units, 100 tablets of triple sulpha and 100 capsules of Achromycin — a barbiturate and three antibiotic lines held in a camp cupboard — with the attending doctor separately supplying narcotic drugs, penicillin for injection, anaesthetic material, adrenalin, steroids and intravenous sets, plus a snake bite kit where required.

Eileen Mayotte's CCA executive profile of February 1978 records: "During her illustrious career in camping, Eileen has had responsibility for camps and campers in four provinces — Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, and B.C. Her camping endeavors have lead her into church camping, YWCA and camps for underprivileged children. In the distant past she was the Secretary of the Quebec Camping Association. She was one of the founders of the Saskatchewan Camping Association, and for many years was its President." She was appointed CCA Secretary at Squamish in April 1977 and elected Vice-President at Moncton in November on Belanger's departure.

Jack Pearse, CCA President 1977-1979, of Waterloo, began directing camps in 1949 with the YMCAs of Charlottetown and Ottawa, has been Director of Camp Tawingo, a year-round camp, since 1961, was first President of the Eastern Ontario Camping Association, and is a past president of the Ontario Camping Association and chairman of its Past Presidents' Council.

Ron Johnstone's CCA profile of February 1978: YMCA camps in Ontario and Saskatchewan; settled in London in 1955; operated Camp White Bear on Lake Temagami until the fall of 1976; joined the Ontario Camping Association in 1946; Conference and Standards Chairman before becoming OCA President 1972-74, and "combined this presidency with that of the Society of Camp Directors in 1973"; founding executive of the Council of Outdoor Educators; first President of Canoe Ontario; and President of the Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association.

The Quebec Camping Association's executive met at the Montreal YMCA on 13 February, 13 March, 10 April, 8 May and 12 June 1978 — the provincial body that accredited Kanawana, presided over by Kanawana's own director, holding its monthly executive meetings in the building of the institution that owned the camp. Its 1978 public programme: 28 February, general meeting, "Looking at Camp Thru the Eyes of a Camper," a panel of four campers; 17-18 March, QCA Conference; 18 April, general meeting, "Let's Get Ready for the Summer"; 27 May, QCA Counsellor Conference and a QCA Standards Meeting.

Elmer Bogyay, food manager at Trinity College School, gave the economics of camp catering in February 1978: "What you can buy today, you cannot buy tomorrow" — he bought a year's coffee in June 1976 and it appreciated "almost 100%"; sugar went from $21 a bag to $91 at peak. He dealt with 25 companies, kept charts by company by month, and carried $35,000-$40,000 of inventory. Practical rules: convert prices ounce by ounce because packaging sizes differ deliberately; test a large purchase on ten or fifteen pounds first; check the weight of the garbage bag every day; and be present when a big delivery arrives, because "once the truck pulls out, they are no longer responsible."

Elmer Bogyay's menu rule of 1978: "NO ROTATING MENUS. I cannot press this point strongly enough... the kids coming into the dining room will know that the first Wednesday is macaroni and cheese, the first Saturday is spaghetti." And on the kitchen against the tripping department: "Don't let your tripping director influence you, even if he has been doing it his way for fifteen years. If you are running the food service he is going to change. His job is to make sure the kids have a good route, your job is to make sure the kids have good food at the best possible price" — with the instruction to buy juice crystals in five-pound packages and have the trip room repackage them, since "75% of the food could come from the kitchen and not the trip room and be bulk packaged."

Trent University Archives holds a Quebec Camping Association fonds, 85-013, covering 1948-1982 — the whole accreditation era. It is cited as source 23 of connections/related-camps/quebec-camp-landscape.md and had never been queried for accreditation records, while the search for the annual Quebec accreditation reports on Kanawana listed the QCA's own archives fourth among places to try. It should be asked first, and asked specifically for QCA Standards Committee minutes.

Eanswythe Flynn's May checklist, written for a mainly Ontario readership, directs directors to "Find out from your provincial camping association whether or not this is your year for a Standards Visitation" — assuming a multi-year cycle, and so confirming from the other side that Quebec's annual re-accreditation was exceptional rather than standard.

Canadian Camping, April 1978, names "Mr. Braverman of Pripstein's Camp, a Q.C.A. member" — so the independent Jewish camp at Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, the same municipality as Kanawana's predecessor Camp Jubilee, belonged to the same accrediting association as Kanawana. The same issue identifies Wilfred A. Jackson, who chaired the QCA English Section's fortieth anniversary conference in March 1977, as "Director of Camps and Conference Centre of the Catholic Community Services, Inc., Montreal."

Wilfred A. Jackson, a Montreal camp administrator, prescribed in April 1978 the records a camp should keep for maintenance: a masterplan showing all buildings present and future; a loose-leaf Maintenance Manual with check lists, directions and "a schedule arranged by seasons, including specific details on opening and closing procedures"; and "A record of each building should be kept showing floor plans, type of construction, history, inventory, and required repairs," with plans of water, electrical and sewage systems and manufacturers' instructions on file. He adds a large master map, a portfolio of buildings with photographs and floor plans, a log of improvements, a list of local suppliers kept in the maintenance building, tagged keys with spares held by the maintenance head, and weekly site tours.

Wilfred Jackson stated a tenure norm in April 1978: "As continuity is very important, a director should be challenged to stay with the camp for at least five years" — the same argument as Bruno Morawetz's "woe to the camp which yearly changes its directors," from a Montreal administrator rather than an Ontario private-camp director. Kanawana had four directors in three years around 1972-74.

John Latimer's keynote to the Geneva Park National Leadership Development Conference on 19 January 1978, "Keys to Success," turned on a Toronto billboard campaign reading "CURE ANONYMITY": "camp is just about the only place in today's society where everyone can be treated as a somebody... and it starts with the director." On his own lineage: "I grew up in camping under the influence of the greats in this country... Charles Plewman, Taylor Statten, Mary Edgar and A.L. Cochrane. I followed in their footsteps up to a point, but... footsteps should only be a guide." On boards: "One of the greatest crimes which a board can commit is to hire a Director... and then start to make him into something which the committee feels he should be, taking away all vestiges of his own personality." On staff: "If our counsellors aren't growing and if they aren't challenged and recognized they'll go somewhere else."

The Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association ran nine canoeing instructor schools in 1978, of ten days each, in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario (two), Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia. No Quebec school is listed — so from 1978 the national canoe-instructor schools no longer ran in Quebec, consistent with Quebec running its own provincial programme instead.

Mary I. Casey's The Nurse and the Health Program at Camp was published by CCA Publication Services at $2.00, with chapters on the camp nurse, organisation of the health programme, health counselling and teaching, emergencies, recording and reporting, camp sanitation, standing orders, supplies and equipment, and health information for counsellors. "Standing orders" and "recording and reporting" name two more camp record classes to ask Concordia for.

The American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement on trampolines, obtained by a Quebec camp director and printed in Canadian Camping in April 1978: "Trampoline accidents have resulted in a significant number of cases of quadriplegia... between 1973-1975 spinal cord injuries with permanent paralysis resulted more frequently from trampolines than any other gymnastic sport. Next to football, trampolines were found to be the highest cause of permanent paralysis," with a recommendation that trampolines be banned from school physical education and abolished as a competitive sport.

Duncan R. Campbell, Executive Director of Labour Market Policy at the Ministry of Employment and Immigration, wrote to CCA President Jack Pearse in 1978: "While it was agreed that job offers made to foreign camp counsellors were not to be exempt from Manpower validation in 1978, our further review of the situation indicates that a change now, to take place for this summer, would pose difficulties... it has been decided that the present exemption from Manpower Certification will be retained for the 1978 summer season, with the change likely coming this fall." So the labour-market-test exemption covered the seasons of 1977 and 1978 and was expected to end that autumn.

Under the revised Immigration Act and Regulations implemented on 10 April 1978, a non-immigrant camp counsellor had to obtain employment authorization before arriving at a port of entry: the camp sent "a detailed offer of employment... The letters should clearly establish that the employer is a member in good standing of the Canadian Camping Association"; the counsellor took it to a Canadian embassy or consulate for Employment Authorization Form Imm. 1102; both were presented at the border; and a social insurance number was required. Consulate addresses were printed for Britain, France, Israel and fifteen American cities — a map of where Canadian camps recruited.

C. R. Blackstock's author note of May 1978 records that he had been involved with camping for fifty years and had directed Bolton Fresh Air Camp, Camp Pinecrest and Camp Mazinaw, and was a consultant with the National Sport and Recreation Centre in Ottawa — the federal body that designed and printed this newsletter. His Pine Crest directorship is relevant to the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs question: the Pine Crest Games began in 1940 and Kanawana adopted the format in 1947, so if his tenure overlaps either date he is a candidate for the person through whom it travelled. He is not the Brian Blackstock who edited this newsletter; no source seen states a relationship.

C. R. Blackstock's history of Canadian camping (May 1978) records that L. B. Sharp, director of the Life Magazine Camps out of New York, "came to Toronto in 1940, and told us it was time to give camping back to the campers," arguing for stated purposes and camper-chosen programme in groups of eight with two leaders. On the origins of accreditation: the thirties brought the "tests and measurements" wave, after which "camping became self-conscious and began measuring the effects of the experience... Soon we had all kinds of standards established against which camps could be given performance ratings. The Camping Associations 'policed' their members and made conforming to the standards a necessary condition for membership."

The Canadian Camping Association sold audio cassettes of eighteen sessions from the Geneva Park national conference of 19-22 January 1978 at $3.50 each, ordered from M. Lee, R.R. No. 1, Port Sydney, Ontario. The titles include "Maintenance and Building" (Wilf Jackson of Catholic Community Services, Montreal), "Expectations" (Bruno Morawetz), "Will Staff Return" (Bob Slingerland), "High A.Q. Programs" (Mayotte and Delainey), "Finance and Legislation" (Ron Johnstone), "Effective Administration" (Ken Willis) and "To Whom Directors Answer" (Shanley Parkinson) — a dated, itemised recording of Canadian camp directors talking about their work in 1978.

The Canadian Camping Association's Liaison with National Agencies Committee wrote to over 40 national agencies in 1978 and ranked them in three tiers. Tier A: Boys and Girls Clubs of Canada, Boy Scouts of Canada, Canadian Recreational Association, Canadian Red Cross Society, Canadian Yachting Association, Royal Life Saving Society of Canada, the Salvation Army, the National Council of YMCAs of Canada, Girl Guides of Canada, National Interchurch Camp Committee and Christian Camping International. Tier C includes the Canadian Bar Association — a sign of where the liability worry of these years was heading.

Dr. S. M. L. Kirkpatrick's talk to the Society of Camp Directors on asthma at camp, summarised in May 1978, describes camp medical procedure for a chronic condition: a question about medical problems on the initial application form, a fuller form sent to parents weeks ahead so the dispensary can be stocked and the child placed "in an environment as free of allergens as possible," all medications held and dispensed by medical staff with counsellors briefed before out-trips, and breathing exercises before medication. His safety warning: "There have been two recent deaths from anaphylactic reaction following an allergy injection in a doctor's office. We advise that campers not be given their allergy injection in the camp setting."

Eanswythe Flynn's June checklist directs directors to "check to see that you have this year's Test Sheets for canoeing and swimming awards"; to distribute the Staff Manual to all staff by the end of the first week of June; to check with Lands and Forests or Natural Resources "about canoe routes and hiking areas, and the cost, if any, of sending groups over Government owned property"; and to "Set up the Infirmary. Check supplies (see page 7 of February's Canadian Camping)" — using the Ebbs list as an operational instruction, which is evidence the magazine functioned as a working manual.

Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 4 (June 1978) is a summer number aimed at counsellors — a quotation page, safety and comfort articles, one reprinted American piece on wilderness navigation, and the publications catalogue. It contains no Kanawana material, no Quebec material and no new Canadian institutional fact. The null is recorded explicitly so that a later pass can tell a read issue from an unread one.

The Alberta Camping Association's "Director's Guide for Counsellor Training" was in print by June 1978, listed in the CCA publications catalogue at $3.00 and asterisked as a Canadian book. The Alberta "Practical Guide to Hebertism" announced in the same breath in 1976 is not in the catalogue, so as of June 1978 it had not appeared and searches should not assume a 1977 imprint.

Canadian Camping's lightning-safety article of June 1978 states plainly: "From time to time, upsetting fatal accidents have taken place in camping situations," adding that "loss of young lives could have been avoided in each case with serious training and forethought." The unnamed plural of fatal accidents at Canadian camps is treated as known to the readership.

The lightning advice printed for Canadian camps in June 1978: everyone indoors as soon as a storm breaks; outdoors, lie flat on the ground and "forget the soaking," never shelter under a tree; on the water, "Get out and get off... On The Double!"; indoors, go low, close windows, avoid the telephone, lamps and taps, and stop all dishwashing and showers; in a vehicle, pull over but not on a hilltop. For electrocution, mouth-to-mouth immediately and continued "whether or not there are signs of life." And with young campers awake at night, "get them singing songs... the louder the better to out-sound the storm. They like the excitement of sitting in a circle on the cabin floor."

Marvin Granek's master's thesis in Recreation at the University of Waterloo, "An Investigation Into the Attitudes of Resident Camp Administration Towards Critical Problems in Resident Camping," summarised in Canadian Camping in October 1978, surveyed Canadian camp administrators on 33 attitude statements across eight areas against thirteen background characteristics. Two findings are reported by region: "Generally speaking, all camps are having some difficulty filling their quota of campers, although church camps less so than others. Quebec camps are having more difficulty getting campers than are camps in other regions," and "Historically the tradition of resident camping has been centred mainly in Ontario and Quebec. As a result, the popularity of resident camping in these two regions may have peaked... Demographic changes in the population, however, have also contributed to a diminishing supply of campers."

Granek's 1978 survey is the first external, dated, quantitatively grounded statement this project has of the market Kanawana was operating in during its thinnest documented decade. It is regional rather than about Kanawana, but it changes how the thin later-1970s record should be read: a Quebec residential camp in 1978 was working against a peaked and demographically shrinking pool, in the province where that pressure was sharpest.

Granek's other 1978 findings: all administrators agree there is a problem holding the interest of older campers, with private and boys-only camps finding it easier; agency camps are "more positive to change, especially in the area of professional development," which he attributes to "a kind of spillover effect from the practices of the agencies themselves, which tend to be involved in in-service training and program evaluation on a regular basis"; private camps "enjoy the luxury of being accountable only to themselves" and "give indications of being least likely to challenge the status quo"; administrators were unanimous that resident camping should be provided for more children who cannot afford it; and camps in eastern Canada are least worried about losing staff to other employers, which he attributes to higher regional unemployment. His three recommendations to the CCA were a higher public profile, a feasibility study for camp director certification, and short-term staff exchanges between camps in different provinces or of different types.

The provincial association contact list of October 1978 gives "Quebec Camping Association, Inc. — Dr. Ken R. Willis, President — 2233 Belgrave Ave., Montreal — Secretary: Miss Frances Kelly." Derek Walsh was in the second year of a two-year term in June 1977, so his presidency ran roughly spring 1976 to spring 1978 and Willis succeeded him. Frances Kelly was still the section's secretary, extending her run in that office to at least twenty-five years.

The provincial camping association officers of October 1978: ACQ — M. Rene Rousseau, Camp Edphy, Val-Morin; ACQ-QCA Provincial Board — Abbe Robert Maisonneuve, 1415 est rue Jarry, Montreal, Executive Director M. Raymond Hade; British Columbia — Dr. Don Arnold; Alberta — Lou Lanier; Saskatchewan — Laverne Jantz; Manitoba — Shanley Parkinson; Ontario — Jocelyn Palm; New Brunswick — Robert Cameron; Nova Scotia — George Matthews; Newfoundland — Elizabeth Wegenast; national office — Jack Pearse.

C. R. Blackstock wrote in October 1978 that "Ernest Thompson Seton through his writings and the programs he developed for his Pioneers put the emphasis on learning the skills and knowledge of the Indian culture, and those that the explorer, trapper and pioneer used to survive in the wilderness," and that early camp programmes were shaped by their staff: "The schedules used in camping were patterned after the school timetables which was only natural as most camp directors were school teachers... the same teaching methods were applied to camp activities and took much of the risk and fun out of them." He reads the later standards movement as liberating rather than constraining: "the educators, the psychologist and the health and safety specialist got into the act. They put back more of the risk and chance to explore the unknown."

Camp Newfound's "cubies" — 6 by 6 foot private dressing rooms, one per camper and counsellor, in a long building in front of every two sleeping cabins — were founded with the camp in 1914 by Elizabeth Horton, "who felt that it was the right of every girl to have a certain amount of privacy no matter where she was." Campers decorated them with six yards of fabric bought from the outfitter's list, a senior staff member inspected each daily and wrote a score out of ten on a calendar on the door, and counsellors' cubies had "private lights, rocking chairs and NO inspection." A deliberate design choice against the open-cabin norm every other camp in this run assumes.

The editorial in Canadian Camping, December 1978: "The tragedy at the beginning of the wilderness trip attempted recently in Quebec brought camping people up short. We have become somewhat complacent during the past ten or twelve years assuming our performance standards are satisfactory and well known to all camp people to the point where they will protect all of us. A review of this incident indicates this is not so. Even government regulations are not broadly known nor publicized well enough." No camp, party, date or water is named, and the incident has not been identified.

The December 1978 editorial reaches for a precedent: "In the 1920s a camp in Southern Ontario had a similar experience at Balsam Lake. Out of that came the slogan 'Hang on to the canoe — for three days and three nights'. It was also the spur to camp people to establish standard strokes." That is a dated 1920s origin for two things any Canadian camp tripper would recognise.

The second half of the 1970s is when the safety framework around Kanawana's canoe trips was rebuilt — the November 1975 federal flotation regulation, and the association's own reckoning after the 1978 Quebec wilderness-trip fatality — and neither change originated at the camp.

F. M. Van Wagner was made President Emeritus of the Canadian Camping Association in December 1978, with his handwritten reply reproduced in facsimile. The notice states: "He shared in the founding of the C.C.A. in 1936 and is one of its Charter Members. The next year he organized the Quebec Camping Association, English Section, and became its first President." It also gives CCA President 1958 to 1961, honorary member 1974, born Hyde Park New York, Camp Nominingue founded 1925 on Petit Lac Nominingue, the Award of Merit from the ACQ-QCA Provincial Board and the Centennial Medal.

F. M. Van Wagner is the second charter member to date the Canadian Camping Association's founding to 1936 in the association's own pages, after Charles Plewman in February 1977 — which bears on the competing 1946 date the project also holds.

Jack Pearse's travel report of December 1978 records a Montreal visit in October 1978: "the afternoon was spent participating on a panel concerning staff recruitment, training and supervision with BARB PATTERSON, RON BRAVERMAN and BOB LAZANIK organized by KEN WILLIS, HERB FINKELBERG and the English Section of Q.C.A." Then "BOB MAISONNEUVE chaired a superb dinner meeting of A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. en deux langues" at which Pearse and John Latimer received woodcarvings by Rene Rousseau. Pearse was met by Rosaire Corbin, visited "old friends Tony Shorgan and Yves Beauregard at the Society for Crippled Children," lunched with Maisonneuve, Raymond Hade and Lucille Cardinal, and was driven by past-president Zave Ettinger to the Lazaniks'.

The CCA board agenda at St. John's in late 1978 records "a nation wide request for all Camps to submit statistics for our use with the Immigration Department, for the national promotion of Camping by DEREK WALSH and the P.R. Committee, and for a C.C.A. National Directory which will be assembled by GEORGE MATTHEWS and the N.S.C.A." So Derek Walsh's national Public Relations chairmanship was still running in late 1978 — the year he ceased to be QCA president and his last full year at Kanawana.

Eileen Mayotte resigned from the Canadian Camping Association executive in December 1978 to work full-time in the Regina schools' counselling department. Jack Pearse: "In the 10 years she has been involved in the National Camping scene, no one has given greater service or dedication to Canada's campers. She has truly been our 'First Lady'." That dates her national involvement from about 1968.

Alan F. Klein's "For a Happy Camper," an address to a Canadian Camping Association conference in Montreal in 1960, was reprinted in December 1978 as still current. Klein was Professor of Social Group Work at the University of Pittsburgh; the piece applies Maslow's hierarchy to camp admissions — "if we have certain kinds of facilities and staff, the level of needs evidenced in a camper may clearly indicate that we have no business accepting him" — and Bettelheim's Love Is Not Enough: "Love them and limit them. A child who is not limited is a deprived child, a frustrated child, a rejected child and hence an unhappy child." A national CCA conference was therefore held in Montreal in 1960, during the three years the national office was there under Van Wagner.

Alan Klein's test of a camp's honesty about its own purposes, reprinted in 1978: "If you do not screen the youngster intake, group them by plan and programme for the purpose, I can only conclude that you are fooling yourself in thinking that you are clear and comfortable about your purpose. If you employ callow young staff and give them a once over lightly pre camp session, I must conclude also that you do not mean your purpose." His analogy: camps engage a dietitian because "a trained dietitian knows which foods in what combinations produce a balanced diet... Then they hire a programme director. His or her skill in devising a programme menu should be as precise as the dietitian's."

The Canadian Camping Association's national office moved before 31 March 1979 to 1806 Avenue Road, Toronto, still sharing with the Ontario association; its submission to the federal government for 1979-80 "totals more than $86,000.00" from Fitness and Amateur Sport. Doug McEwen was revising the constitution, last done by Stan Wild in 1971. Kirk Wipper's Woodsmanship Leaders' Guide was nearly complete and being translated by Rosaire Corbin.

Jean Funk's Leadership Training Committee expected to complete a national model for C.I.T. and Counsellor Training in January 1979 "which could be used by Provincial Associations and individual camps," and the Nova Scotia association had produced a camp song book which it planned to "put to music" — a Canadian camp songbook of 1978.

The Winter Woodsmanship Pilot School at Camp Kandalore, 7-12 February 1979, covered winter trail skills, non-mechanized travel, winter ecology and safety, cooking, clothing, skiing, snowshoeing, snow studies, wildlife and first aid, with "the underlying theme... the principle of living in harmony with the environment." Twenty candidates from across Canada attended, each provincial association allotted places, with travel and board paid by Fitness and Amateur Sport; Quebec had places.

Paul Potter's report on the Nova Scotia Camping Association's 1978 summer project records a real Canadian camp songbook: "May and June also saw the development of a song book. Although some camps had been working on their own song book, none was large enough to hold all of the songs from every camp. Therefore a provincial song book with more than five hundred songs was published. Since its publication, the book has been in constant demand and may soon require a second printing. The cost is $3.00 and it is available from: Nova Scotia Camping Association, Box 696, Halifax, Nova Scotia B3J 3H5."

A five-hundred-song collection compiled from the repertoires of every camp in a province is the best available comparator for deciding which Kanawana songs are house compositions and which are movement-wide — the question the camp-songs-and-cheers article cannot currently answer.

The Canadian Camping Association's own self-description in February 1979: "It began in 1936 and became incorporated in 1949. At present, there are member associations in all provinces except Prince Edward Island." The association reads its two dates as founding and incorporation rather than as rival founding dates.

This project's own sources disagree by one day on the CCA's Letters Patent: canadian-camping-movement.md source 8c gives 4 November 1949, while the association's own 1976 directory gives 5 November 1949. A transcription slip on one side or the other, flagged rather than silently harmonised.

The Canadian Camping Association's stated purposes in February 1979: to further camping "as an educative, character building and constructive recreational experience"; to liaise between provincial associations and act for them internationally; "to speak for organized camping on a national level and to represent their collective interests with the Government of Canada"; to encourage high standards "and the implementation and maintenance thereof through the provincial and territorial camping associations"; to study, interpret and disseminate; to run national training and conferences; to publish; "to further research into camping and to publish the results of such research"; and to encourage audio-visual material.

The Canadian Camping Association's membership rule, stated in February 1979: "Any camp or individual members in good standing of a federated Provincial and/or Territorial Camping Association are automatically members of the Canadian Camping Association." That is why Kanawana was a CCA member without ever having applied to be one. The facing page states: "All C.C.A. program and projects are made possible by financial contributions from the Fitness and Amateur Sport Branch of the Ministry of National Health and Welfare."

Paul Potter's account of the Nova Scotia association's 1978 summer, funded by a Secretary of State grant with three staff from 8 May: they turned the provincial standards for resident youth camps into a checklist format "to make them more useful during the actual visitations"; ran the annual training programme for fifty counsellors and directors; ran the first Provincial Woodsmanship School in June for thirty people; produced the songbook; and visited forty-six camps between 6 July and the end of summer. On how the visits were received: "In most cases, the visitors were met with hesitation, mainly because they were felt to be inspectors. After some time talking and sharing ideas, the camps showed great interest in the project and the N.S.C.A. They left most camps wishing that more time was available."

The Quebec camping calendar for 1979 includes "1-9 March, ACQ-QCA Semaine des camps" — Camp Week for a third consecutive year, now nine days — along with ACQ Formateur multiplicateur modules on 6-8 February and 9-11 March, a Seminaire des directeurs on 27-29 April with the theme "La communication," the ACQ-QCA annual meeting on 10 May, and a session for moniteurs on 25-26 May. The QCA English Section's own monthly executive meetings drop out of the printed calendar this year.

Kevin Redmond's "No Trace Camping" (Canadian Camping, March 1979) brings leave-no-trace ethics into Canadian camping, aimed squarely at camp tripping practice and at the camping tradition itself: "Beware of the traditions — axes, saws, elaborate latrines, garbage pits and material shelters, all of which can be found in camping texts." Its creed: "I believe that man can travel through the wilderness and leave no trace. I will keep my groups small. I will not cut down trees or branches. I will not build fires or if I do I will keep them small and scatter their remains... I will LEAVE NO TRACE." Its test: "Will the next traveller, be he a couple of hours or years away, know that you have been there?"

Kevin Redmond's 1979 specifics: "Large groups do not belong in the wilderness. The organization of trips with more than 20 people is bound to leave its mark on the ecology... it is difficult to imagine how more than 10 people could spend a night in an undeveloped spot and leave no trace"; fires never on the forest floor, on mineral dirt or rock or with the thin forest floor lifted and saved for replacement, kept small enough that "any wood small enough to break with your hands will be suitable"; and because "charcoal is pure carbon and will last forever, wood ashes on the other hand will dissolve in the soil with the next rain," stop adding wood and scrape the embers together to burn out. Human waste fifty feet from water in a hole 8 by 10 inches and "not more than 6" to 8" deep, to stay within the biological disposer layer of soil."

Between 1975 and 1979 a Quebec camp running wilderness trips was told by federal regulation, by its association's editorials and by its association's published ethics to change how it travelled. Kanawana's later environmental commitments arrive in a movement where this argument had already been made in print.

The Canadian Camping Association's committee, project and task force chairmen for 1978-79: Archives, Helen Stewart (succeeding Adele Ebbs); Federal Government Relationships, Jack Pearse; French Language, Rosaire Corbin; Immigration, Barry Lowes; Leadership Training, Jean Funk; Liaison with National Agencies, Larry Bagnell; Membership Promotion, Eileen Mayotte; National and International Conferences, John Latimer; Newsletter, Brian Blackstock; Oral History, Jay Haddad; Professional Development, Linda Arnold; Publications, Fred Okada; Public Relations and Promotion, DEREK WALSH; Skill Schools, Jim Winter; Woodsmanship, Kirk Wipper.

Derek Walsh chaired the Canadian Camping Association's Public Relations and Promotion Committee for a second consecutive year in 1978-79, from the association's own lists, and remained the only Quebec name on the slate. With the 1980 committee list and the 1983 award citation, his tenure in that office is continuous from 1977 to at least 1983.

The Canadian Camping Association's Woodsmanship Leaders' School had been operating for four years by March 1979 — so from about 1975 — funded by Fitness and Amateur Sport, and was publishing an Instructor's Manual in both French and English. Its Skill School Project planned instructors' schools in "Social Recreation (songleading, storytelling, campfire program, games leadership), Pioneer and Native Crafts, Fitness at Camp, Camp Administration, Program Planning and Nature Awareness," with the aim "to decentralize all the schools, once competent leaders have been trained to a national set of standards." A national songleading school was therefore planned in 1979.

The Canadian Camping Association reported in March 1979 that "The content of each Conference is gathered together and each of these reports may be obtained through the Publications Committee at the National Office," naming the French Language Camping Conference of 1976 and the Outdoor Education Conference of 1974 — two conference reports, one of them the first French-language camping conference in Canada, existing as purchasable documents in 1979.

Bob Slingerland's advice on senior campers (March 1979) characterises them as feeling "that with maturity they should be getting more privileges and responsibilities as well as free time and opportunities to be lazy and to be alone to think... they appreciate privacy and the value of a few close friends, and are sensitive to criticism." His levers were atmosphere, a programme set a week in advance, and an optional evening programme followed by a campfire in which non-participants "would have to make other arrangements to constructively use their time" and 75-80% joined anyway. His section avoided swimming until the counsellors swam in the class themselves, after which "swimming became rather popular even in August... possibly because the campers got a chance to show up their counsellors."

Alice Bullwinkle and Howard Galloway's Finding Summer Staff (1979), reviewed in Canadian Camping in March 1979, "for the first time... Canadian listings are included" and carries "specimen forms for use in staff selection... a job application form, an interest and training-need inventory form, a form for obtaining useful information from persons listed as references, and staff employment agreement" — another instrument in the camp staff-records cycle.

C. R. Blackstock's obituary (Canadian Camping, May 1979) dates his Camp Pine Crest directorship: "In 1936 he directed Bolton Camp and for some years after that was the inspired and creative director of Camp Pinecrest," with Camp Mazinaw beginning in 1940. So he ran Pine Crest for roughly 1937 to 1940 — the window in which the Pine Crest Games began. No source says he authored the Games; what this establishes is that the man directing Pine Crest when Lumbermen-versus-Voyageurs started had national reach, which is why a format begun there could travel to a Montreal YMCA camp seven years later.

C. R. Blackstock's 1979 obituary gives a full chronology: a Camp Kitchikewana "original" who "started the first year of that 'Y' camp on Beausoleil Island in 1921 as a very young counsellor" under director Ernie Thurlow; at Pickering College in 1928 "during the same period as the late Taylor Statten"; waterfront director at Camp Ahmek in 1930 and 1931; later full-time staff of the Canadian Red Cross Society as Director of Water Safety; Head Master of the Junior School and Director of Athletics at Pickering College, where he began "the first winter school-camping for a number of seasons at Limberlost Lodge"; a B.Sc. from McGill; an honorary LL.D. from York University in 1974; Camp Mazinaw established 1940; executive secretary of CAHPER; a Founding Fellow of the Society of Camp Directors; and Honorary Life Member of the OCA.

C. R. Blackstock had Fred Hagan carve over the fireplace in the lodge at Camp Mazinaw: "May Wakonda whose messenger is the Thunderbird, smile upon His children and send down the sacred fire from Heaven." His obituary explains it: "Council Ring and Indian Lore is a part of Mazinaw because Blackie had a 'feeling' for our native people."

Three Canadian camps used the same borrowed deity name across sixty years: Kanawana's council ring script ends "Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe"; Jack Eastaugh remembered the Taylor Statten camps closing council ring with "Wakonda dhe dhu"; and C. R. Blackstock — Camp Ahmek's waterfront director in 1930-31 — had the name carved into the fireplace at Camp Mazinaw. The transmission route is the one Eastaugh describes, from Seton through Statten's camps into the leaders trained there.

C. R. Blackstock's obituary records that "He gave input to the current research being done by the Society of Camp Directors, of which he was a Founding Fellow, when he alleged that canoe trippers should be trained to handle risk and to anticipate it." So within months of the 1978 Quebec wilderness-trip fatality, a named body distinct from the CCA had research under way on canoe tripping risk. His own position on flotation is recorded there too: "on the issue of life-jackets he believed that sufficiently trained persons would know under what conditions they should be worn" — the argument the November 1975 regulation had just overridden.

Camp Amy Molson of Montreal advertised a "CHILD LEADERSHIP TRAINING COURSE, June 24 - August 27, 1979. Participatory Training for 16-18 year old girls interested in child care and activity programming for 5-8 year old campers. NO FEE," from Miss Frances Owen, Executive Director, Camp Amy Molson Inc., 1430-A St. Marc Street, Montreal H3H 2G2 — a nine-week free leadership training programme for teenage girls, run by a Montreal camp charity in the same city and season as Kanawana's CIT programme.

A three-week "Workshop in Outdoor Adventure Education," 23 July to 10 August 1979, was held at the University of Ottawa Camp seventy miles north of Ottawa, conducted by Professor Claude Cousineau of Ottawa, Professor Bob Pieh of Queen's and Professor Kirk Wipper of Toronto, for six academic credits, on "the man/nature relationship within the context of adventurism" — the Gracefield camp again, now hosting a credit-bearing university course taught by the two founders of the canoe instructor schools and the founder of Outward Bound Canada.

Dr. Elsie Palter, Honorary Member of the OCA and former director of Camp Kawagama, wrote on discipline in May 1979: "discipline is taken to mean 'to educate, to train, to instruct disciples'. It does not refer to chastisement or punishment." On corporal punishment: "It is most important to realize that corporal punishment does not teach respect. It may achieve immediate results, but no learning occurs... the only thing learned by the child is to use this means of control when he becomes a parent and the vicious circle is perpetuated. There is no place in camping for corporal punishment." On docking: "To 'dock' a child from having dessert does not teach him to be polite at the table. Similarly to 'dock' a child from his favourite activity destroys his trust in you."

Elsie Palter wrote in May 1979 of agency camps specifically — Kanawana's type: "In an agency camp where the children may come from culturally deprived homes, one is more likely to find the adult is regarded as an antagonist. This provides a challenge to you, as a leader, for the child to learn that an adult can be trusted." She argued for "as few rules as possible," naming two — never swim alone and only in supervised areas, and be prompt at meals — and held that camp rules "have grown out of the experience of staff and campers for years back." Period terminology recorded as written.

The Canadian Camping Association's annual meeting was held at Acadia University, Wolfville, Nova Scotia, on Friday 25 May 1979, with "the Installation of the new President, Clifford Labbett, and Vice-President, Derek Walsh." The 1979-81 executive: President Emeritus F. M. Van Wagner; President Clifford Labbett; Immediate Past President Jack Pearse; Vice-President Derek Walsh; Secretary Elizabeth Greenway; Treasurer Wayne Perkins.

Kenneth Willis extended an invitation at Wolfville in May 1979 to hold the next Canadian Camping Association annual meeting in Quebec in the spring of 1980 — which would be the first national camping meeting on Kanawana's home ground since 1976.

Opening the CCA annual meeting at Wolfville in May 1979, Jack Pearse "emphasized the fact that organized children's camping began in Nova Scotia in 1890." This project's canadian-camping-movement.md states 1889 for Big Cove YMCA Camp, sourced to an encyclopaedic entry. Pearse, speaking to the Nova Scotia association on its own ground, said 1890. Neither date is documented from a primary record, a single year may be the difference between founding and first full season, and Kanawana's position as Canada's second-oldest camp is unaffected either way.

Twenty Environmental Maintenance Standards, developed at a Conference of Canadian Interpreters and reprinted from the Alberta Camping Association Newsletter of May 1979, open on exactly Kanawana's 1970 problem: "Most of our camps have occupied the same site for many years... Since large investments in buildings have been made on those sites, the protection of the environment of our camps must therefore be a major concern." Among them: "Privies and outhouses to be considered one of the best ways of disposing of body wastes — superior to the flush toilet"; "Question the use of motor boats in the camp program"; "'Camping without a trace' may be a slogan that could be used more and more. Question the idea of permanent out-trip sites that tend to become over-used"; trails rested and re-surfaced when over-used; "erosion areas become a fine program area for campers to see the results of poor land management"; and noise pollution reduced with "silent hikes and canoe trips."

Canadian Camping printed a four-page removable "Closeup Checklist" in June 1979 whose framing sentence names the problem this project keeps meeting: "It could be very useful in camps where continuity of leadership is not always easy." Several of its items are inventory instructions with two copies and two named holders — food inventory, dishes, cutlery, pots and pans, each with blanks for "____ has one copy / ____ has the other" — which is a camp record class with a known form, worth asking Concordia for by name.

The June 1979 closing-up checklist for Canadian camps: freezers left open with a screen over the top "to prevent animals from being trapped inside"; mattresses on their sides; screens removed and labelled on the edge; tents dried, rolled and labelled; tent platforms lifted to an angle so water drains; packs scrubbed and hung upside down; paddles and oars hung up or laid flat to prevent warping; fire extinguishers checked and containers emptied and stored upside down; piano lids left open to prevent the wires rusting; chimneys covered; ashes down the privies; and boats painted in the fall so the coat hardens.

Canadian Camping reported in June 1979 that "Departments of health are now suggesting with increased urgency that camps have sufficient 'ablution tables' (handwashing areas)," illustrated with an outdoor structure from Camp Onondaga near Huntsville — a dated instance of provincial health departments pressing camps on a specific fixture.

The Canadian Camping Association's "Anyday Ideas" for counsellors (June 1979) record what filled unstructured time at a Canadian camp: "Leave Something Behind" — build new steps, a pathway, a railing, or split wood for the fireplace; a Games Day with "a waterboiling contest, cutting seats in a log, caber toss, three legged race, fire fighting contest, egg throwing contest and log sawing"; a natural-object scavenger hunt; a night walk with no flashlights, "stopping just to listen"; campers making Christmas cards for each other in the summer for the counsellor to post in December; "'Battleship' — a camp classic — ask about it!"; and raft-building, since "camp may provide them with the only opportunity they will ever have to try this activity."

Madelene Allen's tribute to Edgar Blais (Canadian Camping, October 1979) is the only piece about a camp cook in the whole run: "Last week we lost our chef who had been with us for seven years. No famous man whose death would make headlines, but a simple man who did so much for camping by making campers happy with what came from the kitchen. No executive post on the association, no articles written, just work at a hot stove for long hours... spare a thought for an unknown to you, Edgar Blais." The verse gives his hiring and his death: "To our door he came, out of work, dejected. Sent to camp's winter door by Manpower. 'Can you cook? Do you like children?' 'Mais oui.'... But a notice in a small town paper was the final severance: 'est decede accidentellement M. Edgar Blais.'" Seven years at Camp Ouareau, so from about 1972, hired through Canada Manpower.

At Kanawana as at Camp Ouareau, kitchen staff appear in no plaque, no directory and no accreditation report. Madelene Allen's 1979 tribute to a chef of seven years is a reminder that the absence is a property of the records rather than of the camps.

Canadian Camping reprinted a long piece on acid rain from The Probe Post in October 1979, introduced as "a topic which should interest every citizen, particularly those of us who are concerned with children living near 'living lakes'." Its figures: uncontaminated rain pH about 5.6 against a mean of 3.95 to 4.38 in south-central Ontario and one snowfall at 2.97, "over 400 times the acidity of normal precipitation"; of 209 lakes tested near Sudbury, 20% "dead" and 50% threatened; Muskoka-Haliburton acidity "now as bad or worse than that in Scandinavia"; and Inco's 1,250-foot super-stack emitting "an average of 3,600 tons of sulphur dioxide daily." Ontario "emits large quantities of acids that cause acid rains in the province and in Quebec, Eastern Canada and Northeastern U.S."

Acid rain is the first environmental threat in this run that a camp could do nothing about from inside its own fence. Nothing in the 1979 article is about Kanawana and no measurement of its own lakes from this period is known, but it is the context for any later water-quality record from Lake Kanawana, Lake Wilson or Round Lake.

Hartwick, Jorgenson and Gear's "Canoe Tripping in the Twentieth Century" (October 1979) states the problem plainly: "The irony of canoe tripping is that it has the potential of destroying the very environment the tripper seeks out to enjoy... It is unlikely that the number of users will decline voluntarily, therefore the answer must lie in lessening their impact." Their rules: carry out everything "and a little of what others have left"; small stoves or a metal fire container; let the fire burn to ash "leaving no charcoal"; "if you find several fire pits at your site, clean up the best one or two and eliminate the others"; gather firewood by canoe at a distance even when wood is available on the site; and "do not blight the campsite for your own comfort (e.g. trenches, bough beds, tables, natural shelters, garbage pits)" — four techniques standard in camping manuals, abandoned.

Three separate statements of leave-no-trace ethics appeared in Canadian Camping within seven months in 1979 — Redmond in March, the Environmental Maintenance Standards in June, and the canoe tripping article in October. The movement was rebuilding its tripping ethic at speed.

Kirk Wipper's Woodsmanship Leaders' Guide was published by the Canadian Camping Association in 1979, 155 pages, $6.00, "in 3 ring loose-leaf form, to allow for easy up-dating," with three components — "an exploration of the land ethic; a compendium of ideas on the theme of leadership; and... a set of practical materials on land pursuits" — covering Trail Skills, Survival, Program Planning, Navigation, Food and Menu Planning, Human Waste Disposal and Basic Ecology. It was being translated into French by Rosaire Corbin.

From October 1979 all American Camping Association books became available to Canadians through the CCA's Publication Service at American catalogue prices payable in Canadian funds, with the CCA paying postage — dating the moment the American camping literature became cheap and easy for Canadian camps to buy.

A classified advertisement in Canadian Camping, October 1979, offers for rent "75 acres, 3 lakes, large wharf, diving board and tower, playing field, buildings, electricity, central water system, former boys' camp... 70 miles from Montreal near Lachute, Quebec" — an unnamed Laurentian boys' camp that had closed by 1979 and was letting its site. The advertisement gives only a Montreal telephone number and the property is not identified.

The counsellors' page of October 1979 records a documented method by which camp songs were composed and transmitted: "Make up a CAMP SONG using the tune from a popular camp song. Each camper could send one verse to you and then you could return a copy of the completed song to each of them. Follow this up by singing it to the new camp when it assembles next spring." Some camp songs were written in the winter, collectively, by post.

The Canadian Camping Association appointed its first Executive Director in November 1979: Miss Marjorie A. Booth of the Montreal YWCA, on a Fitness and Amateur Sport grant. Her immediately preceding post is given plainly — "most recently as the director of Camp Oolahwan, the Montreal Y.W.C.A. camp, located north of Montreal." She was a native of Toronto with an honours degree in Recreation from the University of Waterloo, several years full-time with the Saint John YWCA, and a Fellow of the Society of Camp Directors since 1977.

Marjorie A. Booth is the second named director of Camp Oolahwan the project holds — camp-oolahwan.md names nobody in charge between Mary Edgar's departure in 1919 and the final season in 2004. Her appointment establishes that Oolahwan was an operating YWCA residential camp in the late 1970s with a professional director recruited from another province, not a survival running on inertia.

The Quebec Camping Association English Section disappears from Canadian Camping's printed list of provincial associations between October 1978 and December 1979. The October 1978 list carried three Quebec entries — the Quebec Camping Association Inc. under Dr. Ken Willis at 2233 Belgrave Avenue, the ACQ under Rene Rousseau, and the joint Provincial Board under Maisonneuve; the December 1979 list carries only "Association des Camps du Quebec — M. Raymond Bonneau, President — 1415 est, rue Jarry." Absence from a list is weak evidence, but it is consistent with the citation for Derek Walsh's 1983 CCA award, which thanks him "as a Past President of the former English Section – Quebec Camping Association."

CCA President Cliff Labbett wrote in December 1979: "Derek Walsh, the Vice-President, is a past-president of Q.C.A. and will retain the Chairmanship of the C.C.A. Public Relations and Promotions Committee, a position he has held for the past two years, along with his duties as V.P." — independent confirmation from the association's president of the 1977-79 span built from the two committee lists.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1979-81 executive was almost entirely YMCA and YWCA staff: Elizabeth Greenway, Secretary, Director of Camping for the Toronto YWCA; Wayne Perkins, Treasurer, Director of Camp Wanakita for the Hamilton YMCA; Derek Walsh, Vice-President, a former Quebec YMCA camp director; and Marjorie Booth, its first Executive Director, from the Montreal YWCA. That is the institutional world Kanawana belonged to.

Cliff Labbett's report from the CCA board meeting of 1-2 November 1979 states the association's decentralisation model: "C.C.A. started the Canoe Instructor's Schools which have now been turned over to the Provinces and also the Woodsmanship School which is almost ready to be turned over," with new schools under consideration in Social Recreation, Nature Awareness, Fitness, Camp Organization and Administration, Native and Pioneer Crafts and Communication, "once they have been developed it is hoped that they too will be taken over by the Provinces." The records of the Quebec versions of these schools would therefore be in Quebec, not Toronto.

The Canadian Camping Association approved in principle in November 1979 an international camping conference in Toronto in 1983, "with the Canadian Camping Association, the Ontario Camping Association and the American Camping Association joining forces. It is hoped that representation will also come from several European countries, Japan and India," John Latimer chairing.

The Victoria YM-YWCA put a forestry counsellor on Camp Thunderbird's 1,300-acre site from early May 1979: with foresters Mark Atherton and Vlad Korelus, campers used an increment borer, chain, diameter tapes, compass and clinometer to age trees, calculate height and compute wood volume, while property lines were located and marked, a base map at 1:5000 was drawn, forest units needing treatment were identified and a fire-safety programme implemented — "By the end of August, a base map and forest cover management plan were completed." Advice was available from the Canadian Institute of Forestry, c/o Macdonald College, Montreal.

Canadian Camping recommended in December 1979 that camps number each canoe by purchase year and sequence — "this was the sixth canoe purchased in 1975" — which "aids in easy camper and staff identification as well as instilling an attitude of care and respect... makes it easy to assign canoes for trips as well as checking for damage upon their return." If Kanawana used a numbering scheme of this kind, its canoe fleet is datable from photographs.

Canadian Camping began serialising the Quebec Camping Association's Director Education Program in February 1980, printed in French as "Formateurs-multiplicateurs" and dated in the accompanying note: "Ce programme... etait prepare par l'Association des Camps du Quebec en fevrier 1976." It is the only Quebec camp training document this project has seen in full, and it covers the period of Kanawana's thinnest records.

The ACQ's 1976 training programme names its recruitment sources — "le personnel actuel, les anciens du camp, le milieu scolaire, collegial, universitaire," specialised faculties in "recreologie, education physique, psychologie," the centre de main-d'oeuvre, and "le service offert par l'A.C.Q.", so the association ran its own placement service — and records that it issued a standard interview sheet to member camps: "un formulaire est necessaire pour obtenir les renseignements utiles... (cf. feuille A.C.Q.)."

The ACQ's 1976 interview guidance: "Le style de l'entrevue determine le style de leadership d'un camp." Questions must draw out ideas and feelings, not yes or no, and must not be confined to the camp; the printed samples include "Qu'est-ce que tu respectes chez les autres?" and "Quel genre de musique preferes-tu ecouter lorsque tu es joyeux?" The interviewer must then evaluate himself: "Avez-vous ecoute ou avez-vous trop parle?... Avez-vous vraiment ecoute ou si vous etiez impatient d'entendre la reponse que vous desiriez? Avez-vous trop insiste sur vos propres valeurs plutot que de laisser le candidat s'exprimer?"

The Canadian Camping Association's 1980 committee list reads "Archives and Oral History — Miss Helen Stewart": the separate oral history project under Jay Haddad has been merged into the Archives committee under one chairman. The tapes and the 1976 pioneer list should therefore be wherever the Archives committee's material went, which Adele Ebbs says was Trent.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1980 slate gives Derek Walsh two chairmanships — Public Relations and Promotion, and Legislation — while he was Vice-President. The rest: Education, Linda Arnold; Finance, Wayne Perkins; Leadership Development, Jean Funk; Constitutional Review and Nominations, Jack Pearse; Concerns, Murray Wickwire; French Language, Abbe Rosaire Corbin; Liaison, Larry Bagnell; Publications, Fred Okada; Skill Schools, LaVerne Jantz; Conferences, John Latimer; Woodsmanship, Kirk Wipper; Newsletter, Brian Blackstock; Immigration task force, Barry Lowes; Membership, Shanley Parkinson; Recreation Canada, Ron Johnstone; Standards task force, Peter Van Wagner.

The Canadian Camping Association moved its executive meeting from Halifax on 17 February 1980 to Montreal on 13-14 March 1980, and the ACQ's Semaine des Camps was moved to 12-18 March 1980 — so the national executive met in Montreal during Quebec's camp week.

Bruce Harris asked thirty-five experienced camp people at Geneva Park why they returned for a second summer: "Out of 35 responses, salary was only mentioned once, and as a secondary reason." They returned "because it was a satisfying experience, they felt needed, they enjoyed the atmosphere, the feelings of responsibility." His principles include: "The first efforts of a staff member must be simple enough to insure success... Frustration at the outset is death to the efforts of a staff member"; "It is difficult to lose a cook in the middle of a summer. But what about a person doing dishes? It could take only one set of dishes done poorly to lead to an outbreak of disease, serious sickness, possible loss of health license and closing of camp"; and on burnout, "Can your head of sailing be effective four summers in a row? Where is the challenge?"

Bruce Harris proposed in 1980 that a director open pre-camp by announcing "As of this moment we have no camp policies regarding days-off, curfew, drugs, alcohol, use of the camp kitchen after regular hours, staff lounge... in fact no major policies at all," and asking the staff to write them. That list is itself a record of what a Canadian camp in 1980 had policies about.

Marjorie Booth's first column as the CCA's Executive Director asked provincial associations to keep the national body on their newsletter mailing lists: "Many times I've come across great articles in provincial newsletters. If each province can continue (or begin?) to include C.C.A. on their mailing list for a few copies of newsletters, conference programs, etc., 'Canadian Camping' will be able to carry articles from all parts of the country." Much of what the run prints from 1980 onward is therefore reprinted from provincial newsletters — a parallel body of material this project has never touched.

The Ontario Camping Association sold a kit of "Suggested Camp Forms" at $3.30 per set, 8.5 by 11 inches, from the Avenue Road office it shared with the CCA, containing nine documents: Camper Application Form; Camp Staff Application Form; Staff Health Certificate; Camper's Health Certificate; Staff Contract Letter; Staff Reference Form; Counsellor Evaluation Form; Camper Evaluation Report Form; Accident Report Form — with the note "These forms may be copied or you may add or delete anything that may be desirable or undesirable for your own special situation."

Every camp document class this read has reconstructed piecemeal existed as a standardised, purchasable set of nine forms by 1980. Anyone searching Kanawana's records should ask for them by these names. Two of them are sensitive on their face: the Counsellor Evaluation Form and Staff Reference Form are the instruments behind the project's embargoed staff-assessment material, and the Camper's Health Certificate carries medical and, for girls, menarche information.

The Camper's Health Certificate reproduced in Canadian Camping in March 1980 shows the record a Canadian camp kept on each child. The parent's checklist covers chicken pox, asthma, hepatitis, red and german measles, frequent colds, hernia, hay fever, rheumatic fever, fainting spells "of any kind," heart condition, sinus trouble, severe stomach aches, diabetes, mumps, recent whooping cough, sleep walking, bed wetting — and, for girls, "Has girl menstruated? Yes/No. If not, has she been told about menstruation? Yes/No." The physician certifies immunisation against poliomyelitis, tetanus, pertussis, diphtheria and smallpox with booster dates, records allergies, and states "any physical or emotional abnormalities." The parent grants advance surgical consent. The foot of the form is headed "FOR CAMP USE ONLY" with columns for date admitted and discharged, diagnosis, treatment and "admissions as bed patients" — so the same sheet served as the infirmary's own log.

Part 2 of the ACQ's 1976 training programme prescribes three levels of staff integration: into the world of camps, where new staff must understand "la dimension et la particularite du phenomene loisir et camp de vacances" and answer "Le loisir au Quebec, comment est-il organise? Les camps de vacances se sont regroupes en association, pourquoi?"; into the specific camp, under "milieu physique, milieu administratif, milieu humain"; and into the specific task, with the staff categories named as "les cuisiniers, le personnel de soutien, les animateurs, les moniteurs, les specialistes" — cooks and support staff listed first, the opposite of every English-language treatment in this run.

Peter Moon's interview method, reprinted in March 1980 "from an early edition of Canadian Camping," holds that "you can judge the quality of the interview by the ratio of talk between the interviewer and interviewee. The poorer the interviewer, the more he talks"; that the application itself is evidence — "Is it neat or careless in format?... What is his skill with language?"; that family and personal questions "require a maximum of sensitivity and tact"; and that a director should "leave medical questions to the physician." Its second half is a taxonomy, "Interview Signs Related to Personality Factors," listing observable indicators under emotional maturity, dependability, self-confidence, objectivity, values, attitudes and social intelligence — the vocabulary in which a camp director of the period would have written down a judgement of a young staff member.

Bruce Harris wrote on camp pay in March 1980: "no matter what the salary, it must be the same for everyone who is doing the same job with the same experience... I sincerely believe that salary has absolutely no bearing on how well a person does their job." And on turnover: "most camps, because of their financial limitations, cannot realistically provide the necessary monetary needs over an infinite amount of time. Staff must move into permanent jobs... and they must move on from the camp family to allow younger staff the opportunity to grow."

Canadian Camping printed about fifty free-text answers to question 139 of the Society of Camp Directors' canoe-tripping questionnaire — "Do you have any thoughts or concerns on the matter of canoe tripping in camps?" — unattributed and unedited, in May 1980. The questionnaire therefore ran to at least 139 questions and its results were tabulated.

Canadian camp directors did not agree about tripping standards in 1980, and the disagreement is the finding. For regulation: "standardization is necessary"; "In our province, canoe tripping is carried on by too many inexperienced or unqualified leaders." Against: "we need standards, but let's beware of setting standards so rigid or impractical that we cannot function properly," with a four-head case against certification — "a) who sets criteria b) dogmatism in tripping c) bureaucratization and government regulation d) inappropriateness of tests to area/culture." The recurring objection: "proliferation and dependence upon qualification — the majority of which assess skill but not either experience of leadership or judgement," and "the key attribute of any trip leader must be good judgement. This cannot be taught, but comes with experience."

Other free-text answers to the 1980 tripping survey: on liability, "nothing can be done when an accident occurs on a safe well-planned trip, but something can and should be done when the accident is clearly the result of criminal negligence"; on ethics, "the pioneer ethic is out of date and replaced by the wilderness ethic and minimal impact technique. Don't push the trip"; on conduct, "I sincerely feel that many camps in our area abuse campsites, the garbage left is terrible... the axe should be illegal"; and on purpose, "tripping allows children a chance to 'shine' who ordinarily would not in camp living" and "trip leaders, once they sever their group from the relative safety of base camp, have their responsibilities and concerns multiplied tenfold."

The Ontario Camping Association distributed written emergency procedures to all member camps and adopted a reporting policy "effective February, 1980." The fifteen-step procedure for a serious accident or death on camp property is legal as much as medical: confirm care is under way and "if death has occurred, cover body and keep others away"; "begin to log each action; both the time and procedure, including all phone calls"; call legal counsel, and in the case of death the police, who "MUST be called"; inform staff, then campers, then the parents named on the camper application; take written statements from everyone involved, each writing their own, plus a record of conditions before the accident and photographs "if at all possible"; and "only the Camp Director or his designate speaks to the press."

The Ontario Camping Association's 1980 reporting policy required a member camp to telephone the president within 24 hours of a serious accident or death and to file a written report within 20 days naming the person injured or deceased with date, time and place; the association would then decide "the position to be taken by the O.C.A. at the inquest," who would appear as its witness, and "methods by which the learning gained as a result of the incident might be usefully shared with the membership." This is Ontario policy and there is no evidence here of what Quebec adopted — but by February 1980 the reporting of a camp death to a provincial association was a written rule with a deadline.

The off-camp emergency procedure adopted by the Ontario Camping Association in 1980 requires the trip leader to delegate first aid, send a message by the fastest route with someone kept at the telephone, log every call in and out, and gives the senior person on the trip the recommendation "concerning the remainder of the trip, that is, to be continued, aborted, altered." It closes: "The Camp stands behind its staff members and expects each member to perform to the best of his/her capabilities and training."

The mailing label on the back page of Canadian Camping Vol. 32 No. 3 (May 1980) reads "Trent University, Archives Dept., Peterborough, Attention: K. Johnson" — the archivist Adele Ebbs named in October 1976. The Internet Archive run of Canadian Camping that this project is reading is Trent's own deposit copy, addressed to the man who received the Canadian Camping Archives.

Camp Tawingo published "Sing with Jack Pearse" in 1980 — the CCA catalogue gives it as 37 pages, 31 songs with music, "delightfully illustrated, many actions included," at $4.00 through the CCA Publications Service, the first Camp Tawingo Publication, by Jack Pearse, immediate past president of the CCA. Two sequels were announced: "Campfire Programs with Jack Pearse" and "Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse." Unlike the Nova Scotia collection it carries the tunes.

Larry Bagnell dates the Canadian equivalent of the American national agency camping group: "that historic, first meeting of the C.C.A. National Agency Group which met for the first time in the Board Room of the National Council of Y.M.C.A.'s on February 7, 1979." The Canadian entry in the international contact list is "Larry Bagnell, C.C.A. Liaison w/National Agencies, Y.M.C.A. Camping Service, 36 College Street, Toronto" — the YMCA's own camping service acting as the CCA's liaison arm.

Ruth Wortman's article on children of separated parents, reprinted in May 1980, gives camp administrative practice: at the interview establish who pays and get both natural parents' signatures where possible, since "the camp is not bound by the parent's own agreement"; ask directly about visiting — "an inquiry regarding 'more than one visiting day' is often a clue to separation of parents" — and request a copy of any court order, because "if there is no court order, the camp cannot stop a parent from seeing a child"; provide alternative visiting days so estranged parents can come separately; and on letter-writing day, "write the mother on one writing day and the father the next, rather than requiring two letters each time." It warns that counsellors "from certain backgrounds might tend to pass moral judgments on divorce."

Michael Hoyer, assistant camp director of Camp Oconto, wrote up the Society of Camp Directors' canoe-tripping survey in Canadian Camping, June 1980, with thanks to Mary Northway and the Neathern Trust for "moral and financial support." Its first paragraph explains the whole 1979-80 exercise: "Following a number of tragic canoeing and tripping accidents in Canada, the Society of Camp Directors became alarmed to hear of the number of organizations and associations which initiated plans to establish yet more sets of standards and rules which many felt should then be imposed on camps... There seemed to be little direction or concerted purpose in these deliberations. The Society felt that perhaps our greatest contribution to wilderness travel safety in this country would be to gather information as to the practices which presently exist in Canadian Camps." Note the plural: "a number of tragic canoeing and tripping accidents."

The Society of Camp Directors' 1980 tripping survey sent about 120 questionnaires to resident, agency, church, private and outdoor-education camps and tripping businesses and received about 60 responses, mostly resident camps, a majority Ontario members but with eight provinces represented. Trips were classified as short (1-2 nights), moderate (3-5), long (6-9) and extended (10 or more).

National norms for Canadian camp canoe trips in 1980: leaders a minimum of 18 on short and moderate trips and 19 to 21 on extended; Bronze Medallion the usual swimming qualification throughout; canoeing qualification usually "experience or a test set by the camp," with Senior OCA or CRCA III/IV only on longer trips; one to two years' experience minimum, two to four on extended; assistants 17, or 18 on extended; ratios about 1:5, tightening to 1:3 on long trips; and campers from eight on short trips (average ten) to fourteen on long and extended.

The equipment Canadian camps carried on canoe trips in 1980, in ranked order: first aid boxes, water purifiers, towing ropes, stern lines, bailers, swede saw, spades, long handled axe, wanigans and hatchets — with "many camp directors expressed the concern away from the use of hatchets or axes, stating that there is usually enough brush available," the leave-no-trace argument reaching the kit list. Bailers were cans, cups, Javex bottles, sponges, billy cans, pots and buckets.

In 1980 the canvas canoe was still the Canadian camp's normal boat: "Two thirds of the camps still use the canvas canoe; half, the aluminum or fibreglass. Few are using the newer plastic models." Standard length was 16 or 17 feet with a few war canoe types; half required a spare paddle per canoe; three to a canoe was most favoured; and trips ran from six canoes minimum with nine or twelve average. This bears on how any undated photograph of Kanawana's fleet is read.

Five years after the November 1975 federal flotation regulation, "about a third of the camps maintain a standard that makes wearing a lifejacket mandatory on trips. Others just expect it in rough weather, when the leader deems it." The law required a device to be carried; two-thirds of Canadian camps had not gone on to require that it be worn.

Canadian camp tripping practice in 1980: a rest day about one in five on longer trips; night tripping not favoured; existing campsites preferred; garbage "burned and carried out"; town visits discouraged; campers not allowed to smoke, staff smoking divided, alcohol "overwhelmingly rejected for staff on trips"; campers "quite involved in route and menu planning, packing and the program"; and the trip group met the director before departure in two-thirds of camps.

The 1980 tripping survey records the records camps kept: "Logs are kept for future occasions, evaluations of campers for post camp evaluations, staff evaluations for future reference, are all carried on in some form or other" — a fourth record class to seek in Kanawana's papers alongside the nine standard forms: trip logs, and camper and staff evaluations written from trips.
