Only 15 of the camps surveyed in 1980 treated white water canoeing as integral to their programme; where it was taught the skills were river reading, position in white water after upset, scouting the shore, high and low braces, lining and tracking, rescue procedures and eddy turns. On accident prevention directors preferred discussion over instruction, and on emotional stress in campers admitted "there were two opinions. One was that directors did not really cover this aspect in pre-camp, and expected their staff to be on top of this. The other group did discuss it but suggested that probably they did not do it justice."

Michael Hoyer's closing note on the 1980 tripping survey — "the questionnaire and the tabulated responses can be obtained from the C.C.A. office" — means a full data set once existed on paper. Neither the report nor the free-text answers names the 1978 Quebec incident.

The Canadian Camping Association printed the distinction beside its cut-out logo sheet in October 1980: "Your camp can only be accredited by your Provincial Camping Association and not by the C.C.A. Therefore your camp is a member camp of the C.C.A. and not an accredited member." Kanawana was accredited by the Quebec association and a member camp of the Canadian one, the membership flowing automatically from the accreditation.

The Canadian Camping Association's "A Counsellor and C.I.T. Training Program" (October 1980) sets out nine headings for in-camp staff training, of which the first is Camp History, containing: "organization history, camp's history, rationale for founding, camp traditions, site: how secured and legal status, facility developments: past, present and future, program development, administration and policy setting procedures." A Canadian camp in 1980 was expected to give its counsellors and CITs an annual account of its own founding, its traditions and how it came by its land.

The 1980 national training outline recommends where a camp's own history would be written down: "A CAMP MANUAL covering the specific details of each section will be most helpful... 1) a written reminder of details for the staff 2) a method of consolidating and finalizing your thoughts 3) a written report for future directors and boards." This retrospectively explains a document this project already holds: the "Kamp Kanawana History" presented at a staff training course in 1951 is exactly the historical sketch such an outline prescribes, which suggests the practice was old at Kanawana and may have produced others.

Christine Nixon of Camp Oconto described how a camp's songs were passed on, in October 1980: "Because they are new to camp, many of the camp songs, graces, chants etc. that staff and older campers take for granted, will be unknown to younger campers. Counsellors should give these campers an 'intensive course' in the learning of these old favourites during the first few days of camp — singing them over and over, anywhere and anytime! This will help them to quickly feel like a part of camp and that they really belong."

A camp repertoire lived in the memory of returning campers and staff and was reinstalled in newcomers by deliberate repetition in the first days of each season. That is why camp songs survive for decades with no written source, why a break of a season or two can lose one completely, and why the song functioned as a membership rite rather than an entertainment — the stated argument for the intensive course being belonging.

Christine Nixon's 1980 method for teaching camp songs: echo songs and songs that build; teach slowly in very small parts; look at each child individually; repeat often; and choose by mood, because "there is nothing like a singsong to bring a rowdy group of youngsters down to earth." The occasions music filled were "waiting periods, energy-spending device, or fearful times (ie thunderstorms)," plus sea shanties "to maintain a steady stroke in canoeing."

Bill Mason's Path of the Paddle was published by Van Nostrand Reinhold in early November 1980, 160 pages, with a foreword by Pierre Elliott Trudeau: "I have known Bill Mason for many years. I have paddled with him, traded outrageous stories with him about past canoeing expeditions." The notice records that "Mason is no stranger to resident camping in Canada having learned a great deal about the art of canoeing at Pioneer Camp in Manitoba while on staff there," and that his four Path of the Paddle films of 1978 "have become the most popular films ever produced by the NFB."

The Canadian Camping Association's Leadership Training Committee invited camps into a national counsellor exchange in October 1980, through Bev Bullock of Kamloops, with an argument about retention: "How often is camp manpower lost simply because kids tire of repeating the same or similar experiences. Staff could be motivated to continue in the camping field if offered the exciting opportunity of a new camp experience in a different part of the country." The idea had been recommended by Granek's 1978 thesis and by Blackstock the same year.

From October 1980 Canadian Camping was mailed from the National Sport and Recreation Centre in Ottawa off a computerised list — a change in the distribution chain, and a reason the Trent deposit copies exist.

The Nova Scotia camp songbook has a title and an exact count: "Come On... Let's Sing — Nova Scotia Camping Association, 156p, 1979, $3.75. Words to 583 favorite camp songs compiled by the N.S.C.A." It is words only, without music, and is searchable in library catalogues.

The printed camp song repertoire a Canadian camp could buy in 1980, from the CCA's first full bilingual publications catalogue: Come On... Let's Sing (583 songs, words only, NSCA 1979); Sing! (ACA/World Around Songs, revised 1978, words and music); Tent and Trail Songs (116 songs, 1966); Sing with Jack Pearse (37 pages, 31 songs with music, Camp Tawingo Publications 1980); and Tobitt's A Counselor's Guide to Camp Singing, with Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse due early 1981. That is the comparison set for deciding which Kanawana songs are house compositions.

Camp Amy Molson's December 1980 advertisement for an executive director requires "formal training in a child related profession... working knowledge of French and fluency in English; meet age and experience requirements of A.C.Q." By 1980 the Association des camps du Quebec set minimum standards for the director's post, not only for the camp's facilities and programme, and a Montreal camp advertised compliance as a condition of employment.

YMCA Camp Howdy near Vancouver packed a "Camper Care Package" into every camper's luggage on the last day, not to be opened until the child was home. Its eight contents included "the words for some of the more popular camp songs, announcements, graces, etc."; a poem about camp; age-banded craft and game activities; a list of January-to-June camp and local YMCA programmes; "an evaluation form for parent(s) and child to complete together and return to our camp office"; and a family activity. Where a camp did this, its repertoire left the site in writing, in a child's suitcase — one route by which a camp song sheet can survive in a family's papers when nothing survives in the camp's.

Walter Mingie wrote a Canadian Camping Association publication: "Outdoor Education — Guidelines for Camp — W. Mingie, 17p, CCA, revised 1981. Information for Camp Directors on campsite use for school programs." Mingie appears in this run as the Quebec association's Outdoor Education chairman and the author of its 1972 hebertisme article.

The Alberta Camping Association's Director's Guide for Counsellor Training is dated 1976, not 1978: "Director's Guide for Counsellor Training — Alberta Camping Assoc., 41p, 1976. Reprinted in 1980 by C.C.A." It existed by 1976 and the CCA reprinted it four years later.

The Canadian Camping Association's constitution provided three regional vice-presidents from 1980: "Derek Walsh of Montreal" agreeing to stay on as the representative of Quebec and Ontario until May 1981; George Matthews for the Atlantic provinces until May 1983; and Gary Luthy for the West until May 1981. The description "of Montreal" contradicts the Camp Thunderbird, Victoria entry recorded elsewhere for Walsh in 1979.

The planned 1983 International Congress lost its American partner: "Finances proved to be too big an obstacle so that regretfully the joint effort of C.C.A./O.C.A. and A.C.A. has been dropped. However, C.C.A. and O.C.A. have agreed to jointly sponsor the International Congress in Toronto in March of '83." A Leadership Resources Workshop at Camp Wanakita, 16-18 October 1980, produced "a three to five year plan for the C.C.A."

The Canadian Camping Association "is the sole distributor in Canada for books published by the American Camping Association," and its first full bilingual catalogue of December 1980 carries only about fifteen asterisked Canadian titles among more than a hundred entries. ACA health forms are listed individually at 5 cents each with the note "These forms are not to be reproduced by any other agency" — Accident Report Form, Health Record Card, Camp Health Record Form, Girl's Health Examination Card, Boy's Health Examination Card, Camp Health Examination Form and Camp Staff Application.

The Project Reach series from the University of Kentucky, funded by the US Department of Health, Education and Welfare and sold through the CCA in 1980, supplies six counsellor-training modules and four job-specific manuals — Camp Food Service Supervisor, Camp Maintenance Supervisor, Camp Nurse and Camp Secretary — the first published treatments this read has seen of the camp jobs that leave no trace in camp records.

Canadian Camping's "Camp Staff Issue" of February 1981 specifies the camp staff manual in full: "A STAFF MANUAL is a booklet prepared by the camp for the purpose of informing its future staff about the camp and their role in it," in seven parts. Part II, Facts About Camp, requires a directional map, "a sketch of site showing trails, program areas, buildings," a description of the setting's special features and "special problems which site gives rise to"; statements of traditions and philosophy; "a brief historical sketch of the camp"; and "explanation of role that camping plays in the total program of the sponsoring organization." Personnel Policies must cover "sickness allowance; employment and dismissal procedures; salary scales and payment procedures; travel to and from camp, charges for laundry."

A single surviving Kanawana staff manual would carry, in one binder, the camp's own historical sketch, a site map with its problems named, its dismissal procedures, its salary scales, its blank forms and its job descriptions. The 1981 specification also explains the "Kamp Kanawana History" presented at a staff training course in 1951: it is exactly the "brief historical sketch of the camp" the list prescribes, so it was probably extracted from or written for a manual of this kind.

Part IV of the 1981 staff manual specification lists the sample forms used at camp: "test sheets (swimming, canoeing, camp crafts, etc.); tripping reports, what to take, hints for safety; parent reports, reports to section heads, etc.; counsellor evaluation." Part III's counsellor curriculum lists under Discipline "meaning of discipline; what kinds of punishment, if any; factors in group discipline; building of esprit de corps"; under The Cabin Counsellor the routines "rising, ablutions, meals, clean-up, rest-hour, parent letters, parcels, prayers"; under Counsellor Duties "night patrol; life guard; evening snacks; records and reports"; and under Public Relations "deportment on days off; consideration for cottagers, neighbors, nearby communities."

Ron Johnstone, Executive Administrator of Camp Tawingo, asked a senior staff member to canvass the rest on why they returned, and reported the answer in February 1981: an atmosphere where "I can express myself... in many different ways... through developing programme with our campers... through experimentation with my own philosophy," with "a feeling of being able to express creativity without threat — without ridicule." His questions to directors: "Do we as Camp Directors really appreciate and encourage initiative? Or do we as Camp Administrators see initiative as a threat? Do we hire staff because of their personality and then say to them... 'this is the way I want you to do it'? Do we let our staff make mistakes?... What a terrific way to teach!" And: "Our staff are people with the same basic needs and desires as our campers."

The counsellors' page of February 1981 on homesickness: "All homesick campers do not act the same way. There is not always tears and stomach aches. Some homesick campers become very reserved, withdrawn, and even very temperamental, angry and resentful. Be sensitive to this very real 'sickness'." It advises "be cautious with ghost stories" under knowing when campers are scared, and on discipline: "Don't use 'archaic' physical punishment or 'torture and endurance' tests. Make the punishment fit the crime."

Ralph H. Raymer died on 20 November 1980 at Beaver, Pennsylvania. With his late wife Elizabeth he was co-director of Camp Tanamakoon from 1953 to 1974; they were founding members of the Society of Camp Directors and Honorary Life Associates of the Ontario Camping Association. He chaired the OCA's Finance Committee, where "he organized the books and recording methods," and its Standards Committee in 1965-66.

Paul Pichard's "Voyage, fantaisies et aventures en plein air," 212 pages, Distributions Reliv inc., Isle-Verte, Quebec, $9.95, is the only francophone outdoor title the Canadian Camping Association drew attention to in this run, and was "published in French only." Its argument is domestic rather than expeditionary: "nul n'est besoin d'escalader de hauts sommets... avec un peu d'originalite et de fantaisie, de nombreuses aventures peuvent se derouler a proximite de votre cour ou de votre chalet."

W. J. Babcock, owner-director of Camp Richildaca, Kettleby, names a further camp record class in February 1981: "Get permission from the director. Draw a sketch of the route of the hike. A list of all those going on the hike should be attached to it along with the proposed time of departure and return. Keep this all on file." The road rule of the period: "Two counsellors go on each hike, with one at the head of the group and one at the rear. When on the road, walk at the left side, single file, facing the traffic."

Canadian Camping's Indigenous-themed material shifts across three years: February 1978, Ernest Thompson Seton's "The Indian's Creed" printed entire and unattributed to any Indigenous source; May 1979, Chief Dan George's "And My Heart Soars" printed in full; April 1981, "Great Spirit Make Me," headed "Translated from the Sioux." The framework of borrowing is unchanged; the sources it draws on are not. But the shift is real only for the material the editors foregrounded: the back cover of the June 1981 issue prints "legend of the white canoe," the Victorian Niagara human-sacrifice invention, unattributed and uncommented. The sourcing had been supplemented, not replaced.

Professor F. M. Chapman, teaching Camp Administration at the University of Minnesota, published "Security and Disaster at Camp" in April 1981, naming nine catastrophic camp occurrences — "Accidents, Asphyxiation, Bombs, Drowning, Epidemics, Murder, Rape, Storms, Theft" — with footnotes to actual American incidents including a 1962 bomb at a Wisconsin Scout camp and the 1977 Oklahoma Girl Scout murders. "There is no longer room for naivety nor carelessness when it comes to securely guiding the camp community... The term 'security' now presents itself as a fact of life," and "Today's camp director can no longer assume that disaster happens only at the other camp." It is American in evidence and general in application, and nothing connects it to Kanawana; it is the clearest statement in the run of how the liability and security anxiety of these years felt from inside.

The research behind the HELP posture was Canadian and dated: in 1971 a team at the University of Victoria — Dr. John Hayward, Dr. Martin Collis and Dr. John Eckerson — began studying the body's response to long-term immersion, over more than 500 immersions in water from 4 to 15 degrees Celsius. Their findings: holding still rather than swimming increases survival time by a third; in 10-degree water an average person can swim "a little less than a mile before being completely incapacitated by cold"; drownproofing, then widely taught, cools 35% faster than treading water because of heat loss from the head; and the HELP posture for individuals and the Huddle for groups roughly double survival time, to nearly four hours in 10-degree water. Their conclusion: "A P.F.D. is not really a life jacket unless it provides a measure of thermal protection."

The fire-safety guidelines reprinted for Canadian camps in April 1981 require a named safety officer responsible for a written fire emergency plan distributed to every staff member with evacuation routes posted; fire drills within the first 24 hours of each camping session; fire watches in all buildings sleeping more than 12 persons where no detection system exists; a posted roster of fire departments, physicians, hospitals, police and ambulance at every telephone; weekly checks of alarms and extinguishers; smoke detectors in all separate sleeping cabins; 100 feet of hose with an adjustable nozzle as a minimum; backpack water pumps by the door of every large tent; and a written camp policy on smoking, fuel storage and refuelling. Two record classes follow — the written fire emergency plan and the weekly safety inspection.

The mailing label on the Internet Archive copy of Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 2 (April 1981) reads "Camp Richildaca, Mr & Mrs W. J. Babcock, Kettleby" rather than Trent — a reminder that the cached run is assembled from more than one deposit.

Camps, Their Planning and Management was written by Robert E. Wilkinson, Ph.D., Professor in the Department of Physical Education at McGill University, Montreal, and published by C.V. Mosby, Toronto, in 1981, 291 pages, $19.95, sold through the CCA's own publications service. The publisher describes the author as a "Member of Canadian Camping Association through the Association des Camps du Quebec," and Eanswythe Flynn's review adds "and Camp Nominingue" — F. M. Van Wagner's camp.

Wilkinson's Camps, Their Planning and Management (1981) prints the Canadian Camping Association's national code of ethics in full, and, per Eanswythe Flynn's review, "scores of charts, sketches, plans and specimens of every kind of business form any camp records would require," with fifty-two sketches and charts by Mrs. Wilkinson. Flynn: "Not since Dimock and Hendry's Camping and Character (1929) has a Canadian textbook of this size and depth been so all embracing." A book with specimens of every camp business form, by a member of Kanawana's own provincial association, published in the year the camp's own record is thinnest.

The Canadian Camping Association issued a memo in May 1981: "Remember, camps are only accredited by Provincial Associations NOT by the C.C.A... It has come to our attention that some camps are still using the wording 'accredited by C.C.A.' on their literature. This is incorrect and should be changed." Any Kanawana printed material claiming accreditation by the national body is using wording the association was actively trying to stamp out, and should not be read as evidence of a second accreditation.

The Canadian Camping Association's executive met the Fitness and Amateur Sport Directorate in Ottawa on 7 April 1981 for a review of its work and federal funding, with Jay Haddad giving a slide presentation. Cliff Labbett reported the department's concern: "Ottawa is concerned with the continuing accidents resulting from poorly-equipped and ill-trained (or untrained) persons who go on camping trips, canoe trips, mountain climbing and wilderness travel." Three years after the 1978 tragedy the federal funder was still pressing the point, and the association's answer was its "HOW TO" series of monographs, for which it was soliciting authors.

Jocelyn Palm was elected Canadian Camping Association President for two years in 1981; Jane McCutcheon succeeded Derek Walsh as Vice-President of the Central Region; Gary Luthy was elected for the West and George Matthews continued for the Atlantic. Cliff Labbett's closing judgement: "C.C.A. has made tremendous strides forward in the past ten years."

John Latimer's list of what parents expect of a camp counsellor (May 1981) runs to twenty-one items. The custodial ones come first: a counsellor who "constantly watches out to see the child is healthy and CLEAN including TEETH"; who checks "that toilet habits are regular"; who "will not let sunstroke strike"; who "is aware of the whereabouts of their child at all times"; and who "sees to it that P.F.D's (life jackets) are properly used." The developmental ones come last: a good listener and "a sounding board for their child's values, ideals, dreams and perceptions of the world"; "has a sense of humour ALL summer"; "does not expend too much time with friends on staff and ignore the children in consequence"; and "senses when a camper is homesick or lonely." One in the middle: "supports established values such as religious beliefs."

John Latimer's survey of visiting-day practice in May 1981 is the only one in this run: "Some camps have it any time and some camps do not allow the parents to visit the camps at all. Other camps, probably the majority, will have one day or period put aside." The argument against is disruption, difficulty for the counsellor, and that "it is often very difficult for those children whose parents do not attend." The argument for is that "it is a very rewarding experience for a parent to meet their child's counsellor, probably the most significant person in the child's life at camp." And: "Counsellors should be given some training before visiting times."

Larry Bagnell's "White Water Canoeing — Should Camps Offer White Water Canoeing?", summarising an OCA conference session and printed in June 1981, opens on the frame: "The decision one makes regarding what high risk activities and styles he adopts for himself are entirely different from those he makes for someone else's children under his guardianship." Bagnell was then Director of Algonquin Experience, a programme for disadvantaged youth run by the Toronto YMCA and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, and the CCA's Liaison with National Agencies.

Larry Bagnell set out in June 1981 the five precautions taken at the National Canoe School "where some of the best canoeists in the country are taught to be instructors": a day of specialised-stroke practice on the lake; capsize and rescue drill in safe slow-moving water; "proper life jackets and helmets... worn at all times"; long bow and stern painters on every canoe; and rescue personnel with throwing lines on both banks with rescue canoes and crews above and below the rapids. "Camps should not attempt white water instruction with any less than the above."

Larry Bagnell argued in 1981 that white-water safety is a whole-camp matter rather than a specialist one: "It does no good if a camper from a capsized canoe is drifting or swimming toward a strainer or souse hole if the guide is the only one who knows what a strainer or souse hole is." All staff and campers on any trip encountering white water, "whether planning to shoot or not," were to be trained to detect and avoid fourteen named dangers, of which he calls the foot-trap and strainers "the greatest killers."

Larry Bagnell's closing image, June 1981: "A wild river is like a wild animal — indecipherable unless one knows it and what to look for... The largest standing waves in the world (15-20 feet high in the Ottawa River) could be harmless, while a tiny, one foot dam on the Humber River can be a killer, constantly taking lives... A river alone cannot create a tragedy... but tragedy may await the laughing, naive and unaware campers and staff innocently floating along."

The back cover of Canadian Camping, June 1981, prints "legend of the white canoe" unattributed and uncommented — the Victorian Niagara tourist legend of an annual human sacrifice "paddled over the terrible cliff by the fairest girl of the tribe who had just arrived at the age of womanhood." It is a nineteenth-century white invention of a custom no Haudenosaunee nation practised, and it appears two months after the April 1981 prayer "translated from the Sioux." Both registers were live in the same volume.

Jocelyn Palm was installed as Canadian Camping Association President at the annual meeting held in Moncton, New Brunswick, 21-24 May 1981, in conjunction with the New Brunswick Camping Association conference. Her record: staff member at Camp Memphremagog, Glen Bernard Camp and the Ontario Camp Leadership Centre, now owner-director of Glen Bernard; President of the Ontario Camping Association 1977-1979; "Managing Director of 'Canadian Camping' Magazine from 1974 to 1977"; and Executive Director of the Royal Life Saving Society of Canada.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1981-1983 executive: President Jocelyn Palm; Past President Cliff Labbett; Eastern Vice-President George Matthews; Central Vice-President Jane McCutcheon, the office Derek Walsh had held; Western Vice-President Gary Luthy; Secretary Jan James; Treasurer George Ross. They were to implement "the Action Plan adopted by the C.C.A./A.C.C. Board last January" — a January 1981 national planning document named here and nowhere else in the run.

The Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association's revised Standards Manual, announced in June 1981, sets out a five-level national canoeing award scheme: "Revised Standards Tests of Achievement in Canoeing" including binder $10.00, checklists at 50 for 10 cents each down to 500 for 5 cents each, and "Award Cards, Levels 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, each 5 cents" — with "All Standards, Checklists and Awards are available in both French and English." A Quebec camp could therefore have issued CRCA award cards, and any Kanawana canoeing certificate of this period should be checked against these five levels before being read as a camp-invented award.

The Canadian Camping Association launched its "HOW TO" monograph series by June 1981 with two titles in both languages: "How To Promote Your Camp" / "Comment promouvir votre camp vacances" and "Composting for Pleasure and Profit" / "Le compostage pour le plaisir et la gain," at 75 cents each or both with a CCA three-ring binder for $4.00. The May 1981 issue shows the series was still soliciting authors in April, so Derek Walsh's pamphlet was written and printed inside about two months, by the man who had just finished four years as the association's national Public Relations chairman.

Mary I. Casey's The Nurse and the Health Program at Camp appeared in a revised and expanded edition of 101 pages at $6.50 in 1981. The read first met the book in 1978 as a CCA publication at $2.00; at fifty-one pages more and three times the price the 1981 edition is a different book, and it is the one to seek for any account of what a camp infirmary was expected to keep and record.

Rev. E. J. Dinsley's letter to CCA Executive Director Marjorie Booth, condensed in June 1981, is the only description of organised camping in the territories in this run: "I understood that there was some evidence of a Yukon Camping Association several years ago and that C.C.A. records of 1972 mentioned a Mr. W.A. Farley of Yellowknife, N.W.T. in connection with a Territorial Youth Camping Association. Both of these are now defunct." He found an inter-denominational church camp at Braeburn Lake outside Whitehorse, thirteen years old; a resident camp at Marsh Lake; and a Christian camp at Watson Lake — with his own caveat, "I would suggest that the above list would include one half or two-thirds of the resident camps in the Yukon."

The 1981 National Wilderness Travel Leadership School was held at the Yamnuska Centre, "the Calgary YMCA's outdoor recreation headquarters," about two hours from Calgary, with twelve participants from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. The programme ran triangulation and mountain navigation, emergency response and "the generic leadership model that provided the basis for the whole course," an ascent of Mount Yamnuska, sessions on tripping nutrition and thermal balance, formal one-to-one instructor-participant meetings, and a four-day hike with participants taking turns leading, one-to-one evaluation of each day leader, and simulated accidents staged to test emergency response.

The Association for Experiential Education held Experience '81 at Harbourfront, Toronto, 30 September to 3 October 1981, with pre-conference programmes across Ontario from 27 September — the American association's conference coming to Canada.

The mailing label on the Internet Archive copy of Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 4 (June 1981) reads "Miss Marion Babcock, Newmarket" — a third deposit hand in the cached run, after Trent University and Camp Richildaca.

Canadian Camping's national camping statistics for 1980-81, printed in October 1981, give by province: Newfoundland 29 camps, 12,974 and 353; Nova Scotia 37, 7,704 and 1,078; New Brunswick 21, 35,764 and 4,497; QUEBEC 125, 63,243 and 5,694; Ontario 197, 91,281 and 13,339; Manitoba 33, 10,047 and 2,228; Saskatchewan 19, 3,677 and 422; Alberta 62, 60,804 and 8,356; British Columbia 51, 19,459 and 1,723; total 574 camps, 313,953 and 37,690. The column headings are set in rotated type and are illegible in this scan, which is a defect of the copy and not an absence in the source.

Quebec had about 125 organized camps in 1980-81 and Kanawana was one of them, in a national field of about 574. The second and third columns of the 1980-81 table total 313,953 and 37,690, which sit in line with the association's 1976 figures of 260,000 campers and 32,000 staff, so campers and staff is the natural reading — an inference from the totals, not from a heading, and a clean copy of the page should be obtained before the columns are labelled in any article.

Rosaire Corbin, directeur general of the Association des Camps du Quebec, explained in October 1981 why the national statistics table existed: "Quoi de plus difficile d'entamer une discussion ou une negociation lorsqu'aux premieres questions posees: 'qui representez-vous?, combien d'enfants accueillez-vous dans vos camps? combien de personnes engagez-vous?' il faut faire preceder les reponses des mots 'a peu pres'." He notes the figures "ont la valeur objective de savants calculs d'extrapolation effectues afin de remedier aux 45% des non-repondants" — extrapolations covering a 45% non-response rate, which must travel with any number taken from the table.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1981 catalogue names the authors of its HOW TO monographs: "'How to Promote Your Camp' — D. Walsh, CCA/ACC, 1981" and "'Comment promouvir votre camp vacances' — D. Walsh, CCA/ACC, 1981," each asterisked as a Canadian book at 75 cents, with the companion "'Composting for Pleasure and Profit' — S. Hambly." This is the first place in the run where Derek Walsh's authorship is stated as authorship rather than inferred from the committee he chaired.

Rosaire Corbin is named as "directeur general — A.C.Q." in October 1981, over a signed special report — the Association des Camps du Quebec's chief executive, and the same Corbin who translated Kirk Wipper's Woodsmanship Leaders' Guide into French and appears in the QCA directory listings of 1975 and 1978 as the French section's contact at 952 rue Cherrier.

The National Survival Institute's fact sheet "Preservation of Wildlife and its Habitat," reprinted in Canadian Camping in October 1981, states that "we are destroying wildlife, and this deprives native people of their traditional way of life," and gives specific Canadian cases: in Ontario alone "some 200 lakes are already 'dead' and 48,000 may be lost by the turn of the century"; "Between 1962 and 1970 Dryden Chemicals Ltd. dumped nearly 10,000 kilograms (20,000 lbs) of mercury into the English-Wabigoon River system... making its fish — the staple diet of the Indian villages of White Dog and Grassy Narrows — unsafe to eat"; the 1979 federal regulation allowing Amax of Canada to dump molybdenum tailings at "concentrations 16,000 times higher than allowed by the Fisheries Act" into "the traditional fishing ground of the Nishga Indians"; the Dempster Highway bisecting the Porcupine caribou range; and the George River herd endangered by excessive hunting in Northern Quebec.

The same magazine that filled its June 1981 back cover with an invented Victorian legend of an Indian maiden sacrificed at Niagara printed, five months later, an account of mercury poisoning at Grassy Narrows and tailings dumped on Nishga fishing grounds. Both registers were live in the same volume, addressed to the same readership of camp directors.

Three of the Canadian Camping Association's small list of asterisked Canadian titles have Quebec authorship: Robert Wilkinson's textbook Camps, Their Planning and Management; Derek Walsh's How to Promote Your Camp; and Walter Mingie's Outdoor Education — Guidelines for Camps (17 pages, CCA, revised 1981, $1.00). Mingie is recorded in this run in June 1961 as "Director, Canoe Trips and Intermediate Section, Camp Nominingue" — F. M. Van Wagner's camp, and Wilkinson's. The association whose publications list looks overwhelmingly American was drawing more of its own writing from Quebec than the run's Ontario centre of gravity suggests.

ACA health forms sold through the CCA doubled in price from 5 to 10 cents each between December 1980 and October 1981, still with the note "these forms are not to be reproduced by any other agency," and the list is unchanged: Accident Report Form; Health Record Card; Camp Health Record Form; Girl's Health Examination Card; Boy's Health Examination Card; Camp Health Examination Form for Children, Youth & Adults; Camp Staff Application Form — with the ACA Health Record Log, "a stitched log book with numbered pages (8.5 by 11), space for 25 entries per," at $3.25.
Robert Wilkinson's Camps, Their Planning and Management was listed at $23.50 with a "special price of $19.95 until December 31, 1981" — so a copy inscribed or invoiced at $19.95 is from 1981.

New Canadian camping titles of 1981 in the CCA catalogue: Jack Pearse, Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse, Camp Tawingo, 1981 — "53 great 'singing songs' with music," a companion to the 31 songs of the 1980 volume; Jack Pearse, Clouds on the Clothesline and Other Games, 225 pages, Tawingo, 1981, 201 games; and Laurie Macintosh, The Kitchen Makes the Camp Go 'Round, 88 pages, 1981 — "lots of good recipes in quantities to serve 50 campers, by a camp cook."

The Canadian Camping Association sold Margaret Bemister's Thirty Indian Legends of Canada to camp directors in 1981 — 153 pages, J.J. Douglas, 1973, $5.95, "Mythology of Canada's Indians, a rich source of story and legend," described as "a reset, handsomely illustrated edition of Ms Bemister's collection," first published in 1912. The campfire-story supply line was a commercial one, and it ran through the association's own bookstore.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1981 catalogue restates its founding year as 1936 in both languages — "The C.C.A. was founded in 1936 as a non-profit organization" / "creee en 1936" — a further printing of the date against the competing 1946 and 1949 claims. Members of the Canadian Camping Association and Christian Camping International were entitled to member registration fees at the American Camping Association's 1982 national convention, a reciprocal arrangement that made the American convention affordable to any accredited Canadian camp's director.

Canadian Camping changed shape with Vol. 33 No. 6 (Winter 1982): for the first time in this run it opens with an "IN THIS ISSUE" cover panel and carries a full contents page with page numbers and bylines, a signed Editorial under a stated Editorial Policy, a Letters to the Editor column, a photo credit line and a designed two-column layout. After six years as a typewritten newsletter or plain-set bulletin it is a magazine again — a fourth structural break in the run.

Jay Haddad interviewed Charles Plewman on 15 August 1976 at his Haliburton rest home; excerpts were printed in Canadian Camping in Winter 1982 after Plewman's death on 28 December 1981, the notice giving his dates as 1890-1981, Honorary Member and Past President of the Ontario Camping Association and founder of Camp Kilcoo in 1932.

Charles Plewman, at 86, described the founding of the Canadian Camping Association: "We did know there were camps in Quebec, so we invited them to a meeting and we all met in Ottawa and decided to have a Canadian Camping Association — and Taylor Statten was its first President. He had a lot of charisma — both Americans and Canadians took to him as he was their (A.C.A.) President too." This project's canadian-camping-movement.md says the association was founded at the Central YMCA in Toronto on 20 May 1936. Plewman agrees with 1936 and differs only on the city.

Charles Plewman said in 1976: "A lot of people don't realize that boys' camps were operating in 1894 and '95 but it was 20 years after that that girls even camped." He names no camp; what he supplies is independent testimony from inside the movement that 1894 is when this kind of camp began in Canada — the year Kanawana dates itself from.

Charles Plewman's account of where organized camping came from: "Fathers would go out canoeing with their sons — after all, the canoe was the main method of navigation in this country for 100 years — one didn't have roads. So canoeing was in our blood; then along comes a guy like Cochrane (and others) who says: 'I'll run some boys on a canoe trip', without any thought of running a camp at all... Camps started as a supply base for canoe trips." And explicitly not from the churches: the evangelical family camps of the 1800s "had no semblance to organized camping for youth."

Charles Plewman recorded that Canadian camping began as a unit of the American association: "About 1930 I was asked to sit in with a group — there were about 4 or 5 people there; they were meeting and went down to the States once a year to the American Camping Association Convention. We were a part of one of the A.C.A. units, along with many other units from the northern states." The Ontario break came "around 1930, 31 or 32," spearheaded by Taylor Statten and Mary Edgar, and the argument at the time was "whether we were concerned with private camps or the broader scope to include agency camps. We had broader visions and wanted to include both" — the decision that made a YMCA camp like Kanawana eligible to belong. He adds that "agencies in the first 10 or 15 years didn't play too much of a role... nothing like today."

Charles Plewman on founding the magazine: "I got out the first bulletin which was the forerunner of the Canadian Camping magazine. I felt we didn't even know each other in Ontario — we had to find out where all these camps were and let's bring them all together through communications."

Charles Plewman on director turnover, from his own worst years of 1940-45 when the Red Cross took him as Secretary of the Toronto branch: "I found myself hiring about 4 or 5 Directors in a period of about 4 or 5 years. This was not a good thing. To bring a man who didn't understand your mores, your customs, your tradition, and had no real Kilcoo blood in his veins, placed authority over people who had been there for several years... well, it was bad business, that's all. My philosophy is that I'd jump over a hurdle of pretty serious proportions to use a man from the camp that knew the place from the ground up." And on the office itself: "In the earlier days, the camp director played the role of a star — not a team player but an individual star... Camps were built around Directors in earlier days, but camps today are built around the team, the camp's reputation, the camp's programme."

Charles Plewman on girls and coeducation: "Girls were supposed to be able to faint at the right time — they were supposed to have lily-white hands — to go out and rough it in the woods for a lady was unheard of! In my first days of camping, they wouldn't let anyone with skirts in the camp — not even the cookhouse or kitchen — it had to be a man." And on Taylor Statten: "I remember when Taylor Statten's chief financial supporter discovered that he was going to run a girl's camp on the SAME lake as the boys' camp, he nearly hit the roof. He said 'Don't do it, Taylor, don't do it — you're making a big mistake'. This was before anything known as co-ed camping!" His own conclusion: "camps allowed females to grow in the out-of-doors and camps were in the forefront of this change."

Charles Plewman's closing line to Jay Haddad in 1976: "You better take a good look at me because I'm a product of the Victorian era — still living and still kicking. With two exceptions, I'm the only one left of our group of camping pioneers — it's a lonely feeling at times."

Canadian Camping printed at the foot of the Plewman interview in Winter 1982: "The CCA/ACC Archives are located at Trent University. The Oral History Interview Tapes reflect the efforts of many volunteers to record the history of the camping movement in Canada. Anyone wishing further information on the CCA/ACC Archives should communicate his specific area of interest to: Mr. Ken Johnson, Archivist, Thomas J. Bata Library, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8, (705) 748-1413."

The Plewman interview printed in Winter 1982 is one of the CCA oral history tapes, transcribed in excerpt — so the tape series contains full interviews of which the magazine printed only parts, and a request to Trent should ask for the recordings and any transcripts rather than only for the printed text. Any Quebec or Montreal interview in that series would be a first-order source for this project.

The first International Camping Congress was held at the Sheraton Centre, Toronto, 26 to 29 January 1983, at $160 full registration ($125 before 20 December 1982), described by the CCA's Central Region report as "the CCA/ACC's biggest event ever," with the French slogan "ENSEMBLE ON EST PLUS FORT." Leaders in camping "from all over the world are being contacted and invited to attend as speakers or delegates," and a National Workshop on Promotion was scheduled to coincide with it.

Raye Kass of Concordia is recorded in this project as having presented on camp leadership at "the International Camping Congress," undated and sourced to Wikipedia. The CCA's own congress was the first of its name in Canada, held in Toronto in January 1983, which makes it a candidate for the one she spoke at — and would put a Montreal academic from Hedley Dimock's own centre on the programme. It is a candidate, not a confirmation: international camping congresses were also held elsewhere.

The Canadian Camping Association offered every member camp a free ACID RAIN EDUCATION KIT in both languages in 1982, from the National Survival Institute's Acid Rain Awareness Twinning Project, "suitable for 10-13 year-olds." It contained a colouring poster for every child, a map of North America showing all areas subject to acid rain, take-home information, leaders' fact sheets on causes, effects and proposed solutions, resource information, and project ideas and discussion questions. Camps ordered by sending their name, director, address, number of campers participating and number of leaders' kits required — so a list of participating camps once existed at the National Survival Institute. Kanawana was a member camp and eligible; whether it ordered a kit is not known.

Canadian Camping's editorial of Winter 1982, "Camp Director Certification: THE TIME IS NOW!", opens: "Doctors are licensed to practise their profession. Teachers are certified before entering a classroom. Nurses are registered before being allowed to care for patients. Yet, just about anyone is allowed to direct a camp and care for other people's children. This is not right! There are no national standards as to the professional qualifications of a camp director." It proposes a curriculum plus an internship in an organized camp, and states the threat behind it: "this situation opens up the very real possibility — in fairness to the public — of the imposition of regulations on us by the government." So in 1982 there was no national qualification for a Canadian camp director, and the association's own editors were arguing that this was a scandal.

Mike Budd, a teacher at Dr. E. P. Scarlett High School, Calgary, wrote in the same Winter 1982 issue that "Certification courses simply legalize errors in judgment" and that "the development of wilderness leaders can't simply be done with the skills school approach" — eight pages after the editorial demanding camp director certification. The Editorial Policy note printed beside the editorial exists precisely because the editorial committee had begun taking positions the association had not adopted.

Mike Budd's framework distinguishes objective dangers — "avalanche, white-outs, bears, lightning — which man has no control over" — from subjective dangers — "hypothermia, getting lost, river crossings — which through skill, precautions, and equipment, man can minimize." His diagnosis of the period: "there has been a drastic rise in the number of accidents causing serious injury or death. A major reason... is that the number of inexperienced wilderness users has risen at a much faster rate than has the proportion of knowledgeable wilderness leaders," and "regulating bodies have been under pressure to do something — anything!" His five legal requirements of outdoor pursuits include "completing route cards, medical cards, and following established back-up procedures in the event that the leader is late" — two more camp record classes. And: "good judgment comes from experience and experience is the result of poor judgment."

The Society of Camp Directors' tripping research exists as a titled, authored, dated paper: "Canoe Tripping Practices in Canada. (John R. Latimer, Research Chairman, 1979)." The Society donated a limited number of copies, given away free with any order to the CCA National Office in 1982. Latimer — Kilcoo's director and a CCA past president — is named as the Society's Research Chairman.

The Canadian Camping Association's Public Relations and Promotion chairman in Winter 1982 was "Marnie Ellis, our Public Relations and Promotion Chairman, and an active A.C.Q. member," heading a National Workshop on Promotion for the 1983 Congress — Derek Walsh's old portfolio, now held by a second Quebec association member.

The Association des Camps du Quebec's 1982 conference was held at Laval, 18-20 March, with the CCA executive attending and some presenting sessions. The provincial offices list in the same issue gives "Association des Camps du Quebec, 1415 est rue Jarry, Montreal, Quebec H2E 2Z7, Telephone: (514) 374-4700 ex 447" and no separate Quebec English-language body — the third printed list in four years to carry one Quebec entry where October 1978 carried three.

The Canadian Camping Association's semi-annual board meeting at Halifax, 20-22 November 1981, with travel and meeting rooms paid by Fitness Canada, decided against committing to a second National Wilderness Travel Leaders Course "since many provinces did not meet with their delegates from last May's" — so the 1981 school at Yamnuska may have been the only one of its kind. A submission to Fitness Canada requested $109,617 for several projects, and reports were received from twenty committee and task force chairmen on their responsibilities "as outlined in the Action Plan." The 1982 annual meeting was set for Camp Rayner, Saskatchewan, 30 April to 2 May.

Peter Rasberry, chairman of the Canadian Camping Association's Environment Committee, reported in Winter 1982 that "the first task of the committee is to prepare an Environmental Ethic — a statement of our values and concerns for our natural world. This ethic will become the basis for a set of principles and practices (personal and institutional) to guide us in continued enjoyment, appreciation, and sensible interaction with Nature." A national environmental code was therefore being drafted in 1982, and if finished it would have gone to every accredited camp.

Bruce Elkin, Assistant Director of Programs at the Rocky Mountain YMCA, described "Earth Ways" in Winter 1982 — "a twenty-two day 'experience in personal and environmental exploration'" in the Exshaw Valley of the Alberta Rockies with fourteen teenagers and three staff. Instead of a top-roped rock school, mountaineering began by running the boulders in a creek bed: "No instruction. No teaching. No show and tell. Running creeks is all 'share and do', learning from example." His observation about fear: "Most people do not suffer from balance problems. They suffer from exposure problems... kids who routinely fell off logs crossing the creek could easily walk the same log placed on land."

Jay Haddad's group dynamics exercise, printed in Winter 1982, gives fifteen relationship pairs — CHEF-DINER, PARENT-CHILD, SALESMAN-CUSTOMER, HOST-GUEST, POLICEMAN-CITIZEN, JUDGE-DEFENDANT, SUPERVISOR-EMPLOYEE, SERGEANT-MAJOR-SOLDIER, DOCTOR-PATIENT, GARDENER-FLOWER, POTTER-CLAY, MISSIONARY-HEATHEN, FRIEND-FRIEND, COACH-TEAM, PERFORMER-AUDIENCE — with staff asked which most and least resembles the counsellor-camper relationship. His rules: "no one wins or loses" and "conflict is important and necessary — it can be a creative experience, as long as no one is attacked personally." The inclusion of MISSIONARY-HEATHEN in a 1982 list is recorded as printed.

Canadian Camping's "Energy Tips" of Winter 1982 describes the Canada Oil Substitution Program, part of the National Energy Program — a ten-year federal grant scheme to convert heating from oil to gas, electricity, wood, solar or propane, with the Ener$ave toll-free line. That is the funding context for any Kanawana heating conversion of the early 1980s.

Canadian Camping's masthead of Spring 1982 states its particulars for the first time in this run: "Canadian Camping (ISSN 008-3119) is published quarterly. CCA/ACC membership includes a subscription; non-member subscription $6.00 a year or $15.00 – 3 years... Material in Canadian Camping may not be reproduced in any form, without written permission of the editor. Copyright 1982." Editor Jay Haddad; Editorial Board John Latimer, John Walker and Murray Wickwire. The six-times-a-year cadence of the newsletter era has become four.

Canadian Camping's editorial of Spring 1982, printed entire in English and French, tells member camps to abolish competition, prizes and badges: "As soon as a race is organized with ten children where one child wins, you have nine losers; if four relay teams compete, three are losers; if you have a first prize, you have losers!... our cities, through competition, create losers — MILLIONS OF THEM! Our camps, unfortunately, are doing the same thing! Awards, prizes, badges, competition, material success should all be discouraged in camp programming." Its five instructions: eliminate competition with winners and losers; give no material reward; encourage co-operation through tasks, chores, canoe trips and games; make the activity an end in itself; and "Never belittle or berate a person; a behaviour or remark, yes; the person, never." It closes: "Competition, as we know it, is a destructive force in our society — it should NOT be tolerated, reinforced or accepted in our camps!"

In the spring of 1982 Kanawana was running an inter-section competition with an annual trophy and a shield, and an honour society with an award ceremony, while the national association's own editorial board was telling every member camp that trophies, prizes and badges were destructive and should be dropped. There is no evidence that Kanawana changed anything; this is the argument its competitive traditions were operating against, dated and in the camp's own trade press.

John Latimer's update on the first International Camping Congress, Toronto, January 1983, names the speakers committed so far: Sir Edmund Hillary at the opening session on 26 January, Dr. Leo Buscaglia at the closing banquet on 29 January, and among session leaders "Bruce Werber from the Colorado Outdoor Education Center for the Handicapped; Barbara Hertell, Youth Programmes Alberta Forest Service; Bryce Taylor, one of Canada's most significant authorities on Indian Lore and Culture; Dr. Hedley Dimock; Steve Van Matre; Dr. Betty van der Smissen; Chuck Kujawa; Nelson Weiters; Ron Johnstone; Barry Lowes; Bruno Morawetz; Brian Law; Kirk Wipper; Ken Low; Bill Mason; and Richard Underwood (N.A.S.A.)," with speakers committed from Tokyo and New Delhi.

Hedley Dimock — the Concordia professor who conducted the 1960-61 counsellor-effectiveness research at Kanawana, built the Department of Applied Social Science out of the Montreal YMCA, and gave the CCA's 1967 keynote urging camps to move from repressive to participative programming — was a committed session leader at the first International Camping Congress, Toronto, January 1983.

The 1983 International Camping Congress's backers, recorded in its fund-raising appeal: the Society of Camp Directors donated $1,500, with each member asked to match it by giving $19.83; the Protocol Office of the Ontario Government gave a grant; the Nova Scotia Camping Association sent a cheque; the Estate of Flora Morrison donated "a sizeable amount in memory of one of Ontario's camping leaders"; and the Camp Services Co-Op gave $2,000. The Department of External Affairs sent information to 32 countries. The appeal promised that "every member who makes a donation... will be acknowledged in our printed programme material" — so the printed programme contains a donor list.

Jocelyn Palm's President's Perspective of Spring 1982 lists committee chairmen by province and records that "Derek Walsh (Que.) is investigating the realities of publishing a Canadian Camping Magazine" and that "Marnie Ellis (Que.) is gearing up her Public Relations and Promotions Committee for a Workshop in Toronto prior to the '82 Congress." The national president assigning her own volunteers by province puts Walsh in Quebec in 1982 — the third Quebec attribution after 1979 and December 1980, against a single 1979 line placing him at Camp Thunderbird, Victoria.

Rosaire Corbin held the Association des Camps du Quebec's chief executive post and the Canadian Camping Association's French Language chairmanship at once in 1981-82: "Rosaire Corbin (Que.) chairs the French Language Committee and we are constantly seeking his input in order to develop an adequate picture of the French Language members of CCA/ACC." The national body was still trying to get "an adequate picture" of its French-language membership.

The Canadian Camping Association's committee chairmen in 1982: Eileen Mayotte (Saskatchewan) Archives; Dorothy Walter (Ontario) Education; Rick Ryan (BC) Funding; Linda Arnold (BC) Research; Jay Haddad (Ontario) Newsletter; Wendy Wren, Judy Richards and Beth Moon (Ontario) Publications Service; Dinny Biggs (Ontario) Leadership Development; Peter Rasberry (Ontario) Environmental Issues; John Latimer (Ontario) the 1983 Congress; Brian Law (Manitoba) a review of provincial Standards; Wayne Perkins (Alberta) a National Consultation and Speakers' Bureau; Barry Lowes (Ontario), who "continues to monitor and represent the CCA/ACC membership to the Federal Ministry of Employment and Immigration"; Ivan Robinson (Ontario) an annual executive workshop; Jack Pearse (Ontario) a study of a national conference in 1985; and Janet Adamson (Ontario) product sales. Executive Director Marjorie Booth, Office Administrator Mary Roy.

Jocelyn Palm presented "Miss Frances Kelly, former secretary of the English Section of the Quebec Camping Association, with a CCA/ACC Certificate of Appreciation" at the ACQ Conference at Laval in the spring of 1982. "Although Miss Kelly was honoured in Quebec, her long service to the camping movement was recognized by the CCA/ACC Board." This is the second national Certificate of Appreciation to a Quebec English-section officer — Derek Walsh received his in January 1983 with the same "former English Section" wording.

Members of the Canadian Camping Association executive were interviewed at the Laval conference in March 1982 by a Globe and Mail writer for a national article on "Choosing a Camp for your child," to appear in the June 1982 Lifestyles issue — a findable press item carrying the association's own advice to parents, and a possible source of a camp list.

Ron Johnstone of Camp Tawingo argued against camp director certification in Spring 1982: "We in Ontario seem to have a tendency to think that all camping in Canada is the same... in reality it isn't! There are whole degrees of difference in sophistication in camping in Canada. I have no difficulty at all in seeing the Camping Associations as educational and inspirational organizations but I have some real trouble when we start into the business of regulating the industry." On protecting the public: "If 'camping' was a high profit business that attracted unscrupulous operators I would be concerned, but that is not so, all that wheeler-dealers have to do is look at the balance sheets of most Camps in Canada and they couldn't run fast enough to stay out of the business." And: "I know some of our numbers who claim ten years experience in camping but in reality have had one year ten times."

Lorne Bowering, President of the British Columbia Camping Association, replied qualifiedly in favour of camp director certification in Spring 1982: "The American Camping Association Certification system seems cumbersome to me — too many levels and a rat's nest to administer. I have always thought certification of Directors is at least as important as the Facilities/Program standards approach... The topic has been considered for years though and the problem is usually the 'How' to do, rather than the 'Why'. Camping people are diverse and what may be a high standard for one may be a very low standard for another." The American association had a director certification system in 1982 and the Canadian one did not, by settled position rather than oversight.

Jay Haddad interviewed June Labbett at the Royal York Hotel on 8 March 1980. Her account of acquiring Camp Oconto: she first went to Camp Ahshunyoong on Lake Simcoe, then Oconto at about twelve, then Glen Bernard at seventeen under Miss Edgar; she directed Camp Tapawingo for the YWCA from about 1944, her first directorship; she met Cliff Labbett on a ski train going to Sainte-Adele in 1948, married him on 4 March 1949, and "we told Miss Halliday we would buy Oconto on 24 May 1949." Ferna Halliday "was 55 years old," was nursing her mother "who died in May of 1949," and "had other people look at the camp and had openly talked to some of her own staff about taking over"; she stayed at Oconto through the 1949 season with the Labbetts.

June Labbett on camp awards, in the same issue as the editorial against them: "There used to be a cup given for the Best All-Around Camper and I just couldn't live with that; we changed it our first year to a tribe Shield (camp has two tribes) and this was a fun thing, not a competitive thing; any silly little game or challenge earned points toward this shield; everyone worked together for this." And on the trend: "we had many [tests and awards], but there has been a definite decrease. Tests are available, but they're not stressed or emphasized now... The skill level is perhaps as good or better than when they were motivated by badges."

June Labbett's first-hand account of the earliest Ontario camp standards dispute, which was about showers: "I remember these fights and arguments over showers! We had a meeting at the Royal York Hotel and I remember A. L. Cochrane standing up and saying, 'What's the matter with having showers? You can get a watering can and fill it full of water and pour it over somebody's head and call it a shower'. I remember one camp pulling out of O.C.A. because of that... others thought you should have the freedom to soap up and dive into the lake. You must remember that no one had showers at all in those days. Clothes were washed in the lake; I remember all of us diving deep with our toothbrushes in our mouths to ensure we were getting fresh water!"

June Labbett described Glen Bernard's "Indian night" from the inside, as a camper in the 1930s: "they have a real indian night at Glen Bernard; I had never been exposed to any kind of indian programme at Oconto so this was unique for me. My friends told me to wear a robe and dress a certain way and line up and then O-kee-mak-wah will come out of the woods... I remember Miss Edgar tripping down out of the trees and everyone saying chants and prayers. This was a very significant part of the programme and I grew to love it, respect it and understand it." The same structure as Kanawana's council ring, at a girls' camp, with the director's own assumed Indigenous-styled name.

June Labbett records that two five-minute hurricanes hit Camp Oconto on Sundays, the first taking eighteen tents, after which cabins were built; that staff girls were allowed to smoke in their tents in the late 1940s until it was stopped as unsafe; and that every counsellor was addressed as "Miss" until a staff vote dropped it about 1976. On leadership qualification: "we can pass leaders on their Bronze and so on, but how do you measure what's really important — maturity of judgement?"

Jane McCutcheon's Central Region report of Spring 1982 records two sixtieth anniversaries — "(Ont) Glen Bernard Camp — 60 years; (Que) Camp Ouareau — 60 years" — putting both foundings at 1922, which independently corroborates the 1922 date this project holds for Camp Ouareau against the competing 1920 claim. Gary Luthy's Western report dates Camp Elphinstone's 75th anniversary celebration to 22 May 1982, putting its founding at 1907.

J. Harry Ebbs summarised the standing medical advice on blackflies in Spring 1982, from a February 1980 Medical Post report: "There are 76 known species in Canada and the U.S.A."; the fly "breeds in shallow running water"; they are "attracted to humans by the carbon dioxide and water vapour in the breath"; they "bite at partially covered areas — the wrists, ankles, neck, scalp and waist"; and the bite "deposits a small amount of fluid into the skin which acts as an anaesthetic and also keeps the blood from clotting." Four known human reaction types, with severe reactors told to see a doctor and be desensitised.

Jay Haddad's "Lost At Sea" group dynamics exercise was printed in full with worksheet and answer sheet in Spring 1982, "a good one because it can be used effectively with campers as young as 8 and 9 years, as well as older campers, CIT's and Counsellors": fifteen items ranked individually in five minutes, then by group consensus — "there should not be voting or majority rules... each item should be 'talked out' until everyone feels comfortable with it" — scored against the U.S. Merchant Marines' order. Its two printed principles: "1) The group score should always be better than each individual score. 2) Conflict is a necessary ingredient toward creativity." A complete, usable 1982 staff-training instrument; a copy surfacing in Kanawana's papers would be datable to this printing.

The Great Canadian Canoe Exposition was held at Harbourfront, Toronto, 12-13 June 1982, free: craftsmen building wood and canvas, birchbark, stripper, fibreglass and kevlar canoes in public view; exhibits from the Kanawa International Canoe Museum; a group from Ste. Marie Among the Hurons; Bill Mason's films; Omar Stringer; and a Voyageur Rendezvous of North Canoes with tumplining races, pipelighting contests and tug-of-war — the voyageur pageantry Kanawana built a whole section around, staged as a public exhibition.

Agriculture Canada's food safety guidance for camps, reprinted in Spring 1982, is addressed to "you in the camp kitchen" with sixteen rules and a temperature threshold of 40 degrees Fahrenheit for four hours, and states the period assumption plainly: "If the camp cook attends to the simple rules listed below she will do much to reduce the risk."

The Royal Life Saving Society Canada's advertised waterfront kit of 1982: an eleven-foot fibreglass paddleboard; California-designed rescue cans "employed in over 30,000 rescues per year in North America"; a windsail PFD, noting that "federal government regulations require an approved PFD or life jacket be worn by board sailors"; first aid kits "designed by lifeguards"; and an Audiopack portable PA "that projects your voice in full circle, loud and clear up to a block away... hands-free camp communication" at 6.5 pounds.

May Brown, interviewed by Jay Haddad in Vancouver on 25 November 1976 and printed in Canadian Camping in Summer 1982, gives her first recollection of the national association: "I attended one of the first meetings on the CCA in Ottawa in the spring of 1947; I was really there as a Director of Camp Oolahwan which is the YWCA camp in Montreal." She met Mary Edgar there for the first time, and Marion Henderson Penney of British Columbia, introduced by "Blackie" Blackstock.

Four separate items now point at Ottawa and the later 1940s for the Canadian Camping Association's constitution: Charles Plewman's "we all met in Ottawa and decided to have a Canadian Camping Association"; the Camp Stephens Alumni claim that Nelson McEwen founded the CCA in 1946 with Statten; the Newfoundland association's statement that the CCA "was incorporated by Letters Patent at Ottawa November 5, 1949"; and May Brown at one of its first meetings in Ottawa in the spring of 1947. Together they describe a national body being constituted at Ottawa across 1946-49, which is compatible with a 1936 founding of a different, Ontario-centred thing. This is the leading reconciliation to test, not a finding; the document that would settle it is the minutes, at Trent.

May Brown's own account of her Montreal years: "In 1945 I went back to Montreal to go to University and began to work for the YWCA at Camp Oolahwan as programme director and then as Director after a few summers," leaving for British Columbia "in the fall of 1947" to join the UBC faculty. She was a McGill graduate, and went on to be President of the Canadian Camping Association from 1965 to 1967.

May Brown places F. M. Van Wagner teaching outdoor education at McGill in the mid-1940s: "Mr. Van Wagner used to lead our outdoor education excursions at McGill; he was just marvelous!... He had that quiet way about him; he could take any group of students out and it wouldn't matter what the weather was like, 'Van' would set us up someplace where we were going to have lunch — before you knew it, fires were blazing and shelters were up."

May Brown dates C. R. Blackstock's McGill studies to about 1945-47: "Blackie at that time had his own camp (Mazinaw) but he was up at McGill improving his academic qualifications and I had just graduated from McGill and we became good friends." He is a fourth figure in the McGill-camping thread, after Arthur S. Lamb, the McGill camping school of 1937-40, and Robert Wilkinson.

May Brown was President of the Canadian Camping Association from 1965 to 1967, having proposed at the 1965 annual meeting at Parkesville, British Columbia, that the executive move west; her predecessor was Don Smith of Alberta, 1963-65. She says the presidency then "went to Manitoba with Doug McEwen as President," where this project's records give Doug McEwen as Ontario, of Camp Wa-Sa-Ah-Dun, St Catharines — a province discrepancy, recorded and not resolved.

The federal government did not fund the Canadian Camping Association during May Brown's presidency of 1965-67: "The CCA had no funds for me to travel as President." She visited every provincial association only because she sat on the National Advisory Council for Fitness and Amateur Sport from 1964 and could take side trips from Ottawa meetings, dating the Fitness advisory committee to "about 1962 or 63" under Bill C-131, "and we were really groping at that time to try to figure out which groups we could fund." Federal money began under her successor.

May Brown records a Canadian Camping Association programme this project had not held: work "with the Secretary of State on inter-cultural camping; bringing ethnic children into the organized camping experience. This is very much taken for granted today, but at that time we were really pushing it," with a large Secretary of State seminar in Winnipeg. She confirms the Centenary Journey with John Latimer as Chairman in 1967 and that "we did have some funding under that Centennial Project."

May Brown describes how western Canada saw the national body in the 1960s: "We basically viewed the CCA as essentially Ontario and Quebec, because they carried the load in those early years... it was mainly the 'names' of people that we knew by association in those early years — the Van Wagner years, the Anne Vail years." And on what held it together: "travel is what tied the CCA together, in my view."

May Brown records that her husband Lorne Brown co-founded the British Columbia Camping Association in the 1930s — "it's an old association, older than the CCA" — with Gertrude Moore of Moorecroft and "several people from the 'Y'", and was involved with YMCA Camp Elphinstone for 25 years; they found land at Deka Lake in the Cariboo in spring 1958, took three summers to build, and opened Camp Deka in 1961. Lorne died in January 1976 and May directed alone that summer. His philosophy: "a skilled camper is a safe camper; over protection was not necessary, but he felt that risks really weren't taken if you're skilled... skills were important, but not as an 'end' in themselves."

Derek Walsh's Magazine Task Force report, printed in full over his name in Summer 1982: "Formed after last year's annual meeting, this task force was mandated to study the feasibility of the CCA (re)launching a magazine... These included: circulation, advertising, format, editorial policy, financial implications, etc. The results of the study essentially suggest that the CCA should not re-launch its magazine per se, but should make some distinct and conscious efforts to broaden/change its current 'newsletter' in three (3) areas: 1) Initiate a major subscription campaign to attract as many camp staff subscribers as possible. 2) Establish an editorial policy to reflect the change in readership. 3) Actively seek advertising revenue with a view to having the publication be a revenue generator."

Jay Haddad's Newsletter Committee report on the facing pages shows Derek Walsh's three recommendations being acted on: a new typeset format, an editorial board, standard features, sixteen pages an issue, four issues a year with subscription rates reviewed annually, and "when we have a few more issues published, we then hope to chase advertisers with a product they would 'want' to be a part of. This will be a 1982-83 initiative." So the man who ran Kanawana in 1976-78 wrote the study that determined the form of this publication for the rest of its run.

Marjorie Booth's national camping statistics compiled in March 1982 for 1980 and 1981: accredited member camps 590 and 533, with 44 non-accredited member camps in 1981; day camps 126 and 125; resident camps 453 and 468; camper beds 64,276 and 74,762; camper/days 3,962,848 and 4,046,388; volunteer staff 18,405 and 12,247; paid staff 19,282 and 20,539; staff/days 1,125,676 and 1,151,255; staff who were students 18,787 and 16,784; food costs $11,454,000 and $12,607,000; salaries $17,279,000 and $19,448,000; foreign campers 9,790 and 9,130; foreign counsellors 1,076 and 1,268; foreign counsellor salaries $558,000 and $524,331; foreign camper fees $3,125,000 and $3,500,940.

Marjorie Booth's caveats on the 1980-81 national statistics must travel with every figure: "The 1980 data was based on a response from eight provincial associations; the 1981 figures represent provincial totals for six associations"; "some resident camps are also listed as 'extended season' camps"; the rise in camper/days and staff/days "is probably due to the longer summer vacation period (10 weeks) for students"; and on the fall in student staff, "since we do not have an average age for camp staff in each province, it is difficult to conclude why the number of staff who were returning to full-time studies dropped in 1981." The 1981 Foreign Camper/Days figure of 185,609 against 1,503,268 the year before is almost certainly a misprint or a different basis and should not be used.

The labelled 1980-81 national table decodes three of the four columns of the illegible provincial table of October 1981. Column 3 is total staff: 1980 volunteer 18,405 plus paid 19,282 is 37,687, three away from the provincial table's 37,690. Column 1 is camps: 574, against 590 accredited member camps in 1980 and 577 member camps in 1981. Column 2 is campers as a head count rather than camper/days. Column 4 remains unidentified — its values are 10, 18, 15, 40, 60, 15, 20, 40 and 10, and it is not day camps, not accredited camps as a subset (Saskatchewan's 20 exceeds its 19 camps), and not extended-season camps.

The Canadian Camping Association's Archives Committee report of 1981-82 names three documents: "Last May a sample questionnaire on camp archives was circulated to all provincial presidents... The oral history (taping) 'Guidelines for Interviews', which were developed by the OCA Archives Committee, were circulated to each provincial contact responsible for archives. The 'Finding Aid for CCA/ACC Archives' stored at Trent University was also forwarded to each province. The ongoing challenge for this committee is to encourage all the provincial associations to store the records of their past in a systematic way. We still lack contacts for Archives Chairmen in some provinces." So a finding aid to the Trent archives existed and copies went to every provincial association, including Quebec's.

Barry Lowes's Immigration Task Force printed a table headed "FOREIGN CAMP COUNSELLORS (CCDO 2333-126)," sourced to Canada Manpower and Immigration, for 1980 and 1981 across all provinces, distinguishing those admitted with Manpower Clearance from those without. National totals: 828 in 1980 and 820 in 1981, of which 763 came with clearance; Ontario dominates at 709 and 654. The provincial columns are unreliable in this scan and the Quebec row cannot be read with confidence, but a Quebec figure exists and is recoverable from a clean copy.

Barry Lowes recorded in 1982 how the foreign-counsellor protocol was enforced: "The protocol worked out with the Federal Ministry of Employment and Immigration, at our annual meeting in Ottawa with senior officials, has worked so well that it was continued without change for 1981... Only three problem situations arose just prior to camp time and again these were caused by camps which did not follow the procedural steps faithfully. One camp brought in a staff member under what appeared to be false pretenses. The person and the camp was castigated by the Regional and Federal offices. The camp is on probation for 1982... The privilege extended by the Federal Government could be revoked if it is believed that any camp or camps is circumventing the agreed protocol." The camp is not named.

Jocelyn Palm reported in Summer 1982: "The CCA/ACC has recently been advised that our application for status as a registered Canadian Charitable Institution has been accepted. This should open up some new funding avenues." A corporate fact checkable against the federal charities register, and a second dating point beside the 1949 Letters Patent.

The Association des Camps du Quebec's annual report for 1981-82, signed by Claire Menard: "Les activites de l'ACQ ont gravite autour de deux poles en 1981-82 soit le Congres 82 et la promotion. Sous le theme: Les Vacances, Facteur de Croissance, le Congres qui s'est deroule au mois de mars a rencontre un franc succes... La promotion de l'ACQ a voulu au cours de l'annee a affermir sa representation et l'image des camps du Quebec par la publication de l'Annuaire 82, par une Semaine des camps intensive, par une presence de plus en plus incitante aupres des media et du publique. Il est a esperer que la frequentation des camps de vacances se maintiendra et s'accroitra." The Annuaire 82 is a named, dated Quebec camp directory in which Kanawana would be listed.

Lorne Bowering reported for British Columbia in 1981-82: "The Government of the Province of British Columbia has abandoned its long history of licensing summer camps. Except for approvals by the Health Department and other specific agencies, the government no longer regulates children's camping. As a result, government agencies and provincial foundations now look to the BC Camping Association's Standards and Accreditation Program as the recognition a camp needs in order to qualify for foundation funding or for government sponsored campers." A provincial government withdrawing from camp licensing and handing the function to a voluntary association.

Provincial reports of 1981-82: Saskatchewan had ten accredited camps, nine reapplying; Nova Scotia got "almost $16,000" from Canada Manpower to employ three people for six months; Manitoba's Sunshine Fund, which sends children to camp, raised $25,241.13 in 1981 against $11,906.35 in 1980, with a handbook on how to run one being compiled; and Ontario records that "in the Fall of 1981 Nelson Wieters led the Directors' Weekend through the challenging task of considering camp directing as a profession and the issue of certification of Camp Directors... although no decisions were reached."

Peter Rasberry reported in 1982 that the Canadian Camping Association's Environmental Ethic "initially... was to be completed by March 1982, as per the CCA/ACC Action Plan, but this date has now been extended to September 1982," with help from Jim Hopkins, Tom Knowlton, Grant Linney, Diane Bertling and Susan Erskine, and later Kevin Moore, Rob McIntosh and John Jorgenson. The committee also discussed "the sharing of the National Survival Institute's Acid Rain Education Kit with CCA/ACC camps" and "the potential for input by our association to the development of skills programs in Canada's National Parks."

Beth Moon's Publications report for 1981-82: "This year four 'HOW TO' publications have been produced. The topics covered include Sailing, Winter Camping, Waterfront, and Fun & Fitness. All were produced in both official languages." So Derek Walsh's promotion pamphlet and Sam Hambly's composting one were the first two of a series that reached six titles within a year. The same report records that "Work is progressing on a brief biography of Mary S. Edgar and her contribution to camping. Also highlighted will be her inspirational writings and ways to use them in quiet time and devotional programs. This publication should be available to the public by July 1982."
