John Latimer's Congress report of Summer 1982 adds detail: speakers booked "from centres across Canada and the United States as well as New Zealand, England, India, Bermuda, and Japan"; a planned deficit of about $4,000; "8 sessions will be given in French, with simultaneous translation being offered at each of the three key sessions," with a bilingual registration form; a third keynote, Dr. Alec Dickson, alongside Hillary and Buscaglia; "80 informative, educational & entertaining sessions"; and the Congress programme and registration mailed to all CCA members in September 1982. The full board met 24-25 January 1983 with Promotions, Standards and Education workshops on 25-26 January.

Dorothy Walter's Education Committee — with Janet Adamson, John Wilkinson, Stan Talesnick, and Carolea Butters observing as chairman of the Ontario Task Force on Professional Development — was tasked in 1982 to "examine, make recommendations for and publicize a variety of educational opportunities for the professional development of camp directors in Canada. (This could include the preparation of a self-directed learning curriculum for use anywhere in Canada)," with all the research "to come from within the Canadian Camping community" and the result to be presented at the Pre-Congress workshop in January 1983 "to determine the basic core curriculum required for professional development of camp directors." Having declined to certify, the association set about defining the body of knowledge instead.

Brian Law's Standards Task Force, funded by Fitness Canada for a January 1983 workshop, lists the questions it would put to every province: "who has mandatory standards; who uses a scoring or percentage system; is there a pass/fail system; question of authority as it relates to provincial legislation; informal/formal ties to provincial licensing bodies; is accreditation/visitation an annual, biennial or triennial process," plus "who qualifies to accredit a camp; what qualifications are required; what training is required yearly; who provides this group with credibility and authority." If the workshop produced a written comparison it would contain the fullest description of the ACQ's accreditation process this project could hope for.

Canadian Camping's Summer 1982 editorial, "The Voice of Camping: Inaudible!", printed in both languages, argues that the associations refuse to speak publicly on the environment, children's rights, boating and waterfront safety, children's health and food regulations: "Camping's silence is in itself a message... And as history clearly has shown: silence gives consent!" And: "How long will our silence keep us guilty by association as camps are branded and tarnished as 'the lake where the four boys drowned' or 'the lake with the broken glass and littered campsites' or 'the lake where the R.C.M.P. made the drug arrests'?" The French version names La Presse where the English names the Globe and Mail.

The only published objection to the Canadian Camping Association's anti-competition editorial came from a French-Canadian member. Raymond Doucet replied in French, congratulating it as "audacieux" but dissenting: "cherchons-nous a proteger le jeune contre la Societe actuelle ou n'est-il pas de notre devoir de fournir a l'adulte de demain les occasions d'exercer ses qualites de leader... Il faut l'aider a devenir responsable et independant."

The Canadian Camping Association launched a National Photo Contest in 1982, four winners a year, first deadline 15 September 1982, with all submitted photographs becoming CCA property — so a collection of camper and staff photographs from 1982 onward accumulated at the national office and should be asked for at Trent. A "Camping Advisor" advice column was announced for the autumn, on "staff, management, leadership, sexuality, program, campers, maintenance, purchasing, legal liability."

The Canadian Camping Association's Legislation Committee reported in 1982 that no federal legislation had passed that year directly affecting camping, but that the Small Vessel Regulations under the Canada Shipping Act were being revised by the Marine Safety Advisory Committee, with Ron Johnstone and Jocelyn Palm representing camping — the same regulations that first required flotation in every canoe in November 1975.

The mailing label on the Internet Archive copy of Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 2 (Summer 1982) reads "Ms. Jane McCutcheon, C.C.A. Vice President, Camp Tawingo, Huntsville" — a fourth deposit hand in the cached run, after Trent University, Camp Richildaca and Marion Babcock, and this time the association's own Central Vice-President.

The Canadian Camping Association printed a boxed appeal over the Trent archivist's name in Autumn 1982: "Children's camping is older than most of us realize. In time for the coming International Camping Congress and for our own information, we need to know who opened the first camp in Canada. As well, we would like to co-ordinate a list of camps in Canada which were opened prior to 1900, 1910, and 1920. Please dig into provincial government departments (education, health, land titles/surveys) as well as those of Church, YWCA, YMCA, Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, CGIT, and private records. This kind of information has never been researched in detail — we may be surprised at the number of early camps established in Canada. Help us know our heritage!" Contact: Mr. Ken Johnson, Archivist, Thomas J. Bata Library, Trent University.

Kanawana dates itself from 1894 and would belong on the "prior to 1900" list the Canadian Camping Association solicited in 1982. Whatever answers came back went to Trent, gathered in time for the January 1983 Congress, and would sit in the CCA/ACC fonds beside the Congress papers. A Quebec answer naming Kanawana would be the earliest independent statement of its founding date outside the YMCA's own papers. The appeal's own admission — "this kind of information has never been researched in detail" — is the national association saying in 1982 that the early history of Canadian camping was unwritten.

John Latimer, interviewed at his Toronto home on 4 August 1982, said of his CCA presidency of 1971-75: "I personally felt uncomfortable about the relationship between French camps and camps in English-speaking Canada. This, unfortunately, is an ongoing concern even today, wrought with political overtones — I know I've made enemies over this issue but I keep thinking we're forgetting the campers and their collective interests which aren't being served by our politics." It is the first time anyone in this run says plainly that the language relationship was a problem, and it is said by the man who was national president in the years the constitution changed.

John Latimer said in 1982 that national camp standards remained unachieved: "When we talked of National Standards, people feared 'regulations' or 'imposed standards' but our intention was always an initiative of education and information — sharing only. This issue still isn't resolved — there are no national standards and I think it would be very difficult to implement the same standards to all camps across the country." On the association's name: "I remember wanting the name changed because we were and still are assumed by the public to be 'that group in charge of trailer camping throughout Canada'... we never did change our name."

John Latimer records the origin of the International Camping Congress: "The idea of an International Congress started several years ago when I was President of the C.C.A. and I was down in New York City at an A.C.A. meeting. John Kirk was their President and a man by the name of Commander Kohli from India was President of the Indian Camping Association. We went out one evening and began to fantasize a little about the possibility of a World Association in Camping." A joint congress with the Americans was explored "but unfortunately, that didn't work out because the financial restrictions presented too many complications," and he notes that "Christian Camping International have had international ventures before but this is really the first sponsored by the C.C.A."

John Latimer describes how the Second World War was present inside a Canadian camp. He first went to Kilcoo in 1938; his first memory of Charles Plewman is "leading songs," and the second is the war: "so many of his Staff were away fighting and Charlie was very close to them. Some, of course, were killed; I remember being very moved when he announced to the camp in the dining hall that last year's swimming instructor was killed or the counsellor of a certain tent had been taken prisoner. Every Sunday night during these war years, Charles Plewman would assemble the entire camp in the dining hall and at one end he had huge maps and he would go through where the allies were, and where the Germans, Italians, Japanese were advancing."

John Latimer bought Kilcoo Camp from Charles Plewman in 1955 after telling him at about nine years old that he would own it. Asked "wasn't there a slight problem in that you couldn't match the offer of another group... And then a mystery offer came to you and your bid matched the other group and the camp was sold to you?" he answered: "Yes, and when I later found out that the donor of the mystery offer was none other than Charles Plewman, I cried!" Plewman took him to his first OCA meeting at the Park Plaza Hotel in the autumn of 1955 and introduced him to Taylor Statten, Ernie Chapman and A. L. Cochrane. His successor at Kilcoo was Hal Hannaford, a former camper and counsellor.

John Latimer credits the idea of the 1967 Centenary Journey to Kirk Wipper: "My first vivid C.C.A. recollection was 1967 when I was asked to Chair the Centenary Journey, an idea formulated by Kirk Wipper." This project's centennial-1967.md records Bruce W. Hodgins of Trent as the primary organiser and Latimer as coordinator — not a contradiction, since originator, organiser and coordinator can be three people, but a third name for the origin.

John Latimer says "My first meeting with the then President of C.C.A., David Hartry was in the basement of a synagogue in Halifax — the year was 1965," where May Brown says she became president at the 1965 annual meeting at Parkesville, British Columbia. Both may be right if the handover fell mid-1965, but the two statements sit awkwardly and are recorded as a minor unresolved discrepancy in the presidential sequence.

Jay Haddad, editor of Canadian Camping, replied in print in Autumn 1982 to a reader who objected to a photograph credited to Camp Gay Venture on the ground that "It disturbs me that a magazine of this caliber would give homosexuality this kind of exposure." Haddad corrected the factual error — Camp Gay Venture is "one of Canada's premiere girls' camps for over 30 years... 'Gay' means 'light and fun' and Gay Venture was the name of a horse back in the 1940's which prompted the camp name" — and answered the substance: "approximately one person in ten is homosexual; whether it's good or bad is not the point — it's just a fact of life. There is obviously a sizeable number of campers and staff in ALL our camps who must deal with this reality; to make them feel unduly shameful, anxious or guilty seems very wrong... you see, one's sexual orientation has little to do with morality. There are surgeons, presidents, lawyers, camp directors, etc. who are homosexual AND are of high moral fabric." It is the clearest surviving evidence of how sexuality was discussed in Canadian camping's own press in 1982. No private individual is identified in the letter or the reply.

The Camping Advisor column of Autumn 1982 answered an unsigned question about a camp director not rehired after an acknowledged relationship with a counsellor. The camp, the province, the board and both individuals are unnamed in the source. The editor's published position is the only statement in this run of a rule about relationships between camp directors and their staff: "The question is not one of homosexuality — it is a question of BEHAVIOUR unbecoming of a camp director! It would have been equally wrong if the camp director was male and the affair was with a female staff member... Your camp director was not guilty of her sexual orientation, but rather of her unwise and untimely expression of it!"

The Camping Advisor's 1982 comparison of canoe hull materials, from Michael Hatton's Lightweight Camping: wood and canvas, 16 feet, about 75 lb, "quiet, good performers and high aesthetic value but allergic to rocks, can become waterlogged and high maintenance"; aluminum, 17 feet, about 75 lb, "very strong but noisy, conducts cold temperatures"; fibreglass, 16 feet, about 65 lb, "light, easy to repair and inexpensive but not as strong"; Kevlar-49, 16 feet, about 48 lb, "high tear resistance, very light but very expensive"; and Royalex, 16 feet, about 75 lb, "very strong but will deform under high stress." With the advice that "few serious canoeists would purchase a hull less than 16 feet in length, and in fact, there is a growing move to 17 and 18 foot models." Read against the 1980 finding that two-thirds of Canadian camps were still paddling canvas, this dates the moment the fleet was changing.

Canadian Camping's Autumn 1982 editorial, "Beer in the Ballparks — Camps are Next!", printed in both languages, argues that camps should let staff drink on site: "Industrious, sensible, committed staff members, who care for our campers all week long with enormous responsibility, become drunken, reckless, irresponsible, immature 'adolescents' on their days off... at its worst, we witness violent automobile accidents causing severe bodily injury and even death!" Its diagnosis: the no-drinking rule displaces the drinking off-site, "like the Ontario Government's policy of 'no beer in the ballparks' which never did stop people from drinking but it did stop stadium officials from effectively controlling it." In 1982 most Canadian camps had a "NO DRINKING IN CAMP" policy and the national editor thought that a mistake.

The Autumn 1982 editorial gives the fullest description in this run of what a camp counsellor's day consisted of — wake-up bell, washing and teeth, breakfast, activity periods, control of the noon meal, rest period, afternoon activities, supper, an evening challenge or campfire, bed, a story and lights out — "and all this assuming no discipline problems arise... or a camper gets sick in the middle of the night and the counsellor sits with him/her for an hour or two in the infirmary. It's a pressure-cooker of a job but we don't always admit it!" And its argument from comparison: "we entrust a 19 or 20 year-old counsellor with human life... more vital responsibility, I might add, than most 40 or 50 year-olds have with their city occupations."

Pre-Congress events for January 1983 included six Kindred Group meetings, among them YMCA, coordinated by Rob Fleming, c/o Camp Wanakita, Hamilton YMCA, from 25 January 9 a.m. to 26 January noon — a YMCA camping meeting at the Congress, the most likely single occasion for a Kanawana or YMCA of Montreal representative to have been present. The Promotions (Marnie Ellis, Quebec), Standards (Brian Law) and Education (Dorothy Walter) workshops each ran 25-26 January with four representatives per provincial association whose travel was paid by the CCA and Fitness Canada, so the ACQ sent four people to Toronto at national expense and their names would be in the CCA's records.

Claire Menard of the Association des Camps du Quebec and Michel Charron taught "Parachute Play to Music" at the Saskatchewan Camping Association's spring conference at the Kelsey Institute, Saskatoon, on 1 May 1982, "proving that there is no language division where fun and laughter are concerned." The ACQ's own officer travelled to Saskatchewan to teach, with a second Quebec name.

Ian Fowler's report on the third annual New Brunswick Counsellor Conference at Camp Glenburn, 28-30 May 1982 — 82 counsellors from 18 camps — records that the Saturday evening session was "devoted to the development of an Indian Program at camp," led by John Jorgenson of Camp Tawingo as the CCA-funded Consultant/Advisor: "The program began with a slide presentation on a typical Indian Council Ceremony... Following this the group had the opportunity to view first hand many costumes and props all transported by Jorgi from Tawingo. The highlight of the evening was just beginning, however, as everyone paraded to the beach for an Indian Council Ceremony... To many of the delegates this was their first experience with Indian Programs."

The council ring practice this project traces from Seton through Statten into Kanawana's own script of c. 1925-27 was still being actively propagated by the national association in 1982, with federal money: an Ontario camp's director drove his camp's costumes and props to New Brunswick and taught a provincial counsellor conference to run the ceremony, for most of them for the first time — four years after the Seton creed reprint and one year after the white-canoe legend.

Canadian Camping printed a correction in Autumn 1982: "the CCA/ACC questionnaire was sent with the wrong year typed in the Camper Data Section," with camps asked to send 1982 totals — a known data-entry fault in the national statistics series for that year. A subscription offer to camp directors of two subscriptions at $6.00 and any further at $4.00 a year is Derek Walsh's first magazine recommendation in action within a quarter.

Jay Haddad's "Alligator River" group dynamics exercise, supplied by Jude de Guerre of Wolfville, Nova Scotia and first seen by the editor at Camp Hillis, Paradise, N.S., in June 1982, was printed in Autumn 1982 with the warning that "very volatile feelings will erupt with regard to issues like honesty, morality, fidelity, proper parenting, friendship, love and emotions" and that a time limit is needed — a second complete, datable 1982 staff-training instrument after "Lost At Sea."

The Canadian Camping Association's HOW TO series, complete in the 1982-83 catalogue, comprises six 4- or 6-page monographs, each in English and French: "Composting for Pleasure and Profit" by Sam Hambly (1981, $0.75); "How to Promote Your Camp" by Derek Walsh (1981, $0.75); "Fun and Fitness at Camp" by Marjorie Booth (1982, $1.00); "Maximum Participation at the Waterfront" by Jocelyn Palm (1982, $1.00); "Organizing a Sailing Program" by Catherine Thomas (1982, $1.00); and "Winter Camping Skills" by Mors Kochanski (1982, $1.00). The binder is "a good quality, dark green plastic binder" at $4.00 including any two monographs.

Derek Walsh's "How to Promote Your Camp" is confirmed at 4 or 6 pages, 1981, 75 cents, and the series it opened had reached six titles within eighteen months, written by the association's own executive director and its president among others.

The Canadian Camping Association sponsored an Outdoor Education Conference at La Caleche, Quebec, in 1974, at which a committee chaired by Walter D. Mingie developed the guidelines published as "Outdoor Education — Guidelines for Camps," covering "the administrative, staffing and camp resources necessary for such programs" for camps letting outside groups use the site in the off-season. A national conference held in Quebec in 1974, chaired by a Camp Nominingue man, on a subject that bears directly on what a Quebec camp could do with its buildings outside July and August.

Mary S. Edgar's poem "Legacy to a Camper" is printed in the 1982-83 CCA catalogue signed "Mary S. Edgar, Honourary President, Canadian Camping Association 1960-1973" — a dated thirteen-year national office for the founder of the programme at Camp Oolahwan.

The Canadian Camping Association's planned life of Mary S. Edgar changed shape between the Summer and Autumn of 1982. In the annual report the Publications Committee described "a brief biography of Mary S. Edgar and her contribution to camping," available July 1982; by the autumn catalogue it is "Legacy to a Camper, by Jocelyn Palm... a book of program ideas and poems for quiet times at camp," available Spring 1983. Anyone looking for a CCA life of Mary Edgar should expect to find an anthology instead.

Brian Blackstock and John Latimer's 1975 Camp Counsellor's Handbook was being revised for publication in spring 1983 by Gage Publishing Company. Blackstock died in 1979, so a 1983 revision is posthumous for one author and was being prepared by the other in the months he was chairing the International Camping Congress. A second edition would be a different document from the 1975 one and should be sought as such.

The French edition of Kirk Wipper's woodsmanship manual is listed in the 1982-83 catalogue as "(Le) Manuel du Coureur des Bois, le Professeur Kirk A. Wipper... L'Association des Camps du Canada, 155 p., 1979" at $6.00, the translation Rosaire Corbin carried out. Its French description names the doctrine plainly — "le mouvement 'impact minimum' en camping" — and the English entry counts the code: "the Woodsman's Code, a list of thirty-three points anyone using the wilderness should obey in order to make a minimum impact there."

The Canadian Camping Association's bookstore carried four Indigenous-themed titles at once in 1982: W. Ben Hunt's The Complete How To Book of Indian Crafts ("actual techniques and designs developed and perfected by the Indians... a remarkably interesting source of information about the first Americans"); Bernard S. Mason's Drums, Tom-Toms and Rattles; Arthur C. Parker (Gawaso Wanneh), The Indian How Book — "Elementary level; sound anthropologically" — Parker being himself Seneca and the only Indigenous author on the list; and Margaret Bemister's Thirty Indian Legends of Canada, described here as "a moving introduction to the heritage of Canada's native peoples, Ojibway and Iroquois, Cree and Okanagan showing their sense of identity with the land and its natural wonders." The catalogue's own descriptions run from "the first Americans" to "Canada's native peoples" in the same list.

ACA health forms sold through the CCA doubled again, from 10 cents in 1981 to 25 cents each in the 1982-83 catalogue, with the same list and the same "not to be reproduced by any other agency" rule — so the seven form names carry across all three catalogues. Wilkinson's textbook is now $24.95.

Every page of Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 4 (Winter 1983) was scanned 180 degrees rotated in the cached copy, and the OCR read the rotated glyphs, substituting upright look-alikes. The issue was decoded with a purpose-written script and read end to end, but the decoding is lossy and ambiguous by construction — rotated b and q both come through as b, rotated a arrives as e, B or q — so the output is roughly 80% clean and is not a faithful transcript. Every quotation from this issue is reconstructed, and every figure should be re-checked against a clean copy before being relied on.

Marjorie Booth, the CCA's Executive Director, interviewed in Toronto on 20 November 1982 and asked what percentage of Canadian camps were members of the association, answered "Depending on the area of the country, probably 10 to 12"; the interviewer restated it as "roughly then, only 10% of camps operating in this country are members of their provincial association," and she did not correct him. Quotation reconstructed from a rotated scan.

If association membership was 10 to 12 per cent of the field, Canada had on the order of five thousand camps operating in the early 1980s, and the national statistics of 574 or 590 member camps describe a small, self-selected, better-resourced minority. Kanawana's membership of the Quebec association is therefore not a neutral fact but a marker of a particular kind of camp, and any comparison of Kanawana with "Canadian camps" drawn from CCA data is a comparison with the accredited tenth.

Marjorie Booth explained who stayed out of the camping associations: "there are a number of small organizations or church-affiliated camping programmes in this country that don't have the financial resources — at least in their minds — to meet some of the recommended practices and so they choose not to belong," and "if camp directors don't know we exist, they can't join the association... Nationally, we're not well known." She also states the rule that applied to Kanawana: in "Ontario and Quebec... in order to become a member camp, you must meet the standards or recommended practices and be visited by a consultant or your peers" — so in Quebec, membership and accreditation were the same gate. Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

Marjorie Booth described her Montreal years: "I left Glenburn in the fall of 1976 and started immediately at the Montreal Y.W.C.A. My first summer directing Oolahwan was its sixtieth anniversary so it was an exciting project... That site was beautiful too. We had 160 acres on a completely private lake right in the middle of the Laurentians near Ste-Marguerite. Our campers were 60% French and 40% English so it was a good mixture and announcements were all made in both languages." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

Camp Oolahwan's sixtieth anniversary fell in Marjorie Booth's first summer directing it, 1977, which confirms its founding in 1917 from inside the camp against the competing 1915 date. Its site was 160 acres on a private lake near Sainte-Marguerite in the Laurentians, and in 1977 its campers were 60% francophone and 40% anglophone with announcements made in both languages — a Montreal YWCA camp running bilingually at exactly the period when the Quebec Camping Association's English Section was disappearing from the national directory, and a direct comparator for Kanawana forty minutes away.

Bruno Morawetz's essay "The Importance of the Unimportant" was printed a third time in Winter 1983, and this printing carries an attribution the 1975 and 1977 printings did not: "Reprinted with permission from the CCA Conference Digest, 19[??]". The year is not legible in the rotated scan; the decoded characters are consistent with 1961 or 1971. So the essay this project has quoted from the June 1975 and June 1977 issues is itself a reprint of a paper given at a Canadian Camping Association conference years earlier, and both its origin and the first date of the "woe to the camp which yearly changes its directors" line may need moving.

Bruno Morawetz's geranium parable, from the fullest printing of his essay: a friend admired his wife's tall spindly geraniums and was told they would only grow into beautiful plants "if you keep nipping off the new shoots, just as any fruit tree needs annual pruning" — from which "a camp director is like a gardener, and his geraniums are children. If a youngster grows without structure, without limits, without the occasional pruning, he may come back from camp... saying 'I did not really learn anything at camp, I accomplished nothing, it was a waste of time.'" And his scepticism about credentials: "I am always suspicious when a staff application is accompanied by a long resume listing dozens of qualifications... perhaps he has never taken the time to sit quietly by a brook, to listen to the gay laughter of its ripples." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

John Latimer wrote to Canadian Camping in Winter 1983 on the association's own history of silence: "Until three years ago, in the CCA conferences, there was never a session on sexual attitudes and awareness. We talked about everything else related to a growing, questioning child and adolescent, but we never talked about sex. To some, this was shocking; to others it was a 'breakthrough'." And on the substance: "I would be much more concerned about a heterosexual teacher or counsellor who is cruel, sadistic, and morally corrupt, than I would about a homosexual teacher or counsellor who was kind, understanding, and a human with high values." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

John Latimer's answer to the proposal that camps let staff drink, Winter 1983: "In Ontario the legal age is 19. I have counsellors who are 17 and 18. If I let them drink in camp, I am knowingly condoning the breaking of the law. As a leader, I should be helping young people (through example) not to break the law." He notes he gives "an 18 year old exactly the same responsibility as I have given to a 19 year old (looking after children for 24 hours)," that a split rule would be intolerable — "some of you may only drink milk shakes, while others are allowed that 'adult' stuff. How divisive!" — accepts the danger of the counsellor driving back from a pub, "where the potentially lethal weapon of a car forces a counsellor to play russian roulette on the trip back to camp," and concludes: "As I said, I'm torn and frustrated, and I haven't got an answer... I'm not ready for that yet." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

John Latimer wrote in Winter 1983: "It will be interesting for a young camping researcher to look through the archives of the CCA in the year 2020 and read this particular issue — and study the comments which you will no doubt receive." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

Canadian Camping's Winter 1983 editorial, "Lest we forget our purpose," prints the UN Declaration of the Rights of the Child entire in both languages, with the note that 1979 was the International Year of the Child, "the year, of course, has come and gone. Children still suffer." Its argument: "Camp activities are not an 'end' in themselves; they are a 'means' toward an 'end', the 'end' being the enrichment of a camper's life and development."

Marjorie Booth stated what Fitness Canada paid for in 1982-83: two staff positions, one full-time and one part-time; the travel costs of two Board meetings and two Executive meetings a year; and special project funding. Her justification: "we are a significant delivery system of physical activity for about 600,000 Canadian children every year" — a figure that must cover the whole field rather than the membership, and which should be reconciled with the member camps' reported 313,953 campers before either is used. She dates the Action Plan's origin to the Camp Wanakita workshop of October 1980 and gives its target: "in our Action Plan, we intend to be 50% self-supporting in our core operation by the year 1985-86." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

Marjorie Booth was explicit about what the January 1983 standards workshop was not: "we're not trying at all to introduce a National Accreditation programme; that's years away," though national recognition of recommended practices "might well come at it from a promotional point of view — it would be in our favour to be able to say when asked: 'when you choose a CCA camp, you get assured of...' whatever those areas of common agreement are." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

Marjorie Booth's account of regional difference in Canadian camping: "In the prairies and Atlantic provinces, most of the camps are organization-run, agency-run or religiously based. There is a huge difference in Ontario, Quebec, and to some degree British Columbia, where many camps operate for longer periods of time — two or four weeks for a session. As well, most of the camps are non-denominational and are able to attract a clientele who are able to pay more to go to camp than you would find in other parts of the country. Population density and factors like the economy are therefore significant." And on campers: "this is so foreign to camps in Quebec and Ontario, for example, where you'll often have 16 and 17 year-old campers who return year after year." Quebec and Ontario camps were the long-session, non-denominational, higher-fee, older-camper end of Canadian camping — the category Kanawana sat in. Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

The Camping Advisor of Winter 1983 answered a section director who had found two counsellors smoking marijuana in camp and told no one: the editor held that he was not wrong, but "perhaps you should have shared what happened with the Director and explained how you handled the situation... the Director would most probably have supported your judgement 100%," warning that "a precedent of leniency may have been falsely assumed by others on staff." Reconstructed from a rotated scan.

W. E. (Ted) Yard died on 3 January 1983. His notice gives him as born in Vancouver in 1919, B.A. from the University of British Columbia, M.S. from George Williams College, Chicago, in the YMCA from 1942 in Vancouver, Toronto and Sault Ste. Marie until he bought Camp Hollyburn in 1967, "particularly during his tenure as Director of Toronto's Camp Pinecrest in the '50s and early '60s," and President of the Ontario Camping Association 1949-51 and of the Canadian Camping Association 1953-55.

W. E. (Ted) Yard's reprinted article describes Camp Pine Crest's Voyageur-Lumberman ceremony from inside, including its spoken text: "Let us pause for a moment, and viewing the truly beautiful shades of our Muskoka evening, let us this day drink deep of the beauty in lake and sky and stately pine. Let us cherish the deep friendships discovered at this spot; may they give deeper meaning to lives already dedicated to helpful, purposeful ends." Then the lumberman "clad in high boots, mackinaw shirt, and peak cap. With an axe on his capable shoulders he strode quietly along the shoreline to take his place against a giant pine... silhouetted in the sunset" — "It is the Lumberman... craftsman, pioneer, conservationist... he is a living symbol of Canada's great forest lands." Then "a canoe skimmed into silhouette. The paddler in buckskin coat and tasselled toque, skillfully set his craft ashore, and took his place opposite the Lumberman" — "It is the Voyageur... explorer, adventurer, master of his craft, he looks to new horizons... for he, too, is Canada."

At Camp Pine Crest the Lumbermen and Voyageurs were not only competition teams but a ceremony with a liturgy — a tableau staged at sunset with an axe and a canoe and two spoken parts. Kanawana adopted the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs format in 1947 from Pine Crest, where the competition had run since 1940. No claim is made that Kanawana used this text or anything like it: nothing in Yard's article mentions Kanawana, the ceremony he describes is undated, and he directed Pine Crest in the 1950s, after Kanawana's borrowing.

W. E. Yard's article describes three further Camp Pine Crest observances: a sunset sharing circle where "over a hundred children" watched the sun go down and rose one by one to say "I remember..."; a campfire induction ceremony in which inductees accept the Pine as a symbol of Strength and Fortitude ("as the Pine roots cling to the crevices of solid Muskoka rock to hold firm in all weather, so will we hold firm to the principles of good living"), of Personal Growth and of Purity ("clean speech, clean sportsmanship, and clear minds"); and a widening-circles ceremony in which a boy dropped a stone in the lake and campers rose in turn — "Our widening friendship circles take us to Poland, my homeland" — followed by boys from Holland, Greece, Estonia, Scotland and Australia, dating a postwar YMCA camp's immigrant intake as a programme element.

The first International Camping Congress was held at the Sheraton Centre, Toronto, 26-29 January 1983: "over 1000 delegates from around the world — Japan, England, New Zealand, United States, Australia, Norway and Canada — participated in over 90 sessions," with 1,100 at the closing banquet, and "it was four years in the planning stages." Sir Edmund Hillary opened it with "Camping is for Everyone"; Dave Broadfoot entertained; Dr. Alec Dickson spoke on "Camping and Caring: Crossing New Frontiers"; and Leo Buscaglia closed after a slide presentation, "The Universal Child," by Jay Haddad and Doug Caldwell. The next congress was planned for 1987 in Washington, D.C.

Every session of the 1983 International Camping Congress was recorded and sold: "Audio Cassettes Available — Recorded live at the International Camping Congress," from AUDIO ARCHIVES OF CANADA, 1140 Victoria Park Avenue, Markham, Ontario L3R 1B2, at $9 a cassette with a six-cassette binder free with every order of six, and the full session list printed with codes and speakers. Titles include "Camp Leadership — The State of the Art"; "Legal Liability of Organized Camps & Youth Organizations" in two parts; "Camper Safety and the Law"; "Cults: A Threat to Campers and Staff"; "Your Staff Deserve Good Supervision" in two parts; "Non-Threatening Evaluation — Almost"; and "Safe Whitewater Canoeing at Camp."

Dr. Robert E. Wilkinson of McGill University, Montreal, ran the session "Camper Safety and the Law" at the January 1983 International Camping Congress, "dwelling on legal responsibility for camper injury, common areas of litigation and appropriate preventative measures." He is the author of the movement's textbook and a member of the Canadian Camping Association through the Association des Camps du Quebec, so the Montreal presence at the Congress is confirmed as delivered rather than merely announced.

National Camping Day 1983 was Thursday 14 April, "chosen as April 14 by the Board of CCA at its meeting last May in Saskatoon." This corrects a decoding error in the rotated Winter 1983 scan, which rendered Marjorie Booth's statement of the date as 1 April. Campers were urged "to wear their camp shirts, hats or jackets, or some identification of their camp on this special day."

Marnie Ellis's account of National Camping Day 1983: the project came out of "the CCA Task Force and the original five-year plan," worked on for eighteen months; the pre-Congress workshop of 25-26 January 1983 had 18 delegates from the nine member provinces, of whom the second day was devoted to the day; the date was chosen for the gap after the workshop and because it was "still early enough that the publicity would benefit the majority of camps doing their registration." Jocelyn Palm adds a history: "National Camping Day is not a new idea. Conceived in the 1960's... The B.C. Camping Association spawned the t-shirt day... The idea was endorsed by all provinces at a Halifax meeting in 1981."

"Derek Walsh was awarded the CCA Certificate of Appreciation at the reception prior to the Congress Banquet last January 29th" — 29 January 1983. The citation adds one item this project did not have: "Most recently Derek completed a feasibility study on a proposed magazine."

Brian Blackstock received the Canadian Camping Association's Award of Honour at the January 1983 Congress, "a long-time member of the Ontario Camping Association and Owner/Director of Camp Mazinaw," the award "bestowed as a tribute to Brian's consistent efforts as Editor of Canadian Camping from 1977 to 1981." That dates his editorship exactly and separates him from C. R. "Blackie" Blackstock, who died in 1979.

John Eberhard, past president of the Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association, was honoured at the January 1983 Congress because he "contributed his time as a lawyer to pursue the CCA's application for charitable status through the national Department of Revenue" — naming who did the work behind the association's 1982 charity registration.

Legacy to a Camper: The Story of Mary S. Edgar, by Jocelyn Palm, was published by the Canadian Camping Association, copyright 1982, first edition 1983, at $7.95 — "the biography of Mary S. Edgar who was a pioneer in children's camping and a faithful supporter of the Canadian and Ontario Camping Associations; the YWCA, CGIT and the Girl Guides of Canada," with 38 of her verses and material for campfires, quiet times and chapel programmes, covering Glen Bernard Camp, which she founded in 1922 at Sundridge, Ontario. All proceeds went to the CCA. Palm "worked at Glen Bernard from 1959 until 1965 and knew Miss Edgar well," with input from Dr. Mary Northway and Maria McCollum Wilson and from Barbara and John Gilchrist, and photographs spanning fifty-two years.

Marnie Ellis's review of Legacy to a Camper claims for Mary S. Edgar that she "created the first Canadian private camp for girls." That sits against this project's record of Camp Ouareau as founded in the same year, 1922, and as "one of the two oldest summer camps exclusively for young girls still in operation in Canada." Both were founded in 1922, and both anniversaries were announced in the same sentence in Spring 1982. "First" and "oldest still operating" are different claims and both sources are promotional.

Mary Casey, R.N., author of the camp nursing manual, specified a camp medication cupboard in Spring 1983 in five categories: "analgesics for pain; antihistamines for allergic reactions; antitussives for coughs; decongestants for colds; laxatives for constipation" — "the old motto, 'Keep it Simple'." She prefers salt-water gargles and hard candy for sore throats over lozenges containing an anaesthetic "with a name ending with the letters 'caine'" that "may cause future reaction to novocaine used by the dentist or the surgeon," and quotes Dr. James C. Fallis of Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children: "current knowledge suggests that acetaminophen is probably the antipyretic of choice for stocking a camp infirmary," because of the emerging Reye's Syndrome association with aspirin.

Marjorie Booth printed the camp grace "Thank You Lord" in Spring 1983, noting it "has been sung for years as a chapel hymn or grace in many Canadian camps," that it was used as the grace at the Congress closing banquet and as the youth hymn at the Scout-Guide Thinking Day service on 22 February. Both verses are printed, attributed Anonymous, and the tune is given: "Sung to the tune: Edelweiss" — a grace in the Canadian camp repertoire in 1983 set to a 1959 Broadway tune, the same kind of borrowing this project documented for "Alabama Jubilee."

The Camping Advisor of Spring 1983 answered "M.C., Montreal, Quebec," a director asking how to run pre-camp training when returning staff have heard it "for 5 or 6 years" and whether experienced staff might arrive later. The reply lists what camps actually did: mixed old-and-new teams; emergency procedures sprung at 4:00 a.m. with the staff unaware; "a lot of Ontario camps 'switch' Directors for an entire day in pre-camp in order to hear leadership sessions and philosophy from different, and sometimes neighbouring, Directors"; free sessions from government-funded summer arts groups; and a buddy system pairing each new staff member with a returning one. It advises against later arrival: "this could prove quite divisive as the morale you are trying to achieve in pre-camp far transcends skills and safety training and moves into the arena of 'camp spirit'."

The Canadian Camping Association's member camp certificate system, described in Spring 1983: "there is one for camps accredited by the provincial standards committee and another for member camps who are not accredited. Once the camp receives the member camp certificate, the CCA/ACC forwards the 'year stickers' to all the provincial presidents. These are sent to each camp to keep the certificate up to date." A Kanawana CCA/ACC member camp certificate with year stickers is therefore a specific, describable object to ask about — it would have hung in the office, and its stickers would date the camp's membership year by year.

The Camping Advisor of Spring 1983 on directors playing favourites: "it is undoubtedly natural and 'human'... to have favourites. To play favourites, though, is unprofessional!", with examples — the favourite who "gets to use camp vehicles when others cannot or is allowed to come back to camp later from time off without recourse" — and the observation that a director "needs a confidante, a friend, someone to 'blow off steam' with or have a drink with."

A CIT Manual published by the Canadian Camping Association was available from 1 May 1983 — the manual begun by Jean Funk's Leadership Training Committee in 1978 and redrafted, now in print. The Congress Photo Competition results were printed, including Sharon Hodgins of Camp Wanapitei, David Latimer of Camp Mazinaw and David Godwin of John Bosco Camp, so a set of prize-winning Canadian camp photographs from 1983 existed and was held by the association.

Marnie Ellis's Publicity and Public Relations report for 1982-83, describing the launch of the first National Camping Day: "6,500 posters have been distributed across the country to member camps. Delay in the distribution was unfortunate, and I apologize, but one learns from all experiences and the 1984 posters will be out by January 1. A special public thanks goes to Peter Goddard and the staff of Kamp Kanawana in Montreal for accepting the tremendous task of mailing to every camp."

Peter Goddard is documented at Kanawana in the late winter or early spring of 1983: Marnie Ellis's report was written before 14 April 1983 and describes work already done. This narrows the near end of the 1981-1985 bracket around his directorship from inference to record. The source names "Peter Goddard and the staff of Kamp Kanawana" and does not give his title; that he is named ahead of the staff reads as the person in charge, and his signature as Director on a Kanawana newsletter of 15 November 1982 settles what that role was, but the 1983 item on its own attests presence and responsibility, not the office.

Kanawana took on the national mailing of 6,500 National Camping Day posters to every member camp in Canada for the Canadian Camping Association's largest-ever promotional project — a dated act of national service performed from Montreal, which also means a mailing list of every CCA member camp in Canada passed through Kanawana's office in the winter of 1983.

The Canadian Camping Association's "CCA/ACC STATISTICS 1982 - SUMMER" gives Quebec's column with every heading legible: member camps total 129, of which accredited 129 and non-accredited none; day camps 10; resident camps 117; "other" camps 2; four-season 49; three-season 22; camper beds 15,791; individual campers 52,977; camper/days 820,812; foreign campers 432; volunteer staff 790; paid staff 4,618; staff/days 321,841; foreign staff 33; staff who were students 3,975; food $3,208,000; wages $5,371,000; and a return rate of 48%. National totals: 618 member camps, 500 accredited, 293,941 individual campers, 6,103,253 camper/days, 20,080 paid staff.

Every Quebec member camp was an accredited member camp in 1982 — 129 total, 129 accredited, none non-accredited, the only province in the table where the two numbers are identical. So in Quebec there was no such thing as an unaccredited member camp, and "member of the ACQ" and "accredited by the ACQ" name one status, not two.

The 1982 statistics table prints a response-rate row by province: Quebec 48%, Alberta 75%, Saskatchewan 68%, Nova Scotia 56%, Manitoba 54%, Ontario 51.5%, British Columbia 49%, Newfoundland 24% and New Brunswick 16%. Quebec's figures therefore rest on returns from about half its member camps.

Quebec camping ran on wages where prairie and western camping largely ran on volunteers: in 1982 Quebec reported 4,618 paid staff against 790 volunteers, nearly six to one, where Alberta reported 1,232 paid against 5,000 volunteers and British Columbia 726 against 2,884. Quebec's wage bill of $5.37 million against 52,977 individual campers is about $101 of wages per camper, and its food bill of $3.21 million about $61 a camper.

The Association des Camps du Quebec's annual report for 1982-83, signed Claire Menard: "Le programme d'accreditation de l'Association des camps du Quebec a fait l'objet d'un renouvellement important. Ce programme est oriente vers une auto-evaluation des membres, le respect des normes universelles et du code d'ethique. Une etude de marche a ete realisee cette annee et demontre le haut taux de satisfaction de la clientele. Un guide d'evaluation des services est actuellement en phase de realisation... La Semaine des camps, activite importante et connue au Quebec depuis plus de cinq ans. Salons d'expositions, centres commerciaux, emissions de radio et de television, articles de journaux et revues permettent a l'ACQ de faire connaitre ses membres et sa propre existence... Au printemps, un colloque pour les directeurs, le personnel-cadre et les moniteurs se tiendra les 13-14-15 mai 1983."

The accreditation programme Kanawana was subject to was substantially rewritten in 1982-83, reoriented toward member self-evaluation against universal standards and a code of ethics — so a Kanawana accreditation file from before and after that change would be different documents. An ACQ market study of Quebec camp clientele was carried out in the same year, and a guide d'evaluation des services was in preparation: two named Quebec documents about camp customers and camp service quality not previously known to this project. La Semaine des camps had been running "depuis plus de cinq ans" by 1983, so from about 1977.

Canadian Camping's Summer 1983 editorial was given over entirely to a text headed "This is a speech made in 1851 by Seattle, Chief of the Suquamish," printed in full in English and French on the authority of Buckminster Fuller's Critical Path (1981), which calls it "one of the most beautiful and profound environmental statements ever made." The version printed is not an 1851 speech: it contains "I have seen a thousand rotting buffaloes on the prairie, left by the white man who shot them from a passing train," "talking wires" and "the end of living and the beginning of survival" — wording written by Ted Perry, a screenwriter, for the 1972 film Home, and circulated thereafter as though it were Seattle's. What Chief Seattle said in 1851 or 1854 survives, if at all, only in Henry A. Smith's much later newspaper reconstruction of 1887, which contains none of this.

The sequence of Indigenous-themed material in Canadian Camping runs: Seton's composite creed presented as ethnography (1978); Chief Dan George printed in full (1979); a Sioux prayer in translation (April 1981); the invented white-canoe legend on a back cover (June 1981); and in 1983 a white screenwriter's text presented in two languages as the words of a named historical Indigenous leader, given the whole editorial page and offered to every member camp as the movement's environmental creed. The trajectory is not from invention to authenticity: it is a movement that could not reliably tell the difference, and whose best-intentioned material was as likely to be manufactured as its worst.

The same Summer 1983 issue prints an attributed prayer — "O Father, whose voice I hear in the winds, and whose breath gives life to all the world, hear me, I am a child before You... I seek strength, Father — not to be superior to my brothers, but to be able to fight my greatest enemy, myself" — attributed to Tom Whitecloud and described as a "prayer inscribed on monument at St. Regis Reservation — Akwesane Mohawk." Its attribution is complicated, since the text circulates widely as a Lakota or Sioux prayer and Tom Whitecloud was a Chippewa writer, but the magazine states a specific physical monument at a specific named community, which is checkable.

Bruno Morawetz's Archives report on the January 1983 Congress: "requests went to the Provincial Associations for slide trays depicting camp scenes representative of that province. The following Provincial Associations brought slide carousels and slides which were shown in the Archives Room: Newfoundland, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia. Due to the efforts of a large number of people, but notably Helen Stewart, Bernadine Dodge and Ken Johnston, the Archives Room contained a splendid display of archival material enriched by exhibits from the Kanawa Museum provided by Professor Kirk Wipper... a photographic record of all former CCA Presidents was prepared consisting of two frames with empty spaces for the next five CCA Presidents." He urged members to "send all materials relating to the business of the Provincial Association to the CCA office for deposit at Trent University." Quebec is not among the six provinces that sent slides.

Provincial camping association business records were to go through the Canadian Camping Association's national office to Trent University, on the Archives chairman's explicit 1983 instruction — so anything the Quebec association sent is at Trent, not in Quebec.

Brian Law's National Standards Workshop of 25-26 January 1983 had two objectives — to "update the existing comparative analysis of provincial standards for organized camping" and to "review and document extensively the visitation process" — with delegates preparing their provincial comparisons in advance, so a written comparative analysis of provincial standards including Quebec's exists. Its conclusion: "The Workshop has proposed that CCA/ACC should not accredit camps but should promote good camping practices through education of camp directors. This, of course, has important implications for our future action plan and for provincial camping associations."

The Canadian camping movement settled two questions in a single year: no national certification of camp directors (1982) and no national accreditation of camps (January 1983). Accreditation stayed provincial, which is why Kanawana's status was always an ACQ matter.

The first National Camping Day was held on 14 April 1983 and its results were printed: "Quebec coordinated their annual 'Semaine des camps' or camp week to coincide with April 14th and featured a media blitz... Senator Ray Perrault greeted CCA/ACC representatives and two camp counsellors presented him with a Special T-Shirt... Calgary Herald did a feature article on Youth Camping... Kitchener-Waterloo Record gave full page coverage... Over 600 weekly papers received information on National Camping Day and sample articles... New Brunswick Premier Richard Hatfield declared Camp Week for the province... Nova Scotia's Minister, Fisher Hudson, declared April 14 as Camp Counsellor Acknowledgement Day." So Quebec press coverage of camping in the week of 14 April 1983 is findable, and Kanawana was a member camp that had just mailed the national posters.

The Canadian Camping Association's 1983-85 executive was elected by acclamation, taking office at the annual meeting of 6 May 1983: President Jocelyn Palm (Ontario); Eastern Vice-President George Matthews (Nova Scotia); Central Vice-President Louis Jean (Quebec); Western Vice-President Terry Burkhalter (Manitoba). Louis Jean is the first Quebec regional vice-president since Derek Walsh, succeeding Jane McCutcheon of Ontario. Pauline Rondeau was confirmed as Chairman of the French Language Committee in March 1983 after the post "was vacant for several months this year."

Jane McCutcheon's French Language Committee report records what was delivered at the January 1983 Congress: "the provision of simultaneous interpretation of all key-note speakers at the Congress, in addition to three French sessions offered to francophone delegates. The bilingual text provided in the promotional literature and program of the Congress also reflected the effort to include both language groups." Eight French sessions were planned in 1982; three were delivered.

John Latimer's summary of the January 1983 Congress: "over 1,000 delegates... speakers and delegates from Canada, U.S.A., Norway, Japan, Great Britain, Jamaica, Mexico, Australia and New Zealand. After four years of hard work... Special thanks should go to all the 60 volunteers who worked on the organizing committees." Provincial delegations: Alberta 45, "the largest delegation outside of Ontario"; Nova Scotia over 30; Saskatchewan 15-16 on a $5,000 SASKSPORT grant; British Columbia 12. No Quebec delegation figure is given anywhere in the annual report.

Janet Adamson reported that 1983 was the Ontario Camping Association's fiftieth anniversary, with a celebration on 25 April at its annual meeting, and that "The Archives Committee is publishing a booklet of the OCA's history to commemorate this anniversary. This will be available in the Autumn." A 1983 booklet history of the Ontario Camping Association therefore exists. She also reports forty-nine Standards visits in the summer of 1982 and a "last minute placement camper service" matching parents to camp vacancies by telephone.

Two provincial associations confirmed Marjorie Booth's 10-12% membership estimate from the ground in 1983. Nova Scotia: "our staff... visited all the camps to carry the message of the Association... Interestingly enough, and maybe not so, but some of the Directors operating camps had never heard of the Association! Apparently, our message and material is not filtering down to the camp level." Saskatchewan: "We speak for about twenty camps but there are probably more than one hundred other camps out there who may or may not know we exist to speak for them."

Lorne Bowering reported for British Columbia in 1982-83: "Despite careful monitoring in previous years, our system of visits and subsequent accreditation had broken down. As a result of this summer project the records were updated and visits were completed," with government funding retaining Dr. Don Arnold & Associates, a major November meeting on accreditation "Myth or Mandate," and "regular meetings of the B.C. Camping Association were not held during the winter of 1982-83" for want of participation.

The Camping Advisor of Summer 1983 answered a director who had argued at the Congress for spanking campers — "several of us felt that children grow up with too much leniency today and that a good spanking is often a way of letting a child know you care about him" — unequivocally: "if you strike anyone — camper or Staff — you are committing the crime of ASSAULT... If a leader in a camp situation strikes a child, we are of the position of siding with the child, IRRESPECTIVE OF CIRCUMSTANCES." It is the clearest statement in this run of the Canadian camping movement's position on corporal punishment.

The Royal Life Saving Society's Aquatic Emergency Care programme was introduced in 1978, grew 50% a year, and certified over 2,300 staff in 1982 — about twenty hours for a Bronze Medallion holder, endorsed by St. John Ambulance, with a syllabus covering near-drowning physiology, spinal injuries, hypothermia and CPR. "Municipalities and camps most often use AEC as the core of their pre-season or in-service training," so an AEC card is a 1980s camp waterfront qualification to look for.

Pam Robbins of the Taylor Statten Camps contributed a natural history of the loon to Canadian Camping in Summer 1983, whose closing paragraph joins the acid rain thread: "in the next few years many lakes in the eastern part of the continent may lose their ability to neutralize acid rain... Unless something is done, a painful silence may descend on our cherished lakes." Her photograph won first prize in the Canadian Nature category at the January 1983 Congress.

Bruno Morawetz's Archives Update of Autumn 1983: "Cliff Labbett, Immediate Past President, is currently canvassing all the CCA Past Presidents for ideas to celebrate CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986." In the autumn of 1983 the association's immediate past president and its archives chairman were jointly planning a fiftieth anniversary for 1986, which places the founding in 1936 and not in 1946 or 1949 — the association speaking about itself, through the two officers most likely to have checked. It does not touch the Ottawa-versus-Toronto question, on which Plewman and the archival holdings disagree while both giving 1936.

Jack Pearse's tribute to Mary Roy on her departure gives the national office's history from 1975 to 1983: "Mary came to the CCA at the tail-end of John Latimer's presidency in the spring of 1975 and she served the camping community with great commitment and quality supporting John's successors in office — Ron Johnstone, Jack Pearse, Cliff Labbett and Jocelyn Palm... She negotiated a super arrangement with the American Camping Association for the distribution of their books throughout Canada — not only to camping folk but to libraries, schools and university courses. She was meticulous in co-ordinating Canada's participation and involvement in the first international conference on camping which was jointly sponsored by CCA and ACA at Minneapolis, Minnesota in 1979. With Brian Blackstock's leadership, Mary designed the format, layout and distributions of the new Canadian Camping Newsletter, beginning in the fall of 1976 and through her good friend, Ken Smith, the Director of the Non-Residents Branch of the National Sport & Recreation Centre, Mary Roy and Cliff Labbett arranged for the nationwide distribution of Canadian Camping."

The Canadian Camping Newsletter began in the autumn of 1976, its format and layout designed by Mary Roy under editor Brian Blackstock, whose named editorship of the magazine ran 1977-1981. National distribution was arranged by Roy and Cliff Labbett through Ken Smith at the Non-Residents Branch of the National Sport and Recreation Centre in Ottawa, the same body that printed it. The CCA was the Canadian distributor of American Camping Association books by a negotiated arrangement into libraries, schools and university courses — which is why ACA titles fill the Canadian catalogue, and why an ACA book in a Canadian camp library of this period is not evidence of an American connection.

Jack Pearse credits Mary Roy with "preparing grant submissions to the Federal Government and... the reconciliation of the financial statements for each project that was federally funded," and with encouraging provincial associations to exchange "Provincial Newsletters, Board Minutes and Conference Reports" with the National Office — which means Quebec material may sit in the national office's files and thence at Trent.

Bruno Morawetz reported in Autumn 1983: "We have a new archivist working on our collection at Trent University. Congratulations to Mrs. Bernadine Dodge on her recent appointment at Trent. Interested members may contact Bernadine Dodge at: Bata Library, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9L 7B8." So the CCA fonds had a named professional custodian from 1983. He repeated the deposit instruction in a narrower form: "as many of you head into a new season of workshops, conferences and training events, now is the time to send copies of last year's conference programs to the CCA Archives c/o the National Office" — so provincial and camp conference programmes, including any Quebec ones, were actively solicited into the fonds in 1983-84.

National Camping Day 1984 was fixed for 21 March, the first day of spring, on the argument of Dennis McLelland that "the first day of Spring is one that everyone knows but no other group «has» as their official day," with the theme "Don't Wait for Summer — Think Camping Now!" Posters went to the provincial offices in early November 1983 for distribution at pre-Christmas meetings or in seasonal mailings to member camps, each with a letter to the Director and an inquiry form, and "each province should have a list of all its member camps ready to send out to those filling in the inquiry form." So the 1984 mailing did not route through Kanawana as the 1983 one did, and the ACQ was to hold a ready list of Quebec member camps in the winter of 1983-84.

The whole front of Canadian Camping's Autumn 1983 issue — a bilingual editorial, the Camping Advisor's lead question, a four-page Council on Mind Abuse feature and a commissioned reply from a Presbyterian minister — is given to the death of twelve-year-old John Yarbough over the weekend of 3 July 1983 at the House of Judah camp, "his neck and wrists... locked into the camp's stocks and, hunched over, he was beaten thirty times on his behind with a stick the size of a broom handle," with an autopsy finding at least one blow to the spine, sixty-six other children removed by court order and a manslaughter charge laid. It is the event behind the Summer 1983 Camping Advisor's unequivocal statement on striking children, and it dates precisely when the Canadian camping movement's public position on corporal punishment hardened.

John Vissers — a Presbyterian minister, former director of Glen Mhor Camp and former vice-president of Christian Camping International Canada — wrote the movement's most careful statement on religion in camping in this run, arguing that "a neutral position of a 'no belief system' under the name of secularism or humanism is a myth" and that the test is not the content of a camp's beliefs but the method of communicating them. Kanawana was a YMCA camp whose religious character moved from explicit Protestant devotion to none; Vissers's frame is the contemporary vocabulary for that change.

Canadian Camping Vol. 35 No. 3 (Autumn 1983) contains no mention of Kanawana, of any Quebec camp, or of the ACQ anywhere in the issue. The Quebec-facing content of this run stops after the Summer 1983 annual report. The null is recorded explicitly.

The second annual British Columbia Leadership Development Camp of 1983, with over fifty counsellors from about twenty-five camps, had Jack Pearse as its special guest for two and a half hours on song-leading technique, gave every participant a copy of his Lead on... Counsellor, and ended with Pearse leading "Let There Always Be a Song, that great new song by Mark Baldwin that everyone who was at the International Camping Congress will remember" — a datable 1983 camp song spreading by exactly the mechanism that carries songs between camps, a national figure teaching at a provincial leadership camp.

Canadian Camping Vol. 35 No. 4, Winter 1984, prints Jocelyn Palm's President's Perspective listing the membership of the association's International Year of Youth Task Force chaired by Hugh Phillips as "IAN FOWLER (N.B.), JOHN LATIMER (Ont.), PETER GODDARD (Que.) and SYLVIA HAYNES (B.C.)". The passage is on a page printed 180 degrees rotated in the Internet Archive scan and the reading is a reconstruction; the name PETER GODDARD was verified glyph by glyph against the raw OCR string "( ano) OHVdOOO H313d" rather than trusted to the decoder.

The Winter 1984 task force listing identifies Peter Goddard by province (Que.) and does not name Kanawana or give his title. It establishes him as an active figure in Quebec camping at the turn of 1983-84, which is a third dated fixed point inside the 1981-1985 Kanawana directorship bracket, alongside his November 1982 signature as Director and the early 1983 national poster mailing at Kamp Kanawana.

Canadian Camping Winter 1984 National Office News reports: "LOUIS JEAN has joined the staff of the Association des Camps du Quebec. As employees are not permitted to serve in Executive roles, Louis has resigned as Central Vice President. Good wishes Louis! A new vice president has not yet been named." (Reconstructed from a 180-degree rotated page; corroborated in clean type at issue 151.)

Louis Jean, elected Canadian Camping Association Central Vice-President by acclamation and taking office 6 May 1983, held the office for under nine months and had resigned it before the winter of 1984. This corrects the record written from issue 147, which recorded only the election. Quebec's seat on the national executive was vacant when the Winter 1984 issue went to press.
The Canadian Camping Association had a written rule barring employees of the association from serving in executive roles, stated in the Winter 1984 explanation of Louis Jean's resignation.

Jeff Reading of Kilcoo Camp, "Acid Rain: Understanding the Problem at Camp," Canadian Camping Winter 1984: "In Quebec the problem may be more serious. When the glaciers retreated across this region they removed much of the buffering material from the northern lakes and deposited them in the south. Most lakes north of the St. Lawrence River have already been acidified. Further, eighty percent of the lakes and streams in the Laurentian Shield have acid levels high enough to kill plankton and interfere with fish reproduction."

Reading's Winter 1984 acid rain feature gives the national average pH of Canadian rainfall as 4.3, describes the "spring shock" of acid stored in snow releasing at melt, and states that acid kills or deforms fry before acid levels reach a point dangerous to adult fish - so a lake could be failing while still looking and fishing normal to a camp.

The bilingual Winter 1984 editorial "Acid Rain: Not Just A Catchphrase!" cites TIME's figure of "some 1,300 [lakes] in Quebec... in the process of being destroyed" and a Gallup finding that 77% of Canadians thought acid rain the gravest environmental problem the country faced.

The Winter 1984 editorial of Canadian Camping states: "Yet the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain has indicated that the Canadian Camping Association is not even a member!! Why is it that those with so much to lose often have little to say?... We have, on paper, a national environment committee and still no word on acid rain, no position, no dissemination of information, no commitment! To be selectively mute in this area is to be irresponsible and out-of-touch with a growing movement." The masthead attributes editorial opinion to the editor, not to the association.

Doug Caldwell of the Federation of Ontario Naturalists, in a letter in Canadian Camping Winter 1984, lists the fifty organizations in the Canadian Coalition on Acid Rain - from the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada to Resorts Ontario - and writes: "noticeably absent in this list is the Canadian Camping Association or any Provincial Camping Associations. Is it the mandate of your Association to remain apolitical?... I challenge the Camping Associations of Canada to take a stand."

Reading's Winter 1984 feature sets out five acid-rain experiments a camp could run: wind charts traced back to the emitting region; a four-container pH comparison of rainwater, distilled water, vinegar and ammonia; daily pH logging of lake water, rainfall, post-rain lake water and tap water as part of a camp weather station; a bedrock-sensitivity experiment comparing marble against crushed local granite; and "Experiment 4: Canoe Trip Testing" - "if you are a camp that has a reasonably extensive canoe tripping program (to distinctly different water sheds) then test the pH levels of the various lakes visited over the course of the summer... examine how the pH of frequently visited lakes changes during the summer."

No evidence exists that Kanawana ran acid-rain pH testing on its canoe trips. What is documented is the dated, published 1984 proposal that a tripping camp turn its routes into a monitoring transect; Kanawana was a camp with an extensive canoe tripping programme of the kind the proposal addresses.

Canadian Camping Winter 1984 National Office News reports Mrs. Irene Knapp appointed Secretary at the CCA National Office, a native of Glasgow who came to Canada on a working holiday, with secretarial and bookkeeping experience, hours Monday to Friday 9:00 to 4:00; and Sharon Freedman, office typist since November 1982, who worked on the tasks surrounding the International Camping Congress of January 1983, leaving in October 1983 before the birth of her second child. (Reconstructed from a rotated page.)

Mary Roy left the Canadian Camping Association national office in September 1983 after eight years of service and continued freelancing from home, still available by phone for bookkeeping questions. The rotated Winter 1984 scan decoded her tenure as "8 1/2 years"; the Executive Director's report in issue 151, in clean type, gives September and eight years.

Jean Funk of Alberta, back from world travels and working as a freelance consultant to the Alberta Forest Service, became chairperson of the CCA Environment Committee, announced in the Winter 1984 President's Perspective. The rotated scan decoded the name as "Jean Punk"; issue 151 prints it in clean type as Jean Funk.

Paul Potter of Nova Scotia, a programme consultant developing emergency training and physical fitness programmes for offshore oil rigs, became CCA Leadership Development Programs chairman and coordinator of the Consultant/Advisor programme, announced Winter 1984.

Three CCA task forces were wound up and disbanded as reported in Winter 1984, their chairmen thanked: Jack Pearse for a feasibility study on a national conference, Janet Adamson for the hasti-notes trial, and Terry Burkhalter for the Volunteer Executive Development seminar. (Reconstructed from a rotated page.)

Marjorie Booth, "Volunteer Leaders Sharpen Executive Skills," Canadian Camping Winter 1984: twenty-one provincial and national leaders met at Bolton Camp and Conference Centre, 13-15 October 1983, chaired by Terry Burkhalter and facilitated by Arnie Cohen, a long-time camp leader then a consultant in psychological matters in Winnipeg, on goal-setting, consensus decision-making, "Synergistic Planning" against "Traditional Planning," managerial grid theory and communication. Fitness Canada paid the delegates' airfares.

The printed delegate list for the October 1983 Volunteer Executive Development Workshop names representatives of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario (Liz Greenway, Fred Okada, Dorothy Walter), Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. Quebec is absent - an explicit null, at a national leadership event held six months after Louis Jean's election and around the time he left the executive for the ACQ's staff.

The contents page of Canadian Camping Vol. 35 No. 4, Winter 1984, announces a "SPECIAL INSERT - 1984 PUBLICATIONS CATALOGUE" which is not present in the Internet Archive scan. The 1984 CCA publications catalogue is therefore a known, named, missing document, on the pattern of the 1981 and 1982-83 catalogues.

The Winter 1984 subscription card offers, after the first two full-rate subscriptions at $6.00 a year, additional one-year subscriptions at $4.00, pitched at directors subscribing their senior staff, with the note that "many counsellors are requesting reprints of articles and/or entire issues."

The Camping Advisor column in Canadian Camping Winter 1984 answers a parent of a newly-disabled ten-year-old on integrated versus specialty camps - "many people feel that integration is a better philosophical stand than segregation" - and promises that "the next issue of Canadian Camping will deal specifically with some of the issues facing disabled campers." Recorded as period language and period practice, dated, and not adopted in this project's own voice.

Colin Lumby reports in Canadian Camping Winter 1984 that Alberta's 1983 pre-camp workshops used 33 volunteer resource people for 120 camp personnel, at Yo-Wo-Ch-As and Yamnuska; Rick Ireland describes Alberta Education's Environmental Education Manual for Grades 1-12, a provincial curriculum an outdoor centre could sell into.

Correction to the record taken from issue 148: the mailing label on the Internet Archive copy of the Winter 1984 issue reads "CAMP RICHILDACA / MR. & MRS. R. J. BABCOCK / KETTLEBY ON". The sixth deposit hand in this run is therefore a camp, Camp Richildaca of Kettleby, Ontario, and the initials are R. J. rather than the "Hugh Babcock" recorded from issue 148. Issue 150's label on the same subscription OCRs the initials as "W. J."; the camp name is the stable part and the initials should not be relied on.

Canadian Camping Vol. 36 No. 1, Spring 1984, contains no mention of Kanawana, the Association des camps du Quebec, or any Quebec camp anywhere in the issue, and Quebec's seat on the national executive is still recorded as unfilled after Louis Jean's resignation. Explicit null from a word-for-word read of the whole issue.

The Ontario Camping Association's fifty-year history was published as BLUE LAKE AND ROCKY SHORE, 112 pages, illustrated, written by a selected committee of OCA Executive Members, published by Natural Heritage, Toronto, and launched to coincide with the OCA Annual Conference of 23-25 February 1984 at the Inn On The Park, Toronto. It was available from the CCA Bookstore for $8.95.

The Canadian Camping review of Blue Lake and Rocky Shore frames it as the first published history of Canadian children's camping - "a book of this calibre, looking at the world of children's camping from the turn of the century, has never before been written" - appearing ten years before Kanawana's own centennial. The review says only that the OCA was "founded in the early Thirties'", which is consistent with the 1930-1933 uncertainty in this project's records and settles nothing.

Jocelyn Palm's President's Perspective, Canadian Camping Spring 1984: "Our Association has been awarded a grant of $10,000 by The Neathern Trust. The objectives of the grant are to provide projects which foster: the acquisition of appropriate practices in simple outdoor living; the appreciation and increased understanding of the natural world; the expansion of education to reflect the concern for conservation of our environment and energy resources. The principal and interest are to be expended after 10 years... This grant was instigated by Dr. Mary L. Northway, a long time camper and friend of CCA."

The Neathern Trust grant of $10,000 to the CCA was a ten-year endowment whose principal and interest were to be expended after 10 years, placing its projects in 1984-1994 - the decade running up to Kanawana's centennial.

Jocelyn Palm gives Dr. Mary L. Northway's camp biography, Canadian Camping Spring 1984: "Dr. Northway was a camper then staff member at Glen Bernard Camp near Sundridge, Ontario from 1922-1939. In 1940, Dr. Northway and Flora Morrison founded Windy Pine, a tripping camp near Minden, Ontario."

Canadian Camping Spring 1984 prints John Latimer's Group Dynamics Exercise on sociometry, comparing "the counsellor's perception vs. the camper's perception" of friendship, trust and leadership within a cabin group, with worked questions and a sample sociogram. The magazine does not link this to Mary Northway, whose academic reputation was made in sociometry and who instigated the Neathern Trust grant announced in the same issue; no link is claimed here.

Canadian Camping created a new column, "Camping... The Last Word!", in the Spring 1984 issue expressly to hold exchanges too long for the letters page. Its first subject was co-ed sleeping accommodation.

In the first "Camping... The Last Word!" column, A.B. Thiessen of Winnipeg - twelve years in corrections, six in education, three in mental health - challenges the editor's earlier endorsement of a proposal that boys and girls share dorms, cabins or tents, demanding "that you make available the studies you refer to" and raising the short camp period, "the varied ethnic, religious and cultural backgrounds of many campers," and "the difficulties and problems experienced by early sexual involvement."

Editor Jay Haddad answers Thiessen at more than a page in Canadian Camping Spring 1984, naming the original correspondent as Harry Rokkos, citing Humber College's daycare with shared washrooms, Mary Calderone of SIECUS, Alex Comfort and the NFB's Why Men Rape, and arguing that "close to 90% of the world's population from the beginning of time to the present day has lived communally... Our society is, in fact, the historical and statistical anomaly" - closing with a bibliography of twenty titles offered as containing "well over 300 studies." The masthead attributes editorial opinion to the editor, not to the association.

The Spring 1984 Canadian Camping exchange on co-ed sleeping accommodation documents the state of the argument in Canadian organized camping seventeen years after Kanawana's coeducation pilot, at a period when Kanawana's own section structure had settled into parallel girls' and boys' sections. The exchange says nothing about Kanawana.
