The bilingual Spring 1984 editorial "segregation... It Still Exists!!!" recounts an experiment initiated in the summer of 1983 in "a large, private Ontario camp which sees 600 able-bodied campers pass through its gates each summer": "6 physically-disabled adolescents co-existed with their own little camp and camp programme within the framework of the larger camp. A few ramps were built leading into the dining hall and dormitory; otherwise, there was little disruption." The editor argues the six hundred gained more than the six. Recorded as period language and practice, dated, and not adopted in this project's voice.

Rick Ireland in Canadian Camping Spring 1984, on adapting a camp for disabled campers: "Our ramps are a little too steep and our showers are a little too narrow. The mud on the paths becomes a little too muddy but now we know. We now know the value of obtaining advice from the 'real' people as well as the experts."

Sylvia Haynes, "Camping is Fun! And it is For Everyone!", Canadian Camping Spring 1984, includes a detailed accessibility audit checklist - shower stalls with regulated water temperature, ramps at one foot rise in twelve, non-slip surfaces, handrails, washbasin and mirror heights, drinking fountains under 34 inches with knee room, picnic tables accessible from both sides, flashing lights for the deaf, bells in washrooms - and suggests a target of 20-30% disabled campers in an integrated programme. This is the contemporary standard against which any future evidence of Kanawana's accessibility in this period should be read; no Kanawana integration practice of this period is documented.

The Camp Counsellor's Handbook, 2nd edition, by Brian Blackstock and John Latimer, "totally revised," $9.95 paperback, was advertised in Canadian Camping Spring 1984 for publication March 1984, covering "programs, daily life, the needs and characteristics of various age groups, counselling the physically or mentally handicapped, activities."

The CIT Instructor's Manual and CIT Manual ($14.95 with binder; the camper manual $9.95, or $8.00 for ten or more) are reviewed by Mary Milne in Canadian Camping Spring 1984, in eleven chapters whose first is "Camp History & Philosophy" - evidence that a camp's own history was a formal element of Canadian counsellor-in-training curriculum by 1984.

The Canadian Heritage Rivers System was announced 18 January 1984 by the federal Ministers of the Environment and of Indian and Northern Affairs, its board meeting for the first time 19-20 January 1984 with representatives of the federal government and of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, Manitoba taking the chair. The first candidate rivers were the Athabasca and the South Nahanni, with the Bloodvein and the French to follow. Quebec is not among the participating governments.

The Society of Camp Directors, "in cooperation with the Canadian Camping Association," announced $450 in Awards Papers prizes - $200 director, $150 staff, $100 camper - for articles on camping in French or English, deadline 15 November 1984, winners to be published in the Summer 1985 issue of Canadian Camping.

The Canadian Camping Association's annual meeting for 1983 was set for Friday 4 May 1984, 7:30 p.m., at the Nova Scotia Agricultural College, Truro. The spring 1984 leadership-development calendar lists events in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Ontario only, with no Quebec entry.

Sam Hambly of Camp Allsaw gives full construction and operating instructions in Canadian Camping Spring 1984 for the Allsaw Composter, a styrofoam-insulated year-round composting unit charged with horse manure and earthworm culture - the most detailed camp composting method in this run of the magazine.

Bruce Elkin of the Yamnuska Mountain School argues in Canadian Camping Spring 1984 that camps should become "integrated centres for personal growth" teaching "generic skills" - Will, Wisdom and Wherewithal - and quotes Masuda's The Information Society on personal computers lifting education "out of the restrictions of formal schools."

The Association des camps du Quebec's 1983 report to the Canadian Camping Association, signed Claire Menard: "Les activites de l'ACQ, cette annee, ont [ete] ajustees aux besoins des membres. Un questionnaire a ete envoye a l'automne, pour connaitre les besoins des camps et les services qu'ils attendent de leur Association. Des journees thematiques sur 'La gestion par informatique', 'Les nouveaux jeux', et 'La place des parents au camp' ont retenu l'interet de plusieurs membres."

The ACQ's 1983 report states: "La Semaine des Camps du 23 au 28 avril sera la principale activite de promotion au printemps. Un projet special, en collaboration avec le Ministere du Loisir, de la Chasse et de la Peche, nous permettra d'avoir un 'message radio' durant cette semaine." This dates a Quebec camp promotion week to 23-28 April 1984 with a radio campaign run jointly with the Ministere du Loisir, de la Chasse et de la Peche.
entities: Ministere du Loisir, de la Chasse et de la Peche

facts.claim: The ACQ's 1983 report states: "Au Quebec, la Loi de la protection du consommateur a fait l'objet de plusieurs rencontres avec differents intervenants afin d'obtenir une exemption pour les camps de vacances." The Quebec camping association spent 1983-84 lobbying for camps to be exempted from Quebec's Loi sur la protection du consommateur - a regulatory question bearing directly on how camp fees, refunds and contracts with parents were governed under Quebec law.

The ACQ sent a questionnaire to member camps in the autumn of 1983 to establish their needs and the services they expected of the association. Kanawana was an accredited ACQ member camp at that date, so a Kanawana response to that questionnaire may exist in ACQ records; the magazine does not name any respondent.

The 1983 CCA annual report's provincial table gives Quebec 117 member camps, all 117 accredited and none non-accredited - the second consecutive year in which Quebec's membership and accreditation figures are identical, after 129 of 129 in 1982.

Quebec's other figures in the 1983 CCA provincial table: 103 resident and 5 day camps plus 9 "other"; 50 four-season and 18 three-season; 16,568 camper-beds; 75,768 individual campers; 790,595 camper-days; 239 foreign campers; 1,395 volunteer and 3,788 paid staff; $3,285,885 food and $4,894,456 wages; and a return rate of 41%, down from 48%.

Quebec's membership in the CCA statistics fell from 129 camps in 1982 to 117 in 1983, a loss of twelve, at the same time as its survey response rate fell seven points from 48% to 41%. Year-on-year movement in the Quebec column therefore mixes real change with sampling change and should not be read as either alone.

The 1983 provincial statistics table printed in Canadian Camping Summer 1984 does not add up: the national "Paid Staff" total of 38,592 is roughly twice the sum of the provincial columns, and Alberta's camper-days are given as 5,403 where neighbouring provinces run to hundreds of thousands. The provincial figures are usable; the 1983 national totals in that table are not, and the four-year national series printed above it is the better source. Recorded as a defect in the source.

Colette Pouliot-Marier, writing in Canadian Camping Summer 1984: "Qu'il me soit permis de rappeler que ce comite qui a ete mis sur pied a l'automne 1974 a pour but d'assurer une presence active des camps francophones et de faire entendre le point de vue des camps de langue francaise au sein de l'Association." The CCA's French language committee was founded in the autumn of 1974.

Pouliot-Marier also records: "rappelons, entre autres, le congres du printemps 1976 qui a reuni des directeurs de camps de vacances et personnes interessees au phenomene des camps, venus de toutes les provinces, autour du theme de 'L'activite pedagogique du camp de vacances'", after which "bien des membres ont maintenu des contacts" - a spring 1976 national congress of French-language camps drawing directors from every province.

Colette Pouliot-Marier told Jocelyn Palm on 22 April 1984 that she would succeed Pauline Rondeau, directrice du Camp Claret, as president of the CCA's French language committee. Ken Willis's committee report adds that Rondeau "resigned as Chairman at the end of this year due to severe time restraints," and that Pouliot-Marier "plans to continue with the tasks of generating articles in French for Canadian Camping and establishing priorities and procedures for translation."

The Executive Director's report in Canadian Camping Summer 1984 states in clean type: "Ken [Willis] replaced Louis Jean who resigned after accepting a position with ACQ" - corroborating the substantive finding recovered from issue 149's rotated pages and naming Louis Jean's successor.

The Canadian Camping Summer 1984 annual report records "Plans for CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986 from Cliff Labbett" - corroborating in clean type the issue 148 finding that the association dated its own founding to 1936.

Adele and Harry Ebbs, "Memorable Quotes from 'Blackie' Blackstock," Canadian Camping Summer 1984, state the source of the several hundred words of his speech they print: "The following quotes are excerpts from the Camping Archives at Trent University." This is the first explicit statement in this run of the magazine that the Trent collection contains transcribed interviews with camping figures, not only institutional paper.

The Ebbs tribute adds to C. R. "Blackie" Blackstock's biography: he was at Pickering College in 1928, in Taylor Statten's time; he was a Kitchikewana "original," starting the first year of that YMCA camp on Beausoleil Island in 1921 as a very young counsellor under Ernie Thurlow, boys' work secretary for Simcoe County, rising to assistant director under Win Smith; he was a Founding Fellow of the Society of Camp Directors and an Honourary Life Member of the OCA; he took summer courses at Wisconsin in outdoor education, a B.Sc. at McGill and an honorary LL.D. at York in 1974; he introduced winter school camping at Limberlost Lodge through Pickering College; he founded Camp Mazinaw in 1940; and he was later executive secretary of the Canadian Association of Physical and Health Education.

Blackstock on camp conservation teaching, quoted from the Trent Camping Archives in Canadian Camping Summer 1984: "conservation isn't something that needs to be taught; you expose people to the situation, and they're sharp enough to see." On canoe tripping he "alleged that canoe trippers should be trained to handle risk and to anticipate it," given as input to research then being done by the Society of Camp Directors.

Hugh Phillips's International Youth Year Task Force, struck March 1983 and meeting in Toronto on 16-17 April and 22-23 October 1983, settled three national projects: "1. National Celebration Event: a special summer day in Aug. of 1985 where all campers in CCA help celebrate the international year of youth. Program kits for the themes of fitness, environment, historical roots and peace will be developed by the IYY Task Force. 2. Youth Camp Director Institute: proposed for Jan. 31-Feb. 1, 1985 at Bolton Camp, Ontario... 3. Special CCA Magazine Edition: an entire issue of Canadian Camping will be devoted to our youth."

A CCA "historical roots" programme kit was to be developed and distributed to member camps for a national celebration day in August 1985. Kanawana was an accredited ACQ member camp and in Quebec every member camp was an accredited one, so the kit was due to reach Kanawana in the summer of 1985. Nothing is claimed about what Kanawana did with it; the kit's despatch is what is documented.
The Youth Camp Director Institute is advertised in Canadian Camping Summer 1984 as running 31 January to 3 February 1985, $145 all inclusive, at Bolton Camp.

Paul Potter's Leadership Development report in the 1983 CCA annual report tabulates every Consultant/Advisor visit of 1983-84 with its cost - Jack Pearse to B.C., George Matthews to Newfoundland, Jane McCutcheon to New Brunswick, Jay Haddad to Nova Scotia, Alberta and B.C., Martha Knowlton to New Brunswick, Mickey Johnston to Manitoba, $2,474.45 in total - and records: "The Association des camps du Quebec could not use their Consultant/Advisor due to insufficient registration for their Winter Conference."

Marnie Ellis, who thanked Peter Goddard and the staff of Kamp Kanawana for the 1983 national poster mailing, was herself based in Montreal: the president's report in the 1983 CCA annual report lists her as "Marnie Ellis of Montreal," and her own Publicity report describes Marjorie Booth helping "the chairman, in Montreal," and Jocelyn Palm doing National Camping Day interviews "out West, and by phone to Quebec."

Jean Funk's environment committee report in the 1983 CCA annual report: "October 1983 saw a fresh start for the Environment Committee," with a revised action plan, review of Environment Canada material, a recommended liaison with the National Trail Association, correspondence with forestry industries, a proposed Energy Camp as a joint venture with the Terry Fox Centre in Ottawa, and "drafted the 'CCA Environmental Ethic'... I am looking forward to... the acceptance of the 'CCA Environmental Ethic' in 1984." The Environmental Ethic tracked since 1982 was therefore still only a draft in the spring of 1984.

Clifford Labbett's 50th Anniversary Task Force report lists five ideas for 1986: "1. Kite flying across Canada. 2. Be a part of the annual July 1st celebrations in Ottawa. 3. Tie in with National Camping Day and sponsorship by private industry in a salute to Children's Camping across Canada. 4. Official recognition from UNESCO for camping's contribution to protection of our environment. 5. Across Canada campfires." Labbett also records that he "was President of CCA when this concept [the International Congress] was first established."

Bruno Morawetz's archives report in the 1983 CCA annual report describes the collection method: "Each Provincial Association was sent a large brown envelope marked 'Archives' under which are listed the kinds of materials that should be saved and placed in the envelope for mailing at a later date when the envelope is about to burst." Provincial deposits at Trent therefore arrive as irregular bulk envelopes rather than ordered transfers.

Brian Law's Standards report in the 1983 CCA annual report sets as an objective for the autumn of 1984 "a new provincial comparison of existing practices, the education of visitors, and an examination of the process of accreditation" - a second edition of the provincial standards comparison.

The Second International Camping Congress was fixed for 3-5 March 1987 at the Shoreham Hotel, Washington, D.C., theme "Our Fragile World - A Challenge for the Outdoor Community," jointly sponsored by the American, Canadian, Jamaican and Japanese camping associations and cooperating with fourteen bodies including the World Alliance of YMCAs and the European YMCA Camping Group. This is the only point in this run of the magazine where Kanawana's parent movement appears as an institutional partner of the camping associations.

The Newsletter Committee report in the 1983 CCA annual report gives Canadian Camping's production chain: Jay Haddad editing, Marc Cote on layout and photographs, Therese Wong typesetting, and Ken Smith at the National Sport & Recreation Centre guiding it "through the printing and mailing process in Ottawa" - with the editor noting "we are now in the enviable position of having too much material for some issues."

The Publications Committee report (Wendy Wren and Judy Richards, succeeding Fred Okada) records CCA Book Store gross sales up $8,776 on the year, a second printing of the CIT Manual required by 30 June 1984, and a Fitness Canada-funded market study by Jack Zoubie into a family-camping publication. The Education Committee (Dorothy Walter) has the "Curriculum for Camp Directors" onto word processing, assisted by Stan Talesnick and John Wilkinson.

The foreign camp counsellor table (CCDO 2333-126) in the 1983 CCA annual report is printed with its columns broken in the OCR; the province headings and the number pairs do not align and the Quebec column cannot be read with confidence. Only the totals are recorded: 732 foreign camp counsellors in 1982 and 708 in 1983. The per-province figures are deliberately not extracted.

The mailing label on the Internet Archive copy of Canadian Camping Vol. 36 No. 2, Summer 1984, reads MISS JANE MCCUTCHEON, C/O CAMP TAWINGO, HUNTSVILLE ON - a seventh deposit hand in this run, identifying a figure who recurs throughout it with a camp of her own. (OCR'd on this copy as "CAMP TANINGU"; corrected against the label on issue 156, which reads CAMP TAWINGO.)

Four readings taken from issue 149's 180-degree rotated pages are corrected by the same material printed in clean type in issue 151: the environment chairman is Jean Funk, not "Jean Punk"; the International Youth Year is 1985, not the "1986" the decoder produced, with the celebration day in August 1985; the Washington congress is 3-5 March 1987, not "1-2 March"; and Mary Roy left in September after eight years, not "8 1/2 years". This is a second demonstration, after the issue 146 date correction, of the unreliability the rotated-scan decoder warning exists for.

The 1984-85 CCA Publications Catalogue, bound as a twelve-page insert into Canadian Camping Vol. 36 No. 3, Autumn 1984, opens: "The Canadian Camping Association was founded in 1936 as a non-profit organization" and "L'Association des camps du Canada, creee en 1936". This is a flat assertion of the founding year in the association's own commercial literature, in both languages, as distinct from an inference drawn from anniversary planning.
The 1984-85 catalogue's statement of a 1936 founding says nothing about whether the Canadian Camping Association was founded at Ottawa or at Toronto, which remains the open part of conflict c_029.

The 1984 CCA Publications Catalogue announced in issue 148 and missing from the Winter 1984 scan is present in Canadian Camping Autumn 1984 in its 1984-85 edition. The named gap recorded from issue 149 is closed.

Editor Jay Haddad, replying to a critical letter in Canadian Camping Autumn 1984, names his complete interview series: "I published interviews I held with Charles Plewman, June Labbett, May Brown, John Latimer, Marjorie Booth and Leo Buscaglia."

Haddad's Autumn 1984 list of every editorial he wrote in three years and every feature the magazine ran matches this project's word-for-word read of the same issues item for item: all six named interviews and every named feature and editorial, including "The Voice of Camping: Inaudible!", are already recorded in the read. This is an external check on the completeness of the read, supplied by the run itself, and the read passes it. It is a fact about the research, not about camping.

Jane McCutcheon, writing as Business Manager of Camp Tawingo in the Autumn 1984 "Camping... The Last Word!" column, objected: "I am tired of the articles on sexuality, homosexuality, masturbation and virginity... I for one feel the focus of this magazine is all wrong." Recorded as a dated statement of the disagreement, not adopted in this project's voice.

Jay Haddad's reply in Canadian Camping Autumn 1984 discloses three things about himself and his appointment: his involvement with the subject "began at a Director's Conference in Bolton around 1978 where so much ignorance was flying around the room that I was ASKED to prepare a session on sexuality and homosexuality"; he is "a Teaching Master in Psychology with a specialization in gender and sexuality"; and Jane McCutcheon "was the central CCA Vice-President when I became editor of Canadian Camping". He also names Mickey Johnstone as "a nationally renowned educator on sexuality, values and youth development" who had led at Tawingo.

Bruno Morawetz, "Are You Taping Your Leaders?", Canadian Camping Autumn 1984, crediting "the inspiration of Helen Stewart, the Ontario Archives Chairman": "In order to record these events, it is a good idea to make use of tape recorders to tape interviews with individual Camp Directors and to tape addresses that are given at conferences and workshops... send copies to the CCA Archives at Trent University, Peterborough, if it is of national importance."

Morawetz's 1984 archives column also states: "The Ontario Archives Committee has just finished writing the history of the Ontario Camping Association in a handsome booklet entitled 'Blue Lake and Rocky Shore' to mark the 50th Anniversary of its founding and it is hoped that other provinces will start thinking about the writing of their own histories." The provinces were formally encouraged in 1984 to write their own association histories.

The 1984 national instruction to tape camp directors and conference addresses and send copies to Trent, taken with the Blackstock transcript excerpts printed in issue 151, indicates that the CCA Archives at Trent University holds audio recordings and not only paper, and gives a date from which such recordings would begin accumulating.

The full four-day programme of the Youth Camp Director Institute, Bolton Camp, 31 January to 3 February 1985, chaired by John Latimer, is printed in Canadian Camping Autumn 1984. Sessions include "Values & Morals of Youth" (K. Grant Kerr, United Church of Canada, OCA President); "Stress & Addiction" (Norm Panzica, Council on Drug Abuse); "Volunteerism & Youth" (Marguerite Hudson, Girl Guides of Canada); "Responsibility, Loyalty & Commitment of Youth" and "Child Abuse", both by Arnold Cohen of the Child Guidance Clinic of Winnipeg; "'I've done it all' - Apathetic Youth" (Barry Lowes, Camp Timberlane); "The Family" (Alan Ingram, Litigation Counsel, Official Guardian Branch, Province of Ontario); and sessions by Michael Brandwein of Chicago, Bruce Harris of Camp Kawabi and Craig Copland of Camp Mini-Yo-We.

"Child Abuse" as a named session on the programme of the Youth Camp Director Institute of 31 January to 3 February 1985 is the first appearance of child abuse as a named agenda item at a national gathering of Canadian camp directors in the first 152 issues of Canadian Camping read word for word by this project. It establishes when the subject entered the profession's formal training programme.
Ron Johnstone is listed under the Alberta Camping Association in Canadian Camping Autumn 1984, having appeared throughout the earlier run of the magazine as an Ontario figure.

Walter D. Mingie's Outdoor Education - Guidelines for Camps, which originated "at an Outdoor Education Conference sponsored by the CCA/ACC at La Caleche, Quebec in 1974", was revised in 1981 according to the 1984-85 CCA Publications Catalogue.

The 1984-85 CCA Publications Catalogue gives Robert Wilkinson's Camps: Their Planning and Management unambiguously as hardbound, C.V. Mosby, 291 pages, 1981, by "Robert E. Wilkinson, Ph.D., of McGill University's Physical Education Department and Camp Nominigue, Quebec" - settling the edition question left open at issue 143 in favour of the Mosby 1981 hardback.

Derek Walsh's "Comment promouvoir votre camp vacances," CCA/ACC, 4 p., 1981, $0.75, is catalogued in 1984-85 as one of six titles in the bilingual "(LA) SERIE COMMENT FAIRE," alongside Marjorie Booth on fitness, Catherine Thomas on sailing, Sam Hambly on composting, Mors Kochanski on winter camping and Jocelyn Palm on the waterfront.

Mary Casey, R.N., "Standing Orders - For Us?", Canadian Camping Autumn 1984, sets out what Standing Orders are and why a camp with nurses and no resident physician legally needs them: written protocols for illness and accidents on and off site, written medical directives for every non-prescription medication with dosage and route, and "the annual signature of the camp physician" - with the advice to draft them in September "when the summer problems are fresh in your mind." This is the contemporary standard against which any Kanawana infirmary record of the period should be read.

The letters column of Canadian Camping Autumn 1984 carries an unsigned letter from a Saskatchewan camp director: "I feel as though I cannot sign this letter because of my very public position as a camp director... the time is not yet right for some of us who are supportive of the rights of lesbians and homosexuals to come out of the closet publicly - no matter what our own orientation may be. The risks are still too high." No individual is identifiable. Recorded because it is a dated statement about what a Canadian camp director in 1984 believed could and could not be said in public.

The same letters column carries a rebuke from Jerry Vander Veen, Atlantic Director of the Canadian Sunday School Mission: "it would be devastating if parents of our campers assumed that we would be the proponents of homosexuality." Recorded as period language, dated, and not adopted in this project's own voice.

Jocelyn Palm's Legacy to A Camper is catalogued in 1984-85 as "more than the history of Mary S. Edgar and Glen Bernard Camp," with programme ideas for "Special Days, Evening Program, Indian Council Ring, Quiet Times, Campfires and Thanks" - the Council Ring still a saleable programme category in 1984. The Blackstock/Latimer Camp Counsellor's Handbook is given a publisher: Methuen, 124 p., 1984, $11.95. Blue Lake & Rocky Shore is listed at $10.75, $8.95 to members. Helen E. Stewart's Cookery for Kids, Kamp n' Kicks is "an anthology of recipes used extensively at Camp Wahcahmie in Ontario", placing the Ontario archives chairman at a camp of her own.

Jocelyn Palm's editorial "CCA - In Transition", Canadian Camping Vol. 36 No. 4, Winter 1985: "In October 1984, the CCA began searching for an individual to replace Marjorie Booth. Since the position was supported by Fitness Canada, permission is required prior to selecting the replacement. At the end of November we were advised by the Director of Fitness Canada, Mr. Michel Bedard, that Fitness Canada would no longer provide funds for the position. In addition, Mr. Bedard advised that support of all management aspects, re travel for meetings, office functions, administrative assistance, would be reduced each year by 33-1/3% to terminate completely in 1988."

The Internet Archive run of Canadian Camping read by this project ends in 1988 because the federal Fitness Canada grant that paid for the CCA national office, the executive director, delegates' travel and special projects was cut by one third a year from 1985 and terminated completely in 1988. The end of the magazine's run is therefore an explained event, not an unexplained gap in the source, and every judgement about the thinness of the record after 1988 must carry it.

Palm's Winter 1985 editorial dates the CCA's own institutional history: the national office with paid secretarial staff and a permanent address was established in 1971 - "prior to that time, the CCA office resided in the home of the elected President"; a full-time Executive Director was funded from 1979; Marjorie Booth held the post until October 1984; and the CCA shared the Ontario Camping Association's office space.
Palm's Winter 1985 editorial records that CCA National Conferences were held in 1972, 1973, 1975 and 1978, before the International Congress of 1983.
Palm's Winter 1985 editorial states that the Canadian Recreational Canoeing Association "was an outgrowth of CCA with an initial board of CCA personnel."

Palm's Winter 1985 editorial states that a 1982 decision to reduce the CCA's dependence on Ottawa produced "a hefty increase in CCA fees paid through the provincial associations." The national dues Kanawana paid through the ACQ therefore rose in 1982 as a consequence of a national funding strategy.

A consultant, Mr. John Fisher, was engaged by the CCA in March 1985 to advise on restructuring after the Fitness Canada cut, reporting first to the Regina board meeting and AGM of 25-26 April 1985. Palm framed the choice: "Shall we return to the methods of the CCA pioneer camp directors of the '30s, '40s, '50s and '60s? Shall we withdraw from some or all of the national initiatives that we have begun?"

Jocelyn Palm's figures for the Canadian Camping Association in the winter of 1985: some 400,000 campers, approximately 11,000 of them from outside Canada; over 38,000 paid staff and over 16,000 volunteer staff; an estimated 80% of staff aged 13-24.

Jean Funk, writing to CCA member camps in Canadian Camping Winter 1985: "This summer you received the Canadian Camping Association Environmental Ethic, and the accompanying sheet 'We, the campers and staff of Camp ______'... we encourage you to have all participating campers and staff sign the 'We, the campers and staff of Camp ______' sheet and post it in a visible place, near the Ethic Statement, at your camp." The Environmental Ethic, still only a draft in the spring of 1984, was adopted and distributed in the summer of 1984.

The full text of the CCA Environmental Ethic printed in Canadian Camping Winter 1985 comprises a preamble on "the finiteness of the earth's natural resources," the "sensitive dynamic balance... among all living organisms and the non-living elements," and "the moral and ethical responsibility of each person to care for the earth, both now and for future generations"; a personal and a professional pledge; and five undertakings - aesthetic appreciation, the rights and responsibilities of all people, lifelong environmental attitudes, the essential concepts of ecology, and "the wise use of our natural heritage - woods, water, wildlife, air and soils."

Kanawana was an accredited ACQ member camp and in Quebec every member camp was accredited, so the CCA Environmental Ethic and its "We, the campers and staff of Camp ______" pledge sheet reached Kanawana in the summer of 1984. The pledge sheet was designed to be signed by campers and staff and posted at the camp - a physical object bearing the camp's name and a summer's signatures that may survive in the camp's papers or in a photograph. No Kanawana copy is documented.

Jean Funk's accompanying suggestions to member camps in Winter 1985: adopt a stream or a series of out-trip sites; water, light, heating, waste-recycling and transport conservation; "plan for the campers of 2085, by planting trees this year"; nest-box trails and winter bird feeding; and "where does your waste water go?"
Alta R. Kahn died on Thursday, 7 March 1985. Her obituary in Canadian Camping Winter 1985 is signed by Frances Kelly and Robert Lazanik.
Alta Kahn's 1985 obituary states: "From 1960-1962, Alta Kahn was President of the English section of the Quebec Camping Association."

Alta Kahn's 1985 obituary states that she "was a major contributor to the realization of the founding of the Provincial Board (co-ordinating board of the English and French sections) and served as the Board's second President from 1963 to 1965." This names the second president of the Conseil Provincial and her term, and credits Kahn with its founding.

Two printings in Canadian Camping twelve years apart disagree on Alta Kahn's service as Executive Secretary of the Jewish Community Camps of Montreal: the 1973 tribute gives 1946 to 1949, the 1985 obituary gives 1946 to 1969. A single-digit typesetting or OCR slip (4/6) is the most economical explanation, but this is two documented sources disagreeing and is not resolved here. Recorded as conflict c_030.

The Camping Advisor in Canadian Camping Winter 1985 prints the Attorney General of Ontario's guidance over the name of the Hon. R. Roy McMurtry, answering counsellors who feared being sued for intervening on a canoe trip: "While no specific 'Good Samaritan' statute exists in Ontario, you can feel confident that if you act reasonably in giving emergency assistance you will not be found liable... the courts expect you to do only what is reasonable, considering the situation and your skills," with the rule that "once you have accepted responsibility for giving emergency assistance... you must continue to give help until another person is able to take over." This is Ontario law, not Quebec's, whose Civil Code duty to rescue is materially different, and it is not applied to Kanawana.

1985 was Heritage Year in Canada, marking a century since land was set aside near Banff. Canadian Camping Winter 1985 prints seventy-plus suggestions in both languages for camps, schools, individuals and organisations, including: "Record the oral history of your community on audio or video tape by interviewing senior citizens and local historians"; "produce an historical atlas of your community... use old maps, photographs, diary accounts and memoirs"; "produce an historic newspaper, reprinting the reports of important and interesting things that have happened in your community"; and "compare the local natural environment with various periods in the past, using archives, oral histories, wildlife and bird counts."

Three separate national prompts to Canadian camps to record their own history landed in the same year: the CCA archives chairman's 1984 taping instruction, the August 1985 "historical roots" programme kit, and the Heritage Year 1985 suggestions to record community oral history. If Kanawana ever produced heritage material outside its annual reports, 1985 is the year to look.

Jane McCutcheon's article in Canadian Camping Winter 1985 is excerpted from her keynote at The Camp Directors' Workshop, Bark Lake, Ontario, June 1984, and by-lined "Co-ordinator of Development at Camp Tawingo." The mailing label on the Internet Archive copy reads MR & MRS J. JORGENSON, HUNTSVILLE ON - an eighth deposit hand, and the John Jorgenson who co-authored the Tawingo books.

Jocelyn Palm's President's Perspective, Canadian Camping Vol. 37 No. 1, Spring 1985 - the International Youth Year special edition: "The CCA salutes and thanks Hugh Phillips of Edmonton, our IYY Chairman and his Committee Sylvia Haynes, Vancouver, Peter Goddard, Montreal, John Latimer, Toronto and Ian Fowler, Moncton. Each has done an excellent job over many months to bring the CCA's focus on youth to the forefront in this special year."

The colophon of the Spring 1985 International Youth Year special edition of Canadian Camping: "This Special Edition of Canadian Camping has been produced by the CCA International Youth Year Task Force. The IYY volunteers are: Marjorie Booth (Ontario), Ian Fowler (New Brunswick), Peter Goddard (Quebec), Sylvia Haynes (British Columbia), John Latimer (Ontario), and Hugh Phillips (Alberta)."

The clean-type printing of "Peter Goddard, Montreal" and "Peter Goddard (Quebec)" on the same IYY Task Force in Spring 1985 retroactively confirms the reading recovered glyph by glyph from the 180-degree rotated page of issue 149. The decoder was right on this passage; the caution accompanying it was still correct to state, and the reconstruction flag can now be joined by a clean-type citation rather than removed.

Five dated documents now fall in or on the span of Peter Goddard's association with Kanawana: 15 November 1982, a Kanawana newsletter signed "Peter G. Goddard, Director"; early 1983, the CCA Publicity report thanking "Peter Goddard and the staff of Kamp Kanawana in Montreal" for mailing 6,500 posters; winter 1983-84, "Peter Goddard (Que.)" on the IYY Task Force; spring 1985, "Peter Goddard, Montreal" and "Peter Goddard (Quebec)" on the same task force, credited with "an excellent job over many months"; and FY1986, the YMCA of Montreal Metropolitan Staff roster listing "Goddard, P. (Director of Kamp Kanawana)". What is documented is continuous presence in Montreal camping at national level from November 1982 to FY1986, with the office stated at both ends and not in the middle.

Ian Fowler, National Co-ordinator, in Canadian Camping Spring 1985: "The Canadian Camping Association will provide each member camp with a kit of program material suitable for the day's event. The kit will be directly mailed to each camp in early May. Kit contents include: Historical Roots Activities - Dr. Bruno Morawetz, Camp Ponacka; Environmental Activities - Mike Walters, Camp Chief Hector; Fitness Activities - Fitness Canada; Peace Activities - Canadian Peace Congress; IYY Campfire Program - Jack Pearse, Jane McCutcheon, John Jorgenson, Camp Tawingo."

The CCA's National Celebration Event for International Youth Year was fixed for Wednesday, 24 July 1985, and every member camp was asked "at least [to] use the special IYY campfire program giving the CCA salute to youth one common denominator."

A named document about how to do camp history - "Historical Roots Activities" by Dr. Bruno Morawetz, the CCA's own archives chairman - was posted directly to every member camp, Kanawana included, in early May 1985, for use on 24 July 1985. This falls in a period for which no Kanawana season report survives. A copy would be at Trent University if it survives anywhere.

Peter Goddard of Montreal sat for Quebec on the CCA task force that commissioned the May 1985 "historical roots" kit mailed to every member camp. That he was therefore party to sending a history kit to his own camp is an inference from two documented facts, not a fact: no source states his office in 1985.

The IYY campfire programme, written by Jack Pearse, Jane McCutcheon and John Jorgenson of Camp Tawingo, was designed to be the one element every camp in Canada used on the same evening, 24 July 1985. If any Kanawana record of that date survives, a Tawingo-written campfire is what it should show.

Bob Stewart's "Tracing Your Roots" is the historical-roots theme article of the Spring 1985 IYY edition: a genealogy primer for children at camp. It advises making a family tree, "be very careful and organized if you are to have a tree that is accurate," starting with one side at a time, and - because "you are a long way from old diaries and photographs and archives" - doing at camp the one thing that can be done there, telling and listening to family stories. Its questions for campers: "Do you know how your parents met?... Most of our families immigrated to Canada at one time or another. Do you know when your family did?... Do you have a favourite family relation?"

Stewart's 1985 camp genealogy article carries the caution: "Gather family 'stories'. But treat them with a bit of care. Time has a way of adding to old family stories... Sometimes they can be very interesting without being very true." His four-book reading list heads with Angus Baxter, In Search of Your Roots: A Guide for Canadians Seeking Their Ancestors (Macmillan of Canada, 1978).

Jocelyn Palm's figures in Spring 1985 - "Over 450,000 campers and 70,000 staff will be at CCA member camps this summer" - are larger than the 400,000 campers and roughly 54,000 staff she gave three months earlier in the Winter 1985 issue. Both are estimates, not returns, and the movement between them within one association year is a caution against treating either as a count.

Milton McClaren of Simon Fraser University argues in Canadian Camping Spring 1985 that ecological thinking needs eight processes - knowing, imagining, valuing, connecting, judging, opening, inquiring, acting - and that "every day that we decide NOT to act on acid rain we are in fact DOING something by NOT ACTING, because time is still operating."

Fred Weir of the Canadian Peace Congress writes the peace article in the Spring 1985 IYY edition, the only explicitly disarmament-political piece in this run of the magazine, proposing a Canadian nuclear-weapons-free zone, a superpower freeze and an end to cruise missile testing. The CCA's IYY themes, distributed to every member camp, therefore included a politically contested one.

Canadian Camping Spring 1985 records that Scouts Canada's 6th Canadian Jamboree was set for 3-12 July 1985 at Guelph, with 15,000 Scouts and Venturers and 2,000 leaders, and that the CGIT planned its first national camp since 1956, at Camp Brereton, Manitoba, 16-27 August 1985, for its 70th anniversary - forty-eight girls from eight regions.

Two poems by Mary S. Edgar, "One World" and "To Youth", close the Spring 1985 International Youth Year edition: "When the atom re-employed / Shall build the bridge of peace." No mailing label is legible on this copy - an explicit null, the deposit-hand series having run to eight.

A letter in Canadian Camping Vol. 37 No. 2, Summer 1985, is signed "Ken Willis, Magog, Quebec." Louis Jean's successor as CCA Central Vice-President was therefore a Quebecer, not an Ontarian. Ken Willis is already recorded in this project as the man who invited the CCA to hold its 1980 annual meeting in Quebec.

Quebec's representation on the CCA national executive was interrupted for a matter of months after Louis Jean resigned the Central Vice-Presidency in late 1983, not lost: the Winter 1984 issue records the seat unfilled, and the seat was then taken by Ken Willis of Magog, Quebec. The picture of a province drifting out of national affairs after 1983 - which the October 1983 Bolton delegate list and the unused Consultant/Advisor seemed to support - is stronger than the evidence sustains.

Ken Willis was Central Vice-President when the CCA's French Language Committee reported through him in the 1983 annual report - a Quebec vice-president receiving the francophone committee's report, not an Ontario one.

Ken Willis, writing in Canadian Camping Summer 1985 as a member of the board and executive at the time, gives the stated reason for the Fitness Canada withdrawal: "I was on the Board and Executive at the time discussions centred around what the Canadian Camping Magazine could do for the Association in its present financial crisis ... resultant upon Fitness Canada's thinking that camping is not within their jurisdiction." The cut was a jurisdictional judgement rather than a general austerity measure.

Madelene Ferguson Allen, director of Camp Ouareau, won a Society of Camp Directors Awards Paper prize with "The Kid Who Doesn't Speak English... How Do We Help?", printed in English and in full French translation in Canadian Camping Summer 1985: "We all know these children. They are the ones who step off the bus with big frightened eyes... They are 'the kids who don't speak English'... In too many cases the most short changed children at our summer camps are these children who don't speak English. Camps are not in tune with this growing segment of our camper population."

Allen's 1985 prize essay prescribes, before the francophone child arrives at an English camp, a letter from the director in translation ("translation can be expensive, but it is a worthwhile and necessary investment. You will find language students at your local university more than willing") with the daily timetable and "a dictionary of fifty or so basic camp words... words such as assembly, bug juice, morning dip... words that he would never meet in his English class."

Allen's 1985 essay advises against putting the non-English-speaking child in a cabin with a fluent speaker of his own language - "Like a drowning man clinging to a life preserver, Jean Pierre will cling to that camper" - and against giving him a counsellor fluent in his language, "a little is better than a lot in this case," while having one staff member free for a few minutes daily with a method shared across the whole staff. She sets out the "core phrase" method, demonstrated with a swimming instructor teaching the word "dive" by having other campers do it first.

Allen's 1985 essay describes predictable withdrawal at bedtime - "It is absolutely exhausting to live in a foreign language. It is an indescribable form of fatigue which attacks body and soul as well as brain" - with the instruction not to short-change the child a tuck-in even so, "he will recognize the kind tone of his voice"; the ten-day regression, "a well documented effect of immersion," explained by the analogy of driving in a snowstorm; and the rarer fear "especially in a young child, [of] an irrational fear of losing his own language and following from this the fear that his parents will not understand him when he returns home."

Allen's 1985 essay gives the 25% rule - "assume that he understands about 25% of what he appears to understand. Living in another language makes one a wonderful actor" - the cabin dictionary compiled at rest hour and illustrated by the whole cabin with the francophone child teaching the French word beside each English one, and the ethical line: "A camp should not, under any circumstances, accept a child who does not speak English unless it is willing to become totally involved in giving the child the time and the teaching necessary."

Allen's 1985 essay is the fullest treatment in this run of the magazine of the French-speaking child at an English-language camp, written by a Quebec director. Kanawana is an English-language YMCA camp in the Laurentians drawing on a bilingual city, and its own French-language provision is undocumented in this period. The essay is the contemporary standard against which any evidence of Kanawana's practice should be read; no claim is made here about that practice.

The other Society of Camp Directors Awards Paper printed in Canadian Camping Summer 1985 is by Gail McClintock of St Lambert, Quebec, "The Challenge of Camping" - a practical essay on preparation, new projects, encouraging new staff, "those magic moments of camping," and flexibility, with a set-piece on a "chocolate cakewalk" invented as a whole-camp project. Her camp is not stated. Both prize papers in the issue come from the Montreal region.

Janet Adamson took office as CCA president at the Regina annual meeting in April 1985, succeeding Jocelyn Palm. Her first President's Message describes the association as having "an impressive archival collection... in place at Trent University," a new "Curriculum of Study for camp directors," and 609 member camps - against 616 in 1983 and 618 in 1982.

John Fisher's preliminary restructuring report was received at the CCA's Regina meeting of April 1985, with a final report due to the Executive in June 1985, and a copy of the CCA's 1984 Annual Report was available from the national office on request. That 1984 annual report - the last full one before the funding cuts bit - has not been seen by this project.

Canadian Camping launched a reprint feature, "Camping... A Retrospective," in Summer 1985, reprinting older addresses "each issue... back many many years to a previously spoken or published work," explicitly so readers could "examine to what degree the atmosphere, thrusts and initiatives of bygone days are relevant today." Later issues of this run may therefore carry material predating the magazine itself.

The first "Camping... A Retrospective" reprints Barry Lowes's address to the Ontario Camping Association annual banquet, Inn-on-the-Park, 19 March 1966: camping threatened by summer schools, cottage real estate, teenage travel abroad and the possibility of a longer school year; "we talk a better game than we play"; "the claims have been mostly shadows without substance." The OCA had just appointed its first executive secretary, Mr. Stan Wild, and Lowes warns that "the strength of OCA has been its voluntary nature." He attacks the profit/non-profit distinction as "anathema... A camp is a camp, and a child is a child."

Barry Lowes, three months before Canada's centennial year began, in his March 1966 OCA address: "Canada stands in danger of coming apart at the seams, after 100 years... If the 3 1/2 millions of dollars that have been poured down the drain on the Bilingual and Bicultural Commission had been spent instead to exchange young people, getting them into homes and camps across Canada, to live together for a time. What a bridge of understanding such exchanges could form!" - almost exactly the inter-cultural camping exchange the Secretary of State went on to fund and which this project traces through the 1967 Centenary Journey.

Terry Burkhalter, CCA Western Vice-President and executive director of "Camps with Meaning," announced in Canadian Camping Summer 1985 that he was leaving Manitoba for the Lakewood Retreat Centre in Brooksville, Florida, effective 1 August 1985, saying "the Conference of Mennonites in Manitoba do not have a very high profile of camping as a profession."
No mailing label is legible on the Internet Archive copy of Canadian Camping Vol. 37 No. 2, Summer 1985. Explicit null.

Canadian Camping Vol. 37 No. 3, Autumn 1985, reprints Douglas G. McEwen's presidential article of Autumn 1967 under "Camping... A Retrospective," containing the sentence: "For the first 20 years of its life the Canadian Camping Association's strength has lain in strong provincial associations." Twenty years before 1967 is 1947: the sitting president in 1967 described the span of his own association's life as beginning two decades back, not three.

The same issue that reprints McEwen's c.1947 dating also carries Janet Adamson's president's message opening "In 1986 CCA/ACC will be celebrating fifty years of service to children and youth in Canada," and a bound-in 1985-86 catalogue repeating in both languages that "The Canadian Camping Association was founded in 1936." The association printed both datings in one issue without noticing. The 1936 dating is what the association said about itself in the 1980s; the c.1947 dating is what its president said about itself in 1967, closer to the event and from a Manitoba executive. Neither is preferred here.

McEwen's 1967 dating is the strongest single piece of evidence yet for the two-stage reading of the CCA's founding - a 1936 Ontario-centred founding, then national incorporation at Ottawa across 1946-49 - because it shows people inside the association operating on both datings at once.

Douglas G. McEwen may be related to Nelson McEwen, whom the Camp Stephens Alumni blog credits with founding the CCA in 1946 and who directed Kanawana c.1927-47. No source establishes the relationship and no weight is placed on it here; it is flagged because if it held, the coincidence of two McEwens both placing the founding in the later 1940s would stop being a coincidence.

McEwen's 1967 presidential article lists the association's gaps: "There are still camps and groups of camps who have not sought membership in the National Association. No Association exists in Saskatchewan, some camps in the Maritimes are not members of the Association and the French section of the Quebec Camping Association are still not members of the Canadian Association."

Joining the Quebec provincial body did not make the French section a member of the national association: as late as 1967 - six years after the Conseil Provincial and four years before the CCA took its bilingual name - the francophone half of Quebec camping was formally outside the Canadian Camping Association. The 1971 name change and the 1974 French Language Committee were therefore the machinery of bringing a French section in, not the movement catching up with one it already had.

McEwen's 1967 article records: "With the adoption this year of a set of Desirable Practices, camps now have a guide from their camping association." The CCA's first national statement of practice dates to 1967 and was explicitly a guide rather than standards.

McEwen's 1967 article records: "During the past four years... the CCA executive has been in the Western Provinces," and "at present the entire National Executive resides in Manitoba" - a Winnipeg-run national association from about 1963 to 1967 - with the admission that "no response from Provincial Associations is taken as assent." No full-time executive officer existed; McEwen argues one should be employed, which the association did not manage until 1979.

McEwen's 1967 article records: "The Centenary Journey project, now in its final stages, received a grant of $12,000.00 from the National Centennial Commission", with travel grants for board members and "a sizeable grant... for the conduct of five regional training events" from the Fitness and Amateur Sport Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare.

McEwen's 1967 article records that at "the Symposium of Recreation in Montreal," a group of twenty-five could not discuss the issues Kirk Wipper had raised "because of an involved discussion that developed as to what was meant by the word, camping."

The 1985-86 CCA Publications Catalogue lists as new: "High Above the Thundercloud, Jack Pearse and Bruce Taylor, Camp Tawingo Publications, 165 p., 1985" - "a one-of-a-kind resource for developing a full and rewarding Indian lore program... complete Indian council ceremonies which include a call to Council, traditional prayers, games, contests, story dances, legends, and closing events... how to build a magic fire, how to set up a council ring, how to teach native dance steps, how to make a drum... The authors have had over 70 years' involvement with Indian traditions and ceremonies."

A full instructional manual for staging council ceremonies, sold by the national camping association in 1985, shows the practice was being systematised rather than winding down - which bears on the arc this project traces from Seton's creed reprinted in 1978, an invented legend in 1981, and Ted Perry's screenplay text printed as Chief Seattle's speech in 1983.

Elizabeth Raymer of Camp Tanamakoon, addressing the Ontario Conference in March 1963 and reprinted in Canadian Camping Autumn 1985, lists the five-minute counsellor-training topics a director should be ready with at general staff meetings: "What is leadership. What to do about 'mush mags' and comic books. Why we teach children to be courteous - or tidy, etc. Open your eyes to nature. Vandalism. Homosexuality. Discipline." Recorded exactly as printed; nothing in the source says what the session would have contained.

Elizabeth Raymer on staff evaluation forms, March 1963: "only God Himself could have sufficient insight into human nature and character to fill out some of the evaluation forms that comes to one's notice," and directors should tell supervisors what is useful "to avoid setting up a system which invites the supervisor to hyper-critical observations, and delving into personalities almost to the extent of psychoanalysis. What we need to know really is - is the job being done well?" She also recommends asking staff to "tell all of us what the Psychology Dept. at McGill teaches on this matter."

Janet Adamson reports in Autumn 1985 that the CCA reorganization continued, with a board meeting at Fredericton in October 1985 and Karen O'Neill as the Fitness Canada consultant now taking part in discussions, and the reassurance that "our funding although changing is not disappearing" - a softer account than Jocelyn Palm's of nine months earlier.

The 1985-86 catalogue's new Canadian titles include Doreen Kronick's three learning-disability guides for CACALD/ACETA (1984), each in English and French - Camp Directors' Guide on Integration / Guide d'integration pour Directeurs de Camps, Guide for Directors of Specialized Camps, and Parents' Guide to Camping - the largest single addition of French camp literature in any catalogue in this run.

The SofterWare "EZ-Camp" advertisement in Canadian Camping Autumn 1985, from Fort Washington, Pennsylvania, "the ACA-recognized supplier of computers for camp management," is the first camp-management software advertised anywhere in this run of the magazine.

Correction to the record taken from issue 151: the mailing label there was OCR'd as "MISS JANE MCCUTCHEON, C/O CAMP TANINGU, HUNTSVILLE ON"; the label on the Autumn 1985 copy of the same subscription reads CAMP TAWINGO, which is Jane McCutcheon's camp throughout this run. "Taningu" was an OCR error.

Janet Adamson's tribute in Canadian Camping Vol. 37 No. 4, Winter 1986: "For four and a half years Jay Haddad edited this magazine in a volunteer capacity... Jay is now retiring as editor." Four and a half years back from Winter 1986 places his appointment in the middle of 1981, matching the editorial-board notice found at issue 139.

The CCA executive report in Winter 1986 states: "The Newsletter under the Communications Committee will be the responsibility of a group from Camp Tawingo. This edition of the magazine is a transitional issue. With the Spring issue we will have a 'new look'." From Spring 1986 the magazine is made by a camp rather than by an editor.

Canadian Camping Winter 1986 is twelve pages with no editorial, no letters column, no Camping Advisor and no French translation of the main article - the handover issue between Jay Haddad's editorship and the Camp Tawingo group. The magazine's character changes here for institutional reasons, not editorial ones, and anyone reading the last eight issues of this run needs to know it.

Canadian Camping Winter 1986 prints in both languages: "CELEBRATE CCA's 50th BIRTHDAY WITH AN ADVENTURE INTO THE PAST - 1936-1986. 1986 is the CCA's fiftieth birthday. Your camp can take part in the celebration this summer! All across the country camps will participate by including one or all of the following activities in their programs: historical journeys; re-enactment of early camping lifestyles; ceremonies and theme events. Each participating camp will be recognized with a wall certificate and those camps pre-registering will receive cards for each of their campers."

For the second year running every CCA member camp was asked to put its own past into its summer programme - the International Youth Year "historical roots" kit mailed in early May 1985, then "An Adventure into the Past" in 1986, registered through the provincial associations. The 1986 scheme produced physical objects: a wall certificate for the camp and a printed card for every participating camper. Whether Kanawana registered is not documented and is not assumed.

The 1986 anniversary notice prints "1936-1986" as the span and the French text "le cinquantieme anniversaire de l'ACC" - a further statement of the 1936 dating that the same magazine's reprint of Douglas G. McEwen's 1967 article contradicts.

The "Between the Covers" new-additions list in Canadian Camping Winter 1986 is almost entirely French: "I. SERIE 'UN CAMP A FAIRE' - A) MANUEL DE GESTION: 1. Aspects generaux de l'administration; 2. Gestion des ressources humaines; 3. Gestion des programmes; 4. Gestion des equipements; 5. Gestion financiere. B) 1. Evaluation du rendement; 2. Les objectifs et le programme; 3. La planification des ressources humaines et selection du personnel. II. Les colonies de vacances d'expression francaise en Belgique (communaute Wallonie-Bruxelles) et les camps de vacances au Quebec."

A comparative study of French-language holiday camps in Belgium (Wallonie-Bruxelles) and camps in Quebec was sold through the Canadian Camping Association in 1986 - a description of the Quebec camp sector from outside, previously unknown to this project. Neither its authorship nor its publisher is given in the catalogue entry, and the attribution of the "Un camp a faire" management series to the ACQ or to the Quebec government would be an inference the source does not support.

Gordon C. Allan, Director of Program & Personnel, Camp Nominingue, Quebec, contributes "Dolittle for Camping" to Canadian Camping Winter 1986 - an allegory in which a bored kingdom turns a bequest of one acre, two wooden boats and a pet dragon into a camp, and a boy from the far richer Camp Wakanda, with "seven boats, six pet dragons and lots of neat things," discovers that "it was not the facilities that made a camp great, but the spirit of wanting to do things."

Jan James of Edmonton, who appears earlier in this run as the CCA's secretary, is Vice-President by Winter 1986. Her article on preparing parents of new campers is a fifteen-point list drawn from the Fund for the Advancement of Camping, the ACA, and a 1971 Margaret Mead piece in Redbook, "How Summer Camp Changes a Child."

The CCA committee reorganization is reported nearly complete in Winter 1986: Nancy Barker of Camp Gay Venture chairs Publications, Glenn Barned of New Brunswick the new National Conference and Workshop Committee, and a new promotional pamphlet for parents was to go to the provincial associations in early February 1986. The Youth Science Foundation's Science Is..., "four years in the making," 400 pages in a three-ring binder at $12.75, was to appear in March 1986 - an all-Canadian science activity book for campers aged 7 to 14, field-tested in camps.

The Canadian Wildlife Service's northern-delta poster notice in Canadian Camping Winter 1986 records that "60% of the St. Lawrence River estuary marshes" had been lost to development within three decades, alongside 88% of southern Ontario's wetlands.

The cover of Canadian Camping Vol. 37 No. 4, Winter 1986, is credited "Archives Photo; Sherwood Forest Camp, 1957" - the first time in this run that the magazine put a picture from its own archives on its cover. The mailing label reads MISS JANE MCCUTCHEON, C/O CAMP TAWINGO, R.R. #1, HUNTSVILLE ON.

Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 1, Summer 1986, the 50th anniversary issue, is the first made by the Camp Tawingo group: Jack Pearse editor-in-chief, Jane McCutcheon and John Jorgenson senior editors, Brenda McFarlane and Liz Greenway regional editors, printed by Cober Printing of Kitchener, editorial address R.R. #1, Huntsville.

Adele Ebbs, Taylor Statten's daughter and secretary to the founding circle, interviewed in the CCA's 50th anniversary issue: "CC: Our records show that the OCA became a reality in 1933 and then the CCA became a reality in 1936. Do those dates sound right? AE: '36 sounds early to me but I ... '33 sounds right... CC: I read that your Dad helped with the formation of the Quebec Camping Association along with F. M. VanWagner in 1937. AE: Well that is why I thought the Canadian Camping Association was not until... CC: After that had happened? AE: My impression was that it was 1938. CC: We may be celebrating 50 years under false pretenses, so let's not upset that apple cart. AE: No, 50 years makes it '36. Well, I'll buy that."

The best-placed living witness to the founding of the Canadian Camping Association said in 1986 that the year was wrong and was overruled on the ground that the anniversary was already being celebrated. Her reasoning was specific: she remembered her father helping F. M. Van Wagner form the Quebec Camping Association in 1937 and placed the national body after it. The exchange is printed verbatim under a headnote asserting that Taylor Statten "was the Founder and first President of the Canadian Camping Association" fifty years earlier.

Three different datings of the Canadian Camping Association's founding all come from inside the association: its 1980s literature says 1936; its own president said c.1947 in 1967; its founder's daughter, who kept the minutes, said 1938 in 1986. A 1937 Quebec association and a 1938 national one is the sequence a founding-circle secretary would remember, while 1936 is what the corporate record of a later reorganisation would show.

Adele Ebbs describes the pre-association supper club: "in the early 30's there were regular meetings, mostly social - Edgar, Hamilton, Halliday, Chapman, Cochrane and Statten, those six," gathering in each other's homes "4 or 5 times a year," and "a great deal of it was social and anything they talked about was sort of trivial in a way because they had secrets. Nobody ever knew what anybody paid their staff." The six are Mary S. Edgar of Glen Bernard, Mary G. Hamilton of Camp Tanamakoon, Ferna Halliday of Camp Oconto, Ernie Chapman of Camp Kagawong, A. L. Cochrane of Camp Temagami and Taylor Statten.

Adele Ebbs became secretary to the founding circle and "finally started to take notes sometime before I got married, and that was 1935" - so minutes of the pre-founding meetings exist from about 1934-35. Charles Plewman and the Dansons (Sadie and Joe) joined "very soon after." Of Arnold Ward she notes that "these are private Camp Directors and maybe because Arnold Ward was an agency Camp Director" he was not in it.

The early CCA presidential sequence is given in the 1986 anniversary interview as Taylor Statten, Dais Gass, Anne Vail, Ted Yard, Irv Haladner, F. M. Van Wagner - placing W. E. Ted Yard, whose Pine Crest council ceremony text this project recorded from issue 145, among the first CCA presidents.

The Quebec column of Canadian Camping Summer 1986, in French and English: "La rencontre estivale des directeurs de camp aura lieu cette annee au Camp Trois-Saumons au debut du mois d'aout. A cette occasion, les membres souligneront a nouveau le vingt-cinquieme anniversaire de l'Association des Camps du Quebec. Le regroupement des responsables des camps des communautes anglophone et francophone avait lieu notamment en janvier 1961."

The Quebec association celebrated its twenty-fifth birthday in 1986, dating itself from the January 1961 amalgamation of its French and English sections rather than from the 1937 founding of the English Section. Quebec, like the national association, was running on two datings at once: 1937 is the English Section, 1961 is the bilingual association. The amalgamation is fixed to January 1961 from the association's own mouth, corroborating the provincial charter of that year.

The ACQ's 1986 report in Canadian Camping: "Dans le cadre du programme d'accreditation, quatre consultants visiteront pres de soixante (60) camps de vacances. Ce programme exige que les camps accredites soient visites tous les deux ans. Les camps de vacances qui ont connu des changements majeurs au cours de l'annee (le changement de directeur, par exemple) sont egalement visites." Quebec had moved from annual visitation to a two-year cycle by 1986, worked by four consultants covering about sixty camps.

On the ACQ's stated rule that a camp changing director in a given year is visited regardless of its cycle position, Kanawana should have received an accreditation visit in 1986: its directorship passed from Peter Goddard to Jay Netherwood inside the YMCA of Montreal's FY1986. An ACQ visitation report for Kanawana in 1986 should therefore exist.
The ACQ's 1986 report records a new parents' guide and directory in members' hands that year.

Adele Ebbs on Camp Couchiching, the Toronto Central YMCA camp her father Taylor Statten directed near Orillia: "That Camp Couchiching just stopped and as far as I know it went up to Torrance and became Pine Crest." Camp Couchiching ran as a boys' camp until about 1912; Geneva Park "didn't exist in the Y's eyes until 1908."

Adele Ebbs on the Council Ring: "of course, he [Ernest Thompson Seton] started the Council Ring," and on whether Seton would let Statten preside, "I don't think he would let anyone be Chief except Ernest Thompson Seton." Of Camp Couchiching before 1912: "I don't think there was any Indian influence... There was no Council Ring at Camp Couchiching as far as I know or have any record of or any pictures," and Seton "was later. I don't think he had anything to do with Dad until they were doing the CSET bit."

On Adele Ebbs's account the Council Ring entered Canadian camping after 1912 and by way of Ernest Thompson Seton personally, not out of the YMCA camp tradition to which Kanawana belonged. She names Ellsworth Jaeger and his Camp of the Red Gods as a parallel figure, and describes the ceremony's form: "It was always done very precisely, very organized, and well planned... the beginning and ending were always the same and most inspirational," adding that her father "always loved the theatre and I think this is why the Council Ring, because it was a spectacle."

Adele Ebbs reprints Herbert B. Bell's complete 1926 outfit list for a ten-day Algonquin canoe trip for two - bacon, cheese, flour, rolled oats, dried apples, dried peaches, rice, raisins, macaroni, dried whole milk, butter, carrots, sugar, four loaves of bread, Crisco, coffee, syrup, pepper, baking powder; and for equipment a medical kit, six candles, two small pails, a frying pan, two cups, two knives, three plates, three bowls, two packsacks and a length of rope - with the totals: "Food $11.18, Equipment $6.60, Canoe (rental) $8.00 = $25.78 (approximately $1.25 per person per day)."

The Summer 1986 officer list carries F. M. Van Wagner, Point Claire, Que., as President Emeritus - the founder of the Quebec association's English Section, alive and honoured in 1986 - and Ken Willis, Magog, Que., as Central Vice-President, confirming in a printed officer list the correction made at issue 155.

The CCA's French Language Committee, chaired in 1986 by Gerard Bachand of Rawdon, Quebec, reports "la publication d'un repertoire des camps francophones hors Quebec... rendue possible grace a la collaboration du Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique. Vingt-quatre camps figurent dans la premiere edition" - a 1985 directory of French-language camps outside Quebec, twenty-four in its first edition.
entities: Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique

facts.claim: "Under Open Skies" in Canadian Camping Summer 1986 describes Mary S. Edgar as "an Honourary President of the Canadian Camping Association, and the Founder of Canadian Camping Magazine." This sits beside, and may complicate, Charles Plewman's account that he produced the first bulletin that became the magazine. Recorded as a discrepancy, not resolved: "founder" and "produced the first bulletin" may describe the same thing from two angles.

Camp Tonakela is explained in the 1986 Ebbs interview: Wally Forgie, Taylor Statten's brother-in-law, went to India as a YMCA man after his wife died in Calgary in 1925, broke with the Y because "trying to convert the Indians to Christianity was going to be [no] good at all," and "virtually became a Hindu"; the camp twelve miles from Madras was named Tonakela when Mr and Mrs Statten opened it in 1938, after Mrs Statten's own Ojibway camp name.

Adele Ebbs states that Hedley Dimock came to Camp Ahmek "in the late 20's," and "it was Hedley Dimock that started the TOF - 'the other fellow'," an Ahmek practice that outlasted him; an editor's note dates Talks with Counsellors to 1939.

Taylor Statten was born at Erindale in 1882, left Streetsville High School without graduating, worked in the Post Office, and believed himself related to P. T. Barnum ("the 'T' in Barnum's name stood for Taylor"). Tom Thompson drowned in Canoe Lake in July 1917, helped build the camp fireplace, and Charles Plewman helped carry his casket up the hill; Tom Thompson sketches were borrowed from the National Gallery in 1932 or 1933 and carried up to the Tom Thompson Totem.

The CCA's foreign-counsellor immigration protocol was amended after a meeting with the Hon. Jake Epp, Minister of Health and Welfare, on 22 April 1986: foreign counsellors would get form MS 1017 from the nearest consulate, have their own doctor complete it, and hand it in at the border.

The Second International Camping Congress dates are given as 2-5 March 1987 in Canadian Camping Summer 1986, against 3-5 March in issues 151, 155 and 159 - an internal inconsistency in the source, recorded as such.

Shirley Yard, interviewed in Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 2, Fall 1986, listing her husband W. E. Ted Yard's work: "There was a project of the Boys' Work Committee of the National Council YMCA. It is a survey of costs and factors in Canadian YMCA Camps. This is probably what he did his thesis on when he completed his Master's degree at George Williams College in 1958/59."

A national YMCA survey of costs and factors in Canadian YMCA camps, dated 1958-59, is unlikely to have omitted the YMCA of Montreal's own resident camp. It is the first concrete lead this read has produced to a document that would give Kanawana's late-1950s operating figures from outside the YMCA of Montreal's own files, in a period for which Kanawana's records are a gap.

A second Ted Yard document was still in circulation in 1986: the Ted Yard Camp Director's Calendar, month by month through the year, put together in 1959 during his Masters at George Williams College - "as a matter of fact, it is still in use."

An editor's note in Canadian Camping Fall 1986 states: "At that time, the Quebec Camping Association was the only Provincial Association east of Ontario," describing the period of Ted Yard's CCA presidency (1953-55). The interviewer adds: "up until that time, the President of the Canadian Camping Association was either from Quebec or from Ontario (and even more specifically from Montreal or Toronto) and, shortly after you made your cross-Canada trip, it began that Presidents and Executives and Boards of the Canadian Camping Association were provincially-located."

Montreal was one of the two cities that ran Canadian camping until the mid-1950s, and the deliberate decentralisation that ended that arrangement is dated in the magazine to Ted Yard's cross-Canada trip of 1953-55. Quebec's slow drift from the centre of national affairs through the 1980s is the far end of that decentralisation.

The CCA celebrated a "50th Birthday Party" at its Moncton national workshop in 1986, with cake provided by the New Brunswick Camping Association, and ran a "50th Anniversary Patrons' Fund" through the year. These are the same anniversary Adele Ebbs was told not to upset, not independent witnesses to a 1936 founding.

The full-page notice in Canadian Camping Fall 1986 reads "OUR FRAGILE WORLD - A CHALLENGE FOR THE OUTDOOR COMMUNITY / SECOND INTERNATIONAL CAMPING CONGRESS / March 3-5, 1987 Shoreham Hotel Washington, D.C.", jointly sponsored by the American Camping Association, the Canadian Camping Association, the Jamaica Camping and Hiking Association and the National Camping Association of Japan. The Canadian contributors named are Dorothy Walter, Jack Pearse, Fred Okada, Jocelyn Palm and Rob Heming - no Quebec name among them.

Shirley Yard on Indian Lore at Camp Pine Crest under her husband's direction, 1946-1963: "Only a Council fire once a week, if it was even that... not that people don't respect the Indian... but he felt that we should not make a big thing out of Indian Lore by imitating them but by celebrating with them. This was a different sort of concept... that he didn't want to play up an Indian theme as such." The family camp took a Coast Salish place name from British Columbia rather than an "Indian name": "there again was another reason why we didn't call our Camp an Indian name."

Ted Yard Jr. on the practice as it stood in 1986: "even when we do our Indian Councils now, we are actually teaching them what the ceremony is because it is a very serious thing we do. From what I remember of Pine Crest, it was very much like that." The Pine Crest ceremony itself: "their most vivid memory is of Dad coming across in a canoe standing up being paddled by his Medicine Man coming to the Council Ring," in costume, unrecognised even by his own children, and "there were only three campfires for the three periods."

The same issue that prints Ted Yard's objection to imitative Indian Lore also prints an unattributed Council Closing and a set of inter-tribal gift speeches - Onondaga to Seneca, Cayuga to Onondaga, Tuscarora to Oneida, Oneida to Cayuga, Mohawk to Tuscarora - written for campers to deliver in the persona of the six nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy ("We the people of the Onondaga tribe offer this table to you the people of the Seneca tribe"). The magazine prints the objection and the practice objected to in the same twenty-eight pages, without comment on either.

Shirley Yard on why Camp Hollyburn took both sexes: "the reason it was a Boys' and Girls' Camp as against a Boys' Camp... was because of our daughter Judy and me... Ted was adamant about making the distinction between what was a co-ed camp and what was a Boys' and Girls' Camp. He felt that boys want to be boys and girls want to be girls, but the family idea, there would be enough mixing naturally in a Camp setting without calling it Co-ed." She credits the Family YMCA at Sault Ste. Marie as the other influence.

The ACQ's 1986 summer report records that Employment and Immigration Canada funded a three-person team that spent the summer reclassifying all of the ACQ's archives and camp dossiers. This is the summer that determined the present shape of the ACQ's own archive.

The ACQ's 1986 report names its three accreditation consultants - Leo Venditti, Yves Legault and Louis Jean - who visited 76 camps, four of them new members. Jean-Marc Amyot of the R.L.Q.'s audio-visual service shot 400 slides at Quebec camps for a bilingual slide show. A pamphlet produced with the M.L.C.P. promoting outdoor-education classes was printed in 50,000 French and 8,000 English copies and sent in September to every school principal and pedagogical consultant in the province.

The CCA's French-language commission reports in Fall 1986 the launch of the second edition of the Repertoire de l'Inventaire des Camps d'Expression francaise (INCEF), with M. Jean-Luc Cote of the Conseil de la Vie Francaise en Amerique, 59 rue d'Auteuil, Quebec G1R 4C2, gathering the data, and names as its next step "elaborer notre politique linguistique pour l'Association des Camps du Canada." A new committee member, M. Michel Gratton of Hearst, Ontario, gives the committee "two 'out-of-Quebec' members."
entities: Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique

facts.claim: The CCA's 50th Anniversary Patrons' Fund appeal, over the names of Janet Adamson (President) and Jack Pearse (Chairman, CCA/ACC Patrons' Foundation), repeats an April 1986 letter: "An additional income of $30,000.00, this year, represents the difference between a giant step forward and an irretrievable step backward... We are sending this plea to approximately 100 people." Two years after the Fitness Canada withdrawal, the national association was passing the hat among a hundred camp directors to cover an operating shortfall.

The CCA National Workshop at Moncton, 1-5 October 1986, was led for its first two days by Bob Latimer, a trainer from the National Training Institute (no relation established to John R. Latimer). Delegates worked on Dorothy Walter's Curriculum for Camp Directors, built "three sample prototype workshops" for provincial associations, spent a day on volunteer board development, and attended Michael Brandwein's sessions at the First Regional Conference held in Eastern Canada as a training exercise in delivery style. It closed with "A contract was produced which the delegates were asked to sign along with the President of CCA."

A proposal was taken up at the October 1986 CCA workshop "to ask the Executive of CCA to produce a certificate to acknowledge a Camp Director's completion of, or attendance at, training" - the certification question traced in this run since 1982, reappearing as a certificate for attendance rather than a licence to practise.

Camp Pine Crest under W. E. Ted Yard, 1946-1963, went from a camp "subsidized because it had just gone through the war years and things were not in good shape either financially or physically" to a self-supporting Branch of the Toronto YMCA that "paid all the salaries, it re-built... all paid out of the operation." A photo caption reads: "The 'new' winter lodge at Camp Pine Crest and some of the earliest winter camping in Canada." His last summer there ran 85 staff and 210 campers; Camie Cameron ran Pine Crest for about twelve years afterwards.

Sass Peepre came to Canada and to Camp Pine Crest in 1950 speaking no English, was taught by Ted Yard an hour a day, and "introduced orienteering to North America... back in the late 50's."
