Kirk Wipper learned to paddle a canoe at Pine Crest - "when Kirk first came to Pine Crest I don't think many people know that he couldn't paddle a canoe at all." John Wadland wrote his doctoral thesis on Ernest Thompson Seton because Yard, a Seton collector, lent him the books while he was a Pine Crest counsellor.

W. E. Ted Yard's dates as given in the 1986 profile: born 1919, died 1983; memorial service at Camp Hollyburn, Rosseau, 15 January 1983; Vancouver YMCA work from about 1941-42; UBC degree about 1945; Camp Pine Crest 1946-1963; General Secretary, Sault Ste. Marie Family YMCA 1963-1967, where he supervised the building of "the first Family Y in Canada" (opened 1964, cornerstone laid by Lester Pearson); Camp Hollyburn 1968-1982; OCA President 1950-52 and Treasurer 1971-74; CCA President 1953-55. He also surveyed YMCA Camp Stephens for Don Phelan, who "went to Winnipeg YMCA in 1962." He was "by far the most prolific writer for the CANADIAN CAMPING MAGAZINE."

Janet Adamson's "A Pioneer Centre" describes the log-cabin museum at Camp Gay Venture, whose fourth component is a Camp Archival Collection - "old camp photos, crests, brochures, letters, manuals... displayed in one area of the cabin for campers to browse through... this collection grows as former campers and staff donate items," so that a camper can "look for a picture of their mother in the photo collection." This is a 1986 statement of what a camp of this movement expected its own historical record to be and where it expected it to live.

Canadian Camping's subscription terms as printed in Fall 1986: published four times yearly, non-member subscription $8.00/year, single issue $2.00, submission deadlines 1 October, 1 December, 15 February and 1 May, editorial office R.R. #1, Huntsville, Ontario P0A 1K0. A standing offer is printed: "If you would like to receive a complete English translation of any article in Canadian Camping Magazine, send a stamped self addressed envelope" - and the same in reverse for French. The French-language material in this run was therefore not systematically translated, and the two columns are not always the same text.

Ken Willis, C.C.A./A.C.C. Vice-President (Quebec Region), in the Quebec column of Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 3, Winter 1987: "The organized camping movement in Quebec was born in 1938. Tony Shorgun, who has been involved in camping during many of the intervening years, is already at work laying plans for the 50th Anniversary of this birth which, obviously, will be held next year."

A fourth date now exists for the origin of Kanawana's provincial association: 1937 from the archival holdings and Alta Kahn's 1958 coming-of-age party; 1958 for the French section; January 1961, used by the ACQ itself in 1986 for its twenty-fifth; and 1938, from the Quebec seat on the national board in 1987, with a fiftieth anniversary being planned around it for 1988. The date was the premise of an event, not a slip in a column.

Adele Ebbs dated the national association to 1938 because her father helped form the Quebec association in 1937; Ken Willis dated Quebec camping itself to 1938. The two recollections cannot both be right in the way each was offered, and between them they show that the 1937/1938 boundary was genuinely unclear to the people who were there.

If a 50th anniversary of Quebec camping was held in 1988 as planned, it would have produced a programme, a press notice or a commemorative publication assembled by Tony Shorgun - a name new to this project. Such a document would be a history of Quebec camping written by a participant, and Kanawana would be in it.

Kelley Byrne, President of the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and Director of Big Cove YMCA Camp, writes in Canadian Camping Winter 1987 under the heading "A TRIBUTE TO THE OLDEST CAMP IN CANADA!": "The Maritime YMCA, based in Truro, held the first Maritime Boys' Camp in 1891. This Camp quickly became an annual event, and the area of Big Cove in Pictou County became the gathering grounds for large numbers of boys and men." The French summary reads: "Big Cove Camp en Nouvelle Ecosse etait etabli en 1891 par le Y.M.C.A. de Pictou County."

The founding date of Canada's oldest camp now has three values in this project's records - 1889 from Big Cove's encyclopaedic entry, 1890 from Jack Pearse speaking to the Nova Scotia association in 1979, and 1891 from the camp's own director and the province's association president writing a commemorative history in 1987. None is preferred here, and Kanawana's position as Canada's second-oldest camp is unaffected by any of them: 1894 follows all three.

Byrne's 1987 tribute to Big Cove YMCA Camp records: floorless bell tents pitched on the grassy hills overlooking Merigomish Harbour; the site "officially became known as Big Cove YMCA Camp" and passed to the Halifax YMCA about 1905; girls came in 1939, and the first building - a dining hall - was put up for them; about 100 boys per session, with "particular emphasis... on providing spaces for underprivileged youths"; support from the Halifax Y's Men's Club and New Glasgow Gyro Club; a ten-day Girls Camp in 1961 that became regular sessions; closed in 1976 for want of repairs and reopened in 1980.

Big Cove YMCA Camp's traditional pageants in 1987 include "Indian Ceremonial Night", described as still running, and "Our Voyageur program dates back to this time [the late 1940s], challenging older youth to develop expert outtripping, canoeing, axemanship and woodcraft skills." A YMCA camp in Nova Scotia adopting a Voyageur programme in the late 1940s is the same decade in which Kanawana took up the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition in 1947. Nothing connects the two beyond the YMCA; the coincidence of date and idiom is recorded, not explained.

John Gilchrist on Mary S. Edgar and the influence of Pauline Johnson, in Canadian Camping Winter 1987: "Pauline Johnson's type of writing inspired Mary to write legends, Indian legends of her own, built around Lake Bernard and the tribes of Glen Bernard which, in fact, were make-believe but she made them sound the real thing in her story." Of the storytelling bench in her cabin: "How many of them were her own fertile imagination or she had read about was hard to say."

The Gilchrist testimony is a camp legend's own manufacturers describing the process in print and naming the effect they were after. It says nothing about Kanawana's Chopsy legend, but it removes a step from the argument: the default assumption for an undated camp legend of this period should be deliberate authorship dressed as tradition, because that is what a documented practitioner says she was doing.

Barbara Gilchrist describes the handover of the Glen Bernard directorship at the last Council Ring of the summer of 1955: Mary Edgar "had been corresponding with Dawendini, the daughter of the Chief of the Mohawks in Brantford, and received the recommendation that Yehjenhiosta meant 'she who takes over someone else's job or she who keeps the fire burning brightly'." Edgar's own council-ring name had been Ogimaqua, given as Ojibwa for "Friend of Children"; Gilchrist used Yehjenhiosta "twice each Saturday night from our first year 1956 through to our last year."

Consulting a named Indigenous person about the meaning of a name before taking it, as Mary Edgar did in 1955, is a third position alongside Ted Yard's refusal of an Indigenous name and Jack Eastaugh's 1973 defence of Indian Lore. It appears in the same interview as the make-believe legends and as Edgar learning "the customs of the Indians... and the peace pipe... and initiations and challenges" on "her trips west" and introducing them into the Council Ring - consultation and invention in the same programme, from the same person.

The Glen Bernard Council Ring in operating detail: two rings on the same night - juniors at seven in a hollow, seniors at eight in the natural glen - every Saturday for eight weeks; senior campers elected as Chiefs by their fellow campers, "given reference books to refer to, to learn of the various tribes in North America," each choosing a tribe name, colour scheme, tribal song and yell in the first day or two of camp; an initiation Council Ring, then weekly ones, with "the whole Camp program built around tribal events" and a winning tribe announced at the end of the summer. The opening liturgy was John Oxenham's "Kneel always when you light a fire, kneel reverently and grateful be." That is Kanawana's own structure - elected chiefs, named tribes, season-long inter-tribal competition - in a girls' private camp in Ontario, and the two are not known to be connected.

The CCA masthead changed between Fall 1986 and Winter 1987: the three regional vice-presidencies (Eastern, Western, Central) became four - Eastern (Ian Fowler), Western (Jan James), Quebec (Ken Willis) and Ontario (Sally Moore, newly appointed). Quebec is no longer half of a "central" region shared with Ontario but a named seat on the national executive in its own right.

Ken Willis on the ACQ at the start of 1987: "The A.C.Q. has, over the past years, received very significant funding from the Provincial Government. The degree of this funding has been reduced somewhat over the past couple of years and the A.C.Q. now expects there will be significant cut backs due to the financial condition of the Government." Members "will be expected to contribute much more of their time... or they will have to dig further into their pockets."

ACQ membership is given as "holding well at about 110" at the start of 1987 - against 117 in 1983 and 129 in 1982 - "with a few being dropped each year because they do not meet standards and a few new ones being added," and the board "each year agonizes over a few camps which seem careless about the paperwork involved in meeting standards."

The cover photograph of Canadian Camping Winter 1987 is captioned "taken at a Canadian Camping Association Conference at Banff, Alberta in February, 1963," adding a month to the 1963 Banff annual meeting at which the affiliation-formula question was first raised. Jocelyn Palm's 1985 list of national conferences ("1972, 1973, 1975 and 1978" before the 1983 Congress) should therefore be read as post-reorganisation conferences, not as the complete series; the Edgar interview independently mentions a CCA Conference at Geneva Park in 1973.

The Winter 1987 cover key names eleven office-holders photographed in 1963: Dr. J. Harry Ebbs (first President, Society of Camp Directors); Adele Ebbs (President OCA, President Society of Camp Directors, Chair CCA Archives Committee); June Labbett (President Soc. Camp Dirs., Chair OCA Education Cte.); May Brown (President CCA, President BCCA); Cliff Labbett (President, VP and Treasurer CCA; President and Treasurer OCA; President Soc. Camp Dirs.); John Gilchrist (VP and Treasurer OCA, President Soc. Camp Dirs.); Barb Gilchrist (President OCA, CCA board, Chair OCA Archives Cte.); Lorne Brown (President BCCA, first President of the BC Outdoor Educators, Chair CCA Nature Lore Cte.).

Mary S. Edgar's route into camping, from the Winter 1987 profile: "it was her background in the YWCA when she was introduced to camping at YWCA Camp Oolahwan in Quebec. That was her first taste of Camping" - and she came to it already trained, having "took training for girls' work in the Y in New York," not as a camper. The Quebec YWCA camp that visited Kanawana repeatedly through the 1940s is therefore where the first editor of Canadian Camping and Honorary President of the CCA learned the work.

Further details of Mary S. Edgar from the Winter 1987 profile: her father was a Sundridge general merchant who supplied the lumber mills, was eventually MPP for Parry Sound District, and bought the lumber for the first cabins; all four Edgar daughters were educated at Havergal College; Glen Bernard opened in 1922 with "about 30" campers ("under 40... but over 30") against the 38 this project records, and more than doubled in year two; the property, an abandoned farm, grew to 590 acres; Mary Northway was one of her earliest campers; the fireplaces were built by Angus Buchanan, a Sundridge stone mason; the New Lodge went up in 1932 (builder Hugo Grimm) and the new Dining Room in 1966, with a bronze plaque carrying her motto "The best of each for the good of all."

Mary S. Edgar handed Glen Bernard to the Gilchrists at the last Council Ring of 1955; they ran it from 1956; and Jocelyn Palm - who "came recommended from Dais Gass' Memphremagog," a Quebec camp, and whose predecessor as CCA president Gass had been - succeeded them about 1977. Edgar's world tour with her parents was in 1921; her Sundridge park at High Rock, five and a half acres bought with stock-market money and landscaped at her expense, was her 1967 Centennial project, given to the town of Sundridge and Strong Township; and she received the Centennial Medal on 9 March 1968 at the Ontario Camping Association's closing banquet, the citation read by Dr. Mary L. Northway.

Two documented disagreements about Mary S. Edgar's bibliography, recorded and not resolved: the Winter 1987 "Under Open Skies" attribution line dates Under Open Skies to 1955 (Clarke, Irwin & Company) where this project records 1956 from her fonds description; and the same feature calls her "author of three delightful, inspirational books" where this project records four, adding The Christmas Wreath of Verse (1967).

The music for "God Who Touchest Earth With Beauty" was written by Magistrate James Edmund Jones, founder of the Aura-Lee Boys' Club, whose cottage was on Lake Bernard; the hymn was translated into many languages, and in Japanese the pine had to be replaced by a straight tree. A second Edgar hymn is printed with music by Jack Pearse (copyright 1979 Jack Pearse Limited), "God of the night, the stars, the skies."

John Gilchrist, independently of Adele Ebbs, names the same six founders: "she was in with the founding fathers... I should mention the six of them. There was Taylor Statten, Ferna Halliday, A. L. Cochrane, Mary Hamilton, Ernie Chapman... and Mary S. Edgar. They got together and decided they wanted to form a Camping Association as a vehicle where they could exchange ideas and learn things from one another." The interviewer supplies: "That was the Ontario Camping Association. Taylor Statten was the first President, in 1933," and Edgar the second, in 1939.

The "founding circle" of six that Adele Ebbs described as a social supper club whose secretary she became is, on John Gilchrist's independent testimony, the founding group of the Ontario Camping Association in 1933 - not of the national association. Whatever happened nationally in 1936, 1938 or 1947 is a separate act, which removes one source of confusion from the founding-date question.

Barry Lowes's immigration committee report in Winter 1987 records that a new requirement of "a Medical Examination for all foreign camp counsellors" disrupted the protocol in 1986; a personal meeting with Jake Epp, Minister of Health and Welfare, in early May got it amended, and a November meeting in Ottawa simplified it further. "Hiring foreign camp counsellors is a privilege granted, not a right of Canadian camps." The liaison at Employment and Immigration is named as Rick Morrison.

Bruno Morawetz reports in Winter 1987 that the provincial associations were asked to send newsletters, minutes and notices to Trent "in order that they would constitute a permanent record of camping in Canada during 1986," and that the archivist Mrs. Bernadine Dodge "has received several of the brown envelopes commonly known as the 'Brown Bag'." He adds that "some Provincial Associations have their own archives where they collect printed material about their member camps and it is hoped that before long all Provincial Associations will establish their own archives committees." The committee's framing: "It has always been difficult to make people aware that the events of today will form an interesting piece of history in two or three decades."

With the ACQ's 1986 archive reclassification recorded at issue 159 and the CCA archives chairman's 1987 note that some provincial associations keep their own archives, there are two independent reasons to ask the Quebec association what it holds rather than only Trent.

Over one hundred Canadians were expected at the Washington congress of March 1987, every province represented, with a reception at the Canadian Embassy; the printed programme lists the Canadian sessions, and no Quebec presenter appears among the nineteen. Janet Adamson planned visits to British Columbia in March, Newfoundland in April and Quebec in May 1987. The French Language Committee would present "a first copy of the language policies of the CCA/ACC" at the January meeting and send a needs questionnaire to identified French-language camps early in 1987; INCEF 87, the second edition, was in production.

Camp Oconto's dining hall burned at about 5:45 a.m. on 24 June 1986, three days before camp opened; the Wilsons' account of feeding 300 people from rented ATCO trailers, with the Army supplying stoves, tables and chairs, is the most detailed camp-crisis document in this run. Lisa Wilson is the daughter of June and Cliff Labbett. Camp Cheboygan, on the south shore of Skeleton Lake, Muskoka, lost its lodge to fire on the evening of 25 August 1937; the Archives Committee was appealing for information about it and its director Blyth Thomas.

The contents page of Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 4, Spring 1987, lists "BETWEEN THE COVERS - Nancy Barker" and the OCR of the Internet Archive scan contains no such section: page 7 produced no machine-readable text. Nothing is known about the page beyond its title and author. This is a gap in the tool, not an absence in the record.

Canadian Camping Spring 1987 reports the result of the CCA's 50th Anniversary Patrons' Fund appeal for $30,000: "To date, the donations total $11,918.11" - forty per cent of the target, from a list of fifty-five individuals and eighteen camps, printed in full.

Every one of the eighteen camps that gave to the CCA's 50th Anniversary Patrons' Fund is Ontarian - Canadian Adventure, Gay Venture, Haliburton Hockey Haven, Kawabi, New Moon, Oconto, Robin Hood, Tanamakoon, Tawingo, the Taylor Statten Camps, Trailfinder, Wahanowin, White Pine, YMCA Wanakita among them. No Quebec camp appears, and no camp from any province west or east of Ontario. A national appeal sent to about a hundred people produced money from the private Ontario camps and from individual officers elsewhere, but not one institutional gift from a Quebec camp.

Six of the individual donors to the 1987 Patrons' Fund are Quebec names or Quebec-connected: Gerard Bachand of Rawdon, chairman of the French Language Committee; Maurice Blaquiere; Jacqueline Lavoie; Dr. Ken Willis of Magog, the Quebec vice-president; Peter & F. M. Van Wagner of Pointe-Claire, the President Emeritus; and Eileen Mayotte - the QCA secretary of the 1940s, here alive, findable and giving money in 1987, which is the latest fixed point this project has for her.

Canadian Camping issue 159 printed an unattributed "Council Closing" for camper delivery - "May the Peace of the Forest, / The Song of the Birds, / The Inspiration of the Hills, / The Warmth of the Sun, / The Strength of the Trees, / The Fragrance of the Flowers, / The Joy of the Wind, / The Calm of the Lake, / In All of Which is the Creator of Good Things be in Your Hearts Tonight and Always."

Two issues later, "Under Open Skies" prints "A BENEDICTION", submitted by Madelene Allen, Camp Ouareau, St. Donat, Quebec: "May the Silence of the hills, / The Joy of the wind, / The Music of the birds, / The Fire of the sun, / The strength of the trees, / And the Faith of youth, / In all of which is God, / Be in our hearts / Now and evermore." Same construction, same closing turn, different nouns and a different name for God. Neither text is attributed to an author.

The two benedictions printed two issues apart in Canadian Camping are a camp liturgy circulating orally and being written down in variants - one an anonymous council-ring text, the other from a named director of a Quebec girls' camp forty minutes from Kanawana. This is the first time in this read that the same formula has been caught twice in different words, and it shows the Quebec end of the circulation.

The Second International Camping Congress at Washington, March 1987, drew 1,700 delegates from sixteen to eighteen countries, over 150 CCA members of whom 27 presented, 160-plus exhibitors and 73 sessions on the Tuesday alone. Opening night featured Nancy Reagan, T. N. Kaul giving the Otto Rosahn Memorial Lecture, and Up With People; the Canadian reception was at the residence of Ambassador Allan Gotlieb. Alberta reported 27 delegates and the Atlantic provinces 18.

"Camping From Coast To Coast" in the Washington congress issue of Canadian Camping has no Quebec entry: Atlantic, New Brunswick, Ontario, Nova Scotia, Alberta and British Columbia file reports and Quebec does not, in the issue devoted to the largest international gathering the movement had held. This is a null result and does not establish that no Quebec delegates attended.

The International Camping Fellowship was founded at the Washington congress of March 1987. Delegates from the USA, Canada, Jamaica, Japan, India, Australia, England, Ghana, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Bermuda, Kenya, Israel, Belgium and the People's Republic of China adopted a five-point agreement presented by Tom Slater of Australia: to coordinate internationally and facilitate exchanges; to evaluate direction within two years; to ask the ACA to produce an international newsletter, first copy deadline 1 June; to ask the ACA to convene five or six delegates within twelve months; and "to do these things under the name of the International Camping Fellowship." The CCA - Kanawana's national association - is one of the two hosts.

Gerard Bachand's committee note in Canadian Camping Spring 1987: "Des la fin janvier nous publiions la deuxieme edition du repertoire des camps d'expression francaise, hors Quebec (Incef '87), et ce grace au Conseil de la Vie Francaise en Amerique et du Ministre des Affaires Intergouvernementales. Des exemplaires sont disponibles au bureau de l'ACC/CCA a Toronto." A mini-survey of the INCEF camps was under way to identify their needs.
entities: Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique

facts.claim: Bachand also reports: "Nous avons aussi elabore une politique linguistique pour l'ACC/CCA afin de nous rendre conformes aux lois du bilinguisme des organismes nationaux," with a translation policy attached for Board approval by spring. The Canadian Camping Association acquired a formal language policy only in 1987 - thirteen years after founding a French Language Committee in autumn 1974 and sixteen after taking its bilingual name in 1971 - and did so to comply with federal bilingualism requirements on national organisations rather than on its own initiative.

Bruno Morawetz reports in Canadian Camping Spring 1987 that "in February of this year a letter was sent to all Provincial Archives Chairmen, or to the Provincial President concerning the collection of material for C.C.A./A.C.C. Archives at Trent University," instructing: "I would urge your member camps to collect as much written material as possible and have it lodged in your own provincial archives... One of the ways of collecting archival material is to interview persons who are playing important roles in camping - these too can be lodged and catalogued in an archival collection."

A letter went to the Quebec association in February 1987 asking it to gather its camps' records and to tape its people. With the ACQ's own archive reclassification of summer 1986 and Morawetz's note that some provincial associations already hold their own archives, that is a third documented prompt in eighteen months for Quebec camping records to be assembled somewhere other than Trent.

Shannon Etkin of the Family Service Association of Metropolitan Toronto, writing on quality assurance in Canadian Camping Spring 1987: "In a recent court case, one of my camp staff was accused by a mother of physically assaulting her son... The proceedings took a year before the judge threw the case out saying it was based on pure fabrications. One crucial part of the evidence that led the judge to his decision was based on the camp providing detailed documentation showing its hiring and training procedures, supervisory system and written policies and practices. We also had to show that management enforced its rules." This is a dated, concrete statement of the institutional reason camps of this period kept personnel records.

Nancy Reagan's opening address to the Washington congress is printed in full in Canadian Camping Spring 1987: a camper at "Camp Katchewa" run by "the three Ross sisters," every summer from about age nine "until the age limit forced me to stop," sleeping in tents, brushing teeth with salt water, and expert at removing leeches; her message is self-esteem, quoting Martin Luther King Jr., "First teach them to believe in themselves."

Canadian Camping began taking commercial advertising again in Spring 1987 "for the first time in some time," and adopted a "look back to look forward" policy of reprinting each new advertiser's own item from thirty years earlier - here Starkman Chemists' advertisement from the April 1957 issue beside its 1987 successor, and a Tandy Leather advertisement noting the company had been "in the camp craft business for over 60 years."

The CCA's Curriculum for Camp Directors was printed in binders and delivered on the eve of the Ontario conference in January 1987, distribution to the provinces beginning at once; Nova Scotia's May conference at Camp Hillis was built around it. The Ontario-Belgium counsellor exchange with Jeunesse et Sante, an International Youth Year project run with the Ontario Ministry of Tourism and Recreation, sent twelve Belgian counsellors to six Ontario camps in July 1986 and eleven Ontario counsellors to Belgium in August.

Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 1, Summer 1987, dates YM-YWCA Camp Stephens on the Lake of the Woods to 1891 in two separate items: "Y.M.-Y.W.C.A. Camp Stephens has been providing resident camping experiences for youth since 1891. It is one of the oldest resident camps in North America and has been continuously operated by the Y.M.C.A. of Winnipeg... Camp Stephens is looking forward to celebrating its 100th anniversary in 1991"; and "Originally known in 1891 as the Lake of the Woods Institute, the Y.M.C.A. Camp Stephens took its present name in 1896. G. F. Stephens, a successful businessman and the founder of the Stephens Paint Co., was a long time member and President of Winnipeg Y.M.C.A."

If Camp Stephens has run since 1891, this project's assertion in three places that Kanawana, founded 1894, is "Canada's second-oldest camp, after Big Cove (1889)" is wrong: Kanawana would be third at best. The difficulty is sharper than a stranger's claim, because this project already carries a conflicting date for the same camp from a Kanawana founder - T. Duncan Patton's memoir gives his first visit to the Lake of the Woods islands as July 1894, "and from that date on camps were promoted and held annually," with the islands passing to the Winnipeg YMCA only in 1907.

The Camp Stephens dating is two documented sources from inside the same institution, three years apart: the camp's own directors writing in the national magazine in 1987 and planning a centenary around 1891, and T. Duncan Patton writing about the Winnipeg association he served and giving 1894. The 1891 "Lake of the Woods Institute" may have been a conference-and-encampment for men rather than a children's resident camp, which would reconcile them, but nothing in either source says so and the reconciliation is not asserted here. Opened as conflict c_031.

Three of the four candidate dates for "Canada's oldest camp" now cluster on 1889-1891 - Big Cove at 1889, 1890 or 1891, and Camp Stephens at 1891 - and Kanawana's 1894 sits behind all of them. What is not in doubt is that Kanawana is Quebec's first residential summer camp and among the oldest in Canada; the "second-oldest" claim has been qualified rather than restated.

Wendell White, Director of Camp Quin-Mo-Lac, writing in Canadian Camping Summer 1987 as someone "relatively active in native affairs for seventeen years" and describing a United Church camp theme built around the church's "Dialogue with Native Peoples" mandate: "The immediate concern became - How do you create a sense of appreciation and understanding of a contemporary people while at the same time be sensitive to the subtle and not too subtle stereotypes?... no child would leave camp without hearing or seeing, that native peoples in 1986, do not live in a tipi, nor do they wear a head dress or moccasins every day."

Wendell White, 1987: "What concerns me... is that, so often native programs begin and end at the traditional level. Native programs, innocently, often fall short of establishing native people in the twentieth century and consequently build upon the imagery of the noble purist conservationist, captured in a vacuum, more comfortable with the past than with the present." He dates his exasperation to "the recent lack of success at the First Ministers Conference on Aboriginal Rights (March 1987, the last of four such conferences)." He proposes a method rather than an abolition: "One of the first ways to achieve this is by first inviting a native person to your training week to discuss nativeness."

White's 1987 critique is the fourth and last position on camp "Indian programming" that this run of the magazine supplies - after Jack Eastaugh's 1973 defence, Ted Yard's 1950s restraint and Mary Edgar's invented legends - and the only one that names the problem as stereotyping. Fourteen years after Eastaugh answered "I think not" to the minstrel-show comparison, a serving camp director says in the same magazine that the programme as usually run leaves campers believing Indigenous people live in the past.

The same article prints "Sweet Grass and Candle," words by Rev. John W. Oldham, music by R. Henry Kilborn and Oldham, written 26 March 1987 after a joint Roman Catholic-Protestant service attended by native and non-native people "to pray for recognition of native rights."

The CCA Board of Management and President's Council held their annual meeting in Quebec City on 1-3 May 1987, the ACQ hosting, with visits arranged to the Camp Keno headquarters office (Marist Fathers, chemin Saint-Louis) and to Camp Oasis Notre-Dame (lac Simon, comte de Portneuf), where Pere Paul Belanger, a former CCA Vice-President, greeted the President's Council. Colette Pouliot-Marier reports the ACQ "very pleased to report an increase in its members' participation." Quebec had not hosted the national body in the whole span this read covers from 1983 onward, and did so in the same year it gained a vice-presidency of its own.

The ACQ's own annual colloque of 2-5 April 1987 was held at the Base de plein air La Vigie, lac Saint-Joseph, comte de Portneuf, under the theme "Demain... c'est maintenant," with more than 125 camp directors, cadres and moniteurs attending. This Lac Saint-Joseph is not the Laurentian lake of the same name where Camp Jubilee began in 1894; the names coincide and the places do not.

The "Changes!!" notice in Canadian Camping Summer 1987: "We welcome Gerard Bachand as Vice-President for Quebec. To retiring Quebec VP, Ken Willis, we offer a thank you for a job very well done over the past six years. The CCA/ACC Certificate of Honour that Ken received is indeed very well deserved." That fixes Willis's national tenure at roughly 1981-1987. Colette Pouliot-Marier of Quebec City takes the French Language committee chair from Bachand, so both Quebec seats are held by Quebec people and the French Language chair sits in Quebec City rather than Rawdon.

Fitness Canada returned to the CCA in 1987 with project money rather than operating money: "PARC STANDS FOR PHYSICAL [ACTIVITY] RESPONSIBILITY CENTRE, so named by Fitness Canada. Through PARC, and our new PARC employee, Aniko Varpalotai, the CCA/ACC plans to take an active leadership role in increasing the quality and quantity of physical activity in Canadian Camps," under five headings - Awareness, Leadership, Programs, Network, Management. Fitness Canada also "received, reviewed and applauded" the Curriculum for Camp Directors and had funded its printing.

After the November 1984 withdrawal of its operating grant, the national camping association survived by becoming a delivery agent for a federal programme rather than a body with its own funded staff. This is the shape of the settlement reached by 1987.

Mary L. Northway died 26 February 1987. Jocelyn Palm's memorial records that she "attended Northway Lodge, Camp Wapomeo, and Glen Bernard Camp"; founded Windy Pine, a canoe-tripping camp, with Flora Morrison; took an MA at Toronto, studied at Cambridge, returned for a PhD; lectured for many years at the Institute of Child Study and on retirement founded the Brora Centre; and received an honorary doctorate from Trent in 1979. Windy Pine was deeded to Trent University in 1983.

Jocelyn Palm's 1987 memorial states of Mary Northway: "She established the OCA Research Committee and also engineered the collection and organization of the OCA and CCA Archives now at Trent University." Her gift funded the Neathern Trust.

Jocelyn Palm records in 1987: "In 1981, I interviewed Dr. Northway in order that the tape could be added to the CCA Archives. I have just listened to that tape..." A 1981 Palm-Northway interview tape exists in the CCA fonds at Trent, and Palm was still able to play it in 1987. Northway's advice to Palm on taking over Glen Bernard: "You'll get lots of advice on how to run the camp and here's mine... Do your own thing."

Armand Ball, executive vice-president of the American Camping Association, keynoting the January 1987 OCA conference and printed in full in Canadian Camping Summer 1987, lists what changed in camping over 1977-87: a dramatic drop in the camper-age population followed by a mini baby boom, forcing diversification into adults, seniors and disease-specific weeks; agencies closing camps ("we had five camps and then three"); private camps sold for lakefront development; camper fees roughly doubled in ten years; sessions shortened; insurance tripling and quadrupling in one to two years, at "$1600 for horse insurance per horse," with rappelling, trampolines and ropes courses becoming uninsurable; 35% of children not living with both biological parents; day camps roughly doubling; a 25% shrinkage in the young-adult population making international staff "25% or more" in many camps; year-round schooling; and referral agencies taking 10-15% of fees.

Armand Ball on child abuse, January 1987: "it exists in camps, it always has... I think we have always dealt with that issue, those of us who have faced it in camp in the past, we have dealt with it as honestly and as humanely and as well as we could given the circumstances of the situation. But that was a different age, today we don't have that freedom. Because suddenly in our country every state requires the reporting of such an incident to a state body." He reports an award of "a quarter of a million dollars for one child that has been allegedly abused in a camp situation," that "most insurance policies in our country today will not cover sexual abuse in a camp setting," and an ACA crisis hotline run for two summers.

Armand Ball on the second-order effect, January 1987: "We have children getting off the camp bus at camp and saying to the camp counsellor 'Don't you touch me'... an arm around the shoulder or a hug or walking with a child along the path and talking becomes a very precarious situation for a counsellor." Ball repeatedly warns his Canadian audience that this is the American picture and not to assume it applies, but it is the fullest account in this run of why camp record-keeping and camp physical practice changed in the 1980s, and it dates the change.

Over 400,000 children and youth were expected in CCA camps in the summer of 1987. A CCA/ACC National Conference was announced for 1989, though the magazine itself stops in 1988. The magazine's price rose from $8.00 to $10.00 a year and from $2.00 to $3.00 an issue, and an ISSN appears for the first time: 0834325.

Canadian Camping Summer 1987 prints "Francophones... a l'aide" - a direct appeal for French copy: "Nous voulons savoir, en francais, ce qui ce passe chez-vous," with the standing offer to translate any article on request.

A new CCA publication, "Exploring Environmental Change," co-authored by Jan James, comprises five illustrated panels showing the same lakeside camp in the 1940s-50s, 1960, 1970, 1980 and 1986, with a 42-page leader's guide, at $48 to members - a purpose-built teaching kit about a camp watching its own landscape change.

Camp Stephens is described in Canadian Camping Summer 1987 as running twelve-day sessions for boys and girls aged 8-15, a Wilderness Adventure Program for 13-17s with trips up to six weeks, a fourteen-boat sailing fleet, a fifteen-year-old kayaking programme, Lount Lodge built by camp staff from local logs 1980-82, and a standing international-education programme with a half-day session in its ten-day pre-camp training.

Provincial changes reported in Canadian Camping Summer 1987: Judy May of Corner Brook replaced Frank O'Connor as Newfoundland president; Jean Bowering replaced Jack Way for British Columbia; Calvin Desmarais replaced Grant Platts for Manitoba; Jane McCutcheon became Ontario's representative and OCA president; and Dorothy Walter, Anne Prewitt-Eaton and Bruno Morawetz were made OCA Honorary Life Members. The New Brunswick association was fighting minimum-wage legislation it had been refused exemption from.

The editor's note in Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 2, Fall 1987, states what the issue is missing and why: "What it doesn't contain are a number of provincial reports, committee news items and our Personality Profile. The postal system blocked the first two and a confounding phone/dictaphone blocked a transcontinental interview concerning Lorne Brown." A postal strike is therefore the reason several provinces are silent in this issue, which must be known before reading any absence in it as significance.

Two further gaps in the Internet Archive scan of Canadian Camping Fall 1987: page 13, carrying Nancy Bramm's prize-winning Bubby Nash article, and page 19, produced no machine-readable text. These are gaps in the tool, not absences in the record.

Mary Northway's 1968 Ontario Camping Association banquet speech, printed posthumously in Canadian Camping Fall 1987: "From the many events going on in the external or internal environment at any one moment, we select from among the millions of possibilities those which our perceptual equipment is capable of receiving and from these, those which have most meaning for or bring most satisfaction to us. In doing so, we stamp them with our own qualities. They become our experience. Indeed, 'We see things not as they are, but as we are'. As time passes, our past experience becomes transformed and modified, for remembering is in essence a creative process, by which we continually recreate past experiences into novel forms that have importance for us in the present... It is not what really happened that matters; it is what we have reconstructed out of it and what we make out of it."

Northway on camp memory specifically, 1968: "our return is not to the blue lake and rocky shore as they were; they are to what we have created from them... Our present campfire is always aglow with all the campfires we have known in the past."

Northway's account supplies the mechanism behind this project's standing subordination of oral history to documents: not that memory decays, but that it is actively reconstructed to serve the present, by a process that feels from the inside exactly like recall. It comes from a professional research psychologist who was also a camper, addressing camp directors about their own camps.

Mary Northway on Glen Bernard Camp's first season, 1922: "This was the first year of the camp - and everything was new to all of us and everything was an adventure. The camp was divided across age groups into Indian Tribes. Although I had never seen an Indian and far less knew anything of our historical dealings or misdealings with them, being an Indian seemed a fine idea to me... There were three tribes, the Micmacs, the Tuscarora and the Kashigabagamogs. We elected the big girls to be tribal chief and scroll reader and to other important positions. But I, a little girl, was elected runner. What an honour to be formally titled 'Runner of the Kashigabagamogs!'"

Two of Glen Bernard's three 1922 tribe names are real nations from opposite ends of the country - Mi'kmaq of the Maritimes and Tuscarora of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy - and the third is not a nation at all, apparently an Ojibwe-sounding coinage. Set beside John Gilchrist's statement that Mary Edgar wrote "Indian legends of her own... which, in fact, were make-believe but she made them sound the real thing," this is what that practice looked like in the camp's first season: two borrowed nations and one invented one, with elected chiefs and scroll readers.

Henri Chalifoux, ACQ President, reports on the 1987 Quebec season in Canadian Camping Fall 1987 that attendance was excellent, "with the no-vacancy sign up throughout the summer for most of the province's camps and many had a long waiting list," and that "Over eighty (80) camps were visited this past summer by five consultants. Out of this number ten (10) were trying to gain provincial recognition and become part of the provincial association for the first time." Against 76 camps visited by three consultants in 1986, that is a larger visitation programme, and ten camps applied for first-time membership in one year.

Chalifoux reports the ACQ's three-part triennial development plan - an orientation plan accepted in May 1987, a revision of each programme's specific objectives due before spring, and a finance-committee plan "that will allow self-financing for the camps in future years" - and that the executive was working closely with the provincial government on l'assurance responsabilite civile, "devenu complexe pour les directeurs de camps, depuis quelques annees."

The ACQ commissioned a study to identify who actually went to Quebec camps, funded by the ministere des Loisirs, de la Chasse et de la Peche, renewing user research done in 1982. It is the closest thing to a demographic survey of Quebec camp clientele this project has encountered, and it would describe the population Kanawana drew from. The magazine's English translation garbles the funder into two ministries; the French text names one, the M.L.C.P., and is the one to trust.

The CCA's Commission des camps d'expression francaise for 1987-88 is named in full: "Carmelle Deveau, Nouveau-Brunswick; Michel Gratton, Ontario; Eileen Mayotte, Saskatchewan; Ken Willis, Quebec," chaired by Colette Pouliot-Marier, who re-accepted the chair in May 1987. Eileen Mayotte, the Quebec Camping Association's secretary of the 1940s, was still sitting on a national committee in the autumn of 1987 - a second fixed point for her in one year - and Ken Willis stayed on as the committee's Quebec member after retiring from the vice-presidency.

Pouliot-Marier credits Gerard Bachand's two years with the INCEF '87 needs analysis and with the linguistic policies "dont les recommendations faites au Conseil des presidents furent acceptees" - so the CCA language policy traced in this project since 1974 was formally adopted by the President's Council in 1987. An INCEF 1988 was planned, to carry "un bilan des Inventaires des camps d'expression francaise realises depuis les trois dernieres annees."

The "Jackpot!" archives appeal in Canadian Camping Fall 1987 records that the previous winter's Camp Oconto fire article brought in "a goldmine of material which might otherwise have been lost... from one person who worked on staff at one small camp in Ontario for two years in 1936 and 1937," and draws the lesson: "We must recognize that today's snapshots, camp brochures, crests, cards and programs are tomorrow's priceless archives. Every camp should be actively archiving. Every camping association should be actively archiving as well. Without gathering our histories together, in a safe organized way we are all losers."

The "Jackpot!" notice states that the magazine would publish suitable material "before forwarding it to the Canadian Camping Association Archives at Trent University or to the appropriate provincial camping association archives in the camp's home province." That is a third statement in three issues that provincial associations held their own archives, so Quebec material sent to the magazine in 1986-88 may have gone to the ACQ rather than to Trent.

Aniko Varpalotai reports in Fall 1987 that "an assessment of the current status and needs of physical activity programs at Canadian camps has now been completed," with a very high return rate, and promises a summary of results "in the next issue" - which is issue 164, the last the magazine published. She answers Ken Willis's objection directly: many camping people "echoed the concerns expressed by Ken Willis... The fear that camps will be turned into aerobic exercise clubs or competitive sports centres is not without foundation given the image of physical activity in the media," but Fitness Canada's 1988-89 mandate "has embraced the concept of holistic fitness which 'includes the integration of physical, mental, emotional, spiritual and social elements'."

Volume 1 Number 1 of the International Camping Fellowship newsletter came off the ACA presses in the autumn of 1987, edited by Armand Ball, with articles on camping in Australia, Ghana, India, Belgium, Japan, Venezuela, the United Kingdom, Europe, Latin America, the USA and Canada; a year's subscription in Canada cost $7.00. The Washington meetings are given here as 25 delegates; the planning group was chaired by Terry Lucas of Venezuela; the agreement is dated 12 March 1987; and Jack Pearse was appointed "International Representative for the Canadian Camping Association," hosting Adamson and Chamberlain at Camp Tawingo on 9-10 July 1987.

The CCA board structure changed again in 1987 to five regional vice-presidencies: Atlantic (Ian Fowler), Pacific (Jan James), Prairie (Jennifer Perron, Winnipeg), Quebec (Gerard Bachand) and Ontario (Sally Moore) - the West split in two and Quebec's separate seat retained. Ontario's members gave over $2,700 to the Patrons' Fund within two weeks of Jane McCutcheon's September appeal, and Dorothy Walter agreed to organise a major fund-raising event for March 1988.

"The Tree of Great Peace," an account of the founding of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy by Deganawidah and Hiawatha, appears in "Under Open Skies" in Canadian Camping Fall 1987 signed "Negwnta-la-ay-ha / Red Dog" - the only Indigenous byline found anywhere in this run of the magazine, and a marked contrast with the camper-persona gift speeches printed anonymously in issue 159.

A classified advertisement in Canadian Camping Fall 1987 reads: "YOUNG INVESTOR - Young investor with 5 years experience as supervisor in summer camps interested in investing in a summer camp with intentions of long term acquisition. Please contact: Alan Leibovitch, [Montreal home address]." A Montreal name sought to buy a camp in 1987. The advertiser's full home address as printed is preserved in kb/reread/cc_findings.md, block 163; it is not repeated here or in any wiki article, being a private individual's home.

Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 3, Winter 1988, the final issue of the digitized run, carries "L'Etranger / The Stranger," printed in full in both languages with the French set first and bylined "by Jay Netherwood, Camp Kanawana." It is the only article by a Kanawana person in 164 issues of the magazine.

Jay Netherwood, Camp Kanawana, opening "L'Etranger / The Stranger," Canadian Camping Winter 1988: "Would you let a stranger walk around your camp with a chain saw, cutting down all the mature trees? Of course not. Well in fact we camp directors in Quebec are doing exactly that. The stranger's name is acid rain, or more properly, acid precipitation, for melting snow is the deadliest form this stranger assumes."

Netherwood, 1988: "If your camp is located in the Canadian Shield (especially the Laurentians) or south of the St.-Lawrence River then your flora and fauna have been irreparably damaged... The problem with acid precipitation is that it is a slow killer; our lakes look healthy, the outer branches of our coniferous trees look green and vibrant... But walk away from your birches and maples and look at the top, where the new growth should be - notice the bare branches? Look at the inside part of the branch of your pines and spruces - are the needles brown? Have you seen more dead tadpoles floating near the edge of your lake? Have you noticed how much quieter your site is on a warm July night when you used to be able to drift off to sleep, serenaded by a frog chorus?"

Netherwood, 1988: "Our lakes are becoming vinegar. Our mature trees are suffering from die-back, caused by stress from acid precipitation which weakens the trees and makes them prone to shoestring root-rot... Our amphibious life is dying. And what are we doing? Nothing. In 1978, concerned maple syrup producers banded together to form a body to lobby governments and industry, but in 1987 what have we camp directors done? Surely we have as much to lose as the maple syrup producers."

Netherwood's closing appeal, 1988: "Our responsibility must expand beyond ensuring that our campers have a safe and rewarding summer experience, it must also include that we are guardians of our fragile environment... it's an industry devoted to people - an industry that is concerned and scared... Individually, we should as educators, promote environmental literacy, for our campers and staff of today will become tomorrow's industrialists and politicians... Let's become acquainted with this stranger. Let's take the chain saw out of its hands."

Correction to this project's earlier catalogue-based record: "L'Etranger" is printed in both French and English, with the French set first, not in French only. For a Quebec YMCA camp in 1988 the ordering is itself a statement.

Netherwood's 1988 article is an independent, dated, printed document placing Jay Netherwood at Camp Kanawana as its public voice, over his own name. Every other document for his directorship is an internal YMCA of Montreal roster or his own director's report; this one is outside the institution.

Netherwood's article completes a thread this project has followed for nine years: the movement put acid rain to camp directors as their own problem from October 1979, the National Survival Institute's teaching kit was posted to member camps in 1982, Jeff Reading's "Acid Rain: Understanding the Problem at Camp" appeared in 1984, and the CCA Environmental Ethic was adopted the same year. In 1988 a Kanawana director answers it in print in his own words. Nothing else in this run shows a Kanawana person acting on the movement's programme rather than being counted by it.

Netherwood does not name Lake Kanawana, Lake Wilson or Round Lake and gives no measurement, but "if your camp is located in the Canadian Shield (especially the Laurentians)... then your flora and fauna have been irreparably damaged" is written by the director of a camp in exactly that position, and the signs he lists - bare crowns on the birches, brown needles inside the spruce branches, dead tadpoles, a silent July night - read as things he had looked for. This is a general statement by a person with particular knowledge, not a record of Kanawana's water chemistry.
A. Ross Seaman died on 23 October 1987, the date given in the founding notice of the A. Ross Seaman Leadership Development Fund in Canadian Camping Winter 1988. This project had only "October 1987."

The A. Ross Seaman Leadership Development Fund: "a group of family, friends, and colleagues met in early November and proposed a living memorial through the establishment of a fellowship/scholarship/bursary fund... Our aim is to use only the interest of the fund, leaving the capital intact... we have set as our minimum goal the sum of $25,000.00." Its address is "Fonds Commemoratif A. Ross Seaman, Universite Concordia, Bureau des finances AD 130, 7141 ouest, rue Sherbrooke, Montreal, Quebec H4B 1R6," with the explicit note in capitals: "THIS IS NOT AN OFFICIAL CCA/ACC FUND-RAISING EFFORT. IT HAS BEEN ORGANIZED FOR AND THROUGH CONCORDIA UNIVERSITY."

The 1988 memorial notice describes A. Ross Seaman as "a community leader, educational innovator, and consummate teacher and mentor... on the leading edge of bringing the best possible resources to bear on the issues that engaged his energy - camping and leadership training, recreation leadership, and community organization, particularly as it relates to adolescent life and latterly as it related to an aging population. One colleague refers to him as a cheerleader of the human race." It records that "One of Ross' philosophies was to 'pass it on' whenever he was on the receiving end of something meaningful."
The last issue of Canadian Camping carries a memorial to one Kanawana director and an article by another. It is the only issue in the whole run in which Kanawana appears twice in its own right.

Janet Adamson's president's message in the last issue of Canadian Camping: "For those intimately involved with the Canadian Camping Association, 1988 is an historic year. It is this year that the Canadian Camping Association is no longer receiving funding for its operating expenses from the Federal Government through Fitness Canada. Will we survive? For many years the C.C.A. received handsome funding for its general operation from the Federal Government. We had an executive director's salary, twice yearly board meetings to which all provincial presidents were flown at government expense, conferences funded by government, and Federal Government administrative money. This funding has been phased out over the past three years, and despite economies, budget cutting and fund raising we are now operating at a deficit each year." She counts the association at "nine provincial associations and six hundred camps and their directors... for fifty years."

Adamson records in the last issue: "Because we are facing a deficit in this year, Camp Tawingo is underwriting the complete cost of production of this winter issue of the magazine" - so the final issue of Canadian Camping was paid for by a single camp - and, of the foreign-counsellor protocol, "Each year Barry [Lowes], at his own expense, flies to Ottawa and negotiates the foreign camp counsellor agreement for C.C.A. He donates his time, the office work involved and the airfare." The board's minutes, printed two pages later, read: "There is no money left in the budget to produce this very C.C.A./A.C.C. Magazine you now hold in your hands" and "Deep concern was expressed by all over the financial outlook."
The board minutes in the last issue record plans that do not appear in this corpus: a third International Congress proposed for Toronto, a 1989 Directors' Institute, and a 1989 national conference.

May Brown, CCA president 1965-67, interviewed in the last issue: "Don Smith from Alberta was President just before I was and I think that was the first move out of Ontario and Quebec. It really solidified our whole country, because, for the next 10 years, it moved from Alberta to B.C. to Manitoba, where Doug McEwen was President and, eventually, David Hartry in Nova Scotia became the President."

May Brown, herself the second president from outside Ontario and Quebec, dates the CCA's decentralisation to Don Smith of Alberta in about 1963-65 - a decade later than the "shortly after" the magazine's own interviewer attached to Ted Yard's 1953-55 cross-Canada trip. Both are printed recollections; the named sequence is the more precise and is preferred. Brown adds the mechanism: "The CCA, at that stage, was very small and we had no money so I took advantage of those trips [on the National Advisory Council for Fitness and Amateur Sports] to go all across the country, stopping off with my air ticket and going to camping meetings in Alberta and Winnipeg."

May Brown on 1947: "I had directed Camp Oolawhan out of the Montreal YWCA... I was going to be directing Camp Oolawhan for the summer but I was looking for something for the fall so I was sent by the Montreal YWCA to a meeting in Ottawa which was the first meeting of the... when they were going to establish a Canadian Camping Association. Blackie Blackstock was there and he introduced me to Marion Henderson Penney from U.B.C." She had taken her Physical Education degree at McGill, finishing in 1947.

May Brown is a third named director of Camp Oolahwan, after Mary S. Edgar (1915-19) and Marjorie Booth (late 1970s), filling a name into a thirty-year gap; and she was sent to the Ottawa founding meeting of 1947 by the YWCA of Montreal, which sharpens an existing item pointing at Ottawa and the later 1940s rather than adding a new one.

Gerard Bachand, in his first Quebec regional report as CCA vice-president: "I also want to extend a warm thank you to Mr. Ken Willis for all the years he spent working for the QCA... By the same token, I wish to welcome Mrs. Madelene Allen who will be taking Ken's place" - "qui prend la releve de Ken au sein du Conseil d'Administration." The director of Camp Ouareau joined the ACQ's board of directors at the start of 1988.

Bachand reports the ACQ's position at the start of 1988: a new leadership programme for administrators; a new advanced course for directors ("Directeur 2") begun in December, with a "Formateur-plus" course for those responsible for training inside camps; two major studies with the M.L.C.P., one on insurance and one on summer-camp clientele - confirming from a second source the study Henri Chalifoux described in the previous issue; and the development plan going to the Conseil d'administration in mid-January after the orientation plan of May 1987.

Bachand records: "une Foire des Camps se prepare pour le debut de 88, ou l'ACQ est le maitre d'oeuvre. Le tout se deroulera au Complexe Desjardins de Montreal" - a camp fair at Complexe Desjardins in Montreal in early 1988, organised by the ACQ, which Kanawana as a member camp would have had reason to attend. No Kanawana attendance is documented.

The PARC national survey, reported in the last issue of Canadian Camping: of "close to 600 CCA member camps" sent the questionnaire, 197 (33%) replied - 70 religious camps, 52 private, 50 agency, 14 special-needs and 11 other; 179 residential and 18 day camps. Findings: 53% call physical activity "very important"; 67.5% say more than half their programme is physical activity; the top five priority programmes are swimming, religion, canoeing, boating and land sports; 70% have water, forest and fields on site and 28% large hills or mountains; campers are mostly 8-15 with almost equal numbers of girls and boys; objectives are new skills, lifelong leisure activities and fitness, with competition preparation rare.

The PARC survey also records that "a large number of camps expressed a preference for cooperative 'New Games', as opposed to the more traditional, competitive, team and individual sports," and names the problems as finding qualified staff for non-waterfront activities, the cost of facilities and equipment, motivating sedentary campers, and the want of cheap new ideas. It is the only statistical portrait of Canadian camp programming in this whole run built from a designed survey with a stated response rate, and its composition - a third religious, a quarter private, a quarter agency - is the best available answer to what kind of institution a "Canadian camp" was in 1987.

The Personality Profile of Lorne Brown (1908-1976) completes the magazine's series on "some of the pioneers of camping in Canada" - Taylor Statten, Mary S. Edgar, Ted Yard and Brown - and the editor promises "the start of a different series of personalities in our next issue," which never came. Brown directed Camp Deka in the Cariboo 1961-1975 (property bought 1958, lodge begun 1960, opened 1961 with 24 campers, never larger than 48 boys), was at the Vancouver YMCA's Camp Elphinstone from 1925 and co-director in 1950, founded the B.C. Outdoor Educators, chaired the CCA's first Nature Awareness Committee under John Latimer's presidency, was president of CAHPER 1955-57 and chaired UBC's Physical Education department.

May Brown on the British Columbia Camping Association's founding date, recorded as disputed at issue 160: "as far as I can trace, I believe B.C.C.A. started in 1940... I think it was incorporated in 1940."

Camp Deka's council-ring practice is described by May Brown with unusual candour: "it came out of an Indian Council idea, but it wasn't too formal. We used to have a Challenge Night and Lorne was the Chief and actually did have an Indian jacket that he wore at it... because we had loons on the lake, we called it 'The Camp where wild loons call.' The boys called him Chief Loony Loon" - a fifth position on the question in this run, and the most casual.

Camp Massad in the last issue of Canadian Camping is the Manitoba camp fifty miles north of Winnipeg, thirty-five years old in 1987 and the only Hebrew-immersion camp in western Canada. It is not the Camp Massad Montreal (1947, Lac Quenouille) recorded in this project's Quebec camp landscape; the two share a name and should not be conflated.

Colette Pouliot-Marier reports in the last issue that Quebec francophones were now providing the magazine's translation under the new language policy - "des Francophones du Quebec assument, depuis quelques mois, la tache delicate de traduire les textes anglais en francais, et vice versa" - and appeals twice for French copy: "Il est up to us, Francophones. Our contribution is lacking." INCEF 88 was expected early in the year.

The word-for-word read of all 164 cached issues of Canadian Camping (1949-1988) is complete. Kanawana is named in the run perhaps two dozen times across thirty-nine years, almost always in a list, and exactly once does one of its own people write in it. The camp was a member of the ACQ and through it of the CCA for the whole period, and the national magazine of its own movement recorded that membership almost entirely as an absence. The Quebec material that does exist - the ACQ's founding datings, its accreditation regime, its statistics, its French-language commission, its officers - was found by going page by page through issues that never mention Kanawana at all.

The YMCA of Greater Halifax/Dartmouth's own 165th anniversary yearbook states on page 8: "Our very own Big Cove YMCA Camp, in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, is the oldest continuously running residential camp in Canada."

The same YMCA of Greater Halifax/Dartmouth yearbook, in its historical timeline on page 28, records: "1975 - 1980 Big Cove Camp operated the last season since opening as the children's residential summer camp, until 1980 when it reopened for resident camping once again." Resident camping therefore ceased after the 1975 season and resumed in 1980 -- four missed summers, 1976 through 1979.

One publication of the YMCA of Greater Halifax/Dartmouth contains both the claim that Big Cove is "the oldest continuously running residential camp in Canada" (p. 8) and a timeline entry recording that its resident camping stopped after 1975 and did not resume until 1980 (p. 28). The two statements are twenty pages apart and the publication does not reconcile them.

Big Cove's four-summer gap was a closure and recovery, not a planned fallow period. Kelley Byrne, the camp's own director, wrote in 1987 that it "closed in 1976 for want of repairs and reopened in 1980"; the owner's 2023 yearbook independently records 1975 as the last season before it "reopened for resident camping once again" in 1980. Both sources describe a cessation followed by a reopening, and the stated cause is the physical condition of the plant.

Big Cove YMCA Camp's current website claims it is "Canada's oldest overnight camp" with roots "back to 1889" and makes no mention of the 1976-1979 interruption. Its Wikipedia article likewise gives a 1889 founding and records no closure. Explicit null on both surfaces.

The Camp Stephens Alumni blog states in a December 2020 post that COVID-19 "Restrictions made it impossible to open camp this past summer (the first closure since 1917)." The alumni association therefore dates the camp's First World War closure to 1917. Secondary summaries of the camp's history give 1918 instead; the two are not reconciled here and no source consulted gives both. [RESOLVED 2026-09-05, see f_4838: the year is 1918. This blog's own 125th-anniversary chapel service and the Lake of the Woods Museum newsletter both give 1918 and both give the mechanism -- not enough men left to staff the season. The '1917' here is a parenthesis in a fundraising appeal, and is superseded as a date while being kept as a record of what the post said.] [RECLASSIFIED 2026-09-05: confidence disputed -> stated, after c_061 resolved. The fact accurately records what a December 2020 fundraising post said; that remains true. The DATE it gave is superseded, which the note above states. A fact can be an accurate record of a wrong claim, and this is one.]

An August 2020 Camp Stephens Alumni post records that "Due to the pandemic, in the best interest of the health and safety of campers, staff and the surrounding community, camp and the wilderness canoe program was cancelled in May," and that "With no campers, camp has no income. Yet the work still has to get done." Camp Stephens therefore lost the 2020 season. Camp Stephens is at Kenora, Ontario, so the prohibition that closed it was Ontario's, not Manitoba's.

The Camp Stephens Alumni blog claims that "One of the reasons why Camp Stephens is the longest-serving summer camp in Canada is due to the generosity of alumni and our donors." This is a third distinct superlative in play, alongside Big Cove's "oldest continuously running residential camp in Canada" and Kanawana's withdrawn "second-oldest."

EXPLICIT NULL: whether Camp Stephens operated in the summer of 2021 could not be established. Its own site, its About Us page and the alumni blog's 2021 archive say nothing about that season, and the alumni blog's only 2021 post concerns an unrelated island preservation effort. Recorded as unknown, not as evidence that it ran.

Camp Stephens' own current pages give 1891 for the first Winnipeg YMCA camp at Keewatin Beach on Lake of the Woods, 1893 for the location of the five-island site, 1896 for the adoption of the name Camp Stephens, and "over 130 years" of operation. EXPLICIT NULL: they record no closure of any kind, neither the wartime one their own alumni association documents nor the 2020 one.

Big Cove YMCA Camp also lost its overnight seasons to COVID-19 and, like Kanawana, kept its site in alternative use rather than ceasing operations: in 2020 it did not run overnight camp but allowed families to rent cabins, and in 2021 it operated as a campground offering canoeing and archery and sustained itself through its leadership training programme, returning to normal operations in 2022. The distinction between a camp that closed and a camp that kept staff and site working therefore does not separate Kanawana from Big Cove in 2020-21.

All three claimants to "Canada's oldest camp" lost overnight seasons to COVID-19 in 2020, and at least Kanawana and Big Cove lost 2021 as well. The pandemic interruption is therefore common to the sector and does not distinguish any claimant from another; it is the interruptions BEFORE 2020 that differ.

Measured as the longest unbroken run of consecutive seasons, Kanawana leads every claimant: 1894 to 2019 inclusive is 126 consecutive seasons. Camp Stephens, closed in 1917 by its alumni association's own account, has a longest run of about 102 seasons (1918-2019). Big Cove, whose resident camping ceased after 1975, has a longest run of about 87 seasons (1889-1975) and only 40 since reopening (1980-2019). This holds on any of Big Cove's three candidate founding dates.

The 126-consecutive-season figure for Kanawana depends on the camp having missed no season between 1894 and 2019. No source records a missed season, and the years most likely to have broken the run are documented as operating: the camp ran through both world wars with boy-weeks flat to rising across 1940-45, ran in 1918 with 223 campers while Camp Stephens did not run, and stayed open through the 1946 polio outbreak on Dr. Cushing's advice with only canoe trips cancelled. But the attendance series has no figure at all for many years, and absence of a figure is not evidence of operation. The claim is stated on that basis and the assumption is named.

Camp Dudley, founded by Sumner F. Dudley, dates its origin to 1884, when Dudley "was asked in 1884 to take 'young honor YMCA members' camping," and to 1885, when "he took seven boys for a week's encampment at Orange Lake, N. J." It describes itself as "the oldest continually running boys camp in the United States."

THE GOLDEN LAKE 1884 CLAIM APPEARS TO BE AN ARTEFACT, NOT A CANADIAN CAMP. The February 1955 Ontario survey asserted "In Canada in 1884, the Ottawa Y went camping at Golden Lake and in all probability established the first Canadian camp." 1884 is Sumner Dudley's date -- the year the American YMCA camping movement's founder was asked to take boys camping, a year before the first camp at Orange Lake, New Jersey. The Ottawa YMCA did not reach Golden Lake until 1908, on the independent agreement of Ace Milks's own account and a Lost Ottawa photograph caption. The survey appears to have grafted the American movement's origin year onto a Canadian site the Ottawa Y occupied twenty-four years later.

Camp On-Da-Da-Waks, the Ottawa YMCA's camp at Golden Lake, was founded in 1908 -- agreeing with Ace Milks's account in Canadian Camping that he attended the Ottawa YMCA camp at Marshall's Bay in 1907 and that it moved to Golden Lake in 1908 "because there was too much sawdust in the water." Golden Lake is therefore not a candidate for the earliest Canadian camp.

With the Golden Lake 1884 claim resolved as an artefact, the surviving pre-1894 rival to Kanawana from the Ottawa YMCA is 1893 -- the date Charles Plewman, who directed for the Ottawa Y himself, gives in December 1964: "When the Ottawa YMCA in 1893, and Camp Temagami in 1900, began taking older boys to camp, they were really breaking new ground." That is one year before Kanawana's first season and remains untested. [AMENDED 2026-09-05: it has now been tested (p_405). The claim is not withdrawn -- 1893 is still the surviving pre-1894 Ottawa date -- but the tail of this fact, 'remains untested', is no longer true, and what the test found weakens the claim: the documentary half of it is an Ottawa YWCA board minute rather than a YMCA record (f_4835), and the North American Year Books of 1893-1897 record no camp for Ottawa, nor for Montreal, which is why that null settles nothing either way (f_4836).]

YMCA Camp Pine Crest states on its own pages that it has been "Operating continually since 1910 on Clear Lake" and is "one of the longest operating summer camps in North America." Its longest possible unbroken run to 2019 is therefore about 110 seasons, against Kanawana's 126.

The YMCA of Greater Toronto states: "Since 1940, the Pine Crest community has come together every summer for The Pine Crest Games" -- a two-day all-camp competition between two teams, the Voyageurs and the Lumbermen. Pine Crest's version therefore predates Kanawana's 1947 adoption by seven years.

EXPLICIT NULL ON THE TRANSMISSION OF L&V. Neither the YMCA of Greater Toronto's account of the Pine Crest Games nor any source consulted says who created the Games, why the teams were named Lumbermen and Voyageurs, or whether the tradition moved between camps. How the competition reached Kanawana in 1947 is undocumented on every surface searched. The camp's own centennial history, "Lumbermen & Voyageurs: The YMCA Pine Crest Story," is the most likely place for an answer and has not been read.

Kanawana's L&V Games began in the summer of 1947, and Roy D. Locke "became Camp Chief during the summer of '47" in the same season. No source consulted connects Locke to Camp Pine Crest or to Toronto, and no document states who introduced the competition. The coincidence of dates is recorded as a lead, not as an explanation.

BIG COVE HAS NO LUMBERMEN-AND-VOYAGEURS COMPETITION ON THE EVIDENCE AVAILABLE. Its programme sections are Little Big Cove, Juniors, Seniors and Leadership (L1 and L2), and the tradition its Wikipedia article names is "the Keeper of the Cove." There is no Voyageur section, no Lumbermen team and no colour-war competition. What Big Cove does have is a "Voyageur program" dating to the late 1940s -- an advanced outtripping track "challenging older youth to develop expert outtripping, canoeing, axemanship and woodcraft skills" -- and a place on site called the Voyageur Trail. The shared word is fur-trade vocabulary common to Canadian camping, not a shared institution.

The 1989 relay campfire marking the Centenary of YMCA Camping in Canada involved Kanawana and twenty-eight other YMCA camps, each burning a campfire for one hour of a twenty-nine hour relay. That gives a count of approximately twenty-nine YMCA camps in Canada in 1989.

YMCA overnight camps identifiable in Canada in 2026 across the surfaces searched: Camp Kanawana (Saint-Sauveur, Quebec); Big Cove (Sutherlands River, Nova Scotia); YM-YWCA Camp Stephens (Lake of the Woods, near Kenora, Ontario, run from Winnipeg); YMCA Camp Pine Crest (Torrance, Muskoka, Ontario, YMCA of Greater Toronto); YMCA Wanakita (Haliburton, Ontario, YMCA of Hamilton-Burlington-Brantford); and YMCA Camp Elphinstone (Gibsons, British Columbia). YMCA Camp Kanannaq near Prince George runs day camps only. This is a floor, not a complete roster: ymca.ca's national camps page names no individual camps at all.

The number of YMCA camps in Canada appears to have fallen sharply since 1989, when twenty-nine took part in the centenary relay. Stan Symington's 1953 tour of eastern Canada alone named nine YMCA camps -- Naskapie, Pascobac, Wapomeo, Barachois, Magaguadavic, Y's Acres, Sherbrooke, Holland Cove and Big Cove -- of which only Big Cove is identifiable as still operating. This is a comparison of two lists gathered by different methods, not a measured decline, and is recorded as an observation requiring proper testing.

YMCA Hayo-Went-Ha Camps (founded 1904, Central Lake, Michigan) use "Woodsmen" and "Voyageurs" as programme group names, and the wider "colour war" genre is documented by historian Leslie Paris as originating with "Red and Gray Week" in 1916 at Schroon Lake Camp in the Adirondacks. Kanawana's L&V is therefore best understood as a Canadian YMCA fur-trade-themed variant of a North American camp form, rather than as a tradition unique to Pine Crest and Kanawana.

YMCA CAMP KITCHIKEWANA RUNS THE LUMBERMAN AND VOYAGEUR GAMES -- A THIRD CANADIAN YMCA CAMP WITH THE TRADITION. Its programmes page names the "Lumberman and Voyageur Games" among the special programmes of its two-week Traditional Camp, alongside the Annual Musical, Sailing Regattas and Talent Show. This corrects this project's earlier statement that only Camp Pine Crest and Kanawana are documented as running the competition.

YMCA Camp Kitchikewana is on Beausoleil Island in Georgian Bay Islands National Park, Honey Harbour, Ontario, operated by the YMCA of Simcoe/Muskoka and founded by the Midland YMCA. Its own pages state "YMCA Camp Kitchikewana has been in operation since 1919" and "For the last 105 years YMCA Camp Kitchikewana has been offering a values based camp experience."

A DATE CONFLICT ON KITCHIKEWANA'S FOUNDING, CARRIED IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN RECORDS. The camp and this KB give 1919, but C. R. "Blackie" Blackstock's 1979 obituary and the 1984 Ebbs tribute both describe him as a Kitchikewana "original" who "started the first year of that 'Y' camp on Beausoleil Island in 1921 as a very young counsellor" under Ernie Thurlow. Two years apart, and the 1921 version comes from a man who says he was there. Not resolved here. [EXTENDED 2026-09-05: a third statement of 1919 is on record, the Rooted podcast's 'In 2019, Camp Kitchikewana celebrated its 100th anniversary' (f_4842). It is not independent of the camp, which took part in the programme, so the conflict with the 1921 of Blackstock's obituary and the Ebbs tribute stands.]

EXPLICIT NULL: when the Lumberman and Voyageur Games began at Camp Kitchikewana, and whether they arrived from Camp Pine Crest, travelled to it, or developed independently, is not stated on the camp's own pages or on any surface searched. The camp's founding in 1919 predates Pine Crest's Games (1940) by twenty-one years, so Kitchikewana cannot be ruled out as an earlier or parallel source of the tradition on present evidence. Know History's commissioned study "Rooted: Beausoleil Island" has a chapter on the camp and is the most likely published source; it returns HTTP 403 to this project's fetch tool and has not been read. [EXTENDED 2026-09-05: the Know History source named here as unread has now been heard -- it is a podcast, not a study, and its Camp Kitchikewana chapter says nothing about the Games (f_4841). The null therefore now covers the source that was expected to break it.]

Kitchikewana already has documented points of contact with Kanawana independent of the L&V Games. Austin Matthews, General Secretary of the Midland YMCA and Director of Camp Kitchikewana, described a fully documented school-camp week in autumn 1967 -- 170 grade-four children of the Midland public school system in three five-day groups -- which is the clearest model in the Canadian Camping run of the arrangement that later became Kanawana's own outdoor-education work with schools. Charles Plewman was "instrumental in organising some thirty-five camps, notably the training camp at Beausoleil Island, Georgian Bay." And Camp Kitchikewana supplied the name of YMCA Camp Wanakita, taken from its own Wanakita Beach.

Camp Kitchikewana is a seventh YMCA overnight camp operating in Canada in 2026, missing from this project's earlier list of six, which was explicitly recorded as a floor rather than a roster. Its presence confirms that the floor was too low and that no complete list of Canadian YMCA camps has been assembled from any national source.

Kitchikewana's "in operation since 1919" and "for the last 105 years" is a fourth long-continuity claim among Canadian YMCA camps, alongside Big Cove's "oldest continuously running residential camp in Canada", Camp Stephens' "longest-serving summer camp in Canada" and Camp Pine Crest's "operating continually since 1910". Founded 1919, its longest possible unbroken run to 2019 is about 101 seasons, behind Kanawana's 126. Whether it lost seasons to the wars or to COVID-19 is not stated on its own pages.
