A FOURTH CAMP RUNS THE TRADITION. RKY Camp at Parham, Ontario, on Eagle Lake, states: "The RKY Games is a special 3-day camp-wide competition in 4th Session between the Lumbermen and Voyageurs." With Camp Pine Crest, Kanawana and Camp Kitchikewana, that makes four Canadian camps documented as running a Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition.

RKY Camp's initials stand for Rotary, Kiwanis and YMCA: it was founded jointly by the Rotary Club of Kingston, the Kingston Kiwanis Club and the Kingston YMCA, and is described as the only camp in Ontario jointly owned by three service clubs. The Chair of the YMCA Committee, Professor C. E. Walker of Queen's University, approached the two service clubs in 1929; on 3 July 1930 a 25-acre site was purchased from W. Goodfellow and J. Snider for $925.00, with the YMCA supplying about $500.00 of equipment. "The name RKY Eagle Lake Camp was decided to be both 'representative and pronounceable'."

The Kingston YMCA had offered annual camping experiences for local boys as early as 1902, before the permanent RKY site was acquired -- another instance of the pattern by which an association's camping predates the camp it is remembered by, as at Montreal (1891-93 before 1894), Winnipeg (Keewatin Beach 1891 before the islands) and the Maritimes.

RKY CAMP CLOSED FOR THE WAR AND KANAWANA DID NOT. RKY's own history states: "In 1943 RKY Camp was forced to close down due to a lack of staff. It reopened in 1945." Kanawana ran both of those seasons -- the attendance series gives 1,343 boy-weeks for 1943 and 1,450 for 1944, the second of those its highest figure of the war. This is the second documented wartime closure among the camps compared in this project, after Camp Stephens in 1917 or 1918, and Kanawana operated through both.

EXPLICIT NULL: RKY Camp's own history page does not date the RKY Games or say where the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs idea came from, exactly as Camp Kitchikewana's and Camp Pine Crest's pages do not. Three of the four camps running the tradition give no origin for it, and the only dated adoption in the group is Kanawana's own, 1947.

ALL FOUR CAMPS RUNNING THE LUMBERMEN-AND-VOYAGEURS COMPETITION HAVE YMCA ROOTS, AND THREE OF THE FOUR ARE IN ONTARIO. Camp Pine Crest (Muskoka, YMCA of Greater Toronto), Camp Kitchikewana (Georgian Bay, YMCA of Simcoe/Muskoka) and RKY Camp (Eagle Lake near Kingston, founded in part by the Kingston YMCA) are Ontario camps; Kanawana, in the Quebec Laurentians, is the outlier. Kanawana is also the only one of the four whose adoption of the tradition carries a date, 1947. The shape of the evidence is an Ontario YMCA camp tradition that reached Quebec, but the direction and the mechanism remain undocumented.

The count of camps documented as running the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition has risen from two to four within a day, both additions supplied by the operator rather than by any search this project ran. The working conclusion should be that the tradition is more widespread than the evidence assembled here shows, and that the number four is a floor.

P_409 SURVEY, INSTRUMENT FOUND. The Ontario Camps Association publishes a browsable member directory of 163 camps and outdoor education centres at ontariocampsassociation.ca/find/camp-directory/, paginated alphabetically by a ?alpha=N parameter. Its Y page carries 61 YMCA and YWCA entries. This is the systematic instrument the earlier attempt to count Canadian YMCA camps lacked, and it was not found by any of the general searches run before.

THIS PROJECT'S EARLIER COUNT OF YMCA CAMPS WAS BADLY LOW. The points-of-contact article named six, then seven, YMCA overnight camps in Canada and called the number a floor. The OCA directory alone lists 61 YMCA and YWCA entries in Ontario, of which more than a dozen are overnight camps or outdoor education centres rather than branch day camps -- Pine Crest, Kitchikewana, Wanakita, Waabanaki, Belwood, Ki-Wa-Y, Heidelberg, Tillicum, John Island, Camp Henry, Camp Queen Elizabeth, Otonabee, Geneva Park, Cedar Glen and Rotary Youth Camp Presqu'ile among them. The earlier figure was assembled from famous names and should be read as a count of what this project had heard of, not of what exists.

TWO YMCA CAMPS SHARE BEAUSOLEIL ISLAND. YMCA Camp Kitchikewana (YMCA of Simcoe/Muskoka, from 1919) and YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth (YMCA of Southwestern Ontario, since 1953) both operate on Beausoleil Island in Georgian Bay Islands National Park. Charles Plewman was recorded as instrumental in organising the training camp at Beausoleil Island, and C. R. Blackstock started at Kitchikewana there.

NEGATIVE RESULT, CAMP QUEEN ELIZABETH: no Lumbermen or Voyageurs teams and no camp-wide two-team competition were found on the camp's pages or in searches of them. "Voyageur canoe" appears as a craft type only. A YMCA overnight camp on the same island as one that does run the competition apparently does not run it.

NEGATIVE RESULT, CAMP WAABANAKI, AND IT CONFIRMS THE BIG COVE DISTINCTION. The YMCA of Three Rivers' Camp Waabanaki runs a "Voyageur Extended Tripping Program" for ages 13-15 -- Killarney canoe routes, the La Cloche Silhouette trail, sea kayaking on Georgian Bay -- with no Lumbermen team and no two-team competition. This is the same shape as Big Cove's Voyageur programme: "Voyageur" as an advanced tripping RANK is a separate and commoner thing from "Lumbermen versus Voyageurs" as a two-team GAMES tradition, and the two must not be conflated.

P_409 RESULT AS OF 2026-09-05: four camps confirmed running a Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition (Pine Crest, Kanawana, Kitchikewana, RKY); three checked and negative (Camp Queen Elizabeth, Camp Waabanaki, Big Cove); the remaining dozen-plus Ontario YMCA overnight camps unchecked. No camp beyond the four was found, and no camp's Games were dated beyond Pine Crest's 1940 and Kanawana's 1947. The survey did not settle the direction of travel.

A SECOND ROTARY-YMCA HYBRID CAMP EXISTS: the OCA directory lists "YMCA Rotary Youth Camp Presqu'ile", alongside RKY Camp, whose initials stand for Rotary, Kiwanis and YMCA. Joint service-club-and-YMCA ownership is therefore not unique to RKY, and camps of that kind may be a category worth searching for the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs tradition rather than searching YMCA-owned camps alone.

General phrase searching does not find camps running the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition. Searches on "Lumbermen" with "Voyageurs", and on the exact strings "Lumberman and Voyageur" and "Lumbermen and Voyageurs", returned Kanawana's own TikTok, unrelated colour-war material and lumber-themed video games -- but not Kitchikewana's or RKY's programme pages, both of which use the phrase. Camp programme pages sit too deep in site structures to rank. Enumeration through an association directory is the method that works; phrase search is not.

P_409 ENUMERATION COMPLETE FOR ONTARIO'S YMCA OVERNIGHT CAMPS: TEN CHECKED, TEN NEGATIVE. Camp Belwood, Camp Ki-Wa-Y and Camp Waabanaki (YMCA of Three Rivers); YMCA Wanakita (Hamilton-Burlington-Brantford); Camp Henry and Camp Queen Elizabeth (Southwestern Ontario); Camp Tillicum and John Island Camp (Northeastern Ontario); Camp Otonabee (National Capital Region); and Rotary YMCA Camp Presqu'ile (Owen Sound Grey Bruce) were each checked for a Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition. None runs one. The count of camps with the tradition stands at four: Camp Pine Crest, Kanawana, Camp Kitchikewana and RKY Camp.

THE COLOUR-WAR GENRE IS COMMON AT ONTARIO YMCA CAMPS; THE LUMBERMEN-AND-VOYAGEURS NAMING IS NOT. John Island Camp (YMCA of Northeastern Ontario) lists among its traditions "evening programs, theme days, and Colour Wars" -- the genre under its generic name. Rotary YMCA Camp Presqu'ile runs "Presqu'ile Bound," described as "an epic adventure where campers conquer challenges and earn valuable points to determine who will reign over camp" -- the same competitive form under a local name. Neither uses the fur-trade naming. The question worth asking is therefore not which camps run a camp-wide competition, which many do, but which use the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs names, which is the narrow thing Kanawana shares with three others.

SERVICE-CLUB AND YMCA JOINT OWNERSHIP IS A COMMON ONTARIO PATTERN, NOT AN ODDITY OF RKY. Three examples are now documented: RKY Camp (Rotary Club of Kingston, Kingston Kiwanis Club and Kingston YMCA, from 1930); Rotary Camp Tillicum (YMCA of Northeastern Ontario in partnership with the Rotary Club of North Bay); and Rotary YMCA Camp Presqu'ile (YMCA of Owen Sound Grey Bruce with the Owen Sound Rotary Club, providing overnight camp "for the past 90+ years", so from about 1935). Of the three, only RKY runs the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition.

THE ENUMERATION DID NOT SETTLE THE DIRECTION OF TRAVEL, AND ON PRESENT EVIDENCE NOTHING SHORT OF THE TWO CAMP HISTORIES WILL. Ten Ontario YMCA overnight camps were checked and none runs the Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs competition; no camp's Games were dated beyond Camp Pine Crest's 1940 and Kanawana's 1947; and neither Camp Kitchikewana (founded 1919) nor RKY Camp (founded 1930) dates its own. The remaining routes are the two published camp histories -- "Lumbermen & Voyageurs: The YMCA Pine Crest Story" (p_404) and Know History's "Rooted: Beausoleil Island" chapter on Kitchikewana (p_408) -- and the archival records of the four camps.

That the four Lumbermen-and-Voyageurs camps are Pine Crest, Kitchikewana, RKY and Kanawana -- and that ten other Ontario YMCA overnight camps are not among them -- makes the tradition a minority practice within its own movement rather than a general YMCA camp form. Three of the four are in Ontario and one is in Quebec; the ten negatives are all Ontario. Whatever carried the competition between camps was specific rather than systemic, which makes a personal route more likely than an association-wide one and raises the value of finding who moved between Pine Crest, Kitchikewana, RKY and Kanawana.

THE LOCKE HYPOTHESIS IS DEAD: ROY D. LOCKE WAS A MONTREAL YMCA MAN THROUGHOUT, AND DID NOT COME FROM PINE CREST OR ONTARIO. The YMCA of Montreal's own annual reports track his career: the 1947 report lists him among secretaries who secured Certification by the Association of Secretaries; the 1948 report records that the Executive Secretary of Eastern Communities Branch "was succeeded by Roy D. Locke, Boys' Work Secretary of Notre Dame de Grace Branch"; and the 1949 report records "ROY D. LOCKE, Executive Secretary of Eastern Communities was appointed Metropolitan Boys' Work Secretary." He rose through Montreal branches -- Notre Dame de Grace, then Eastern Communities, then Metropolitan -- and became Kanawana's Camp Chief in the summer of 1947 from inside the Montreal association. The coincidence of his arrival with the first L&V season is therefore just a coincidence, and he is not the route by which the tradition reached the camp.

THE EARLIEST CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT MENTIONING THE L&V TRADITION AT KANAWANA IN THIS PROJECT'S CACHE IS THE 1950 ANNUAL REPORT, AND IT ALREADY CALLS IT ESTABLISHED: "'Lumbermen~ Voyageur' Week, as a closing feature of camp programme has become a whorthwhile tradition of Kanawana. A striking, lerge fireplace mural in the dining hall makes use of this motif. Division of the entire camp into two teams for this final week of goodenatured competition again met with tremendous enthusiasm on the part of campers." (OCR as cached.) The word "again" and the phrase "has become" both imply prior seasons.

EXPLICIT NULL, AND A POINTED ONE: the YMCA of Montreal annual reports for 1947, 1948 and 1949 do not mention the Lumbermen-and-Voyageur tradition at all, although the 1949 report describes Kanawana's programme in some detail, noting that swimming and paddling tests "reached 'four-star' proportions". And the camp's own "Kamp Kanawana History", presented at a training course on 6 June 1951, never mentions the tradition either, though it lists Roy Locke's innovations since 1947 -- a new main wharf, a cabin for the Senior Section Director, electrification, an automatic chlorinated water system and electric refrigeration. Three annual reports and the camp's own history are silent on a tradition the 1950 report calls established.

[SUPERSEDED 2026-09-05: wrong on both halves. The 1947 date does NOT rest only on the edition count -- the camp's own 1988 report states it outright, and the perpetual trophy's first shield reads 47. And the arithmetic does yield 1947: only ONE season was lost, 2021, not two. See the reconciliation fact f_4798.] THE 1947 START DATE FOR KANAWANA'S L&V GAMES RESTS ON A MODERN EDITION COUNT, NOT ON A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT, AND THE ARITHMETIC DOES NOT CLEANLY YIELD 1947. This project's basis for 1947 is the YMCA's statement that 2025 saw the 78th edition. If the Games ran every year without a gap, the 78th edition in 2025 implies a first edition in 1948. If the two COVID years of 2020 and 2021 are excluded from the count, 78 editions span eighty calendar years and imply a first edition in 1946. 1947 is what neither reading yields. The earliest contemporary mention in this project's cache is the 1950 annual report. The 1947 date should be treated as approximate, and the discrepancy resolved before it is relied on.

A CACHED FILE THAT IS NOT WHAT ITS NAME SUGGESTS: sources/cache/web-pages/pine_crest_book.txt is the Shopify PRODUCT PAGE for "Lumbermen & Voyageurs: The YMCA Pine Crest Story" -- HTML, title, price of $25.00 CAD and a marketing blurb -- and not the book's content. Priority p_404 to read the book is therefore not satisfied by anything on disk, and the file should not be mistaken for the source.

RESOLUTION of the L&V start date (p_410): 1947 is CONFIRMED, and this project's own doubt of 2026-09-05 (f_4796) was an error. Three independent lines converge. (1) THE OBJECT: the perpetual Kanawana Annual Trophy for Lumbermen Voyageur Games carries a shield for every season, and the first reads 47 -- 1947, Voyageurs. (2) THE CAMP'S OWN RECORD: "Kanawana... A Place to Grow" (YMCA of Montreal, 1988) lists under PROGRAMME HIGHLIGHTS: "1947 Kanawana introduces new camp wide event to highlight the final session of camp. Lumbermen and Voyageurs competition is created." (3) THE ARITHMETIC, CORRECTED: YMCA Quebec calls 2025 the 78th edition. 1947 through 2025 inclusive is 79 calendar seasons; exactly one was lost, 2021, which has no shield -- 2020 WAS contested, remotely, and does have one. 79 minus 1 is 78. The count lands on 1947 to the year, and independently confirms 2026 as the 79th edition. The earlier arithmetic failed only because it deducted two pandemic seasons where the trophy and the operator's account both record one. What survives of the doubt is narrower and still open: the annual reports for 1947, 1948 and 1949 are silent on the tradition and the camp's own 1951 history does not mention it (f_4795), so no CONTEMPORARY document from the founding seasons has yet been found -- the 1988 report is retrospective and the trophy's early shields could in principle have been back-filled. That is a gap in the contemporary record, not a competing date: nothing anywhere proposes a year other than 1947.

Dr. Amy Ornstein's credential line on the Dalhousie University Department of Pediatrics faculty page reads "Amy Ornstein, MDCM, MSc, FRCPC, FAAP". The degrees and granting institutions listed are BSc (Concordia University), MDCM (McGill University), MSc (Dalhousie University) and FRCPC (University of Toronto). She is Professor in the Department of Pediatrics, Division Head of General Pediatrics, and Medical Director of the IWK Suspected Trauma and Abuse Response Team (START); she previously worked in the Suspected Child Abuse and Neglect programme at the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, where she did her residency and fellowship. TWO OF THE FOUR DEGREES ARE FROM MONTREAL INSTITUTIONS, and in the order a Montreal upbringing would predict -- an undergraduate degree at Concordia followed by medicine at McGill. Concordia is itself the YMCA-descended institution that holds the YMCA of Montreal fonds this project reads.

OPERATOR TESTIMONY, 2026-09-05 (Matt Aronson): Amy Ornstein is a Halifax-based doctor who grew up in Montreal and worked at Camp Kanawana. This is first-hand knowledge from someone who was at the camp, and it directly contradicts this project's earlier assertion that no connection to Kanawana, YMCA Quebec or Montreal existed. The Montreal half is independently corroborated by her Concordia and McGill degrees; the Kanawana employment rests on the operator's testimony and has not yet been found in a document.

[CONFIRMED 2026-09-05, same day: see f_4803. Matt Aronson, a member of the Pip Awards committee, states the 2019 recipient was Dr. Amy Ornstein. This fact's hedging is superseded -- it was written before that confirmation and correctly declined to assert the attribution on inference alone. Kept as the record of the reasoning that pointed the right way before the answer arrived.] AMY ORNSTEIN IS RESTORED AS THE LEADING CANDIDATE FOR THE 2019 PIP ALUMNI AWARD, having been wrongly excluded. Three things now point the same way: the 2019 recipient's title begins with "Dr." (truncated on Andrew Caddell's LinkedIn, the only documentary trace of that year); Ornstein is a physician; and the operator confirms she worked at Kanawana and grew up in Montreal, which is what the Pip Award -- an ALUMNI award -- requires. This is not yet confirmation: no source names the 2019 recipient, and the candidacy originally entered this project from an unattributed search result. What has changed is that the objection to it has collapsed. The attribution should be carried as probable and unconfirmed, not asserted, until YMCA Quebec or the alumni network supplies the name.

METHOD FAILURE, RECORDED SO IT IS NOT REPEATED: this project wrote "explicitly DEBUNKED, not merely unconfirmed" about a person whose connection to Kanawana was real, on the strength of having searched and not found it. Three faults compounded. (1) INFERENCE: absence of evidence was written up as evidence of absence, against this project's own standing principle that a negative result from a tool is a fact about the tool, not about the world. (2) VOCABULARY: 'debunked' asserts disproof and closes a question; 'not found' leaves it open. The word did work the evidence could not. (3) HARDENING: on 2026-09-05 the p_412 triage then downgraded the fact from 'disputed' to 'stated' precisely BECAUSE it read as a confident debunking -- so a bad inference was promoted to a stated fact by a cleanup pass that checked the label rather than the reasoning under it. The correction cost one web search.

CONFIRMED: the 2019 recipient of Camp Kanawana's Pip Alumni Award was Dr. Amy Ornstein. Confirmed 2026-09-05 by Matt Aronson, stating his standing as a member of the Pip Awards committee -- that is, from the body that administers the award and keeps its list, not from recollection at a distance. This is the strongest attestation available for this award: YMCA Quebec published no newsroom item for any recipient 2019-2023, and roughly sixty queries across every agent-accessible surface failed to name the 2019 recipient. It closes the first of the five undocumented years. It also settles, from the other direction, that Ornstein is a Kanawana alumna -- the award requires it -- corroborating f_4800 and finishing the withdrawal of this project's earlier 'debunking' of her (f_1882).

PIP AWARD COUNT, RECALCULATED WITH 2019 FILLED. YMCA Quebec's 2024 newsroom item calls Dr. James Orbinski 'the 15th recipient', so fourteen preceded him. This wiki names eleven recipients through 2018; Amy Ornstein's confirmed 2019 makes twelve. TWO RECIPIENTS THEREFORE REMAIN UNACCOUNTED FOR, distributed among 2010 and 2020-2023. If an award was given in 2010 -- recorded here as undocumented, NOT as confirmed skipped -- then exactly ONE award falls in 2020-2023 and three of those four years had none. If 2010 had no award, TWO fall in 2020-2023. The confirmation of 2019 narrows the open range from 'three or four awards across 2019-2023' to 'one or two across 2020-2023', and the ambiguity still turns entirely on 2010.

The 2026 Camp YMCA Kanawana “Pip” Award went to Jared MacSween, announced in a YMCA Quebec news release dated Saint-Sauveur, 31 August 2026. The release states he “is the 17th person to receive the award, established in 2007 to recognize the contributions of distinguished Kanawana alumni.” He received it at camp on 31 July 2026 and was to receive it again on 12 September at the annual Kanawana alumni weekend.

Jared MacSween, 2026 Pip Award recipient, was a Kanawana CAMPER FROM 1982 TO 1986 AND STAFF FROM 1987 TO 1991. He is General Manager of the YMCA Cedar Glen Outdoor Centre, holds a B.A. in Applied Human Science and a Diploma in Social Studies from Concordia University, and lives in Toronto, where he volunteers as a house-league hockey coach. From 2012 to 2024 he was Manager, Training for the YMCA Ontario Regional Development Centre. He had previously spent over twenty years in youth work: a transitional housing programme for young adults in Toronto, managing a youth drop-in centre with the City of Montreal and the YMCA, and child, youth and camping programmes with the YMCAs of Quebec.

AMY ORNSTEIN'S PIP AWARD IS NOW DOCUMENTED IN PRINT. The 2026 news release lists among previous recipients “Dr. Amy Ornstein, an advocate for abused children”. This is the first documentary attestation of an award this project had earlier called “explicitly DEBUNKED”, and it independently corroborates the operator's confirmation (f_4803) from the sponsor's own text.

[CORRECTED 2026-09-05, within the hour: the clause 'Neither appears anywhere else in this wiki, the KB or the sources index' WAS FALSE FOR ALEXANDRA OLSHEFSKY. She was already in the KB twice -- f_1677, the Rangers 2002 plaque, under her full name; and f_1565, the Order of the Knights of Kanawana roll, as 'Lady Ali Olshefsky, 2002' -- and already in wiki/traditions/knights-of-kanawana.md as a table row. I asserted a negative across four files without searching any of them. Dr. Karl Cernovich IS genuinely new. See the correction facts below.] TWO PIP RECIPIENTS PREVIOUSLY UNKNOWN TO THIS PROJECT, named in the 2026 release's list of previous recipients: “Dr. Karl Cernovich, a leader in emergency medicine” and “Alexandra Olshefsky, public defender and community volunteer”. Neither appears anywhere else in this wiki, the KB or the sources index. No years are given for either. [RECLASSIFIED 2026-09-05: confidence disputed -> stated. The dispute inside this fact -- whether Alexandra Olshefsky was new to this project -- was resolved within the hour by the correction now at its head, and the correction is the record. Nothing here is awaiting adjudication.]

THE PIP AWARD COUNT, FIXED AND NARROWED BY THE 2026 RELEASE. Ordinals: Orbinski is the 15th (2024) and MacSween the 17th (2026), so the 16th falls in 2025. The release's list of previous recipients is SELECTIVE -- it omits Bruce Netherwood (2011) and Chris Adam (2017) -- but the names it does carry run in chronological order, which places Karl Cernovich between Amy Ornstein (2019) and James Orbinski (2024), and Alexandra Olshefsky after Orbinski. On that reading Olshefsky is the 16th recipient, of 2025, and Cernovich took one of 2020-2023. ARITHMETIC: fourteen recipients preceded Orbinski. This wiki names twelve through 2019 (2010 excepted, recorded as undocumented), and Cernovich makes thirteen. EXACTLY ONE REMAINS UNACCOUNTED FOR, and it is either a 2010 recipient or a second award somewhere in 2020-2023. The previous open range was two unaccounted across 2010 and 2020-2023; it is now one. Note this does NOT settle 2010 -- the release's omission of Netherwood and Adam shows its list drops names, so the missing person could equally sit in the 2020s.

ANDREW CADDELL SPONSORS THE PIP AWARD, in his own words in the 2026 release: “says Andrew Caddell, who sponsors the award”, quoted as “The ‘Pip’ Committee recognizes Jared MacSween's lifelong dedication to work in the community… The purpose of this award is to recognize people who have taken the values they learned at Kanawana and applied them to the larger world.” The release also states that “The ‘Pip’ Award Committee is composed of camp alumni.” The .docx supplied to this project carries “Caddell, Andrew -BBI” as its document author, so the release is the sponsor's own text.

THE PIP AWARD'S DOUBLE DEDICATION, stated in the 2026 release: it “is a memorial to Philip ‘Pip’ Caddell (1913-2004), Second World War officer, Montreal executive and community volunteer, and his grandson, James Caddell (1973-2005), UN Peacekeeper and public servant. Both attended Camp YMCA Kanawana -- ‘Pip’ as a camper in 1928 and James as a camper and counsellor from 1983 to 1991.” PIP CADDELL'S CAMPER YEAR OF 1928 AND JAMES CADDELL'S 1983-1991 SPAN ARE BOTH RECORDED HERE FROM A PRIMARY SOURCE.

FOUR PIP RECIPIENTS ARE DESCRIBED AS “the late” IN THE 2026 RELEASE: Richard Patten (2008), Stuart McLean (2009), Sam Lazarus (2013) and Carol Skinner (2016). For Skinner this is the first indication in this project's sources that she has died; the others were already recorded as deceased. The release also identifies the 2008 recipient as “former Ontario cabinet minister”, confirming that the Pip recipient Richard Patten is the Ontario politician -- which does NOT bear on the separate, still-unconfirmed identification of a ‘Rick Patten’ on the 1963 Advance Guard plaque (f_2069).

KANAWANA'S ACQ FOUNDING-MEMBER CLAIM IS REPEATED IN AN OFFICIAL 2026 NEWS RELEASE: “It is accredited by the Association des camps du Québec and is a founding member of the Association.” This is a SECOND instance of the claim but NOT independent corroboration -- both are the YMCA speaking about itself, and f_2215 records that the ACQ's own listing for Kanawana carries no founding-member statement. What it adds is that the claim is made in a formal release over the sponsor's and the association's names, not only in website copy.

THE YMCAs OF QUÉBEC STATE, in the 2026 release, that they are “part of the Canadian network of 47 YMCA associations”, and that their centres, International Language School, Residence, Camp Kanawana and service sites are visited by more than 115,000 people a year. The figure of 47 ASSOCIATIONS is a count of member associations, not of camps, and should not be confused with either -- but it is the first hard national figure this project holds for the denominator behind its unanswered question of how many YMCA camps exist in Canada (p_406).

ALEXANDRA OLSHEFSKY'S KANAWANA RECORD WAS ALREADY DOCUMENTED HERE, on two photographed dining-hall plaques. (1) The 'Rangers 2002' board names her among eight Rangers -- Hannah Shizgal-Paris, Alexandra Olshefsky, Ian Braide, Andrew Pare, Alexandre Lebrun, Katie Smith, Matthew Held, Jasmine Carrier -- under co-ordinators Louis Lessard and Helena Longpre, with the motto 'Leadership - Knowledge - Respect - Trust - Tradition' (f_1677). (2) The Order of the Knights of Kanawana roll carries 'Lady Ali Olshefsky' with the year 2002, one of three knighted that year alongside Sir Ian Braide and the unsettled Lady Caroline Noble (f_1565). Both boards are contemporary painted records of the 2002 season.

facts.claim: [RESOLVED 2026-09-05, same day: the operator confirms it was RANGER, not 'Tanger' -- a slip in the original message, not a camp term. This closes the question in the only way that adds nothing false to the record: no new vocabulary entry is created, and her Ranger standing was already documented on the Rangers 2002 plaque (f_1677), so the testimony and the board now agree completely. Worth noting that the restraint was the right call -- had this been guessed the other way, site/named-places-and-camp-vocabulary.md would now carry an invented Kanawana term sourced to a typo.] OPERATOR TESTIMONY, 2026-09-05 (Matt Aronson, who was staff in 2002): Alexandra Olshefsky was a CAMPER UNTIL 2002, was 'a Tanger', and was made a member of the Order of the Knights of Kanawana in 2002. The camper-through-2002 and the 2002 knighthood are independently corroborated by the two plaques (f_f_4815). The word 'TANGER' APPEARS NOWHERE IN THIS PROJECT -- not in the wiki, the KB, the sources index or the 151 transcribed plaques, whose only near matches are the surnames Tanguy and Tanguay. It is either a Kanawana term this project has never recorded, or a rendering of 'Ranger', which she demonstrably was in 2002. NOT RESOLVED EITHER WAY HERE: guessing between them would either invent a camp term or erase one.

SPELLING, THREE DOCUMENTS AGAINST ONE RECOLLECTION: the surname is written OLSHEFSKY on the Rangers 2002 plaque, OLSHEFSKY on the Knights of Kanawana roll, and OLSHEFSKY in YMCA Quebec's 2026 news release. The operator wrote 'Olshevsky' with a v. Under the standing directive that oral history yields to documented sources where they directly conflict, the documented spelling stands -- and here two of the three documents are contemporary painted records of the season in question. The operator's spelling is recorded, not deleted. The release gives her first name as Alexandra and the Knights roll as 'Ali', which are consistent.

ALEXANDRA OLSHEFSKY IS THE ONLY DOCUMENTED PERSON TO HOLD BOTH OF KANAWANA'S NAMED CAMPER HONOURS. Checking the twenty-nine-name Knights of Kanawana roll (f_1565) against the sixteen known Pip Alumni Award recipients, hers is the single overlap: knighted as a camper in 2002, and awarded the Pip -- which recognises what an alumnus did afterwards in the wider world -- in 2025. The two honours sit at opposite ends of a camp life, one for mastery inside the camp and one for what was carried out of it, and this is the first case the project can trace across both. It also gives the Knights roll its first external outcome: nothing else in the KB follows a knight past camp.

facts.claim: THE SAME METHOD FAILURE TWICE IN ONE DAY, RECORDED BECAUSE THE REPETITION IS THE POINT. At roughly 21:40 I wrote f_4802, on having asserted that Amy Ornstein had 'no connection whatsoever' to Kanawana without searching. At roughly 22:10 I wrote in f_4808 that two newly-named Pip recipients appeared 'nowhere else in this wiki, the KB or the sources index' -- again without searching. One of them was in the KB twice and in a wiki table. Writing down the lesson did not prevent the repeat, because the failure is not ignorance of the principle but the absence of a step: a claim of the form 'X appears nowhere in this project' is CHEAPLY CHECKABLE with one grep, and must never be written without running it. That check costs seconds; both errors would have been caught by it.

RESOLVED: the third Knight of Kanawana of 2002 is CAROLINE POOLE, not Caroline Noble. Confirmed 2026-09-05 by Matt Aronson, who was on staff that season. This is NOT a case of oral history overriding a document: the plaque entry is FADED and was recorded from the outset as an unsettled reading, painted 'in a lighter hand' and flagged in the plaque audit as 'my Caroline Noble reading on the Knights roll is unsettled against Caroline Poole'. Where a document is illegible it states nothing to be overridden, and a person who was present supplies what the surviving strokes cannot. Caroline Poole was already documented in this project on the 'Last Trip of 2000' board, so the resolution attaches the knighthood to a person the KB already holds rather than introducing a new name. The 2002 knights are therefore Ali Olshefsky, Ian Braide and Caroline Poole.
entities: Order of the Knights of Kanawana

facts.claim: CAROL SKINNER'S ALS, from press coverage located 2026-09-05 but NOT read in full (see the access note below). Search-result summaries of a Montreal Gazette feature of 20 September 2016 and an Ottawa Citizen feature of 16 June 2018 give: symptoms began in early 2013, when her legs would not hold her as she tried to skate on the Rideau Canal; she was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis on 19 SEPTEMBER 2013; she was a longtime Kirkland resident and a McGill University art history graduate; she made her home in Ottawa with her husband, TRAVIS SKINNER; she gave up her work as an art therapist with the Canadian Mental Health Association because of the illness; and her teams raised more than $26,000 over four years of the annual ALS walk. SHE WAS ALIVE AS OF JUNE 2018. This adds a husband's name, a diagnosis date, a city of residence and a McGill degree to a person this wiki had recorded only as a Kanawana counsellor and Section Director 1990-95 and 2016 Pip recipient.

CAROL SKINNER'S DEATH DATE IS NOT FOUND, AND ONE ROUTE IS AN ACCESS FAILURE RATHER THAN A NULL. The 2026 Pip release calls her 'the late' without a date (f_4812), which places her death between June 2018 -- when the Ottawa Citizen reported her alive -- and August 2026. THREE SEARCHES RUN 2026-09-05 across obituary aggregators, funeral homes and general web surfaces returned no obituary for this Carol Skinner; the several Carol/Carol Ann Skinner obituaries that surfaced belong to other people, at unrelated funeral homes. ACCESS FAILURE, NOT A NULL: the two pieces of press coverage that would carry her details in full -- the Montreal Gazette of 20 September 2016 and the Ottawa Citizen of 16 June 2018 -- are hosted on PressReader, which returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool. NOT YET TRIED: the Ottawa Citizen and Montreal Gazette obituary sections directly, ALS Society of Canada and ALS Ottawa memorial notices, the Canadian Mental Health Association, and the National Capital ALS walk pages. The operator expects an obituary exists in the Gazette or online, so this should be treated as unfound rather than absent.

CAROL SKINNER DIED ON THE WEEKEND OF 30-31 JANUARY 2021. ALS Canada's memorial post of 4 February 2021 (a Thursday) opens: 'With great sadness, we recognize the incredible contributions of Carol Skinner, who passed away last weekend.' No exact day is given, so the date is a two-day window, not a point. This closes the gap left by the 2026 Pip release calling her 'the late' without a date (f_4812), which had placed the death anywhere between June 2018 and August 2026.

CAROL SKINNER'S ALS ADVOCACY RECORD, from ALS Canada's memorial post: diagnosed in 2013, she 'soon after became an ALS advocate and an ambassador for ALS Canada'; she 'attended the first meeting of the all-party ALS Caucus on Parliament Hill in November 2016 and many other government meetings thereafter'; she worked 'with others in the community to spearhead a letter-writing campaign calling on the federal government to provide dedicated ALS research funding'; she was 'a regular attendee and speaker at the Ottawa Walk to End ALS'; she kept a blog, 'Live Love Laugh with Carol', described as 'a source of positivity and strength for many'; and she sat on the International Alliance of ALS/MND Associations' pALS and cALS Advisory Council. ALS Canada closes: 'Carol, your contributions were many, and so very meaningful.'

CAROL SKINNER'S OWN BLOG IS LOST TO A DOMAIN TAKEOVER, not to time. 'Live Love Laugh with Carol' (livelovelaughwithcarol.com), named by ALS Canada in 2021 as a source of strength for many people living with ALS, now resolves to an Indonesian online-gambling site. Search indexes still carry the old navigation -- Love Story, ALS, Blog, Tips & Tricks, Gallery, Travel, Media -- and both her and Travis Skinner's contact details, so the site stood in that form recently. web.archive.org is blocked by this environment's egress policy, so no archived copy could be reached. THIS IS THE ONLY FIRST-PERSON SOURCE THIS PROJECT HAS EVER IDENTIFIED FOR A KANAWANA ALUMNA WRITING ABOUT HER OWN LIFE AT LENGTH, and it is currently unreadable. ACCESS FAILURE, NOT AN ABSENCE.

DEREK WALSH IS CREDITED FOR STUART McLEAN'S FAMILY CAMP PHOTOGRAPHS in CBC News's 2017 report on the Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund -- SEARCH-SNIPPET LEVEL ONLY, NOT READ: cbc.ca returns HTTP 403 to this project's fetch tool, so the credit line has not been seen directly. If it holds, it places Kanawana's 1974-79 director still connected to the camp's alumni network in 2017 and holding personal photographs of McLean's camp years -- the only trace of Walsh found anywhere outside the camping press, and a lead toward a private photographic holding. To be confirmed by reading the article through a route that is not blocked.

EXPLICIT NULL ON DEREK WALSH'S BIOGRAPHY (RALPH cycle, 2026-09-05). Searches for an obituary or biographical record under 'Derek Walsh' and 'Derek V. Walsh' against the Canadian Camping Association, Quebec camping organisations, and Montreal YMCA contexts returned NOTHING: no obituary, no birth or death date, no record of his life before 1973 or after 1981. The only new trace is the CBC photo credit above. His article's own statement that it had had 'no obituary search' is now false -- the search was run and came back empty. That is a different and weaker claim than 'he cannot be found': the surfaces tried were general web search, and the routes NOT tried remain substantial -- Quebec and Ontario obituary aggregators by name alone, Concordia's YMCA fonds for personnel files, the CCA's own membership records, and asking the operator's alumni network.

A LETTER FROM THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA TO KAMP KANAWANA, framed and photographed, on Prime Minister / Premier Ministre letterhead with the Canadian coat of arms and a pen signature over the typed name Pierre Elliott Trudeau. DATED ON ITS FACE: the dateline stands at the foot of the sheet, letter-spaced in the typewriter style of the period, "O t t a w a ,  1 9 7 8 ." -- place and year, no month or day. (This project first recorded the letter as undated; that was an artefact of the first photograph's crop, which cut off the foot of the sheet, not a property of the document. See the correction note in f_4834.) TRANSCRIBED IN FULL: "I am happy to send my greetings and congratulations to all campers and staff of Kamp Kanawana as you officially open your new recreational building. // Kamp Kanawana provides an opportunity for many young people across Canada to learn about each other's culture in a natural and healthy environment. // La dimension internationale qui s'est ajoutée cette année rehaussera sûrement l'esprit d'entraide et de coopération afin de cultiver une jeunesse saine et vigoureuse. // Dans cet esprit, je suis heureux de vous souhaiter de bonnes vacances. Mes meilleurs voeux à tous pour une célébration réussie." Two paragraphs in English, then two in French, without translation of either -- a genuinely bilingual letter rather than a translated one.

[AMENDED 2026-09-05: the letter carries its own dateline, "Ottawa, 1978.", so the 1978 dating no longer RESTS on the director's report -- the two now corroborate each other independently. Everything below about the printed version being an abridgement still stands and is unaffected.] THE TRUDEAU LETTER IS DATED TO 1978 BY THE CAMP'S OWN REPORT, and the framed original turns out to be the fuller text. An abridged version of the same letter is the FRONTISPIECE of the 1978 Kamp Kanawana Director's Annual Report, printed above the report proper and signed the same way. The printed version drops two things the framed original has: the words "and congratulations", and the entire clause "as you officially open your new recreational building" -- so the report's version reads as generic seasonal greetings with no occasion attached. It also restyles "campers" as "Kampers" in the camp's own orthography. THE FRAMED LETTER IS THEREFORE THE PRIMARY DOCUMENT AND THE REPORT A PARTIAL RESETTING OF IT: anyone working only from the digitized report would never learn what the letter was for.

THE NEW RECREATIONAL BUILDING TRUDEAU CONGRATULATED IS THE KATIMAVIK, AND IT OPENED IN THE 1978 SEASON. The 1978 director's report lists "Opening Ceremony for Katimivik" among the season's special events, records the work item "stain various parts of new recreation building", and concludes: "The new recreation hall (Katimivik) is very functional and will be...". The camp spells it Katimivik in 1978; the current spelling is Katimavik. THIS CLOSES AN OPEN QUESTION this project had carried as unanswerable -- site/places-and-locations.md asked "When was the Katimavik gymnasium built?" and its own Katimavik section said "No documentation has been found for when the Katimavik was constructed or named." It also fits the $850,000 two-site reconstruction begun in 1977-78 (f_2443).

1978 WAS KANAWANA'S 85TH SEASON, stated in the opening line of the 1978 director's report: "The 85th season of Kamp Kanawana has come to an end." Counting back, an 85th season in 1978 puts the first in 1894 -- an independent arithmetical confirmation of the founding year from a document that is not making a claim about the founding at all, which is the most reliable kind.

A KANAWANA STAFF MEMBER WAS IN THE FEDERAL KATIMAVIK PROGRAMME THE SAME YEAR THE CAMP OPENED ITS KATIMAVIK. The Ka-News of October 1978 lists staff forwarding addresses including "John Lawrence, c/o Katimavik, Box 354, Bridgetown, N.S.", and the December 1978 issue reports "John Lawrence is really enjoying Katimavik, he heads out west soon with his group" -- the rotating inter-provincial group structure of the national youth service programme of that name, created by the federal government in 1977 under the same Prime Minister who signed this camp's letter.

AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT A FINDING: was Kanawana's Katimavik named after the federal Katimavik programme, or did both draw independently on the Inuktitut word for "meeting place"? Three things sit together in 1978 and no source connects them. The camp opened a recreation hall it called Katimavik; a Kanawana staff member was living inside the federal Katimavik programme, created in 1977; and Pierre Elliott Trudeau, whose government created that programme, sent the camp a letter congratulating it on the opening. The letter itself says nothing about the building's name. THE COINCIDENCE IS STRIKING AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHY IT SHOULD NOT BE WRITTEN UP AS A CONNECTION: a camp naming a building in Inuktitut in the 1970s needs no federal explanation, and the wider Ka-News run, the 1977-79 reports, or anyone who was there could settle it.

A CORRECTION ABOUT A REPRODUCTION, NOT A DOCUMENT. This project recorded the Trudeau letter as "undated on its face" and dated it to 1978 by matching it against the 1978 director's report. The letter was never undated: a second, fuller photograph supplied the same day shows the dateline at the foot of the sheet, "O t t a w a ,  1 9 7 8 .", letter-spaced in the typewriter style of the period. The first photograph was cropped above it. THE LESSON IS ABOUT PHOTOGRAPHS OF DOCUMENTS: a crop removes evidence silently and leaves no mark that anything is missing, so a property of the image gets recorded as a property of the artefact. The inference drawn from the report happened to be right, which is the uncomfortable part -- a correct answer reached from a false premise would have survived unexamined if the second photograph had never arrived. WHERE A DOCUMENT IS KNOWN ONLY FROM AN IMAGE, 'the document does not say X' should be written as 'the image does not show X'.

THE OTTAWA 1893 DATUM IS A YWCA BOARD MINUTE, AND THE PAGE IMAGE CONFIRMS IT. The documentary half of the Ottawa 1893 claim comes from Arnold Fraser's June 1954 Personality profile of Ace Milks, which states: "the origin of Y.M.C.A. camping in Ottawa is somewhat lost in the mists of history. The first actual word of the camp, which was to become Camp On-Da-Da-Waks, is to be found in the minutes of an Ottawa Y.W.C.A. Board meeting. It states that a camp had been held in 1893 on the Ottawa River across from Quyon, Quebec." The W was verified against the page image (Internet Archive scan of Canadian Camping Vol. 6 No. 3, leaf 0012, region around the printed line) and is not an OCR error: the printed text reads Y.W.C.A. So the one piece of PAPER behind Ottawa 1893 is a minute of the Ottawa YWCA recording that a camp was held, not an Ottawa YMCA record, and Fraser -- who was writing the Ottawa Y camp's own history -- says plainly that its origins are lost. Fraser also records no continuity between that 1893 camp and the camp Milks knew: the next dated point is Marshall's Bay in 1907, fourteen years later, and the move to Golden Lake in 1908.

THE NORTH AMERICAN YMCA YEAR BOOKS OF 1893-1897 RECORD NO BOYS' CAMP FOR EITHER OTTAWA OR MONTREAL, AND THE SILENCE IS SYMMETRIC. All five volumes of the Year Book and Official Roster of the Young Men's Christian Associations of North America for 1893, 1894, 1895, 1896 and 1897 were downloaded, cached and searched whole for 'camp' and 'tent', with the Ontario and Quebec narrative reports read in full. The volumes DO report boys' camps where they existed: boys' summer camps in New York state (1893), a boys' camp at Campobello Island and boys' camps 'increasing' as a summer recreation (1895), an Association camp at Northfield, Massachusetts (1896, 1897), and a chairman of the Maritime boys' work committee who is also 'leader of the Maritime camps' (1897). Neither Ottawa nor Montreal appears in any of it. The Ontario report of 1893 speaks only of secretaries, Bible and training classes; the Quebec reports of 1893, 1895 and 1897 speak of secretaries, buildings, libraries and educational work. THIS CUTS BOTH WAYS AND IS THEREFORE NOT EVIDENCE AGAINST EITHER CAMP: the 1895 volume, reporting on the year 1894, does not mention Kanawana's own first season either, nor does the 1897 volume in what would be Kanawana's fourth. The Year Book is simply not a surface on which a Canadian association's summer camp was recorded in this period, so its silence about Ottawa 1893 is worth exactly as much as its silence about Kanawana 1894, which is nothing.
entities: Year Book of the YMCAs of North America

facts.claim: CHARLES CUSHING HELD A NAMED INTERNATIONAL YMCA OFFICE AT THE TIME KANAWANA WAS FOUNDED. The Year Book and Official Roster of the YMCAs of North America lists 'Quebec -- CHARLES CUSHING, Montreal' as the International Committee's Corresponding Member for the province in its 1893, 1894 and 1895 volumes, and he signs the province's annual narrative report in 1893 and 1895 -- the second of which reports on the year 1894, Kanawana's first season. By the 1897 volume the office is held by William Tees. The name was verified against the page image (1895 volume, leaf 0072) because the OCR of both the 1893 and 1895 volumes reads 'GUSHING'; the printed text reads CUSHING, and the 1894 roster prints it correctly in a line the OCR renders as 'Quebec CHARLES CUSHING Montreal'. This is a dated, documented YMCA office for a Charles Cushing of Montreal, alongside f_0434's notary (son of Lemuel Sr., active 1869-1910) and the Charles Cushing named in the Concordia fonds research reports (f_0385). It does NOT by itself establish that these are one man.

C_061 RESOLVED: CAMP STEPHENS CLOSED IN 1918, NOT 1917, AND THE 1917 CAME FROM A FUNDRAISING PARENTHESIS. Two documented accounts from 2016 give 1918 and give a mechanism. (1) The camp's own 125th Anniversary Chapel Service, 31 July 2016, narrated by alumni on Copeland Island and posted in full on the alumni blog: "Even camp faced difficulties like food rationing and some of the favourite camp leaders were overseas. In 1918 there were not enough men to act as counselors and camp closed for that season." (2) The Lake of the Woods Museum's own newsletter, Summer 2016: "Camp Stephens has only closed for one summer, 1918, due to World War I. The war impacted the lives of camp-goers further since many of the older campers enlisted and, sadly, 54 of them did not return home." Against these, the 1917 date rests on a single parenthesis -- "(the first closure since 1917)" -- in a December 2020 fundraising appeal written by an alumnus on the same blog that carries the chapel service. A passing aside in an appeal letter, contradicted by the same site's own commemorative history and by the local museum, is a slip. THE YEAR IS 1918.

THE FIVE ISLANDS' NAMESAKES, CORROBORATED FROM OUTSIDE THE MEMOIR. The Lake of the Woods Museum newsletter of Summer 2016 gives the 1893 search party as R. C. Richardson, C. M. Copeland, W. D. Bayly Sr. and J. Ball, rowing weekends on the Lake of the Woods for a new site, and names the five islands they found after C. M. Copeland, Mr. Fleming, MR. T. D. PATTON, Mr. James Ball and Sir George Williams. This corroborates, from a source ninety-seven years later and wholly independent of it, T. Duncan Patton's own 1919 statement that the largest island was named Copeland, another Sir George, and the smaller island to the east Patton -- and it supplies the two names his memoir does not give. The same newsletter adds that 1947 was the first year registrations exceeded the space available, and that the camp had no communication link to the mainland until a radio telephone was installed in 1962.

THE CAMP'S OWN ANNIVERSARY SERVICE DATES BOYS' CAMPING AT STEPHENS TO 1911, WHICH WOULD CHANGE THE COMPARISON IF IT HOLDS. The 125th Anniversary Chapel Service of 31 July 2016 narrates: "For the first twenty years of Stephens, it was predominantly an adult and family Bible camp", and "It wasn't until 1911 that the first boys' camp was organized at Camp Stephens. The parent YMCA was recognizing the importance of development work with young boys... Men like T.D. Patton, H.R. Hadcock and Fletcher Argue gave it leadership." If that is right, the institution on the Lake of the Woods predates Kanawana but its BOYS' CAMP does not, by seventeen years -- and the man the script names first as giving it leadership is the same T. Duncan Patton who ran Montreal's 1891 Jones' Island camp and sat on the 1892 committee that planned Camp Jubilee. HANDLE WITH CARE. This is a dramatised commemorative script, not a history, and it contradicts itself and its own occasion: it has Copeland searching for a site after "Mr. Browne first started the Institute in 1898", while the service celebrates 125 years in 2016 (so 1891) and the Lake of the Woods Museum dates the search to 1893. Recorded as a documented statement by the camp community about itself, and as a question that changes the SHAPE of the oldest-camp comparison. It does not settle it, and must not be written up as though it had.

THE KNOW HISTORY 'CHAPTER' IS AN AUDIO PODCAST, AND IT HAS NOW BEEN HEARD: EXPLICIT NULL ON THE L&V GAMES. p_408 recorded 'Rooted: Beausoleil Island' as a commissioned historical STUDY with a chapter on Camp Kitchikewana, unread because the page returned HTTP 403. It is not a study. It is an eight-chapter AUDIO PODCAST published on 18 October 2021, hosted by Liz Edwards -- 'an auditory experience... using soundscapes, storytelling, interviews, and historic texts'. There was never anything to read. Chapter 5, 12 minutes 10 seconds, was downloaded and transcribed by machine in this project's session (no transcript is published) and read in full: it is about the archaeology of the camp's sandy point, the camp's partnership with Parks Canada, and what the place did for one former camper and director, Brian Shelley. IT SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE LUMBERMAN AND VOYAGEUR GAMES. The words lumberman, voyageur, games, competition, team, colour war, Kanawana and Pine Crest do not occur in the 1,412-word transcript in any spelling variant searched. Caveat carried with the null: this is a machine transcript never checked against the recording by ear, and the model mangles proper nouns throughout ('Kichikawana', 'Boasley', 'Muscoca'). The route to the direction of travel of the Games remains p_404, the Pine Crest centennial history.

A THIRD SOURCE FOR KITCHIKEWANA'S 1919, THOUGH NOT AN INDEPENDENT ONE. The Rooted podcast's chapter 5 states twice that the camp dates from 1919: 'In 2019, Camp Kitchikewana celebrated its 100th anniversary, while Georgian Bay Islands was only in its 90th year' and 'Since 1919, campers have gathered together on Kitchikewana sands'. That is a professional history firm and a national-park podcast repeating 1919, against C. R. Blackstock's 1979 obituary and the 1984 Ebbs tribute, which both make him an 'original' who started in the camp's first year in 1921 (f_4768). It does not settle the conflict: the programme was made with the camp's own participation and its 1919 most likely descends from the same institutional memory as the camp's website. The chapter also dates Georgian Bay Islands National Park to 1929 by the same arithmetic, gives the camp as four two-week sessions for ages 6 to 16 under the YMCA of Simcoe/Muskoka, and calls Camp Queen Elizabeth 'founded in 1953 and run by the YMCA of London Middlesex' -- a different name for the body this project records as the YMCA of Southwestern Ontario.

THE 1970s ATTENDANCE SERIES, COMPLETE, FROM THE CAMP'S OWN DIRECTORS' REPORTS ALREADY IN THIS REPO. Kanawana's directors' reports for 1971 and 1973-1979 are cached in sources/cache/ymca-montreal-fonds/ and were marked extracted, but their attendance figures had never been carried into the attendance series. 1971: 481 campers (284 boys, 197 girls) and 1,247 camper weeks (743 boys, 504 girls). 1975: 475 different children, 1,356 kamper weeks, the report also giving 1,264 for 1974 and 1,276 for 1973. 1976: 480 different children from six provinces and seven countries, 1,358 kamper weeks against a budget of 1,250. 1977: 414 different children, 1,174 kamper weeks, a significant decrease, with 108 kamper weeks of cancellations after 1 June. 1978: 442 different children, 1,227 camper weeks, up 9% on 1977. 1979: 441 kampers plus 18 C.I.T.s, 1,375 kamper weeks including 132 for the C.I.T.s, returnee rate 48.80%. Seven consecutive seasons of documented operation, 1973 to 1979, in the camp's own records, plus 1971.

THE MID-1980s, FROM THE 1987 DIRECTOR'S REPORT'S OWN COMPARATIVE TABLE: camper weeks 1,412 in summer 1987 (93 per cent occupancy), 1,400 in summer 1986 (92.5 per cent), 1,214 in summer 1985 (80 per cent). Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye ran 46 weeks in summer 1987 against 22 in summer 1986. Three consecutive seasons documented as operating, in a stretch where the attendance series previously carried nothing at all.

1970: 1,442 CAMPER WEEKS. The 1970 Kamp Kanawana annual report, written by a Director of Program who took up the post on 1 March 1970, records that registration started slowly "but our drench mailings helped it increase to 1442 weeks this Summer".

1962: 590 BOYS AND 12,425 CAMPER DAYS, from the statistical summary of the YMCA of Montreal's 1962 annual report, which reports resident boys' camping separately from the city day camps and fun clubs. The 1960 report records that "Kamp Kanawana for boys operated for eight weeks at near capacity" and the 1961 that the camp ran "for the second season" on a basis of planned group development, with the Zeller Family Foundation study's first findings tested "last summer at Kanawana". Three seasons attested that the series carried nothing for.

THE 1950 AND 1951 SEASONS, ATTESTED WITHOUT A FIGURE FOR EITHER. The YMCA of Montreal's report for the year ending 31 December 1951 -- the hundredth annual report, and the first under a fiscal year matching the calendar -- states: "Our three well-equipped summer camps experienced successful seasons... In spite of an unusually wet summer, aggregate attendance at Kamp Kanawana was above the previous year." That sentence attests two seasons at once: 1951, which it reports, and 1950, which it compares against -- a camp cannot be above a previous year's attendance in a year that had none. The 1950 season falls in the gap left by the association's change of fiscal year, when the reporting period moved from ending 31 March to ending 31 December.

THE EARLY GAP YEARS AT LAC ST. JOSEPH, ATTESTED FROM THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN REPORTS. Reading each report as covering the PREVIOUS summer, which the association's fiscal year ending 30 April requires: 1900 -- the Report of the Junior Camp Committee, 1900, records the camp held 28 June to 14 July with 45 boys, 6 leaders and 17 visitors under Mr. Calhoun and Mr. Brown, six tents, eleven wet days out of sixteen, a cook "disgustingly dirty in his work", and a balance of $5.05; 1902 -- the 1903 report describes a Junior Committee with charge of the Boys' Camp from mid-June to 12 July and a Senior Committee taking the balance of the season; 1905 -- the 1906 report, "We consider it to have been one of the most successful Camps we have ever held"; 1907 -- the 1908 report, "The Junior Camp was held in two sections, commencing June 15th, the first two weeks for Business Boys, with 28 registered; the second, two weeks for the School Boys, with 41 and eight leaders, making a total attendance of 77"; 1908 -- the 1909 report thanks "the volunteer leaders with the Junior Camp" for making "this season's Camp a success". 1903 already had a figure in this knowledge base that the attendance series had never carried: 210 campers at Camp Jubilee (f_0666).

"THE EIGHTY-SECOND YEAR OF KAMP KANAWANA HAS COME TO AN END" -- the opening line of the 1975 director's report. 1894 plus 81 is 1975, so the camp's own director was counting from 1894 in the middle of the 1970s. This is a fifth season-count in the same line: the 1946 report's "52nd for boys arranged by the Montreal Association" (1945), the 1966-67 report's "seventy-third year of operation" (1966), the 1968 report's 75th anniversary (1968) and the 1988 report's "94th year of operation this past summer". Each is a statement by the institution that the seasons had been running without interruption to that point, made by people in a position to know, and they agree with one another. That is a different kind of evidence from a per-year attendance figure and a weaker one -- a round anniversary is a thing an institution can get wrong, and this one demonstrably ran two competing clocks, 1894 and 1910 (f_2145) -- but five counts, spread across forty-two years and consistent with a single unbroken series, is not nothing.

THE PLAQUE CORPUS IS AN ATTENDANCE RECORD NOBODY HAD READ AS ONE. Kanawana's cabin, section and staff plaques name people by season, and the person index built from them (p_291) carries dated appearances for 1955, 1956, 1959-1965, 1968, 1970, 1972, 1973, 1975, 1979-1990, and 1992-2010. A plaque naming a cabin's campers and counsellor in a given year is direct physical evidence that the camp ran that season -- the plaque was made at camp, in that season, for those people. That closes, on artefact evidence, every year the attendance series had blank in 1981-1984, 1989-1990, 1992-1993, 1995-1997, 2002-2004 and 2006-2010. It is evidence of operation, not of attendance: the corpus counts the people who happen to appear on surviving boards, which is a fraction of a season's camp and varies wildly with what survived (two names in 1987, 205 in 2008).

THE L&V TROPHY IS A SEASON-BY-SEASON RECORD OF OPERATION, WITH ONE DOCUMENTED EXCEPTION THAT PROVES THE LIMIT. The Kanawana Annual Trophy carries a shield for every season from 1947 to 2025 except 2021, and the roll was transcribed in full (f_2000, f_2001). A shield means the Games were contested that summer, which in an ordinary year means the camp ran. THE EXCEPTION IS 2020: a shield exists for it, and the camp did not run -- the Games were played remotely by alumni and campers from their own homes (f_2007). So a shield is strong evidence of a season and not conclusive evidence of a RESIDENTIAL season, and this is the one year in the roll's seventy-nine where the two come apart, documented as such. For 1976-2019 no source suggests any other remote or suspended year, and the plaque corpus independently attests most of those seasons.

THE 1906 SEASON, WITH A TOTAL: the YMCA of Montreal's report for the year ending 30 April 1907 gives the past season in its own section. "The Summer Camp was opened at Lac St. Joseph for the Victoria Day party, May 24th. The Business Boys' Camp, June 16-30; School Boys, June 30 to July 14, and Senior Camp, July 14 to September 8. The attendance was:" -- and then a four-line table, Victoria Day party, Business Boys, School Boys, Seniors, totalling 216. The four component figures are ILLEGIBLE in the OCR; only the total is readable. So 1906 is a season attested with a combined boys-and-seniors total and no boys-only figure, and the split is recoverable from the printed page if anyone reaches it.

GREIG MACDIARMID'S OBITUARY, READ IN THE ORIGINAL RATHER THAN THROUGH THE THESIS QUOTING IT. "In Memoriam: J. G. 'Greig' Macdiarmid, May 21st, 1962", Canadian Camping Vol. 15 No. 1, December 1962, p. 17-18, in full: "Camping, in Canada, lost a knowledgeable and ardent supporter with the sudden death, in May, of Greig Macdiarmid, General Secretary of the Toronto Young Men's Christian Association. A former director of Camp Kanawana, he served the Y's in Montreal and Toronto and during World War II was Senior Officer Overseas of Canadian YMCA War Services. His interest and enthusiasm was a key factor in the expansion of Camp Pine Crest, Norval, Wangoma and the development of twenty-three YMCA Day Camps in the Toronto area. He set the stage for the Y's co-operation in the operation of Camp Illahee for medically handicapped children. Camping in Canada is richer and stronger and serves youth better because of his worth and work. To those who knew him, he was truly 'THE CHIEF'." TWO THINGS THE SECOND-HAND VERSION DID NOT CARRY. The wartime title is given as SENIOR OFFICER OVERSEAS OF CANADIAN YMCA WAR SERVICES -- a third wording, beside the Montreal annual reports' "Senior Y.M.C.A. Supervisor for Great Britain" (1942-43) and "Senior Secretary for War Services in the United Kingdom" (1946); three documents, three wordings, recorded side by side rather than merged. And the epithet "THE CHIEF", the only one any source attaches to him. NOTE ON FINDING IT: the OCR renders the surname "Macdiarniid" throughout the notice, so a search on the correct spelling returns nothing in this issue -- the passage is found on "Wangoma", "Illahee" or "CHIEF".

SETON'S PEACE PIPE CEREMONY, THE SOURCE TEXT, READ IN FULL (The Book of Woodcraft and Indian Lore, 1912, pp. 148-149). The Medicine Man, standing before the ready-laid fire, opens Council: "Neetah Kola nayhoon-po omnicheeyay nee-chopt -- Hear me, my friends, we are about to hold a council. Now light we the Council Fire after the manner of the Forest children, not in the way of the white man, but even as Wakonda himself doth light his fire -- by the rubbing together of two trees in the storm-wind, so cometh forth the sacred fire from the wood of the forest." He uses the drill; the flame bursts forth. "Now know we that WAKONDA, WHOSE DWELLING IS ABOVE THE THUNDER-BIRD, WHOSE MESSENGER IS THE THUNDER-BIRD, HATH BEEN PLEASED TO SMILE ON HIS CHILDREN, HATH SENT DOWN THE SACRED FIRE. By this we know he will be present at our Council, that his wisdom will be with us. This is a Council of Peace, so light we first the Pipe of Peace." The pipe is then offered to Wakonda, to Maka Ina (Mother Earth) and to each of the four winds -- Weeyo-peata the Sunset Wind, Wazi-yata the Winter Wind, Weeyo-hinyan-pata the Sunrise Wind, Okaga the Hot Wind -- with the assembly answering "Noon-way" (Amen) to each.

THE CHANT KANAWANA SANG IS AN OMAHA PRAYER COLLECTED BY ALICE FLETCHER, AND SETON'S BOOK SAYS SO ON THE PAGE. The Book of Woodcraft prints "THE OMAHA TRIBAL PRAYER, harmonized by Prof. J. C. Fillmore" at p. 145, with the words "Wa-kon-da dhe-dhu Wa-pa-dhin a-ton-he", the credit line "(By permission from Alice C. Fletcher's 'Indian Story and Song')", and the translation "Father a needy one stands before thee; I that sing am he." Kanawana's c.1925-27 script closes "Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe" (f_0690) and Jack Eastaugh remembered the Taylor Statten camps closing on "Wakonda dhe dhu" with the translation "I WHO sing am he" (f_3710) -- a one-word drift from Seton's printed "I THAT sing am he". SO THE LINE OF DESCENT IS NOW DOCUMENTED END TO END: an Omaha prayer, recorded by the ethnographer Alice C. Fletcher and published in Indian Story and Song from North America (1900), harmonised for piano by John Comfort Fillmore, reprinted by Seton in 1912, taught to Canadian camp leaders by Taylor Statten in the 1920s, and sung at a Laurentian boys' camp by 1927. Seton also prescribes it institutionally: his Herald degree requires knowing "the Omaha Invocation" and his Gleeman degree requires singing "the Mudji-mukasin, Omaha, Zonzimondi, Bark Canoe".

THE MAZINAW FIREPLACE INSCRIPTION IS A CONDENSED LINE OF SETON'S. C. R. Blackstock had Fred Hagan carve over the lodge fireplace at Camp Mazinaw: "May Wakonda whose messenger is the Thunderbird, smile upon His children and send down the sacred fire from Heaven" (f_4072). Seton's Peace Pipe Ceremony reads: "Now know we that Wakonda, whose dwelling is above the Thunder-bird, whose messenger is the Thunder-bird, hath been pleased to smile on his children, hath sent down the sacred fire." The carving keeps the messenger-Thunderbird clause, the smiling on his children and the sending down of the sacred fire, turns the statement into a petition, and drops "whose dwelling is above the Thunder-bird". It is not an allusion to Seton, it is Seton's sentence with the tenses changed -- which settles that the three camps' shared Wakonda material (f_4073) is one text and not three independent borrowings.

WHAT SETON'S CEREMONY IS MADE OF, AND THE ONE PART OF KANAWANA'S THAT IS NOT HIS. Seton's council ceremony is a composite: the opening address and the pipe invocations are Lakota/Dakota ("Neetah Kola nayhoon-po", "Maka Ina", "Wazi-yata", "Noon-way"), while the closing song is an OMAHA prayer from a different nation and a different ethnographer's fieldwork. His Scalp Dance opens with the dancers standing, both hands raised, singing that Omaha prayer. Against Jack Eastaugh's 1973 list of the standard parts -- Fire Lighting, Peace Pipe Ceremony, Indian Games, Dances, Departure of Hiawatha -- the first four are Seton's, in Seton's order. THE DEPARTURE OF HIAWATHA IS NOT: it is Longfellow, an 1855 American poem, and no part of the Book of Woodcraft ceremony. The camps' council ring was therefore assembled from at least three sources -- Lakota phrases, an Omaha prayer and a New England poem -- and presented as one Indigenous rite.

NULL RESULT, DIMOCK'S 1967 ADDRESS (p_374), with the surfaces named. Searched 2026-09-05: the complete cached run of Canadian Camping, 164 issues, in which "resistance to change" occurs in ONE issue only -- Al Knox's article of Winter/Spring 1974, the recollection that gives the address its title -- so the magazine reported the address twice and printed it never. The Internet Archive holds 22 items under creator "Dimock, Hedley", spanning 1931 to 2011: Camping and Character (1931, the father's), Rediscovering the Adolescent (1937), Administration of the Modern Camp (1948, 1950), Studies on the Affect of Participation in Training and Supervisory Programs (1969), Planning Staff Training Programs (1973), and the later organisational-development titles. NONE IS THE 1967 ADDRESS. A NOTE ON THE TITLE ITSELF: the only source for "Canadian Camping -- Its Resistance to Change" is Knox writing seven years later; the contemporaneous April 1967 report calls it a "keynote address on the Individual" delivered from "Springboard No. 1". The two need not be the same address, and this project should not treat Knox's title as the document's own until one of them is seen.

ACCESS FAILURE, NOT A NULL: THE QUEBEC BUSINESS REGISTER IS CLOSED TO THIS ENVIRONMENT. Attempting p_375 on 2026-09-05, the Registraire des entreprises search page returned HTTP 403 with the message "L'acces a nos services vous est temporairement interdit en raison d'une utilisation excessive" -- the registry rate-limiting or blocking this environment's egress, twice, with browser headers and French language preferences. BAnQ numerique answers 200 but renders its search results in JavaScript, so the returned HTML carries the page furniture and no results. NEITHER IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE 1961 CHARTER. What was obtained: the Association des camps du Quebec's own about page states "Fondee en 1961 a l'initiative de directeurs de camps de vacances" -- the ACQ crediting camp directors collectively for its founding, in the same year the Alta Kahn tribute credits her efforts for the Quebec Camping Association's provincial charter. The two statements are compatible and this project should not merge them: an incorporation and a founding are different events, and whether the 1961 charter IS the ACQ's legal birth is exactly the question p_375 asks. UNTRIED ROUTES, in order of promise: (1) the GAZETTE OFFICIELLE DU QUEBEC for 1961, which publishes letters patent for non-profit corporations and would carry the charter, its date, its corporate name and its petitioners -- BAnQ holds the run; (2) the Registraire from an ordinary Quebec browser, where the same search is free and takes a minute; (3) the Registre des entreprises open dataset on Donnees Quebec, which is bulk and needs downloading rather than searching.

THE MAN WHO FOUND CAMP STEPHENS'S ISLANDS WAS THE YMCA'S OWN PROVINCIAL CHAIRMAN, AND HIS INITIAL IS D. The Year Book of the YMCAs of North America lists "CANADIAN NORTHWEST. Headquarters, Winnipeg, Man. R. D. Richardson, Win'p'g, Man., Chairman" in 1893 and "CANADIAN WEST. Headquarters, Winnipeg, Man. R. D. Richardson, Win'p'g, Man., Chairman. John Norris, Treasurer. George Fleming, Brandon, Man." in 1895, and he signs the province's narrative report in both volumes -- "ROBERT D. RICHARDSON, Cor. Mem." (1893) and "ROBT. D. RICHARDSON, Cor. Mem." (1895). So the man in the rowboats searching the Lake of the Woods for a camp site in 1893 was the chairman of the YMCA's own provincial committee for the Canadian Northwest, and his name was Robert D. Richardson. This settles a small disagreement in the two accounts of the search party: Camp Stephens's own page gives R.D. Richardson, the Lake of the Woods Museum's 2016 newsletter gives R.C. -- the contemporaneous printed record gives D, twice.

A LEAD, NOT A FINDING, ON THE FLEMING ISLAND. One of Camp Stephens's five islands is named for a "Mr. Fleming" whom neither the camp nor the Lake of the Woods Museum identifies further. The 1895 Year Book lists the Canadian West provincial committee at Winnipeg as R. D. Richardson (chairman), John Norris (treasurer) and GEORGE FLEMING of BRANDON, MANITOBA -- a Fleming on the same three-man committee as the man who found the islands, in the years the naming happened. That is a coincidence worth writing down and nothing more: Fleming is a common name, no source connects this one to the island, and the camp's own account says only that the islands were named after influential YMCA members. Recorded so that whoever reaches the Winnipeg association's own records knows which Fleming to check first.

THE YEAR BOOKS CANNOT ADJUDICATE C_063 EITHER. The Manitoba and Canadian West narrative reports in the Year Books of 1893, 1895 and 1897 describe conventions, provincial secretaries, buildings, college associations and corresponding members, and NOT ONE MENTIONS A CAMP -- not the Lake of the Woods Institute, not the islands, not a boys' camp. Neither does any volume mention Lake of the Woods at all (zero occurrences across all five). So the same volumes that fail to record Kanawana's 1894 season and the Ottawa camp of 1893 also fail to record whatever was happening on the Lake of the Woods, and they cannot be used to prefer the 1891 dating over the chapel service's 1911 first boys' camp or the reverse. THE ROUTE TO C_063 REMAINS THE WINNIPEG ASSOCIATION'S OWN ANNUAL REPORTS, which are not in the digitized run searched here.

TONY SHORGAN'S OWN DATED ACCOUNT OF FOUNDING THE FRENCH SECTION, read in full: "Birth of the French Camping Association (l'Association des Camps du Quebec)", Canadian Camping Vol. 17 No. 3, April 1965, pp. 83-84, bylined "by Tony Shorgan, Executive Secretary, Quebec Society for Crippled Children". 1957: as a member of the CCA and QCA and Camp Director of the Crippled Children's Camp at St. Alphonse, Joliette, he attends a committee meeting preparing a joint conference and asks whether a few sessions might be held in French; some doubted French camp directors would be interested. He canvasses friends who direct French camps, calls a meeting at his own office on twenty-four hours' notice, and "Despite one of the worst blizzards we have ever had, there were some 18 French-speaking Camp Directors attending", with Nan Vail, past president of the Quebec and Canadian associations. 12 APRIL 1958: at a joint CCA/QCA meeting at the Windsor Hotel a special French-language session studies forming a French-Canadian section; a committee is struck for a year's trial under Shorgan's presidency and adopts the name ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS CANADIENS FRANCAIS. 17 JULY 1958: at the Crippled Children's Camp, St. Alphonse, under the honorary presidency of Monsignor J. A. Papineau, Bishop of Joliette, the meeting resolves to apply to become part of the QCA. 15 NOVEMBER 1958: permanent officers elected after a full day's study in the Mont St-Louis gymnasium, Shorgan president, with representatives for the Ottawa, Quebec and Montreal regions. 1959: a newsletter every two months and inter-camp visits, French directors visiting English and Jewish camps. 1960: THE NAME CHANGES TO "ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC (SECTION FRANCAISE)". He closes by crediting the merger "with the Quebec Camping Association Inc. (English Section), as recounted by Mrs. Alta Kahn". He had been a QCA member fifteen years by then, so from about 1943. One aside he chose to print: a French director he canvassed early replied that he knew how to run his camp and needed nobody to dictate to him -- "My reply was that we did not need persons like him in the Association" -- and that man later became president of the French section. [DUPLICATION NOTED 2026-09-05, same day: this project had ALREADY extracted this article, as f_3146 (the 1957 approach and the blizzard meeting), f_3147 (the dated chronology 1958-1960), f_3148 (the descent correction for the ACQ name) and f_3149 (the director who did not want to be dictated to). I read the source without first searching the KB for its content, and produced a fourth record of it. WHAT THIS FACT ADDS is the article's own byline and title, the full quotation of the blizzard meeting and the 1960 renaming in one place, and Shorgan's fifteen years of QCA membership; everything else here is a re-statement. Kept rather than deleted, per the no-silent-overwrite rule, and cross-linked so a later pass reads one cluster instead of two. THE LESSON, which is the reason this note is long: the KB is the index to the corpus, and a source should be searched for in it BEFORE being read, not after.]

THE NAME THE MODERN BODY CARRIES IS THE FRENCH SECTION'S, NOT A RENAMED QCA. Shorgan's chronology (f_4863) has the name "Association des Camps du Quebec (Section Francaise)" adopted in 1960 by the French section for itself, two years after that section was founded as the Association des Camps Canadiens Francais and before the merger with the QCA Inc. (English Section). So the association that accredits Kanawana today carries the name the FRENCH SECTION gave itself, which is a different descent from 'the QCA renamed'. THREE FOUNDING DATES NOW SIT SIDE BY SIDE, and they are not interchangeable: the QCA formed 1937 as a chartered unit of the CCA; the French section formed 1958 and named itself Association des Camps du Quebec in 1960; and the ACQ's own website today says "Fondee en 1961 a l'initiative de directeurs de camps de vacances" (f_4859), which is the year of the provincial charter and of the French section joining the QCA. Each date is right about a different event, and this project should say which event it means whenever it gives one.

TWO DISCREPANCIES BETWEEN SHORGAN IN 1965 AND THE CONTEMPORANEOUS REPORTS, recorded rather than smoothed. (1) ATTENDANCE AT THE FIRST MEETING: Shorgan in 1965 says "some 18 French-speaking Camp Directors" came through the blizzard; the June 1958 Quebec report says "Some fifteen persons attended" (f_2821). (2) WHEN AND WHERE IT HAPPENED: Shorgan places that meeting in his own office on twenty-four hours' notice in 1957, before the conference; the June 1958 report describes the meeting as called by him after the programme committee's discussion, chaired by Rene St-Onge, without a date or a place. The two accounts are compatible if the office meeting of 1957 and the conference session of 12 April 1958 are different events, which is the natural reading of Shorgan's own sequence -- but the 1958 report does not say so, and this is a seven-year-later recollection against a contemporaneous minute. Neither is preferred here. Note also that this project's records carry the surname as both SHORGAN (his own 1965 byline and the 1959 report) and SHORGUN (the Winter 1987 issue, on the Quebec association's fiftieth-anniversary planning); the byline spelling is the better authority.

KANAWANA'S ENTRY IN THE CCA DIRECTORY ISSUE, JANUARY 1975, field by field as printed: "KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)"; director DEREK V. WALSH; camp address P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts, Que. (514-227-2414); winter office 1441 Drummond St., Montreal, H3G 1W5 (514-849-5331); activities TRIPPING, SWIMMING, SAILING, ARTS & CRAFTS, C.I.T. PROGRAM; capacity 90 BOYS 8-15 AND 90 GIRLS 8-15. Three unlabelled columns follow the address in every Quebec entry and read "X X C" for Kanawana; THE HEADER ROW IS NOT RECOVERABLE FROM THIS OCR and the columns are therefore left uninterpreted here rather than guessed at -- C plausibly marks co-educational or 'camp' against R for resident, but the directory does not say so on any page this read can reconstruct. The capacity is the useful new number: an even 90 and 90, seven years after coeducation began, in a year for which this project's Kanawana record is otherwise thin.

KANAWANA IS THE OLDEST CAMP IN QUEBEC BY THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN 1975 DIRECTORY, AND BY TWELVE YEARS. The January 1975 Directory Issue lists 64 Quebec camps with a founding year printed beside each name. Sorted, the earliest are: KANAWANA 1894; Brewery Mission 1906; Oolahwan 1917; Lewis 1918; B'nai B'rith 1921; Ouareau 1922; Oasis Notre-Dame 1924; Nominingue and Sante Bruchesi 1925; Wa-Thik-Ane, Kinkora and Ste-Jeanne d'Arc 1926. Kanawana's 1894 is the earliest in the province by a twelve-year margin over the next entry, and the directory prints that date as a plain fact of the listing rather than as a claim anyone was arguing about. NOTE WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT: it is the CCA's own compilation of what its Quebec member camps told it in 1974-75, not an independent test of any founding date, and it covers association members only -- a Quebec camp outside the association is not in it. It says nothing about the national question (see oldest-camp-question.md), only about the province.

THE QUEBEC CAMPS KANAWANA SAT AMONG IN 1975, from the same directory: 64 member camps, of which six were founded after 1970 and a quarter before 1940.
