The list names camps this project already tracks -- Oolahwan (1917), Lewis (1918), Ouareau (1922), Nominingue (1925), Kinkora (1926), Weredale (1933), Crippled Children (1938, Tony Shorgan's camp), Perrot Day Camp (1948), Carowanis (1958) -- alongside many it does not: Brewery Mission (1906), Sante Bruchesi (1925), Wa-Thik-Ane (1926), Frontier Lodge (1933), Enfants Infirmes (1938), Quebec Lodge (1943), Amy Molson (1944), Massad (1947), Pembina (1947), Fatima and Notre-Dame du Lac Sept-Iles (1948), Pine Valley and Trail's End (1949), Massawippi (1951), Olier (1954), St-Michel and Mere M. L. Clarac (1957), Robinson, Val Heureux and Wilvaken (1958), Demetelin (1960), Savio (1961), Elgin Gym Camp (1962), YM-YWHA Country Camp (1963), Richelieu Quatre-Saisons (1964), Green Acres (1966), Kennebec (1967) and Maro Mac (1968). The francophone and anglophone camps are interleaved in one alphabetical list, fifteen years after the French section formed and fourteen after it joined the QCA.

JACK PEARSE'S "SONG LEADING" (Canadian Camping, June 1970, p. 8) sets out the period's own taxonomy of camp singing in five categories, each with a named repertoire. 1. NOVELTY NUMBER, "our broadest category" -- tongue twisters, nonsense songs, familiar songs given a novel touch: One Flea Fly; Hole in the Bottom of the Sea; Tipperary; Pack up Your Troubles; Long, Long Trail; She'll be Coming Round the Mountain; Bingo; My Bonnie; Beans in my Ears; Old MacDonald. "These kinds of songs are the backbone of the sing song... Find some novelty numbers. INVENT SOME." 2. ACTION SONGS -- "the novelty number makes the sing song successful, action songs make the song LEADER successful": My Hat it Has Three Corners; The Old Mill Stream; Deep and Wide; Under the Spreading Chestnut Tree; Heads and Shoulders, Knees and Toes; This Old Man; Little Cabin in the Wood; One Finger, One Thumb, Keep Moving; Grand Old Duke of York. 3. ROUNDS, with an eight-step teaching method and three sub-groups -- ROUSERS (Little Tommy Tinker; Row, Row, Row Your Boat), FUN (Kookaburra; Three Blind Mice), QUIET (Fire's Burning; Oh How Lovely is the Evening; Rosen Fra Fjun; Hey Ho). 4. SPIRITUALS AND FOLK SONGS: Swing Low Sweet Chariot; Steal Away; He's Got the Whole World; All Night, All Day; Ezekiel Saw a Wheel; Where Have All the Flowers Gone; This Land is Your Land; We Shall Overcome; I'm On My Way; KUM BA YAH; Go Tell It On The Mountain; Down By the Riverside -- with the complaint that "some commercial folk singing groups have spoiled for us some excellent spirituals and folk songs". 5. QUIET SONGS: Stephen Foster songs; Harvest Moon; Moonlight Bay; Tell Me Why. THE RULE, printed in capitals: "ALL SING SONGS SHOULD END WITH QUIET SINGING."

KANAWANA'S SONG RECORD AGAINST PEARSE'S TAXONOMY: the common stock overlaps, the camp's own songs are exactly what the movement told leaders to make. Two items in Kanawana's recorded repertoire sit inside Pearse's named lists -- KUM BAH YAH, which he classes under spirituals and folk songs, and "My Old Kentucky Home", a Stephen Foster song, and Foster is the first entry in his quiet-songs category. Those are movement-wide material, not Kanawana property, and a later pass should not treat either as evidence of anything camp-specific. What IS camp-specific -- "On My Way to Kanawana", the Kamp Kanawana Marching Song, "Dear Old Kanawana" to the Battle Hymn of the Republic, and the local adaptation of "Alabama Jubilee" -- falls precisely under Pearse's instruction for the novelty category: "Find some novelty numbers. Invent some." CAMP-SPECIFIC SONGS WERE ADVISED PRACTICE IN THE MOVEMENT KANAWANA BELONGED TO, taught as technique in the association's own magazine, not an accident of local invention. Pearse's closing rule -- all sing songs should end with quiet singing -- also matches the shape of Kay McClelland's 1956 campfire structure already in this knowledge base (f_2725).

ACCESS FAILURE, NOT A NULL: EVERY BIBLIOGRAPHIC SURFACE THAT WOULD CATALOGUE THE ACQ'S ANNUAIRE 82 IS EITHER BLOCKED TO THIS ENVIRONMENT OR OUT OF QUOTA. Searching for the Annuaire 82 on 2026-09-06 (p_326): (1) BAnQ's own catalogue, iris.banq.qc.ca, was refused at the network gateway -- CONNECT answered 502, logged by the agent proxy as "policy denial or upstream failure", so no query reached it and NOTHING is known about what BAnQ's catalogue holds; (2) LAC's national union catalogue Voila, voila.bac-lac.gc.ca, was refused the same way; (3) WorldCat, search.worldcat.org, returned HTTP 429; (4) the Google Books API returned HTTP 429 with "Quota exceeded for quota metric 'Queries' ... 'Queries per day'", so the three Google Books queries attempted returned no results for a reason that has nothing to do with Quebec camping. WHAT DID RUN AND WAS GENUINELY EMPTY: Internet Archive advancedsearch for the exact phrase "Association des camps du Quebec" (numFound 0) and for title:(annuaire) AND (camps OR colonies) (three hits, all French municipal or trade directories, none Quebec camping). The correct statement of the result is that the reachable full-text surface does not hold the Annuaire and the catalogue surfaces WERE NOT SEARCHED. UNTRIED ROUTES, all needing a browser or a letter: BAnQ's IRIS catalogue and its legal-deposit holdings, on which the Annuaire would be registered; Concordia P145/12N04 (see f_2262); the CCA/ACC fonds at Trent; the ACQ itself at campsquebec.com; and Montreal university libraries.

BANQ NUMERIQUE DOES HOLD THE ACQ'S OWN ANNUAL REPORT, BUT THE RUN BEGINS THIRTY YEARS TOO LATE. The catalogue record "Rapport annuel ... / Association des camps du Quebec" (BAnQ numerique notice 52327/3671752) describes an annual serial published by the association at Montreal and states that it COMMENCES WITH 2012/2013. It is digitized but cannot be shown in the online viewer -- the record says the document must be downloaded to be seen and that access is from "les postes informatiques securises dans les edifices de BAnQ", the item being protected by copyright. So BAnQ has the association's modern reporting and, on the evidence of this record alone, nothing of its 1980s publishing; the Annuaire 82 is not reachable through BAnQ numerique. This does NOT establish what BAnQ's IRIS catalogue holds, which could not be searched (f_4871).

WHAT AN "ANNUAIRE" WAS IN THIS MOVEMENT, AND WHERE THE NEAREST SURVIVING ACQ VOLUME IS. The word is not particular to the ACQ's 1982 report: in the movement's own paper it names the annual members' directory that a camping association published. (1) January 1975, in a French article on choosing a camp for a child, the writer's "source principale" is "la section de l'Annuaire des Membres et Associes de Camps de l'Association des Camps de l'Ontario, intitulee 'In Choosing your Child's Camp Be Sure'" -- so the Ontario association's Annuaire was a members-and-associates directory carrying a parents' guidance section. (2) January 1976 carries the title page "Annuaire National des Camps 1976", the French title of the CCA's own national directory issue. So when the ACQ reported spending 1981-82 affirming the image of Quebec's camps "par la publication de l'Annuaire 82", it was publishing in an established genre of the movement, and a Kanawana entry would be a directory line in it. THE NEAREST SURVIVING VOLUME OF THE ACQ'S OWN SERIES IS ALREADY LOCATED, in this project's own notes and not previously connected to this question: Concordia P145/12N04, box HA1888, holds "Annuaire 1979, liste des membres. - 1979" (f_2262). Its own title calls it a members' LIST, which is a caution: what an ACQ Annuaire contained is not established, and the assumption that the Annuaire 82 carried address, director, capacity, ages and session structure on the pattern of the CCA's directory issues is an assumption, not a finding.

THE OFFICIAL TOPONYMIC RECORD FOR KANAWANA, READ FROM THE COMMISSION DE TOPONYMIE'S OWN FILE (2026-09-06). Four names are officially registered at the camp. (1) LAC KANAWANA, no_seq 31996, entity Lac, 45.85126 / -74.19633, Saint-Sauveur (Ville), MRC Les Pays-d'en-Haut, map sheet 31G16-0102; officialised 1968-12-05, published 1969-03-15; Origine_linguistique in the open dataset: ALGONQUIN. (2) KANAWANA, no_seq 31995, entity LIEU-DIT, 45.85 / -74.18333, same dates, also Algonquin -- the settlement name as distinct from the lake. (3) LAC WILSON, no_seq 67247, entity Lac, 45.84374 / -74.1954, same dates; Origine_linguistique: ANGLAIS. (4) CAMP KANAWANA, no_seq 144200, entity type CAMP, 45.85444 / -74.19305, officialised 1985-11-07 and published in the Gazette 1986-08-30; Algonquin. The fourth is new to this project: the camp itself is a registered Quebec toponym with its own entity class and its own date, seventeen years after the lake.

QUEBEC'S OWN NAMING AUTHORITY SAYS IT DOES NOT KNOW WHAT "KANAWANA" MEANS, AND ASKS THE PUBLIC. All four Kanawana-area fiches -- the lake, the lieu-dit, the camp, and Lac Wilson -- carry the identical sentence under "Origine et signification": "L'origine de ce nom et, le cas echeant, sa signification n'ont pu etre determinees jusqu'a maintenant. La Commission de toponymie invite toute personne detenant une information sur l'un ou l'autre de ces aspects a lui en faire part." Each fiche is stamped "Date de la derniere mise a jour: 7 octobre 2020". So the Commission de toponymie du Quebec holds NO etymology for Kanawana and NO explanation of Lac Wilson, and has an open standing invitation for anyone who does. THIS BEARS DIRECTLY ON OPEN QUESTION 1 of indigenous-names-and-land.md: the question is not merely unanswered in this project, it is unanswered in the provincial record. It is also ACTIONABLE IN THE OTHER DIRECTION -- this project holds the 1951 camp history's statement that the lake was renamed from Lake St. Louis (f_2372) and that Lac Desjardins was renamed Lake Wilson for J. W. McConnell's son (f_2371), which is precisely the kind of information the Commission is asking for.

THE 1968 DATE ON THESE TOPONYMS IS A BULK REGISTRATION, NOT A RENAMING -- A CONTROL WORTH KEEPING. 26,229 of the 131,634 rows in the Toponymes officiels file carry the decision date 1968-12-05, a fifth of the whole Quebec register; the next largest dates are 1978-08-17 (4,930) and 1973-10-24 (3,307). So "Date d'officialisation 1968-12-05" on the Lac Kanawana and Lac Wilson fiches records the Commission registering names already in use, not a decision about those two lakes, and must never be read as the date either lake was renamed. Camp Kanawana's 1985-11-07 sits in a smaller batch of 1,201 rows and is subject to the same caution.

THE PROVINCE'S REGISTER OF DE-OFFICIALISED NAMES CARRIES NO TRACE OF EITHER KANAWANA RENAMING, AND ONE NEAR-MISS COULD FOOL A LATER PASS. Searched 2026-09-06, all 13,951 rows of Toponymes desofficialises: no row names the Saint-Sauveur Lac Kanawana or Lac Wilson as either an ancien nom or a nom officiel, so the change from Lake St. Louis to Lake Kanawana (f_2372) and from Lac Desjardins to Lake Wilson (f_2371, f_1206) are recorded in the camp's own history and NOT in the provincial register -- consistent with both changes happening decades before the Commission's file on these lakes begins. THE NEAR-MISS: a DIFFERENT Lac Saint-Louis, at Morin-Heights (45.92 / -74.2775, about 8 km northwest), WAS de-officialised on 1985-11-07 and is now LAC FRANC. It is not Kanawana's lake and must not be read as it. Three other lakes within a few kilometres were renamed in the same era -- Lac Raquette to LAC LORANGER on 1988-09-15 (45.8606 / -74.1917, about 1 km north of Lac Kanawana), Lac Black to LAC DAWSON on 1985-11-07 at Mille-Isles, and Lac Thibault to LAC AUX CASTORS in 2000 -- so this stretch of the Laurentians was actively re-registered in the 1980s while Kanawana's two lake names were left exactly as the camp had made them.

"KANAWANA" IS CLASSED AS ALGONQUIN IN ONE PROVINCIAL FILE AND IS ABSENT FROM THE OTHER, AND THE TWO STATEMENTS SHOULD BE HELD APART. The Toponymes officiels dataset gives Origine_linguistique = ALGONQUIN for all three Kanawana entries; the Commission's own fiche for each says the origin and meaning have not been determined (f_4875). Those are not the same claim: the dataset field classifies the LANGUAGE a name is taken to belong to, the fiche reports whether an ETYMOLOGY is known, and the Commission asserts the first while disclaiming the second. Separately, the Noms traditionnels autochtones register -- 2,675 Indigenous traditional place names collected by the Commission -- contains NO Kanawana entry and nothing at all within half a degree of the camp; the nearest entries are Moziosagan (Abenaki, for Deux-Montagnes) and Quenechouan (Algonquin, for the riviere Quinchien at Vaudreuil-Dorion), both far to the south. So the province classifies the name as Algonquin in origin, does not know what it means, and does not list it among the traditional Indigenous names of Quebec. That is the sharpest form the naming question has taken in this project and it does not settle it either way.

THE 1900 REPORT IS READ. "Seventh Annual Report of the Current Camp Committee", 10 December 1900, is eight pages of cursive manuscript, which is why the Internet Archive scan carries no OCR text (f_2322, now superseded). The page images were read by eye and transcribed on 2026-09-06. It is addressed "To the Chairman Permanent Camp Committee" -- so the YMCA of Montreal ran TWO camp committees, a Permanent one and a Current one, the second reporting annually to the first -- and it is signed "signed on behalf of the committee" by Frank [L.] Benedict, Chairman, and a Dawson, Secretary. THE CAMP IT REPORTS ON IS LAC ST. JOSEPH, NOT KANAWANA: the suggestions name Rock Island, Corbett Island and "all the Islands in Lac St. Joseph". Kanawana's first season was 1910. Every place name in this document belongs to the original site at Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard.

THE 1900 SEASON IN THE COMMITTEE'S OWN WORDS: THREE PARTIES, AND ONE OF THEM WAS THE BOARD. "We think we have come through the banner year in the Camp's history." The committee handled three parties: (1) THE 24 MAY PARTY, "composed of some of the most prominent members of the Association to the number of TWENTY FOUR, including the PRESIDENT, TREASURER and FOUR DIRECTORS", lasting four days -- the committee expected the camp to "profit very materially" because "the impression formed by the 'Fathers of the Association' was a very favorable one"; (2) the regular summer party; and (3) A FALL PARTY OF TWELVE that left town on 21 SEPTEMBER and returned on the 26th, photographed "in duck suits" for next year's prospectus, with a different and better chef. The Annual Regatta is named as a camp fixture, and campers attended the STE AGATHE REGATTA in a body, taking the chef with them and winning ELEVEN PRIZES -- the committee notes they would have won more with skiffs to enter the rowing events. A PROSPECTUS was issued by this committee for the season and enclosed with the report.

THE 1900 ATTENDANCE FIGURE WAS LEFT BLANK BY THE WRITER, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. The report reads "The attendance of __ members shows an increase of __ over last season" -- two gaps in the manuscript where numbers were to be filled in and never were. So this document, which looks from its title like the obvious place to get a 1900 attendance number, does not carry one, and a later pass should not go back to it expecting one. It does establish that 1900 attendance was UP on 1899.

THE FIRST CAMPER SATISFACTION SURVEY IN THIS RECORD, 20 OCTOBER 1900. "On Oct. 20th this Committee sent a letter to every member of the Association who had been to Camp during 1900, calling for criticisms favorable or otherwise and also suggestions." The replies were "almost without exception favorable and many were exceedingly complimentary", except on the food: those who came late in the summer "complained about the manner in which the meals were cooked and served up, but in every case stated that it was not a fault of this committee, as the food supplied was of the best, the trouble emanating entirely from the chef." The committee asks that a more proficient chef be secured. The report then prints ABOUT THIRTY-FIVE SUGGESTIONS VERBATIM, underlining those that several letters repeated -- a stated methodology. That is a designed, dated, written consultation of camp users in 1900, eighty-seven years before the CCA's own 1987 national questionnaire, and the replies themselves would be a further document if they survive.

THE PHYSICAL CAMP AT LAC ST. JOSEPH IN 1900, FROM THE SUGGESTIONS THEMSELVES. Named features: a HOUSE with a GALLERY and a KITCHEN; an ICE-HOUSE badly built and blocking the view from the gallery, which the writers want moved nearer the kitchen and lined with at least six inches of sawdust with the ice raised a foot off the floor; a KITCHEN WHARF (and a demand for a permanent wharf, "where is the one advertised in the accompanying prospectus?"); TENTS on prepared ground, with a named tent site called "HIGH BLUFF" where blocks were set in the ground for the poles so they could not sink; a SPRING whose water they want pumped to the house; ROCK ISLAND, where they want a lean-to "to rough it in while fishing", and which they want the camp to buy; CORBETT ISLAND, where they want an athletic field; the CAMP ISLAND ITSELF, which was unnamed -- "Why not name the camp island and also the one opposite, that is now called 'Corbett Is'?"; DIVING ROCK, "an ideal swimming place", wanting a spring board; and a LUMBERMEN'S SHANTY AT THE RAPIDS which they want purchased. Equipment asked for: a couple of canoes AND A FULL SIZED WAR CANOE, decent diving boards bought in town, aluminium spoons and forks to replace worn-out plate, dinner plates rather than only soup plates, white oilcloth for the tables, two blankets a man, tent flies because the tents all leaked, and four boats repaired that "leaked all the past season". Also asked for: A DARK ROOM AT CAMP, and a covered waggon and carriage for campers and baggage. Two named local suppliers appear, both complained of: BERGERON, blamed for milk arriving so late that breakfast waited until half past nine, and BERGIN THE CARTER, of whom the committee reports "We are informed that Bergin the carter sells liquor."

[RESOLVED 2026-09-06 for BENEDICT, still open for DAWSON: the 1899 annual report prints "F. L. BENEDICT" twice in type, on the Permanent Camp Committee and as Chairman of the Summer Camp committee (f_4908, f_4909), so the flourished middle initial in the 1900 signature is L. The Dawson monogram is unaffected and remains unresolved. The original claim follows.] THE 1900 SIGNATURES PUT THE SAME TWO MEN TOGETHER AS THE 1898 PHOTOGRAPH, AND THAT IS AS FAR AS IT GOES. The report is signed by a Chairman whose surname is plainly BENEDICT and whose middle initial is a flourished capital, and by a Secretary whose surname is plainly DAWSON and whose initials are a single interlocking monogram inside an enclosing loop. THE MONOGRAM CANNOT BE RESOLVED from this scan: the second letter reads as a capital B, the first as R or A. This project already holds the 1898 Camp Jubilee photograph caption naming FRANK L. BENEDICT and RALPH H. DAWSON among four men (f_0021, f_0930), and Ralph H. Dawson wrote the 1933 "History of Kamp Kanawana" (f_0049). The same two surnames signing the camp's own annual report two years after that photograph is strong circumstantial evidence that these are the same two men, and it would be the FIRST DATED OFFICE this project has for either -- but the initials on the page do not confirm it and this fact does not assert it. A clean copy of the signature block, or the Permanent Camp Committee minutes of 1899-1901 at Concordia (f_2237), would settle it.

THE 1900 CAMP HAD THREE COMMITTEES AND TWO CLIENTELES, AND THE TWO 1900 REPORTS FIT TOGETHER. The two Current/Junior camp reports digitized from 1900 are complementary, not duplicates, and read together they show how the Lac St. Joseph camp was actually run. A PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE sat above the season; a CURRENT CAMP COMMITTEE ran the ADULT MEMBERS' camping and reported to it on 10 December 1900 (f_4879) -- the 24 May party of twenty-four senior Association men, the summer party, the September fall party of twelve; and a JUNIOR CAMP COMMITTEE ran the BOYS' CAMP, reporting on 30 November 1900 that it was held 28 June to 14 July with 45 boys, 6 leaders and 17 visitors under Mr. Calhoun and Mr. Brown, in six tents, with eleven wet days out of sixteen and a balance of $5.05 (f_4848). SO ONE SITE CARRIED TWO PROGRAMMES IN DIFFERENT WEEKS OF THE SAME SUMMER, each with its own committee and its own annual report. That is the same two-stream structure the 1894-95 annual report shows at the very beginning (f_2141), still running six seasons later, and it is why a single 'attendance' figure for these years is the wrong shape of question. Both committees complained about the cook, independently, in the same season.

ACCESS FAILURE, TESTED FOUR WAYS: THE MONTREAL GAZETTE CANNOT BE FULL-TEXT SEARCHED FROM THIS ENVIRONMENT (2026-09-06). (1) Per-issue search at books.google.com/books?id=<volumeId>&q=<term> returns HTTP 200, but the result snippets are rendered by JavaScript and NOTHING appears in the served HTML -- the only _OC_Page token in the response is the default PA1, so a query that matches and a query that does not look identical. (2) The screen-reader plain-text view of the same page, &output=html_text, returns HTTP 403; so do &output=text and &printsec=plaintext on the news.google.com viewer. (3) Corpus-wide search, news.google.com/newspapers?q=<term>, redirects to Google Search and returns HTTP 429 with a JavaScript challenge. (4) The Google Books API is out of daily quota (HTTP 429, already recorded today at f_4871). This is a fact about the environment, not about the Gazette. UNTRIED ROUTES: a browser session; a different egress; Newspapers.com or ProQuest through an institutional login; BAnQ's own Gazette holdings; and asking the operator to run a named query in a browser.

WHAT DOES WORK ON THE GAZETTE ARCHIVE, AND TWO TRAPS IN IT. The browse index and the page images are both reachable, so any issue whose DATE is already known can be read by eye. METHOD: fetch news.google.com/newspapers?nid=Fr8DH2VBP9sC&dat=YYYYMMDD, and parse the embedded JSON for start_date / end_date and the volume id and sjid; then fetch news.google.com/newspapers?id=<id>&sjid=<sjid>&pg=1&dq=<anything> and take the list of "pid" values, one per page; then request each page as .../newspapers?id=<id>&sjid=<sjid>&pg=<pid>&img=1&hl=en&zoom=3. TRAP ONE: THE IMAGE ENDPOINT NEEDS A REFERER. Without one it returns a 43-byte transparent GIF with HTTP 200 -- a silent failure that looks like a served image. With a Referer of the viewer page it returns a real PNG of about 150 KB. TRAP TWO: ZOOM STOPS AT 3. zoom=4 and zoom=5 return the same 43-byte placeholder. zoom=3 gives roughly 748x1000, at which HEADLINES AND MASTHEADS ARE LEGIBLE AND BODY TEXT IS NOT -- enough to locate a story on a page, not to read it. TRAP THREE: THE DATE LABELS IN THE BROWSE INDEX ARE NOT RELIABLE. The volume filed under dat=19420805 has a masthead reading "THE GAZETTE, MONTREAL, THURSDAY, AUGUST 6, 1942" (Vol. CLXXI No. 187), while the volume filed under dat=19420804 reads "TUESDAY, AUGUST 4, 1942" (Vol. CLXXI No. 185) and matches. Read the masthead; do not trust the label.

THE GAZETTE OF 5 AUGUST 1942 WAS NOT REACHED, AND MAY NOT BE IN THE ARCHIVE AT ALL. Trying to recover the article behind f_0851 -- "Y.M.C.A. Boys Stage Parade and Circus", naming Camp Director R. H. Hanagan and Resident Director E. E. Smee -- the browse index for that week lists volumes labelled 19420803, 19420804, 19420805, 19420807 and 19420808, with NO ENTRY LABELLED 19420806. The volume labelled 19420805 turns out to be the issue of Thursday 6 August (Vol. CLXXI No. 187), and the volume labelled 19420804 is Tuesday 4 August (No. 185). No. 186, the issue of Wednesday 5 August, is therefore either absent from Google's archive or filed under a label this pass did not identify. THE ARTICLE WAS NOT RECOVERED and src_gazette_1942_parade remains an unverified backfill. Its content is known only from the earlier Newspapers.com reading recorded at f_0851, f_0855, f_0862 and f_0868.

JONES' ISLAND IS LOCATED, ON GEOGRAPHY RATHER THAN ON A DOCUMENT. Quebec's toponymic register holds exactly ONE island named Jones: ILE JONES, no_seq 31476, at 45.5199 / -74.2924 in Saint-Andre-d'Argenteuil, MRC Argenteuil, officialised 1968-12-05, origine linguistique Anglais. The Commission's fiche places it "a l'entree de la baie de Carillon, entre l'ile de Carillon et la terre ferme, dans l'estuaire de la riviere des Outaouais" and gives a full etymology: "Son nom reprend celui du premier proprietaire de l'ile, MARTIN JONES (1747-1843). Apres avoir combattu aux Etats-Unis durant la Revolution americaine, il arriva en 1788 au Canada avec sa femme, HANNAH BRANT (1761-1854). Le couple s'installa a l'extremite sud-est de la seigneurie d'Argenteuil", Martin farming while Hannah attended births and the sick. The Commission cites Benjamin N. WALES, 'Memories of old St. Andrews and historical sketches of the seigniory of Argenteuil', Watchman Press, Lachute, 1934, 135 pp. THE MATCH TO PATTON: he wrote in 1919 that he took the first Montreal boys' camp to "Jones' Island, about 40 miles north-west of Montreal in the Ottawa River" (f_2291). Ile Jones is in the Ottawa River, about 56 km -- 35 miles -- west-north-west of downtown Montreal, and it is the only Ile Jones in the province. THIS IS AN IDENTIFICATION BY GEOGRAPHY AND BY THE UNIQUENESS OF THE NAME, NOT A DOCUMENT SAYING THE CAMP WAS THERE. Two things are not checked: the Ontario toponymic register, which was not searched and which covers the far bank further upstream; and whether any smaller unregistered island carried the name locally in 1891.

KANAWANA'S THREE LAKES ALL HAVE OFFICIAL QUEBEC NAMES, AND ROUND LAKE'S IS LAC ROND. From the Toponymes officiels register, everything officially named within about 3 km of the camp (2026-09-06): LAC KANAWANA 45.85126/-74.19633 (Saint-Sauveur, 1968-12-05, Algonquin); LAC WILSON 45.84374/-74.19541 (Saint-Sauveur, 1968-12-05, Anglais); LAC ROND 45.84582/-74.20147 (Saint-Sauveur, officialised 1970-02-27, Francais) -- the camp's own "Round Lake", which this project had never matched to an official name or a coordinate; the lieu-dit KANAWANA and CAMP KANAWANA themselves (f_4874); LAC DES BECS-SCIE 45.84855/-74.20959, immediately west, confirming f_1428's finding that it is a separate lake and not one of the camp's three; LAC LORANGER 45.86080/-74.19051, a kilometre north, formerly Lac Raquette until 1988; LAC PREVOST, LAC LEONARD, LAC BEAUCHAMP, LAC DES CHATS, LAC AUX CASTORS (formerly Lac Thibault until 2000), LAC TOR and LAC LAPOINTE in Saint-Sauveur; and to the south in Mille-Isles, LAC TAMARACOUTA 45.82995/-74.19451 -- registered as ALGONQUIN in origin -- with LAC DAWSON (formerly Lac Black) and LAC GEORGE. NO ISLAND IS REGISTERED IN ANY OF KANAWANA'S THREE LAKES.

THREE OTHER CAMPS ARE REGISTERED TOPONYMS IN KANAWANA'S OWN DISTRICT, WHICH IS A SMALL MAP OF THE LAURENTIAN CAMPING TRADE. Quebec's register carries the entity class "Camp" for named camps, and within a few kilometres of Kanawana it holds CAMP KANAWANA itself (Saint-Sauveur, 1985-11-07), CAMP OLIER 45.82833/-74.15333 and CAMP DE L'AVENIR 45.83555/-74.15889 (both Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs, 1985-11-07 and 2005-12-08, both Francais). Neither Olier nor l'Avenir appears anywhere in this project. Further north at Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, beside the old Otoreke site, CAMP KINKORA is in the DE-OFFICIALISED register: "Camp-Kinkora" was replaced by "Kinkora, Camp" on 1984-09-06 at 46.006944/-74.313333 -- a form change rather than a renaming, but it confirms the camp Msgr. McShane founded in 1926 as a mapped, officially named place. Camp Tamaracouta, the Scouts' camp joined to Kanawana by the 1964 lot purchase, is NOT registered as a Camp; only its lake is.

CAMP JUBILEE'S ISLANDS AT LAC SAINT-JOSEPH ARE NOT IN QUEBEC'S TOPONYMIC REGISTER AT ALL. Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard carries 120 official toponyms, of which exactly ONE is an island: ILE CHRISTIE, 45.974066/-74.384710, officialised 1985-11-07, origine linguistique Anglais. LAC SAINT-JOSEPH itself is registered at 45.974310/-74.331879. Searched province-wide, there is NO Corbett anything in the Laurentians -- the only two Corbett toponyms in Quebec are lakes at Senneterre and Lac-Nilgaut, hundreds of kilometres away -- and no island of any name is registered within 6 km of Lac Saint-Joseph except Ile Christie. SO THE NAMES THE 1900 CURRENT CAMP COMMITTEE REPORT USES -- ROCK ISLAND, CORBETT ISLAND, and the camp island that one writer complained had no name at all (f_4883) -- NEVER ENTERED THE PROVINCIAL REGISTER. That bears directly on camp-otoreke.md's open question about whether the three islands are still identifiable: they are not identifiable by name from the official record, and whether Ile Christie is one of them is not established here.

THE TOPONYMIC REGISTER'S "CAMP" CLASS IS MOSTLY HUNTING AND FISHING CAMPS, NOT SUMMER CAMPS -- AND IT STILL YIELDS SEVEN NEW NAMES. Swept province-wide 2026-09-06: Quebec's Toponymes officiels file holds 87 entries of entity class Camp. THE HYPOTHESIS THAT THIS IS A DIRECTORY OF CHILDREN'S CAMPS IS WRONG and is corrected here: roughly forty of the eighty-seven are on ILE D'ANTICOSTI (Jupiter-12, Jupiter-24, Chicotte-la-Mer, Baie-de-la-Tour and so on) and most of the rest are outfitters' camps in the Laurentides and Jacques-Cartier wildlife reserves; 32 of the 87 were officialised in 2026 alone, in two batches on 11 March and 11 June, which is a mapping exercise rather than a wave of camp founding. Linguistic origins: 72 French, 7 English, 3 Autre, and one each Cri, Mohawk and Algonquin. WHAT THE RESIDUE IS WORTH: a real band of CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMPS runs through the Laurentians and Lanaudiere -- Camp Kinkora (Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard), CAMP HIAWATHA (Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts, 46.08389/-74.24667, officialised 1984-09-06, ORIGINE LINGUISTIQUE MOHAWK), Camp Kanawana, Camp Olier and Camp de l'Avenir (Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs), Camp Ouareau (Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci), Camp-Nominingue, Camp Quatre-Saisons (La Macaza), OLD BREWERY MISSION (Wentworth-Nord, 45.89028/-74.42083, officialised 1986-06-12), Village-des-Jeunes (Saint-Come), CAMP MARIAN and CAMP AURELDA (both Mandeville, both 1981-07-09), Colonie de Granby (Clarenceville), Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc (Contrecoeur), Camp Bosco (Coteau-du-Lac) and Camp Gatineau (Pontiac). SEVEN OF THESE APPEAR NOWHERE IN THIS PROJECT: Camp Hiawatha, Camp Olier, Camp de l'Avenir, Camp Aurelda, Village-des-Jeunes, Colonie de Granby and Camp Glen Emma (Routhierville). Only two of Kanawana's own three registered camp neighbours are known to this wiki.

KANAWANA'S TWO NEAREST REGISTERED NEIGHBOURS ARE BOTH CATHOLIC ORDERS' CAMPS, AND THE COMMISSION SAYS SO. CAMP DE L'AVENIR (no_seq 393822, Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs, 45.83555/-74.15889): "Ce camp de vacances, situe sur la rive sud du LAC OUIMET, fut fonde en 1964 par les CLERCS DE SAINT-VIATEUR." A dated founding, a named order and a named lake, in three lines, for a camp three kilometres from Kanawana that appears nowhere else in this project. CAMP OLIER (no_seq 145208, Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs, 45.82833/-74.15333, officialised 1985-11-07): "Son nom rappelle le souvenir de Jean-Jacques Olier" -- Jean-Jacques Olier de Verneuil (Paris 1608-1657), founder of the COMPAGNIE DES PRETRES DE SAINT-SULPICE, who with Jerome Le Royer de La Dauversiere and Pierre Chevrier founded "Les Messieurs et Dames de la Societe de Notre-Dame de Montreal", the society that founded Ville-Marie. The fiche gives no founding date for the camp itself. SO WITHIN THREE KILOMETRES OF THE YMCA'S CAMP THERE IS A CAMP OF THE CLERICS OF SAINT VIATOR AND A CAMP NAMED FOR A FOUNDER OF MONTREAL AND OF THE SULPICIANS -- the same confessional density this project already describes for Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, twenty kilometres north, but on Kanawana's own doorstep and never noticed here.

CAMP HIAWATHA AND OLD BREWERY MISSION ARE BOTH "ORIGIN NOT DETERMINED", WHICH IS NOW THE COMMISSION'S ANSWER FOR SIX CAMP-RELATED NAMES IN THIS DISTRICT. The fiches for CAMP HIAWATHA (no_seq 137664, Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts, officialised 1984-09-06, origine linguistique recorded as MOHAWK in the dataset), OLD BREWERY MISSION (no_seq 150335, Wentworth-Nord, 1986-06-12), CAMP MARIAN and CAMP AURELDA (105558 and 105559, both Mandeville, both 1981-07-09) all carry the same sentence as Lac Kanawana, Lac Wilson, Camp Kanawana and the lieu-dit Kanawana: "L'origine de ce nom et, le cas echeant, sa signification n'ont pu etre determinees jusqu'a maintenant", with the standing invitation to anyone who knows. CAMP HIAWATHA IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS TO THIS PROJECT: its origine linguistique is recorded as MOHAWK while its fiche disclaims knowing the origin -- exactly the split found for Kanawana's own ALGONQUIN classification (f_4878) -- and it sits about twenty kilometres from Kanawana, so the pattern of Laurentian camps carrying names of that kind is not peculiar to Kanawana.

CAMP OLIER IS A SULPICIAN CAMP, FOUNDED 1954, AND THE CCA DIRECTORY GIVES IT FIELD BY FIELD. From the January 1975 CCA Directory issue and repeated in January 1976: "OLIER (1954) -- M. COME LALANDE, PSS -- 1931 ouest, Sherbrooke, Montreal H3H 1E3, (514-933-7869) -- R.R. no. 1, Piedmont, Ste-Anne des Lacs, (514-224-2004) -- 60 GARCONS 12-16", activities "Arts plastiques, Exp. corporelle, Artisanat, Hebertisme, Camping". THE POST-NOMINAL PSS IS PRETRES DE SAINT-SULPICE, so the Commission de toponymie's note that the camp's name "rappelle le souvenir de Jean-Jacques Olier" understates it: the camp was RUN BY THE ORDER OLIER FOUNDED, not merely named after him (f_4894). It was a boys' camp of sixty, aged 12 to 16, eight kilometres from Kanawana, with a director who is himself a Montreal address on Sherbrooke Street West. A COINCIDENCE WORTH FOLLOWING RATHER THAN ASSERTING: the de-officialised toponymic register records "Freres, Lac des" renamed "COME-LALANDE, LAC" at Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs on 2005-12-08 (f_4877's sweep) -- almost certainly the same man commemorated, but nothing read here says so.

CAMP HIAWATHA WAS A PRIVATE CO-ED CAMP FROM 1932, THIRTY-SIX YEARS BEFORE KANAWANA ADMITTED GIRLS. The January 1975 CCA Directory: "HIAWATHA (1932) -- Mr. & Mrs. B. JACOBSON -- 6595 Cote St. Luc Rd., No. 203 [Montreal] -- R.R. no. 2, Ste. Agathe des Monts, (819-326-0577) -- 85 BOYS 5-16, 85 GIRLS 5-16", activities Tennis, Golf, Ice Hockey, Fine Arts and Riding (extra); the January 1976 issue repeats the entry and adds the season, JUNE 24 - AUGUST 18. A camp of 170 children in equal numbers of boys and girls, from age five, twenty kilometres from Kanawana, founded in 1932 and family-run. KANAWANA DID NOT ADMIT GIRLS UNTIL 1968 and declined an internal recommendation to do so in 1965; Hiawatha had been mixed since before the war. That is a fact about the Laurentian camping market Kanawana operated in and belongs beside the coeducation question, not as a criticism of the YMCA's decision but as the context in which it was taken.

VERIFY CORRECTION (p_284): THE 1938 "CAMP DOCTOR" ITEM IS A JOKE-COLUMN LETTER, NOT A DIRECTOR'S RECORD. camp-lighthall.md presented the Green Triangle of 29 July 1938 as the paper recording, "over the signature 'Chief' -- the camp director", that "Our camp doctor is dividing his time between Kanawana and the Junior League", and read it as documentary evidence of a shared medical officer. THE SOURCE SHOWS OTHERWISE. The full item reads: "Dearest Do: / Our camp doctor is dividing his time between Kanawana and the Junior League. It worries me, and I want to know if something can be done about it. / 'Chief.'" That is the paper's spoof advice column -- the same format the article itself notes for 13 August 1932, where a letter is signed "A Junior League Girl" -- with "Chief" written IN as a pseudonymous correspondent, not signing off as director. THE UNDERLYING FACT MAY WELL STILL HOLD, since the joke only works if the doctor really was splitting his time, but it is a joke told about an arrangement, not an administrative record of one, and the article's weighting was too high. Corrected in place 2026-09-06.

THE STRONGEST GREEN TRIANGLE ITEM ON THE JUNIOR LEAGUE CAMP WAS CITED AND NEVER USED. The issue of 17 AUGUST 1935 is listed in camp-lighthall.md's note 10 among eleven issues but nothing from it appears in the article, and it is the most concrete record of contact in the whole run: "It was a very beautiful day, in fact almost perfect... but best of all, SOME TWENTY GIRLS FROM JUNIOR LEAGUE WERE OUR WELCOME VISITORS. We certainly were glad to have them here -- especially the directors and certain counselors. In fact, we have it on good authority that THEY HAVE BEEN ASKED BACK FOR TO-MORROW." The same issue records an evening entertainment at which "there were present besides our own campers several visitors from Junior League, who declared that it was a rare treat." That is a dated visit of about twenty girls to Kanawana, a return visit the following day, and a second occasion in the same issue -- an actual programme of visits rather than boys walking over the hill. ALSO RECOVERED, from the 1 July 1939 christening item already quoted: the staff made "a second trip made next day... for the alleged purpose of aiding the Junior League Girls' preparations for their FIRST BATCH OF CAMPERS THAT EVENING", which dates the Junior League Camp's 1939 season opening to late June 1939, and names STEVE GANNON, the guide of one car, who lost his way.

SIX PER CENT OF THIS PROJECT'S SOURCE CACHE IS THE SAME TEXT FILED TWICE, WHICH MAKES EVERY GREP-BASED COUNT OVER IT WRONG. Measured 2026-09-06 after the p_284 verify pass had to notice by hand that the Green Triangle issue of 1938-07-29 sat in the cache under two filenames: of 921 non-empty files in sources/cache, 51 are BYTE-IDENTICAL copies of another cached file, in 50 groups. The largest overlap is sources/cache/green-triangle/ against sources/cache/ymca-montreal-fonds/ -- EVERY ONE of the 42 files in the green-triangle directory has an identical twin elsewhere, and not one is unique -- with sources/cache/brochures/ duplicating the fonds directory as well. Only 5 source records point at green-triangle/ against 625 at ymca-montreal-fonds/. CONSEQUENCES, both real: a grep across the cache double-counts hits, so 'this appears in N issues' is inflated; and a coverage sweep of 'how many issues are cached' overstates -- the two directories together hold 42 and 38 files for 37 distinct Green Triangle issue dates. NOTHING WAS DELETED. These are cached primary texts, which copy is canonical is a decision for a person, and the five source records pointing at the redundant directory would break. data_integrity.py now reports the duplication as an advisory with the groups named, so it cannot be forgotten again. Separately, the 0-byte file that stood at the 1900 Current Camp Committee report's path for years has been replaced by a POINTER to the transcript made on 2026-09-06, because an empty file is what anyone grepping the cache found.

THE MISDATING TRAP IS SHARPER THAN f_2078 RECORDS: FOUR CACHED FILES CARRY 1990 OR 1991 IN THEIR NAMES AND TWO OF THEM ARE NINETEENTH-CENTURY. Checked file by file 2026-09-06. sgw-ymca-annual-report-1990-1991.txt opens "Annual Report, Young Men's Christian Association of Montreal, 1890-91" and announces the new DOMINION SQUARE building; sgw-ymca-annual-report-1991-1992.txt opens "41st Annual Report... 1891-92". BUT sgw-ymca-annual-report-1990.txt IS GENUINELY 1990 (chairman Claude Lemay, referring to September 1989) and sgw-ymca-annual-report-1991.txt IS GENUINELY 1991 (opening on the dismantling of the Berlin Wall), with French counterparts beside each. So the four files sit adjacent in the same directory, two of them a century older than their names, and sorting or globbing that directory by name puts 1890 next to 1990. NOTE THAT THE INTERNET ARCHIVE'S OWN METADATA IS CORRECT -- title "YMCA Annual Report 1890-1891", date 1891-05-28 -- and only the IDENTIFIER and the inner _djvu.txt filename are wrong; a fetch of archive.org/metadata/<id> gives the right year. THIS PROJECT PROPAGATED THE ERROR: three source records carried dates taken from the identifier rather than the document ("1990", "1991-19-92", "1889-18-90"), and all three were corrected on 2026-09-06.

[QUALIFIED 2026-09-06, HOURS AFTER THIS FACT WAS WRITTEN: there is now a strong alternative reading of "Volunteer Camp work" and this fact overreached in implying it was boys' camping. The 1893-94 report shows the association ran a tent at the LAPRAIRIE MILITIA CAMP, with Patton in charge in June 1893 and the work running "for many years" before that (f_4906) -- and f_1537 already recorded that in the 1901 Historical Sketch every "camp" reference is militia, not summer camping. So the 1890-91 report's "Volunteer Camp work... under Mr. Patton" may well be the Laprairie tent rather than a boys' camp, which would also dissolve the oddity noted below about "successfully carried out". THE PHRASE IS NOT DECIDED EITHER WAY and this fact should not be cited as evidence for boys' camping in 1890-91. The original claim follows.] THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN 1890-91 REPORT CREDITS PATTON WITH CAMP WORK, THREE YEARS BEFORE 1894 AND CONTEMPORANEOUS WITH HIS 1891 CAMP. Under EXECUTIVE, the Annual Report of the YMCA of Montreal for 1890-91 (presented 28 May 1891) states: "THE VOLUNTEER CAMP WORK WAS SUCCESSFULLY CARRIED OUT UNDER THE [affiliation] AND ASSISTANCE OF MR. PATTON." (The OCR reads "ahielation"; the word is affiliation or affiliation-like and the sense is not in doubt.) UNTIL NOW PATTON'S 1891 CAMP WAS ATTESTED ONLY BY HIS OWN MEMOIR OF AUGUST 1919, twenty-eight years after the fact (f_2291). This is the association writing about camp work in its own annual report for the year of that camp, and it says the work was carried out successfully -- which sits oddly beside the memoir's account of a camp broken up on its first day by a drowning, and the two are not obviously about the same outing. WHAT IT DOES ESTABLISH: the YMCA of Montreal had something it called VOLUNTEER CAMP WORK in 1890-91, and Patton ran it. The same report also dates his departure: "EARLY LAST SPRING, OUR LEADER MR. PATTON RESIGNED TO ENTER THE SPRINGFIELD SCHOOL for training secretaries", which independently puts him at Springfield from the spring of 1891 and therefore in place for Naismith's first basketball game that December.

A CORBETT LEAD FOR CORBETT ISLAND, OFFERED AS A LEAD AND NOT A FINDING. The 1900 Current Camp Committee report names CORBETT ISLAND at Lac St. Joseph as an established name (f_4883), and no source read here explains it. The association's own reports carry three Corbetts. (1) D. W. CORBETT, assistant secretary, in charge of the boys' department: the 1892-93 report records that "D. W. Corbett, as assistant secretary, having in charge this department... has accepted the position as secretary of the Honolulu" association, and the 1893-94 report twice laments "the departure of Mr. D. W. Corbett in June, 1893", who "was the main-stay of this work", with P. H. Cushing secured as his successor. (2) E. M. CORBETT, in a 1893-94 list. (3) JOHN CORBETT, a subscriber in the 1900 report. THE HYPOTHESIS: the island is named for D. W. Corbett, the boys'-work secretary of the years immediately before the camp. AGAINST IT: he left Montreal in June 1893, a year before the 1894 camp, so if the island is his it was named in his memory rather than during his tenure, and nothing read here says so. He also appears alongside Patton in the 1890-91 report -- "our old friends, Messrs. Corbett and Patton, with Mr. W. H. Davis, of the Springfield School, spoke on 'The Race of Life'" on 22 March -- which places the two men together in the association at exactly the period of the first camp work. RECORDED SO A LATER PASS CAN TEST IT, NOT AS AN ANSWER.

R. L. CHARLTON SAT ON THE MONTREAL YMCA BOARD'S TRAINING CLASSES COMMITTEE FOR 1892-93, WITH THE ENTIRE FOUNDING CAST. The 41st Annual Report of the YMCA of Montreal (1891-92) prints "COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD, 1892-93", and under TRAINING CLASSES: "D. A. Budge, D. W. Corbett, T. D. Patton, W. H. Ball, R. L. CHARLTON." The same report's staff list gives D. A. BUDGE General Secretary, D. W. CORBETT Assistant Secretary, T. DUNCAN PATTON (role garbled in the OCR), and W. H. BALL Physical Director. THIS ANSWERS HALF OF rl-charlton.md's OPEN QUESTION 2, which asked whether Charlton held any formal position and noted that his camp involvement was inferred. He held a documented seat on the association's board committee structure in 1892-93 -- the year the camp syndicate was formed -- alongside the general secretary, the assistant secretary in charge of boys' work, the man who ran the 1891 camp, and the physical director who took the 1894 one out. IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH A CAMP ROLE: Training Classes is not a camp committee, and nothing here puts him at Lac St. Joseph. WHAT IT DOES CHANGE is the standing of his 1943 manuscript "Notes re Early Days of YMCA Camps at Lake St. Joseph and Kanawana": he was in the association's committee rooms in 1892, so he wrote it as a participant fifty-one years on, not as a later compiler. That raises its value among the Concordia asks.

PATTON IS ON THE MONTREAL STAFF LIST IN 1891-92, AFTER RESIGNING FOR SPRINGFIELD, WHICH FITS HIS OWN MEMOIR. The 1890-91 report says "Early last spring, our leader Mr. Patton resigned to enter the Springfield School" (f_4902), yet the 41st Annual Report for 1891-92 prints T. DUNCAN PATTON in its staff list between the assistant secretary and the physical director, and on the Training Classes committee for 1892-93 (f_4904). The memoir supplies the reconciliation in its own words: "DURING THE VACATION PERIOD OF 1891 I RETURNED TO MONTREAL and took out to Jones' Island... the first Montreal Boys' Camp" (f_2291). So the sequence that the documents and the memoir agree on is: Montreal staff to spring 1891 -> Springfield -> back in Montreal for the 1891 vacation period and the Jones' Island camp -> at Springfield again in December 1891 for Naismith's first game -> on the Montreal staff and board committee through 1892-93. THIS BEARS ON p_286(b), the overlapping Montreal and Winnipeg date ranges in the basketball-player exhibit timeline: the Montreal end is not a competing claim, it is a man moving back and forth between a city job and a training school.

THE MONTREAL YMCA RAN A TENT AT THE LAPRAIRIE MILITIA CAMP FOR YEARS BEFORE 1894, AND PATTON HAD CHARGE OF IT. The 1893-94 annual report, under MILITARY CAMP: "The Association placed a tent with full equipment for reading-room, library, games, etc., in the grounds at LAPRAIRIE IN JUNE LAST. MR. T. DUNCAN PATTON HAD CHARGE, and conducted evangelistic meetings every night amongst the men. He was assisted by members from the city. THE INFLUENCE OF THIS WORK FOR MANY YEARS has been most beneficial upon the whole character of the camp life, and many men date their conversion from these services." TWO THINGS FOLLOW. (1) The association had institutional experience of running a tented operation -- equipment, staffing, a season, a site -- for years before the first boys' camp of 1894, and the phrase "for many years" is the report's own. (2) Patton is the association's camp man for a THIRD time in a third form: the militia tent in June 1893, the Volunteer Camp work of 1890-91 (f_4902), and the boys' camp at Jones' Island in 1891 (f_2291).

AN EXPLICIT NULL IN THE YEAR THE CAMP SYNDICATE WAS FORMED. The YMCA of Montreal's annual report for 1892-93 contains NO camp content of any kind -- searched 2026-09-06 for camp, tent, fishing, Agathe and Ste. Agathe, and the only hits are the surnames Campbell and Camperdown and unrelated words. The 1951 camp history dates the founding committee to the fall of 1892 (f_2177 and the syndicate account), and the association's own annual report covering that year does not mention it. That is consistent with the camp beginning as a private syndicate of members rather than as association business, which is how the 1951 history and the 1919 memoir both describe it, and it should be read as corroboration of that framing rather than as evidence against the 1892 date.

THE CAMP'S COMMITTEE STRUCTURE IN 1899, PRINTED IN FULL, AND IT NAMES THE MEN THE 1900 REPORT IS SIGNED BY. The YMCA of Montreal's annual report for the year ending 30 April 1899 prints three relevant committees. PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE: "CHAS. CUSHING, Chairman. John W. Ross. W. E. Cushing. C. S. Paterson. F. L. BENEDICT." SUMMER CAMP [committee]: "F. L. BENEDICT, Chairman. R. C. Paterson. F. S. Macfarlane. A. G. Burton. G. A. Gatehouse. Jas. Greig." JUNIOR DEPARTMENT: "R. B. Ross, Jr., Chairman. F. A. Crowe, Secretary. R. L. CHARLTON. Geo. Lyman. Harold Beall. W. E. Cushing. L. Cushing. F. M. H. Cushing. Geo. C. Wells. C. S. Paterson. A. L. Paterson. E. C. Budge." FOUR THINGS FOLLOW. (1) CHARLES CUSHING CHAIRED THE PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE in 1899 -- the same Charles Cushing the North American Year Books record as the International Committee's Corresponding Member for Quebec in 1893-95 (f_4837). (2) The 1900 Current Camp Committee report is addressed "To the Chairman Permanent Camp Committee" (f_4879): this names him. (3) W. E. CUSHING, who wrote the 1943 "Historical sketches -- Lake St. Joseph", sat on BOTH the Permanent Camp Committee and the Junior Department in 1899, so like Charlton he wrote as a participant. (4) R. L. CHARLTON sat on the JUNIOR DEPARTMENT committee in 1899 -- a second documented seat, and one in boys' work rather than Training Classes.

THE BENEDICT INITIAL IS SETTLED: F. L., NOT F. B. Reading the 1900 Current Camp Committee report's signature block on 2026-09-05, the chairman's middle initial was recorded as a flourished capital read as L on the strength of the 1898 Camp Jubilee photograph caption alone, with B explicitly not ruled out (f_4884). THE 1899 ANNUAL REPORT PRINTS IT TWICE IN TYPE: "F. L. BENEDICT" on the Permanent Camp Committee and "F. L. BENEDICT, Chairman" of the Summer Camp committee (f_4908). Together with the 1898 photograph caption naming FRANK L. BENEDICT, that is three independent typeset instances against one ambiguous signature. The man who signed the 1900 report as Chairman of the Current Camp Committee is FRANK L. BENEDICT, and he chaired the Summer Camp committee the year before and sat on the Permanent Camp Committee under Charles Cushing.

A PHOTOGRAPH OF THE ORIGINAL CAMP SITS IN THE 1899 ANNUAL REPORT AND HAS NEVER BEEN LOOKED AT. The report for the year ending 30 April 1899 carries a plate captioned "THE ASSOCIATION SUMMER CAMP, LAKE ST. JOSEPH." The caption is all the cached OCR text preserves -- the plate itself is an image, and the digitized page has not been fetched. IT IS ONE OF THE EARLIEST KNOWN IMAGES OF THE CAMP THIS PROJECT'S OWN HISTORY BEGINS WITH, five years after the first season, and camp-otoreke.md's open questions ask for exactly this. THE ROUTE IS KNOWN AND CHEAP: the Internet Archive item for this report has jp2 page images, and the method used on the 1900 manuscript (download the jp2 zip, convert, read by eye) applies unchanged. NOT DONE HERE.

C. B. POWTER RAN THE YMCA'S OWN CAMP AT LAKE ST. JOSEPH FOUR YEARS BEFORE HE FOUNDED HIS. The Permanent Camp Committee's report in the annual report for the year ending 30 April 1899 states of the senior camp season: "The camp was under the charge of the following: Messrs. A. MACKELLAR, C. B. POWTER, A. R. ROSS, and W. H. BALL." This project holds thirteen facts about C. B. Powter and NOT ONE of them connects him to the YMCA of Montreal's camp: they are all about Powter's Camp, "Sans Egal", which N. B. Powter's 1962 account of his father says was founded in June 1902 when "a group of 50 boys from the Montreal area under the leadership of the late C. B. Powter arrived on the shores of Lac St. Joseph near Ste. Agathe des Monts" (f_2986). THE SAME LAKE. So the man who founded the neighbouring camp in 1902 was one of four in charge of the YMCA's camp on that lake in 1898, alongside W. H. Ball, the association's Physical Director. That is a direct documentary link between Kanawana's predecessor and Powter's Camp, and this wiki has treated them as parallel institutions. A. MACKELLAR and A. R. ROSS are otherwise unrecorded here in a camp role.

THE 1898 SEASON IN THE COMMITTEE'S OWN DETAIL, INCLUDING A LENGTH-OF-STAY BREAKDOWN NOBODY HAS. From the same report. THE LOG CLUB HOUSE: "the Log Club house at Lake St. Joseph was COMPLETED IN SEPTEMBER, and has been greatly admired by all who have seen it", built on member subscriptions and "FREE OF DEBT", with furnishing and "a number of needed improvements" planned for the coming season. NOTE A POSSIBLE OFF-BY-ONE: this report covers the year ending 30 April 1899, so "September" is SEPTEMBER 1898, while meta/attendance-series.md carries "Log clubhouse opened, cost $700" against 1899. The two may be the completion and the opening, or the series may be a year late; NOT RESOLVED HERE. THE SENIOR SEASON: open "from the 9th of July to the 4th of September", with parties out in May and September; attendance "first week 19, second 11, balance of summer 42, May and September 13, TOTAL 85" -- a figure the attendance series already carries, but the weekly split is new. LENGTH OF STAY, which nothing in this project has: "two, four weeks; one, three weeks; three, two and one half weeks; one, two weeks; twenty-eight, between one and two weeks; fifteen, one week; twenty-eight, odd days." That is 78 men accounted for against a stated total of 85. Finances: receipts $984.32, expenditures $939.71, balance printed as $41.62 -- THE ARITHMETIC DOES NOT WORK, the difference is $44.61, and the printed figure is either a transposition in the report or in the OCR.

THE 1898 JUNIOR CAMP, WITH ITS SUPERVISORS NAMED. Same report: "The report of the Junior Camp shows that their camp was open from the 23RD OF JUNE TO THE 7TH JULY, and that there were 20 BOYS at camp, and also a party of FIVE VISITORS spent DOMINION DAY with them. The camp was under the supervision of W. F. CHAPMAN and C. S. PATERSON, to whom much of the success of the camp is due. They were also fortunate in having with them for a short time, DRS. HARRY SHAW and CHARLES OGILVY, who are old members of the Junior Department." Finances: receipts $220.23, expenses $207.48, balance $12.75 (this arithmetic does work). The dates and the count of 20 are already in meta/attendance-series.md; W. F. CHAPMAN, HARRY SHAW and CHARLES OGILVY are new to this project, and C. S. Paterson is here in a camp role for the first time -- he also sat on the Permanent Camp Committee and the Junior Department committee the same year (f_4908). The visit of two doctors described as OLD MEMBERS OF THE JUNIOR DEPARTMENT is the earliest evidence in this record of camp alumni returning.

THE EARLIEST KNOWN PHOTOGRAPH OF THE CAMP, FOUND AND DESCRIBED 2026-09-06. The plate in the YMCA of Montreal's annual report for the year ending 30 April 1899, captioned "THE ASSOCIATION SUMMER CAMP, LAKE ST. JOSEPH.", is printed on page 13, immediately below the list of members who died during the year and the signatures of C. T. WILLIAMS, President, and D. A. BUDGE, Secretary. WHAT IT SHOWS, read from the page image: a view from above and behind the camp, looking out over the lake. FOUR TENTS. Left of centre and largest, a WALL TENT or marquee with its side walls raised, and immediately in front of it A FLAGPOLE WITH A FLAG FLYING. Lower left foreground, a pale CONICAL OR BELL TENT on guy ropes. Right of centre, a smaller wall tent half screened by brush. Right foreground, an A-FRAME OR WEDGE TENT seen side on. Between them, what appears to be stacked cut poles or a woodpile. The ground is rough scrub with low bushes and a bare sapling in the foreground; it falls away through brush to the shore, and the lake runs across the frame with a long low wooded far shore behind. NO PERMANENT BUILDING APPEARS IN THE FRAME -- which is worth stating as what the IMAGE SHOWS and not as what the site held, since the Log Club house was completed in the September of the year this report covers (f_4912) and could simply be out of shot. THE PLATE WAS INVISIBLE TO EVERY TEXT SEARCH THIS PROJECT HAS RUN: the OCR preserves the caption and not the picture. Cropped and filed at assets/images/documents/1899-association-summer-camp-lake-st-joseph.jpg.

THE CAMPERS' SURVEY OF OCTOBER 1900 WAS ACTED ON, AND THE REPORT SAYS SO. The YMCA of Montreal's annual report for the year ending 30 April 1902, under SUMMER CAMP, ST. AGATHE: "The Permanent Camp Committee has to report THE MOST SUCCESSFUL YEAR SINCE ITS OPENING. 147 senior and 60 junior members spent their vacation at this delightful spot... THE COMMITTEE ENLARGED THE KITCHEN AND BUILT A NEW ICE-HOUSE. These improvements will greatly facilitate the work." READ AGAINST THE CIRCULAR OF 20 OCTOBER 1900 (f_4882, f_4883), in which campers asked for "a proper pantry & Ice-house built near kitchen", "Shelves are needed in the worst way in the kitchen", and complained that the ice-house was "not built properly" and "now spoils view from gallery" -- the two things the committee reports building are the two things the campers asked for. THIS IS THE CLEAREST EVIDENCE IN THE RECORD THAT THE 1900 SURVEY CHANGED THE CAMP. FINANCES for the same year: the Junior Committee received $617.26 and expended $478.67, handing a balance of $138.59 to the Permanent Camp Committee; the Senior Camp received $1,306.85 and expended $1,106.96, handing over $199.89; $490.89 was spent "on needed improvements and permanent equipment"; and "The Camp Committee has received a loan from the Association of $384.27. This should be repaid next year."

A DATED ISLAND PURCHASE, AND IT SAYS THE ASSOCIATION HELD ONE ISLAND IN 1901. Same report: "On NOV. 26TH, 1901, THREE ISLANDS IN LAC ST. JOSEPH WERE SOLD BY PUBLIC AUCTION, and the Committee purchased A SMALL ONE ADJOINING OUR PRESENT ISLAND, FOR $50." TWO THINGS THIS SETTLES AND ONE IT DOES NOT. It settles that on 26 November 1901 the association bought ONE small island at auction for fifty dollars, and that at that date it already held an island it called "OUR PRESENT ISLAND" -- SINGULAR. So immediately after this purchase the association held TWO. THAT BEARS ON c_008, the unresolved two-versus-three island count, which rests on two secondary sources (QAHN's "three islands" and BaladoDecouverte's "two islands acquired in 1897") neither of which could be quoted cleanly when re-checked in July 2026. This is a PRIMARY source with a date and a price, and it fits neither secondary account: one island before 26 November 1901, two after. IT DOES NOT RESOLVE c_008, because a third island could have been acquired at any point after 1901 and this project has not read the later reports for it. THE OTHER TWO ISLANDS SOLD AT THAT AUCTION went to buyers this document does not name.

A CAPTION SWEEP FOR PLATES ACROSS THE PRE-1912 ANNUAL REPORTS FINDS EXACTLY ONE, AND ITS LIMIT MATTERS. Searched 2026-09-06 across every cached YMCA of Montreal annual report from 1856 to 1912 for isolated all-capitals lines ending in a period and mentioning camp, lake, Joseph, Kanawana or tent -- the shape of a halftone caption. THE ONLY PLATE CAPTION NAMING THE CAMP IS THE 1899 "THE ASSOCIATION SUMMER CAMP, LAKE ST. JOSEPH." (f_4914). Everything else the sweep returned is a SECTION HEADING, not a caption: "PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE." in 1896-97 and 1899, "SUMMER CAMP, ST. AGATHE." in 1902, "SENIOR CAMP." and "SUMMER CAMP." in the 1904 Men of Montreal, "SUMMER CAMP." in 1907 -- each followed immediately by prose. The sweep also turned up the militia-camp headings of 1883, 1884 ("MILITIA CAMP, ST. JOHNS, QUE., JUNE, 1884."), 1885-86 and 1886-87, corroborating that "camp" in these volumes usually means militia (f_4906, f_1537). THE LIMIT: THIS FINDS ONLY CAPTIONS THE OCR RENDERED LEGIBLY. A plate whose caption was mangled, or printed in a face the OCR dropped, is invisible to it, and so is any plate with no caption at all. A NULL FROM THIS SWEEP IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT A VOLUME HAS NO PHOTOGRAPH; only a page-image pass can say that, and p_425 holds it.

THE 1904 ANNUAL REPORT IS A SUMMER CAMP NUMBER, AND ITS COVER IS A PHOTOGRAPH OF THE LOG CLUB HOUSE. The YMCA of Montreal's 1904 report is titled "MEN OF MONTREAL... FIFTY-THIRD ANNUAL REPORT AND SUMMER CAMP NUMBER, 1904", and its front cover carries a halftone captioned "CAMP CLUB HOUSE, LAKE ST. JOSEPH." WHAT THE PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS, read from the page image 2026-09-06: a substantial gable-ended two-storey building with a masonry chimney and windows in the gable; a WIDE COVERED VERANDA running across the front and down the visible side on posts, with a canvas blind or awning let down at the left end; a flight of steps from the middle of the veranda down to a path. ROUGHLY A DOZEN TO FIFTEEN BOYS AND YOUNG MEN are in the frame -- on the veranda, on the steps, and on the path -- several in bathing dress. The lake shows at the right beyond the building with a low wooded hill on the far shore; scrub and a low stone or log edging in the foreground. THIS IS THE LOG CLUB HOUSE COMPLETED IN SEPTEMBER 1898 (f_4912), and its veranda is the "gallery" whose view the 1900 campers complained the ice-house spoiled (f_4883). The cover was invisible to the caption sweep of the cached OCR (f_4917) because the OCR runs the caption into the surrounding cover text; it was found by ranking the item's djvu pages by word count and looking at the sparsest.

THE ASSOCIATION COUNTED FROM 1894 IN 1904, IN ITS OWN ORDINAL. The 1904 Summer Camp Number opens: "On JULY 16TH, THE ELEVENTH ANNUAL SUMMER CAMP of the Association for senior members will open at Lac St. Joseph, in charge of MR. H. BALLANTYNE, EDUCATIONAL SECRETARY." An eleventh annual camp in 1904 counts the first at 1894. IT THEN TELLS THE FOUNDING STORY AT TEN YEARS' DISTANCE: "TEN YEARS AGO a small party of our members, AFTER PRELIMINARY EXPLORATION, PITCHED THEIR TENTS ON ONE OF THE ISLANDS IN LAC ST. JOSEPH. Their enthusiastic description of their experiences created wider interest amongst the members on their return and LED TO THE ACQUIRING OF THE ISLANDS FOR THE ASSOCIATION and to the establishment of the summer camp at that spot. Later, through the efforts of well-known interested campers THE PRESENT SPLENDID LOG CLUB HOUSE WAS ERECTED." THIS MATTERS BECAUSE THE ASSOCIATION LATER CONTRADICTED ITSELF: the 1931 report says "IN 1898, OR FORTY YEARS AGO, THE FIRST BOYS CAMP OF THE ASSOCIATION WAS OPENED AT LAC ST. JOSEPH" (f_2146), which is wrong twice over. The 1904 ordinal is contemporaneous, arithmetically checkable, and agrees with the 1894-95 annual report's own account (f_2178). NOTE ALSO that H. Ballantyne is very likely the HARRY BALLANTYNE who wrote "A Short History of the Canadian Y.M.C.A. 1851-1944", a source this project already holds -- the author of the movement's standard short history ran the Montreal senior camp in 1904. That identification is NOT confirmed here.

THE CAMP'S WHOLE PLANT, PROGRAMME AND PRICE LIST IN 1904. From the Summer Camp Number. PLANT: "the Association now has IN ADDITION TO THE CLUB HOUSE, A WELL FURNISHED LOG KITCHEN ADJOINING, AN ICE HOUSE, PUMP, SMALL CAMP LIBRARY, EIGHT LARGE TENTS EQUIPPED WITH FLY AND BOARD FLOOR, TEN BOATS, FISHING AND SWIMMING WHARVES, etc." -- the enlarged kitchen and the new ice-house the campers asked for in October 1900 and the committee built by 1902 (f_4915), now standing, with board floors and flies on the tents that had "all leaked" in 1900. "Through the generosity of MR. JAS. W. TESTER, A GASOLINE LAUNCH will be at the disposal of the members this year." PROGRAMME: "Tenting, boating, bathing, fishing, exploring are the chief means of enjoyment. There are facilities also for TENNIS, BASE BALL, BASKET BALL, QUOITS"; "In wet weather the club house brings the men together." "A camera adds greatly to the pleasure of a visit." GETTING THERE: "Sixty-four miles from Montreal to Ste. Agathe... and EIGHT MILES BY ROAD brings one to the shores of Lac St. Joseph"; transport Saturday afternoon out, Monday morning back. RATES, "a member's privilege" representing "the actual cost of operation with a small margin to maintain the camp property": one week including railway fare and drive both ways $10.00; subsequent weeks $5.00; Saturday to Monday $4.00. THE CAMP CLOSED 6 SEPTEMBER. CAMP COMMITTEE 1904: B. S. R. WATSON, Chairman; JAS. R. GREIG, W. JARRETT, C. D. TWEEDIE, H. G. BEALL.

BY 1904 THE ASSOCIATION OWNED THE MAIN ISLAND AND "SEVERAL ISLANDS IMMEDIATELY ADJOINING". The 1904 Summer Camp Number: "On A LARGE WELL-WOODED ISLAND in the lake the camp is situated. THE ASSOCIATION ALSO OWNS SEVERAL ISLANDS IMMEDIATELY ADJOINING." SET BESIDE THE 1902 REPORT (f_4916), which says the association held "our present island" -- singular -- until it bought "a small one adjoining" at auction on 26 November 1901 for $50, this gives a sequence: one island through 1901, two from November 1901, and SEVERAL by 1904. So the acquisitions continued between 1902 and 1904 and are not all recorded here. IT ALSO MEANS c_008's "three islands" and "two islands acquired in 1897" are both attempts to fix a number on a holding that was still growing, which may be why neither secondary source can be made to agree with the other. The 1904 text does not say how many "several" is.
